units.la: Ibrorum (domine amplissime) haud aliter quàm foliorum arborum, adolescente jam vere, permagna est copia: scripturire quam parturire mallet hoc sæculum, & vitam chartaceam nemo non optat. Quorsum ego itaque scriberem? an quia stultum & ignavum peritura parcere charta? an vero, quod verius est, quoniam hoc habent miserrima & deflenda ecclesiæ fata, senescente jam mundo, ut veritas, quæ nullum forum reformidat, nullum tribunal perhorrescit, nunquam non in jus & quæstionem rea petrahatur, & theologia jam tantum non arena gladiatoria fiat? Huic malo remedium, pacem & concordiam animorum optare possumus, quod obnixè orandum, at præstare non possumus, imo vix sperare, quod seriò dolendum est. Atqui hujusce rei causa forte veritati potius quam humanitati imputanda est, eo quod ipsa sit ardua, intricata, perplexa, tenebricosa, & errorum spinis & senticetis scateat. At non ita est: illa nuda, bone Deus, quam clara, quam facilis, quam expedita! Sed disputacissimi sunt mortales, præsertim qui subactioris ingenii videri volunt, & maleferiata ingenia malunt disputationum & concertationum montes creare, de barbâ caprinâ, de Ulyssis patria, de Nili ortu, imo de litera y, quam pacem animorum sectari. Inde est quod Natio Jesuitica theologiam obvelarit, ut nos qua itur, non qua eundum est, circumgyrare unicè satagat, idque per tot distinctionum & cavillationum Μαίανδρος [?], respectuum & notionum labyrinthos, & subtilitatum Scholasticarum gyros & anfractus, ut periculum jam non mediocre fit, ne veritas intermoritura videatur. Hinc Conciliorum,
units.tr: Of books (most distinguished sir) there is no less abundance than of leaves on the trees when spring is already in its prime. This age would rather spawn writings than bear children, and nearly everyone wishes for a life on paper. Why, then, should I write? Is it because it is foolish and lazy to spare paper that is going to perish? Or rather, as is truer, because the most wretched and lamentable fate of the Church is this, that as the world now grows old, truth, which fears no forum and dreads no tribunal, is always being dragged into court and into the dock as a defendant, and theology is now almost turned into a gladiatorial arena. For this evil we can wish for a remedy, namely peace and concord of minds. We must pray earnestly for it, but we cannot bring it about, and we can scarcely even hope for it, which is a matter for serious grief. Yet perhaps the cause of this should be laid to the charge of truth rather than of human nature, on the ground that truth itself is steep, tangled, perplexing and dark, and abounds in the thorns and brambles of error. But it is not so. Good God, how bare truth is, how clear, how easy and how open! But mortals are very fond of disputing, especially those who wish to seem of a sharper wit, and ill-cultivated minds prefer to heap up mountains of disputes and quarrels, about the goat's beard, about the homeland of Ulysses, about the source of the Nile, or even about the letter y, rather than pursue peace of mind. Hence it is that the Jesuit nation has veiled theology, and it labours only to lead us round in circles, so that we go by the way we should not go rather than the way we ought to go. It does this through so many labyrinths of distinctions and cavils, of respects and notions, through the meanders [Μαίανδρος] and windings of scholastic subtleties, that the danger is no small one that truth itself may seem about to die out. Hence the more fervent and forward minds of councils,

units.la: Scholarum, Academiarum & doctorum ferventiora & petulantiora ingenia coguntur disputare, non credere, opinari, non scire, digladiari, non addiscere, quae scitu necessaria sunt; & tantum non seculum sufficiat spinosarum quaestionum strophas litigiosas detegere, tricas involutissimas enodare, sophismata viscata diluere, imposituras Dædaleas explicare. At vero immortales, per nos, ferant disceptationes, si non impetiginosos, in Dei providentiam, & gratiam efficacem, calamos strinxissent. At quis vere Christianus, se non multis nominibus devinctum fateretur divinae gratiae? de qua, si simul actum & conclamatum sit, totam Theologiam in extrema regula stare, nemo non scit. Nimis exploratum habeo communem, & decantatam Arminiana scholae cantilenam esse, nostrum decretum absolutum, & gratiam Dei irresistibili vi operantem, esse ipsissimum fatum. At probare, causam dicite, tabulas proferre
units.tr: of schools, of academies and of teachers are compelled to dispute rather than believe, to opine rather than know, to wrangle rather than learn what it is necessary to know. And scarcely a whole century suffices to unravel the contentious knots of thorny questions, to untangle the most involved trifles, to refute the sticky sophisms and to explain the Daedalian deceptions. Yet, by us, may the immortal gods bear such disputes, if they had not drawn their pens, not against the mere cavils, on the providence of God and on efficacious grace. But what true Christian would not confess that he is bound to divine grace by many ties? Concerning it, if it is both discussed and loudly proclaimed, that the whole of theology stands on its final rule, no one fails to know. I have learned well enough that the common and hackneyed tune of the Arminian school is that our absolute decree, and grace working by irresistible force, is simply fate itself. But prove it: state your case, bring forward your tables

units.la: Nam sophistae ita argutanti: Quod ego jam sum tu non es: homo autem ego sum: homo igitur tu non es, respondens Diogenes, à me (inquit) incipe, & vera erit conclusio. Ita nos, non esse dicimus, quales sunt Arminiani, nempe qui Deum ipsum fato adamantino constringunt: nos vero fati assertores esse contendunt illi, sed Tribunitia & dictatoria affirmatione, nulla ratione solida. Quin & nos vobiscum dicimus
units.tr: For when a sophist argues thus: What I now am, you are not; but I am a man; therefore you are not a man, Diogenes replied, "Begin with me, and the conclusion will be true." So we say that the Arminians are not what they are: namely, men who bind God himself with adamantine fate. They, however, insist that we are the advocates of fate, but by a tribunician and dictatorial assertion, with no solid reasoning. Indeed we say with you:

units.la: Et—Quem fata cogunt is cum venia est miser. Fati ista culpa est, nemo fit fato nocens.
units.tr: And—the man whom fate compels is pardonable and wretched. The fault lies with fate; no one is made guilty by fate.

units.la: At si fatum hoc sit, [ita fatus est Jehova exercituum: & faciam. Et Iehovah inivit consilium & quis irritum faciet?] tum nos tale fatum, frustra obstrepente invidia asserimus, credimus, propugnamus. Quas vero contra nos adfertis disputationes, vidimus, deprehendimus, probavimus Leotrephide & Thavmantide (ut dicitur?) macilentiores. Argumenta quid aliud sunt, quam larvae, umbrae, fuci, fumi, ceroma, purpurissa? Sed errori opus est vestibus purpureis, ne perpluat. Et ex hac radice usque adeo luxuriantur, & sobolescunt, silvescente, jam praesertim hisce extremis diebus, humani ingenii petulantia immani, errores Pelagiani, Sociniani, utinam non Arminiani & Epicurei, ut omnes promissiones novi fœderis sint tantum μορμολύκεια[?] verba & venti. Hoc imputamus Iesuitis vestris, hoc lasciviæ ingenii humani: quippe nullum magnum ingenium sine mixtura dementiæ. At si Cynicus ille philosophus, conspecto adolescente vertiginoso, inculto, & profligato, præceptorem ipsius verberibus cædi jusserit, vestri certe præceptores, Iesuitæ intelligo, quibus doctrinam vestram, & nova dogmata debetis, & vos cum illis digni estis, qui flagris cædamini. Interim in promptu vobis erit coccysmus vester fatalis, penes Deum me quidem esse, quo minus cædamini. Dicite enim per Deum immortalem, nec conscientias candidiores obtestari verebor, & qua Deo libertas salva esse posset, salvâ vestra scientiâ mediâ, & actuum contingentium decreto conditionato. Nam obtinente hoc dogmate, futuritionem habente, antecedenter ad Dei tum scientiam, tum decretum, omnes quotquot ærumnæ, mortalibus, ministerio causarum ego provinciam appuli, & in sacrosancti ministerii in ecclesia Christi, curriculo, licet non qua debeam, attamen qua possim, animi contentione militantem, spe, re, consilio, authoritate in dies adjuvare, complecti, & promovere, non gravate tulisti, te vindicem & assertorem appellant, salutant, patrocinium exoptant, & in authoris obsequii & gratitudinis, amplitudine tuae Chirographum, sese dicant, consecrant, & amoris sigillum testatissimum appendunt, quo confidentius, & animosius, tua fretus authoritate, ad alia quae libelli inscriptio spondet, promovear. Ista φιλοσοφω-[illegible, ~3 letters] & abstrusiora, quam par est, si quis incusabit, pro me respondeo, malo nodo, malum cuneum deberi; & amaram bilem. non nisi amaris pharmacis, diluendam, & hostes divinae gratiae vel in aliena castra, extra septa theologica fugientes, persequi non esse inutile & invitissimo delinquenti veniam dandam esse. Interim qua possum animi submissione, quo debeam mentis ardore, Deum patrem D. Iesu Christi invoco, ut te, & familiam tuam, omni benedictionum genere
units.tr: But if this is fate, [thus has Jehovah of hosts spoken: and I will do it. And Jehovah has taken counsel, and who will make it void?] then we assert, believe and defend such fate, while envy frets in vain against us. As for the disputations you bring against us, we have seen, detected and proved them to be (as they are called?) Leotrephides and Thaumantides thinner than thin. What are the arguments but ghosts, shadows, drones, smoke, wax-paint and rouge? But error needs purple garments, lest it be rained upon. And from this root such errors grow so lush and multiply, the more so now, in these last days, when the wild wantonness of the human mind has run riot in a forest: the errors of Pelagians, Socinians, would that they were not Arminians and Epicureans, so that all the promises of the new covenant are merely bugbears [μορμολύκεια] and words and wind. This we charge to your Jesuits, and to the wantonness of the human mind, for no great mind is without a touch of madness. But if that Cynic philosopher, on seeing a dizzy, uncultivated and dissolute youth, ordered his teacher to be beaten with blows, then your teachers, I mean the Jesuits, to whom you owe your doctrine and your new dogmas, and with whom you are worthy, are surely the ones who should be whipped. Meanwhile your fatalistic mockery will be ready at hand, that it is in God's power, not mine, that you are not beaten. For tell me, by the immortal God, and I shall not shrink from calling your consciences to witness, how liberty could be safe for God, with your middle knowledge and your conditional decree of contingent acts kept safe. For while this dogma holds, which makes future events depend on causes, anterior to both God's knowledge and his decree, I have brought to myself, by the ministry of causes, the task of helping, embracing and advancing day by day all the troubles of mortals, and of serving in the course of the sacred ministry in the Church of Christ, not as I ought, yet as I can, with the strenuous effort of my spirit, by hope, by deed, by counsel and by authority. You have not borne this reluctantly. They call you their champion and defender, they greet you, they desire your patronage, and in the largeness of their obedience and gratitude they dedicate and consecrate themselves to you by this written pledge, and attach the most solemn seal of their love, so that, relying more confidently and boldly on your authority, I may advance to the other things that the title of this little book promises. If anyone criticises these philosophical and rather too abstruse matters, I answer for myself that a hard knot deserves a hard wedge, and that bitter bile can be diluted only with bitter medicines; and that it is not useless to pursue the enemies of divine grace even into foreign camps, outside the theological fences, and that pardon should be given to a most unwilling offender. Meanwhile, with all the humility of mind I can muster, and with all the ardour my spirit owes, I call upon God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, that he may bless you and your household with every kind of blessing.

units.la: DEDICATORIA.
units.tr: DEDICATORY.

units.la: nere quam cumulatissime complectatur, ut possis esse ecclesiæ ornamento, patriæ subsidio, bonis omnibus solatio. Non enim ignoras in hac valle miseriarum minime sistendum, neque tentorium figendum, ad æternitatem ipsam (quod vere magnum est nomen & ineffabile) te vocari, crescere iter, decrescere diem, omnia alia aliena, tempus tantum nostrum esse, si modo nostrum est. Ista profecto, quorum amore nos miseri inescati tabescimus, nostra non sunt. Quid vero nobilitas? Omnis sanguis concolor est, diversitatem parit virtus, imo pietas. Hæc unica nobilitas, hæc sapientia ad patriam nostram, quam possumus, commoda & concitatiore velificatione contendere. Illuc enitere & Vale.
units.tr: may He embrace you with every kind of blessing as abundantly as possible, so that you may be an ornament to the Church, a support to your country, and a comfort to all good people. For you are not unaware that in this valley of miseries we must not settle down or pitch our tent, and that you are called to eternity itself (which is truly a great and unspeakable name), that the journey lengthens while the day shortens, that all other things are foreign to us, and that only time is ours, if indeed it is ours at all. Those things, by whose love we wretches are enticed and waste away, are certainly not ours. What then is nobility? All blood is of one colour; virtue, and indeed piety, produces the difference. This is the only nobility, this is the wisdom that lets us make for our homeland, as best we can, with a quicker and more eager sailing. Strive towards that: and farewell.

units.la: Immanem insaniam delirarunt nuperi Turbones foederata Belgico-Germania, qui, primusquam Durdrechtana Synodi felici exitu everterentur, cum ecclesia remp. in discrimen maximum pertraxerunt. Deum opt. max. nimium quantum depressere, hominem in immensam sublimitatem extulerunt. Eo dissimiles idololatriæ, quod illi hominum condituram insignem infra ligna & lapides abjiciant, isti pulverem & cinerem, quin potius lutum sanie corruptionis macera-tum supra contrave Deum elevarint. Ita e dissimili genere fatuitatis an perfidiæ diversa facinora manarunt. Seipsos Remonstrantes sublimant cum injuria Dei & hominum peccatorum. Libertatem eam humanæ voluntati attributum eunt, qua Divinæ providentiæ nexibus emancipata in throno confideat absoluta dominationis. Deus autem humanæ voluntatis regimine & dominio eversus, maxima caret parte regni illius quod scriptura nullis limitibus circumscribi affirmat. Alteram cladem intulerunt Divinæ gratiæ in Christo, quum Christum nihil nobis acquisivisse sed hoc Deo ipsi acquisivisse docent, quod fœ-dum dum cum homine lapso inire novum possit certumque modum statuere, quo homines (dummodo velint & si velint) restituantur. Iam homini lapso, perdito, polluto, misero vires dant, quibus opus sit ad apprehensionem boni oblati. Voluntatem igitur, qua non subest Deo, nisi in quantum ipse totam, quam condidit, abolere potest, non qua flectatur ab eo & ab ipsius motu & nutu pendeat, ita non impeditis lacertis quaquaversum semet agitare tradunt in salutis negotio, ut sibi, non Deo debeat vim illam nobilissimam, qua instar manus, qua ὄργανον ὀργάνων [?] philosopho praedicatur, sumit, quod in Evangelio proponitur. Hanc ipsam actionem esse formalem illam causam, qua ad iustitiam imputetur. Sedet exspectans Deus, quid illi Domina voluntati sit placiturum, frustratur saepe & excidit eo, quod anhelat, quia homini aliter visum. Si voluisset homo potuisse in immensum extendi regnum Dei, quod nunc exiguus finibus terminatur. Fieri & hoc potuisse ut Christus rex esset sine regno, nomen inane sine re, vana dominator, non dicam in aula sed ditione. Ut mors ipsius sine fructu sine effectu, tantum sacrificium sine expiatione ullius mortalium periret. Ut propheta tantum suaderet nec persuaderet quem-
units.tr: The recent troublemakers of the United Netherlands raved with monstrous madness. Before they were overthrown by the happy outcome of the Synod of Dort, they dragged the Church and the commonwealth into the greatest danger. They cast down almighty God to a great depth and raised man to an immense height. Their idolatry differs from the older kind in this: the older idolaters cast the outstanding creature of man beneath wood and stone, while these men have lifted up dust and ashes, or rather mud soaked in the filth of corruption, above and against God. So from one kind of folly, or from one kind of faithlessness, different crimes flow. The Remonstrants exalt themselves to the dishonour of God and of sinful men. They attribute to the human will that freedom by which, released from the bonds of divine providence, it may sit confidently on an absolute throne of dominion. But God, overthrown by the rule and dominion of the human will, is deprived of the greater part of that kingdom which Scripture affirms is bounded by no limits. They inflicted a second blow on the grace of God in Christ, since they teach that Christ acquired nothing for us, but only acquired this for God himself: that he could enter into a new covenant with fallen man and establish a certain manner by which men are restored, provided they are willing, and if they are willing. Now they give to fallen, lost, polluted, wretched man the powers needed for laying hold of the good that is offered. They therefore teach that the will, which is subject to God only so far as he can destroy the whole nature he has made, is not bent by him, nor does it depend on his motion and nod. So, with its limbs unhindered, it moves itself in every direction in the business of salvation, so that it is to itself, not to God, that it owes that most noble power, which is called, like a hand, the organ of organs [ὄργανον ὀργάνων] by the philosopher, and which it takes up when the gospel is set before it. They maintain that this very action is that formal cause by which righteousness is imputed. God sits waiting to see what his mistress, the will, will be pleased to do; he is often frustrated and falls short of what he longs for, because man has decided otherwise. If man had willed it, the kingdom of God, which now is confined within narrow borders, could have been extended without limit. It could also have happened that Christ was king without a kingdom, an empty name without a thing, a vain ruler, not to say in a court but in a dominion. His death would have perished without fruit and without effect, a sacrifice so great that it expiated no mortal at all. A prophet would have persuaded only in name and not in fact.

units.la: Admodum in turbidis Gracia Concionibus venalis orator. Scilicet illud est Deum suo honore & providentia communis & gratia deturbare, homines etiam cum dispendio salutis & solatii intumidare, nixos in vanum prædicatis falso liberi arbitrij facultatibus aut etiam Communi gratia quā fallax & inefficax, multos, quibus contigit, in cœno destituit. Hoc est pietatem & religionem in exilium agere, dum homines docentur semet potius suasque opes respicere & conando agendoque eniti, quàm supplicus[?] muliebribus, reflexisque in Deum cordibus, ejus auxilium implorare.
units.tr: Just as a hired orator in the turbulent Gracian sermons. Clearly this is to cast down God from his honour, his common providence and his grace, and to puff up men, even to the loss of their salvation and comfort, by leaning them on the vain faculties of a free will that is falsely preached, or even on a common grace which, being deceptive and ineffective, leaves many whom it reaches stuck in the mire. This is to drive piety and religion into exile, while men are taught to look rather to themselves and their own resources, and to strive by effort and action, instead of, with suppliant and humble hearts turned towards God, imploring his help.

units.la: Adeo universam Theologiam non turbant, sed exturbant novi dogmatistæ, fabri ψευδῶν[?] δοξῶν[?] vere παραδόξων[?], quas, ut tueantur[?], in omnes se formas vertere, modo Scriptura dicta planissima & evidentissimos S. S. sensus torquendo eludere, modo philosophiam advocare, ut qui propter habitum mentes suas in Scripturis subegissent, nec offusis nebulis à tramite recto in pravum abduci possent, acumine spinarum rationis humanæ punctì[?] aut sinuosis anfractibus exotica sapientia turbati de via veritate dubitare inciperent. Ista artes imperitis & inexercitatis successu haud pœnitendo imposuerunt. Solet autem sapiens be[?]ignitas numinis, cum ad juvandum accedit, ingenia excitare, idonea temporibus & in remedium amovendarum calamitatum. Solet dare שֹׁפְטִים[?] & Suffetes tales, qui eo genere certaminis polleant & armorum, quo hostis exsultat. Plurimi excellentissimi viri genere docendi populari & scriptura robore simplicissimo, pestilentissimam perfidiam ea tempestate, cum ista ferverent, velut agmine facto confecerunt. Ita pestis ea confecta est ut Scriptura puritate & analogia fidei vindicata oculi aperti fuerint multis, qui parum in hac causa viderant. Verum caput factionis & quidam duces ad Philosophia auxiliares copias confugere. Cum se hic altius inferrent & triumphum jactabundi canerent, ostendere viri Dei complures veritatem non esse oppositam veritati, caeterum duo tresue introgressi adyta philosophia & scholastica Theologia puriores, (quae philosophia germana filia est) secreta omnia in apertum produxerunt docueruntque ὀφθαλμοφανῶς[?] nihil hic pro hostibus divina providentia & gratia praesidii inveniri. Britanni gloriam istam, tanquam infula sua propriam & a majoribus traditam vindicarunt. Inter eos hic scriptor est acutissimus, qui acerrime divinam gratiam propugnaus armis philosophia & rationis docet quomodo libertas humana voluntatis subjecta sit Dei decreto & voluntati & inde fulcimen potius quam impulsum accipiat, fundetur non evertatur. Ita voluntatem nostram a gratiâ potenter penetrari ut inde accipiat vires, quibus e servitute edu&a libere assurgat ad bonum, infra quod ante per libertatem subsidebat. Brevi ambitu verborum & oratione nervosa convenienter istas subtilitates enuntiat, vocibus technicis propriisque, qua popularem dictionem respuunt. Itaque multa hic constricta uno obtutu plerumque comprehendes, quae alii laxe diffuderunt. Lege & arbitrare lector. Age Deo gratias quod pestiferos antiqui draconis hic quoque conatum eliserit & elusrit, uti pristina puritas ecclesiis nostris constaret. Contende abeodem ardentibus votis, quo veritatem Evangelii indies propaget ad laudem gloria gratia tua in Christo & in eo Vale.
units.tr: In this way the new dogmatists do not so much disturb all theology as tear it up by the roots. They are makers of false and paradoxical opinions [ψευδῶν δοξῶν, παραδόξων]. To defend these, they turn themselves into every shape: now they try to evade plain sayings of Scripture and the most evident senses of the Holy Scriptures by twisting them, now they summon philosophy to their aid, so that men whose minds had been subdued to Scripture by habit, and who could not be led from the right path by the mists cast over them, might be drawn astray by the sharp thorns of human reasoning or by the winding turns of foreign wisdom, and begin to doubt the way of truth. These arts have brought no regrettable success to the unskilled and the untrained. The wise Godhead, however, is accustomed, when it comes to help, to stir up men of talent, fitted to the times and to the remedy for removing calamities. It is accustomed to give judges and Suffetes [שֹׁפְטִים] of such a kind as excel in that sort of combat and in those arms in which the enemy rejoices. Many most excellent men, with a popular manner of teaching and the simplest strength of Scripture, overthrew that most pestilential faithlessness in that season, when these men were raging, as if by forming a battle line. So completely was that plague overthrown that, with Scripture vindicated by its purity and the analogy of faith, the eyes of many were opened who had seen little in this cause. But the head of the faction and certain leaders fled to philosophy for auxiliary troops. When they pushed themselves further in here and sang their boastful triumphs, several men of God showed that truth is not opposed to truth. Moreover, two or three men who had entered the inner sanctuaries of philosophy and the purer scholastic theology (which is philosophy's true daughter) brought all its secrets into the open, and taught that, manifestly [ὀφθαλμοφανῶς], no protection is to be found here for divine providence and grace against the enemies. The British claimed this glory as their own, like a crown handed down from their forefathers. Among them this writer is the most acute, who, most keenly defending divine grace with the arms of philosophy and reason, teaches how the liberty of the human will is subject to the decree and will of God, and receives from it a support rather than a push, being founded and not overthrown. So powerfully is our will penetrated by grace that, being drawn out of slavery, it receives from grace the strength to rise freely to the good, below which it had sunk before through its freedom. In a brief compass of words and a vigorous style he states these subtleties fittingly, in technical and proper terms, which reject popular speech. Hence you will often grasp at one glance much that others have spread out loosely. Read and judge, reader. Give thanks to God that he has here too crushed and repulsed the pestilential attempt of the ancient dragon, so that the former purity may stand firm in our churches. Strive with equally ardent prayers that he may daily spread the truth of the gospel, to the praise of his glory and grace in Christ, and farewell in him.

units.la: EXERCITATIONES APOLOGETICÆ pro divina gratia, contra JESUITAS & ARMINIANOS. Exercitatiò I. De divinis decretis & divinæ voluntatis cum libertate humana amicâ consociatione.
units.tr: EXERCITATIONES APOLOGETICAE for divine grace, against the Jesuits and Arminians. Exercitation I. Concerning the divine decrees and the friendly association of the divine will with human liberty.

units.la: CAP. I. De natura humana libertatis, & an Suarez, & Arminiani satis Philosophico-theologicè ipsum naturam esse doceant, potentiam ad agendum vel non agendum positis omnibus requisitis ad agendum.
units.tr: CHAP. I. On the nature of human liberty, and whether Suarez and the Arminians sufficiently teach, philosophically and theologically, that it is the power to act or not to act, with all the requisites for acting having been posited.

units.la: THES. I. Causa ex communi sententia, alia est naturalis, quæ [illegible, ~20 letters] ut habet Philosophus, & agit necessario, ut ignis; alia libera, quæ potest vel operari, vel non; sic, vel alio modo, ut libertas humana, quæ quamvis naturaliter, ex interno principio, hoc est oppositè ad violentum & fortuitum, vel etiam ad supernaturale, agat, ideoque hoc sensu causa naturalis dici debeat, tamen non determinatur ad unum effectum producendum, & sic jure, non naturalis, sed libera causa censetur, voluntas itaque non est contingenter sed necessario libera, ut fabulatur Tho: Lackfonus, sed contingenter agit, libertas enim non esse, sed operari, respicit.
units.tr: THES. I. By common opinion, one cause is natural, which, as the Philosopher says, acts necessarily, like fire; another is free, which can either act or not act. Or there is another way, such as human liberty, which, although it acts naturally, from an internal principle (that is, opposed to violent and chance action, or even to the supernatural), and so in this sense ought to be called a natural cause, nevertheless is not determined to produce one effect. Thus, rightly, it is judged a free cause, not a natural one. The will, therefore, is not contingently but necessarily free, as Tho: Lackfonus fabricates; rather it acts contingently, for liberty concerns not being but acting.

units.la: Et libertas naturalis proprietas est voluntatis, hæc finem; & quidem necessario, illa contingenter & liberè media respicit. Nescio an jure Scholastici docent voluntatem non carere libertate exercitii, quoniam quamvis non posset non velle beatitudinem, si circa eam actum eliciat, potest tamen nullum, circa eam, actum elicere, avocando intellectum ab actuali cogitatione. Nam libertas tanquam potentia imperatrix & voluntatem & intellectum ad agendum applicat, vel ab agendo revocat, non vero voluntas est, quæ hoc facit.
units.tr: And natural liberty is a property of the will: the will regards the end necessarily, while liberty regards the means contingently and freely. I do not know whether the Schoolmen rightly teach that the will does not lack liberty of exercise. For although it cannot not will happiness, if it elicits an act concerning it, it can nevertheless elicit no act concerning it, by withdrawing the intellect from actual thought. For liberty, as the commanding power, both applies the will and the intellect to acting and recalls them from acting; it is not the will that does this.

units.la: 2. Itaque voluntas qua libera agit, in seipsam quatenus est voluntas per naturam ad bonum volendum determinata, & libertas hæc in actu primo nec radicaliter, nec formaliter est in intellectu, quippe facultas hæc appetens immediatè inhæret animæ, absque ulla mentis ratiocinio intermedio, & non parum miror, qui potentia libera conveniat voluntati, mediante potentia intellectiva, quia voluntas tam immediatè & per se est libera, quam mens est cognoscitiva. At an libertas in est radicaliter intellectui, quia judicium est libertatis fundamentum ? At, per parem rationem, dic potentiam cognoscitivam esse in voluntate radicaliter, quod est inauditum, quia intellectus non cognoscit, nisi quatenus voluntas ipsum ad agendum applicat, ideoque ex hoc argumento sequitur libertatis exercitium & usum esse radicaliter, aut verius directivè in intellectu, formaliter & effectivè in voluntates quod non gravate concedo.
units.tr: 2. Therefore the will, by which it acts freely, is, insofar as it is will, determined by nature to will the good; and this liberty, in first act, is neither radically nor formally in the intellect, since this appetitive faculty inheres immediately in the soul, without any intermediate reasoning of the mind. I do not much wonder how free power belongs to the will through the intellectual power, since the will is as immediately and per se free as the mind is cognitive. But is liberty radically in the intellect, because judgement is the foundation of liberty? By the same reasoning, however, say that the cognitive power is radically in the will, which is unheard of; for the intellect knows only insofar as the will applies it to acting. Therefore from this argument it follows that the exercise and use of liberty is radically, or more truly directively, in the intellect, and formally and effectively in the will; which I concede without difficulty.

units.la: 3. Objectum liberi arbitrii est duplex, vel materiale vel formale. Materiale est bonum, malum, . Formale est tantum hoc eligibile qua bonum ad finem conducens [illegible, ~20 letters] ἀγαθόν. Nec hoc bonum est tale sensibus sed moraliter bonum, non enim vivere, esse, dormire proprie eligimus (ista enim natura, non libertas nostra appetit.) nisi quatenus ista ad esse morale conttahuntur. Hoc bonum etiam est cognitum, nec tamen credo cognitionem esse de formali ratione objecti, sed tantum conditionem in objecto requisitam, ideoque bonum quod est in mente, non quatenus est in mente, est objectum finalizantis. Vide Scheble, & Rutgersium in Metaphys.
units.tr: 3. The object of free choice is twofold, either material or formal. The material object is good or evil. The formal object is only that which is eligible as a good leading to the end [ἀγαθόν]. Nor is this good such to the senses, but morally good; for we do not properly choose to live, to be, or to sleep (for our nature, not our liberty, desires these), except insofar as they are referred to moral being. This good is also known; yet I do not believe that knowledge belongs to the formal character of the object, but is only a condition required in the object. Therefore the good which is in the mind, not as it is in the mind, is the object of what gives the end its direction. See Scheibler and Rutgersius in the Metaphysics.

Malum qua malum appeti, vel ita intelligitur, ut reduplicatio referatur ad malum, vel ad appetentem; priore modo nimis, proh dolor, verum est, malum quod formaliter & in se malum est, ut adulterium, homicidium &c. appeti, posteriore modo appeti non potest, nam in omni mali appetitione, (esto quod

In the former way, alas, it is only too true that evil which is formally and in itself evil, such as adultery, homicide, and so on, is desired. In the latter way it cannot be desired, (granted that

units.la: §. Voluntas consideratur 1. ut natura; & hoc ei commune est cum aliis agentibus, ut in bonum feratur. 2. ut est talis natura, & sic fertur in beatitudinem, inclinatione essentiali libertatem antecedente, ut innuit Thomas, non mentis deliberatione, aut libere. 3. ut est libera. 4. ut est bona vel mala. Ut est libera simpliciter, ipsius actus sunt indifferentes, ut bona vel mala, legi subjicitur; libertas ad agendum vel non agendum physica competit libertati in omni statu, quamvis semper contracta ad ⁊[?] bene vel male velle. Inclinatio vero indifferens ad bonum vel malum nunquam est in natura, (quicquid contra somniant sophistæ) nam post lapsum est inclinatio ad malum in non renatis, & inclinatio in regenitis ad bonum, quatenus sunt spiritus, ad malum quatenus habitat in iis caro, at hic nulla est pura indifferentia Arminiana sed indifferentia non contracta per carnem & spiritum, non magis est, quam existit natura generica animalis extra hominem aut brutum. At vero in Adamo ante lapsum, non erat inclinatio ad malum, nam voluntas ipsius sancta inclinabatur ad Dei legem præstandam. At dices in Adamo fuit actuale peccatum, ergo erat antea in eo inclinatio & potentia ad peccandum; actus enim in creaturis non fluit nisi a præexistente potentia. Respondeo, Erat in eo potentia naturalis ad ⁊[?] comedere, & ad ꝛ [?] non comedere fructus, quierant actus natura mere indifferentes, & accedit iis actibus ut quid extrinsecum, quod effent legi cohibiti aut determinati, Adamus autem tantum actuabat potentiam naturalem, Potentia enim peccandi vel respicit actum entitativum peccati, & haec ex se non erat potentia moralis indifferens, vel ἀνομίαν ipsam, & haec non fuit proprie potentia, sed naturalis ipsa potentia quatenus legi subdita, quae quidem potentia nulla fuisset, si Deus legem, (uti potuit, liberae enim suae creaturae leges ponit) non praescripsisset homini; servitus quidem & vitiosa ad peccandum inclinatio inest homini post lapsum, ea vero non tam potentia est, quam curvitas potentiae, nec magis est de natura liberi arbitrii, quam potentia claudicandi, est de formali ratione facultatis locomotivae. Hinc infero libertatem gratiae non superaddere libertati naturae novam libertatem, sed tantum novam potentiam, libertatem naturae qualificantem & elevantem. Nam si esset nova libertas, essent in regenito duae libertates distinctae, & sic duae voluntates, & quidni etiam intellectus duo? Nam si multiplicentur proprietates, etiam & subiecta. 2. libertas proprie est facultas vitalis ad nolle & velle, & promt legi subest ad peccandum, vel non peccandum; at quis diceret homini regenito per gratiam inesse potentiam peccandi? Gratia enim disponit ad non peccandum, non vero ad peccandum. 3: Sicut velle, & velie bonum non sunt duo actus distincti, ita neque libertas volendi, & libertas volendi bonum, sunt duæ distinctæ libertates, est enim par ratio utrobique, & per has rationes libertas naturæ, & libertas peccati non sunt duæ distinctæ libertates.
units.tr: §. The will is considered 1. as nature; and in this it is common to it with other agents, that it is borne towards the good. 2. As it is such a nature, it is borne towards blessedness by an essential inclination that precedes liberty, as Thomas hints, not by deliberation of the mind or freely. 3. As it is free. 4. As it is good or evil. As it is free simply, its acts are indifferent, as good or evil, and subject to law. Freedom to act or not to act belongs physically to liberty in every state, although always restricted to willing well or ill. But an indifferent inclination to good or evil is never in nature (whatever the sophists dream to the contrary). For after the fall there is an inclination to evil in the unregenerate, and in the regenerate an inclination to good insofar as they are spirit, and to evil insofar as flesh dwells in them. Yet here there is no pure Arminian indifference, but an indifference not restrained by flesh and spirit, which is no more than the generic nature of animal exists outside man or beast. But in Adam before the fall there was no inclination to evil, for his holy will was inclined to perform God's law. But you will say that in Adam there was actual sin, and therefore before it there was in him an inclination and power to sin, for an act in creatures flows only from a pre-existing power. I answer: there was in him a natural power to eat and a natural power not to eat the fruit. These acts were merely natural and indifferent, and there was added to them, as something extrinsic, that they should be restrained or determined by law. Adam, however, only actuated natural power. For the power of sinning either regards the entitative act of sin, and this of itself was not an indifferent moral power, or it regards lawlessness itself, and this was not properly a power, but natural power itself insofar as it was subject to law. This power would indeed have been nothing if God had not prescribed law to man (as he could, for he lays down laws for his free creature). A servile and vicious inclination to sin does indeed dwell in man after the fall; yet this is not so much a power as a crookedness of power, and it belongs no more to the nature of free will than the power of limping belongs to the formal character of the faculty of locomotion. Hence I infer that the liberty of grace does not add to the liberty of nature a new liberty, but only a new power, liberty qualifying and elevating nature. For if there were a new liberty, there would be two distinct liberties in the regenerate, and so two wills, and why not two intellects too? For if properties are multiplied, so too are subjects. 2. Liberty properly is the vital faculty to will and not to will, and it is subject to law for sinning or not sinning. But who would say that a power to sin is present in a man regenerate by grace? For grace disposes to not sinning, not to sinning. 3. Just as to will and to will the good are not two distinct acts, so neither are the liberty of willing and the liberty of willing good two distinct liberties; for the reason is equal on both sides. By these reasons the liberty of nature and the liberty of sin are not two distinct liberties.

units.la: 6. Forma liberi arbitrii, non est spontaneitas, aut non coactio, hæc intellectui & voluntati in relatione ad summum bonum conveniunt. Et quamvis Calvinus, hac voce, ob penuriam vocum, abstrusam libertatis naturam explicet, attamen non-coactioni, approbandi, respuendi, enitendi vim superaddit. Sed hoc etiam pontificii vitio dent suis angelicis doctoribus. Ita Aquinas: homo non quoad libertatem naturalem, quæ est à coactione, sed quantum ad libertatem, quæ est à culpa lib. ar. perdidit. Ita Lombard. libere moveri est voluntarie & spontaneo motu moveri. Necesitas coactionis (inquit Bonaventura) repugnat libero arbitrio, non necessitas immutabilitatis. Non-defuerunt (inquit Fra. Zuarez) aliqui moderni Catholici, qui negaverunt ad libertatem actus esse necessariam indifferentiam seu carentiam necessitatis, sed satis esse carentiam coactionis. Quin & Augustinus per non coactionem libertatem explicat; eum excusat Estius, ita Bellarmin. excusat Prosper, contra Collat. sed Calvinus accusabitur, & tamen hic scripturæ adhæret, 1. Pet. 5. 2. pascite gregem μὴ ἀναγκαστῶς, ἀλλ' ἑκουσίως.
units.tr: 6. The form of free choice is not spontaneity or non-coaction; these belong to intellect and will in relation to the highest good. And although Calvin, with this word, for want of words, explains the obscure nature of liberty, nevertheless he adds to non-coaction the force of approving, rejecting and striving. But the Papists give this fault to their angelic doctors too. Thus Aquinas: man has lost liberty not as to natural liberty, which is from coaction, but as to the liberty which is from fault. Thus Lombard: to move freely is to be moved voluntarily and by spontaneous motion. The necessity of coaction (says Bonaventure) is repugnant to free will, not the necessity of immutability. Some modern Catholics, says Fr. Suarez, have not been lacking who denied that indifference, or the absence of necessity, is necessary for the liberty of an act, and held that the absence of coaction is enough. Indeed Augustine explains liberty by non-coaction; Estius excuses him, as Bellarmine also excuses him; Prosper does so against the Collations. But Calvin will be accused, and yet here he adheres to Scripture: 1 Pet. 5. 2. feed the flock not by constraint, but willingly [μὴ ἀναγκαστῶς, ἀλλ' ἑκουσίως].

units.la: 7. Theologi nostri immunitatem à coactionene & naturali etiam necessitate ortam ex judicio rationis practico, naturam libertatis esse statuunt, in quo veritati obediunt. Nam revera hæc imperatrix, illa interna vitalis & electiva vis qua lib. arbi. proposito objecto per intellectum, sub ratione boni, sese ad agendum applicat, est formalis ratio liberi arbitrii.
units.tr: 7. Our theologians hold that the nature of liberty is an immunity from coercion and also from natural necessity, arising from the practical judgment of reason, by which the will obeys truth. For indeed this judgment is the governing faculty, while that internal, vital and elective power by which the free will, once the object has been proposed through the intellect under the aspect of good, applies itself to acting, is the formal reason of free will.

units.la: 8. Iesuitæ Zuarez, Vasquez, Fonseca, Iod. Molina, Becanus & Iac. Armin. Remonstr. in script. Synodorum, Corvinus, volunt naturam ipsius esse potentiam ad agendum vel non agendum, etiam positis requisitis ad operationem omnibus, quod an non sacrilego in Dei providentiam, & gratiam ausu fiat, cum bono Deo videbimus. Ista interim observari velim. 1. nor.[?] Potentia volendi vel nolendi est ın. 1. not. Potentia volendi vel nolendi [?]est una & simplex potentia, si enim essent duae potentiae, vel una respiciens utrumque copulativè, tum non repugnaret voluntatem secundum eandem potentiam velle, & secundum eandem potentiam nolle, & nolle & velle idem, secundum idem, ad idem, & eodem tempore, quod est grave ἀντινομία. 2. Not. potentia libera spectatur dupliciter. 1. ut est res individualis, & terminus individualis divinae creationis uti creatio distinguitur ab actu providentiae & sic est simpliciter indifferens ad nolle & velle, quia secundum naturalem agendi modum, non magis τὸ velle, quam τὸ non velle spectat ad essentiam libertatis. 2. ut eadem potentia providentiae subjicibilis est, sic disjunctiva potentia determinatur ad unam partem (salva potentiae natura) non ad aliam: Deo enim sive scientia ipsius spectemus, quippe omnia scit, sive voluntatem, quae ad nihil creatum vel creabile est sulpensa, sed ab aeterno determinata, nulla est potentia disjunctiva; considerari quidem potest potentia creata, non considerato divino decreto, & in signo rationis decretum Dei antecedente, sed in tali chymerica consideratione, adversarii nobis litem vitiosa nuce haut emptitanda, frustrâ ferunt; at vero non est ulla potentia creata, nisi quae subest aeterno Dei decreto, nisi quis cum ἀΐδιος[?] divinae providentiae renuntiare velit, priore consideratione potentia quidem est actu ens determinatum, at actus potentiae sunt tantum possibiles & esse habent tantum in relatione ad omnipotentiam, non ad Dei decretum: at vero posito decreto, praesertim conditionato, tum quaestio an potentia libera sit indifferens ad agendum vel non agendum, vana est; nam potentia tum sub eo casu est determinata, & idem est ac si quaestio esset, an potentia non indifferens sed determinata, sit indifferens, & indeterminata, & posito decreto absoluto de rebus omnibus, insulse quaeritur an potentia libera sub eo decreto sit indifferens, nam decretum absolutum ponit futuritionem determinationis, & ablationem futurae fore indifferentiae, ideoq; sensu Iesuitico-arminiano, nempe prout illi sumunt vocem indifferentiae, inanis & vana est quaestio, at vero vox indif-feferentiæ si[?] referatur ad objectu, nempe pro indifferentia objectiva judicii proponentis objectū, quod nempe voluntas velle vel nolle potest, pro sua natura quippe quia non magis læderetur essentia libertatis, si libertas hoc potius quā illud amplecteretur, tum facile solveretur quæstio: sed quia difficile est cum protervis adversariis limites quæstionis figere, quo fata disputationis nos ducant, sequi & persequi hostes oportet.
units.tr: 8. The Jesuits Suárez, Vásquez, Fonseca, Luis Molina, Becanus, and Jacob Arminius and the Remonstrants in the writings of the Synods, Corvinus, hold that its nature is the power to act or not to act, even when all the requisites for the operation are posited. Whether this is done without sacrilegious presumption against God's providence and grace, we will see with the good God. Meanwhile I would have these points observed. 1. Note: the power of willing or not willing is one and simple. For if there were two powers, one embracing both conjunctively, then it would not be contradictory for the will to will and not will the same thing according to the same power, in the same respect, toward the same object, and at the same time, which is a grave contradiction. 2. Note: a free power is viewed in two ways. First, as an individual thing and term of divine creation, insofar as creation is distinguished from the act of providence; and thus it is simply indifferent to willing and not willing, since according to its natural mode of acting, willing rather than not willing does not belong to the essence of liberty. Second, as that same power is subject to providence; thus a disjunctive power is determined to one part (the nature of the power being preserved) and not to the other. For whether we look at God's knowledge, since he knows all things, or at his will, which is not suspended on anything created or creatable but determined from eternity, there is no disjunctive power. Indeed a created power can be considered without regard to the divine decree, and in the order of reason the decree of God can be considered as antecedent. But in such a chimerical consideration, our adversaries carry on a quarrel not worth buying with a worthless nut, and they bring it in vain. Truly, however, there is no created power except what lies under the eternal decree of God, unless someone wishes to renounce the eternal providence of God. In the former consideration the power is indeed a determinate being in act, but the acts of the power are only possible and have being only in relation to omnipotence, not to the divine decree. But when the decree is posited, especially a conditional one, the question whether a free power is indifferent to acting or not acting is vain. For the power is then determined under that condition, and it is the same as if the question were whether a power that is not indifferent but determined is indifferent and undetermined. And with an absolute decree concerning all things posited, it is foolishly asked whether a free power under that decree is indifferent; for the absolute decree posits the futurity of determination and the removal of the indifference that would otherwise come. Therefore, in the Jesuit-Arminian sense, as they take the word indifference, the question is empty and vain. But if the word indifference is referred to the object, namely to the objective indifference of the judgment proposing the object, which the will by its nature can will or not will, then the essence of liberty would not be harmed any more if liberty embraced this rather than that, and the question would easily be resolved. But because it is difficult to fix the limits of the question with stubborn adversaries, one must follow and pursue the enemies wherever the fates of the dispute lead.

units.la: At contra hanc indifferentiam objicient, talem indifferentiam competere causæ naturali, nam non-calefactio non magis lædit essentiam & actum primum ignis, quam calefactio. Sed respondeo, quamvis in casu miraculi salvetur essentia ignis sub non-calefactione, non tamen salvatur naturalis modus agendi in igne. At nec actus primus, nec actus secundus potentiæ liberæ lædituer, sive voluntas hoc velit, sive non. Dabimus itaque duplicem indifferentiam in potentia liberâ, aliam objectivam, nempe quando intellectus proponit eligibile libertati ut medium summo bono absolutè intento non necessarium, aliam internam, vitalem, electivam, qua voluntas libera ex se potest tam hoc velle, quam nolle, salva tum essentia libertatis, tum salvo naturalissimo agendi modo suo.
units.tr: But against this indifference they will object that such indifference belongs to a natural cause, for non-heating harms the essence and first act of fire no more than heating does. But I answer: although in the case of a miracle the essence of fire is preserved under non-heating, the natural mode of acting in fire is not preserved. But neither the first act nor the second act of a free power is harmed, whether the will wills this or not. We will therefore grant a twofold indifference in the free power: one objective, namely when the intellect proposes something eligible to liberty as a means, not necessary to the supreme good absolutely intended; the other internal, vital and elective, by which the free will of itself can will this as well as not will it, the essence of liberty being preserved and its most natural mode of acting being preserved too.

units.la: 9. Hinc prima nostra assertio. Voluntati liberæ in se & formaliter convenit indifferentia hæc & objectiva & interna, & per hanc à non coactione, à spontaneitate, & ab omnibus causis naturalibus formaliter distinguitur. libertas, & hæc indifferentia convenit libertati per se & primo conceptu. Nam si quæris quid sit libertas, Resp. est potentia electiva quæ ex se, & respectu naturalis modi agendi ex interno, & vitali suo imperio, tam potest hoc medium eligere, quam non eligere & per hoc ab aliis causis distinguitur. Ergo hæc est formalis ratio libertatis. 2. illa est formalis libertatis ratio, per quam relinquitur voluntati tale actus dominium, quale convenit enti creato, at per has indifferentias tale convenit libertati sui actus dominium, Ergo♦ Majorem concedent adversarii. Prob♦ minor. Quia positis his indifferentiis, nullum agens externum, ne quidem Deus, potest evertere libertatem in naturali agendi modo, Ergo semper relinquetur voluntati dominium sui actus♦ prob. anteced♦ Ratio formalis electionis, est unio objectiva boni non ut necessarii fini intento propositi ab intellectu♦ atqui ipsa libertas est causa intrinseca & vitalis, & quidem sola hujus unionis. Quod hypothesi sic declaro, Vult ex sua libertate Cyrus populi Dei liberationem. Deus quidem adhanc Cyri volitionem contribuit esse effectivum, Quippe excitavit Jehovah spiritum Cyri, at vero nullum esse vitale aut formale contribuit Deus in illam volitionem, tum quoniam causa efficiens utpote externa non potest[?] esse formale aut internum effectui contribuere, nisi efficiens causa evaserit, causa vel concausa formalis: Atqui Deus non fuit causa vel concausa formalis volitiopis Cyri. Sic enim non voluntas Cyri, sed Deus in Cyro formaliter & vitaliter eam liberationem voluisset, quod plane ἀθεόλογον[?]: & rationi repugnans; tum etiam quoniam Deus non majorem unionem objectivam, inter Cyri libertatem & populi liberationem facit quam ut effective approximet objectum illud indifferens vitali suæ causæ, excitando rationes efficaces illius volitionis, & physice predeterminando libertatem Cyri, ut illud velit, & tamen Cyrus eam liberationem ut medium tantum suæ fælicitatis cognovit, & ipsius libertas, & in actu primo, & in naturali agendi modo permansisset illæsa[?], sive eam liberationem voluisset, sive non. Imo quæ mea est infantia, fateor me videre non posse, qui causa efficiens infinita possit causam formalem in agendo lædere, nisi efficiens fiat causa formalis: exemplum esto tinctor, qui efficiens est in lana tingenda, applicando activa passivis, esto quod operam obnixius & solito impensius intendat, & ingredientia fortiora & anxiora superaddat, semper tamen coloratur lana modo connaturalissimo: eodem plane modo, esto quod Iehovah unionem objectivam inter voluntatem Cyri & populi liberationem faciat, non intendit esse objectivum supra gradus causationis formalis, ideoque semper libertas modo sibi connaturali aget, quamvis haud negem causam finitam posse lædere causam formalem in agendo, ut si quis ex alta turri corpus grave præcipitaret, fortius quam fert natura ipsius gravitatis, sed tum præcipitans est causa efficiens adhuc, non formalis illius motus.
units.tr: 9. Hence our first assertion. This indifference, both objective and internal, belongs to the free will in itself and formally, and through it liberty is formally distinguished from non-coercion, from spontaneity, and from all natural causes; and this indifference belongs to liberty per se and in the first concept. For if you ask what liberty is, the answer is: it is the elective power which of itself, and with respect to its natural mode of acting, by its own internal and vital command, can choose this means as well as not choose it, and by this it is distinguished from other causes. Therefore this is the formal reason of liberty. 2. That is the formal reason of liberty by which the will is left such dominion over its act as befits a created being; but through these indifferences such dominion over its act belongs to liberty. Therefore the adversaries will grant the major. I prove the minor: because, these indifferences being posited, no external agent, not even God, can overturn liberty in its natural mode of acting; therefore dominion over its act will always be left to the will. I prove the antecedent: the formal reason of choice is the objective union of a good, not as necessary, with the end intended and proposed by the intellect; but liberty itself is the intrinsic and vital cause, and indeed the sole cause, of this union. I declare this by a hypothesis: Cyrus wills the liberation of the people of God from his own liberty. God indeed contributes to this volition of Cyrus as an effective cause, for Jehovah stirred up the spirit of Cyrus; but God contributes no vital or formal element to that volition, since an efficient cause, being external, cannot contribute anything formal or internal to the effect unless it becomes a formal cause or concause. But God was not the formal cause or concause of the volition of Cyrus. For otherwise it would not be the will of Cyrus, but God in Cyrus who formally and vitally willed that liberation, which is plainly atheological and repugnant to reason. Also, God does not make a greater objective union between the liberty of Cyrus and the liberation of the people than that he effectively brings that indifferent object near to its vital cause, by stirring up efficacious reasons for that volition and physically predetermining the liberty of Cyrus to will it. Yet Cyrus knew that liberation only as a means to his own happiness, and his liberty would have remained unharmed, both in its first act and in its natural mode of acting, whether he had willed that liberation or not. Indeed, I confess I cannot see, and this is my childishness, how an infinite efficient cause could harm the formal cause in acting unless the efficient cause becomes a formal cause. Let the example be a dyer, who is the efficient cause in dyeing wool, applying active things to passive ones. Let him apply his effort more earnestly than usual and add stronger and sharper ingredients; still the wool is coloured in its most connatural mode. In exactly the same way, let Jehovah make an objective union between the will of Cyrus and the liberation of the people; he does not intend this object to be beyond the degrees of formal causation, and therefore liberty will always act in its own connatural mode. Although I do not deny that a finite cause can harm a formal cause in acting, as when someone casts a heavy body from a high tower more forcefully than the nature of gravity itself bears; but then the one casting is still the efficient cause of that motion, not its formal cause.

units.la: 10. Affert. 2. Nuda indifferentia objectiva non est formalis ratio libertatis. Hoc tamen sensu contra nos militant argumenta, Suarez. de divina grat. & in Metaph. sic enim objicit: Origo & radix libertatis, non est formalis ratio libertatis sed indifferentia objectiva est radix tantum & origo libertatis: E. Resp. Conceded major: & negando minor. Nam indifferentia objectiva tantum, non est origo libertatis, nos vero dicimus hanc indifferentiam objectivam una cum indifferentia vitali, & interna, qua libertas potest hoc vel eligere vel non eligere, fine læsione fui, vel in actu primo, vel in actu fecundo, esse formam liberi arb. Obj. 2. Voluntas in habitudine ad beatitudinem potest elicere actum circa eam, vel non elicere: nam interdum intellectus actu non cogitat de beatitudine. Ergo esse indifferens ad nolle, vel velle absque læsione essentiæ & naturalis agendi modi non est propria ratio libertatis. Resp. concedendo totum: requiritur enim præter internam indifferentiam ad nolle & velle, etiam externa indifferentia objectiva: at vero beatitudo non est tale objectum indifferens, sed necessarium. Obj. 3. Potest Deus libertati proponere medium ad felicitatem, cum tam claro, & evidenti lumine, ut non possit objectum non videri bonum, at in hoc casu voluntas libere eligeret. Ergo hæc indifferentia objectiva non est necessaria ad libertatis naturam. Resp: Deum posse objectum libertati ita proponere non negamus, sed actum voluntatis tunc esse liberum negamus. 2. Indifferentia interna non tantum respicit nolle & velle indifferenter, sine voluntatis violatione, sed etiam superaddit huic indifferentiæ vim quandam imperialem & vitalem, qua libertas & sese & alias omnes potentias ad opus applicat imperio plane vitali. Unde dicimus ista includi in formali ratione libertatis: 1. Non-coactionem. 2. Superaddere non-coactioni indifferentiam objectivam. 3. Superaddere indifferentiam etiam internam & vitalem, qua voluntas libera velle hoc vel nolle potest, citra actus primi & secundi dispendium & jacturam. 4. Tandem omnibus superaddi vitalem illam electivam & imperatricem vim ab ipsis libertatis visceribus (utsic loquar) manantem, & hisce libertas ob omnibus potentiis distinguitur.
units.tr: 10. Assertion. 2. A bare objective indifference is not the formal reason of liberty. Yet in this sense arguments militate against us from Suarez, On Divine Grace, and in the Metaphysics, for he objects thus: The origin and root of liberty is not the formal reason of liberty, but objective indifference is only the root and origin of liberty; therefore Reply. I grant the major, and deny the minor. For objective indifference alone is not the origin of liberty. We, however, say that this objective indifference, together with the vital and internal indifference by which liberty can choose this or not choose it without harm to itself, whether in the first act or the second act, is the form of the free will. Objection 2. The will, in relation to happiness, can elicit an act about it or not elicit one, for at times the intellect is not actually thinking about happiness. Therefore, to be indifferent to willing or not willing, without injury to its essence and natural mode of acting, is not the proper reason of liberty. Reply. I grant the whole: for, besides the internal indifference to unwilling and willing, external objective indifference is also required; but happiness is not such an indifferent object, but a necessary one. Objection 3. God can present to liberty a means to happiness with so clear and evident a light that the object cannot fail to appear good; yet in this case the will would choose freely. Therefore this objective indifference is not necessary to the nature of liberty. Reply. We do not deny that God can present the object to liberty in this way, but we deny that the act of the will is then free. 2. Internal indifference not only regards unwilling and willing indifferently, without violence to the will, but also adds to this indifference a certain imperial and vital power, by which liberty applies both itself and all the other powers to the work by a wholly vital command. Hence we say that these are included in the formal reason of liberty: (1) non-coaction; (2) objective indifference added to non-coaction; (3) internal and vital indifference added as well, by which the free will can will this or not will it, without loss or damage to the first or second act; (4) lastly, that vital elective and commanding power, flowing from the very bowels (as I may so speak) of liberty, is added to all the powers, and by this liberty is distinguished from all of them.

units.la: II. Indifferentia Iesuitarum & Arminianor: qua volunt positis omnibus ad operandum antecedenter requisitis, esse in potentia libera ut existat vel non existat τῷ[?] nolle vel velle, non est ullo modo de formali ratione libertatis, imo cum providentia divina adversis frontibus conflictat. Prob. 1. ex orationibus sanctorum, quibus petunt ex fide & Dei verbo, ut Iehovæ inclinet cor ipsorum ad observanda Dei mandata, ut det cor sanum, ut gressus dirigat secundum ipsius verbum, ut ducat ipsos in via justitiæ, ut agglutinet cor timori Dei. Hinc argumentor. Quod sancti ex Dei verbo & fide orant, id Deus iis gratiose indulget. Hæc major est scripturæ Joh. 14. 13, 14. Quicquid petieritis in nomine meo, dabitur. Et Matth. 7. 7. Atqui sancti hisce testimoniis & infinitis aliis orant ex Dei verbo & fide liberrimam obedientiam, non vero talem, qua voluntas indifferenter obedire potest, vel non obedire. E. Deus iis talem obedientiam indulget, ac proinde libertatem, qua obediant, cui repugnat talis absoluta indifferentia. Prob. Minor.
units.tr: II. The indifference of the Jesuits and Arminians, by which they hold that, all things antecedently required for acting being posited, there is in a free power the ability to exist or not exist, or to be unwilling or willing, is in no way part of the formal reason of liberty; indeed it clashes head-on with divine providence. Proof. 1. From the prayers of the saints, in which they ask, from faith and the Word of God, that Jehovah would incline their heart to keep God's commandments, that he would give a sound heart, that he would direct their steps according to his word, that he would lead them in the way of righteousness, that he would bind their heart to the fear of God. Hence I argue: what the saints ask from the Word of God and in faith, God graciously grants them. This major premise is from Scripture: John 14:13, 14: Whatever you ask in my name, it will be given; and Matthew 7:7. But the saints, by these testimonies and countless others, pray from the Word of God and in faith for the most free obedience, and not for that obedience by which the will can obey indifferently or not obey. Therefore God grants them such obedience, and consequently the liberty by which they obey, with which such absolute indifference is incompatible. Proof of the minor.

units.la: 1. Non petunt sancti ut Deus libertatem destruat (quod necessario peterent ex JesuitoArminia: si petunt obedientiam quæ à tali indifferentia fluit) tales enim petitiones, essent miraculorum postulationes, citra fidem aut Dei verbum, imo suavi providentiæ, cujus est rerum naturas conservare, non evertere, adversissimæ. 2. Hoc, Agglutina cor meum timori tui, non fert hunc ridiculum sensum, ita Jehova cor meum ad obedientiam flecte, ut possim, vel te timere, vel pro indifferentia libertatis meæ, abjecta numinis tui reverentia, à timore nominis tui prorsus deficere: sic e. Propheta tam inobedientiam quam obedientiam oraret. Imo quis non videt tales petitiones è diametro pugnare cum votis, sanctis desideriis, intentionibus piis, fide & consolatione fautor[?]? Tam e. credendum esset sanctis, Deum non exauditurum quam exauditurum. Quid hic Jesuitæ petunt (inquit Gob. Vazquez) ut Deus congruo motu excitet voluntasvoluntatem, ut actu Deo adhaereant, quamvis motioni tali liberum sit iis vel obtemperare, vel resistere. R. Audio Chymaeram Iesuiticam. Motio congrua (ut habet Petrus Fonseca) in suo conceptu quid ditativo includit obedientiam congruè moti, sicitaquè orat: quando præscias, Iehova, antecedenter ad actum voluntatis tuæ, cor meum tibi agglutinatum iri, oro ut velis agglutinare; imo tam sana ratione petitur quod jam est, quam si Iesuitæ hodierno die, Deum pro creatione mundi, multis retro seculis elapsa, precibus solicitarent.
units.tr: 1. The saints do not ask that God destroy liberty (which they would necessarily have to ask, on the Jesuit and Arminian view, if they asked for the obedience that flows from such indifference). For such petitions would be requests for miracles, without faith or the Word of God, and indeed wholly opposed to a gentle providence, whose task is to conserve the natures of things, not to overturn them. 2. The words Bind my heart to your fear do not bear this ridiculous sense: "Jehovah, bend my heart to obedience so that I may either fear you, or, by the indifference of my liberty, having cast off reverence for your majesty, fail altogether from the fear of your name." On that reading the prophet would be praying for disobedience as much as for obedience. Indeed, who does not see that such petitions run diametrically against vows, holy desires, pious intentions, faith and consolation? Thus it would have to be believed by the saints that God would not hear them just as much as that he would. What do the Jesuits ask here? (says Gabriel Vázquez) That God by a congruous motion should excite the will, so that it may actually cling to God, although it is free to either obey such a motion or resist it. Reply. I hear a Jesuitical chimera. A congruous motion (as Pedro de Fonseca holds) includes in its very concept an obedience to the congruously moved will; so the one who prays says: "Since you foreknow, Jehovah, antecedently to the act of your will, that my heart will be bound to you, I pray that you will bind it." Indeed, what is already so is asked for on sound reasoning, just as if the Jesuits today were to beseech God, many ages after the creation of the world, for the creation of the world.

units.la: 12. Idem 2. proba. ex promissionibus divinis, quibus Deus liberrimam obedientiam in nobis effecturum pollicetur. Ezech. 36. 27. Faciam ut in statutis meis ambuletis. Arminianis solennis est cantilena, Deum ista in nobis efficere ex promissis suis, non absolute sed conditionate, faciam ambuletis, siquidem vos velitis ambulare. Tuissius scholasticorum[?] ingeniorum flos illibatus; jure quærit hic conditionem, præsertim in actibus voluntatis elicitis; Faciam (diceret Deus) ut velitis ambulare, siquidem velitis. Digna hostibus gratiæ responsio. At certum est τὸ velle ambulare in præceptis Dei promitti, at ut objectum promissionis, seu res promissa antecedat ipsam promissionem, idem est, ac si Deus, hodierno die, promitteret ortum solis hesternum aut mundi creationem; satin' sana sunt ingenia talium Davorum? At suboleo, quid hic sint responsuri: Deum promittere, ut efficiat in nonobis velle, non ex hypothesi quod velimus (hoc enim esset nimis crasse Philosophari, magno praesertim Arminio) sed ex hypothesi quod nostra voluntas incipiat collaterali influxu suum influxum accommodare Deo volenti concurrere. Sed sit ita: 1. qui inter influxum voluntatis nostrae & ipsam volitionem distinguet, nae ille spiritum admodum metaphysicalem sapit, & erit mihi magnus Apollo. 2. Hic influxus providentiae Dei eximitur, si Arminio credendum, prius enim natura hic influxus in actus supernaturales, fidei, amoris, spei &c. influit, quam Deus incipit concurrere, & quidem ex mero naturae arbitrio, sine ulla gratiae divinae motione, & sic Deus non operatur in nobis velle, uti docet Apostolus, secundum ipsius beneplacirum, sed ex beneplacito humani naturalis influxus. 3. Si voluntas independenter a Deo influat in actum legi & euangelio conformem, influxus ille erit legi & euangelio conformis adeoque supernaturalis, & sic dabitur actus supernaturalis citra adjutorium gratiae, absque primae causae concursu, & actus etiam positivus peccato substratus absque actione primae causae. 4. Ipse actus est liber propter libertatem influxus; ideoque ipse influxus est magis liber. Nam propter quod unum quodque tale, id ipsum est magis tale. Hinc sequitur omnem obedientiam supernaturalem esse primario a mera natura. 5.[?] Et cum illi influxus sint entitates positivae, tot entia positiva quot sunt astus contingentes hominum & angelorum existent sine concursu primæ causæ. Vereor tamen ne Arminiani apud se negent concursum Dei in actibus creaturæ, ut facilius in folium Dei evehatur nova Dea contingentia.
units.tr: 12. I prove the same second point from the divine promises, in which God promises that he will effect in us the most free obedience. Ezekiel 36:27: I will cause you to walk in my statutes. To the Arminians it is a set refrain that God effects these things in us from his promises not absolutely but conditionally: "I will cause you to walk, provided you are willing to walk." Truly the spotless flower of scholastic wit! Here they rightly ask for a condition, especially in acts elicited by the will: "I will cause you to be willing to walk, if you are willing." A reply worthy of the enemies of grace! But it is certain that the willingness to walk is promised in God's precepts; yet that the object of the promise, or the thing promised, should precede the promise itself is the same as if God today were promising yesterday's sunrise or the creation of the world. Are the minds of such Davuses sound? But I suspect what they will reply here: that God promises to effect in us the willing, not on the hypothesis that we will (for that would be too crude a philosophy, especially for the great Arminius), but on the hypothesis that our will, at the same time, begins to adapt its own influx to God's willing that it should concur. But let it be so. (1) Whoever distinguishes between the influx of our will and the volition itself savours of a very metaphysical spirit, and he will be a great Apollo to me. (2) According to Arminius, this influx of providence is excluded, for by nature this influx flows into supernatural acts of faith, love, hope and so on before God begins to concur, and indeed by the mere choice of nature, without any motion of divine grace. Thus God does not work in us the willing, as the Apostle teaches, according to his good pleasure, but according to the good pleasure of human natural influx. (3) If the will influences, independently of God, an act conformed to the law and the gospel, that influx will be conformed to the law and the gospel and therefore supernatural; and so there will be a supernatural act without the help of grace, without the concurrence of the first cause, and even a positive act underlying sin without any action of the first cause. (4) The act itself is free because of the liberty of the influx; therefore the influx itself is more free. For that by which each thing is such, is itself more such. Hence it follows that all supernatural obedience is primarily from mere nature. (5) And since those influxes are positive entities, there will exist as many positive entities as there are contingent acts of men and angels, without the concurrence of the first cause. I fear, however, that the Arminians deny among themselves the concurrence of God in the acts of the creature, so that a new goddess, Contingency, may more easily be raised up to the throne of God.

units.la: 13. 3. Si talis fit formaliter potentia libera, quæ possit omnibus ad agendum requisitis agere vel non agere, tolletur Dominium Dei in entitates creatas, at hoc est absurdum. E. etiam antecedens. Prob. major. Si ꝥ[?] velle vel non velle, etiam posito decreto Dei fit in voluntate Petri, erit in potestate hominis, non Dei, ut Christus generetur ex fœmine Davidico, vel non, per actus liberos generandi, item quodulli sint in rerum natura credentes, item quod Cyrus liberet Dei populum, quod Babylonii a Medis, Tyrii a Babyloniis, Iudæi ab Assyriis vastentur. Nam Deus ista quæ fiunt per agentia libera, nec procurare nec avertere potest, quando illa absolutè sint indifferentia arbitrii humani, & sic providentia, fiducia in Deum propter bonum aut salutem, per ministerium hominum libere agentium, gratitudo, patientia, spes, &c. plane tollerentur: ut enim homines libere aliquid faciant, vel non, est pœnes libertatem indifferentem, vel penes Deum est. Resp. Suarez. & cum eo verbosus declarator Nicol. Grevinchov. Deum concurrere cum voluntate, non est uti suo dominio, sed est sinere ut voluntas utatur suo dominio ad dominium Dei satis est ut possit [illegible, ~6 letters] creaturam, & ut actus creaturæ jam [illegible, ~3 letters] oducti Dei dominio subsint. R. 1. Paulus Dei dominium extendit ad ea, quæ nondum sunt, quæ vocat quasi jam essent Rom. 4. 16. An non ergo Deus actus liberos è potentia voluntatis pari jure vocare potest? Sed nolunt Deum uti dominio suo in actus liberos futuros, ne injuria fictet reginæ libertati. 2. Summunt pro oppositis quæ non opponuntur, nempe Deum uti suo dominio in creaturas, & ipsas in actibus suis juvare. Nam quando Deus concurrit cum pluvia, nive, grandine, imbribus cadentibus, testantur & ubique clamant oracula sacra Deum uti suo dominio erga homines, vel beneficia præstando, vel pœnas irrogando 4. Sæpius in rerum conservatione, quam in annihilatione cernitur Dei dominium. Alia argumenta alibi addemus. Hæc prænotasse consultum duxi, ut ad profundiora via sterneretur.
units.tr: 13. 3. If free power is formally such that it can either act or not act, when all the things required for acting are present, then God's dominion over created beings is abolished, and that is absurd. Therefore the antecedent too is absurd. I prove the major premise. If willing or not willing, even when God has decreed something, comes about in Peter's will, then it will be in the power of man and not of God, whether Christ is born of a woman of David's line or not, through free acts of begetting; likewise whether there are any believers in the world, that Cyrus should free God's people, that the Babylonians should be laid waste by the Medes, the Tyrians by the Babylonians, and the Jews by the Assyrians. For God could neither bring about nor avert those things that come about through free agents, when they are wholly indifferent to the human will. Thus providence, trust in God for good or for salvation, through the ministry of men acting freely, gratitude, patience, hope, and so on, would plainly be abolished. For whether men do something freely or not lies either in indifferent freedom or in God. Suarez replies, and with him the wordy expounder Nicolaus Grevinchovius: for God to concur with the will is not to use his dominion, but to allow the will to use its own dominion. It is enough for God's dominion that he is able [illegible] the creature, and that the acts of the creature, once brought forth, are subject to God's dominion. Answer 1. Paul extends God's dominion to things that are not yet, which he calls as though they already were (Rom. 4. 16). Can God not, by the same right, call free acts out of the power of the will? But they are unwilling that God should use his dominion over future free acts, lest they do injury to liberty, that queen. 2. They assume as opposites things that are not opposed, namely that God uses his dominion over creatures and helps them in their actions. For when God concurs with rain, snow, hail, and falling showers, the sacred oracles testify and cry out everywhere that God uses his dominion towards men, either by bestowing benefits or by inflicting punishments. 4. God's dominion is seen more often in the preservation of things than in their annihilation. We shall add other arguments elsewhere. I thought it wise to premise these things, so that a road might be laid down to deeper matters.

units.la: CAP. II. An Arminiani candidè fateantur æternita- tem, & immutabilitatem divinorum de- cretorum.
units.tr: CHAPTER II. That the Arminians candidly admit the eternity and immutability of the divine decrees.

units.la: DE divina libertate pauca præmitto. I. Not. Actus liberi in Deo non sunt extrinsecæ tantum denominationes (ut quidam somniant) ratione cujus Dei velle nihil aliud, quam fieri mutationem ad extra in re à Deo volita: cum enim Deus sit spiritus vivens & intelligens, sunt in Deo actus vitales, &c. scriptura attribuit Deo quod intelligat, velit, amet. Itaque 2. Not. Intelligere, velle, & amare, quoad entitativam perfectionem quam includunt, Deo insunt necessario. Nec potest Deus esse Deus, si hisce destitueretur. At vero quoad terminationem ad objectum creatum, insunt tantum necessario ex hypothesi, poterat enim mundum non creasse. 3. Not. libertas essentialiter non dicit dependentiam appetitus ab objecto, ideoque objectum est per se terminativum, non perfectivum appetitus, quare libertas Dei non dependet ab objecto, nec ab eo perficitur.
units.tr: I shall first set down a few points about divine freedom. (1) Free acts in God are not merely extrinsic denominations (as some dream), by which God's willing is nothing other than a change outside of him in a thing willed by God. Since God is a living and intelligent spirit, there are vital acts in God, etc. Scripture attributes to God that he understands, wills and loves. Hence (2) understanding, willing and loving, as far as the entitative perfection they involve, belong to God necessarily. Nor could God be God if he lacked these. But as regards their termination on a created object, they belong to him only necessarily on a hypothesis, for he could have not created the world. (3) Freedom essentially does not imply the dependence of the appetite on the object, and so the object is terminative of the appetite in itself, not perfective of it. Therefore God's freedom does not depend on the object, nor is it perfected by it.

units.la: 4. Dei libertas in se non est indeterminata, sed per eminentiam sui actus ab aeterno determinata, ut recte Scotus. Hinc privatio actus secundi, qualis reperitur in libertate creata, in Dei libertatem non cadit, & per eandem rationem Dei libertas non est in potentia vel activa vel passiva, ideoque ut recte docet Alvarez, Indifferentia illa quæ opponitur libere determinationi, & importat quandam potentialitatem & suspensionem actus secundi, non est de essentia libertatis: nam in Dei libertate non reperitur. Ideoque cum dicimus Deum posse nolle, vel velle, illud (posse) non importat potentiam in Deo actuabilem, sed solum indifferentiam actus ut ad hoc objectum terminetur, vel non terminetur, quod est admirandum: ita recte annotat Fr. Suarez.
units.tr: (4) God's freedom is not indeterminate in itself, but is determined from eternity by the eminence of his act, as Scotus rightly holds.
