Hence the privation of a second act, such as is found in created freedom, does not fall within God's freedom; and for the same reason God's freedom is not in potency, either active or passive. Therefore, as Alvarez rightly teaches, that indifference which is opposed to free determination, and which implies a certain potentiality and suspension of a second act, is not of the essence of freedom, for it is not found in the freedom of God. So when we say that God can not-will or will, that "can" does not imply a potency in God that could be actualised, but only an indifference of the act as to whether it is terminated on this object or not terminated on it, which is a wonder. So rightly observes Fr. Suarez.

units.la: 5. Actus liber in Deo est actus simplex, & actus simplex est essentia simplex, non potest autem Dei essentia aliter se habere, aut habuisse, quam est, absque divinæ naturæ mutabilitate. Idem omnino est actus volendi secundum rem, qui sine ulla mutatione ad varia terminatur, & idem actus prout ad hoc terminatur volitio & est odiū. Nec sunt ulli in Deo, ut in nobis actus vere contrarii aliquid reale addentes: quare iidem fuissent actus decretorum Dei, qui nunc sunt, & eodem modo se habuisset essentia Dei, quo nunc se habet: si qui jam reprobi, fuissent electi, & qui jam electi, reprobi. Nam libertas in creaturis est ad actus indifferentes: in Deo vero est ad alia tantum atque alia objecta extra se, & hinc videre possunt Arminiani, quomodo immutabilitas Dei cum absoluta libertate consistat.
units.tr: (5) A free act in God is a simple act, and a simple act is a simple essence. But the essence of God cannot be otherwise disposed, or have been otherwise disposed, than it is, without a mutability of the divine nature. The act of willing is altogether the same in reality, though it is terminated on various objects without any change; and the same act, as terminated on this object, is called volition, and as terminated on that, is called something else. Nor are there in God, as in us, acts that are truly contrary and add something real. Hence the acts of God's decrees would have been the same as they are now, and the essence of God would have been disposed in the same way as it now is, even if those who are now reprobate had been elected, and those who are now elected had been reprobate. For freedom in creatures is towards acts that are indifferent; but in God it is only towards one object outside himself or another. From this the Arminians can see how the immutability of God is consistent with absolute freedom.

units.la: 2. Nos vel accuratoribus Jesuitis & Scholasticis litem amandamus. An Arminiani digna divinæ majestatis ter tremendâ immutabili natura doceant, qui ut hæretico Vorstio & suo genio lenocinentur, statuant multos esse actus liberos in Deo, qui nunquam in eo fuissent, nisi antecederent humanæ & angelicæ quædam volitiones. Sed ad rem, præsentem disquisitionem ad duos fontes revoco, ad Arminiana placita de prædestinatione, & de justificatione, & [illegible, ~14 letters] εἰς τὸ ἀλληγορῶ[?] exercitationes scribenti lectori dabit veniam, si nostram doctrinam de justificatione obiter vindicare tentavero.
units.tr: (2) We leave this dispute to the more careful Jesuits and the Schoolmen. Do the Arminians, who in order to flatter the heretic Vorstius and their own disposition, hold that there are many free acts in God which would never have been in him unless some human and angelic volitions had preceded them, teach things worthy of the awesome majesty of the immutable nature? But to the matter in hand: I recall the present inquiry to two sources, to the Arminian tenets on predestination and on justification. [Here some words are illegible in the scan.] The writer of these exercises will pardon me if, in passing, I attempt to defend our doctrine of justification.

units.la: 3. 1. Forensis illa distinctio electionis in peremptoriam, completam & irrevocabilem, & non peremptoriam, incompletam & revocabilem, volitiones Dei & mutabiles, & temporales, nostrique lubrici & inconstantis arbitrii passibus coævas esse, fatis manifeste astruit. Nam quoties homo credit, est in Deo decretum electionis, quoties eadem horâ diffidit Deo promittenti, facit fe formale reprobationis objectum, & oritur in Deo novum decretum reprobationis; rursus idem credit, postea non credit, graviter peccat, denuo & resipiscit & credit, en Euripi more, Dei decreta singenda, indies mutanda, ad humani arbitrii revolutiones vel currus rotulis mutabiliores; & quis ignorat ecclesiam Pfal. 77. & sanctos, Davidem Pfal. 6. Iobum cap. 2. in eadem oratione ad Deum, & triumphos sacros agere, & etiam cum Deo, ex carnis prævalentis diffidentiâ, expostulare, imo Deum oblivionis, inconstantiæ & mutati propositi, non procul à blasphemiarum aspersione, postulare? An ecclesia eadem horâ etiam inter orandum in chorum electorum cooptatur, denuo & reprobis & tenebrarum Angelis, in Dei voluntate simplicissima accensetur? Quid hic Arminiani? Agnoscimus (inquiunt) electionem & reprobationem peremtoriam, ex præscientia finalis in fide vel infidelitate perseverantiæ omnium in ecclesia viventium. R. Quorsum ergo illa decantata distinctio, quam in scripturis haberi clamitant Arminiani? Quare Deus vitæ adjudicaret, quem juxta præscientiam infidelitatis finalis in peccato in spiritum sanctum obstinatione horrendâ moriturum præscit? Nonne illa contumacia Deo omnia scienti, &que[?] præsens objectivè singularis fidei actus impedire deberet, quo minus Deus præmio & & mercedi æternæ gloriæ destinaret, quem mercede æternorum cruciatuum dignum fore, & gloriæ bravium indigne rejecturum præscit?
units.tr: (3) (1) That forensic distinction of election into peremptory, complete and irrevocable, and non-peremptory, incomplete and revocable, sufficiently shows that the volitions of God are both mutable and temporal, and keep pace with the steps of our slippery and inconstant will. For as often as a man believes, there is in God a decree of election; as often as in the same hour he distrusts God who promises, he makes himself a formal object of reprobation, and a new decree of reprobation arises in God. Again, he believes, afterwards does not believe, sins grievously, again repents and believes. Behold, in the manner of the Euripus, the decrees of God are to be feigned, changed daily, to suit the revolutions of the human will, more mutable than the wheels of a chariot. And who does not know that the Church, Psalm 77, and the saints, David in Psalm 6, Job in chapter 2, in the same prayer to God, both celebrate sacred triumphs and also, from the distrust of a prevailing flesh, complain with God; indeed they ask God to forget, to be inconstant and to change his purpose, not far from the spatter of blasphemy? Is the Church, in the same hour, even while praying, enrolled among the elect, and again among the reprobate and the angels of darkness, in the most simple will of God? What do the Arminians say here? They acknowledge (they say) an election and reprobation that is peremptory, from the foreknowledge of final faith or unbelief of all who live in the Church. Answer: then to what purpose is that much-vaunted distinction, which the Arminians loudly claim is found in Scripture? Why would God adjudge life to one whom he foreknows will die in final unbelief, in the dreadful obstinacy of sin against the Holy Spirit? Would not that obstinacy, which God, knowing all things, foresees, have to prevent God from destining for the reward of eternal glory the one whom he foreknows to be worthy of the wages of eternal torments and to reject the prize of glory unworthily?

units.la: 2. Considerari percupio verba Remonstrantium in apologia sua cenf. cap. 17. pag. 187. Quia enim (inquiunt) comminetur pœnam ei, quem peremptorio decreto à pœna immunem esse vult, quem gratia ejusmodi donare vult, quâ posita fieri non potest, ut pœnam incurrat &c. Assumo, Atqui Arminiani volunt Deum comminari pœnam ei quem præscit in fide moriturum, & quem gratia efficaci Arminiana donare vult, quâ posita fieri non poterit, ut pœnam incurrat. Ita Arminii. Antiperk. pag. 665. Vocat enim electos (inquit) decreto prædestinationis contradistincto à decreto providentiæ, eâ gratiâ, quâ posita, certo scit eos ad finem crediturosas, & pœnam euasuros æternam, & tamen comminatur pœnam æternam. At hoc Remonstrantium dicunt loc. citat. sapientiæ 'divinæ non convenire, atque adeo ab omni rectâ ratione alienum esse. Sed quia Arminiani credunt ab æterno neminem peremptoriè ad gloriam esse destinatum, ideo est quod omnibus comminationes fieri velint, quia possibile est omnes pœnam æterdam incurrant. Nam vel electio peremptoria est non æterna, sed temporalis, & pro arbitrii humani actibus mutabilis; vel Deus contra suam sapientiam & omnem rectam rationem comminatur peremptorie electis poenam, sed hoc est mysterium, nemo est peremptorie electus ab æterno, sed tum demum est peremptorie electus in tempore, quando in fide mortem obit, unde incipit in Deo nova electio temporalis peremptoria, quæ vera est mutatio, imo & nova scientia, unde peribit Dei præscientia æterna.
units.tr: (2) I am eager to consider the words of the Remonstrants in their Apology, chapter 17, page 187. For (they say) since he threatens punishment to the one whom he wills by a peremptory decree to be free from punishment, whom he wills to bestow such grace that, grace being given, it cannot happen that he incurs punishment, etc. I assume: but the Arminians hold that God threatens punishment to the one whom he foreknows will die in faith, and whom he wills to bestow the efficacious Arminian grace, grace being given, it cannot happen that he incurs punishment. So Arminius, Antiperkins, page 665. For he calls the elect (he says) by a decree of predestination distinct from the decree of providence, by that grace which, given, he knows for certain that they will believe to the end and escape eternal punishment; and yet he threatens them with eternal punishment. But the Remonstrants say, in the place cited, that this does not agree with divine wisdom, and is therefore alien to all right reason. But because the Arminians believe that no one from eternity has been peremptorily destined to glory, therefore they wish threats to be made to all, because it is possible that all may incur eternal punishment. For either election is peremptory but not eternal, but temporal, and changeable according to the acts of the human will; or God, against his own wisdom and all right reason, peremptorily threatens punishment to the elect. But this is a mystery: no one is peremptorily elected from eternity, but only then is he peremptorily elected in time, when he dies in faith; whence a new temporal and peremptory election begins in God, which is a true change, indeed a new knowledge, whereby the eternal foreknowledge of God would perish.

units.la: 4. Sed aliud patet Arminiūs[?] hic refugium lepidum sane. Deus (inquit) credentes pro tempore eligit, non credentes reprobat, & Deus ab æterno absolute & immutabiliter decrevit homines credentes eligere, non credentes reprobare, ex præscientia fidei vel infidelitatis, ideoque æterna adhuc & immutabilia sunt Dei decreta. Sed Resp. 1. Divinæ mutationes non desinunt esse mutationes, quia sunt immutabiliter decretæ. Pari ratione si quis immutabiliter, & constantissimo decreto apud se statueret, fidem cum locis, personis, rege, aula, belli fatis, adversis vel secundis rerum humanarum ventis, commutare, & etiam pro illo decreto immoto semper se componat ad omnes religiones, euangelicam, papisticam, mahumeticam, an propterea dicendus esset immutabilis? An quasi Deus immutabilis erit, quia ab æterno immutabiliter statuit decreta sua in horas cum nova Dea Contingentia, & humana libertate mutare? Apage theologiam orco relegandam: Simili modo Deus ab æterno statuit ut homo esset mutabilis, an propter tale decretum, erit immutabilis? 2. Decretum est statutum beneplaciti, advocata sapientia, edictum: at vero quæ sapientia, quæ determinatio est illud hodie decernere, figere, quod cras refigendum est? Hoc ne[?] in virum sapientem cadit?
units.tr: (4) But Arminius here reveals another, certainly a witty, refuge. God (he says) elects believers for a time, and reprobates unbelievers; and God decreed from eternity absolutely and immutably to elect men who believe and to reprobate those who do not, from the foreknowledge of faith or unbelief; and therefore the decrees of God are still eternal and immutable. But I answer: (1) divine changes do not cease to be changes because they are immutably decreed. By the same reasoning, if someone were to decide in himself, immutably and with most constant decree, to change his faith according to places, persons, the prince, the court, the fates of war, and the adverse or favourable winds of human affairs, and were always to adapt himself to every religion, evangelical, papist, Mahometan, on the strength of that unmoved decree, should he therefore be called immutable? Or will God be immutable because from eternity he immutably decided to change his decrees hour by hour with the new goddess Contingency and with human freedom? Away with such a theology, fit to be banished to hell! In the same way, God from eternity decreed that man should be mutable; will man therefore be immutable on account of such a decree? (2) A decree is a determination of good pleasure, a sovereign edict, issued with wisdom counselling it. But what wisdom, what judgement is it to decree and fix today what must be re-fixed tomorrow? Does this befit a wise man?

units.la: §. 2. Verba Arminianorum idem probant Nam Remonstran. in apo. Concludimus ergo (inquiunt) falsum esse. {quanquam habent id plerique tenuerunt} electionem in scripturis usquam ab æterno fastam[?] diti[?], aut eam (nisi cum pro decreto sumitur) in scripturis proponi ut rationem Dei interna[m], sive immanentem, quæ in Deo, ab æterno fuerit, & contra verissimum esse, quod electio in scripturis prædicatur, ut actio Dei externa & transiens, & quæ in tempore cepta est, contra quam habent fere creditum est. Sed. 1. Quis non videt hanc horariam fidem Iac. Arminii, qui definit reprobationem decretum, quo ab æterno statuit infideles damnare &c. & prædestinatio quam alibi vocat electionem thef. 3. Finit eodem modo thef. 6. Decreto isto (inquit) æternitatem tribuimus, quia Deus nihil in tempore facit, quod ab æterno facere non decrevit. Et thef. 10. Hoc decretum est secundum electionem, ut inquit Apostolus.
units.tr: §. 2. The words of the Arminians prove the same point. The Remonstrants, in their Apology, say: "We conclude therefore (they say) that it is false {although most have held it} that election is set forth anywhere in Scripture from eternity, or that it (unless it is taken for a decree) is proposed in Scripture as God's internal or immanent reason, which was in God from eternity; and that on the contrary it is most true that election is preached in Scripture as God's external and transient action, which began in time, contrary to what most have commonly believed." But first: 1. Who does not see that this is the temporal faith of James Arminius, who defines reprobation as a decree by which from eternity he resolved to condemn unbelievers, etc., and who elsewhere calls predestination election (thesis 3)? He ends in the same way in thesis 6: "To this decree (he says) we ascribe eternity, because God does nothing in time that he did not decide from eternity to do." And in thesis 10: "This decree is according to election, as the Apostle says."

units.la: Ergo Arminius ipse vere censet prædestinationem æternam fieri secundum electionem æternam: nam si electio sit temporalis, non poterit esse regula secundum quam fit prædestinatio æterna, ut Arminius ait: Electio est decretum Dei quo apud se æterno statuit &c. 2. Electionem interdum significare vocationem in tempore. I. Cor. 1. 26 27. non negamus, sed haec non est destinatio hominum ad vitam aeternam, de qua Rom. 9. & Eph. 1. quae in scriptura ab aeterno est. Eph. 1. Antequam pueri quicquam boni vel mali fecissent. Nec Arminiani electionem pro vocatione sumunt: nam electio, quam illi defendunt, in apolo. loc. citat: est electio eorum qui vere credunt, ut habetur confess. c. 18. th. 2. Imo eorum qui jam conversi sunt & vere credunt, e profana pereuntium turba segregantur &c. Atqui vocatio est nondum conversorum, sed convertendorum, imo vocatio iisdem doctoribus, confess. c. 17. th. 2. est eorum qui non credunt, imo fieri potest (inquiunt) ut vocati nunquam reipsa credant, ac salventur. Ergo credunt electionem & destinationem ad gloriam esse temporariam, & ex hominum arbitrio, qui credere vel non credere possunt, adeoque immutabilem[?] esse. 3. Electio haec temporaria credentium ad gloriam, vel est actualis gloriae datio, & sic glorificatio. (At quis glorificationem ad gloriam vocet? Non scriptura, non scriptor ecclesiasticus,) vel est Dei destinatio in mente & voluntate, qua voluit gloriam dare: at vero haec est actio immanens & aeterna: nulla enim Dei volitio est temporaria aut transiens; quod Deus vult, ab aeterno voluit. Arminiani tercium dare non possunt, vel est actus omnipotentiae divinae, & sic oportet ut fit glorificatio, quod non dicerent: vel intellectus & voluntatis, & sic erit actus immanens & æternus. Hic hærebit ipsis aqua.
units.tr: Therefore Arminius himself truly holds that eternal predestination is made according to eternal election. For if election is temporal, it cannot be the rule according to which predestination is eternal, as Arminius says: "Election is the decree of God by which he decided within himself from eternity, etc." 2. We do not deny that election sometimes signifies calling in time (1 Cor. 1.26, 27), but this is not the destining of men to eternal life, of which Rom. 9 and Eph. 1 speak, and which in Scripture is from eternity: "Before they had done anything good or evil" (Eph. 1). Nor do the Arminians take election for calling. For the election they defend, in the Apology cited above, is the election of those who truly believe, as is found in the Confession ch. 18, th. 2: "Indeed, those who are already converted and truly believe are separated from the profane crowd of the perishing, etc." But calling belongs not to those already converted but to those to be converted. Indeed, by the same teachers (Confession ch. 17, th. 2), calling belongs to those who do not believe: "It can happen (they say) that the called never actually believe, and are saved." Therefore they hold that election and destination to glory are temporary, and depend on the decision of men, who can believe or not believe, and so are mutable. 3. This temporary election of believers to glory is either the actual bestowal of glory, and so glorification (but who calls glorification a calling to glory? Not Scripture, not any ecclesiastical writer); or it is God's destination in mind and will, by which he willed to give glory. But this is an immanent and eternal act, for no volition of God is temporary or transient: what God wills, he has willed from eternity. The Arminians cannot offer a third option. Either it is an act of divine omnipotence, and so the glorification must be what happens, which they would not say; or it is an act of intellect and will, and so it will be an immanent and eternal act. Here the water will stick in their throat.

units.la: 6. 3. Corvinus vult (Hoc fac, & vives). suisse legale decretum, de ultimo fine creaturarum rationalium: at vero quoniam lex est abrogata, ipsis fatentibus, necesse est ut decretum hoc legale desierit in Deo, multis abhinc annis, nempe statim à lapsu Adami. Dicent non esse abrogatum decretum, quia non fuit peremptorium, respectu hominum, sed conditionatum. At quid tum? An est, quæso, jam in Deo decretum salvandi homines, siquidem legem præstiterint? At ipsi docent nullam esse salutem per legem. Ergo Deus vel illud decretum refixit & abjecit, vel sic apud se dicit, quamvis statuerim apud me nullos salvare per opera legis, sed tantum per fidem, tamen adhuc decerno salvare omnes, siquidem legem servaverint. Hic insulsum erit in Deo decretum legale; & inane, & erunt in Deo duo decreta plane contradictoria, adeoque voluntates contrariæ, quod est blasphemum.
units.tr: 3. Corvinus holds (Do this and you will live) that there was a legal decree concerning the ultimate end of rational creatures. But since the law has been abrogated, as they themselves confess, it must be that this legal decree ceased in God many years ago, namely immediately after the fall of Adam. They will say the decree was not abrogated, because it was not peremptory with respect to men, but conditional. But what then? Is there now in God, I ask, a decree to save men, provided they have fulfilled the law? Yet they teach that there is no salvation by the law. Therefore God either revoked and cast off that decree, or he says to himself: although I have decided within myself to save no one by the works of the law, but only by faith, nevertheless I still decree to save all, provided they keep the law. Here the legal decree in God will be foolish and empty, and there will be in God two plainly contradictory decrees, and so contrary wills, which is blasphemous.

units.la: 2. Penes voluntatem Adami fuisse præstare legem, qua præstita nullum fuisset in Deo decretum evangelicum, vel non præstare, qua non præstita, fuit in Deo decretum evangelicum, & sic decretum evangelicum in Deo causatur à volitione temporali humana, adeoque non est æternum. At (inquiunt) Deus ab æterno præsciens lapsum Adami, ab æterno fecit decretum evangelicum; sed hic videant Arminiani qualem sibi Deum fingant, ab æterno, sic statuentem apudfe[?]. Decerno ut Adamus & posteri ipsius salventur, siquidem legem præstiterint, vel si non, ut salventur siquidem crediderint, vel si nulli crediderint, ut damnentur: hic Deus fuit anceps, pendulus & decretis figendis varius, pendens plane in decretis suis æternis à temporariis hominum actibus. 3. Fecit decretum euangelicum vel præsciens quosdam creditu-ros, vel non præsciens: si primum, tum decretum de certis quibusdam personis salvandis, erit prius decreto generali de salvandis fidelibus, quod invertit decretorum Arminianum ordinem: si posterius, Deus nulla providentia, quia nulla scientia, fecit totum euangelium, & ignoravit in eo decreto utrum assequeretur illustrationem gloriæ misericordiæ, vel justitiæ. 4. Quare fecit Deus decretum legale non peremptorium? certe vel quia præscivit Adamum lapsurum, & sic quare omnino fecit, quod abrogandum fore, & incasso[?] fine futurum prævidit? id enim non est scientis, præscito fine frustraneo, aliquid facere, vel fecit non peremptorium, quia non præscivit, sed conjecturam fecit, fieri posse, ut homo, qui est creatura mutabilis, peccet; & sic non opus fuit in eo signo rationis decreto legali, quorsum decerneret, quod refigendum sit?
units.tr: 2. It lay in Adam's will either to fulfil the law, in which case there would have been no evangelical decree in God, or not to fulfil it, in which case there was an evangelical decree in God. So the evangelical decree in God is caused by a temporal human volition, and so is not eternal. But (they say) God, foreseeing the fall of Adam from eternity, made the evangelical decree from eternity. Let the Arminians see, however, what kind of God they imagine, who so decides within himself from eternity: I decree that Adam and his posterity shall be saved, if they have kept the law; or if not, that they shall be saved if they have believed; or if none believed, that they shall be condemned. Here God is doubtful, dangling and varying in fixing his decrees, plainly hanging in his eternal decrees on the temporal acts of men. 3. He made the evangelical decree either foreseeing certain ones who would believe, or without foreseeing. If the first, then the decree about certain persons to be saved will precede the general decree about saving believers, which reverses the order of decrees held by the Arminians. If the second, God made the whole gospel without any providence, since without any knowledge, and in that decree he did not know whether it would achieve the manifestation of the glory of mercy or of justice. 4. Why did God make a legal decree that was not peremptory? Certainly either because he foresaw that Adam would fall, and so why did he make at all what was to be abrogated, foreseeing that its end would be in vain? For it is not the mark of one who knows, having foreknown a futile end, to do something. Or he made it non-peremptory because he did not foresee, but only conjectured, that man, being a mutable creature, could sin; and so in that act of reason there was no need for a legal decree, since he would decree something that must be revoked.

units.la: 7. 4. Arminius ait; Certum est Deum velle nonnulla, quæ non vellet, nisi aliqua humana volitio antecederet. Atqui humanæ omnes volitiones sunt temporaneæ, & vult alibi, neminem esse actu reprobum nisi reipsa existentem, & sic reprobatio erit decretum temporale, & homines eligi non nisi in Christo mortuo, atqui mortuus est in tempore, Ergo homines electi sunt in tempore. Figmentum præscientiæ ipsos ne hilum juvabit. Volunt enim electionem & destinationem hominis ad gloriam esse actum justitiæ æque atque actualis datio, quæ est ex ordine justitiæ impossibilis nisi soluto λυτρω. Ergo, inquam ego, perfolutio λύτρω[?] in præscientia non salvat justitiam in Dei electione, sed necesse est actu persolvatur, priusquam Deus possit actu deligere homines ad vitam æternam, sicut actu persolvi debet, priusquam Deus possit actu vitam communicare, hæc consequentia nititur dogmatis Arminianis; illis enim destinare ad gloriam est actus justitiæ, sicut dare gloriam.
units.tr: 7. 4. Arminius says: "It is certain that God wills some things which he would not will unless some human volition preceded." But all human volitions are temporary, and he elsewhere holds that no one is actually reprobate except one who actually exists. So reprobation will be a temporal decree, and men are elected only in Christ who died; but he died in time; therefore men were elected in time. The fiction of foreknowledge will not help them a whit. For they want the election and destination of man to glory to be an act of justice, just as the actual bestowal is, which by the order of justice is impossible unless the ransom [λύτρον] is paid. Therefore, I say, the payment of the ransom in foreknowledge does not preserve justice in God's election; rather, it must be actually paid before God can actually choose men to eternal life, just as it must be actually paid before God can actually impart life. This consequence rests on the Arminian dogma, for to them to destine to glory is an act of justice, just as to bestow glory is.

units.la: 8. 5. Corvinus sic ait, Est vero absurdum, ut cum Deus obedientiam creaturæ vult, legem secundum praescientiam proponat, qua scit creaturam, eam non transgressuram: ratio quia tum eo ipso talem legem proponeret, quam absoluta voluntate nollet permittere, ut cui fertur, transgrederetur: & quamvis in specie hominis libertas maneret, revera tamen ad unam speciem actus, effet per istud determinata. Hinc argumentor: Deus vel legem tulit secundum eam præscientiam, qua scivit Adamum peccaturum, vel secundum nullam præscientiam: si primum, voluntas Dei absoluta antecedet libertate & eam destruet; hæc est enim consequentia. Corv.: Si secundum ullam præscientiam, tum postea quando Deus praescivit, cæpit in Deo nova scientia rei quam antea ignoravit, & etiam novum decretum permissivum temporale. Sed obiter hoc notetur etiam Dei præscientiam rei futuræ liberæ, non minus quam voluntatem determinantem, evertere libertatem, adeoque Arminianos revera negare in Deo præscientia actuum liberorum. 2. Hinc sequitur Deum intendere gloriam justitiæ in remunerando Adami obedientiam, quando ei legem tulit, & tamen ignarum fuisse utrum illum finem assecuturus esset, nec ne: at quis sapiens statueret redimere captivos auro in tali fodina, ignarus sit ne illic reperturus aurum, an non? Hoccine est dictitare digna infinitā Dei sapientiā? 3. Post violatam legem incipit in Deo nova volitio proponendi euangelium, & nova intentio salvandi homines; ignarus, sint ne obedituri, nec ne. Non obtemperant plerique! Oritur volitio nova damnandi, contraria intentioni salvandi. Rursus obtemperant! oritur volitio rursus salvandi. Imo fieri potest, ut quis per totam vitam credat, & in extremo puncto exspirationis credere desinat, ex illo uno actu infidelitatis, oritur peremptoria & irrevocabilis in Deo fixaque volitio in æternum damnandi, & qui per totam vitam flagitiosissimus fuerit, nec credens, nec obediens euangelio, in extremo anhelitu credit, & oritur in Deo nova volitio peremptoria in æternum salvandi. Quis hic non videt infælicem fortunam contingentiæ post se trahere temporaras in Deo & mutabiles volitiones, ut nihil dicam de insigni injuria in Dei justitiam, unum actum fidei vel infidelitatis, forte & contra divinam providentiam & voluntatem, exortum, aeterno exitio, vel ineffabili gloria, remunerantem.
units.tr: 8. 5. Corvinus says: "It is indeed absurd that when God wills the obedience of a creature, he should propose a law according to foreknowledge, by which he knows the creature will not transgress; the reason being that by that very fact he would propose such a law as, by his absolute will, he would not wish to permit to be transgressed, as it is given; and although liberty would remain in the species of man, in reality it would be determined by that to one kind of act." From this I argue: God either gave the law according to that foreknowledge by which he knew Adam would sin, or according to no foreknowledge. If the first, the absolute will of God precedes liberty and destroys it, for this is the consequence. Corvinus: If according to some foreknowledge, then afterwards, when God foreknew, a new knowledge of a thing began in God, which he had previously been ignorant of, and also a new temporal permissive decree. But let it be noted in passing that the foreknowledge of God of a future free thing, no less than a determining will, overturns liberty; and so the Arminians really deny foreknowledge of free acts in God. 2. From this it follows that God intended the glory of justice in rewarding Adam's obedience when he gave him the law, and yet was ignorant whether he would attain that end or not. But what wise man would decide to redeem captives with gold in such a mine, while ignorant whether he would find gold there or not? Is this to prattle things worthy of God's infinite wisdom? 3. After the law was violated, a new volition to propose the gospel arises in God, and a new intention to save men, while he is ignorant whether they will obey or not. Many do not obey! A new volition to condemn arises, contrary to the intention to save. Again they obey! A volition to save again arises. Indeed it can happen that someone believes throughout his life and ceases to believe at the last moment of his breath; from that one act of unbelief there arises in God a peremptory and irrevocable volition, fixed for eternity, to condemn. And one who throughout life was most flagitious, neither believing nor obeying the gospel, believes at his last gasp, and there arises in God a new peremptory volition to save for eternity. Who here does not see that the unhappy fortune of contingency drags behind it temporary and mutable volitions in God? Not to mention the notable injury to God's justice: a single act of faith or unbelief, perhaps even contrary to divine providence and will, arising, rewards with eternal destruction or with ineffable glory.

units.la: 9. 6. Ista defendit Corvinus quae habet Vorstius. Eventum duntaxat particularem a causa secunda contingente pendentem, aliquando mutari dico, cujus deinde respectu decretum Dei per partes seorsim sumptum, aliquatenus mutabile dici possit. Et quid apertius, quam quod ipse Arminius dicit? Potest quis sua incredulitate mereri ut Deus effectum, quo ille obtulit filium redemptorem. mutet in iram, qua illum punire vult. Nihil hic planius quam Dei decreta & effectus mutari, ad mutationem effectuum liberorum: atqui voluntatem humanam in horas mutari, nemo (ut opinor) inficiabitur. Neque Arminianos juvat, quod decreta Dei immutabiliter contemperentur hominum moribus, ideoque non est contraria voluntas, qua Deus Petrum credentem vult salvari, & eundem postea non credentem damnare; quia non est idem objectum, Petrus credens, Petrus non credens, ideoque eadem immutabilis voluntas potest utrumque velle, sed sic diluo. Nam 1. non est eadem voluntas, ubi prius est velle salutem, & postea novum non velle salutem. Nam si Judex terrenus statuit hunc absolvere innocentem, & eundem reum postea damnare, nemo non dicet voluntatem judicis physice mutari;esto[?] quód mutatio accederet ex damnati bonis aut malis moribus, non ex inconstantia judicis. Par enim est blasphemia, sive dicamus Dei decreta mutabilia esse ex interna inconstantia, sive ex objecto externo: non enim vel hoc, vel illo modo, potest esse Iehovah, qui non mutatur. Mat. 3. Sic homines nolentes & volentes Deum è nolente in volentem, & rursus è volente, in nolentem circumagant: non enim aqua è frigida in calidam, & rursus è calida in frigidam retro commeans, propterea definit esse mutabilis, quia hæ mutationes ei accidunt ab externis agentibus, puta aere, aut sole. 2. Arminius disertis verbis ait Deum commutare affectum benevolum in iram, Ergo postquam homines contumaciter rejecerunt Christum, definit esse in Deo decretum tales salvandi, aut voluntas etiam antecedens, & mutatur in decretum damnandi & in odium.
units.tr: 9. 6. Corvinus defends what Vorstius holds: "I say that a particular event, depending on a contingent secondary cause, is sometimes changed; and with respect to this, the decree of God, taken part by part separately, can in some measure be called changeable." And what could be plainer than what Arminius himself says? "Someone may by his unbelief deserve that God change the effect by which he offered his Son as Redeemer into wrath, by which he wills to punish him." Nothing here is plainer than that God's decrees and effects are changed in response to the change of free effects. Yet that the human will changes from hour to hour, no one (I think) will deny. Nor does it help the Arminians that God's decrees are immutably tempered to men's behaviour, so that there is no contrary will by which God wills Peter believing to be saved and afterwards wills him, not believing, to be damned. They say the object is not the same, Peter believing and Peter not believing, and so the same immutable will can will both. But I answer as follows. First, it is not the same will where there is first a will to save and afterwards a new not-willing of salvation. For if an earthly judge decides to acquit an innocent man and afterwards to condemn the same man as guilty, no one would fail to say that the judge's will is physically changed, even though the change came from the condemned man's good or bad conduct and not from the judge's inconstancy. For it is equally blasphemy whether we say God's decrees are changeable from internal inconstancy or from an external object; for in neither way can he be Iehovah, who is not changed. Mat. 3. Thus men, by being willing and unwilling, turn God from unwilling to willing and again from willing to unwilling. For water that passes back and forth from cold to warm and again from warm to cold does not on that account cease to be changeable, because these changes happen to it from external agents, such as air or sun. 2. Arminius expressly says that God changes his benevolent affection into wrath. Therefore, after men have obstinately rejected Christ, the decree of saving such men ceases to be in God, or even the antecedent will does, and it is changed into a decree of damning and into hatred.

units.la: At vero Remonstr, ut ictum hujus argumenti declinent, Iacobum magistrum suum derelinquunt. Ita enim illi in apolog. Mutabilitatis hic ne species quidem est, non enim mutat Deus intentionem salvandi (sed mutare docent Vorstius & Arminius) quia non habuit nisi intentionem hypotheticam. Si vid. homo ipse sponte sua rebellis aut ingratus esse, aut manere nolit, eadem illa hypothetica intentio manet: hypothesi autem non existente, manet constans Dei voluntas, & jam ante liberata intentio puniendi ingratum & rebellem. Speciosa quidem sed fallax evasio. 1. Si non intendit salvare, neque decernit salvare, nisi hypothetice, & sic Deus antecedenter non magis vult omnium salutem quam exitium omnium, an non fucatus erit amor eorum communis, quem in Deo erga omnes mortales fingunt? 2. Posito actu credendi unico, ponitur conditio ex parte, ergo eligit credentes pro tempore, rursus relabuntur in infidelitatem, & removetur conditio, tum rursus ponitur decretum contrarium damnandi: caecus est qui hic in Deo non videat, id poni in esse quod antea ei non inerat, & id non poni sed removeri, quod antea inerat, quod millies circa unum hominem accidere potest: at an non fit haec vera mutatio, lectoris esto judicium. 3. Hic indignissima de Deo efficiunt, nempe postquam Judas est in inferos detrusus, manet hypothetica Dei intentio salvandi ipsum; Estote igitur damnati & reprobi angeli bono animo. Arminiani vobis annunciant idem euangelium, quod vivis praedicatur, nempe, manet etiam adhuc erga vos in Deo constans & deliberata voluntas vos salvandi, siquidem credideritis, & jam in Domino defunctis & coronam gloriae assecutis, est idem evangelium praedicandum, nempe ipsos manere aeternum exitium, siquidem ingrati & rebelles esse velint. Sed in nobis Arminiani conqueruntur, sed salsissime, de Dei amore salvandi ipsos, quos salvari propter obstaculum fatalis decreti impossibile est clamitant; at nos potiore jure, & merito ipfos incusamus, quod graventur Deum voluntate salvandi licet hypothetica ; ipsos damnatos, quos salvari est simpliciter impossibile.
units.tr: But the Remonstrants, to dodge the blow of this argument, abandon James, their master. For in their Apology they say: Here there is not even the appearance of change, for God does not change His intention to save (but Vorstius and Arminius teach that He changes), because He had only a hypothetical intention. If man himself, of his own accord, is rebellious or ungrateful, or refuses to remain, that same hypothetical intention remains; but if the hypothesis does not hold, the constant will of God remains, and the intention to punish the ungrateful and rebellious was already free from the start. A specious but false escape! First, if He does not intend to save, and does not decree to save, except hypothetically, and so God antecedently does not will the salvation of all any more than their destruction, will not the common love which they imagine in God toward all mortals be a pretence? Second, once the single act of believing is posited, the condition is posited on the human side; so He chooses believers for a time; then they fall back into unbelief, and the condition is removed, and then the contrary decree to damn is posited again. It is blind not to see here in God that something is posited which was not previously in Him, and something is removed which was previously in Him; this can happen a thousand times with one man. But whether this is a real change, let the reader judge. Third, here they make the most unworthy assertions about God: namely, after Judas has been thrust down into hell, God's hypothetical intention to save him remains. Be of good cheer, then, damned and reprobate angels! The Arminians announce to you the same gospel that is preached to the living: that God's constant and deliberate will to save you still remains, provided you believe; and for those who have already died in the Lord and obtained the crown of glory, the same gospel must be preached, namely, that they remain in eternal destruction, provided they wish to be ungrateful and rebellious. But the Arminians complain against us, and most unjustly, about God's love for saving those whom they cry out it is impossible to save because of the obstacle of a fated decree. Yet we, with the stronger right and deservedly, accuse them of charging God with a will to save, even if merely hypothetical, toward those whom it is simply impossible to save, namely the damned.

units.la: 4. Si non mutat Deus intentionem salvandi damnatos, ira & odium Dei non potest succedere in locum affectus benevoli, utitait Arminius; unde non est in Deo odium erga rebelles, nisi simul in Deo, sateantur consistere posse, patris, matris, amantissimae Gallinae, clementissimi, adiram tardissimi, benevolum affectum ex vero salvandi desidemio, propensoque amore, una cum odio, & vero justoque aeternae perditionis desiderio, erga unum & eundem hominem, id quod ipsi non admittent. 5. Volunt manere hypotheticam intentionem damnatos salvandi, ne nova in Deo volitio inciperet, aliaque desinaret; sed frustra: velenim Deus odio habet Petrum negantem Dominum, & rursus respiscentem ad vitam aeternam diligit, unde necessario volitiones & nolitiones in Deo incipiunt & desinunt: vel manet Dei voluntas suspensa erga omnes, qui in hac vita justitiam & pietatem colunt, & impietati, & nefariis artibus se dediderunt, quod prorsus absurdum est: ait enim scriptura contrarium.
units.tr: Fourth, if God does not change His intention to save the damned, then wrath and hatred of God cannot take the place of a benevolent affection, as Arminius says. Hence there is no hatred in God toward rebels unless they will admit that the same God can have, toward one and the same man, the benevolent affection of a father, a mother, or a most loving hen, most merciful yet slow to anger, together with a true desire to save and a inclination of love, along with hatred and a true and just desire for eternal perdition. This they will not admit. Fifth, they want the hypothetical intention to save the damned to remain, lest a new volition arise in God and another cease; but in vain. For either God hates Peter denying his Lord and again loves him to eternal life when he repents, and so volitions and nolitions necessarily begin and cease in God; or the will of God remains suspended toward all who in this life cultivate justice and piety and those who have given themselves to impiety and wicked arts. This is utterly absurd, for Scripture says the contrary.

units.la: · 10. 7. Dogma ipsorum palmarium est, Deum omnes vocare eo animo & intentione ut obediant & salventur: Atqui inter vocatos multi sunt ab aeterno peremptorie & irrevocabiliter ex praescientia finalis impoenitentiae Deo exosi & rejecti, atqui intenrio seria & naturalis salvandi e Diametro pugnat cum peremptoriâ in tentione damnandi, responso se egregiè defunctosputant, qua rdo nobis dicunt, Deum antecedenti voluntate velle iis vitam, quibus consequenti voluntate velit mortem æternam ; sed nihil ad rem: dicimus enim absurdum esse in magistratu terreno, si post latam irrevocabilem sententiam de morte prodito ris flagitiosissimi, eunde ad vitam ulla voluntate invitaret, ipse præmiorum proposita, eo consilio atque animo, ut nullus non honoribus aulicis, & omnibus voluptatibus genialiter indulgeret, atqui talis nobis fingitur Deus Arminianus.
units.tr: 10. 7. Their chief dogma is that God calls all men with the intention and purpose that they obey and be saved. But among those called are many who, from eternity, by foreknowledge of final impenitence, are peremptorily and irrevocably hateful to God and rejected. And a serious and natural intention to save stands in direct opposition to a peremptory intention to damn. They think they have answered this well when they tell us that God by His antecedent will wills life for those to whom by His consequent will He wills eternal death. But this is nothing to the point. For we say that it would be absurd in an earthly magistrate, after pronouncing an irrevocable sentence of death on a most notorious traitor, to invite that same man to life by any will, setting before him rewards, with the purpose and intention that every one of them should freely indulge in court honours and all pleasures. Yet such is the God that the Arminians imagine for us.

units.la: 12. Arminianos nihil hic juvare potest, nisi ad illud Vasquesij confugerint, quamvis voluntas Dei libera circa res producendas, nihil addat supra essentiam, praeter respectu rationis, & cum hoc respectu voluntas dicatur libera producendi creaturas, ac proinde si ab æterno Deus non decrevisset creaturas producere, nihil ei deesset nisi respectus rationis, nihilominus in tempore mutari non potest voluntas, nec ille respectus rationis; sed si talis respectus in Deo esse debet, ab æterno esse debet, sicut de scientia dicebamus, non quia mutatio aliqua sequeretur in Deo intrinseca, aut etiam scientiæ ipsius, si respectus in tempore mutari posset, sed quia res futuræ ab æterno suturæ sunt, nec in tempore quidquam potest incipere esse futurum, sequitur respectum ad res producendas non posse in tempore incipere. Unde inferunt quidam Armin. sicut actus creandi, qui non fuit ab æterno, sed in tempore incipit esse in Deo, non ponit in Deo mutationem aliquam: sic neque nova volitio in Deo incipiens in tempore ponit in Deo aliquam mutationem. Sed, respondeo 1.non est par ratio creationis & volitionis:creatio enim est mera denominatio externa,qua res ad extra esse incipiunt per æternam Dei sapientiam, voluntatem & omnipotentiam; volitio vero non est mera denominatio extrinseca, sed & actus vitalis, qui non poteft de novo incipere absque mutatione Dei. Creatio est Dei actio transiens, ideoque non potest non esse æterna, quoniam ens creatum est, ad quod terminatur Dei actio: volitio vero est actus immanens, ideoque non potest non, esse æterna, est enim eadem cum effentia Dei & cum ipsa identificata. At qui putet essentiam Dei esse mutabilem aut non æternam, is putet Deum, non esse Deum, ita etiam Suarez. vide Metaph. Modus ille amandi quo Deus ab æterno mundum condere decernebat, (ut ait Pet. Fonseca in Metaph.) terminandus erat ad mundum pro eo tempore, quo illum condidit; idcirco causalitas effectiva qua illum produxit, erat in fe æterna, quia erat idem reipfa cum æterno Dei decreto, adeoque cum divina effentia identificata: at vero causalitas erat terminative & virtute temporalis. 2. Vasquez sic iis adversatur. Si respectus ille (inquit) ad res volitas in Deo esse debet, ab æterno esse deberet, ac proinde in tempore non potest incipere talis respectus. Creatio vero, quamvis a vitali actu Dei fluat, non est formaliter vitalis actus, sed relativa actio terminata in tempore ad res creatas. 3. Res futurae non possunt non ab aeterno futurae esse, & si Deus in tempore aliquid futurum esse vult, quod ab aeterno non voluit, incipit in Deo nova actio vitalis, quod 'est abfurdum.
units.tr: 12. The Arminians cannot be helped here, unless they take refuge in that saying of Vasquez: although the free will of God regarding things to be produced adds nothing above the essence except a respect of reason; and with this respect the will is called free to produce creatures; and therefore, if God had not from eternity decreed to produce creatures, nothing would be lacking to Him except a respect of reason; nevertheless the will cannot change in time, nor can that respect of reason. But if such a respect must be in God, it must be from eternity, as we said about knowledge; not because any change would follow in God intrinsically, or even in His knowledge, if the respect could change in time, but because future things will be from eternity, and nothing can begin to be future in time; it follows that the respect to things to be produced cannot begin in time. From this some of the Arminians infer that, just as the act of creating, which was not from eternity but begins in time to be in God, does not imply any change in God, so neither does a new volition beginning in God in time imply any change in God. But I answer, first, that the reasoning about creation and volition is not the same. For creation is a mere external denomination, by which things begin to exist outside God through His eternal wisdom, will, and omnipotence; but volition is not a mere extrinsic denomination, but also a vital act, which cannot begin anew without a change in God. Creation is a transient action of God, and therefore cannot fail to be eternal, since the created being, to which God's action is terminated, is eternal; but volition is an immanent act, and therefore cannot fail to be eternal, for it is the same as the essence of God and identified with it. Whoever thinks the essence of God is changeable or not eternal thinks that God is not God. So also Suarez; see Metaph. That mode of loving by which God from eternity decreed to found the world (as Pet. Fonseca in Metaph. says) was to be terminated at the world for the time in which He founded it; therefore the effective causality by which He produced it was in itself eternal, because it was really the same as the eternal decree of God, and so identified with the divine essence; but the causality was terminative and by virtue temporal. Second, Vasquez opposes them thus: if that respect (he says) to things willed must be in God, it would have to be from eternity, and therefore such a respect cannot begin in time. But creation, although it flows from a vital act of God, is not formally a vital act, but a relative action terminated in time at created things. Third, future things cannot but be future from eternity; and if God wills something to be future in time which He did not will from eternity, a new vital act begins in God, which is absurd.

units.la: 13. Doctrina etiam Thom. Jacksoni Angli, theologastri, si quis alius, superficiarii, decreta Dei & temporaria & mutabilia astruit, ait enim, somnium esse cogitare de divino decreto & praedeterminatione rerum futurarum tanquam de actibus [?] jam irrevocabiliter finitis & completis, & consequente errore, tam impossibile esse ullam rem posse aliter esse, quam est, fore, aut fuisse, quam id quod est praeteritum, revocare. Antiquum hunc errorem forte vidit apud Molinam, aut ex Suarez extorsit. Sed 1. videat lectot lepidam distinctionem inter decretum finitum, & completum irrevocabiliter, & decretum finitum revocabiliter, Scriptura ait decretum Jehovae ps. 33. non rescindi, Jacksonus rescindi & revocari vult. 2. Vel loquitur de decreto absoluto, quod omnibus sani finciptis, est irrevocabile; vel de conditionato, quod sive conditio impleatur, sive non, semper est irrevocabile; quoniam includit praescientiam conditionis in objecto. 3. Doceat, an sint in Deo decreta irrevocabilia, & quaenam illa sint? Nam loquitur hic de decretis in genere, sed an decretum electionis Ephesiorum quod fuit ante mundi constitutionem Eph. 1. & eorum quibus data est gratia ante tempora saecu-la-
units.tr: 13. The teaching also of Thomas Jackson, an English theologaster, or of anyone else of the same superficial stamp, asserts that God's decrees are both temporary and mutable. For he says it is a dream to think of the divine decree and predetermination of future things as acts already irrevocably finished and completed. From this follows the error that it is as impossible for anything to be otherwise than it is, or will be, or was, as it is impossible to recall what is past. Perhaps he saw this ancient error in Molina, or wrung it out of Suarez. But: (1) let the reader note the witty distinction between a decree that is finished and completed irrevocably and a decree that is finished but revocable. Scripture says that the decree of Jehovah is not rescinded (Ps. 33), but Jackson wants it rescinded and revoked. (2) Either he speaks of an absolute decree, which every sane person knows is irrevocable, or of a conditional decree, which is always irrevocable whether the condition is fulfilled or not, since it includes foreknowledge of the condition in its object. (3) Let him teach whether there are irrevocable decrees in God, and what they are. For he speaks here of decrees in general. But what of the decree of election of the Ephesians, which was made before the foundation of the world (Eph. 1), and of those to whom grace was given before the times of the ages (2 Tim. 1. 9)

units.la: [?] Printed letter in the marginal reference of the Suarez note is uncertain. laria 2. Tim. 1. 9. Iacobi & Esavi, quorum hic rejectus, ille dilectus est, antequam fecissent aliquid boni vel mali, nondum habuit finem ante mundi constitutione? Estne hoc spiritui sancto obloqui? 4. Si decreta non finiatur, donec res decretae actu executioni mandentur, Deus multa facit in tempore, quae ab aeterno facere non decrevit, & sic erit insipiens agens; vir prudens in arena non capit consilium. §. Decretum de creatione mundi, refuscitatione Christi, jam olim est finitum, alioqui hodierno die Deus decernit mundi creationem, & sic potest mundus non esse creatus, quod est impossibile; dicet decreta finiri, quando res decretae actu existunt: sed tum decretum est temporale, non aeternum, & actu transiens, non immanens, & Deus nulla alia de causa non facit decreta priusquam res decretae actu existent, quam quia ignorat futura contingentia, quod est blasphemum, aut quia decretum finitum irrevocabiliter laederet libertatem Dei: atqui sic Deus nunquam vult actum liberum credendi in Petro, donec actu credat, at sic casu & novo plane & temporario consilio efficit finem, & concurrit cum omnibus casibus contingentibus. 6. Per decreta Dei, omnia futura habent futuritionem completam ab aeterno, alioqui det nobis aliam causam futuritionis. Ergo decretum Dei fuit ab aeterno, sicut rerum futuritio fuit ab aeterno ac proinde decretum erat actu causa rerum omnium sub esse futuro, longe antequam res ipsæ existerent. 7. Deus in scripturis à decreto, rem futuram esse invictè probat Ier. 1. 5. Ef. 14. 24. Atqui si decreta non sunt irrevocabiliter completa ante rerum decretarum actualem existentiam, nulla est Dei consequentia. Deus decrevit Assyriorum vastationem, E. vastabuntur. Posset enim illud decretum utpote nondum finitum rescindi, & sic Assyrij non vastabuntur. 8. Iackson. postea ait vel possibilia omnia à Deo decerni, Ergo multa decreta Dei nunquam erunt completa, multa enim possibilia nunquam actu existent, ut Ægyptiorum transitus salvus per mare rubrum, liberatio Christi per 12. legiones angelorum &c. At absurdum est à Deo decerni multa, & ipsius decreta nunquam compleri, quando nulla sunt obstacula, quæ completionem ipsorum impedire possent. 9. Non sequitur omnia ita evenire, ut tam impossibile fit aliter res fore, quam est præteritum revocare. Nam omnia contingentia futura, poterant nunquam esse futura: at præteritum revocare involvit contradictionem, & est absolute impossibile. 10. Sequitur etiam sapientissimum Dei decretum euangelicum de salvandis hominibus per Christum, nondum est finitum neque finiendum ante dissolutionem mundi, & sic multa in euangelio mutari posse, Deumque illic falsa dixisse. Nec est quod dicat euangelium esse decretum de rebus ab ipso Deo faciendis, ideoque jam finitum esse, licet decretum de rebus faciendis à causis contingentibus, non fit completum, donec causæ contingentes effectus suos produxerint. Nam euaneuangeliū est decretū etiam de multis effectibus contingentibus, ut de Antichristi futuritione, de Iudæorum conversione, de ortu pseudochristorum in extremis diebus; nec video causam, cur Iacksonus non posset dicere, non obstante decreto Dei & prædictione Paulina Rom. 11. fieri posse ut Judæi nunquam convertantur.
units.tr: [?] The printed letter in the marginal reference to the Suarez note is uncertain. laria. 2 Tim. 1. 9. Of Jacob and Esau, of whom the one was rejected and the other loved, before they had done anything good or evil: did this decree not yet have its end before the foundation of the world? Is this not to speak against the Holy Spirit? (4) If decrees are not finished until the things decreed are actually carried out, then God does many things in time which he did not decree from eternity, and so he will be an unwise agent; a prudent man in the arena does not take counsel. §. The decree concerning the creation of the world, and the resurrection of Christ, was finished long ago; otherwise God today decrees the creation of the world, and so the world could not have been created, which is impossible. He will say that decrees are finished when the things decreed actually exist. But then the decree is temporal, not eternal, and transient in its act, not immanent. God makes no decrees before the things decreed actually exist for no other reason than that he is ignorant of future contingent events, which is blasphemous, or that a decree finished irrevocably would harm God's freedom. Yet in this way God never wills the free act of believing in Peter until he actually believes, and so by a chance and entirely new and temporal counsel he brings about the end, and concurs with all contingent events. (5) Through God's decrees, all future things have complete futurity from eternity; otherwise give us some other cause of futurity. Therefore the decree of God was from eternity, just as the futurity of things was from eternity, and so the decree was actually the cause of all things under future being long before the things themselves existed. (6) In Scripture God proves invincibly from a decree that a thing will be future (Jer. 1. 5; Isa. 14. 24). But if decrees are not irrevocably complete before the actual existence of the decreed things, then God's inference is no inference at all. God decreed the devastation of the Assyrians; therefore they will be devastated. For that decree, being not yet finished, could be rescinded, and so the Assyrians would not be devastated. (7) Jackson then says either that all possible things are decreed by God. Therefore many decrees of God will never be completed, for many possible things will never actually exist: for example, the safe passage of the Egyptians through the Red Sea, the deliverance of Christ by twelve legions of angels, and so on. But it is absurd that God should decree many things whose decrees are never fulfilled, when there are no obstacles that could prevent their completion. (8) It does not follow that all things come to pass in such a way that it is as impossible for a thing to be otherwise as it is to recall what is past. For all contingent future things could have never been future; but to recall the past involves a contradiction and is absolutely impossible. (9) It also follows that God's most wise decree in the gospel concerning the saving of men through Christ is not yet finished, nor will it be finished before the dissolution of the world, and so many things in the gospel could be changed, and God would have said false things there. Nor is there any reason for him to say that the gospel is a decree about things to be done by God himself, and therefore already finished; for a decree about things to be done by contingent causes is not complete until those contingent causes have produced their effects. The gospel is also a decree concerning many contingent effects, such as the coming of Antichrist, the conversion of the Jews, and the rise of false Christs in the last days. Nor do I see why Jackson could not say, notwithstanding God's decree and Paul's prophecy (Rom. 11), that it may come about that the Jews are never converted.

units.la: 14. Addit Iackson. 16. Deum nunc non incipere primò omnia decernere, sed eum nunc decernere, & tutius esse unicuique respicere Dei decretum, prout coexistit universo vitæ cursui, quam prout ab æterno factum est. 1. Hoc si verum est, doctrinam non tutam nobis Paulus tradidit, qui vult Ephesios respicere electionem, prout facta est ante mundi constitutionem, item minus tuto docuit gratiam nobis datam ante tempora secularia 2. Tim. 2 9. Quid? an non ipse Deus probat Ieremiae prophetandum esse? Arg. à Dei decreto. Jer. 1.5. Priusquam e ventre exieris, prophetam gentibus te constitui: an non novator iste diceret, nulla necessitas tamen erat prophetandi, quia dum Ieremias recusaret prophetare, decretum illud erat in fieri, & non obstante decreto facto priusquam Ieremias nasceretur, potuit non prophetare, neque tutum fuit prophetæ tale argumentum Dei considerare. 2. Hic etiam omnia decreta ortui & interitui, fixioni refixioni, prout libertas creaturæ vult, exponit. 3. Si non est tutum respicere decretum, prout ab æterno factum est, E. vel illa respectio est inanis & falsa, vel decretum Dei est ab æterno, ideoque irrevocabiliter completum in suo esse, infinitis seculis imaginariis, priusquam res decretæ existant.
units.tr: 14. Jackson adds (16) that God does not now begin to decree all things for the first time, but that he now decrees, and that it is safer for each person to regard God's decree as it coexists with the whole course of life than as it was made from eternity. (1) If this is true, then Paul has handed down a doctrine that is not safe for us, since he wants the Ephesians to regard election as it was made before the foundation of the world. Likewise he taught less safely about the grace given to us before the secular times (2 Tim. 2 9). What then? Does God himself not prove that Jeremiah must prophesy, from the argument of God's decree? Jer. 1. 5: Before you came out of the womb I appointed you a prophet to the nations. Would this innovator not say that there was nevertheless no necessity to prophesy, because while Jeremiah refused to prophesy that decree was still in the making, and that, notwithstanding the decree made before Jeremiah was born, he could have not prophesied? Nor was it safe for a prophet to consider such an argument of God. (2) Here too he explains all decrees in terms of birth and death, fixing and refixing, as the freedom of the creature wills. (3) If it is not safe to regard a decree as it was made from eternity, then either that regard is empty and false, or God's decree is from eternity and therefore irrevocably complete in its being, for infinite imaginary ages before the decreed things exist.

units.la: 4. Ecquid vero periculi est respicere æternitatem decreti; quia (inquit) sic inspiciemus decreta Dei quasi actus irrevocabiliter more statutorum Medorum & Persarum, præteritos; si ita respicere decreta est erroneum, decreta sunt revocabilia & mutabilia, & sic Iehovah mutatur; & sic credere Deum ab æterno præscivisse cogitationes liberas & actus liberos, est periculosum: nam Deo præscienti, non minus quam Deo decernenti, actus liberi sunt irrevocabiles, & sic æternam Dei præscientiam negabit. 5. Agnoscit statuta Medorum esse immutabilia, Dei vero mutabilia. 6. Hodie Deus decernit mundi creationem, filii sui incarnationem, Chaldæorum excisionem &c. quis non diceret Philosophastro huic læsum esse cerebrum, & febricitantem ista in chartam conjecisse. Alteram paginam facit doctrina Arminiana de iustificatione, quæ est Episcopio, actus continuus qui est & durat, quam diu durat ipsius conditionis requisitæ præsentia; interrumpitur vero semper & toties, quoties actus præstantur ejusmodi, qui cum vera fide & conscientia boni consistere nequeunt, & ipse Arminius iustificationem ante exitum vitæ compleri negat, & Deum commutare affectum in Chisto benevolum, quem ergo vere iustificatum habuit, in iram & odium, quod est Deum mutare vo-luntatem suam, pro humani arbitrii libitu, ita ut Deus hodie peccata imputet, cras non imputet, & rursus imputet: id vero ego Ar-minio ipsi , 2. scripturae, 3. & rationi adver-fari existimo, Arminio qui ait. 1. voluntatem Dei esse ipsam essentiam Dei. 2. infinitam. 3. aeternam & immutabilem, quia nihil potest ei de novo aut esse aut videri bonum. At si voluntas Dei movetur à causa externa, nempe Christi satis factione, fide & resipiscientia hominis, ut velit homini nunc credenti peccata non imputare, & postea non credenti imputare, hic ex Arminio mutabilis erit Dei voluntas, adeoque ipsa Dei essentia mutabilis est. 2. Scripturae adversatur, quae Iehovam statuit immutabilem Mal. 3. & Dei electionem esse tum aeternam Ier. 3.3. Esai. 54.7. Psal. Deus tu noster à sæculo usque in sæculum, ejusque dilectionem, etiam actus nostros, & peccata antecedere. Ioh. 3.16. Ita Deus dilexit mundum Ezech. 16, 8. Tempus tuum, tempus amorum, eo autem tempore populus in peccatis tantum non expirabant. 3. Cum, ratione pugnat, si Deus in tempore homini peccata non imputat, & rursus etiam imputet, & justificet & damnet, cum hi actus imputandi & non imputandi sint actus in Deo immanentes, adeoque aeterni, sequetur Deum, eundem hominem ab aeterno ad vitam aeternam dilexisse, & ad externum exitium odio habuisse. 2. Sint Saulo, Iudæ, aliisque ad tempus justificatis peccapeccata permulta remissa, ideoque sanguine Christi deleta & expiata, recidunt in peccata gravissima, ita ut Deus non possit non velle iis æternam damnationem, illa priora peccata semel remissa, vel de novo imputantur vel non. Si imputantur, quaerimus, quo jure id fiat, neque enim vel apostatis Deus facit injuriam, num peccata semel deleta & in Christi sanguine expiata, apostatis etiam in ghenna luenda erunt? Atqui sic duplex satisfactio pro iisdem peccatis præstabitur. Si non imputantur, quaerimus, qua scriptura quaedam unius & ejusdem hominis peccata expientur in Christo, quaedam non, cur Christus pœnam lueret pro quibusdam Iudæ peccatis, pro quibusdam non? Quæ ratio discriminis, an quia præscivit fidem temporalem Iudæ quaedam peccata subsequutura, quaedam vero infidelitatem. Ideoque hæc noluit expiare, illa vero expiavit; nugæ & conjecturæ Siculæ: ' Atqui iplorum est commentum Christum in cruce morientem nullius hominis vel fidei vel infidelitatis rationem habuisse, sed peracta morte Christi, potuisse vel omnes ad fidem convertere & salvare, vel nullos, adeoque omnes damnare. At si dixerint peccata Iudæ fidem ipsius temporariam antecedentia, fuisse in Christo expiata conditionaliter, non absolute, nempe siquidem Iudas in fide perseveraverit, remissa tum nulla omnino peccata sunt in hac vita, nemo hic justificatus contra luculentas scripturas in contrarium Rom. 4. 1Q[?]. Rom. 5°.
units.tr: 4. Yet what danger is there in regarding the eternity of the decree? Because, he says, in this way we would look upon God's decrees as acts irrevocably past, like the laws of the Medes and Persians. If it is erroneous so to regard decrees, then decrees are revocable and mutable, and so Jehovah is changed. And so to believe that God foreknew from eternity free thoughts and free acts is dangerous, for to God foreknowing, no less than to God decreeing, free acts are irrevocable, and so he will deny God's eternal foreknowledge. (5) He acknowledges that the statutes of the Medes are immutable, but God's are mutable. (6) Today God decrees the creation of the world, the incarnation of his Son, the overthrow of the Chaldeans, and so on. Who would not say that this philosophaster's brain is injured, and that he wrote these things on paper in a fever? The Arminian doctrine of justification makes the other page. It is Episcopius': a continuous act which is and lasts as long as the presence of the required condition lasts; it is interrupted always and as often as acts are performed of such a kind that they cannot consist with true faith and a good conscience. And Arminius himself denies that justification is completed before the end of life, and says that God changes his affection, which was kindly toward him in Christ, into wrath and hatred. This is for God to change his will at the pleasure of human choice, so that God imputes sins today, does not impute them tomorrow, and imputes them again. I think this is opposed to Arminius himself, to Scripture, and to reason, since Arminius says: (1) the will of God is the very essence of God; (2) infinite; (3) eternal and immutable, because nothing can newly be or seem good to him. But if the will of God is moved by an external cause, namely the satisfaction of Christ, and the faith and repentance of man, so that he now wills not to impute sins to the man who now believes, and afterwards wills to impute them to the man who does not believe, then by Arminius's own account the will of God is mutable, and so the very essence of God is mutable. (2) It is opposed to Scripture, which declares Jehovah immutable (Mal. 3), and God's election to be eternal (Jer. 3. 3; Isa. 54. 7; Ps.: "God, you are our God from age to age"), and his love to precede even our acts and sins (John 3. 16: "So God loved the world"; Ezek. 16. 8: "Your time was the time of love," yet at that time the people were not expiring in their sins). (3) It fights against reason. If in time God does not impute sins to a man, and then again imputes them, and justifies and condemns, since these acts of imputing and not imputing are acts immanent in God, and therefore eternal, it would follow that God loved the same man from eternity unto eternal life, and hated him unto outward destruction. (4) Let Saul, Judas, and others who were justified for a time have many sins remitted, and therefore blotted out and atoned for in the blood of Christ; let them fall back into most grievous sins, so that God cannot but will them eternal damnation. Are those earlier sins, once remitted, now imputed anew or not? If they are imputed, we ask by what right this is done; for God does no injustice even to apostates. Will sins once blotted out and expiated in the blood of Christ also have to be paid for by apostates in hell? Yet in that case a double satisfaction would be made for the same sins. If they are not imputed, we ask by what Scripture some sins of one and the same man are expiated in Christ and others not. Why would Christ pay the penalty for some of Judas's sins and not for others? What is the reason for the distinction? Is it that he foresaw that Judas's temporary faith would be followed by some sins, and unbelief by others, and so chose not to expiate the one but did expiate the other? These are trifles and Sicilian conjectures! Yet it is their own invention that Christ, dying on the cross, took account of no man's faith or unbelief, and that once his death was accomplished he could either convert all to faith and save them, or none, and so condemn all. But if they say that the sins of Judas that preceded his temporary faith were expiated in Christ conditionally, not absolutely (namely, if Judas persevered in faith), then no sins at all are remitted in this life, and no one is justified here, contrary to the plain Scriptures to the contrary (Rom. 4. 1Q[?]; Rom. 5°.

units.la: 1. Rom.8; 30. Eph. 1. 7. 1. Cor. 6. 11. quin Abrahamus justificatus erat, quando Ifacum obtulit Iac 2. 21. verf. 25. tum etiam satisfactio Christi pro peccatis conditionalis fingi non potest, nisi mortuus esset pro quibusdam conditionaliter, atqui mortuus est absolute pro omnibus, pro quibus obiit mortem: tum dubium ineluctabile est Arminianis, An non Christus Judæ etiam finalem apostasiam luoll anguine expiarit? Si non expiavit, tum iea apostasia vel erat peccatum simpliciter itr misibile, & dato quod Deus Judæ, vita prorogata, indulsisset resipiscentiam & fidem, consequutus tum fuisset Judas veniam illius apostasiæ, absque sanguinis effusione, quod scriptura aperte negat Heb. 9. 22. vel ut illud peccatum foret remissibile, ex ordine justitiæ, Christum denuo mori oportebat, quæ monstra sunt theologica. 3. Qualem remissionem Christus impetravit, talem primo credentibus communicat: atqui impetravit peccatorum omnium remissionem. Nactus æternam redemptionem. Heb. 9. 12. Delevit chirographum mandatorum quod erat contra nos. Col. 2. 13. Pacem fecit in cruce. Col. 1. 20. Ideoque omnia peccata, &c omne inter Deum & nos dissidium amovit. Ergo talem remissionem nobis communicat. Ratio majoris est, quia non plures remissiones aut syngraphas præstitit nobis: ratio enim reddi non potest ab adversariis, cur satisfaceret pro quibusdam peccatis Judæ, & pro quibusdam non, illa enim pro quibus non satisfecit, essent simpliciter irremissibilia, quod est absurdum, neque est ulla ratio cur remissionem impetratam nobis per partes communicaret, nisi eundem ab aeterno dilexerit, & odio etiam habuerit, quae sunt ἃ σύσατα[?].
units.tr: 1. Rom. 8:30; Eph. 1:7; 1 Cor. 6:11. Indeed Abraham was already justified when he offered Isaac (Jas 2:21; ver. 25). Nor can Christ's satisfaction for sins be conditional, unless he died for some people only on condition. But he died absolutely for all those for whom he underwent death. Then the Arminians face an inescapable question: did Christ not also atone with his blood for Judas's final apostasy? If he did not atone for it, then that apostasy was either a sin that could never be pardoned, or, granting that God, by prolonging Judas's life, had granted him repentance and faith, Judas would then have obtained forgiveness of that apostasy without any shedding of blood. Scripture plainly denies this (Heb. 9:22). Or, if that sin were to be remissible by the order of justice, Christ would have had to die again. These are theological monstrosities. 3. The forgiveness that Christ obtained is the forgiveness that he first communicates to believers. But he obtained the forgiveness of all sins: having obtained eternal redemption (Heb. 9:12); he blotted out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us (Col. 2:13); he made peace by the cross (Col. 1:20). Therefore he removed all sins and every division between God and us. Therefore he communicates such forgiveness to us. The reason for the major premise is that he did not grant us several forgivenesses or several acquittances. For the adversaries cannot give a reason why he would have satisfied for some of Judas's sins and not for others. Those for which he did not satisfy would be simply unforgivable, which is absurd. Nor is there any reason why he would communicate to us piece by piece a forgiveness he had obtained, unless he had loved the same people from eternity, and had also hated others. These are [?] matters.

units.la: 15. Arminianus nihil prius est in votis, quam remissionem peccatorum non fieri priusquam quis actu credit in Christum, Nam Remonstrant. in Apolo. dicunt nihil esse salsius, quam homines donari remissione peccatorum priusquam credunt; in quo lenocinantur suo Socino qui ait non posse peccata per actum credendi remitti, si jam sint remissa, antequam credamus, & suo Bellarmino, qui haec habet: quomodo enim vera fides est, qua credo mihi remissa esse peccata, si dum ita credo, nondum sint remissa, sed sint per actum fidei remittenda. Quippe omne obiectum est prius actu suo. istis acclamant Remonst. Hic vero tres actus velim distingui. 1. actum satisfaciendi pro peccatis & nos Deo reconciliandi a Christo praestitum.
units.tr: 15. The Arminian has nothing more at heart than that the remission of sins does not take place before a person actually believes in Christ. For the Remonstrants in their Apology say that nothing is more insipid than the claim that men are granted remission of sins before they believe. In this they flatter their Socinus, who says that sins cannot be remitted by the act of believing if they were already remitted before we believe, and their Bellarmino, who has this: for how is it true faith by which I believe that my sins are remitted, if while I so believe they are not yet remitted, but are to be remitted by the act of faith? Indeed every object is prior to its act. The Remonst. shout these things along with them. Here, however, I would wish three acts to be distinguished. 1. The act of satisfying for sins and reconciling us to God, performed by Christ.

units.la: 2. Dei Patris accipiendi actum quo agnoscit sibi cumulatissime satisfactum esse pro omnibus omnium electorum peccatis. 3. Actum justificandi, cui subordinatur fides tanquam causa organica.
units.tr: 2. The act of God the Father in accepting, by which he acknowledges that full satisfaction has been made to him for all the sins of all the elect. 3. The act of justifying, to which faith is subordinated as an organic cause.

units.la: 16. Actus reconciliandi nihil novi in Deo ponit, neque meritum Christi vel divinam voluntatem movet, vel Deum ex nolente in volentem, ex odio nos habentem, in diligentem (ut fabulatur Grevinchov.) transmutare potest. [?]1. quia Deus est immutabilis. 2. quia divisæ voluntatis causa non magis dari potest, quam ipsius Dei, uti cum Aquinate testantur universa multitudo Scholasticorum, ut Durand, Bonavent. Alensf. Ægidius, Alvar. Estius, Valent. Molina, Suarez, Vasquez, &c. prius natura nos Deus diligit, & æternæ gloriæ nos destinat, quam Christum in mediatorem nobis dare decrevit: hinc vere nos diligit nondum credentes, adeo ut reconciliatorem Christum dare velit nobis adhuc Dei inimicis, nos diligat nondum credentes Ioh. c. 3. verf. 6. Cum inimici essemus, reconciliati sumus &c. Ezech. 16. 6. Dixi tibi in sanguine tuo, vive. Ephes. 2. 4. Deus dives misericordiæ, pro immensa suo in nos amore, etiam mortuos in peccatis una cum Christo vivificavit nos. Arminii hæc eluunt, cum aliquid obganniant de universali communi Dei amore, quasi vero amor ille de quo Ezech. 16. non separaret Hierosolymitanos ab Amorrhæis & Moabitis, & amor ille qui vocatur Ephes. 2. [illegible, ~10 letters] ἀγάπῃ[?] fit communis amor, quo soli pluviis & pane reprobos beare non destitit Deus. Imo nihil salsius dogmate isto Arminiano, neminem diligi in Christo nisi actu existentem in eo per fidem: nam per & propter Christum datur spiritus sanctus, per cujus gratiam credimus Ioh. 7. 36. Ioh. 15. 16. Ergo Deus diligit nos in Christo priusquam credamus. Imo eadem & unica & immutabilis est illa Dei dilectio, & amor quo nos complectitur Deus tum ante, tum post mortem Christi. Et quoniam Dei dilectio ad vitam, nec est actus in Deo naturalis (sic enim non posset non velle nobis æternam vitam, & quæ tum foret gratia, si non libere daretur?) nec actus misericordiæ nec justitiæ formaliter, sed actus supremi Domini: non necesse fuit ut Deus quæreret satisfactionem justitiæ, antequam posset juste nos amare ad vitam æternam, neque necesse fuit ut satisfactio justitiæ compleret hunc actum dilectionis, quasi antea esset incompletus; quoniam satisfactio justitiæ in se fuit Deo libera, & necessaria tantum ex hypothesi, potuit enim Deus absolute, alio modo quam per satisfactionem filii sui ad vitam æternam nos perducere.
units.tr: 16. The act of reconciling puts nothing new in God. It does not move the merit of Christ or the divine will, nor can it change God from unwilling to willing, from hating us to loving us (as Grevinchovius fables). 1. Because God is immutable. 2. Because a cause of a divided will can no more be given than a cause of God himself. So the whole multitude of Schoolmen testify with Aquinas: Durand, Bonaventure, Alensis, Giles, Alvarez, Estius, Valentia, Molina, Suárez, Vásquez, and others. By nature God loves us before he decreed to give Christ to us as Mediator, and he destines us to eternal glory. Hence he truly loves us while we are not yet believing, so that he wishes to give Christ as reconciler to us while we are still God's enemies. He loves us while we are not yet believing (John 3:6). When we were enemies, we were reconciled, etc. (Ezek. 16:6): I said to you in your blood, Live. (Eph. 2:4): God, rich in mercy, because of his immense love toward us, made us alive together with Christ even when we were dead in sins. The Arminians wriggle out of these texts, while they growl a little about a universal, common love of God. As if that love of which Ezekiel 16 speaks did not separate the Jerusalemites from the Amorites and Moabites, and as if the love called in love [ἀγάπῃ] in Ephesians 2 [illegible, about ten letters] became a common love, by which God has not ceased to bless the reprobate with rain and bread alone. Indeed nothing is more insipid than this Arminian dogma that no one is loved in Christ unless he actually exists in him through faith.
