For the Holy Spirit is given through and on account of Christ, and through his grace we believe (John 7:36; John 15:16). Therefore God loves us in Christ before we believe. Indeed that love of God, and the love with which God embraces us, is the same, single and immutable both before and after the death of Christ. And since God's love toward life is not a natural act in God (for thus he could not but will eternal life for us, and what would grace then be, if it were not freely given?), and is formally neither an act of mercy nor of justice but an act of the supreme Lord, it was not necessary for God to seek satisfaction of justice before he could justly love us to eternal life. Nor was it necessary that satisfaction of justice should complete this act of love, as if it had been incomplete before. For satisfaction of justice was in itself free for God, and necessary only by hypothesis. God could absolutely bring us to eternal life by another way than through the satisfaction of his Son.

units.la: 17. Quæres igitur, quid reconciliatio ponit in Deo? Resp. non ponit aliquid in Deo, quod complet actum electionis, ut innuere videtur Anton. Walæus; neque aliquid novi ponit in Dei voluntate, quod in ea antea non inerat; sed tantum facit ut Deus nos liberrime ad æternam vitam diligens, possit[?] bonum in electione æterna nobis volitum rite & convenienter suæ justitiæ, prout libere decreverat, ideoque actu impertiri nobis vitam æternam.
units.tr: 17. You will ask, then, what reconciliation posits in God? Answer: it posits nothing in God which completes the act of election, as Anton. Walaeus seems to hint. Nor does it posit anything new in the divine will which was not in it before. Rather, it only makes it so that God, loving us most freely to eternal life, may bestow the good willed to us in eternal election rightly and fittingly, consistent with his justice, as he had freely decreed, and therefore actually impart eternal life to us.

units.la: Hinc observa fraudem Arminii, qui ubique contendit actum volendi nobis vitam æque restrictū esse justitiæ divinæ, atque actualem darionem[?] vitæ, quod est aperte falsum. Nam actus volendi nobis vitam est actus supremi domini Dei, non actus justitiæ; dita-[?] actualis vero datio vitæ est justitiæ restricta non ordine justitiæ, quasi ipsa justitia formaliter diceret Deo hunc modum perducendi homines ad vitam æternam, quod sic probo. Si Deus qua justus & necessitate justitiæ perduceret peccatores ad vitam per satisfactionem Christi, tum non posset aliter ipsos ad vitam perducere, quam per satisfactionem. At hoc libertatem Dei & infinitam sapientiam angustis nimis cancellis circumscribit. Erg.Ratio Majoris est, quia quod Deus facit qua justus & ex justitia ut ex principio formali, id facit necessitate naturæ suæ, & non liberè, & si illud non faceret Deus injustus foret; atqui non fuisset injustus si omnes ad vitam immediate perduxisset, & gloriæ participes fecisset, quod fecit in unione personali naturæ humanæ cum divina. Hinc sequitur Dei iram erga electos peccantes non esse odium oppositum dilectioni, quo antea ipsos est prosecutus, sed tantum displicentiam & odium immotum in peccata, non in personas, & interdum paternam castigationem, hinc electos Deus semper diligit, reprobos semper odio habet. Notari itaque hic velim, quam ridiculè nostram sententiam de æterna electione Remonstrantes capiant, dum ita delirant. Intentio salvandi efficax, sive irrevocabilis & peremptoria voluntas, qua Deus nominatim Petrum & Paulum salvare vult, cum voluntate executiva, qua iis deinde reconciliari, aut qua mediatorem iis dare vult, per quem ipsis reconcilietur, conjungi non potest: velle efficaciter salutem peccatorum ut finem. & velle deinde reconciliationem & meritum, ut medium quo moveari ad volendum salutem peccatorum, sunt contradicit: sed cum umbris dimicatur: Docemus enim nos Deum velle efficaciter salutem electorum ut finem, & moveri merito Christi tanquam medio justitiæ suæ convenientissimo ut iisdem actu det vitam æternam, non tantum non esse contradicentia, sed secundum scripturas amice subordinata; at velle salutem electis ut finem, & moveri Dei voluntatem merito Christi, ut velit ipsis salutem, Arminiani somniant, nobis nunquam venit in mentem, imo blasphemum est Dei voluntatem ab ulla causa aut agente externo moveri. Quærunt ibid. quis fit effectus formalis meriti Christi? ubi enim (inquiunt) talis efficax voluntas salvandi, præsupponitur, dicere effectum meriti Christi esse actualem restitutionem peccatoris in gratiam Dei, est nugari, restituere enim aliquem in gratiam alicujus, nihil aliud est quam efficere ut aliu efficaciter quis alicui bene velit. at hæc efficax voluntas præcedit meritum Christi. Nullus itaque (inquiunt illi) nostra doctrina, stante, est formalis effectus meriti Christi. Ignorant hi boni viri reformatæ ecclesiæ doctrinam qui ita hariolantur: nam meritum Christi non mutat Dei voluntatem erga electos ex odio in amorem, mutabilem Deum non colunt reformatæ ecclesiæ: effectus formalis meriti Christi est, quod Deus posset non obstante iustitia sua, effecta gratiæ & gratuiti ætetæterni fui amoris, qui quidem prior est meritis Christi, electis actu communicare nempe gratiam, à poena peccati immunitatem & relaxationem & vitam æternam: potest enim Deus nobis efficaciter velle gloriam & gratiam, quam actu dare non potest, absque læsione justitiæ suæ ex libero suo decreto, citra satisfactionem vel nostram, vel Christi, multa efficaciter homines volunt, quæ actu citra injustitiam facere non possunt, potest rex efficaciter velle ut aulicus ejus æris alieni nomine incarceratus, è carcere liberetur, actu tamen liberare non potest sine justitiæ læsione, nisi prius debita aulici persolvenda curet. Deus efficaciter & absolute voluit filio suo dilecto æternam gloriam, non vult tamen eum actu intrare nisi per multas perpessiones. Sed semper Arminiani Deum suo modulo metiuntur, quasi ex odio in amorem, & ex amore rursus in odium humanitus versaretur.
units.tr: Hence observe the fraud of the Arminian, who everywhere contends that the act of willing life for us is restricted to divine justice just as much as the actual bestowing of life, which is plainly false. For the act of willing life for us is an act of the supreme dominion of God, not an act of justice. The actual giving of life, however, is restricted to justice not by the order of justice, as if justice itself formally dictated to God this manner of bringing men to eternal life. I prove it thus. If God, as just and by necessity of justice, brought sinners to life through the satisfaction of Christ, then he could not bring them to life otherwise than through satisfaction. But this confines God's freedom and infinite wisdom within too narrow bounds. The reason for the major premise is that what God does as just, and from justice as from a formal principle, he does by the necessity of his nature and not freely. If he did not do it, he would be unjust. But he would not have been unjust if he had brought all immediately to life and made them partakers of glory, which he did in the personal union of the human nature with the divine. Hence it follows that God's wrath toward the elect when they sin is not a hatred opposed to the love by which he previously pursued them, but only displeasure and an unmoving hatred toward sins, not toward persons, and sometimes a paternal chastisement. Hence God always loves the elect and always hates the reprobate. I would have you note here how ridiculously the Remonstrantes take up our doctrine of eternal election, while they rave thus: The efficacious intention of saving, or the irrevocable and peremptory will by which God wills to save Peter and Paul by name, cannot be conjoined with the executive will by which he then wills to reconcile them, or to give them a mediator through whom they may be reconciled. To will efficaciously the salvation of sinners as an end, and then to will reconciliation and merit as a means by which he is moved to will the salvation of sinners, are contradictory. But they fight with shadows. For we teach that God efficaciously wills the salvation of the elect as an end, and is moved by the merit of Christ as the means most suited to his justice, so that he gives them eternal life in act. These are not only not contradictory; according to Scripture they are friendly and subordinate. But to will salvation for the elect as an end, and for God's will to be moved by the merit of Christ so that he wills them salvation, the Arminiani dream up. This never came into our minds. Indeed it is blasphemous to say that the will of God is moved by any cause or external agent. They ask in the same place what the formal effect of Christ's merit is. For where, they say, such an efficacious will to save is presupposed, to say that the effect of Christ's merit is the actual restoration of the sinner into God's grace is trifling; for to restore someone into someone's grace is nothing other than to bring it about that someone efficaciously wills good to someone. But this efficacious will precedes the merit of Christ. Therefore, they say, on our doctrine there is no formal effect of Christ's merit. Those good men who so conjecture are ignorant of the doctrine of the Reformed Church. For Christ's merit does not change God's will toward the elect from hatred to love; the Reformed Church does not worship a mutable God. The formal effect of Christ's merit is that God, notwithstanding his justice, could bring about the effect of grace and of his free and eternal love, which is indeed prior to the merits of Christ: namely, to actually communicate to the elect grace, immunity from the punishment of sin, relaxation, and eternal life. For God can efficaciously will us glory and grace, which he cannot actually give without injury to his justice, by his free decree, apart from satisfaction either ours or Christ's. Many men efficaciously will things which they cannot actually do without injustice. A king can efficaciously will that his courtier, imprisoned on account of debt, be freed from prison, yet he cannot actually free him without injury to justice, unless he first takes care that the courtier's debts be paid. God efficaciously and absolutely willed eternal glory for his beloved Son, yet he does not will him actually to enter it except through many sufferings. But the Arminians always measure God by their own measure, as if he were turned in a human way from hatred to love, and from love back again to hatred.

units.la: 18. Falsa itaque ab iis assignatur definitio reconciliationis, nempe efficientia voluntatis salvandi, loco voluntatis perdendi, quasi vero in Deo voluntas contraria contrariæ succederet.
units.tr: 18. The definition of reconciliation they give is therefore false, namely that it is the efficacy of the will to save, in place of the will to destroy, as if in God a contrary will succeeded a contrary one.

units.la: 19. Distinguendi etiam hic debent τὸ credere, pro assentiri, & pro actu fiduciali cordis & amplexu quo innitimur in Christum, priore significatu, fide non justificamur, nisi dixerimus Cainum, Iudam aut ejusmodi qui legis comminationibus cum horrore credunt, justisicari, posteriore modo fides innititur rei ut bonæ, non ut veræ aut falsæ. Cor enim & affectus in quibus est actus fiduciæ bonum aut malum, non verum aut falsum apprehendunt, unde non proprie credo peccata vel esse remittenda, vel jam esse remissa. Hinc ut ad rem. Satisfactio ut à Christo præstita non est justificatio, quia est Dei justificantis fundamentum, neque fides ullo sensu est satisfactionis Christi instrumentum: Quis enim credendo efficere poterit ut Christus pro se satisfecerit? Neque fides ulla ratione dici potest causa motiva vel organica etiam divinæ acceptationis, qua satisfactionem Christi pro nobis acceptat. 1. Nos credendo non efficicimus vel ὀργανικῶς ut Deus Christi mortem pro peccatis nostris acceptet, neque ulla causalitas externa movere potest Dei voluntatem, 2. Sive nos credimus sive non credimus, jam post mortem Christi vivimus, imo ab æterno, Deus mortem Christi pro electorum peccatis acceptavit, statuitque antecedenter ad nostram fidem nos non punire, sed gratis in Christo pro filiis habuit. At vero Arminiani innuere videntur fidem esse partem collateralem ἀντὶ λύτρου[?] à Christo Deo persoluti, vel fidem nostram, causalitatem aliquam exercere in Dei voluntatem, qua ipsa ex odio, & ira in dilectionem & gratiam erga nos commutetur, unde & mutabitur Deus, & actus aliquis immanens & vitalis in Deo in tempore incipit, nempe dilectio, & alia interit, nempe actus displicentiæ & odii, quod est blasphemum. Nihil enim Deus de novo aut in tempore vult, ejus volitiones sunt æternæ. Negamus etiam fidem nostram nempe assensum non posse apprehendere remissionem omnium peccatorum ut præteritam, id enim quilibet justificatus vere apprehendit, nempe Christum & satisfecisse jam olim, & Deum ab æterno acquievisse, depositâ displicentia & ira erga ipsorum peccata, tanquam in sufficiente redemptionis pretio, sed hic fides non facit; sed objectum jam factum præsupponit.
units.tr: 19. Here too we must distinguish between "to believe" (τὸ credere) taken as "to assent," and "to believe" taken as the fiducial act of the heart and embrace by which we rest upon Christ. In the former sense we are not justified by faith, unless we say that Cain, Judas, or others like them, who believe the threats of the law with horror, are justified. In the latter sense, faith rests on a thing as good, not as true or false, since the heart and affections, in which the act of trust lies, apprehend what is good or evil, not what is true or false. So it is not strictly correct to say that sins are to be forgiven, or are already forgiven, by believing. To come to the point: the satisfaction made by Christ is not justification, because it is the foundation of God's justifying, and in no sense is faith the instrument of Christ's satisfaction. For who could bring it about, by believing, that Christ made satisfaction for himself? Nor can faith in any way be called the moving or organic cause even of divine acceptance, by which God accepts the satisfaction of Christ on our behalf. (1) By believing we do not bring it about, organically (ὀργανικῶς), that God accepts Christ's death for our sins, and no external causality can move the will of God. (2) Whether we believe or not, we live now after the death of Christ, indeed from eternity: God accepted Christ's death for the sins of the elect, and decreed, before our faith, not to punish them but to regard them freely as sons in Christ. But the Arminians seem to hint that faith is a collateral part of the ransom (ἀντὶ λύτρου) paid to God by Christ, or that our faith exerts some causality on the will of God, by which God is changed from hatred and wrath into love and favour toward us. Thus God would be changed, and some immanent and vital act would begin in God in time, namely love, and another would perish, namely the act of displeasure and hatred, which is blasphemous. For God does not will anything new or in time; his volitions are eternal. We also deny that our faith, that is, assent, can apprehend the remission of all sins as past. For every justified person truly apprehends this: that Christ has long since made satisfaction, and that God from eternity has been appeased, his displeasure and wrath against their sins laid aside, as in a sufficient price of redemption. But faith does not produce this; it presupposes an object already made.

units.la: 20. Justificare sumitur vel active pro actu Dei judiciali, vel passive seu terminative prout in credentem terminatur, priore modo est actus in Deo internus, & immanens, non transiens in subjectum externum, cujusmodi actus sunt electio & reprobatio quæ habent totum esse completum, priusquam homines electi, reprobati, aut justificati, vel esse vivere, credere incipiant aliquid boni vel mali faciunt, & in hoc sensu fides non est instrumentum justificationis: nemo enim credendo efficit ut Deus non velit punire peccata, aut ut velit nos amare ad vitam æternam: At vero justificare terminative & passive est justum hominem & viventem & actu credentem declarare, actu judiciali terminato in conscientiam peccatoris rei & citati coram tremendo Dei judicis tribunali & peccatorum convicti, quo lite forensi peccator absolvitur, & absolutionem declaratâ actu sentit, apprehendit, & fiduciali innixu in Christum jam manifestationem illius sententiae porrigentem recumbit. At vero τὸ[?] justificare, hac usitata in scripturis loquendi forma, non ponit n[?] Deo novam volitionem jam in tempore incipientem, ut nugantur Arminiani cum suo Socino, sed aeternae Dei volitionis intimationem conscientiae jam factam. Quod sic probo, homo non est justificatus ab aeterno, quia homo non est ab aeterno. homini credenti non sunt remissa peccata ab aeterno, quoniam non est ab aeterno. Nam justificatio & remissio hoc sensu non sunt terminis diminuentes. 2. Sicut quando Rex aulico condonat crimen laesae majestatis, haeredibus & gnatis suis etiam nondum natis condonat, sed nondum nati nec regiae irae nec gratiae, sunt capaces actu, sed tantum potestate; ita se habet in hoc negotio reus. Dicent ergo Arminiani nos hic justificationem sumere, pro sensu & notitia justificationis & remissionis, ideoque (homines fide justificantur) idem valet, ac homines tum demum justificantur, quando credunt, hoc est, sentiunt se justificari, cum antea essent justificati. Nugae & tricae Siculae: nam justificari plus est quam sentire se justificari, nam 1. est actus Dei absolventis terminati in conscientiam hominis citati & tracti ad tribunal tremendi judicis, qui actus ante hoc infrans non terminabatur in conscientiam. 2. Hoc actu Deus certum facit conscientiae citati, innitenti fiducialiter in Christum, jam etiam in Christo plenam expiationem omnium peccatorum factam 3. Ipse peccator actu fiduciali recumbit in Christum sufficientem salvatorem credentiū: at vero actus Dei terminatus in nos non potest esse nudus sensus illius actus: quis sanus ita argumentaretur cui paulo magis sobriū est sinciptu[?]?
units.tr: 20. To justify is taken either actively, for the judicial act of God, or passively, or terminatively, insofar as it terminates in the believer. In the former way it is an act internal to God and immanent, not passing over into an external subject; of this kind are election and reprobation, which have their whole being complete before elect, reprobate, or justified men begin to be, to live, or to believe, and do nothing good or evil. In this sense faith is not the instrument of justification: for no one by believing brings it about that God does not will to punish sins, or that he wills to love us unto eternal life. But to justify terminatively and passively is to declare a just man, one who is living and actually believing, by a judicial act terminating in the conscience of a sinner who is guilty and summoned before the dread tribunal of God the Judge and convicted of sins. By this forensic process the sinner is absolved, and he feels and apprehends the absolution as declared, and resting by fiducial trust on Christ, he reclines upon the manifestation of that sentence now offered to him. But to justify, in this usual form of speech in Scripture, does not posit a new volition in God beginning now in time, as the Arminians trifle with their Socinus, but is the intimation to the conscience of the eternal volition of God, now made. I prove it thus: a man is not justified from eternity, because a man is not from eternity; sins are not forgiven to a believing man from eternity, because he is not from eternity. For justification and remission, in this sense, are not terms of diminution. (2) As when a king pardons a crime of treason against his majesty, he pardons it also to his heirs and sons not yet born; but those not yet born are capable of neither the king's wrath nor his grace actually, but only potentially; so it is with the guilty man in this matter. The Arminians will say, therefore, that we here take justification in the sense and knowledge of justification and remission, and so the proposition "men are justified by faith" means the same as "men are then at last justified when they believe," that is, when they feel themselves justified, though before they were already justified. These are Sicilian trifles and quibbles! For to be justified is more than to feel oneself justified. For (1) it is an act of God absolving, terminating in the conscience of a man summoned and drawn to the tribunal of the dread Judge, which act, before this, did not terminate in the conscience. (2) By this act God makes certain to the summoned conscience, which trusts fiducially in Christ, that a full expiation of all sins has now been made in Christ also. (3) The sinner himself, by an act of trust, reclines upon Christ, the sufficient Saviour of believers. But God's act terminating in us cannot be the bare feeling of that act. What sane person would argue this way, unless he were somewhat more soberly disposed?

units.la: 21. Quamvis itaque in mente Dei peccata ab æterno remissa sunt, non tamen homo ab æterno est justificatus, hoc est declaratus in conscientia sua, quando citatur coram tribunali Dei justus in Christo: nam quamvis actus justificandi in Deo connotet Dei actum immanentem & æternum, attamen ille actus non est tota & integra formalis ratio justificationis peccatoris, de qua Paulus epist, ad Galatas, & scriptura loquitur. Formaliter enim justificare est Deum actu declarare, actu nempe judiciali trementem coram judice reum, & absolutionem æternam & jam primo & nunquam antea cessare effectus divinæ adversus peccatum displicentiæ, virtute promissionis divinæ, quâ credenti promittuntur Christus, omniaque ipsius bene-ficia, & actuale jus ad regnum Dei, & dignitas[?] adoptionis. Dices, an non electo, antequam credat, removentur effectus divinæ iræ adversus peccata: si enim pœna inflicta electo priusquam credit, fit satisfactoria, Deus plectit peccata electorum, semel in Christo, & semel in ipsis, antequam credant. Resp. Sane priusquam electus credit, cessit iræ Dei adversus ipsum, omnesque iræ effectus erga ipsius personam, idque propter Christi meritum, sed non virtute illius palmaris promissi euangelici (qui credit in Christum, non venit in condemnationem) nunquam enim removentur effecta irae Dei adversus peccatum electi virtute, illius promissi, donec quis actu credit. Hinc est quod electo nulla fit consolatio, nulla pax conscientiae, priusquam conditionem foederis pacis impleat, hoc est, priusquamcredat, ideoque quamvis electus etiam antequam credit, non subsit irae Dei, idque proper merita Christi & satisfactionem ipsius, & quamvis propter illam satisfactionem baptismatis & euangelii gratia & etiam spiritu sancto, virtute cujus tandem credit, donetur, tamen ista beneficia non habet ille nondum credens virtute foederis gratiae & specialis illius promissi euangelici (qui credit habet filium, qui credit salvabitur) ideoque hoc sensu nondum credenti electo, nondum sunt remissa peccata, nondum removetur ira Dei, hoc est, effectus divinae, adversus peccatum, displicentiae non-dum illi aufertur, eo speciali modo, quo tollitur virtute promissionis euangelicae quam fidem, quae foederis est impletio, postulat, ideoque electus nondum credens habet jus in Christo, non ad Christum, utpote qui nondum credit, iguorat, sicne foederatus ad quem promissiones spectant, ut ad haeredem & filium promissionis, qui vero credit habet jus in Christo & ad Christum, & Christus in illo foedus novum implevit, & tanquam fœderis fidei-jussor. Heb. 7. 22. virtute promissionis & veracitatis Dei, quæ justitia quædam est Dei, specialiori modo pactionis æquissimæ removentur effectus iræ Dei, & hoc est remitti peccata & peccata non imputari juxta phrasin scripturæ Ps. 32. 1. 2. Rom. 4. Aliud itaque est hominem justificari in Christo, idque ab æterno, & justificari hominem in Christo in tempore juxta fœdus & pactum euangelicum. Dico itaque per actum credendi remitti peccata, quia fides apprehendit Christum non ut nudum objectum, sic enim assensus fidei apprehendit Christum & historiam euangelii, sed ut objectum datum, & actu oblatum à Deo in nostram justitiam, sic enim fides Christum quatenus datum & promissum amplectitur, & deosculatur & recipit Iob. 1. 12. Heb. 11. 13. ut juxta fœdus novum, & virtute veracitatis Dei Christus sit ipsius justitia: hinc & specialis est immunitas (ut sic loquar) pactionis ab effectis iræ Dei, & à peccati vi condemnatoria; Hinc illud notari velim, fidem non facere ne quidem organicos justificationem & peccatorum remissionem æternam & immanentem, sed [?]ipsam ut objectum jam olim factum præsupponere, & hoc sensu procedit argumentum Bellarmini, Socini & Arminianorum contra nos. Et nos dicimus cum illis nullum actum facere suum objectum, & per actum fidei non remitti peccata, sed ante illum actum jam olim esse remissa: At vero justificatio pactionalis, seu remissio foederalis (quam ego jam explicavi) est effectus fidei, fidesque illa est natura prior justificatione, neque vero haec pactionalis justificatio superaddit aliquid reale aeternae Dei volitioni de non puniendis electorum peccatis in ipsis electis, sed in Christo, neque est nuda notitia aut sensus justificationis, sed ponit in electo credente novam immunitatem a condemnatione, novam inquam, non secundum substantiam rei, semper enim electi etiam antequam credant sunt in & propter Christi mortem immunes a condemnatione, sed novam in modo rei, quia immunitas haec est remotio effectuum divinae irae juxta speciale pactum evangelicum, quod per Dei gratiam implent, quando credunt, quae remotio ante actum credendi erat plane dispensatoria ex libera Dei constitutione, haec vero nititur veracitate Dei & speciali pacto revelato in evangelio, prior est ab absoluta Dei libertate, haec a voluntate Dei justa.
units.tr: 21. Although, then, in the mind of God sins were remitted from eternity, yet a man is not justified from eternity, that is, declared in his conscience, when he is summoned before the tribunal of God as just in Christ. For although the act of justifying in God implies God's immanent and eternal act, that act is not the whole and complete formal reason of the sinner's justification, of which Paul speaks in his epistle to the Galatians and Scripture generally. For formally to justify is to declare by an act of God, indeed a judicial act, the guilty man trembling before the judge; and the eternal absolution, and the cessation of the effects of divine displeasure against sin, first now and never before, come into effect by virtue of the divine promise, by which Christ is promised to the believer, together with all his benefits, and the actual right to the kingdom of God, and the dignity of adoption. You will say: does not the effect of divine wrath against sin cease for the elect before they believe? For if punishment inflicted on the elect before they believe becomes satisfactory, then God punishes the sins of the elect twice, once in Christ and once in them, before they believe. Answer: Certainly before the elect believes, the wrath of God toward him has ceased, and all the effects of wrath toward his person, and this on account of Christ's merit, but not by virtue of that outstanding evangelical promise (he who believes in Christ does not come into condemnation). For the effects of God's wrath against the sin of the elect are never removed by virtue of that promise until someone actually believes. Hence it is that no comfort, no peace of conscience, comes to the elect before he fulfils the condition of the covenant of peace, that is, before he believes. So although the elect, even before he believes, is not subject to the wrath of God, and that on account of the merits and satisfaction of Christ, and although by that satisfaction the grace of baptism and of the gospel, and also the Holy Spirit, by whose virtue at last he believes, is given, yet the one not yet believing does not have these benefits by virtue of the covenant of grace and that special evangelical promise (he who believes has the Son; he who believes will be saved). Therefore in this sense, for the elect not yet believing, sins are not yet remitted, and the wrath of God is not yet removed; that is, the effect of divine displeasure against sin is not yet taken away from him in that special way in which it is removed by virtue of the evangelical promise, which requires faith, the fulfilment of the covenant. So the elect not yet believing has a right in Christ, not a right to Christ, since he does not yet believe, and is ignorant, as one in covenant to whom the promises pertain, as heir and son of the promise. But he who believes has a right in Christ and to Christ, and Christ in him has fulfilled the new covenant, and stands as surety of the covenant. (Heb. 7. 22.) By virtue of the promise and the truthfulness of God, which is a certain justice of God, the effects of God's wrath are removed in a more special manner by the most equitable compact; and this is to have sins remitted and not imputed, according to the phrase of Scripture (Ps. 32. 1, 2; Rom. 4). It is one thing, therefore, for a man to be justified in Christ, and that from eternity, and another for a man to be justified in Christ in time, according to the covenant and gospel compact. I say therefore that sins are remitted by the act of believing, because faith apprehends Christ not as a bare object (for the assent of faith apprehends Christ and the history of the gospel in that way), but as an object given and actually offered by God for our righteousness. For faith embraces Christ as given and promised, and kisses and receives him (John 1. 12; Heb. 11. 13), so that according to the new covenant, and by virtue of the truthfulness of God, Christ may be his righteousness. Hence, so to speak, there is a special immunity from the effects of God's wrath and from the condemning power of sin, given by the compact. Here I would have this noted: faith does not even organically make justification and the eternal and immanent remission of sins, but presupposes the object itself as already made long ago; and in this sense the argument of Bellarmine, Socinus and the Arminians against us proceeds. And we say with them that no act makes its own object, and that sins are not remitted by the act of faith, but were already remitted long before that act. But pactional justification, or covenantal remission (which I have now explained), is an effect of faith, and that faith is by nature prior to justification. Nor does this pactional justification add anything real to the eternal volition of God, that the sins of the elect are not to be punished in the elect themselves, but in Christ. Nor is it the bare knowledge or feeling of justification; rather it posits in the believing elect a new immunity from condemnation. New, I say, not in the substance of the thing, for the elect are always, even before they believe, immune from condemnation in and on account of Christ's death; but new in the mode of the thing, because this immunity is the removal of the effects of divine wrath according to the special evangelical compact, which they fulfil when they believe. That removal before the act of believing was wholly dispensatory, from God's free constitution; but this one rests on God's truthfulness and on the special compact revealed in the gospel. The former comes from God's absolute freedom, the latter from God's just will.

units.la: 22. Hinc facile est diluere quae contra nostram doctrinam objiciunt Remonstrantes in Apol. nam contra fiduciam specialis misericordiae magisterialiter declamitant 1. fidei objectum est promissio misericordiae, eaq; universalis sicut est universalis praedicatio poenitentiae, uti fatetur Augustana confessio. At misericordia specialis electorum, vel ex electione fluens, non est universalis, omnium, sed electorum propria misericordia. Ergo talis specialis misericordia non est objectum fidei. Resp. Promissio mise-riricordiæ universalis dicitur in illa confessione Augnst. [?] quia indefinite omnibus in ecclesia proponitur. sed revera in se & respectu intentionis divinæ, est electorum propria.
units.tr: 22. Hence it is easy to dissolve what the Remonstrants object against our doctrine in their Apol. For against the confidence of special mercy they declaim dogmatically: 1. The object of faith is the promise of mercy, and that promise is universal, just as the preaching of repentance is universal, as the Augustana confession admits. But the special mercy of the elect, or mercy flowing from election, is not universal, belonging to all, but is the proper mercy of the elect. Therefore such special mercy is not the object of faith. Reply: the promise of universal mercy is spoken of in that confession because it is proposed indefinitely to all in the Church; but in itself, and with respect to the divine intention, it belongs properly to the elect.

units.la: Ob. 2. Specialis illa misericordia non potest promitti, ergo ejus promissio non est objectum fidei. Prob. ante. Talis misericordia, est electorum propria ex vi absoluti decreti, electionis multo antequam promittitur. Resp. Non docent nostri specialem misericordiam formaliter promitti in euangelio: promittitur enim secundum effectus & promitti dicitur, quoniam gratia efficax, fides remissio, & gloria æterna quæ manant ex illa speciali misericordia promittuntur electis, non est absurdū promitti effectus gratiæ postquam secundum decretum gratiosum electionis sumus in gratia.
units.tr: Objection 2. That special mercy cannot be promised, therefore its promise is not the object of faith. Proof of the first part: such mercy is the proper possession of the elect by virtue of an absolute decree, that of election, long before it is promised. Reply: our people do not teach that special mercy is formally promised in the gospel. It is promised according to its effects, and it is said to be promised because efficacious grace, faith, forgiveness and eternal glory, which flow from that special mercy, are promised to the elect. Nor is it absurd that the effects of grace should be promised after we are in grace, according to the gracious decree of election.

units.la: Ob. 3. Quod fides non sit applicatio remissionis peccatorum, prob. sic. Remissio peccatorum, est purus putus actus divinæ mentis aut voluntatis, actus judicialis in Deo immanens, non transiens in subjectum extra Deum: Applicari autem a nobis actum Dei à Deo perfectè immanentem quis capiat? Resp. Satis capi potest omnes actus Dei immanentes, quo Deus decrevit, vocare justificare, & glorificare nos, nobis applicari quando fides actus illos per effecta in nobis gratiosa nobis revelet. 2. Proprie credimus revelata in verbo, at etiam à posteriori decreta Dei interna & immanentia credimus, quamvis non à priore, & etiam nobis sic credita applicamus, quamvis specialis applicatio mihi videtur effectus, non essentia fidei justificantis.
units.tr: Objection 3. That faith is not the application of the forgiveness of sins, proved thus: the forgiveness of sins is a pure act of the divine mind or will, a judicial act immanent in God, not passing into a subject outside God. But who can grasp that an act of God, perfectly immanent in God, is applied by us? Reply: one can well grasp that all the immanent acts of God, by which God decreed to call, justify and glorify us, are applied to us when faith reveals those acts to us through the gracious effects in us. 2. We believe properly what is revealed in the word; but we also believe, a posteriori, God's internal and immanent decrees, though not a priori, and we apply to ourselves what is thus believed. Although special application seems to me an effect, not of the essence of justifying faith.

units.la: Ob. 4. Actus applicans vel est efficiens causa, vel antecedanea conditio misericordiæ specialis, vel tantum nude cum illa coexistit, si prius misericordia erit effectus & posterius applicatione ideoque non objectum: nam objectum applicationis est prius ipsa applicatione, & hæc coexistentia est inanis. Ergo. Resp. Actus applicationis, si proprie loquamur, est causa organica, non ipsius misericordiæ; sed effectuum gratiosorum misericordiæ ideoque nec est efficiens, nec prærequisita conditio: at negamus fidem ullo modo causative movere Dei voluntatem, ut velit vostri misereri: nam voluntas Dei misericors est, ipse Deus misericors, atqui Dei nulla est causa extra ipsum Deum: sic enim esset creatura, non Deus si sui esse haberet causam.
units.tr: Objection 4. The applying act is either the efficient cause or the antecedent condition of special mercy, or it merely coexists with it. If it is prior, mercy will be the effect and application posterior, and so not the object: for the object of application is prior to application itself, and this coexistence is empty. Therefore... Reply: the act of application, properly speaking, is an organic cause, not of mercy itself, but of the gracious effects of mercy; therefore it is neither efficient nor a prerequisite condition. But we deny that faith in any way causally moves God's will to be merciful to us. For God's will is merciful, and God himself is merciful, and there is no cause of God outside God himself; for if he had a cause of his being, he would be a creature, not God.

units.la: Ob. 5. Absurdum est fidem h. est applicationem specialis misericordiæ à Deo præscribi hominibus, sub promisso specialis misericordiæ sive remissionis peccatorum. Resp. 1. non absurdum, sed euangelicum est applicationem effectuum specialis misericordiæ mandari à Deo sub promisso vitæ æternæ. At quis nostrum afferat gratiam electionis promitti nobis? id Arminianis[?] satis arridebit, qui volunt fidem movere Dei voluntatem ad eligendum homines, ideoque hæc ipsis est promissio, crede & electus eris in sanguine Christi. 2. ipsorum commentum est Deum moveri ad actus immanentes remittendi peccata, & eligendi a fide nostra, quod blasphemum est.
units.tr: Objection 5. It is absurd that faith, that is, the application of special mercy, should be prescribed by God to men under the promise of special mercy or forgiveness of sins. Reply: 1. It is not absurd but evangelical that the application of the effects of special mercy should be commanded by God under the promise of eternal life. But which of us asserts that the grace of election is promised to us? That will please the Arminians well enough, who wish faith to move God's will to elect men; for them this is the promise: believe, and you will be elect in the blood of Christ. 2. Their fiction that God is moved by our faith to the immanent acts of remitting sins and of electing is blasphemous.

units.la: Ob. 6. Actus determinatus, qualis est electio, non potest non producere in Dei voluntate alium, gratiosum effectum determinatè distinctum a justificatione: atqui actus ille non potest alius esse quam actus remittendi & salvandi: misericordia itaque specialis necesse est formaliter includatur in electione: eo ipso itaque quod Deus elegit ad vitam peccatorem, determinata est voluntas divina ad remittendum peccatori sua peccata. Deum enim velle peccatori determinata voluntate vitam æternam citra peccatorum remissionem, est in Calvini schola atheologon & Socinianum. Resp. 1. Hoc ipso, quod electio actum remittendi & salvandi producat, hoc ipso non necesse est essentialiter includatur in electione. 2. Non hoc ipso quod Deus elegit, determinata est voluntas ad remittendum, sed necessario determinabitur: sunt enim duæ diversæ determinationes volendi nempe gloriam & remittendi peccata, & prius determinata est Dei voluntas ad salvandum ut ad finem, & deinde ad remittendum tanquam ad medium, nec hoc est atheologon in nostra schola, quanquam si rigidè loquamur, unus actus volendi in Deo non est causa alterius actus, & hoc ipso, quod homines eligat ad vitam, vult dare Christum & remittere hcc[?] est non punire propter Christum, ut possit convenienter justitiæ suæ gloriam intentam, dare, non quia vovoluntas intenta in exitium propter peccatum mutetur in voluntatem salvandi ex fide tanquam ex causa externa, ut somniant Armin.
units.tr: Objection 6. A determinate act, such as election, cannot but produce in the divine will another gracious effect, determinately distinct from justification; but that act can be nothing other than an act of forgiving and saving. Therefore special mercy must necessarily be formally included in election: by the very fact that God has elected a sinner to life, the divine will is determined to forgive that sinner his sins. For for God to will eternal life to a sinner by a determinate will, apart from the remission of sins, is atheism and Socinianism in the school of Calvin. Reply: 1. From the fact that election produces the act of forgiving and saving, it does not follow that this act is essentially included in election. 2. It does not follow from the fact that God elected that his will is determined to forgive; rather it will necessarily be determined. For there are two different determinations of willing, namely glory and the forgiveness of sins: the divine will is first determined to save as to an end, and then to forgive as to a means. Nor is this atheism in our school, although, strictly speaking, one act of willing in God is not the cause of another. By the very fact that he chooses men to life, he wills to give Christ and to remit, that is, not to punish on account of Christ, so that he may suitably give his intended glory to his justice. He does not give because a will set on destruction on account of sin is changed into a will to save from faith, as from an external cause, as the Arminians dream.

units.la: Ob. 7. Iustificatio est actio Dei quam Deus pure pute in sua ipsius mente efficit, quia nihil aliud est quam volitio aut decretum, quo peccata remittere, & justitiam imputare aliquando vult iis qui credunt, id est, quo vult poenas peccatis eorum promeritas iis non infligere, eosque tanquam justos tractare & præmio afficere. Hæc itaque Dei actio quomodo proprie effectus dici possit fidei & quidem fidei quatenus est instrumentum? Certe nos credendo actionem istam Dei efficeremus, quo quid absurdius? Resp. 1. Qui iustificationem volunt esse decretum immanens, ii decrerum æternum vocent necesse est: actus enim omnes Dei immanentes sunt revera ipse Deus agens, ideoque coæterni cum Deo, & quando callide dicunt pro suo more iustificationem esse decretum, quo aliquando vult credentes præmiare, satis judicant hoc decretum immanens aliquando incipere, & ponere ailquando[?] (hoc est in tempore quando homines credunt) novum & temporarium velle inDeo ortui & interitui obnoxiu, prout homo credit & resipiscit, aut non credit, & in peccata gravia relabitur, ideoque Dei decreta & temporanea & mutabilia statuant, necesse est. 2. Iustificatio terminative sumpta non est formaliter decretum, sed actus passionalis declarandi credentem justum. 3. Nos efficere credendo, ut Deus velit aut decernat ab æterno, est absurdum, quod tamen admittunt Remonstrantes, quando docent Deum ab æterno homines eligere quoniam credunt: at vero non absurdum, sed orthodoxum est, nos credendo efficere ut Deus nos in Christo justos declaret conscientiis nostris & pronunciet, adeoque nos credendo efficere ut cessent effectus iræ & displicentiæ Dei modo, pactioni euangelicæ, convenientissimo, quo sensu nos fidem justificationis instrumentum esse credimus, non quod fides qua opus sit nostræ justitiæ pars, sed quod fide amplectamur Christum datum à Deo nobis in justitiam fidem manu quasi apprehendere justitiam Christi aut remissionem attrahere nugas meras vocant, notitiam, assensum aut applicatione esse actionem instrumentalem vocant. Sed quia fide præstita non aliter (inquiunt Rem.) consequimur remissionem peccatorum, ex promisso Dei, quam si fides veluti instrumentum à Deo data esset ad obtinendam remissionem peccatorum? instrumentum justificationis dicitur. Sed R.1.[?] Fidem instrumentum respectu Dei actu justificantis nemo nostrum dixit: at respectu justificationis passive in nostram conscientiam terminatæ instrumentum, hoc sensu appellamus, non quod fides ulla organica causalitate Christi justitiam producat; nugantur qui hoc nobis imputent, aut quod actu reali justitiam Christi attrahat, sicut manus pauperis eleemosynam attrahat (omnis enim similitudo claudicat) sed quod impleta per Dei gratiam fidei conditione, adeoque impleto plenâ[?] per Dei gratiam fidei conditione, adeoque impleto fœdere gratiæ, ex promissione euangelicâ, nos justi declaramur, & ex pacto euangelico cessant effectus iræ divinæ, hinc fide, ex hprafi scripturæ, recipimus λαμ-βάνομεν promissiones Dei Gal. 3. Itaqua[?] justificatio pactionalis non est nuda Dei accetantis nos, æstimatio, quasi nihil poneret in nobis: quamvis enim non ponat in nobis expulsionem habitus, & habitualis gratiæ novam introductionem, ut somniant pontificii attamen ponit aliquid reale in nobis nempe nos nostram propriam justitiam deseruisse, & justitiæ Christi propter remissionem peccatorum, firmiter adhærere coram judice, & aliud (esse) reale ponit in nobis nempe Dei actum justificandi terminatum in conscientiam nostram, quo non aliter quam debitor qui soluto, par fide-ijussorem, ære in quo erat, ita à foro recedimus nacti certificationem solutorum debitorum, quasi syngrapham à Christo absolutoriam.
units.tr: Objection 7. Justification is an action of God which God accomplishes purely in his own mind, since it is nothing other than a volition or decree by which he wills at some time to remit sins and impute righteousness to those who believe, that is, by which he wills not to inflict on them the punishments their sins have deserved, and to treat them as righteous and reward them. How then can this divine action properly be called an effect of faith, and indeed of faith insofar as it is an instrument? Surely we, by believing, would bring about that action of God; what could be more absurd? Reply: 1. Those who want justification to be an immanent decree must call it an eternal decree; for all immanent acts of God are really God himself acting, and therefore coeternal with God. And when they cunningly say, after their manner, that justification is a decree by which at some time he wills to reward believers, they sufficiently show that this immanent decree begins at some time and posits at some time (that is, when men believe) a new and temporary will in God, subject to rising and perishing, as man believes and repents or does not believe, and falls back into grave sins. So they necessarily make God's decrees temporary and mutable. 2. Justification, taken terminatively, is not formally a decree, but a passive act of declaring the believer righteous. 3. That we, by believing, bring it about that God wills or decrees from eternity is absurd; yet the Remonstrants admit this when they teach that God from eternity elects men because they believe. But it is not absurd, rather it is orthodox, that by believing we bring it about that God declares and pronounces us just in Christ to our consciences, and so that by believing we bring it about that the effects of God's wrath and displeasure cease, in a manner most agreeable to the evangelical covenant. In this sense we believe that faith is the instrument of justification: not because faith is some part of our righteousness, but because by faith we embrace Christ, given by God to us for righteousness, and as it were lay hold of him with the hand. They call these things mere trifles, and they call notice, assent or application an instrumental action. But because, having exercised faith, we do not otherwise (say the Remonstrants) obtain forgiveness of sins from God's promise than if faith had been given by God as an instrument for obtaining forgiveness of sins, it is called the instrument of justification. But reply: none of us has said that faith is an instrument with respect to God's act of justifying. We call it an instrument with respect to justification as terminated passively in our conscience; not because faith by any organic causality produces Christ's righteousness (those who impute this to us trifle), or because it attracts Christ's righteousness by a real act, as the hand of a poor man attracts alms (for every comparison limps), but because, when the condition of faith has been fulfilled by God's grace, and so the covenant of grace has been fulfilled, we are declared righteous from the evangelical promise, and from the evangelical covenant the effects of divine wrath cease. Hence by faith we receive the promises of God, according to the phrasing of Scripture, Gal. 3. [λαμβάνομεν]. Therefore pactional justification is not a bare estimation by which God accepts us, as if he posited nothing in us. For although it does not posit in us the expulsion of a habit and the new introduction of habitual grace, as the Papists dream, yet it posits something real in us: namely, that we have abandoned our own righteousness and firmly cling, before the judge, to the righteousness of Christ for the forgiveness of sins. And it posits another real thing in us, namely God's act of justifying, terminated in our conscience, by which we withdraw from the court no differently than a debtor who has paid, with a surety, the money he owed, and who is released, having obtained a certificate of his paid debts, as it were an acquittal from Christ.

units.la: Ob. 8. justitiam Christi nobis imputari propter meritum & obedientiam Christi, in rigore, non est verum, nisi dicamus justitiam Christi nobis impu-tari propter justitiam Christi, quod absurdum: & Episcop. idem habet. Non est itaque justitia nostra justitia proprie Christi, nedum activa aut passiva sed id quod Christus utraque illa promeruit, & nos per solum Christum Iesum censequimur. Non enim justitia Christi proprie id est quod imputatur, sed id quod imputatur, nobis crecredentibus, ipsum est justitia. Hinc ipse Armin. de justificat. art 19. ait, an rrte [?] dici possit justitia Christi gratiose imputari in justitiam? Sed Resp. 1. Nullo modo sequitur, quia justitia Christi imputatur nobis propter Christi meritum & obedientiam, ideo justitia Christi imputatur propter justitiam Christi. Nam Christi obedientia non est justitia ipsius formaliter, sed tantum causativè, est ratio & causa nimirum justitiæ Christi: quia enim Christus plenissime obedivit ad mortem crucis, ideo resurrexit fidei jussor, justus & ab ære solutus, quo nomine Deus nos ab ære solutos & justos censet, & hoc est imputari Christi justitiam nobis, quod in rigore est verum. Nam hæc tria hic subordinantur. 1. Deus ex absoluta libertate censet Christum mori, idem esse ac si nos mortui essemus. 2. Christus obediendo ad mortem, justitiam fide-jussoriam acquisivit. 3. propter talem obedientiam, Christus est justus fideijussorie, & nos in illo: neque recte dici potest Adami peccatum nobis imputari propter Adami peccatum.
units.tr: Objection 8. That Christ's righteousness is imputed to us on account of Christ's merit and obedience is not true in the strict sense, unless we say that Christ's righteousness is imputed to us on account of Christ's righteousness, which is absurd: Episcopius has the same view. Christ's righteousness is therefore not properly our righteousness, nor active nor passive, but what Christ merited by both, and what we obtain through Christ Jesus alone. For Christ's righteousness is not properly that which is imputed, but that which, when imputed to us who believe, is itself righteousness. Hence Arminius himself, On Justification, article 19, asks: can it be rightly said that Christ's righteousness is graciously imputed for righteousness? But the answer is: (1) it does not at all follow that, because Christ's righteousness is imputed to us on account of Christ's merit and obedience, Christ's righteousness is imputed on account of Christ's righteousness. For Christ's obedience is not his righteousness formally, but only causally; it is the reason and cause of Christ's righteousness. For since Christ obeyed most fully, even to the death of the cross, he therefore rose again as surety, just and released from the debt, and on this ground God counts us released from debt and just; and this is to impute Christ's righteousness to us, which is true in the strict sense. For three things are subordinated here: (a) God, from absolute freedom, counts Christ's death as equivalent to our having died; (b) by obeying unto death Christ acquired the righteousness of a surety; (c) on account of such obedience Christ is just as surety, and we are just in him. Nor can it rightly be said that Adam's sin is imputed to us on account of Adam's sin.

units.la: 2. Non dicimus Christi justitiam imputari propter meritum Christi, imo dicimus id quod Christus morte sua nobis commeruit, nempe justitiam Christi nostram esse per imputationem divinam: non enim simpliciter Christi justitia est nostra sed justitia fide jussoria seu cautionaria. 3. Eo inclinant Armin. ut Christi justitia sit nostra, non formaliter, sed effectivè, nempe Christus morte sua promeruit ut noster credendi actus & bona opera habeantur à Deo judice pro justitia nostra, hoc dicunt astute admodum, ne cogantur admittere Christum vice aut loco sive in persona nostri mortuum esse, sed tantum mortuum esse in bonum nostrum, ut possint omnes, por quibus Christus obiit, in aeternum damnari & peccatorum poenas luere, non obstante justitia Dei, quod Christus poenas pro ipsis dederit. Et hoc habent commune cum Pontificiis. Ita enim Franc. Suarez Iesuita, Merita Christi non donantur nobis ut formaliter justificent, sed ut sint pretium quo emamus justitiam, qua formaliter justificemur, sicut qui dat alteri pretium, quo emat vestes, dicitur vestire illum, non formaliter, sed effective, moraliter, ut constat.
units.tr: (2) We do not say that Christ's righteousness is imputed on account of Christ's merit; rather we say what Christ merited for us by his death, namely that Christ's righteousness is ours by divine imputation. For Christ's righteousness is not simply ours, but a righteousness of suretyship, or of security. (3) Arminius inclines to the view that Christ's righteousness is ours not formally but effectively: Christ by his death merited that our acts of faith and good works should be counted by God the judge as our righteousness. They say this very craftily, so that they need not admit that Christ died in our place or stead, or in our person, but only died for our good; so that all for whom Christ died may be damned forever and pay the penalties of their sins, notwithstanding the justice of God, because Christ paid penalties for them. And in this they agree with the Papists. For Francis Suarez the Jesuit says: "The merits of Christ are not given to us that they may formally justify us, but that they may be the price by which we buy the righteousness by which we are formally justified; just as one who gives another a price with which to buy clothes is said to clothe him, not formally but effectively, morally, as is clear."

units.la: Ob. 9. Nolunt in justificatione omnia pecpeccata remitti. Pretium (inquiunt in Apolo:) fuit persolutum pro peccatis electorum omnibus commissis aut committendis, vel non: si non, quomodo pretium istud verum pretium esse velis? Si sic, quid itaque restat electis quam ut securi de reliquo dormiant? Resp. 1. Meritum Christi est verum pretium, licet non gratiam aut favorem Dei emat, quasi Deus ex irato in benevolum commutetur, sed est pretium, quia eo dato, potest Deus actu bene-facere peccatoribus congruenter justitiae suae. 2. Est pretium solutum pro peccatis in posterum committendis, neque est quod sopori & securitati indulgeant; nam iste est abusus ex prava carnis dispositione ortus ex remissione peccatorum omnium, non genuinus foetus remissionis, & talem securitatem non cadere in regenitum credimus, quippe cui Deus ex foederis gratiosa promissio dilertè promisit, se inditurum in cor ipsius timorem sui, ut non recedat à Deo, Ierem. 32. verf. 40.
units.tr: Objection 9. They do not want all sins to be remitted in justification. The price (they say in Apollonius) was paid for all the sins of the elect, committed or to be committed, or not: if not, how can you want that price to be a true price? If so, what then remains for the elect but to sleep securely about the rest? Answer: (1) Christ's merit is a true price, although it does not buy God's grace or favour, as if God were changed from angry to kind; but it is a price, because on its being given God can actually do good to sinners in a way consistent with his justice. (2) It is a price paid for sins to be committed in the future, and there is no reason why they should indulge in drowsiness and security; for that is an abuse arising from the depraved disposition of the flesh, and it is not a genuine fruit of the remission of all sins. We believe that such security does not befall the regenerate, since God has clearly promised, by the gracious promise of the covenant, that he will put his fear into their heart so that they do not depart from God (Jer. 32:40).

units.la: 3. Bene est quod Arminiani velint, peccata electo quaedam remitti, quaedam non, & admissa non imputari, & admittenda imputari, sed quando Deus admittenda praescit, an non ad mortem simul eundem hominem odio habeat, & eundem ad vitam aeternam diligat, quod est contrarias in Deo voluntates ponere?
units.tr: (3) It is well that the Arminians wish that some sins be remitted to the elect, some not, and that sins committed are not imputed, while sins yet to be committed are imputed. But when God foresees sins yet to be committed, does he not at the same time hate the same man unto death and love the same man unto eternal life? Is this not to posit contrary wills in God?

units.la: 4. Satis sese detegunt Arminiani, qui volunt actum justificandi, quem supra vocabant decretum immanens in Deo, esse actum temporalem, coaevum actibus liberi arbitri, quod est Deum Protheo fingere mutabiliorem, qui tot volitiones & decreta figat, refigat, ponat, & rescindat in horas & annos.
units.tr: (4) The Arminians reveal themselves sufficiently when they want the act of justification, which above they called an immanent decree in God, to be a temporal act, coeval with the acts of free will. This is to make God more changeable than Proteus, who fixes, refixes, posits and rescinds so many volitions and decrees by the hour and the year.

units.la: 5. Peccata imputata vel expiata sunt Christi sanguine, & pro ipsis satisfactum irae Dei, vel non, si sic, ergo non obstante quod Deus peccata imputet, electus est in gratia cum Deo, & verum pretium solutum est pro peccatis imputatis: at quae justitia, id imputare in debitum, quod est planè[?] solutum? Si non, ergo fides electi postea credentis, facit ut Deus peccata non imputet, pro quibus tamen non satisfactum est irae Dei, & hic erit remissio sine effusione sanguinis, vel fides erit ἀντίλυτρον[?] pro illis peccatis, quod est absurdum.
units.tr: (5) Either sins imputed are expiated by Christ's blood, and satisfaction has been made for them to the wrath of God, or not. If so, then, although God imputes sins, the elect is in grace with God, and a true price has been paid for the sins imputed. But what justice is there in imputing as a debt what has plainly been paid? If not, then the later faith of the believing elect causes God not to impute sins for which satisfaction has nevertheless not been made to the wrath of God; and this will be remission without the shedding of blood. Or faith will be a ransom [ἀντίλυτρον] for those sins, which is absurd.

units.la: 6. Sed hoc est, quod volunt Arminiani Deum non impetraffe eleðtis[?] plenariam remissionem, sed tantum pro iis obiisse conditionatè si crediderint, quod tamen ipsorum doctrinam evertit, aut fidem nostram aliquid superaddere satisfactioni Christi, quo compleatur, quasi in se insufficiens esset.
units.tr: (6) But this is what the Arminians want: that God has not obtained full remission for the elect, but died for them only conditionally, if they believe. Yet this overthrows their own doctrine, or else it means that our faith adds something to the satisfaction of Christ to complete it, as if it were in itself insufficient.

units.la: 7. Hinc etiam nemo ante obitum est vere justificatus: Deus enim semper peccata admittenda imputabit, cui reclamat scriptura quæ testatur nos habere pacem in hac vita ex justificatione, & accessum ad Deum per Christum Rom. 5. 1. 2. & remissionem peccatorum Ephef. 1. 7. Col. 1. 13. 14.
units.tr: (7) Hence also no one is truly justified before death, for God will always impute sins still to be committed. Scripture opposes this, which testifies that we have peace in this life from justification and access to God through Christ (Rom. 5. 1. 2.) and the remission of sins (Eph. 1. 7; Col. 1. 13. 14.).

units.la: Objectio 10. Aut pretium hoc solutum pro electis est acceptatum & solutum sine conditione, aut non nisi cum conditione: Si sine conditione, quid applicatione aut fide opus est? Quis effectus formalis applicationis? Si persolutum & acceptatum cum conditione; quomodo pro iis persolutum est magis quam pro reprobis, imo quale beneficium quod à conditione suspenditur? Resp.
units.tr: Objection 10. Either this price paid for the elect has been accepted and paid without condition, or only with condition. If without condition, what need is there of application or of faith? What is the formal effect of application? If paid and accepted with condition, how has it been paid for them more than for the reprobate? Indeed, what kind of benefit is it that hangs on a condition? Answer.

units.la: 1. Hoc argumentum etiam torquebit Arminianos, qui volunt absolutè Christum obiisse, ideoque pretium redemtionis solvisse pro omnibus: at tum quæ necessitas fidei? Si solutum est ex conditione fidei, tum Christus tantum mortuus est pro credentibus, quod illi negant, neque potest solvi ex conditione fidei: tum enim, si nos qui jam post mortem Christi vivimus, non credidissemus, quod Arminio est possibile. Christus non obiisset pro nobis, & sic non pro omnibus mortalibus, imo si fides est conditio soluti pretii, debebat solutionem pretii antecessisse, & sic Christus non debebat mori, donec omnes mortales finaliter crederent, quod absurdum, & si mors Christi pendet a fide ut a conditione, si qui non crederent, debebat Christus pro iis non mori, & sic adhuc non mortuus est pro omnibus. 2. Innuunt hic Arminiani Christum mortuum esse pro omnibus absolute, ut alibi docent: at vero divina acceptatione solutum est pretium a Christo & acceptatum a Patre, nomine tantum eorum qui credunt: hoc si volunt tum mortem Christi a pretio misere divellunt, tum mors Christi quia mors, fit λύτρον: qui vero non credunt, pro iis Christus pretium redemptionis non dedit. Ergo fides ipsorum, hoc dato, quod crederent, ne hilum ipsos juvaret: non potuissent enim eo casu redimi, ideoque salvari, cum pro iis pretium sanguinis Christi non sit datum: at vero si volunt fidem causari acceptationem Dei qua mortem Christi pro ipsis credentibus acceptet, cum nondum deletum chyrographum, nec peccata priusquam credamus: at Paulus Col. 2. 15. ait, ista a Christo pendente in cruce, ideoque antequam credamus nos, qui jam post mortem Christi vivimus, deleta fuisse, deinde in filio dilectionis grati & accepti sumus Deo Ephes. 1. 6. in sanguine Christi Heb. 9. 13, 14. non actu fidei. 3. Dicimus solutum esse pretium pro electis absque conditione ut fit solutum, non absque conditione fidei ut fit applicatum, ideoque necessaria est applicatio propter justificationem pactionalem. 4. Nec est pretium illud inane beneficium, secundum nostram doctrinam, quia suspenditur a conditione fidei: nam non agnoscimus conditionem potestativam Arminianam, quam ex Jurisconsultis hauserunt, quae est ad esse & non esse: inanis quidem effet mors Christi, ex tali conditione, sed suspenditur fructus pretii dati a conditione fidei, quam in nobis indeclinabiliter operatur Deus, pro suo beneplacito solo.
units.tr: (1) This argument will also turn against the Arminians, who hold that Christ died absolutely, and so paid the price of redemption for all. But then what need is there of faith? If the price was paid on the condition of faith, then Christ died only for believers, which they deny; nor can it be paid on the condition of faith. For then, if we who now live after Christ's death had not believed, which is possible according to Arminius, Christ would not have died for us, and so not for all mortals. Indeed, if faith is the condition of the price being paid, the payment of the price ought to have preceded faith, and so Christ ought not to have died until all mortals finally believed, which is absurd. And if the death of Christ depends on faith as a condition, then for those who did not believe Christ ought not to have died, and so he still did not die for all. (2) Here the Arminians imply that Christ died for all absolutely, as they teach elsewhere. But in truth the price was paid by Christ and accepted by the Father by divine acceptance, on behalf only of those who believe. If they want this, then they wretchedly tear the death of Christ away from the price, and the death of Christ, because it is death, becomes a ransom [λύτρον]; but for those who do not believe, Christ did not give the price of redemption. Therefore their faith, even granting that they would believe, would not help them at all: for in that case they could not have been redeemed, and so could not have been saved, since the price of Christ's blood was not given for them. But if they want faith to cause God's acceptance, by which he accepts Christ's death for believers, then the bond was not yet cancelled, nor sins, before we believe. Yet Paul says (Col. 2:15) that these were blotted out by Christ hanging on the cross, and therefore before we believe, we who now live after Christ's death, they were already blotted out; then we are accepted by God in the Beloved Son (Eph. 1:6), in the blood of Christ (Heb. 9:13, 14), not by an act of faith. (3) We say that the price was paid for the elect without condition, so that it has been paid; not without the condition of faith, so that it is applied; and therefore application is necessary on account of pactional justification. (4) Nor, according to our doctrine, is that price an empty benefit because it hangs on the condition of faith. For we do not acknowledge the Arminian potestative condition, which they drew from the jurists, the condition of being and not being. The death of Christ would indeed be empty under such a condition; but the fruit of the price given hangs on the condition of faith, which God works in us indeclinably, by his good pleasure alone.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: An contingentia subsint decreto Dei absoluto, & an admittenda sint decreta in Deo con- ditionata? Ad examen vocantur Jac. Ar- minius, Jesuitae, Suarez, Molina, Les- sius &c. Probatur fatum Jesuitico-Arminianum.
units.tr: Whether contingent things are subject to God's absolute decree, and whether conditional decrees are to be admitted in God? Called to examination are James Arminius, the Jesuits, Suárez, Molina, Lessius, etc. The Jesuitical-Arminian fate is proved.

units.la: DEcretum absolutum circa futura contingentia non negant antiquiores, sed recentiores Scholastici, praesertim execrabilis Jesuitarum natio, Lodiv. Molina, Leonard. Lessius, Pet. Fonseca, Greg. de Valentia, Gab. Vasq. Francisc. Suarez, praeceptoribus suis deesse nolunt, Iac. Arminius, Corvinus, Nicol. Grevincho, inter pseudo-lutheranos. Balscha, Meisnerus, Iac. Arminius determinationem quandam agnoscit, qua posita causa libera est absolute indifferens ad agendum, vel non agendum, sed determinationem ad alteram præcisè partem magis quàm ad aliam negavit, ideoque verbis ludit, & ipsius determinatio est non determinatio, sed solutio causæ contingentis à providentiæ nutu, ut docuit Cicero, Epicurus, & quicunque providentiam Dei negabant. Francisc. Suarez opuf. de auxil. lib. 1. de concur. cap. 16. f. 6. 7. agnoscit in Deo prædefinitionem immanentem, quâ finis infallibiliter sequatur, ex congruâ mediorum, juxta Dei præscientiam, applicatione: at tamen decretum hoc præsupponit scientiam contingentium prius naturâ futurorum, quam decernantur, quod est decerni, seu post-decerni contingentia futura, postquam sunt futura, quod non est decretum. Candidiores in hac re Vasq. & Valent. Decretum conditionatum appellant. Sed candorem omnium vincit Fonsc. qui Met. lib. 6. cap. 2. q. 5. f. 7. co. 2. ita loquitur: Possibilis ac vera prædefinitio aliquorum liberorum futurorum, nihil est aliud quam approbativum decretum divinæ voluntatis, quo Deus absolutè vult, ut sint futuri. Alibi rotundè vocat post-definitionem, Atqui boni Angeli & sancti homines approbant bonum futurum, postquam est futurum, & reprobi Angeli & homines approbant omne malum futurum, postquam est futurum: non ergo major est Dei, quam creaturarum intelligentium, circa futura contingentia providentia, si nudam scientiam accipiemus. Gab. Vasq. ponit decretum concomitans, sed eadem in providentiam Dei injuria. 2. Sed antecedaneum & absolutum Dei decretum probo. 1. scripturis. 2. ratione. 3. testimoniis. Ita Scriptura, Ephef. 1. Elegit nos ut effemus fanctì. 2. Theff. 1. 13. Elegit nos ad salutem per fanctificationem spiritus & fidem habitam veritati. E. Deus elegit nos absolute ad actus liberos fanctitatis & fidei. Resp. Suarez. Decretum hoc praesupponere actus futuros libere juxta congruam voluntatis motionem. At diluo sic, vel praescit illud fututum, antequam decernat, vel non: fi prius imponit lectori: nam quod jam est, non magis decerni potest, quam helternus solis occasus, hodie decerni potest, futurum non decernitur postquam est futurum, decretum dat esse rei, ut fit: at quod jam praescitur futurum jam habet esse antecedenter ad decretum: fi uero Deus praescit illud nondum esse, tum decretum antecedit effectum contingentem futurum, quod est institutum. 2. Voluntas vel potest refragari decreto congruo, vel non: fi potest, non est decretum congruum, sed incongruum: fi non potest, tam arcte circumscribitur indifferentia libertatis ab hoc decreto qua ab absoluto; & sic indifferentia no est de effentia libertatis, ut alibi docet Iesuita
units.tr: The older writers did not deny an absolute decree concerning future contingent things; the more recent Schoolmen did, especially the accursed tribe of the Jesuits: Lodovicus Molina, Leonardus Lessius, Pedro Fonseca, Gregorio de Valencia, Gabriel Vázquez, and Francisco Suárez, who are unwilling to depart from their teachers. Among the pseudo-Lutherans, James Arminius, Corvinus, and Nicolaus Grevinchovius, and Balduin, Meisner. Arminius acknowledges a certain determination by which, once the cause is posited, the free cause is absolutely indifferent to acting or not acting; but he denied that it is determined to one part rather than the other. So he plays with words, and his determination is not a determination but a release of the contingent cause from the nod of providence, as Cicero and Epicurus, and all who denied God's providence, taught. Francisco Suárez, in his work on help and concurrence, book 1, chapter 16, pages 6 and 7, acknowledges in God an immanent predefinition by which the end follows infallibly, from the fitting application of the means, according to God's foreknowledge. Yet this decree presupposes knowledge of contingent things as future, by nature prior to their being decreed; so that the contingent future is decreed only after it has become future, and that is not a decree. The more candid on this matter are Vázquez and Valencia, who call it a conditional decree. But Fonseca surpasses all in candour; in his Metaphysics, book 6, chapter 2, question 5, page 7, column 2, he speaks thus: A possible and true predefinition of some free future things is nothing other than an approving decree of the divine will, by which God absolutely wills that they be future. Elsewhere he bluntly calls it a post-definition. "But the good angels and holy men approve good things that are to be, after they are to be; and the wicked angels and men approve every evil that is to be, after it is to be." Therefore, if we take it as mere knowledge, God's providence concerning future contingent things is no greater than that of intelligent creatures. Gabriel Vázquez posits a concomitant decree, but this does an equal injury to God's providence. 2. I prove, however, an antecedent and absolute decree of God: 1. from Scripture, 2. from reason, 3. from testimonies. Scripture, Ephesians 1: He chose us that we should be holy. 2 Thessalonians 2:13: God chose us to salvation through sanctification by the Spirit and faith in the truth. Therefore God chose us absolutely to the free acts of holiness and faith. Suárez replies that this decree presupposes acts that will be free, according to a fitting motion of the will. But I answer thus: either he foreknows that act as future before he decrees it, or he does not. If first, he imposes on the reader; for what already is cannot be decreed any more than today's sunset can be decreed. A future thing is not decreed after it has become future; a decree gives being to a thing so that it comes about. But what is already foreknown as future already has being prior to the decree. If, however, God foreknows that it is not yet, then the decree precedes a contingent effect that is future, which is what was to be established. 2. The will either can resist a fitting decree or cannot. If it can, it is not a fitting decree but an unfitting one. If it cannot, the indifference of liberty is as tightly circumscribed by this decree as by an absolute one; and so indifference is not of the essence of liberty, as the Jesuit teaches elsewhere.

units.la: 3. Esa. 14. 27. Iehovah inivit consilium & quis irritum faciat? v. 24. Ne vivam nisi quemadmodum proposui, ita extiterit. cap. 46. 10. Confilium meum stabit, deleftationem meam faciam. 11. Voco ab oriente (perfide) volucrem (Cyrum expeditissimum bellatorem) effectorem confilii mei, loquutus & adducam. Hinc arg. Quod Deus decrevit, id ita fit, ut non possit non fieri: atqui Deus decrevit liberam Chaldaeorum à Medis & Persis eversionem. Erg. fiet illa libera eversio, ac proinde effectus liber & quidem indeclinabiliter futurus subest decreto absoluto, atque omnium contingentium par est ratio. Jam audi Iesuitae distinctionem. Quis (inquit) non videat decretum antecedere praescientiam effectus sic decreti. At quis tum non videat (inquam ego) Iesuitam credere veritati coactum? Iesuitae & Arminianiani ref. Cyrus necessitate consequente, nulla vero absoluto decreto necessitate antecedente, vastavit Chaldaeos, sed ex praescientia liberi arbitrii Cyri, sed quorsum dent verba Iehovae, an securi Chaldaei hoc in quaestionem vocabant ipsos vastandos fore à Cyro, si modo vastandi essent.
units.tr: 3. Isaiah 14:27: Jehovah has formed a purpose, and who shall make it void? v. 24: Surely as I have purposed, so it shall come to pass. Chapter 46:10: My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure. 11: Calling a ravenous bird from the east (Cyrus, a most ready warrior) the executor of my counsel; I have spoken and I will bring it. Hence the argument: What God has decreed comes about in such a way that it cannot not come about; but God has decreed the free overthrow of the Chaldeans by the Medes and Persians. Therefore that free overthrow will come about, and so a free effect, which will certainly come to pass, falls under the absolute decree; and the reasoning is the same for all contingent things. Now hear the Jesuit's distinction: "Who," he says, "does not see that the decree precedes the foreknowledge of an effect so decreed?" But who, I ask, does not see that the Jesuit is compelled to believe the truth? The Jesuits and the Arminians reply that Cyrus laid waste the Chaldeans by a consequent necessity, but by no antecedent necessity from an absolute decree; he did so from the foreknowledge of Cyrus's free will. But what do the words of Jehovah mean? Did the Chaldeans, if they were in fact to be laid waste, call into question whether Cyrus would lay them waste?

units.la: 2. Logica haec nova facit probationem Dei sophisticam qua si probaret idem per idem: haec est conclusio probanda. Cyrus delebit Chaldaeos. Prob. Deus decrevit decreto invincibili ut Cyrus deleret Chaldaeos. Erg. Cyrus delebit Chaldaeos. Consequen. est ipsius Dei. Arminian. & Iesuitae probabunt antecedens: Certum & fixum est Dei decretum ex praescientia liberi arbitrii Cyri se libere ad bellum determinaturi, & praescientiae certitudo nititur certitudine rei praescitae (quia nempe Cyrus libere delebit Chaldaeos) non enim res est certa, quia Deus praescivit eum fore, sed certa est praescientia, quia res est certa. Ergo a primo ad ultimum ita argumentatur Deus: Cyrus delebit Chaldæos, quia Cyrus delebit Chaldæos. An non hidati omnia turbent? Et pari ratione omnis probatio a Dei decreto, juramento & promissione erit sophistica, & scripturæ veritas peribit. 3. Si certitudo & necessitas vastationis liberæ non pendet a Dei decreto, mihi licebit secundum Iesuit. & Armin. ita argumentari: Deus juravit & decrevit, ut Cyrus Chaldæos deleret. E. Cyrus Chaldæos non delebit, & sic Dei argum. contradicentia probaret, si vastatio libera totam habet entitatem antecedenter ad decretum, & nulla a decreto necessitatem, tam arcta est connexio causativa aut logicalis inter juramentum vel decretum Dei, & non vastationem liberam, quam est inter juramentum vel decretum & vastationem. Neque ipsos juvat Fonsecæ decretum approbativum: nam tam certo res futura, quam si Deus futuritionem approbaret, imo certitudo futuritionis tota est antecedenter ad approbationem, non minus quam ad decretum. Deinde decretum approbativum est repugnans in objecto: nam objectum decreti est, quod potest esse vel non esse, juxta libertate Dei decernentis: atqui objectum approbationis est ens jam existens, & quod jam est, non potest non esse, & Deus existentiam seu futuritionem futurorum contingentium, quæ antecedenter ad decretum Dei futura sunt, non magis non potest non approbare, quam impedire potest, ut illud nunquam fit, quod jam est, quod est simplici. pliciter impossibile vel Iovi, teste Hesiodo.
units.tr: 2. This new logic makes a sophistical proof of God's, which would prove the same by the same. The conclusion to be proved is: Cyrus will destroy the Chaldeans. Proof: God has decreed, by an invincible decree, that Cyrus destroy the Chaldeans. Therefore Cyrus will destroy the Chaldeans. The consequence is God's own. The Arminians and Jesuits will prove the antecedent: "It is certain and fixed that God's decree arises from the foreknowledge of Cyrus's free will, that he will freely determine himself to war; and the certainty of foreknowledge rests on the certainty of the thing foreknown (namely, that Cyrus will freely destroy the Chaldeans). For the thing is not certain because God foreknew that it would be, but the foreknowledge is certain because the thing is certain." Thus God argues from first to last in this way: Cyrus will destroy the Chaldeans, because Cyrus will destroy the Chaldeans. Do not such notions throw everything into confusion? And by the same reasoning every proof drawn from God's decree, oath, and promise will be sophistical, and the truth of Scripture will perish. 3. If the certainty and necessity of the free destruction does not depend on God's decree, then, according to the Jesuit and Arminius, I may argue thus: God has sworn and decreed that Cyrus shall destroy the Chaldeans; therefore Cyrus will not destroy the Chaldeans. So God's arguments would prove contradictories.
