If the free destruction has its whole entity antecedently to the decree, and no necessity from the decree, then the causal or logical connection between God's oath or decree and the free destruction is no tighter than between an oath or decree and the destruction. Nor does Fonseca's approving decree help them. For a future thing is as certain as if God merely approved its being future; indeed, the certainty of its futurity lies wholly antecedently to the approval, no less than to the decree. Moreover, an approving decree is repugnant in its object. For the object of a decree is what can either be or not be, according to the freedom of the God who decrees. But the object of approval is a being already existing, and what already is cannot not be. God no more can fail to approve the existence or futurity of future contingent things, which are future antecedently to God's decree, than he can prevent that what already is should never come to pass; and this is simply impossible, even for Jove, as Hesiod testifies.

units.la: 4. Ioan. 15. 16. Ego elegi vos, & ordinavi, ut vos euntes fructus feratis. Ergo Christus decrevit, ut Apostoli bona opera facerent, orarent, ecclesias plantarent, praedicarent. Quid? an electi ad illa opera ex praescientia liberae determinationis Apostolorum? tum Apostoli eligebant Christum, quod negatur in textu. Deinde de illa libera determinatione redibit quaestio, sit ne decreta conditionate, an absolute? Si conditionate, redibit quaestio infinities de illa conditione. E. necessario sistendum erit in Dei decreto.
units.tr: 4. John 15:16: I have chosen you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit. Therefore Christ decreed that the apostles should do good works, pray, plant churches, and preach. Well? Were they chosen for those works from the foreknowledge of the apostles' free determination? Then the apostles would have chosen Christ, which the text denies. Further, the question will return about that free determination: is the decree conditional or absolute? If conditional, the question will return endlessly about that condition. Therefore we must necessarily stop at God's decree.

units.la: 5. Act. 22. 14. Deus (inquit Paulo Ananias) elegit te, ut voluntatem ipsius cognosceres, & videres justum illum, & audires vocem ejus. Ergo Paulus erat absolute praedestinatus ad annunciandum euangelium liberrime, ut foret testis eorum quae viderat, ut est v. 15. Resp. Armin. electionem illam esse temporalem Pauli designationem ad officium, non decretum aeternum. Resp. 1. Hoc gratis dicitur, non probatur. 2. Sed esto temporalis designatio, erat a matris ventre separatus ad apostolatum, Gal. 1. tum enim absoluta designatio antecedanea consistet cum libertate, quod ipsorum dogmata evertet, & sic aeterna electio absoluta cum actibus liberis consistere posset. Deinde dicunt hanc electionem esse extraordinariam, sed dictata fine probatione quis sobrius audiret? sit extraordinaria, est tamen irrefragabilis, & absoluta sit oportet, non nixa determinatione libera & tamè Paulus obediisse dicitur vocationi Act. 26. 19. Ergo libere euangelizavit: nulla enim est obedientia absque libertate, uti ipsi docent. 2. Frustrà Paulus exemplar omnibus credituris proponeretur 1. Tim. 1. 15, 16. Si Paulus ita obedierit ut non posset non obedire & reliqui pro indifferente libertate, gratia longe minus efficaciore poterant obedire vel non obedire. 3. Ubi comminatio locum habet, ut clamitant adversarii, ibi necessitas parendi non est: atqui Paulus comminationibus obnoxius erat, alioqui quorsum dixisset, Væ mihi si non euangelizavero. Paulus itaque & libere obedivit & absolute, & irrefistibiliter ad actus liberos ordinatus erat, secus non peccasset Paulus, si apostolicam provinciam subterfugio aliquo detrectasset.
units.tr: 5. Acts 22:14: The God of our fathers (says Ananias to Paul) has chosen you to know his will, and to see the Just One, and to hear the voice of his mouth. Therefore Paul was absolutely predestined to proclaim the gospel most freely, so that he might be a witness of what he had seen, as is said in verse 15. Arminius replies that this election was Paul's temporal designation to the office, not an eternal decree. Reply: 1. This is asserted without proof. 2. But granted that it was a temporal designation: Paul was set apart from his mother's womb to the apostleship (Galatians 1). Then an absolute designation antecedent to his act would be consistent with liberty, which would overturn their own doctrines; and so an eternal absolute election could be consistent with free acts. Further, they say that this election is extraordinary; but who of sound mind would hear such a claim, asserted with no proof? Let it be extraordinary; it is nonetheless irresistible, and it must be absolute, not resting on a free determination. Yet Paul is said to have obeyed the heavenly vision (Acts 26:19). Therefore he preached the gospel freely: for there is no obedience without freedom, as they themselves teach. 2. In vain would Paul be set before all who were to believe as an example (1 Timothy 1:15, 16), if he obeyed in such a way that he could not not obey, while the rest, by indifferent liberty, could obey or not obey under a far less efficacious grace. 3. Where a warning has a place, as our adversaries cry, there is no necessity of obeying; but Paul was subject to warnings, otherwise why would he have said: Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel? Paul, therefore, both obeyed freely and absolutely, and was ordained irresistibly to free acts; otherwise Paul would not have sinned if he had shirked the apostolic charge by some evasion.

units.la: 6, Rom. 8. 29, Quos præscivit, eosdem etiam præde-stinavit ut conformes essent imagini filii Dei. Atqui homines libere conformantur imagini filii Dei tum liberrimâ sub cruce patientiâ, tum vera sanctitate, neque præscientia futuræ cooperationis hic locum habet: nulla enim solatio sub cruce erit à Dei prædestinatione absoluta, si conditionatè, hoc est, antecedenter ad Dei prædestinationem, crucem subituri essent.
units.tr: 6, Rom. 8. 29, Whom he foreknew, them he also predestinated to be conformed to the image of his Son. But men are made conformed to the image of the Son of God both by most free patience under the cross and by true holiness, and here there is no room for foreseen future cooperation. For there would be no comfort under the cross from absolute predestination by God if men were to undergo the cross conditionally, that is, antecedently to God's predestination.

units.la: 7. 1. Theff. 3. 3. Ipsi nostris addixit esse positos, hoc est, ab æterno constitutos, ut gravia in mundo patiamur. Ephes. 2. 10. Creati ad bona opera, quæ præparavit Deus ut in iis ambula-tenus[?]. remus. Ergo absolute ordinati sumus ad actus liberos. Resp. Armin. non esse nos creatos ad bona opera absolute, quia in vanitate cordis sui ambulare poterant cap. 4. 17. Resp. 1. non sequitur. 2. pugnat cum scopo Apostoli qui probat nos salvari non ex operibus, quia bona opera (inquit) sunt causaliter ex divina ordinatione gratiosa, sed si antecedant talem ordinationem, non sunt ab ea causaliter. 2. Resp. Suarez. ad summum tantum colligi beneficium praedestinationis qua Deus parat nobis auxilia supernaturalia, quibus adjuvantur ad bona opera. Hinc contendunt Arminiani Deum absolute decrevisse normam sanctè videndi, non vero libertatem ad actus liberos praedeterminasse. Resp. 1. textum jugulant miserè. Nam Paulus non ait nos creatos ad gratiam aut auxilia supernaturalia: quid enim hoc faceret adversus operarios, qui id non negabant, sed ad bona opera ex gratia? 2. Nec est sermo de conditura Evangeli, sed de praeconstitutione nostri ad parendum evangelio: nos (inquit) ipsius creatura sumus v. 10. 3. Non sic Paulus, negatum concluderet. Quid? Deus praeparavit evangelii & auxilia supernaturalia quibus benè operemur: Ergo non salvamur ex operibus, non sequitur. Ipsi negant hanc consequentiam: operarii enim fidem cum operibus, plerique saltem eorum, conjungebant. 4. Armin. vero contendunt decretum absolute fuisse evangelium de salvandis credentibus, & si nullus mortalium salvaretur, quod Iesuitæ merito non ferent: sic enim insanis esset Dei intentio, & frustraneum decretum, ideoque par est ratio, sive Deus absolutè præscripsit euangelium liberè agentibus, sive agentia libera absolutè prædefinivit ad liberam obedientiam euangelio præstandam. Et hoc responso stabilitur nostra sententia.
units.tr: 7. 1 Thess. 3. 3. Ipsi nostris addixit esse positos, that is, appointed from eternity, that we should suffer grievous things in the world. Eph. 2. 10. Created unto good works, which God hath prepared that we should walk in them. Therefore we are absolutely ordained to free acts. Reply: Arminius says we were not created absolutely to good works, because they could walk in the vanity of their minds (Eph. 4. 17). Reply 1: It does not follow. 2: It conflicts with the Apostle's purpose, who proves that we are saved not by works, because good works (he says) are causally from divine gracious ordination, but if they precede such ordination, they are not causally from it. 2. Reply (Suárez): at most there is gathered only the benefit of predestination, by which God prepares for us supernatural helps by which we are aided to good works. Hence the Arminians contend that God absolutely decreed the norm of living holily, but did not predetermine the freedom to free acts. Reply 1: They wretchedly cut the throat of the text. For Paul does not say we were created for grace or supernatural helps; for what would this accomplish against the workmen, who did not deny this, but affirmed good works from grace? 2: Nor is the discourse about the framing of the Gospel, but about the prior constitution of us for obeying the Gospel: we are (he says) his creature, v. 10. 3: Paul would not conclude a denial in this way. What then? God has prepared the Gospel and supernatural helps by which we may work well: therefore we are not saved by works does not follow. They themselves deny this consequence, for the workmen joined faith with works, at least most of them. 4: The Arminians contend that the decree absolutely was the Gospel concerning the saving of believers, even if no mortal were saved, which the Jesuits will rightly not tolerate: for thus God's intention would be insane and the decree pointless; and therefore the reasoning is the same, whether God absolutely prescribed the Gospel to free agents, or absolutely predefined free agents to render free obedience to the Gospel. And by this answer our opinion is established.

units.la: 8. Luc. 24.44. Oportet (inquit Salvator) impleri de me, quæ scripta sunt in lege Mosis, in Prophetis, in Psalmis. v. 26. Oportuit Christum ista pati. Ergo foffipo manuum & pedum, lateris perforatio, derisio, cæsio corporis, Iudæ proditio, & omnia ejusmodi, quæ liberrimè fiebant, ex definito Dei consilio fiebant, Act. 2.24. Quid hic adversarii? Ista omnia fiebant conditionatè. At quâ conditione? Nempe si Deus vellet, apage, decrevit, si decrevit, vel an ex præscita prava inclinatione hostium decrevit permittere? at est hæc nugatoria principii petitio; nam illa prava inclinatio, & malevolus animus Iudæorum in Messiamsuum, principem locum tenet inter illa, quæ Christum absque causa, ut in lege scriptum erat (Ioh. 15.v.25.) exosum, pati necesse fuit, & an illa prava inclinatio fuerit à Deo decreta, quæritur, & si decreta, utrum absolutè, & sic habemus intentum, vel conditionatè, & rursus idem saxum voluntandum redit, qua conditione? Nempe hoc est mysterium φιλίας[?] Arminianæ, postquam omnia de Christo sunt impleta, & futura antecedenter ap ullum divinæ voluntatis actum, Deus ista fieri voluit, hoc est, si jam sunt, vult & decernit, ut sunt, atqui sic ego decerno creationem mundi & peccatorum redemptionem, postquam jam sunt, volo ut sint. Imo hoc modo Diabolus Jobi cruciatus decrevit, quod ad voluntatis actus attinet.
units.tr: 8. Luke 24. 44. It is necessary (says the Saviour) that all things be fulfilled which are written of me in the law of Moses, in the prophets, and in the psalms. v. 26. Ought not Christ to have suffered these things? Therefore the piercing of hands and feet, the opening of the side, mockery, the scourging of the body, the betrayal of Judas, and all such things, which were done most freely, were done by the determined counsel of God (Acts 2. 24). What do our opponents say here? These things were done conditionally. But on what condition? Namely, if God wished it, far be it; he decreed it; if he decreed it, or whether he decreed to permit it from the foreseen wicked inclination of the enemies? But this is a trifling begging of the question; for that wicked inclination and malevolent spirit of the Jews against their Messiah holds the chief place among those things which Christ had necessarily to suffer without cause, as was written in the law (John 15. 25). And whether that wicked inclination was decreed by God is the question; and if decreed, whether absolutely, and so we have what we intend, or conditionally, and again the same stone must be rolled back: on what condition? Namely, this is the mystery of Arminian friendship [φιλίας]: after all things concerning Christ have been fulfilled, and are future antecedently to any act of the divine will, God willed these things to happen, that is, if they now are, he wills and decrees them as they are. But so I decree the creation of the world and the redemption of sinners after they already are; I wish that they should be. Indeed in this way the Devil decreed the torments of Job, so far as an act of will is concerned.

units.la: 9. Jer. I. 5. Priusquam formasfem te in ventre, agnovi te, & quum nondum prodiisses ex vulva, sanctificavi te, Prophetam ipsis gentibus constitui te. Atqui libere prophetavit Ieremias comminatione & promissionibus tractus. c. 1. v. 17. c. 15. 19. 20. Sed & Decreta conditionata cum Dei natura, & proprietatibus omnibus e diametro pugnare evinco, & cum universo hominis officio, & vera contingentia, Deumque fato, res fortunae arbitrio emandare. 1. Argum. est à providentia Dei, quam decretum conditionatum funditus evertit. 1. Si res non sunt decretae, nisi conditionatae, ex praescientia quid jam sint, tum habent esse antecedenter ad Dei decretum: atqui sic praeter intentionem Dei, ideoque casu fient. Resp. Fonseca: non sequitur ea casu fieri, quia postquam ea fore praevidit Deus, intendit, & Leffius ait, id casuale esse, & fortuitum, quod neque praescire, neque declinare possumus. Sed Resp. 1. Ipse Fonseca sui oblitus alibi ait, ista fortuito evenire, quae praeter intentionem causae liberae fiunt. Ita Aristo. 2. Phys. c. 5. Ita Doctor. Conymbricenses 16. Fortuna (inquiunt) fiunt, quae non tantum praeter scientiam, sed etiam praeter intentionem agentis fiunt. 2. Si nuda
units.tr: 9. Jer. I. 5. Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee, and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee; I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations. But Jeremiah prophesied freely, moved by threats and promises: c. 1, v. 17; c. 15, 19, 20. But I also prove that conditional decrees are diametrically opposed to the nature of God and to all his properties, and to the whole duty of man and true contingency, and that they make God subject to fate and things subject to the will of fortune. First argument: it is from the providence of God, which a conditional decree utterly overthrows. (1) If things are not decreed except conditionally, on the basis of foreknowledge of what they already are, then they have being prior to God's decree; but so they come about beside God's intention, and therefore by chance. Fonseca replies that it does not follow that they happen by chance, since after God has foreseen that they will be, he intends them; and Lessius says that whatever we can neither foresee nor avert is accidental and fortuitous. But in reply: (1) Fonseca himself, forgetting himself, says elsewhere that those things happen by chance which come about beside the intention of a free cause. So Aristotle, Physics 2, c. 5; so the Conimbricenses, disputation 16: "Those things are said to happen by chance," they say, "which happen not only beyond knowledge but also beyond the intention of the agent."

units.la: Fonseca Metaph. 7 tex. 7 in Comment. c. 7. Colleg. Coimb. comment. Phys. 2. c. 5. q. 1. [?] nuda noticia rei & volitio, ut fit postquam jam est, sufficit ad providentiam, tum qui invenit thesaurum postquam invenit, habet providentiam perfectam de thesauro: scit enim illic esse thesaurum, & non tantum vult & approbat ut illic fit, sed & non mediocri gaudio perfunditur: at non habet praescientiam thesauri priusquam in ipsum casu incidat, ideoque non habet circa ipsum (forte dicerent) providentiam, sed resp. providentia Dei hoc casu erit humana perfectior, solo praescientiae actu, non voluntatis, atqui providentia formali suo conceptu claudit volitionem rei, non nudam scientiam. 3. Repugnantia dicit Fonseca, nempe Deum praescientem rem fore intendere, ut fit: nam postquam res est, non magis intendi potest, ut fit: quam creatio mundi hodierno die decerni potest. 4. Astrologus praescit futuram eclipsin, & etiam vult ut fit tali tempore, uti ipse praedicit, ut famae suae consulat: at per Fonseca rationem Astrologi habent circa eclipseis providentiam, non minus, quam ipse Deus. 5. Deus non potest declinare futuritionem rei contingentis, postquam futura est, neque ipsam avertere. Ergo habet nudam praescientiam circa ipsam.
units.tr: Fonseca, Metaphysics 7, text 7, in his commentary on c. 7; Coimbra College, commentary on Physics 2, c. 5, q. 1. [?] If bare knowledge of a thing, and willing it as it comes about after it already is, suffices for providence, then the man who finds a treasure, after he has found it, has perfect providence over the treasure: for he knows that the treasure is there, and not only wills and approves that it is there, but is also filled with no small joy. Yet he has no foreknowledge of the treasure before he stumbles upon it by chance, and so (perhaps they would say) he has no providence concerning it. But God's providence in this case will be more perfect than human providence, by the act of foreknowledge alone, not of will. Yet providence, by its formal concept, includes the willing of a thing, not bare knowledge. (3) Fonseca says there is a contradiction, namely that God, foreknowing that a thing will be, intends that it come about; for once the thing exists it can no more be intended to come about than the creation of the world can be decreed today. (4) An astrologer foreknows a future eclipse, and also wills that it occur at the time he predicts, so as to safeguard his reputation; yet on Fonseca's reasoning, astrologers have providence over eclipses no less than God himself. (5) God cannot avert or turn aside the future occurrence of a contingent thing once it is future. Therefore he has only bare foreknowledge of it.

units.la: 10. Peribit etiam Deo laus providentiae particularis, & universa gloria in egressu fortium [?]è gremio, in casione hominis, ut videtur casu, à securi percussi, in responsione linguae, quam scriptura ait esse à Deo, nempe quando tres aut quatuor sunt meditationes
units.tr: 10. The praise of particular providence will also be taken from God, and all the glory in the casting of the lot into the lap, and in the outcome of a man's blow, which seems to be by chance, when a man is struck by an axe, and in the answer of the tongue, which Scripture says is from God: namely when there are three or four meditations in the heart, why one rather than another, the other three being set aside, leaps to the tongue; and no other reason can be given than the determination of divine providence. Hear what Corvinus replies concerning the accidental killing of a traveller, Exod. 21. He says: "God did not expressly will that the axe…

units.la: Argum. 2. in corde, cur una potius, quam alia, posthabitis tribus, exiliat ad linguam, alia ratio reddi non potest; quam divinae providentiae determinatio. Audi quid ad casualem occisionem viatoris Exod. 21. respondeat Corvinus. Non (inquit) expresse Deus voluit, ut securis de manu ejus decideret in caput occisi. Neque juxta eam voluntatem (absolutam) manum direxit, ut & caderet & ita quidem caderet: sed Deus cum casum ipsum providerit, & impedire ac alio dirigere posset, impedire, ac alio dirigere noluit. Resp. 1. Dicit fraudulenter pro suo more (non expresse voluit, ut caderet securis) pro eo, quod debebat dixisse (non absolute voluit, ut caderet securis) sed quaerp an conditionate voluerit, ut caderet? At conditionem flagito, non alia fingi potest, quam ex hypothesi quod securis caderet. En egregium solamen tum caedenti, si forte patrem interemerit, tum caeso moribundo, quod principium interitus sit a securi, non a Deo. At dicerent esse a voluntate conditionata Dei, quod fecuris caderet: at vero quae fingi potest conditio? Nam ex ipsorum placitis securis antecedenter, ad Dei decretum casura erat, o fortunam. An conditio petenda erit a voluntate viatoris illuc libere conferentis, quando securis decidit? Et tum miser viator in sua libertate contingente, non in Deo quaerit solamen, nullus hic locus providentiae. 2. Hic nullum actum providentiae agnoscit praeter solam (nescio quam) praevisionem seu praescientiam: at vero ea nec est causa boni vel mali, sed futuritionem utriusque præsupponit. 3. Deus (inquit) causam prævidit, ac alio dirigere noluit: nullus hic actus est providentiæ positivus, sed negativus, nempe non directio securis. 4. Ergo vero sic: vel alio dirigere noluit voluntate absoluta, vel conditionata: si prius, habeo institutum: tum enim contingens occasio est, absolute à Deo decreta: si posterius detur, quæro, qua conditione noluit alio dirigere, nempe ex hypothesi, quod viator illuc liberè se conferret in eo temporis articulo, quo in caput exciperet ictum securis? At vero tum falso dicitur, Deum potuisse alio securim dirigere, & noluisse, imo sic, ex hypothesi quod exciperet viator ictum; non potuit Deus alio magis dirigere, quam efficere poterit, ut quod jam est, non fit. Imo si securis se ad cadendum determinet antecedenter ad Dei decretum, uti ipsi docent, Deus non potuit alio dirigere securim, sic enim efficeret, ut quod jam est, non fit; quod simpliciter impossibile est; ideoque Deus fato hic constrictus, viatoris occisionem non potuit antevertere, aut præpedire. 5. Si dixerint, Deum potuisse impediisse confluentiam horum trium actuum contingentium, nempe actus cædendi in occisore[?] 2. actus profiscendi illuc in occisio, & 3. dilapsus securis, redintegro argumentum: Hæc tria contingenter agunt tali momento, quo cæditur viator. Ergo Deus vel voluit, ut tali temtempore agerent, absoluta voluntate, & sic habeturinstitutum adhuc, vel voluntate conditionata, & tum requiro conditionem ex hypothesi, scilicet quod tum agerent, & sic Deus non poruit occisionem praepedire, nisi necessitatari consequenti obviam iret, quod est simpliciter impossibile. Hic vides non obstante Dei voluntate occisionem fieri posse, vel non, etiam invito Deo, & deum fato constringi: quem igitur viator mane orarer ut improvisam mortem effugeret, aut cui vel spere, declinatae mortis gratias religiose ageret? Non Deo, cujus voluntate non facta est occisio (fit enim occisio antecedenter ad Dei voluntatem) necesse est itaque Armin. fortunae, seu novae Deae contingentiae aras, & sacrificia stituant, preces concipiant, & Iehovah noster providentia sua cadat. 6. Posita voluntate hac conditionata, Matthias cooptatur in coetum apostolorum, ex hypothesi quod cadat sors super ipsum, & exit ei sors bona ex hypothesi, quod exierit & non potest non Matthias ad apostolatum evehi. Non est ergo quod Deo gratias ageret hoc nomine, quod forte electus fuerit. 7. Dicendum etiam tot injurias illatas innocenti salvatori, tot lapsus hominum & angelorum etiam in nunquam finiendos cruciatus, fieri voluntate Dei conditionata, ideoque antecedenter ad Dei aeterna intentionem & decretu. Mihi crede, Arminianissimus[?] erit merus Atheismos.
units.tr: Argument 2. Why one thought rather than another leaps from the heart to the tongue, with three others set aside, cannot be explained by any reason except the determination of divine providence. Hear how Corvinus answers the accidental killing of a traveller in Exod. 21: "God did not expressly will that the axe should fall from his hand onto the head of the one slain. Nor did he direct the hand according to that (absolute) will, so that it fell, and fell in just that way; but God, since he foresaw the chance itself and could have prevented it and directed the axe elsewhere, was unwilling to prevent it or to direct it elsewhere." Reply 1. He says "not expressly willed that the axe should fall" dishonestly, as is his habit, when he ought to have said "not absolutely willed that the axe should fall." The question is whether he willed it conditionally. I demand the condition. None can be imagined except on the hypothesis that the axe falls. Behold a splendid consolation both for the one who struck, if he perhaps killed his father, and for the dying man, that the beginning of his death is the axe and not God. But they would say the axe fell by God's conditional will. What condition, then, can be imagined? By their own opinions the axe was going to fall antecedently to God's decree. O fortune! Or must the condition be sought in the will of the traveller who freely went there when the axe fell? Then the wretched traveller seeks his consolation in his own contingent liberty, not in God, and there is no room for providence here. 2. Here he recognises no act of providence except a bare foreknowledge or prescience (I know not what kind), but this is not the cause of good or evil; it presupposes the futurition of both. 3. "God foresaw the cause and was unwilling to direct it elsewhere": here there is no positive act of providence, only a negative one, namely the absence of any redirecting of the axe. 4. Then I argue thus: either he was unwilling to direct it elsewhere by an absolute will or by a conditional one. If the former, I have my point, for then the contingent occasion is absolutely decreed by God. If the latter, I ask under what condition he was unwilling to direct it elsewhere: namely on the hypothesis that the traveller freely betook himself there at the moment when he received the axe-blow? But then it is falsely said that God could have directed the axe elsewhere and was unwilling to; indeed, on the hypothesis that the traveller receives the blow, God could not have directed it otherwise, since he could only bring it about that what already is does not happen. Indeed, if the axe determines itself to fall antecedently to God's decree, as they themselves teach, God could not have directed the axe elsewhere, for that would bring about that what already is does not happen, which is simply impossible; and so God, bound by fate here, could not forestall or prevent the traveller's killing. 5. If they say God could have prevented the coincidence of three contingent acts, namely the act of striking in the killer, the act of the victim's going there, and the falling of the axe, I renew my argument. These three contingently act at the moment when the traveller is struck. Either God willed that they should act at that time by an absolute will, and then I still have my point, or by a conditional will, and then I require the condition on the hypothesis that they would act at that time. So God could not have prevented the killing, unless he met a consequent necessity head on, which is simply impossible. Here you see that, despite God's will, the killing could or could not happen, even against God's will, and God is bound by fate. Then to whom would the traveller pray in the morning that he might escape an unforeseen death, or to whom would he religiously give thanks for a death avoided? Not to God, whose will did not make the killing happen, since the killing happened antecedently to God's will. So the Arminians must set up altars and sacrifices to Fortune, or to a new goddess of contingency, and offer prayers to her, and our Jehovah must fall by his providence. 6. Given this conditional will, Matthias is chosen into the company of the apostles on the hypothesis that the lot falls upon him; and the good lot comes out to him on the hypothesis that it comes out, and Matthias cannot but be raised to the apostolate. So there is no reason for him to give thanks to God on this account, that perhaps he was chosen. 7. It must also be said that so many injuries inflicted on the innocent Saviour, and so many falls of men and angels into never-ending torments, happen by a conditional will of God, and so antecedently to God's eternal intention and decree. Believe me, the most Arminian doctrine will be pure atheism.

units.la: ii. Cerrum[?] numerum animarum à Deo absolute decerni certum est. Ergo actus liberi generandi, per quos corporibus uniuntur, absolute à Deo decernuntur. Hic vel dicendum numerum electorum non esse certum, & Deo definitum, quod non ferent aures theologicae, vel cedendum est veritati, quod & facit Suarez, qui dicit omnia moralia media praedestinationis probabiliter à Deo absolute definiri, ideoque probabiliter falsum ille dicit actus liberos non posse absolute à Deo decerni. Neque auditu dignum est, quod ait Fonseca, praefinitas esse animas, prout sunt partes essentiales mundi, non vero respectu infusionis in corpora. Nam 1. quis diceret à Deo praefiniri animas quod sint, non vero quod sint, cum Davidis membra omnia libro Dei inscripta sint. Ps. 139.16. 2. Possibilis est Fonf.thesaurus animarum apud Deum corporibus nunquam uniendarum, siquidem homines nunquam generarent, uti ipsis est liberum: quis tales sustineret conjecturas?
units.tr: Second, it is certain that God absolutely decrees the definite number of souls. Therefore the free acts of generation, by which souls are united to bodies, are absolutely decreed by God. Here one must either say that the number of the elect is not certain and fixed by God, which theological ears will not bear, or yield to the truth, as Suarez does. He says that all the moral means of predestination are probably absolutely determined by God, and so he probably falsely says that free acts cannot be absolutely decreed by God. Nor is it worth hearing what Fonseca says, that souls are predefined as they are essential parts of the world, but not with respect to their infusion into bodies. For 1. who would say that souls are predefined by God as to their existing, but not as to their existing? When all the members of David are written in God's book (Ps. 139:16). 2. A treasury of souls kept with God, never to be united to bodies, is possible, since men might never beget children, as is open to them. Who would endure such conjectures?

units.la: 12. Pugnat hoc decretum cum Dei omnipotentia, ergo non est ferendum. Prob. antecedens: si omnes actus liberi habent esse antecedenter ad Dei voluntatem, tum etiam antecedenter ad Dei omnipotentiam. Prob. con-nexio. Quoniam causa omnium rerum est potentia Dei per liberam ipsius voluntatem determinata. Ideoque ne Deus quidem potest efficere, ut plures sint actus volendi aut nolendi, quam sint, nec est penes Deum ut plures salventur, quam qui salvantur, aut pauciores, aut plures vel pauciores damnentur vel inter homines & angelos,quam qui damnantur & certe si effectus contingentes sunt futuri antecedenter ad Dei decretum, non potest omnipotentia sua Deus efficere, ut non sint futuri, qui jam sint futuri; non magis quam Deus potest efficere, ut id non sit, quod jam est: simpliciter enim impossibile involvit contradictionem, & nullo modo poteft esse objectum omnipotentiae. 4. Pugnat cum Dei sapientia etiam: nam sic divina sapientia nihil statuet omnino de ordine volitionum humanarum aut Angelicarum: atqui ordinem absque primo ordinante nemo philosophorum statueret. Prob. connexio. Nam si Petrus prius hoc est voliturus, quam Deus decreverit, ut vellet, tum non est penes Deum ut Petrus prius vellet A. quam vellet B. & prius vellet B. quam vellet C. Neque est penes Deum quod prius sceptrum Iudae fit ablatum, quam veniret Christus: nam non obstante Dei voluntate, poterant Romani non abstulisse sceptrum Iudae, donec ageretur annus vicesimus post Christi resurrectionem. Item poterat Dominus Asini negasse Domino Asinum certo illo die, quo implenda erat prophetia Zach. c. 9. 9. Poterat homo prius peccasse, quam Angeli non obstante decreto, poterat David Keila non exiisse, donec advenisset Saulus, & infinita alia quae fiunt hoc anno poterant fieri anno superiore, quicquid in contrarium statueret Dei sapientia. §. Pugnat cum absoluta Dei libertate, & Dominio in creaturas. Nam si Petrus antecedenter ad Dei decretum credat, & Judas finaliter non credit, constituunt sese formale electionis, & reprobationis objectum, ita ut cum Dei justitia & constantia pugnet vel non, electio Petri, vel non-reprobatio Judæ. Tollitur itaque Dei libertas in prædestinatione.
units.tr: 12. This decree clashes with God's omnipotence; therefore it is not to be borne. I prove the antecedent: if all free acts have being antecedently to God's will, then they also have it antecedently to God's omnipotence. I prove the connection: the cause of all things is the power of God determined by his free will. Therefore not even God can bring it about that there are more acts of willing or of unwilling than there are, nor is it in God's power that more are saved than are saved, or fewer, or that more or fewer are damned, whether among men or among angels, than are damned. Certainly, if contingent effects are future antecedently to God's decree, God cannot by his omnipotence bring it about that those which are going to be future are not future; no more than God can bring it about that what already is is not. For this simply involves a contradiction, and can in no way be an object of omnipotence. 4. It clashes with God's wisdom too. For thus divine wisdom would decide nothing at all about the order of human and angelic volitions, yet no philosopher would posit an order without a first orderer. I prove the connection. If Peter is going to will this before God has decreed that he should will it, then it is not in God's power that Peter should will A before he wills B, and will B before he wills C. Nor is it in God's power that the sceptre was taken from Judah before Christ came. For notwithstanding God's will, the Romans could have failed to take the sceptre from Judah until the twentieth year after Christ's resurrection. Likewise the lord of the ass could have refused the ass to its lord on that very day on which the prophecy of Zech. 9:9 was to be fulfilled. A man could have sinned before the angels did; notwithstanding the decree, David could have not gone out to Keilah until Saul arrived; and countless other things that happen this year could have happened in the previous year, whatever the wisdom of God might decide to the contrary. 5. It clashes with God's absolute liberty and dominion over creatures. For if Peter believes antecedently to God's decree, and Judas finally does not believe, they constitute the formal object of election and reprobation, so that the election of Peter, or the non-reprobation of Judas, either does or does not clash with God's justice and constancy. Thus God's liberty in predestination is taken away.

units.la: 13. Duo sunt hic effugia. 1. Iesuitæ dicunt Deum per scientiam mediam præscientem fidei & infidelitatis actus, quosdam in tali rerum ordine & circumstantiis collocasse, in quibus eos credituros ad finem præscivit, damnandos vero in contrario ordine collocasse, ideoque Deo constare suam libertatem R. 1. Audio commentum Pelagianum. 2. Cogentur hic admittere hominum salvationem & damnationem ex absoluto decreto & cur non etiam exercitium libertatis ex eodem decreto statuent? Imo postquam absolute decrevit quosdam salvare, illi possunt absolute ad finem non credere ex ipsorum doctrina, & sic frustraneum erit Dei decretum. At dicerent Deum ita movere absolute salvandos, quo modo juxta præscientiam suam videt eos ad finem credituros. At vero sic diluo, si antecedenter ad Dei voluntatem sunt non finaliter credituri, adhibita motione congruissima nunquam credent. 3. Quomodo Deus antecedente voluntate velit salutem omnium hominum citra exceptionem ut docent Iesuitæ ex loco 1. Tim. 2. & tamen quosdam velit absolute damnari & ea de causa locare, in eo rerum ordine, in quo non crediturus finaliter, adeoque damnandos praescit. Credo ego omnibus fanioris cerebri esse prorsus [illegible, ~8 letters]. 4. Neque hi Davi effugient: Obj. enim scientiae mediae est prius ipsa scientia: nam omnis scientia suum objectum praesupponit. Ergo prius natura erat libera Dei collocatio salvandorum in tali rerum ordine, in quo ad finem sunt crediturí, & idem verum est de damnandis, ergo si antecedenter ad Dei scientiam collocantur in eo, quo nunc collocantur ordine, tum etiam & antecedenter ad Dei decretum: nam docent hanc mediam scientiam antecedere Dei decretum. Neque possunt negare, quin libera illa collocatio, & omnes actus Dei liberi, sint objectum scientiae mediae. Ergo adhuc Dei libertas in salvatione & damnatione hominum nulla est, quia sunt salvandi & damnandi ante actum libertatis. 5. Damnandi in tali ordine locati, vel necessario credunt, vel liberè. Si prius, perit theologia Iesuitica: si posterius, possunt ad finem credere, ac proinde non obstante illa locatione, faciunt se antecedenter ad Dei decretum objectum electionis & reprobationis. Et non possunt non salvandi salvari, & qui damnantur, non damnari, etiam Deo invito.
units.tr: 13. There are two ways out here. 1. The Jesuits say that God, by his middle knowledge, foresaw the acts of faith and unbelief, and placed some men in such an order of things and circumstances that he foresaw they would believe unto the end, while he placed the damned in the opposite order; and so God's liberty stands secure. Answer 1: I hear a Pelagian fiction. 2. They will be forced to admit that the salvation and damnation of men come from an absolute decree. Why, then, will they not also say that the exercise of liberty comes from that same decree? Indeed, once God has absolutely decreed to save some, those men can, by their own doctrine, absolutely fail to believe unto the end, and so God's decree will be pointless. But they would say that God moves the elect absolutely in the way he foresees they will believe unto the end. My reply is this: if men are antecedently to God's will not going to believe finally, then, even with the most fitting motion applied, they will never believe. 3. How God by his antecedent will wills the salvation of all men without exception, as the Jesuits teach from 1 Tim. 2, and yet by that same will wills some to be absolutely damned and places them, for that reason, in an order of things in which he foresees they will not believe finally and so are to be damned: I believe that this is utterly [illegible, about 8 letters] to anyone of sound mind. 4. Nor will these men escape by this device. For the object of middle knowledge is prior to the knowledge itself, since all knowledge presupposes its object. Therefore God's free placing of the elect in such an order of things, in which they will believe unto the end, is prior by nature, and the same holds for the damned. So if they are placed in the order they now occupy antecedently to God's knowledge, then they are also placed there antecedently to God's decree, for they teach that this middle knowledge precedes God's decree. Nor can they deny that this free placing and all God's free acts are the object of middle knowledge. Therefore God's liberty in the salvation and damnation of men is still nothing, because they are to be saved or damned before any act of liberty. 5. Those who are damned, placed in such an order, either believe necessarily or freely. If the former, Jesuit theology perishes; if the latter, they can believe unto the end, and so, notwithstanding that placing, they make themselves, antecedently to God's decree, the object of election and reprobation. And those who are to be saved cannot but be saved, and those who are damned cannot but not be damned, even with God unwilling.

units.la: 14. Sed quoniam obiter hoc argumentum evertit praedestinationem Arminianam ex praevisa fide, non erit inutile paulo preffius urgere effugia Arminianorum. Nam Corvinus vult Dei libertatem esse causam electionis, non liberam fidei obedientiam, quoniam (inquit)
units.tr: 14. But since this argument incidentally overturns Arminian predestination from foreseen faith, it will not be useless to press somewhat more closely the evasions of the Arminians. For Corvinus holds that the liberty of God is the cause of election, not the free obedience of faith, since (he says)

units.la: F Deus in genere statuit servare fideles, etiam in genere eligit hunc vel illum credentem in individuo, quatenus sic pari seu id quod habet modum partis imitatur toti. Nam singularia sub universali, tanquam pars sub toto comprehenduntur. Resp. 1. Constat quidem Deo libertas in generali decreto, quo statuit salvare credentes cum posset, si quidem voluit, salvare operarios, sed non constat Deo sua libertas in particulari decreto, quo Petrus, non Judas eligitur. Nam primo fiat hic syllogismus, Deus eligit omnes credentes, atqui Petrus credit, ergo Deus eligit Petrum. Conclusio nullo modo est vera propter veritatem majoris, alioqui etiam conclusio hujus syllogismi esset vera, quoniam vera est major. Omnis arbor est substantia, atqui Petrus est arbor, ergo Petrus est substantia. Atqui vel tyrones in rudimentis Dialecticae vix initiati sciunt, majorem veram non reddere conclusionem veram, sed & majoris & assumptionis veritatem simul junctam esse causam totalem, cur conclusio sit vera. Itaque assumptio (Atqui Petrus credit,) nec est certa, nec vera, quoniam Deus eligit omnes credentes: arenosa [?] itaque est haec consequentia. Deus eligit omnes credentes ex suo beneplacito, ergo ex suo beneplacito eligit Petrum: nam Petrus potest non credere, & tum non est electus, etiam stante veritate hujus, quod Deus elegerit omnes credentes. 2. In generali decreto nullam causalitatem Deus exercet aliam, ad electionem Petri potius quam Judae: nam stante generali decreto de salvandis fidelibus, potest Judas eligi & Petrus non eligi: nulla itaque est Dei libertas in electione Petri potius quam Judae, sed quando Petrus libere creditur antecedenter ad Dei decretum, ve fato coactus & necessitate Deus eliget Petrum vel retractabit decretum generale & desinet esse verax & justus. 3. Quaero an Deus absolute decernat salvare credentes, priusquam praesciat, sintne aliqui crediturI, nec ne, an vero nescius, sintne ulli credituri: si hoc posterius dicetur, tum insulsum & fatuum est decretum generale: poterat enim sic decrevisse liberare salvatorem per plusquam 12. legiones angelorum: si vero prius, praescit sintne aliqui credituri, tum generale decretum non est absolutum, ut statuit ipse Arminius, sed conditionatum, & homines praesciuntur credituri priusquam Deus media fidei dederit, quod invertit ordinem decretorum Arminianorum, sed hoc obiter dici volo.
units.tr: F God in general decreed to save believers, and in general chooses this or that believer individually, insofar as what has the mode of a part imitates the whole. For singulars are comprehended under the universal as a part under the whole. Answer 1. It is indeed certain that God has liberty in the general decree by which he decided to save believers, since he could, if he so willed, save the workers. But it is not certain that God has his liberty in the particular decree by which Peter, not Judas, is chosen. For first let this syllogism be made: God elects all believers; but Peter believes; therefore God elects Peter. The conclusion is in no way true on account of the truth of the major premise, otherwise the conclusion of this syllogism would also be true, since the major is true. Every tree is a substance; but Peter is a tree; therefore Peter is a substance. Now even novices barely initiated into the rudiments of dialectic know that a true major premise does not make the conclusion true, but that the truth of both the major and the minor taken together is the whole cause why the conclusion is true. Therefore the minor (But Peter believes,) is neither certain nor true, since God elects all believers. So this inference is shaky: God elects all believers from his good pleasure; therefore from his good pleasure he elects Peter. For Peter can fail to believe, and then he is not elect, even though it is true that God has elected all believers. 2. In the general decree God exercises no other causality toward the election of Peter rather than Judas. For while the general decree about saving the faithful stands, Judas can be elected and Peter not elected. There is therefore no liberty of God in the election of Peter rather than Judas. But when Peter believes freely, antecedently to God's decree, then either God, compelled by fate and necessity, will elect Peter, or he will retract the general decree and cease to be truthful and just. 3. I ask whether God absolutely decrees to save believers before he foreknows whether there are any who will believe or not, or whether he is ignorant whether there will be any who will believe. If the latter is said, then the general decree is silly and foolish: for he could then have decreed to rescue the Saviour by more than twelve legions of angels. But if the former, then he foreknows whether there will be any who believe; and then the general decree is not absolute, as Arminius himself holds, but conditional, and men are foreknown as going to believe before God has given the means of faith. That inverts the order of the Arminian decrees. But I wish to say this only in passing.

units.la: 1 5. Neque penes Dei libertatem est & Dominium quod Assyrii, Chaldaei, Edomitae, Ammonitae &c. vastent ecclesiam Dei, vel non vastent, quod Sabæi spolient Iobum, vel non, quod decem tribus deficiant a familia Davidis propter idololatriam Salomonis, quod David filios generet, ex quibus nasciturus est Christus. Siquidem haec omnia fiunt liberrime & antecedenter ad Dei decretu. Itaque non obstante Dei Dominio non possunt non fieri, & sic Deus fato nexus est ab hisce theologastris,dum homines fato commentitio eximere conentur.
units.tr: 15. Nor is it within God's liberty and dominion that the Assyrians, Chaldeans, Edomites, Ammonites etc. lay waste the church of God or do not; that the Sabaeans despoil Job or not; that the ten tribes fall away from the house of David because of the idolatry of Solomon; or that David beget sons, from whom Christ was to be born. For all these things happen most freely and antecedently to God's decree. Therefore, notwithstanding God's dominion, they cannot but happen, and so God is bound by fate by these little theologians, while they try to free men from a fate of their own invention.

units.la: 16. Pugnat cum infinita divinae naturae persectione: nam si voluntas Dei pendet a determinatione causae contingentis, tum Dei natura non est infinite perfecta: atqui si Deus non decernat contingentia, donec sint futura, Dei volitio pendebit ab operationibus causae contingentis, imo ficDeus ad agendum determinabitur per entia creata: nam posita futuritione effectus contingentis, necessario movebitur ad decernendum, nam non potest Dei voluntas esse indeterminata circa futura contingentia, inter quae sunt multa bona & actus supernaturales fidei, amoris, refipiscentiae &c.
units.tr: 16. It clashes with the infinite perfection of the divine nature. For if the will of God depends on the determination of a contingent cause, then the nature of God is not infinitely perfect. But if God does not decree contingent things until they are future, then God's volition will depend on the operations of a contingent cause; indeed God will be determined to act by created beings. For once the futurity of a contingent effect is posited, he will be necessarily moved to decree it, since the will of God cannot be indeterminate with respect to future contingent things, among which are many good things and supernatural acts of faith, love, repentance, and so on.

units.la: 17. Pugnat cum primae causae dignitate suprema, quae est ut sit causa omnium entium: atqui haec sententia statuit omnia futura contingentia futuritionem habere, & e statu posfibilitatis ad statum futuritionis ab aeterno transfiisse, antequam accederet nutus & libera primae causae volitio, ideoque Dei voluntas non erit prima causa omnium, contra scripturas luculentas Rom. 11. 36. Act. 17. 28. Prov. 16. 17. Apoc. c. 4. 11. & sic Deus non erit primum efficiens & ultimus finis omnium entium: si enim entia habent esse antecedenter Dei ad determinationem liberam & intentionem, in illo prioritate ob nullum finem sunt, neque gloriae Dei inserviunt, quia omnia media divinae gloriae illustrandae habent esse in Dei intentione: atqui haec antevertunt Dei intentionem.
units.tr: 17. It clashes with the supreme dignity of the first cause, which is that it be the cause of all things. But this opinion holds that all future contingent things have futurity and have passed from the state of possibility to the state of futurity from eternity, before the nod and free volition of the first cause came in. So the will of God will not be the first cause of all, against the clear Scriptures, Rom. 11. 36, Acts 17. 28, Prov. 16. 17, Rev. 4. 11. And so God will not be the first efficient and ultimate end of all beings. For if beings have existence antecedently to God's free determination and intention, then in that priority they serve no end, and do not serve the glory of God, since all the means of displaying the divine glory have their being in God's intention; but these things come before God's intention.

units.la: 18. Pugnat etiam cum Dei aeternitate: nam[?] si Dei volitiones sint posteriores volitionibus creatis & temporariis, non sint æternæ. Atqui si contingentia futuritionem habent ante Dei decretum, erunt priora Dei volitionibus.
units.tr: 18. It clashes also with the eternity of God. For if God's volitions are posterior to created and temporal volitions, they are not eternal. But if contingent things have futurity before God's decree, they will be prior to God's volitions.

units.la: 19. Pugnat cum Dei immutabilitate: nam si Deus antecedenter ad determinationem causæ contingentis ipsam flectit, & quo vult determinat, ut habet scriptura, Prov. 21. 1. vel decrevit antecedenter ad illam determinationem, ita movere & flectere causam contingentem, vel aliquid facit in tempore, quod ab æterno non decrevit facere, quod Deum facit mutabilem.
units.tr: 19. It conflicts with the immutability of God. For if God, before determining a contingent cause, bends it and directs it to what he wills, as Scripture says (Prov. 21. 1.), then either he decreed beforehand to move and bend the contingent cause in that way, or he does something in time that he did not decree from eternity to do, which makes God mutable.

units.la: 20. Cum justitia Dei, quatenus declaranda est, pugnat: fieri enim potuit, ut omnes, siquidem vellent, obedirent, tum homines, tum angeli, & sic locus non fuisset Deo etiam volenti patefacere justitiam vindicatricem; & per eandem rationem poterant omnes non obedire, & sic in æternum, non obstante Dei sapiente decreto, latere potuit misericordia, qua Deus patefacere irresistibiliter decreverat.
units.tr: 20. It conflicts with the justice of God, insofar as that justice is to be displayed. For it could have happened that everyone, if they had wished, would obey, both men and angels, and so there would have been no place for God, even if willing, to display his avenging justice. By the same reasoning, all could have refused to obey, and so, despite God's wise decree, the mercy which God had irresistibly decreed to display could have remained hidden for ever.

units.la: 21. Pugnat cum gratia Dei, & gratuito amore: non enim Deus ex voluntate regenerat nos, ut docet Iacobus c. 1. v. 18. Neque ex immenso erga nos amore, uti ait Paulus Eph. 2. 4. Neque secundum gratiosum beneplacitum, ut ait Christus Matt. 11. 26. sed ex debito & necessitate: nam antecedenter ad actum gratiosæ voluntatis, regeneratio nostra futuritionem habuit, & quod est futurum, Deus non potuit antevertere quin sit futurum.
units.tr: 21. It conflicts with the grace of God and his free love. For God does not regenerate us of his own will, as James teaches (Jas 1. 18.); nor from his boundless love towards us, as Paul says (Eph. 2. 4.); nor according to his gracious good pleasure, as Christ says (Matt. 11. 26.). Rather, it is from debt and necessity. For our regeneration had its future existence before any act of gracious will, and what is going to happen, God could not prevent from happening.

units.la: 22. Hoc decretum etiam invertit euangelium: statuit enim euangelium humiliationem & salutarem tristitiam antecedere exaltationem & gaudium, at vero quatenus haec, sæpe liberæ fiunt, est penes homines prius gaudere, quam sese humiliare, neque potest talis ordo dici Dei decretum, nam antecedenter erat ad decretum, deinde euangelium est liberum Dei decretum de effectione cordisnovi, in electis, de indurandis reprobis, de liberanda ecclesia, per agentia libera; de defendis hostibus Christi per bella cruenta, quae libere fiunt, de humiliatione electorum per ærumnas & tentationes permultas, quae ipsis accidunt per contingentes causas, nempe mundi odium &c. At vero hoc decretum statuit, haec omnia fieri antecedenter ad Dei decretum, imo salvatorem interimi, apostolos flagellari, martyres occidi, antichristum dominari tyrannice, pseudo-christos decipere, & seducere multos, electos perseverare, hypocritas deficere antecedenter ad Dei decretum, & hoc est totum euangelium esse fortuitum retum[?] eventum, & confluxum præter & ante sapiens Dei decretum, contra scripturas, E-phes. 3. 9. 1 Cor. 2. 7.
units.tr: 22. This decree also overturns the gospel. For the gospel sets humiliation and saving sorrow before exaltation and joy; but since these come about freely, it depends on men to rejoice before they humble themselves, and such an order cannot be called a decree of God. For it would have been prior to the decree. Then the gospel is God's free decree concerning the creation of a new heart in the elect, the hardening of the reprobate, the deliverance of the Church through free agents, the defence of Christ's enemies through bloody wars, which are done freely, and the humbling of the elect through many distresses and temptations which befall them through contingent causes, namely the hatred of the world and so on. But this decree holds that all these things happen before God's decree; indeed that the Saviour is slain, the apostles scourged, the martyrs put to death, Antichrist tyrannically rules, false christs deceive and lead many astray, the elect persevere, and hypocrites fall away, all before God's decree. And this means that the whole gospel is a fortuitous series of chance events and a confluence of things apart from and prior to the wise decree of God, contrary to Scripture (Eph. 3. 9.; 1 Cor. 2. 7.).

units.la: 23. Hoc decretum omnem patientiam sanctorum in ærumnis tollit: quorsum enim David in domino se solaretur Psal. 39. Tacui (inquit) quia tu fecisti, si antecedenter ad Dei decretum factum est est ei malum ab hostibus, qui contra Shemei convitia in Deo solatium quaereret, si convitia illa futuritionem habuerint antecedenter ad Dei decretum: nam sanctis ad Deum confugientibus, Deo esset in promptu responsio: ferenda, non flenda (mi fili) sunt ista mala, quae a mundo & causis contingentibus inferuntur: nam evenerunt illa, priusquam ego quicquam de ipsis decreveram, fortuna prius aleam jecerat ab aeterno, ego non potui non subscribere adversae istae fortunae: non est itaque quod in me solamen aerumarum vestrarum quaeratis. An non frigida erit piorum consolatio in Deo?
units.tr: 23. This decree removes all the patience of the saints in their distresses. For why would David console himself in the Lord? Psalm 39. I was silent (he says), because you did it; if it were the case that the insults of Shimei had their future existence before God's decree, what comfort would David seek in God against the enemies who did him evil? For when the saints flee to God, God would have this answer ready: "These evils, my son, which are inflicted by the world and contingent causes, must be borne, not wept over. For they happened before I decided anything about them; fortune had cast the die from eternity; I could not but agree to this adverse fortune. There is therefore no reason for you to seek in me the solace of your miseries." Would not the consolation of the godly in God then be cold?

units.la: 24. Neque fides hic locum haberet: nam quorsum ecclesia in bello in auxilium Iehovæ contra hostes speraret? nam antecedenter ad Dei decretum, rata erat victoria & fataliter statuta, neque contra mortem improvisam & immaturam valeret; quod spiritus sanctus ait Iob. 14. 6. Præcisi sunt dies ejus, numerus mensium penes te est, limites ejus fecisti, quos non transgrediatur. Nego (inquit Corvinus) decreto mere absoluto fixos esse, nisi quatenus concessum est semel mori, & post judicium; sed si horam ac articulum mortis præcisio decreto, ita vis ordinatum esse, ut simul præcise decretum sit, quod homo tali momento, tali modo, per talia media sit moriturus, eo modo terminum vitæ fixum esse nego. Imo contra ait fieri preces pro longæva vita, inde sequi ordinari a Deo, ut quidam sese necarent & frustraneam esse medicinam. Sed resp. 1. Iobus non illic disserit de necessitate moriendi simpliciter, sed tali præcisso tempore. Iobus ait ita fixos esse-menses & dies ut ipsos transgredi homo non possit, atheus novator non verecundatur Deo obloqui, quasi homo per preces, per medicinam possit ultra à Deo praescriptum momentum vitam prorogare. 2. Limites negat absolute esse fixos. Vis ergo figi limites conditionate: at cedo conditionem nempe ex hypothesi quod morbus lethalis tali tempore ipsum invaserit, ac deinde redibit quaestio, an ille morbus lethalis tali tempore invadens fit absolute, an vero conditionate ordinatus: si prius, habetur institutum: si posterius, rogito denuo conditionem, & tandem Sophista nos huc deducet ut dicamus Deum hoc ordinasse, siquidem hoc futurum fit, risum teneatis amici. 3. Modum, horam tenebrarum: qua caperetur Christus, genus mortis, manuum & pedum confossionem, fatellites mortis, sepulturam &c. a Deo fuisse, Christo ordinata ait scriptura, modum mortis Iefabelis, & mortem, Achabi mortem praecise Deus decrevit. 4. Adventum gloriosum Christi oramus, Apoc. 22.20. At Deus diem adventus praeconstituit Act. 17.31. Non aliter hic Sophista argutatur, quam Diabolus cum Christo Matt. 4. Deus praefecit angelos tui custodes, Ergo dejice temet e pinaculo templi. Ita ille: Deus absolute decrevit horam & modum mortis: frustranea ergo medicina, inanes preces, vana periculorum prudens declinatio.
units.tr: 24. Nor would faith have any place here. For why would the Church hope, in war, for the help of Jehovah against its enemies? For before God's decree the victory was certain and fated, and it would not avail against an unforeseen and untimely death. The Holy Spirit says (Job 14. 6.): His days are cut off; the number of his months is with you; you have appointed his limits, which he cannot pass. I deny (says Corvinus) that they are fixed by a purely absolute decree, except insofar as it has been granted that one dies once, and after judgment. But if the precise hour and moment of death were so ordained by decree that it was simultaneously decreed precisely that a man would die at such a moment, in such a manner, by such means, I deny that the term of life is fixed in that way. Indeed, he says the contrary, that prayers are made for long life, and that it follows from this that some have killed themselves, and that medicine is in vain. But I answer: first, Job does not there discuss the necessity of dying simply, but at such a precise time. Job says that the months and days are so fixed that a man cannot pass beyond them; the innovating atheist is not ashamed to contradict God, as if a man could by prayer or by medicine prolong life beyond the moment prescribed by God. Second, he denies that the limits are absolutely fixed. You want the limits to be fixed conditionally, then. But I grant the condition, namely on the hypothesis that a lethal disease has seized him at such a time; and then the question returns: whether that lethal disease, seizing him at such a time, is ordained absolutely or only conditionally. If the former, the point is conceded; if the latter, I ask again about the condition, and in the end the sophist will lead us to say that God ordained this, provided it is going to happen. Hold your laughter, friends. Third, the manner and the hour of darkness in which Christ was taken, the kind of death, the piercing of hands and feet, the executioners of death, the burial and so on, Scripture says were ordained by God for Christ; and God decreed precisely the manner of Jezebel's death and the death of Ahab. Fourth, we pray for the glorious coming of Christ (Rev. 22. 20.); but God has fixed beforehand the day of his coming (Acts 17. 31.). The sophist argues here no differently than the devil did with Christ (Matt. 4.): God has set his angels over you to guard you; therefore cast yourself down from the pinnacle of the temple. So he argues: God has absolutely decreed the hour and manner of death; therefore medicine is in vain, prayers are empty, and the prudent avoidance of dangers is pointless.

units.la: §. Frustra sperarem placidam mortem & repentinae mortis declinationem à Iehova, si-rata rata fuit mors & fixa, quoad modum, genus, media, locum & tempus, prius natura quam Iehova suo decreto quicquam de morte mea statuerit; quorsum enim siderem in Iehova, quod est futurum antecedenter ad ipsius voluntatem, non potest ille vel sua omnipotentia efficere ut non sit futurum.
units.tr: §. I would hope in vain for a peaceful death, or for the avoidance of a sudden death from Jehovah, if death was settled and fixed, as to its manner, its kind, its means, its place and its time, by nature prior to Jehovah deciding anything about my death by his decree. For why should I trust in Jehovah about what is going to happen before his will? Not even his omnipotence can bring it about that it will not happen.

units.la: 25. Fruftraneæ sunt preces, & gratiarum actio, & gratitudo omnis in Deum ex hoc decreto, quorsum deprecarer flagellationem linguæ, latronum in itinere manus violentas, incarcerationem, contagiosas pestilentias ex convictu cum morbidis, mortem inopinam ex ruina ædium, uxoris & liberorum mortem immaturam & acerbam, longævitatem, dierum decurtationem, spoliationem ab hostibus, ædium incendia & infinita alia quæ ministerio contingentium causarum eveniunt mala? Cui usui pro hisce Deum precibus follicitarem, & supplicarem? hæc enim omnia ratam fixamque futuritionem habuerunt ab æterno antecedenter ad Dei scientiam mediam, & multo magis ad Dei voluntatem.
units.tr: 25. Prayers and thanksgiving are in vain, and all gratitude to God, on the basis of this decree. Why should I pray against the scourge of the tongue, violent hands of robbers on the road, imprisonment, contagious plagues from association with the sick, sudden death from the collapse of a house, the untimely and bitter death of wife and children, long life, the shortening of days, plunder by enemies, fires in houses, and the infinite other evils which come about through the work of contingent causes? To what use would I importune and beseech God on account of these things? For all of these have had a fixed and settled future existence from eternity, before God's knowledge of what is possible (his middle knowledge), and much more before his will.

units.la: 26. Quorsum Iobus à Sabæis spoliatus nomini Iehovæ, qui dat & aufert benediceret? spoliatio enim illa totum esse futurum habuit citra & ante omnem Dei volitionem. Quorsum miles rerum potitus victoriis præclarus in dextra Iehovæ in bello præpotentis gloriaretur? Psal. 20. 7.
units.tr: 26. Why should Job, plundered by the Sabeans, bless the name of Jehovah, who gives and takes away? For that plundering had its whole future existence apart from and before any will of God. Why should a soldier who has gained the spoils of victory glory in the right hand of Jehovah, mighty in war? (Ps. 20. 7.)

units.la: 27. Verbum, promissiones, & commigationes[?] frustra plane à Deo adhibentur ea intentione ut homines ad obedientiam perducerent, aut ut reprobi inexcusabiles fierent; per voluntariam suam contumaciam, frustra enim Deus eorum obedientiam intendit, quorum obedientia totum esse habet ante talem intentionem, frustra per negationem auxilii efficacis intendit reproborum contumaciam in poenam scelerum antegressorum, quando Dei volitio nullo modo est talis poenae causa: tollitur itaque omnis ministerii necessitas.
units.tr: 27. Word, promises and threatenings are clearly used by God in vain, with the intention of bringing men to obedience or of making the reprobate inexcusable through their own wilful obstinacy. For God would be intending in vain the obedience of those whose obedience has its whole existence before any such intention; and he would be intending in vain, by withholding effective help, the obstinacy of the reprobate as punishment for their previous sins, when God's will is in no way the cause of such punishment. Thus all necessity of the ministry is removed.

units.la: 28. Frustra etiam spiritus sanctus operatur in nobis salutarem curam & solicitudinem operandi salutem, & studium & zelum bonorum operum; quando illud studium & sollicitudo fataliter antecedunt omnem Dei tum praescientiam tum volitionem, frustanea etiam omnis Dei actio in mentem, voluntatem & affectus, ea intentione ut sanctificemur, quando antecedenter ad omnem Dei intentionem perficitur sanctificatio nostra: idem enim est, ac si Deus id intenderet facere, quod jam factu est.
units.tr: 28. The Holy Spirit also works in us in vain: the saving care and concern to work out our salvation, and the zeal and eagerness for good works, are in vain, when that eagerness and concern necessarily precede all of God's foreknowledge and will. Likewise every action of God on the mind, the will and the affections, undertaken to make us holy, is idle, when our sanctification is accomplished before any intention of God. For it amounts to the same thing as if God intended to do what has already been done.

units.la: 29. Denique non video proclivioriem viam ad Atheismum, Epicurismum & solium fortunae seu contingentiae stabiliendum, qua conscientiae omnium hominum a Deo a providentia avocentur, & ipsis causis fortuitis plane voluntatione operantibus infigantur; Iesuitico-Arminianismus, erit itaque Epicurismus.
units.tr: 29. Finally, I do not see a readier road to establishing atheism, Epicureanism and the throne of fortune, or of contingency, than this: men's consciences are drawn away from God and from providence, and fixed upon chance causes that work entirely by their own will. Jesuitical Arminianism, therefore, will be Epicureanism.

units.la: 30. Stet itaque decretum absolutum, & cadat necesse est decretum conditionatum. At vero Tho. Jackfonus [?] Anglus cudit nobis tertium decretum, quod disjunctivum vocat, cujus objectum jeiunus iste theologus facit. possibile. Ita ille impeccabilis regula æterna æquitatis, quæ ab æterno decernit quicquid pos-sibile est, & præscit quicquid est futurum, mullum statutum ponit quod absolutæ & æternæ suæ potestati dominii adversetur. Semper (inquit) fuit, est, & erit ex æquo indifferens & liber ad retribuendum unicuique secundum opera ipsius. Et alibi dicit, unicuique antecedenti possibili decrevit consequens correspondens. Et 2. par. 2. cap. 17. Nullum est in Deo decretum de contingentibus præterquam disjunctivum, aut erit, aut non erit, aut pluet per totum diem cras aut non pluet per totum diem. Hodie aut Sol splendebit hora decima & secunda, aut non splendebit. Hæc effata cerebri Silvestris & feri ad examen revocare non est inutile. Nam.
units.tr: 30. Let the absolute decree stand, then, and the conditional decree must necessarily fall. But Thomas Jackson the Englishman coins for us a third decree, which he calls disjunctive, and whose object this barren theologian makes "possible." Thus he writes: The eternal and unchangeable rule of equity, which from eternity decrees whatever is possible and foreknows whatever is to be, sets up no decree that opposes its absolute and eternal power of dominion. It always was, is, and will be, equally indifferent and free to render to each person according to his works. And elsewhere he says: To each possible antecedent he has decreed a corresponding consequent. And in part 2, book 2, cap. 17. There is in God no decree concerning contingent things except a disjunctive one: either it will be, or it will not be; either it will rain all day tomorrow, or it will not rain all day. Today either the sun will shine at the tenth and second hour, or it will not shine. It is not useless to call these utterances of a brain of wood and wild beast to account. For:

units.la: 1. Tuissius vir in Palæstra Scholastica bene Deus quantus! Observat objectum decreti divini non esse necessarium: non enim Deus decernit, ut ipse sit infinitus, justus &c. Nam non potest non esse infinitus: atqui objectum decreti disjunctivi est necessarium, quia necesse est ut Petrus vel credat, vel non credat, quia contradicentium altera pars est necessario vera, altera falsa. 2. Multæ prædictiones Dei & promissiones erunt ex hoc decreto disjunctivo aperte falsæ: erit illo die, postremis diebus hoc faciam, dabo vobis cor novum. Zach. 12. 10. & respicient ad me, quem transfixerunt, & clangent &c. ferre possunt contrarium rium plane sensum, non erit illo die; non dabo vobiscor novum. non respicient ad me, non clangent &c. prophetandum tibi est Jer.
units.tr: 1. Tuissius, a man in the Scholastic Wrestling-ground, rightly observes, how great a god he is! He notes that the object of the divine decree is not necessary: for God does not decree that he himself be infinite, just, and so on, since he cannot fail to be infinite. But the object of the disjunctive decree is necessary, because it is necessary that Peter either believes or does not believe, since one of two contradictories is necessarily true and the other false. 2. Many of God's predictions and promises will, on this disjunctive decree, be plainly false. "It shall come to pass in that day," "in the latter days I will do this," "I will give you a new heart" (Zech. 12. 10), "and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and mourn," and so on. These may just as well bear the plainly opposite sense: "it shall not come to pass in that day"; "I will not give you a new heart"; "they shall not look upon me, nor mourn," and so on. "You are to prophesy" (Jer.

units.la: 1. Quare? Constitui enim te prophetā gentibus. Imo ex hac constitutione sequitur, ergo non erit tibi prophetandum; & quis tum decernere potest inter Deum praedicentem hoc fore, & praedicentem hoc non fore? 3. Hinc sequitur Dei voluntatem esse nullorum actuum supernaturalium causam; nullius boni moralis siquidem posito decreto Dei possunt omnes res decretae nunquam esse, imo tam diabolorum quam Dei voluntas est causa boni, siquidem ea posita potest bonum morale esse vel non esse, poterat simpliciter Christus incarnari, vel non, mori & redimere genus humanum, vel non, Judaei in captivitatem abduci a Chaldaeis, vel non, posita Dei voluntate de futuritione horumomnium, imo totum evangelium potest esse vel verum vel falsum, quando multa sunt in evangelio quae interventu agentium contingentium implentur. 4. Omnia fere argumenta contra decretum conditionatum, hoc decretum profligabunt: mihi enim nihil fidei aut spei adversus mala quae contingenter eveniunt in Jehovam esse potest, siquidem posito ipsius decreto, possunt tam evenire, quam non evenire. Ecquid enim solatii foret sanctis in Deo sub onere aerumnarum tantum non exspirantibus, siquidem mala contingentia ipsis vel evenire, vel non evenire possunt, non obstante sapientissimo Dei decreto? tum non est quod oremus Deum vitæ prorogationem, fecundam valetudinem, gratiam fidei & perseverantiæ contra tentationes, constantiam, in adversis patientiam. Quid aliud hic Deus nobis respondere posset, quam? penes me ista vel promovere vel non, non est, nam vel ista vobis eveniunt, vel non; ego fatalibus contingentiæ citra meæ voluntatis actum constitutis subscribo vel invitus.
units.tr: 1. "Why? For I have appointed you a prophet to the nations" (Jer. 1). Indeed, from this appointment it follows: therefore you are not to prophesy; and who then can decide between God predicting that this will be, and God predicting that it will not be? 3. Hence it follows that the will of God is the cause of no supernatural acts, and of no moral good. For once God's decree is posited, all things decreed may never come to be; indeed, the will of the devils is as much the cause of good as the will of God, since, that being posited, a moral good may or may not be. Christ could simply have been incarnate or not; could die and redeem the human race or not; the Jews could be led away into captivity by the Chaldeans or not. Given God's will concerning the futurition of all these things, the whole gospel may be either true or false, although many things in the gospel are fulfilled through the intervention of contingent agents. 4. Almost all the arguments against the conditional decree will overthrow this decree. For to me there can be no faith or hope against the evils that happen contingently to Jehovah, since, with his decree posited, they can happen just as well as not happen. What comfort would there be for the saints in God, under the burden of miseries when they are scarcely breathing their last, if contingent evils could either happen to them or not happen, notwithstanding God's most wise decree? Then there is no reason for us to pray God for prolonged life, fruitful health, the grace of faith and perseverance against temptations, constancy, and patience in adversity. What else could God answer us here than: "It is not in my power to advance these things or not; for either these things will happen to you or they will not. I subscribe to fated contingencies, set up without any act of my will, either unwillingly or against my will."

units.la: 31. Si possibilia sunt à Deo decreta, tum decrevit Deus liberare filium suum per duodecim legiones Angelorum: ea enim liberatio fuit possibilis: at vero quid impedire potuit illius decreti impletionem. Num boni Angeli sunt Deo minus obsequentes? non dicent. Num ipse Deus sua decreta quo minus impleantur, impediat? Tum non creatio mundi, excitatio filiorum Abrahami ex lapidibus, diabolorum redemptio sunt decreta; quis ista audiret prodigia? 2. Decretum nihil statuit nisi quod divinæ sapientiæ consultissimum videtur, ac proinde cujus contrarium Deo minime expediens videtur, alioqui Deus erit agens inconsultum, ac proinde decrevit ut frangerentur ossa Christi, & non frangerentur. 3. Quis sapiens judex terrenus decernit ut sontes vel necarentur, vel non necarentur? At tale decretum Deo affingitur. 4 Si Deus quicquid possibile est, decernit, tum peccata hominum & Angelorum, tum quæ sunt, tum quæ possibilia decrevit. Nunquid igitur Deus erit author peccati? & peccata Dei vo[?]Iuntate fiunt? 5. Hoc dato quod Deus nihil omnino decrevisset, quod fieri potuit, quia liberè & non necessitate & omnia extra se voluit, & creavit, tamen omnia quæ nunc possibilia sunt, fuissent possibilia. In habitudine quippe ad Dei omnipotentiam, non ad Dei voluntatem res sunt possibiles: ergo res possibiles sunt citra omne Dei decretum, neque necesse est ut decernantur. 6. Deus ex infinitâ suâ præscientiâ videt, quæ sunt futura, quæ non: atqui nullâ sapientiâ id fore decernitur, quod decernens vidit nunquam futurum: nam quo fine decernerentur nunquam futura? Nullo certo fine. Certe ad salvandam libertarem humanam possibile decerni dicitur: atqui hinc inclinare videtur, Deum non omnia futura præscire, sed quando fiunt, quod est possibile, ut sic accrescat Deo nova scientia. 7. Quod Deus decernit fore, liberè decernit fore, si iaque Deus non decrevisset possibilia, tum possibilia non fuissent possibilia, quod est contradictorium. 8. Quia futurum aliquid superaddit possibili, quæritur an futurum possibile decernatur à Deo, an non. Si prius, vel absolute, & sic perit decretum disjunctivum: nam eadem res futura, non est, & futura absolute, & non futura, hæc enim sunt contradicentia, vel futurum conditionatè decernitur; at qua conditione? Ex hypothesi quod sit futurum: at quæritur infinities, an hypothesis futura absolute, an conditionatè decernatur, si futurum non omnino decernatur, tum primo falso dicit Iacksò[?]. Omne possibile à Deo decerni, tum etiam futurum esse incipit citra Dei voluntatem, & periclitatur providentia Dei. 9. Vana & nulla effet omnis ratiocinatio scripturae à Dei decreto: nam ex decreto rei possibilis, tam hoc quam non hoc sequitur. 10. Insulsa est collocatio inter Dei consilium quod rescindi non potest, & humanum quod rescindi potest Psal. 33. 10. 11. Quis enim in quaestionem vocet, an Dei consilium de re quae potest tam non esse, quam esse, cujusmodi est possibile, possit rescindi? sic enim humanum consilium aeque fixum esset atque divinum: nam quod homines decernunt, id vel potest esse, vel non esse. 11. Frustra Deum oramus, in eo confidimus, ei voluntatem nostram patienter submittimus in secundis vel adversis, si Dei voluntas nullam causalitatem exercet citra futuritionem rei, vel non futuritionem, sed circa solam possibilitatem, quasi vero David Deum possibilitatem liberationis à Saule, Absalomo, & aliis hostibus, non actualem liberationem oraret; quicquid rerum gerirur id fortunae, non providentiae ascribendum foret. Imo quicquid boni à Dei voluntate petunt impii, id continuo haberent, & nunquam non exaudirentur; nam possibile fuit illud bonum per Dei voluntatem, at vero futuritionem, Dei voluntas velle non potuit, absque insigni injuria in novam Deam contingentiae.
units.tr: 31. If God's decrees concern possibilities, then God decreed to free his Son by twelve legions of angels, for that deliverance was possible. But what could have hindered the fulfilment of that decree? Are the good angels less obedient to God? They will not say so. Does God himself hinder his own decrees from being fulfilled? Then the creation of the world, the raising up of the children of Abraham from stones, and the redemption of the devils would not be decrees either. Who would hear such prodigies? 2. A decree determines only what seems most wise to the divine wisdom, and therefore whose contrary seems least expedient to God; otherwise God would be an agent without counsel, and so he would have decreed that the bones of Christ be broken and not be broken. 3. What wise earthly judge decrees that the guilty either be put to death or not be put to death? Yet such a decree is ascribed to God. 4. If God decrees whatever is possible, then he decrees the sins of men and angels, both those that are and those that are possible. Will God then be the author of sin, and will sins come to be by the will of God? 5. Grant that God had decreed nothing at all of what could come to be, since he freely, and not by necessity, willed and created all things outside himself. Still, all things that are now possible would have been possible. For things are possible in relation to God's omnipotence, not to God's will.
