Therefore possible things are independent of any decree of God, and it is not necessary that they be decreed. 6. God by his infinite foreknowledge sees what will be and what will not be. But no wisdom decrees what the one who decrees has seen will never be; for to what end would things that never will be be decreed? To no certain end. Surely it is said that the possible is decreed in order to save human freedom; but this seems to incline towards God not foreknowing all future things, but only when they come to pass, which is possible, so that new knowledge would accrue to God. 7. What God decrees to be, he decrees to be freely. If therefore God had not decreed the possibles, then the possibles would not have been possible, which is a contradiction. 8. Because the future adds something to the possible, it is asked whether the possible future is decreed by God or not. If first, then either absolutely, and so the disjunctive decree perishes: for the same future thing both is not and is absolutely future and not future, since these are contradictories; or the future is decreed conditionally. But on what condition? On the hypothesis that it will be. And it is asked endlessly whether the hypothesis is decreed as absolutely future or conditionally. If the future is not decreed at all, then the first thing Jackson says is false, namely that every possible is decreed by God; then the future too begins to be apart from God's will, and the providence of God is endangered. 9. All reasoning from Scripture about God's decree would be vain and void: for from the decree of a possible thing, both this and not-this follow. 10. The contrast between God's counsel, which cannot be rescinded, and human counsel, which can be rescinded, is foolish (Ps. 33. 10). 11. For who would call in question whether God's counsel concerning a thing that can be just as much not to be as to be, which is what is possible, could be rescinded? For then human counsel would be just as fixed as divine, since what men decree either can be or can not be. 11. We pray to God in vain, we trust in him in vain, we submit our will patiently to him in prosperity or adversity, if the will of God exercises no causality in the futurition or non-futurition of a thing, but only in its possibility. As if David were praying God merely for the possibility of deliverance from Saul, Absalom and his other enemies, and not for actual deliverance! Whatever happens in the world would have to be ascribed to fortune, not to providence. Indeed, whatever good the impious ask from the will of God, they would continually have it, and would never be refused; for that good was possible through the will of God, but the will of God could not will its futurition without a notable injury to the new goddess of contingency.

units.la: 32. Qui dicit Deum esse, & futurum semper indifferentem & liberum ad retribuendum unicuique secundum opera ipsius, is aeternitatem divini decreti pernegat. Atqui hoc facit hic Iacksonus. Nam ab aeterno Deus suam voluntatem ita determinavit ad tractandum homines secundum opera, ut non possit non ita ipsos tractare, nisi vellet, & promissa, & comminationes rescindere, quamvis nemo afferat Deum, vi decreti cogi ad homines ita tractandos: tam enim liberè Deus decreta exequitur, quam decreta sua facit, si loquamur de libertate naturae, quia necessitate hypothetica, non potest non decreta exequi. Sed Iacksonus vult Deum ne quidem necessitate decreti, & hypothetica hominibus retribuere secundum opera ipsorum, sed volitiones liberas in Deo de novo oriri, secundum ortum & interitum volitionum angelicarum & humanarum, quia vult decreta irrevocabila divinae libertati obesse: imo & futuritio & existentia actualis effectuum contingentium, Iacksono, antecedunt potius quam sequuntur Dei decreta.
units.tr: 32. Whoever says that God exists and will always be indifferent and free to repay each person according to their works denies the eternity of the divine decree. Yet this is what Jackson does. For from eternity God so determined his will to deal with men according to their works that he cannot but deal with them so, unless he wished to rescind his promises and threats. No one asserts that God is compelled by the force of a decree to treat men in this way. God executes his decrees as freely as he makes them, if we speak of freedom of nature, since by hypothetical necessity he cannot but execute them. But Jackson wants God not even to repay men according to their works by the necessity of a decree, even a hypothetical one. Instead, he wants free volitions to arise anew in God, following the rise and passing of angelic and human volitions, because he holds that irrevocable decrees obstruct divine freedom. Indeed, for Jackson, the futurition and actual existence of contingent effects come before God's decrees rather than after them.

units.la: 33. Si unicuique antecedenti possibili decrevit consequens correspondens, age dic, quod consequens mundi non creati, Christi incarnati & non crucifixi? Haec enim sunt possibilia. Imo sic Deus suam gloriam non intendit per media possibilia. Nam tam non glorificationem sui, per antecedens possibile, quam glorificationem intendit. 2. Quae hic sapientia antecedenti, quod Deus praescit nunquam futurum, decernere consequens? num saperet Mater quae vestes & alimenta pararet fœtui quem in ventre certissimè novit enecatum? At (inquiunt) quia possibile antecedens, ideò decrevit consequens, & ex multis possibilibus antecedentibus hoc potest de facto fieri, ideoque consultum est ut paretur ei consequens correspondens. At vero tenet hæc providentia in hominibus futurorum contingentium ignaris, Deo vero ab æterno notum erat, quod antecedens possibile esset suturum, quod non. 3. Consequens possibile vel est contingens, vel necessarium possibili antecedenti; si contingens, posito antecedente possibili, potest nunquam sequi consequens possibile. Ergo cuidam [?]antecedenti possibili, nullum aptavit consequens, sed fallitur plane Dei decretum: si vero consequens fit necessarium, tum vel necessario fit à causa secunda, vel à prima. Si prius, quæro propositioni Iudæ, quod est consequens necessarium? Num à necessaria causa secunda est, quod Iudas laqueo sibi necem crearet? Hoc si dicitur, non peccavit Iudas sese laqueo committendo, si necessarium est hoc consequens à prima causa, à Deo erat necessitas peccati. Idem dici potest de languore & tristitia Achitophelis ex repudiato suo consilio, quod nefarium scelus consequutum est. 4. Non alio tendunt, quæ dictat rudis iste novator, quà ut omnia fortunæ arbitrio gerantur, & per Dei decreta non determinentur ex multis possibilibus, quædam ad futuritionem, quædam ad non-futuritionem, sed ad salvandam fortunam, seu commentitiâ hanc contingentiam, omnia vult à Deo possibilitati relinqui, Dei voluntatem dependentem plane à futuritione possibilis, caeco quodam modo, aptasse consequens quoddam, ne forte antecedens inane videretur. §. Quid intelligit per consequens correspondens? vel intelligit correspondens praemium ex ordine iustitiae, vel id quod proxime sequitur ex antecedente possibili. Si prius, vult Deum neminem nominatim eligere vel reprobasse, sed vitam & damnationem confuso quodam decreto omnibus religuisse ut praemium actuum possibilium bonorum vel malorum, & hoc est Deum non eligere, sed homines. Deinde multi ad tempus credentes & iustificati ex Arminio nullum praemium ex ordine iustitiae consequuntur: deficiunt enim à fide in articulo extremo vitae & praemium aeternae damnationis probe anteactae vitae consequuntur, & multi flagitiosi in extremo vitae exitu credunt & resipiscunt, & consequuntur vitam aeternam; an quaeso vita aeterna est consequens, possibile correspondens antecedenti vitae flagitiosae & profligatae? 3. Peccatum esse peccatorum antecedentium poenam non diffitentur Arminiani & expresse id docet scriptura: itaque peccatum erit correspondens consequens a Deo decretum. 4. Omnibus electis possibilis est defectio & finalis impoenitentia, & reprobis possibilis in fide perseverantia. Ergo Deus non minus electis exitium quam vitam, & reprobis vitam quam exitium decrevit, & sic universalis est electio, quod est repugnans in adjecto, & universalis reprobatio. Si vero consequens correspondens est id quod proxime sequitur ex antecedente possibili, tum Davidis innocentiæ decrevit Deus Sauli animum malevolentiæ & livoris plenum; ut correspondens consequens Christi prædicationi sincerae veritatis Dei immanem & horrendam Domini gloriæ crucifixionem, Chaldeorum in Dei Ecclesiam truculentiæ decrevit regnum florentissimum & bonorum omnium affluentiam: hoc vero correspondens consequens truculentiæ nemo dicet. 6. Quod Deus decrevit id stabit, & indeclinabiliter fiet Esai. 14. At vero consequentia correspondentia antecedenti possibili, plæraque tantum sunt possibilia & nunquam futura; ergo non sunt à Deo decreta. 7. Hoc dicto innuit, omnia bona aut mala simpliciter relinqui in statu possibilitatis, neque à Deo voluntate determinari, quod tollit usum precum, fidei, spei, gratitudinis, submissi in Deum animi, quicquid boni vel mali ex causis contingentibus nobis eveniat.
units.tr: 33. If God decreed for every possible antecedent its corresponding consequent, then come, tell me: what is the consequent of a world not created, or of Christ incarnate but not crucified? These are possible. Indeed, in this way God does not intend his glory through possible means, for he intends the non-glorification of himself through a possible antecedent just as much as the glorification. 2. What wisdom is there in decreeing a consequent for an antecedent which God foreknows will never be future? Would a mother be wise who prepared clothes and food for a foetus she knew with certainty had been killed in the womb? But they say: because the antecedent is possible, he decreed the consequent, and since of many possible antecedents this one can actually come about, it was prudent to prepare the corresponding consequent for it. But such foresight belongs to men who are ignorant of future contingents. God, however, had known from eternity that the antecedent would be future, which it would not be. 3. A possible consequent is either contingent or necessary to the possible antecedent. If contingent, then, given the possible antecedent, the possible consequent may never follow. Therefore for a certain possible antecedent he assigned no consequent, and the decree of God is plainly mistaken. If, however, the consequent becomes necessary, then it is made necessary either by a secondary cause or by the first cause. If by the former, I ask about the proposition concerning Judas: what is the necessary consequent? Is it from a necessary secondary cause that Judas made a noose to bring about his own death? If this is said, Judas did not sin in committing himself to the noose; but if this consequent is necessary from the first cause, then the necessity of the sin was from God. The same may be said of the languor and sadness of Ahithophel over his rejected counsel, which was followed by a wicked crime. 4. These things which this crude innovator dictates tend to nothing else than that all things are governed by the will of fortune, and are not determined by the decrees of God from among many possibles, some toward futurition and some toward non-futurition. But in order to save fortune, or this fictitious contingency, he wants everything left to possibility, and God's will, depending wholly on the futurition of the possible, to have fitted, in a certain blind manner, some consequent, lest perhaps the antecedent seem empty. §. What does he mean by the corresponding consequent? Either he means the reward that follows from the order of justice, or that which most immediately follows from the possible antecedent. If the former, he wants God to have elected and reprobated no one by name, but to have left life and damnation to all by a confused decree, as the reward of possible good or evil acts. And this is not God electing but men. Next, many who believe and are justified for a time, according to Arminius, obtain no reward from the order of justice. For they fall away from faith at the last hour of life and receive the reward of eternal damnation for the life they previously lived; and many profligate men at the end of life believe and repent and obtain eternal life. Is eternal life, I ask, the possible consequent corresponding to a shameful and dissolute antecedent life? 3. The Arminians do not deny that sin is the punishment of antecedent sins, and Scripture expressly teaches this; so sin will be the consequent decreed by God as corresponding. 4. Falling away and final impenitence are possible for all the elect, and perseverance in faith is possible for the reprobate. Therefore God has decreed for the elect destruction no less than life, and for the reprobate life no less than destruction; and thus election is universal, which is a contradiction in terms, and reprobation is universal. But if the corresponding consequent is that which most immediately follows from the possible antecedent, then God decreed for Saul a mind full of malice and envy because of David's innocence; and for the crucifixion of the Lord, the immense and dreadful consequence corresponding to Christ's preaching of the sincere truth of God, he decreed the flourishing kingdom and abundance of all good things for the savagery of the Chaldeans against the Church of God. Yet no one would call that cruelty a corresponding consequence. 6. What God has decreed will stand and will come to pass without change (Isa. 14). But the consequences corresponding to a possible antecedent are for the most part only possible and never future; therefore they are not decreed by God. 7. By this saying he implies that all good or evil things are simply left in a state of possibility, and are not determined by the will of God. This removes the use of prayer, faith, hope, gratitude, and a humble mind toward God, whatever good or evil befalls us from contingent causes.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CAP. IV.

units.la: Contingentia & decreti absoluti conspirationis modum Arminianorum, Suarezij, Vas- quezij, Molina, Lessij, Fonseca rationes ad examen vocantur.
units.tr: Contingency, and the manner in which the absolute decree concurs with it: the arguments of the Arminians, Suárez, Vásquez, Molina, Lessius and Fonseca are brought to examination.

units.la: I. IN hanc arenam descendere vix tutum tyroni praesertim videtur, nisi satius famae quam veritatis dispendium & jacturam facere esset. Primo itaque observari velim, quatuor esse rerum status. Primus est status non entis vel simpliciter impossibilis: ex hoc statu Deus nulla entia extrahit, quia simpliciter impossibile, non est objectum omnipotentiae. 2. Secundus status est vastissimus nempe status possibilitatis, quo omnia sutura contingentia, & omnia tum necessaria tum contingentia, quae sunt nunquam futura, habent esse, hoc est non repugnantiam ut sint, in habitudine nempe ad Dei omnipotentiam, & dato quod nunquam fuisset in Deo decretum producendi ulla entia extra se, omnia quae jam sunt possibilia in eo casu possibilia forent: possibilia enim sunt antecedenter ad Dei voluntatem, hoc modo contingentia omnia sunt antecedenter ad Dei volitiones, & in signo rationis aliquid prius natura est possibile, quam futurum, & futurum aliquid superaddit possibili, sicut species aliquid superaddit generi; hoc sensu contingentia, simpliciter possunt esse vel non esse, & omnia etiam maxime necessaria possunt esse vel non esse. Tertius vero status rerum est status futuritionis, quo res possibiles accipiunt (esse) futurum a Dei decreto, possibile: itaque est terminus a quo, futurum, terminus ad quem, & futuritio motus intermedius, quo res possibilis transit à statu possibilitatis ad statum futuritionis. Sicut itaque res sunt possibiles in habitudine ad aliquam causam, (alioqui essent impossibiles, & hæc causa est omnipotentia), ita etiam res possibiles, è statu possibilitatis ad statum futuritionis evehuntur, & remotius à non ente elongantur per aliquam causam. Jam hæc causa futuritionis, vel est in ente creato, vel in Deo. Non potest esse in ente creato, quia vel in ipso ente futuro, vel in alio ente creato. Non in ipso ente futuro: quia sicut ens præsens non habet esse præsens à se ipso quoniam non habet esse simpliciter à seipso, & præteritum non habet esse præteritum à seipso, ita neque futurum habet esse futurum à seipso, tum enim esset & sui ipsius causa & seipso prius, & posterius, quod absurdum: deinde futurum cum sit ab æterno non habet esse futurum ab alio ente creato, quia nullum erat ens creatum ab æterno, quod possit esse causa futuri, quod est æternum. Itaque causa futuritionis necesse est, sit in Deo, non in Dei intellectu, quia Deus entia intelligendo, entia non facit, quippe non entia intelligit, neque omnipotentia Dei est causa futuri, sed tantum possibilis. Ergo necessario dicendum Dei voluntatem ut libere decernentem esse causam hujus transitus è statu possibilitatis ad statu futuritionis. Quartus rerum status est status actuationis, quo res è statu futuritionis transeat ad statum actuationis & hujus transitus causa est voluntas omnipotentiâ armata; in Deo.
units.tr: I. It seems scarcely safe for a novice to enter this arena, especially unless it would be better to risk his reputation than the truth. First, then, I would have it observed that there are four states of things. The first is the state of non-being, or of the simply impossible. From this state God brings forth no beings, because the simply impossible is not an object of omnipotence. 2. The second state is the very wide state of possibility, in which all future contingent things, and all necessary and contingent things that will never be, have being, that is, have no repugnance to existing, in relation to the omnipotence of God. Even if God had never decreed to produce any beings outside himself, all the things that are now possible would in that case still be possible; for they are possible antecedently to the will of God. In the same way, all contingent things are antecedent to God's volitions, and in the order of reason something is possible before it is future. Being future adds something to the possible, as a species adds something to its genus. In this sense contingent things can simply either be or not be, and even the most necessary things can either be or not be. The third state of things is the state of futurition, in which possible things receive future being, from the decree of God. So there is a terminus from which, which is the possible; a terminus to which, which is the future; and futurition is the intermediate motion by which a possible thing passes from the state of possibility to the state of futurition. Just as things are possible in relation to some cause (otherwise they would be impossible, and this cause is omnipotence), so too possible things are raised from the state of possibility to the state of futurition, and are removed further from non-being, through some cause. Now this cause of futurition is either in a created being or in God. It cannot be in a created being, because it is either in the future being itself or in some other created being. Not in the future being itself: for just as a present being does not have present being from itself, since it does not have being simply from itself, and a past thing does not have past being from itself, so neither does a future thing have future being from itself. For then it would be the cause of itself, and prior and posterior to itself, which is absurd. Moreover, since the future has been from eternity, it does not have future being from some other created being, because no created being existed from eternity that could be the cause of what is eternal. Therefore the cause of futurition must necessarily be in God, not in the intellect of God; for God, by understanding beings, does not make beings, since he understands non-beings, and the omnipotence of God is not the cause of the future but only of the possible. Therefore we must necessarily say that the will of God, deciding freely, is the cause of this passage from the state of possibility to the state of futurition. The fourth state of things is the state of actuation, in which a thing passes from the state of futurition to the state of actuation, and the cause of this passage is the will, armed with omnipotence, in God.

units.la: 2. Observo, esse futurum, quod est, à Dei voluntate commensurandum esse exactissimè ab esse præsente, quod illud futurum in tempore habet & accipit; ita ut esse futurum & esse præsens, sint unum & idem esse, & tantum differant durationis ordine. Hinc illud esse quod effectus contingens habet in tempore, non est aliud quam illud idem esse futurum, quod erat habiturum ab æterno, per decretum divinæ voluntatis liberum; & possibile nunquam transit ad statum actuationis nisi intermedio statu futuritionis. Itaque contingens possibile nullo modo potest immediatè transire ad statum actuationis, quia sic aliquid esset præsens, quod ab æterno non erat futurum: quod idem est ac aliquod ens creatum esse actu, quod nunquam fuit in potentia, quod est simpliciter impossibile. Possibile itaque est quod potest esse vel non esse, hoc est cui non repugnat esse: at vero possibile contingens est quod de facto & actu potest esse vel non esse, non simpliciter sed antecedente futuritione, ideoque quamvis possibilitates superent numero actualitates, at vero futurorum contingentium & effectorum contingentium actū & de facto, planè & idem est numerus, nec illa vel unitate hæc excedunt.
units.tr: 2. I observe that the future being, which is, must be measured most exactly against the present being, which that future thing has and receives in time; so that future being and present being are one and the same being, and differ only in the order of duration. Hence that being which a contingent effect has in time is nothing other than that same future being, which it was going to have from eternity, through the free decree of the divine will. A possible thing never passes to the state of actuation except through the intermediate state of futurition. Therefore a contingent possible thing can in no way pass immediately to the state of actuation, for then something would be present which from eternity was not future; and this is the same as saying that some created being is actually existing which never was in potency, which is simply impossible. Thus the possible is what can either be or not be, that is, what has no repugnance to being; but the possible contingent is what can in fact and in act either be or not be, not simply but by antecedent futurition. And therefore, although possibilities exceed actualities in number, yet the number of future contingents and of contingent effects, in act and in fact, is plainly the same, and the one does not exceed the other even by a unit.

units.la: 3. Hinc tertiò observo. Posito per impossibile, quod nullum esset in Deo absolutum decretum determinans futura contingentia, causa contingens de facto non determinate produceret effectum alium quam qui ab aeterno habuit futuritionem sibi correspondentem exactissimè, & ille effectus contingens qui nullam sibi correspondentem habuit futuritionem, esse non potest, quia impossibile est aliquod ens esse praesens, quod ab aeterno non fuit futurum; ideoque nemo non videt essectus contingentes omnes qui eveniunt in tempore, de facto limitari per futuritionem aeternam: at vero si Dei decretum superveniens eidem futuritioni correspondenti effectui contingenti qui de facto fit, ipsam determinet, non magis evertit naturam causae contingentis, quam si contingens causa sola antecedenter ad Dei decretum se determinaret, praevia aeterna futuritione. Sit itaque libertas humana inclinans ad volendum, A, B, C, D, E, & actu volitura, C, non, A, non B, non D, non E, actualis volitio <bl>τῇ</bl> C sola habuit sibi correspondentem aeternam futuritionem volitionis τῇ [?] C, volitio vero τῇ A, B, D, E, nullam suturitionem ab aeterno habuit, neque potuit voluntas actu velle A, B, D, E, nisi antecedente futuritione aeterna illius volitionis; hoc enim ex observatione nostra secunda est impossibile. Si itaque Dei decretum absolutum determinet ab aeterno voluntatem liberè inclinantem & determinantem se ad volendum, C, cui volitioni correspondebat aeterna futuritio, ex hypothesi quod non fuisset in Deo decretum absolutum, & idem decretum non dedeterminet ab æterno voluntatem libere nolentem [?] A, B, D, E, manifestum plane est Dei decretum absolutum non magis lædere naturam libertatis, quam si per impossibile non esset in Deo tale decretum. Itaque hic oculos convertat in sequens diagramma lector: Decretum absolutum Dei Potens eligere A, possibile futurum æternum B, possibile non-futurum æternum Eligens C, possibile & futuru æternum D. Possibile non-futurum æternum. Libertas humana Potens eligere E, Possibile futurum æternum.
units.tr: 3. Hence, thirdly, I observe. Suppose, which is impossible, that there were in God no absolute decree determining future contingents. A contingent cause would then in fact not determinately produce any effect other than the one that from eternity had a futurition corresponding to it most exactly. And a contingent effect that had no corresponding futurition cannot exist, because it is impossible that any being should be present which from eternity was not future. Therefore everyone sees that all contingent effects which occur in time are in fact limited by eternal futurition. But if a decree of God, coming upon the contingent effect that corresponds to this futurition and that in fact comes about, determines that futurition itself, it does no more overthrow the nature of the contingent cause than if the contingent cause had determined itself alone, antecedently to the decree of God, with eternal futurition going before. Let there be, then, human liberty inclining towards willing: A, B, C, D, E, and it is going to will actually C and not A, not B, not D, not E. The actual volition towards C alone had a corresponding eternal futurition, while the volitions towards A, B, D, E had no futurition from eternity. Nor could the will actually will A, B, D, E, unless an eternal futurition of that volition had gone before; for this, by our second observation, is impossible. If therefore the absolute decree of God from eternity determines the will, freely inclining and determining itself to will C, to which volition an eternal futurition corresponded (on the hypothesis that there was no absolute decree in God), and the same decree does not from eternity determine the will freely to refuse A, B, D, E, it is plainly manifest that the absolute decree of God does no more injure the nature of liberty than if, per impossibile, there were no such decree in God. Let the reader therefore turn his eyes here to the following diagram. The absolute decree of God: able to choose A, a possible future eternal, B, a possible non-future eternal; choosing C, a possible and future eternal, D, a possible non-future eternal. Human liberty: able to choose E, a possible future eternal.

units.la: 4. Necessitas ex hypothesi quod libertas jam actu operetur, & necessitas ex hypothesi decreti absoluti, quamvis respectu termini & principii à quo, sint diversæ necessitatis, tamen respectu termini ad quem sunt eædem: quod sic doceo. Hæ propositiones sibi æquipollent.
units.tr: 4. The necessity on the hypothesis that liberty now actually operates, and the necessity on the hypothesis of the absolute decree, although they are of different kinds with respect to the terminus from which and the principle, are nevertheless the same with respect to the terminus to which. I prove this as follows. These propositions are equivalent to each other.

units.la: Homines prout subsunt decreto Dei absoluto non possunt aliud velle aut eligere, quam volunt aut eligunt, & de facto.
units.tr: Men, insofar as they are subject to the absolute decree of God, cannot will or choose otherwise than they will or choose, and in fact.

units.la: Homines in actuali exercitio libertatis non possunt aliud velle aut eligere, quā actu [?] volunt aut eligunt.
units.tr: Men, in the actual exercise of liberty, cannot will or choose otherwise than they actually will or choose.

units.la: Probatur, illæ sunt eædem necessitates quoad terminum & objectum, quæ removent easdem indifferentias libertatis: atqui necessitas ex hypothesi decreti absoluti, & necessitas ex hypothesi actualis exercitii removent eandem, imo unam & eandem indifferentiam libertatis humanæ. Ergo sunt quoad terminum & ob[?]jectum eædem necessitates. Major est certa ex oppositione inter determinationem factam per necessitatem & indifferentiam. Probatur assumptio, quoniam necessitas decreti aufert indifferentiam ad volendum A, B, D, E^c ut ipsa libertas auferat eandem indifferentiam, non aliam. In eo vero adversarii & fallunt & falluntur, quod ex decreti absoluti vi manare velint, quod voluntas libera ex se & quoad futuritionem in hunc angulum actu inclinatura esset, & volitura, A, B, D, E, & torqueatur contra insitam vim suam per fatale decretum ad volendum C; at vero pernegamus nos libertatem humanam ulla vi decreti, aut fatalitate torqueri ab illo coinclinationis primigeniæ & nativæ angulo ad alium angulum, aut ad aliam potentiæ quasi partem actuandam, quam & ad illam quæ ab æterno actuanda erat, antecedente æterna futuritione, & illam eandem & non aliam, quam ipsa libertas humana ex se erat amplexura, hoc dato per impossibile, quod non fuisset in Deo decretum absolutum, & nulla rerum providentia.
units.tr: It is proved thus: those are the same necessities as to term and object which remove the same indifferences of liberty. But the necessity on the hypothesis of the absolute decree and the necessity on the hypothesis of actual exercise remove the same, indeed one and the same, indifference of human liberty. Therefore they are the same necessities as to term and object. The major premise is certain from the opposition between determination made by necessity and indifference. The minor is proved thus: the necessity of the decree removes indifference to willing A, B, D, E, so that liberty itself removes the same indifference and no other. But the adversaries are both mistaken and misled in this, that they want it to follow from the force of the absolute decree that the free will, of itself and with respect to futurition, would have actually inclined and willed towards this corner, A, B, D, E, and is twisted against its innate force by the fatal decree to will C. But we flatly deny that human liberty is twisted by any force or fatality of the decree from that original and native corner of its co-inclination to another corner, or to actuating another part of the power, as it were, other than that which from eternity was to be actuated, with eternal futurition going before, and that very same thing, and not another, which human liberty itself of its own accord was going to embrace; this being granted per impossibile, that there was no absolute decree in God and no providence of things at all.

units.la: §. At vero duo hic objici posse video. 1. Dicerent me hic nunc non ponere aliam necessitatem in causa libera ex decreto, quàm concomitantem, & talem quæ relinquat potentiæ liberæ omnimodam indifferentiam, quamvis verbis ponam antecedentem necessitatem. Nam si decretum Dei, accedente nimirum in tempore potentia executrice, removet eandem indifferentiam & potentiam particularem, quam removet actuale exercitium libertatis, tum quoniam actuale exercitium removet vel hanc vel illam potentiam indifferenter: sequitur decretum vel hanc vel illam indifferentiam removere non aliam, & sic non praecise actus liberos a decreto absoluto determinari. R. Non sequitur, quia quamvis libertas in actu liberrimo vel hanc vel illam potentiam removeat, tamen non & hanc & illam removet, sed tantum illam removet quae ab aeterno non actuanda erat, & eam ponit quae actuanda erat, & cui aeterna futuritio correspondebat: decretum vero praecise determinat actum illum liberum & futuritionem, quoniam antecedenter locat voluntatem liberam quoad primam vitalem & electivam motionem, in eo vitali situ, quo respicit illam inclinationis naturalis (ut sic loquar) positionem, in qua actuetur illa eadem potentia particularis, quam & Deus ab aeterno absolute actuari voluit, & decrevit, & non aliam, & quam libertas subordinate & dependenter a Deo vult actuari. Sicut itaque aulicus quidam clam Rege statuit proficisci in longinquam regionem, & rex apud se statuit eundem ad illam regionem legare, & re utrique ex votis succedente; ille ut mittat, pro regis imperio, hic ut libere illuc iter faciat, quamvis Rex nullo tali decreto, aut imperio ipsum praefiffet [?], quo casu & rex absolute decernit illud iter, & aulicus liberrime iter conficit, ita Deus absolute de-cernit cernit hunc non illum actum liberum, & in eo situ vitali locat libertatem, quo illum actum liberum & non alium, quam qui quoad æternam futuritionem libertas erat liberrime productura, ita penes Dei providentiam est ut talis actus fit, non alius, non plures vel pauciores, & etiam penes voluntatem sed subordinate & dependenter, quod sint tales actus non plures vel pauciores.
units.tr: §. But I see that two objections could be raised here. 1. They would say that I am not positing any necessity in a free cause from the decree except a concomitant one, one that leaves the free power complete indifference, even though in words I posit an antecedent necessity. For if God's decree, with the executive power coming in at the right time, removes that same indifference and the particular power that the actual exercise of liberty removes, then, since the actual exercise removes either this power or that one indifferently, it follows that the decree removes either this indifference or that one, and not a fixed one; and so free acts are not determined precisely by the absolute decree. Reply: It does not follow. Although liberty in its most free act removes either this power or that one, it does not remove both this and that. It removes only the power that was not to be actuated from eternity, and it posits the power that was to be actuated, the one to which the eternal futurition corresponded. The decree, however, determines precisely that free act and its futurition, because it antecedently places the free will, as to its first vital and elective motion, in that vital position in which it regards the natural inclination (so to speak) in which that same particular power is to be actuated, the power that God from eternity willed and decreed absolutely to be actuated, and no other, and which liberty wills to be actuated subordinately and dependently on God. So, for example, if a courtier secretly resolves with the king's knowledge to set out for a distant region, and the king likewise resolves to send him to that region, and both wishes succeed, the king's part being to send him by command and the courtier's part to make the journey freely there, although the king has not prescribed this by any such decree or command. In that case the king absolutely decrees that journey, and the courtier makes the journey most freely. So God absolutely decrees this free act and not that one, and places liberty in that vital position in which it will produce that free act and not another, namely the one that liberty was to produce most freely in view of its eternal futurition. Thus it lies with the providence of God that such an act comes about and not another, and neither more nor fewer acts; and it lies also with the will, but subordinately and dependently, that the acts are not more or fewer.

units.la: 6. Objici potest, si non poneretur tale decretum, necessitas futuritionis nulla esset, & maneret vera indifferentia naturalis, quia necessitas futuritionis est mere hypothetica, manans à libertate creata; quia enim libertas creata est libere hoc volitu-ra, ideo est futuritio æterna talis volitionis: nam posito, quod res sit futura, necesse est ut sit futura, sicut necesse est res præsens, sit præsens: at vero in signo rationis futuritionem antecedente, libertas est absolute indifferens ad hoc vel illud volendum: quia vero est hoc non illud volitura, ideo antecesit æterna futuritio. Resp. 1. contra omnem sanam rationem, libertas libere volens in tempore statuitur causa futuritionis æternæ. Nullum enim temporale est causa æterni, quia causa est prior effecto, temporale non est prius sed posterius æterno. 2. Concedimus necessitatem futuritionis esse tantum hypotheticam non absolutam, sed tamen est antecedens ne-cessitas respectu actus liberi, quod nobis sufficit ad probandum necessitatem antecedentem non pugnare cum actu liberè, nisi talis sit necessitas, qua vi evellatur aut torqueatur libertas ab illo, quod naturaliter erat volitura, ad illud quod non erat volitura, quod non est verum de necessitate ex hypothesi decreti; 3.[?] Quando futuritio non fit merè nihil, (nam futurum & non futurum per aliquid differunt) tendentiæ à possibili ad statum actuationis aliam causam assignare non possunt, quam liberam Dei voluntatem. 4. Etiam in ligno rationis antecedente futuritionem, potentia libera est quidem indifferens ad nolle vel velle idem sub disjunctione, non vero ad nolle & velle idem copulative. Potentia vero disjunctiva in se & intrinsece respicit tantum unum oppositorum, ideoque vi materiæ potentia unum respicit intrinsece; indifferentia vero tantum formaliter hoc importat quod ꝥ[?] velle A non magis spectet ad naturalem agendi modum in libertate, quam ꝥ[?] nolle A. Ideoque potentia respicit illud tantum oppositum intrinsece, quod per positionem suturitionis, tendet à statu possibilitatis ad statum actuationis, & quia Dei decretum potentiam determinat ad illud idem objectum in habitudine ad quod, habebit in ligno rationis subsequente, futuritionem: quis non videat decretum hic optimè conspirare cum libertate humana? in hoc vero est Dei dominium, quod absolute hunc non illum actum prædefiniat; & quod ita collocat voluntatem, ut voluntas ex insita vi electiva in illud, vitali influxu, & indifferen-ti ti, (quantum attinet ad naturalem modum agendi in libertate) in illud idem numero, & non aliud obiectum erumpat, quod Deus praecise decrevit.
units.tr: 6. It may be objected that if no such decree were posited, the necessity of futurition would be nothing, and natural indifference would remain true, because the necessity of futurition is merely hypothetical, flowing from created liberty. For since created liberty is going to will this freely, therefore the eternal futurition of such a volition exists. For, granted that a thing will be, it is necessary that it will be, just as it is necessary that a present thing be present. But in the order of reason that precedes futurition, liberty is absolutely indifferent to willing this or that. Yet because it is going to will this and not that, the eternal futurition has preceded. Reply: 1. Against all sound reasoning, a liberty that wills freely in time is made the cause of eternal futurition. For nothing temporal is the cause of what is eternal, since a cause is prior to its effect, and what is temporal is not prior but posterior to the eternal. 2. We grant that the necessity of futurition is only hypothetical, not absolute; yet it is an antecedent necessity with respect to the free act. This is enough for us to prove that antecedent necessity does not conflict with a free act, unless such necessity is of a kind by which liberty is forcibly torn or twisted away from what it was naturally going to will, toward what it was not going to will. That is not true of the necessity arising from the hypothesis of the decree. 3. When futurition is not simply nothing (for the future and the not-future differ by something), they cannot assign any cause for the tendency from the possible to the state of actuation other than the free will of God. 4. Even in the order of reason that precedes futurition, the free power is indeed indifferent to not willing or willing the same thing under a disjunction, but not to not willing and willing the same thing conjunctively. Now a disjunctive power in itself and intrinsically regards only one of the opposites, and therefore by the force of its matter the power regards one intrinsically. Indifference, however, formally implies only this: that willing A is no more part of the natural mode of acting in liberty than not willing A. Therefore the power intrinsically regards only that opposite which, by the positing of futurition, tends from the state of possibility to the state of actuation; and because God's decree determines the power to that same object in relation to which, in the subsequent order of reason, it will have futurition, who does not see that the decree here agrees perfectly with human liberty? In this lies the dominion of God, that he absolutely predefines this act and not that one; and that he so places the will that the will, by its inborn elective force, by vital influence, and with indifference (so far as concerns the natural mode of acting in liberty), breaks out into that same object numerically, and not another, which God precisely decreed.

units.la: 7. Hoc 4. etiam observo, libertatis humanae duplicem esse potentiam, universalem & particularem: prior est libertati essentialis, qua libertas ex naturali suo agendi modo, non magis respiciat nolle quam velle, eligere quam repudiare, vel suspendere suum actum. Posterior est accidentalis, accedens vel recedens à libertate, salva ipsius essentia. Haec distinctio potentiae non potest negari. Qui negat potentiam voluntatis ad nolle, velle, vel eligere in genere, is negat libertatis potentiam. Dari vero potentia particularem probo. Antequam Petrus crasdisputet, est in potentia ad disputandū cras. At vero el apsa[?] semel crastina[?] disputatione, perit talis potentia, neq; amplius est in potentia ad talem disputationem, quoniam ad praeteritum actum nulla est potentia.
units.tr: 7. I observe also, in this fourth point, that human liberty has a twofold power, universal and particular. The former is essential to liberty, by which liberty, from its natural mode of acting, regards not being unwilling more than willing, choosing more than rejecting, or suspending its act. The latter is accidental, coming to liberty or departing from it while its essence remains. This distinction of power cannot be denied. Whoever denies the power of the will to be unwilling, to will, or to choose in general denies the power of liberty. That a particular power exists I prove thus. Before Peter disputes tomorrow, he is in potency to dispute tomorrow. But once that tomorrow's disputation has itself taken place, such a power perishes, and he is no longer in potency to that disputation, since there is no power with respect to a past act.

units.la: 2. Cuilibet actui particulari correspondet potentia particularis. At multi sunt actus particulares in voluntate. Ergo sunt etiam potentiae. 3. Sicut Philosophi iure optime ponunt in materia prima duplicem potentiam hanc, ita pari iure tales sunt hic potentiae. Hinc dico decretum Dei non removere potentiam libertatis universalem utpote ei essentialem. At vero potentiae libertatis particulares sunt à Deo ab aeterno determinatae. Prob. 1. Omnes actus, cum sint entitates determinatae à Deo, decreto absoluto præfiniuntur, alioqui præter Dei intentionem evenirent & providentiæ non subessent. Ergo etiam potentiæ particulares determinaatur. Prob. consequens, quoniam opposita ad oppositorum multiplicationem multiplicantur. 2. Potentiæ hæ particulares sunt entia determinata. ergo à Deo absolutè præfiniuntur: alioqui providentiam etiam effugerent. 3. Habent hæ potentiæ esse determinatum & individuale: ergo tale esse à primo ente habeant necesse est. Hinc sequitur libertatem non esse in potentia particulari ad plures paucioresve actus, quam quos actu exercet, quamvis sit in potentia universali ad omnes actus possibiles. At dicent per antecedens decretum ita igitur ligari voluntatem, ut non possit aliter facere, quam facit. Resp.[?] non obstante decreto, potentia universali potest aliter facere, & alia velle, nolle, & eligere, quam quæ de facto vult, non vult, aut eligit. At dices potentia particulari non potest voluntas agere vel non agere. Resp.[?] me id haud gravatè concedere, quoniam ipsa voluntas talem potentiam removet liberrime inclinando se in illum actum, qui quoad futuritionem erat ab æterno producendus, quam futuritionem habuit à decreto Dei absoluto: at vero quia voluntas libero exercitio istam potentiam particularem removet, quam Dei decretum removet, non magis lædiTur libertas per antecedens decretum, quam per suum actuale libertatis exercitium. Si vero Dei decretum aliam potentiam particularem, nempe ad hoc volendum removeret, & ipsa voluntas tali potentia particulari inclinaret ad illud non volendum, tum antecedens decretum libertatem laederet. At hoc tribuitur nobis ab adversariis, sed falso.
units.tr: 2. To every particular act there corresponds a particular power. But there are many particular acts in the will. Therefore there are also powers. 3. Just as the philosophers rightly posit this twofold power in prime matter, so by the same right there are such powers here. Hence I say that God's decree does not remove the universal power of liberty, since that is essential to it. The particular powers of liberty, however, are determined by God from eternity. Proof 1: All acts, since they are entities determined by God, are predefined by the absolute decree; otherwise they would happen outside God's intention and would not be subject to providence. Therefore the particular powers are also determined. Proof of the consequence: opposites multiply in step with the multiplication of opposites. 2. These particular powers are determinate entities; therefore they are absolutely predefined by God; otherwise they would also escape providence. 3. These powers have a determinate and individual being; therefore they must have such being from the first being. Hence it follows that liberty is not in a particular power for more or fewer acts than those it actually exercises, although it is in a universal power for all possible acts. But they will say that by the antecedent decree the will is so bound that it cannot act otherwise than it does. Reply: Notwithstanding the decree, the universal power can act otherwise, and will, not will, and choose other things than those it in fact wills, does not will, or chooses. But you will say that the will cannot, by a particular power, act or not act. Reply: I readily grant this, since the will itself removes such a particular power by most freely inclining itself to that act which, as to futurition, was to be produced from eternity, a futurition it had from God's absolute decree. But because the will by its free exercise removes that particular power which God's decree removes, liberty is no more harmed by the antecedent decree than by its own actual exercise of liberty. If, however, God's decree removed another particular power, namely the power to will this, and the will itself inclined by such a particular power to not willing this, then the antecedent decree would harm liberty. But this is attributed to us by our opponents, and falsely.

units.la: 8 Objiciunt etiam necessitatem ex decreto non esse necessitatem hypotheticam, sed absolutam, ac proinde evertere libertatem; probant sic: necessitas hypothetica est necessitas, qua res alioquin contingens, sive libera, non potest non esse, ex hypothesi, quod fit, ideoque rei contingentis existentiam ponit. At vero necessitas decreti non ponit actum liberum jam poni, aut esse antecedenter ad decretum, sed contra quia prius est decretum, ideo necessario fore actum liberum. Resp. 1. Angusta & arcta nimis est illa definitio necessitatis hypotheticae. Nam non tantum necessitas hypothetica dicitur, quando res contingens ponitur jam esse, sed quando ponitur aliquod antecedens, ex quo posito res contingens necessario est futura ad modum suae naturae, nempe contingenter. Ideo actus liberi sunt necessarii ex hypothesi decreti divini ponentis actus liberos non jam esse, sed futuros esse liberrime per vim decreti; & ratio est manifesta, quoniam necessitas ex decreto ponit causam liberè in talem praecisae oppositionis angulum erupturam vitali & electivo influxu ex judicio rationis, in quem liberè erumperet, posito quod nulnullum esset decretum, sed antecederet per impossibile, sola futuritio aeterna, dico (per impossibile antecederet futuritio aeterna) quoniam impossibile est ullam futuritionem rerum omnium ab aeterno fuisse, nisi per liberam Dei voluntatem. Quid? Si futuritio ab aeterno omnium rerum fuisset, tum invito Deo, & contra ipsius voluntatem, mundus & omnia entia quae jam sunt futura, essent necessario non libere respectu divini decreti, & sic Deus, necessitate naturae, mundum creasset, & per eandem rationem, non-futuritio omnium entium possibilium ponenda esset antecedenter ad Dei decretum, & sic fatali necessitate Iehova entia omnia produxit, ita ut ei simpliciter impossibile fuerit illa non produxisse, & impossibile vel plura vel pauciora, quam sunt producta, produxisse. Nam quod jam est futurum prius, vel contra quam Deus id velit esse futurum, non potest ne per Dei omnipotentiam, non esse futurum. Nam omnipotentia non potest efficere ut propositio identica fit falsa, aut ut futurum non fit futurum, & videat hic lector miserrima ecclesiae fata: en quo rerum devolvimur a subtilioribus sophistis: qui malunt homines esse liberos, quam Deum, & interim libertatem humanam evertunt, & in fatu ne Deo quidem superabile convertunt.
units.tr: 8 They also object that the necessity arising from the decree is not hypothetical but absolute, and so overthrows liberty. They prove it thus: hypothetical necessity is that by which a thing that is otherwise contingent or free cannot fail to be, given the hypothesis that it is done, and so it posits the existence of the contingent thing. But the necessity of the decree does not posit that the free act is already posited or exists before the decree; on the contrary, because the decree comes first, the free act will necessarily come about. Reply: (1) That definition of hypothetical necessity is too narrow and confined. For it is called hypothetical necessity not only when the contingent thing is posited as already existing, but also when some antecedent is posited, from whose positing the contingent thing is necessarily going to be, according to the manner of its nature, that is, contingently. So free acts are necessary by the hypothesis of the divine decree, which posits that the free acts are not yet existing but are going to be, most freely, by the force of the decree. The reason is plain. Necessity from the decree posits that the cause will freely break forth into such an angle of precise opposition, with vital and elective influence from the judgment of reason, into which it would freely break forth if there were no decree but, per impossibile, an eternal futurition went before alone. I say "per impossibile an eternal futurition would go before," since it is impossible that any futurition of all things has existed from eternity except through the free will of God. What then? If there had been an eternal futurition of all things, then, against God's will and contrary to his will, the world and all beings that are now future would be necessary, not free, with respect to the divine decree; and so God would have created the world by necessity of nature. By the same reasoning, a non-futurition of all possible beings would have to be posited before God's decree, and so by fatal necessity Jehovah produced all beings, so that it was simply impossible for him not to have produced them, and impossible to have produced either more or fewer than have been produced. For what is already future beforehand, or future contrary to what God wills, cannot fail to be future, not even by God's omnipotence. Omnipotence cannot make an identical proposition false, or make what is future not future. Let the reader see here the most wretched fate of the Church: see to what we are being rolled down by the more subtle sophists, who prefer men to be free rather than God, and in the meantime overturn human liberty and turn it into a fate that not even God could overcome.

units.la: 9. In eo vero inimici gratiae turpiter hallucinantur, quod ex ingrata & superba creati arbitrii elatione, Dei sapientissimum, & omnipotens in omnia entia creata. Dominium ignorant : quasi Deus non posset in profunditatem libertatis creatæ penetrare, absque læsione ipsius naturæ, & libertatem ad quatuor angulos propendentem; quod ad vero futuritionem æternam in tertium angulum ex illis quatuor actu erupturam liberrime, & non in ullum ex reliquis tribus, non potsit antecedenter decreto suo absoluto in illum tertium angulum præcisè definire. Nos vero, si Deus esset agens finitum, haud ægrè concederemus, fieri haud posse ut antecedenter determinaret voluntatem liberam præcisè ad unum actum, posthabitis aliis possibilibus. At nobis concederent, siquidem concederemus ipsis scientiam mediam, quia Deus antecedenter ad decretum suum infinita sua scientia cognoscit futuritionem actuum contingentium, Deum posse absolute prædefinire actus liberos; at vero hoc verbis dicunt, non argumentorum pondere evincunt. At vero dicimus nos, Deum, qua est infinitate, & absoluto & sapienti dominio in creaturas absolute decernere actus omnes contingentes, & causam contingentem determinare antecedenter in eam partem suæ coinclinationis primigeniæ & radicalis, in quam ipsa contingenter se determinabit, & nisi hoc dicendum, videre nos haud posse, vel intelligere, qui infinita sua providentia & dominio sapienti omnia administret.
units.tr: 9. In this matter the enemies of grace grossly err. Out of the ungrateful and proud elevation of created free will, they ignore the most wise and omnipotent dominion of God over all created beings, as if God could not penetrate into the depth of created liberty, which inclines towards four angles, without injury to its nature. Nor, as regards the eternal futurition, can he, by his absolute decree prior to it, define precisely that liberty will break forth freely into the third of those four angles and into none of the other three. We, indeed, if God were a finite agent, would not readily concede that he could not determine beforehand a free will precisely to one act, setting aside the other possibilities. They would concede to us, if we conceded to them middle knowledge, that God, by his infinite knowledge prior to his decree, knows the futurition of contingent acts, and so could absolutely predefine free acts. But they say this in words; they do not prove it by the weight of arguments. We, on the other hand, say that God, by his infinite and absolute and wise dominion over creatures, absolutely decrees all contingent acts, and determines the contingent cause beforehand into that part of its primal and radical co-inclination in which it will determine itself contingently. Unless this is said, we cannot see or understand how he administers all things by his infinite providence and wise dominion.

units.la: 10. Itaque [?]1.non quæritur, an effectus liberi fiant contingenter, vel an in se sint contingentes. Nam & essentialiter & antecedenter ad Dei decretum effectus contingentes sunt contingentes, non minus quam homo est animal. 2. Non quaeritur, an fiant necessario ex Dei decreto, quasi decretum effectis contingentibus necessitatem inspirarer; ut insulte loquitur Thom. Iack f; sed an fiant necessario ex hypothesi decreti absoluti; hoc est, an postquam Deus absolute decrevit ut actus contingentes sint, an tum ita fiant, ut sub ea suppositione possint non fieri. Nam Dei decretum causarie non facit necessitatem aliam quam ipsa libertas facit. Itaque an causa libera prout subest decreto, possit non agere, quando per decretum determinatur ad agendum; hoc praecipue quaeritur. Nam etiam prout subest decreto potentia universali poterit non agere, & contra id agere, ad quod determinatur, quia decretum nullo modo aufert potentiam universalem. Dici itaque forte poterit, manet potentia universalis sub decreto; tu nihil impossibile poneretur si in actum reducetur ut definit Aristoteles contingens [?] τὰ μὲν ὅτι ἀναγκαῖον[?] τὰ δὲ ὅτ' ὑπάρχειν[?], οὐδὲν ἔχει δὲ διὰ τὸ ἀδύνατον[?]. Ac proinde nihil impossibile esset si libertas ad hanc partem determinata per decretum in actum & contrariam partem se determinaret. Ergo vel falletur, & rescindetur tale decretum, quod non est dicendum; vel tale decretum non determinat libertatem praecise ad unam partem. Resp. Potentia liberae voluntatis ex se & immediate nunquam reducitur in actum, sed semper mediante potentia particulari: jam potentiā particularis non potest reduci in actum, contrarium actui à decreto determinato. Nam repugnat hypothesi decreti divini, imo suæ naturæ etiam repugnat, eo quod decretum potentiam particularem determinat ad eum actum in quem ipsa libere erumpet, & non in alium: nemo autem sanus diceret voluntatem id posse non velle quod actu est volitura, postquam est id actu volitura. Nam necessitas absoluta sive consequentis est, ut recte definit Antonius Andreas, Ipsius rei necessitas quæ consistit in essentiali causæ & effectus dependentia: quando nimirum res requitur ex causa antecedente necessario. Jam vero omnis effectus contingens ita est à decreto Dei ut tamen potuerit non esse: non est enim Patri volitio à Dei decreto, ut lumé à sole, aut calor ab igne, sicut neque talis volitio Petri, tali modo est à libertate Petri. Semper itaq; teneo, decretū Dei determinare præcise voluntatem creatam in tale partem in quam ipse se libere determinabit.
units.tr: 10. Therefore the question is not whether free effects come about contingently, or whether they are contingent in themselves. For contingent effects are contingent both essentially and antecedently to God's decree, no less than a man is an animal. 2. The question is not whether they come about necessarily by God's decree, as if the decree breathed necessity into contingent effects, as Thom. Iack f insultingly puts it. The question is whether they come about necessarily given the hypothesis of the absolute decree: that is, whether, once God has absolutely decreed that the acts shall exist, they then come about in such a way that, under that supposition, they could fail to come about. For God's decree, as a cause, creates no necessity other than that which liberty itself creates. So the chief question is whether a free cause, insofar as it is subject to the decree, can fail to act when it is determined by the decree to act. For even insofar as it is subject to the decree, it retains universal power, and so it can fail to act and act against that to which it is determined, since the decree in no way removes universal power. It might therefore be said that universal power remains under the decree; and nothing impossible would be posited if it were reduced to act, as Aristoteles defines the contingent: [τὰ μὲν ὅτι ἀναγκαῖον, τὰ δὲ ὅτ' ὑπάρχειν, οὐδὲν ἔχει δὲ διὰ τὸ ἀδύνατον]. Accordingly, nothing would be impossible if liberty, determined to one side by the decree, were to reduce itself to act on the contrary side. Either, then, such a decree would be overturned, which must not be said; or such a decree does not determine liberty precisely to one side. Answer. The power of the free will is never reduced to act of itself and immediately, but always through a particular power. Now a particular power cannot be reduced to an act contrary to the act determined by the decree. For this contradicts the hypothesis of the divine decree, and indeed contradicts its own nature, since the decree determines the particular power to that act into which it will freely break forth, and not into another. No sane person would say that the will can fail to will what it is actually going to will, once it is actually going to will it. For absolute, or consequent, necessity is, as Antonius Andreas rightly defines it, the necessity of the thing itself, which consists in the essential dependence of effect on cause, when, namely, the thing is required by a cause that is necessarily antecedent. But every contingent effect is from God's decree in such a way that it could nevertheless not have been: Peter's volition is not from God's decree as light is from the sun or heat from fire, nor is such a volition of Petri from the liberty of Peter in such a manner. So I always hold that God's decree determines the created will precisely to that side to which it will freely determine itself.

units.la: Sed dices, decretum Dei non propterea determinat potentiam liberam in eam partem, in quam potest se determinare voluntas: at vero in quamcunque partem voluntas determinat se, poterat in contrariam partem se determinasse. Resp. 1. ridiculum est Dei decretum determinare voluntatem ad eam partem in quam potest inclinare. Nam potest inclinare se ad omnes actus possibiles, neque ipsa libertas sese determinat in actus possibiles. 2. In quamcunque partem se determinet voluntas, posito quod in actum, qui contrarius est ei, quem nunc ab æterno decretum Dei determinavit, tum dico antecedens decretum futuritionem æternam debuisse isti actui possibili tribuisse, quo è statu possibilitatis, ad statum futuritionis elevaretur. 3. Si stricte loquamur, Dei decretum, cum fit in actus immanens, non ponit aliquid in libertate, ideoque ipsam non determinat; Dei vero determinatio est actus transiens, et temporalis: attamen decretum determinare libertatem dicimus, quia absolute decrevit, ut voluntas in tempore, accedente potentia Dei executrice, se determinaret. Primo hinc dico, falsæ sunt hæ propositiones. 1. Deus decrevit ut effectus contingentes fierent necessario. 2. Deus decrevit ut actus liberi non possent non esse. Veræ sunt hæ. Deus decrevit ut effectus contingentes ita fierent, ut possent non fieri, nempe oblata suppositione æternæ futuritionis, & decreti divini. 3. Deus decrevit ut illi actus liberi essent præcise & non alii quam libertas liberè elicit in tempore. Hinc etiam hæ propositiones observentur. 1. Petrus creditūrus est, quoniam Deus decrevit ut liberrimè per motum efficacis gratiæ crederet. Idem de non credentibus, sano sensu, dicendum, ut postea exponemus. 2. Quoniam Petrus est credituruṡ, ideo Deus decrevit ut libere crederet, hæc est vera, sed ab effectu non à causa, quoniam Deus decrevit ann-teceecedenter ad Petri volitiones, illum actum id quem Petrus quoad æternam futuritionem erat se libere determinaturus, & hoc est ter mirandæ sapientiæ & omnipotentiæ proprium, ut ita in causæ contingentis naturam penetret, ut illam coinclinationis naturalis actuationem extrahat, quam solam, & non aliam, quam causa contingens contingenter extrahi appetit. Luculentius & clarius ista in patria viluti fumus, hæc interim credimus.
units.tr: But you will say that God's decree does not for that reason determine the free power to the side to which the will can determine itself; yet whatever side the will determines itself to, it could have determined itself to the contrary side. Answer 1. It is absurd for God's decree to determine the will to the side to which it can incline. For it can incline itself to all possible acts, and liberty does not determine itself to possible acts. 2. To whatever side the will determines itself, supposing that it determines itself to an act contrary to that which God's decree has determined from eternity, I say that the antecedent decree ought to have granted that possible act eternal futurition, by which it would have been raised from the state of possibility to the state of future existence. 3. Strictly speaking, God's decree, since it is an immanent act, places nothing in liberty and therefore does not determine it; but God's determination is a transient and temporal act. Yet we say that the decree determines liberty, because He has absolutely decreed that the will should determine itself in time, with God's executive power coming to bear. First, then, I say the following propositions are false: 1. God has decreed that contingent effects should come about necessarily. 2. God has decreed that free acts should be unable not to be. These are true: God has decreed that contingent effects should so come about that they could not come about, namely, given the supposition of eternal futurition and the divine decree. 3. God has decreed that those free acts should be precisely what liberty freely elicits in time, and no others. Hence these propositions also are to be observed. 1. Peter will believe because God has decreed that he should believe most freely through the motion of efficacious grace. The same is to be said of non-believers, in a sound sense, as we shall explain later. 2. Because Peter will believe, God has therefore decreed that he should believe freely. This is true, but it holds from the effect, not from the cause, since God decreed, antecedently to Peter's volitions, that act which Peter was to determine himself to freely with respect to eternal futurition. This is the proper work of wonderful wisdom and omnipotence, to penetrate so deeply into the nature of a contingent cause that it draws out that actuation of its natural inclination which alone, and no other, the contingent cause desires to be drawn out contingently. These matters will be set out more brightly and clearly in our homeland, as smoke is to fire; meanwhile we believe them.

units.la: II. Jam discutiamus Adversariorum rationes. I. In arenam primò descendat, Iacob. Arminius: Vna (inquit) & eadem res nequit esse necessaria simul & contingens, quia necessarium & contingens dividunt totam entis amplitudinem. Omne enim ens est vel necessarium vel contingens. Quæ autem dividunt totum ens, illa non coincidunt in ullum ens, seeus non dividerent totum ens. Resp.
units.tr: II. Let us now examine the arguments of our opponents. I. Let Jacobus Arminius first enter the arena. He says: one and the same thing cannot be necessary and contingent at once, because the necessary and the contingent divide the whole extent of being. For every being is either necessary or contingent. But things that divide the whole of being do not coincide in any one being, otherwise they would not divide the whole of being. Reply.

units.la: I. Præter aliquid Sophistici acuminis, ausim dicere, nihil fuisse in impostore isto præter fumos & verba, imò ne umbratilem logicæ aut metaphysicæ notitiam. Age itaque Iacobe, fare quæso, an non causa vel causatum, potentia vel actus, finitum infinitum dividunt totum ens? Omne enim ens est causa vel causatum, actus vel potentia, finitum vel infinitum, & tamen materia prima, elementa, & ferè omnia entia sunt causa respectu aliorum entium, & causatum respectu primæ causæ, elementa sunt actu elementa & mista in potentia, Embryo actu Embryo, & potentia homo. Christus qua homo finitus, nisi velit Sophista cum Arrio, quia finitum & infinitum dividunt totum ens, non posse Christum esse & Deum & hominem. 2. Quia aliqua dividunt totum ens, non officit, quin diverso respectu in idem coincidant, quia diversitas respectuum, maxime distantia uniit in aliquo tertio.
units.tr: I. Apart from some sophistical sharpness, I dare say there was nothing in this impostor but smoke and words, indeed not even a shadowy knowledge of logic or metaphysics. Come then, Jacob, tell me, I beg you: do not cause and effect, potency and act, finite and infinite divide the whole of being? For every being is either a cause or an effect, act or potency, finite or infinite. Yet prime matter, the elements, and nearly all beings are causes with respect to other beings and effects with respect to the first cause. The elements are actually elements and potentially mixed bodies; the embryo is actually an embryo and potentially a man. Unless the sophist sides with Arius, who argues that because finite and infinite divide the whole of being, Christ as finite man cannot also be God and man, he must admit that the two can coincide. 2. Even where some things divide the whole of being, nothing prevents them from coinciding in the same thing under different respects, since a difference of respects, especially a wide one, unites them in some third thing.

units.la: 2. Ob. p. 141. Differunt (inquit) contingens & necessarium integris essentiis & tota definitione: Nam necessarium est quod non potest non esse, vel fieri. Contradictorie[?] scilicet ista opponuntur quae oppositio est infinita. Resp. 1. Audite nugas metaphysicales, differunt integris essentiis relatum & correlatum, & tamen Iacobus Arminius fuit & pater & filius, & doctor & discipulus, causa & causarum, album & quantum differunt totis essentiis, & idem tamen est & causa & causatum, causa hujus ut Polycletes statuae & causatum illius, filius patris, a quo ut homo generatus, idem paries albus & quantus. Diversitatem respectuum, quando contradictio non est πρὸς τὸ αὐτὸ[?], κατὰ τὸ αὐτὸ[?], ἅμα καὶ ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ χρόνῳ[?] ut ait Aristoteles, tollere contradictionem norunt in schola decantatissimum esse pueri. Iacobus grandis metaphysicus plane contra vult contradictionem, quae non est contradictio nisi in ipsius cerebro, evertere diversitatem respectuum. 3. Laxe & dissolute definit contingens quod potest non fieri; atqui sic sol, luna, plantae, & etiam maxime necessaria sunt contingentia. Deo enim ita volenti possunt omnia
units.tr: 2. Objection, p. 141. Contingent and necessary, he says, differ in their whole essences and in their whole definitions. For the necessary is that which cannot not be or not be made. Clearly these are opposed as contradictories, and this opposition is absolute. Reply 1. Hear the metaphysical trifles! Relative and correlative differ in their whole essences, and yet Jacobus Arminius was both father and son, both teacher and pupil, both cause and effect. Something can be both cause and effect, the cause of one thing, as Polyclitus is the cause of his statue, and the effect of another, as a son is the effect of his father, from whom he was begotten as a man. The same wall is both white and large. Schoolboys know well, as is repeated in the school, that a difference of respects removes contradiction, when there is no contradiction in the same respect, in the same way, and at the same time [πρὸς τὸ αὐτὸ, κατὰ τὸ αὐτὸ, ἅμα καὶ ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ χρόνῳ], as Aristotle says. Jacobus, the great metaphysician, plainly wants to overturn the difference of respects, which is a contradiction only in his own brain and nowhere else. 3. He defines the contingent loosely and carelessly as that which can not happen. Yet in that case the sun, the moon, the plants, and even the most necessary things are contingent, for all things could not be if God so willed. For God made all things freely.

units.la: Idem ibid, p. 142. nia non esse: nam liberè omnia fecit. Contingens est quod respectu naturalis modi agendi in causa potest non fieri, ut actus credendi in Petro, & tamen respectu decreti non potest non credere.
units.tr: The same author, ibid., p. 142. The contingent is that which, with respect to the natural mode of acting in the cause, can not happen, as the act of believing in Peter. Yet with respect to the decree, he cannot not believe.

units.la: 3. Necessitas (inquit) vel contingentia eventus non ex una causa, sed ex omnibus simul junctis est æstimanda. Si enim positis decem causis ex quibus res non necessario sed contingenter producitur una accedat ex qua res necessario conficiatur, tota illa res dicitur non contingenter, sed necessario, extitisse. Resp. 1. Sed audi quid tute, alibi, magne Gamaliel, tanquam è tripode docueris, si plures causæ concurrant ad unum effectum producendum, jam quidem effectum illud relationem habet & assectionem ad singulas suas causas, sed nomen non fortitur, nisi ex modo quo [?] causis simul junctis exsistit & producitur: qui modus si fit necessarium, necessarium dicitur, si contingens, contingens. Tum infero ex tuis placitis effectuum contingens ex decem causis; & ex una necessarium, esse partim contingens, partim necessarium. 2. An non motus solis est contingens seu liber in relatione ad Deum? nam Deo ita libere volenti olim constitit sine motu sol, & respectu solis est naturalis: doce tu ergo utrum motus solis sit necessarius an contingens: hic cogeris dicere esse diverso respectu & contingens & necessarium, & sic quæ infinitè opponuntur, in idem coincidunt. 3. Si decem illæ causæ sunt proximæ, totum effectum denominatur contingens, & quia Deus decrevit concurrere cum illis decem causis, erit essectum etiam necessarium in relatione ad Deum.
units.tr: 3. Necessity or contingency of an event (he says) must be judged not from one cause but from all causes taken together. For if, when ten causes are posited from which a thing is produced not necessarily but contingently, one more cause is added from which the thing is necessarily brought about, the whole thing is said to have come into being not contingently but necessarily. Reply 1. But hear what you yourself, great Gamaliel, have taught elsewhere as from a tripod: if several causes concur to produce one effect, then that effect indeed bears a relation and affection to each of its causes, but it takes its name only from the mode in which it exists and is produced by the causes taken together. If that mode is necessary, the effect is called necessary; if contingent, contingent. Then I infer from your own tenets that an effect which comes from ten causes and from one necessary cause is partly contingent and partly necessary. 2. Is not the motion of the sun contingent, or free, in relation to God? For when God freely willed it, the sun stood still without motion, and with respect to the sun the motion is natural. Teach me then whether the motion of the sun is necessary or contingent. Here you will be forced to say that it is both contingent and necessary under different respects, and so things that are infinitely opposed coincide in the same thing. 3. If those ten causes are proximate, the whole effect is called contingent; and because God has decreed to concur with those ten causes, the effect will also be necessary in relation to God.

units.la: 4. Si Dei modus concurrendi vel agendi fit partim necessarius, partim liber, qualis erat mundi creatio? Deus enim absolutè ab æterno mundum decrevit creare, & tamen liberè creavit mundum; vel volitio creationis in Deo orta est in tempore, & sic mutabilis est; vel creatio mundi erit & & libera & necessaria diverso respectu, §. Petrus mutabiliter & defectibiliter credit, uti omnis causa fecunda facit: Deus vero impedibiliter & immutabiliter, ut credat. Videat Arminius qui illa contradictorie opposita commisceat.
units.tr: 4. If God's mode of concurring or acting is partly necessary and partly free, what kind of creation of the world was it? For God absolutely decreed from eternity to create the world, and yet he created the world freely. Either the volition of creation arose in God in time, and so he is mutable; or the creation of the world will be both free and necessary under different respects. Peter believes changeably and defectibly, as every secondary cause acts; but God believes unhinderedly and immutably. Let Arminius see who mixes together these contradictory opposites.

units.la: 4. Obj. Decretum Dei, cum fit interna Dei actio, non est rei causa immediate, sed quicquid facit, per potentiam facit, unde nihil est necessarium respectu decreti. Refp. Non sequitur: posito decreto, necessario effectus contingens fiet, non quia decretum influit immediate in effectum, sed quoniam decretum applicat in tempore omnipotentiam ad determinandum voluntatem.
units.tr: 4. Objection. The decree of God, since it is an internal act of God, is not the immediate cause of a thing; but whatever he does, he does by power. Hence nothing is necessary with respect to the decree. Reply: It does not follow. Given the decree, the contingent effect will necessarily come about, not because the decree flows immediately into the effect, but because the decree applies omnipotence in time to determine the will.

units.la: §. Ob. Sic respondet Iacob. objectioni sibi propositæ: olfa Christi fi naturam ossium quis consideret, frangi potuerunt; fi decretum Dei, non potuerunt frangi. Respondeo (inquit) me negare, quod respectu decreti divini non potuerunt frangi. Deus enim non decrevit, ut non possent frangi, sed ut non frangerentur. Fractionem enim non impediit potentia irrefiftibili: sed levi fuafione, argumento ducto, ab inutili. {*}Otili. Resp. 1. Non potuit imprudens sophista clamosius sibi contradicere. Concedit enim Deum decrevisse ut non frangerentur offa Christi, & tamen argumentum ab inutili, milites frangebant contingenter. Ergo fractio illa respectu Dei decreti erat necessaria: alioqui Dei decretum rescindi potuit, & respectu militum erat contingens, quod est institutum.
units.tr: §. Objection. Jacobus answers the objection put to him thus: if one considers the nature of bones, the bones of Christ could be broken; if one considers God's decree, they could not be broken. I answer (he says) that I deny that they could not be broken with respect to the divine decree. For God did not decree that they could not be broken, but that they would not be broken. For the breaking was not prevented by an irresistible power, but by a light persuasion, by an argument drawn from what is useless. {*}Useless. Reply. 1. The imprudent sophist could not have contradicted himself more loudly. For he concedes that God decreed that the bones of Christ would not be broken, and yet by an argument from what is useless the soldiers broke them contingently. Therefore that breaking, with respect to God's decree, was necessary; otherwise God's decree could have been rescinded, and with respect to the soldiers it was contingent, which is what was laid down.

units.la: 2. Dicat quis nostrum[?], afferat Deum decrevisse, ut offa Christi non possent frangi; hoc illi in somniis[?] venit in mentem.
units.tr: 2. Let one of us say, let him bring forward, that God decreed that the bones of Christ could not be broken. That idea came to him in dreams.

units.la: 3. Dicimus Deum decrevisse ut milites non frangerent offa, id quod Iacobus ait, sed quaero, an potuerint non frangere. Certè fatetur id Iacobus Arminius, quando negat vi irresistibili milites fuisse à Deo impeditos, vult vi resistibili milites fregisse. Nam negat suasionem determinare voluntatem: quaero quomodo itaque Deus decrevit ut frangerentur; decretum illud rescindi potuit à militibus libere frangentibus, hoc est ita frangentibus ut potuerint non frangere. Quid hic, Iacobe, respondeas aveo scire, nempe ex praescientia determinationis liberi arbitrii militum, decrevit ut non frangerentur. Itane? Ergo praevidit prius ipsos non velle frangere, & tum decrevit ut non frangerentur, hoc est, si velit lector nugas audire, postquam praescivit Deus è fenestra scientiæ mediæ, fore ut milites liberè non frangerent: decrevit ut ab iis non frangerentur. Pudeat itaque theologos, superficiarium rudem, & logicæ plane ignarum impostorem deperire, & ut doctorem demirari. 4. Quasi vinolentus nihil non molitur, ut defendat efsectum non esse diverso respectu & contingens sive liberum & necessarium, & tamen resp. ad art. 6. p. 142. ait Mundus[?] vero ; ut & omnia alia secundum absolutam considerationem, contingentia sunt, & contingenter a Deo libere operante producta. At vero posito quod Deus vult mundum condere potentia infinita ; & posito quod Deus alia iflam potentiam usurpat ; jaih[?] dicetur mundum non potuisse non existere ex ista causa. Illic verbis videtur fateri mundum & contingenter & necessario a Deo creatum esse.
