Sed velim, ut lector vafriciem miselli theologastri observet; non dicit mundum necessario existere hoc posito quod Deus infinita potentia vult mundum condere, sed vult aliam poni conditionem, nempe hoc posito quod Deus actu istam potentiam usurpet. At quis dubitet Deum necessario condere mundum, quando actu condit? Sed quaero, cur non sufficit ad necessitatem creationis mundi hoc poni, quod Deus velit mundum condere infinita sua potentia. Hoc si Arminius fateatur sufficere, cogetur dicere actum liberum & decretum absolutum adversis frontibus haud pugnare, & idem esse contingens in se, & necessarium respectu decreti divini. Sed aliud forte heterodoxius subest, nempe quod fieri posset ut Deus decreverit mundum infinita sua potentia creare,{1} & tamen non necesse est ut creetur, nisi Deus etiam actu potentiam infinitam usurpet; quia forte oritur in Deo nova scientia & mutatio voluntatis, aut quia nihil ab æterno decrevit, sed volitiones ipsius temporales sunt, etiam in effectibus a solo Deo productis, & sic Deus inconsultius aget, quam homines.
units.tr: 3. We say that God decreed that the soldiers would not break the bones, which is what Jacobus says; but I ask whether they could have failed to break them. Certainly Jacobus Arminius admits this when he denies that the soldiers were hindered by God with an irresistible force, and wants them to have broken the bones by a resistible force. For he denies that persuasion determines the will. I ask then how God decreed that they would be broken; that decree could have been rescinded by the soldiers breaking the bones freely, that is, breaking them in such a way that they could have not broken them. Here, Jacob, I am eager to know how you would answer. You will say, no doubt, that from foreknowledge of the determination of the soldiers' free will God decreed that the bones would not be broken. Really? So he first foresaw that they would not wish to break them, and then decreed that they would not be broken; that is, if the reader wishes to hear trifles, after God foresaw, through the window of middle knowledge, that the soldiers would freely not break them, he decreed that they would not be broken by them. Let theologians be ashamed, then, to dote on this crude superficial fellow, an impostor utterly ignorant of logic, and to admire him as a teacher. 4. Like a drunkard he attempts everything, so as to defend that an effect is not both contingent and free and necessary under different respects; and yet, in reply to article 6, p. 142, he says: The world, indeed, as all other things considered absolutely, is contingent and produced by God acting freely and contingently. But granted that God wills to found the world by infinite power, and granted that God uses that power, it will be said that the world could not have failed to exist from that cause. In these words he seems to admit that the world was created by God both contingently and necessarily. But I would have the reader notice the cunning of this wretched little theologaster. He does not say that the world necessarily exists given that God wills to found the world by infinite power; he wants a different condition posited, namely, given that God actually uses that power. But who would doubt that God necessarily creates the world when he actually creates it? Yet I ask, why is it not enough for the necessity of the world's creation that it be posited that God wills to create the world by his infinite power? If Arminius admits that this is enough, he will be forced to say that a free act and an absolute decree do not fight against each other on opposite fronts, and that the same thing is contingent in itself and necessary with respect to the divine decree. But perhaps something more heterodox lies beneath, namely, that it could happen that God decreed to create the world by his infinite power, and yet it is not necessary that it be created unless God also actually uses that infinite power; because perhaps a new knowledge arises in God and a change of will, or because he decreed nothing from eternity but his volitions are temporal, even concerning effects produced by God alone, and so God would act more carelessly than men.

units.la: 12. Objest. 6. Contradicens (inquit) est in adjecto contingenter aliquid fieri, hoc est, ita fieri, ut possit non fieri, & tamen idipsum esse determinatum ad alteram partem, ut non possit non fieri id, quod determinatum est (per Dei decretum absolutum) ut fiat, nec sufficit manere libertatem quoad naturam creaturæ, nam ad contingentiam non sufficit, ut adsit potentia, quæ libere agere possit secundum naturam; sed requiritur, ut usus illius potentiæ & libertatis nullo modo impediatur, & quæ insania est concedere potentiam in creatione, & cum jam usurpanda est, ipsam auferre. Hoc est potentiam concedere, quum illius usus non est, & cum usus ejus & necessitas est, tum libertatem in actu impedire. Idem etiam in anal. Rom. 9. ait ad libertatem requiri potentiam & δυνάμει & ἐνεργείας non impeditam, & Remonst. in confess. volunt non tantum potentiam esse liberam, sed & usum liberum, atque ad opposita indifferentem. Resp. 1. Contradicens in adjecto non est aliquid fieri contingenter respectu causæ secundæ, & esse determinatum respectu Dei decreti, quod statuit futuritionem æternam illius actus, quem voluntas determinatè ex insita sua libertate producet, sicut non est re-
units.tr: 12. Objection 6. He says: "It is a contradiction in terms that something should happen contingently, that is, in such a way that it could fail to happen, and yet that the same thing is determined to one side, so that what has been determined (by God's absolute decree) to happen cannot fail to happen. Nor does it suffice that freedom remains with respect to the nature of the creature, for contingency does not depend only on the presence of a power able to act freely according to its nature. Rather, it requires that the exercise of that power and freedom be in no way hindered. And what madness it is to grant a power in creation and then, when it is about to be exercised, to take it away! This is to grant a power when it has no exercise, and when its exercise and necessity are at hand, to hinder its freedom in act. The same author, in his commentary on Romans 9, also says that freedom requires a power, both potency [δυνάμει] and act [ἐνεργείας], unimpeded. And the Remonstrants in their Confession want not only the power to be free but also its free exercise, and indifferent to opposites." Answer 1. There is no contradiction in terms in something happening contingently with respect to the secondary cause and yet being determined with respect to God's decree, which establishes the eternal futurition of that act which the will will produce determinately from its innate freedom. Nor is this inconsistent, just as it is not inconsistent that, if God's decree were removed, the will could will this or not will it, and yet, with respect to eternal futurition, will only this and not will the opposite. For it cannot both will and not will the same thing, as the Sophist hints, unless there had been from eternity both an eternal futurition of the volition and an eternal non-futurition of this same volition, which is a palpable contradiction.

units.la: Resp. ad art. 7. p. 144. Remonst. confess. c. 6. pugnans; si auferatur Dei decretum, voluntatem posse velle hoc, vel nolle, & tamen quoad aeternam futuritionem determinate tantum hoc velle, non nolle, non enim potest & velle & nolle idem, ut innuit Sophista, nisi ab aeterno praecesserit & futuritio aeterna volitionis, & aeterna non futuritio volitionis hujus, quae palpabilis est contradictio. 2. Bene est quod fateatur Arminius posito decreto absoluto, manere potentiam liberam. 3. Ait requiri ad libertatis naturam, ut usus ipsius non impediatur; sed quomodo probat Sophista ex decreto absoluto impediri usum libertatis? certe hic obmutescit, nihil adfert nec syllabam qua probet. Semper videbis illum, quando ad probationes ventum est, silere, quasi hiatus oris aut inanis conatus cerebri profligandae veritati par esset. Neque Remonstrantes verbulo probant impeditionem usus liberi, quin & nos ditimus[?] posito Dei decreto, tandem omnipotentiam adjuvare, non impedire libertatem, & libertati quasi gravidae actus quoad futuritionem producendi, obstetricari, & cum libertate in hunc non in aliam actum propendentem, concurrere ad extractionem actuationis e potentia libertatis, quam illa sola suis viribus extrahere non posset. 4. Hic lector videat, quam dissimulate & minus candide nostram sententiam exponant. Nam voluntas non magis impediri potest, quam cogi, imo voluntatem liberam velle impeditam, est simul velle & non velle & velle coactam, quia impeditio est impedimentum ponere voluntati, ne velit, hoc est efficere, ut velit contra suam insitam propensionem, ideoque non velle, quia τὸ velle in suo conceptu claudit vitalem propensionem.
units.tr: Answer to art. 7, p. 144. Remonstrant Confession, ch. 6. 2. It is good that Arminius concedes that, with the absolute decree posited, the power remains free. 3. He says that for the nature of freedom it is required that its exercise not be impeded. But how does the Sophist prove that the exercise of freedom is impeded by the absolute decree? Certainly here he falls silent; he brings forward nothing, not a syllable by which he might prove it. You will always see him, when it comes to proofs, going quiet, as if a gaping of the mouth or an empty effort of the brain were a match for overthrowing the truth. Nor do the Remonstrants prove the hindering of the free exercise by a single word. Indeed we say that, with God's decree posited, omnipotence at last aids freedom and does not hinder it; it acts as a midwife to freedom, as it were pregnant with an act with respect to its futurition, and, concurring with freedom which inclines toward this act and not another, it brings about the drawing forth of the actuality from the power of freedom, which freedom could not draw forth by its own strength alone. 4. Here let the reader see how dishonestly and how uncandidly they set forth our opinion. For the will can no more be hindered than be compelled. Indeed, to will while hindered is at once to will and not to will, and to will under compulsion; for to hinder is to place an obstacle to the will so that it does not will, that is, to bring it about that it wills against its innate inclination, and therefore does not will, since the notion of willing [τὸ velle] includes in its concept a vital inclination.

units.la: §. Arminius dicit auferri usum libertatis cum opus est, & forte hoc est actum impedire, sed falso & absurde, bone Deus, quia hoc innuunt voluntatem inclinare ad volendum A B. C. D. & decretum absolutum vi torquere inclinationem à volitione τὸ A. B. D. & efficere, ut impedita & constricta velit C, non A, non B, non D, hoc omnium est ipsorum non doctrina nostra, imo volumus voluntatem ex se posse velle, A, B, C, D, & quoad aeternam futuritionem volituram esse liberrime C, non A, non B, non D, etiam posito per impossibile, quod non esset in Deo decretum, at vero Dei decretum superveniens & antecedens volitionem τὸ C, non constringit voluntatem; de voluntatem in eo vitali situ locat, in quo electione liberrima, admiranda conspiratione, id est, volitura, & non aliud, quod Deus absoluto decreto definivit volendum, & rursus Deus absoluto decreto illud praedefinit; & non aliud, quod libertas humana actu eliget: jam quaerant hi Davi impeditionem suam commentiam.
units.tr: §. Arminius says that the exercise of freedom is removed when there is need, and perhaps this is to hinder the act; but falsely and absurdly, good God, because they imply that the will inclines to willing A, B, C, D, and that the absolute decree by force twists the inclination away from the volition of [τὸ] A, B, D, and brings it about that the hindered and constrained will wills C, not A, not B, not D. This is not our doctrine, nor is it the doctrine of any of them. Rather, we hold that the will of itself can will A, B, C, D, and with respect to eternal futurition it will will most freely C, not A, not B, not D, even supposing, which is impossible, that there were no decree in God. But the decree of God, both superveniing and antecedent, does not constrain the will to the volition [τὸ] C. Rather, it places the will in that vital situation in which, by the most free choice and by an admirable conspiring, that is, it will will this and not another, which God by his absolute decree defined to be willed; and again God by his absolute decree predefines it; and not another, which human freedom will actually choose. Now let them find an impediment for their David, a made-up one.

units.la: §. 6. Accuratius Arminius? uti vulgo vendicatur, vult potentiam esse δύναμις[?] hoc est; potentia libera, quae nugae? Potentia potentia libera.
units.tr: §. 6. Is Arminius more accurate, as is commonly claimed, when he wants the power to be [δύναμις], that is, free power? What trifles! Power, free power.

units.la: §. 7. Usum esse indifferentem ad oppositā est repugnans in adjecto, ita tamen loquuntur Remonstrantes: nam usus liber est actus libertatis, actus libertatis est actualis determinatio voluntatis, at vero determinationem libertatis esse indifferentem ad opposita, est determinationem esse determinabilem, & non determinationem, & album esse nigrum, deinde potentia dicitur indifferens ad opposita, non actus, vel usus libertatis: nam quando adest usus, tollitur indifferentia ad actus oppositos. Sed Remonstrantes in apolog. cap. 6, pag. 70 dicunt se velle nullam circumstantiam adesse vel abesse a voluntate cum qua non possetconsistere ipsum non agere, hoc itaque est actum absolute posse fieri, vel non; & sic ita loquuntur, non tantum potentia sed & usus debet esse indifferens hoc est non tantum actus liberi possunt esse vel non esse sed etiam possunt esse vel non esse. Nam Sophistae non docent, quod non-impeditio actus superaddat non-impeditioni potentiae.
units.tr: §. 7. That the exercise is indifferent to opposites is a contradiction in terms, yet the Remonstrants speak thus. For a free exercise is an act of freedom, and an act of freedom is an actual determination of the will. But to say that the determination of freedom is indifferent to opposites is to say that a determination is determinable and not a determination, and that white is black. Next, power is said to be indifferent to opposites, not an act or exercise of freedom. For when the exercise is present, indifference to opposite acts is removed. But the Remonstrants, in Apology ch. 6, p. 70, say that they hold that no circumstance is present or absent in the will with which it could not be consistent for it not to act. So it is that an act can absolutely come about or not. And so they speak thus: not only the power but also the exercise ought to be indifferent, that is, not only can free acts be or not be, but they can also be or not be. For the Sophists do not teach that the non-hindrance of the act adds to the non-hindrance of the power.

units.la: 13. Obj. 7. Ex hac determinatione sequitur 1. Deum esse authorem peccati, 2. Deum vere & proprie & solum peccare, quia posita lege vetante, istum actum, & praedeterminatione tali, qua actus ille non potest non pati, sequitur Deum ipsum esse qui legem transgrediatur, utpote qui faciat ipse actum contra legem, quomodo actus homini est inevitabilis. Resp. 1. quia Deus effectivè determinat actus positivos illegalitati in peccato substratos, nullo modo sequitur eum esse peccati authorem, sed alibi cum bono Deo diputabitur de Dei circa peccatum volitione. 2. Injurius est in providentiam, qui Dei efficientiae & decreto admit actus positivos in peccato, neque sequitur Deum esse, qui legem transgrediatur. Nam creaturae vetuit actusquofdam: ut doceat qua lege cautum sit, ne Deus mundum administret, omnia entia aeterno decreto, modo, mensura, numero & circumstantiis determinet, ne tanquam prima causa cum actu positivo in peccato concurrat. Num Arminius, Deo lege prohibitum esse velit, ne in eo creaturae vivant, moveantur, & esse habeant? Act. 17. 3. Quaero an actus positivi in peccato nullo Dei decreto, ne quidem conditionato fiant, aeterna Dei voluntate: ait Arminius Deum velle omnia illa quae ex infinitis sibi possibilibus entibus, per extremum sapientiae judicium facienda decrevit, & quidem vult illa facere. Asserit Dei voluntatem omnium rerum esse causam mediante potentia, inter quas, eo loci numera actus contingentes. Ibid. hinc voluntas Dei ex Arminio erit causa actuum lege prohibitorum, qua sunt actus. Ergo ex Arminio Deus vere, proprie, & solus peccat, & peccare decrevit, utpote qui facit ipse actum contra legem. Item difp. 10. th. 15. citra omnem in justitiam, efficientiam Dei in concurrendo astruit. Ergo, inquam, ab aeterno decrevit concurrere, ideoque actu positivo voluntatis suae mediante potentia, actum peccaminosum efficere. At scio Arminium dicere Deum velle illum actum voluntate non absoluta sed conditionata. Age itaque Iacobe, quid est voluntas conditionata, nempe Deus praesciens creaturam libere actum peccatum minosum efficere, vult. hoc est postquam actus est, actum esse vult. At mendacem oportet esse memorem. An Dei voluntas, mediante potentia, erit causa actuum contingentium, uti fassus est supra, nempe postquam est actus contingens. tum enim quia vult hoc esse postquam habuit esse, Dei voluntas est ipsius causa. Apage, Sophista, ineptias.
units.tr: 13. Obj. 7. From this determination it follows, first, that God is the author of sin; second, that God truly, properly, and alone sins, because, given a forbidding law and such a predetermination that the act cannot fail to occur, it follows that God himself is the one who transgresses the law, as the one who himself makes the act against the law, just as the act is unavoidable for a man. Answer. 1. Because God effectively determines positive acts that underlie illegality in sin, it in no way follows that he is the author of sin. But elsewhere, with the good God, we shall discuss God's volition concerning sin. 2. It is an injury to providence to deny that God's efficiency and decree admit positive acts in sin. Nor does it follow that God is the one who transgresses the law. For he forbade certain acts to the creature, so as to teach by what law it is provided that God, in administering the world, by his eternal decree determines all beings in mode, measure, number and circumstances, so that as first cause he does not concur with a positive act in sin. Does Arminius wish that God is forbidden by law to let creatures live, move, and have being in him? Acts 17. 3. I ask whether positive acts in sin come about by no decree of God, not even a conditional one, by his eternal will. Arminius says that God wills all those things which, from the infinite beings possible to him, he has decreed by the extreme judgment of wisdom to be done, and indeed he wills to do them. He asserts that the will of God is the cause of all things through power, among which, in that place, number contingent acts. Ibid. Hence, according to Arminius, the will of God will be the cause of acts forbidden by law, which are acts. Therefore, according to Arminius, God truly, properly, and alone sins, and has decreed to sin, as the one who himself makes the act against the law. Likewise, in disputation 10, thesis 15, he asserts God's efficiency in concurring, without any injustice. Therefore, I say, he decreed from eternity to concur, and so by a positive act of his will, through power, to bring about the sinful act. But I know that Arminius says God wills that act not by an absolute but by a conditional will. Come then, Jacob, what is a conditional will? Namely, God, foreseeing the creature freely bringing about the sinful act, wills it; that is, once the act is, he wills the act to be. But a liar ought to have a good memory. Will God's will, through power, be the cause of contingent acts, as he confessed above, namely once the contingent act is? For then, because he wills this to be after it has come to be, the will of God is its cause. Away with you, Sophist, with your nonsense.

units.la: 2. Vide, qui Arminius Deum excuset, vult ipse vere & proprie & solus facere actum lege prohibitum, non absolute, sed conditionata voluntate, nempe praesciens creaturam illum actum efficere, at vero velle seu approbare actum lege prohibitum, postquam est, non est minor injustitia, quam illud velle & intendere absolute, antequam fit, ac proinde hoc argumentum in detrimentum non mediocre cedet doctrinae Arminianae.
units.tr: 2. See how Arminius excuses God. He holds that God himself truly, properly and solely performs an act forbidden by law, not absolutely but by a conditional will, namely by foreseeing that the creature will perform that act. Yet to will or approve an act forbidden by law after it has happened is no less injustice than to will and intend it absolutely before it happens. Therefore this argument will count for no small harm to the Arminian doctrine.

units.la: 4. Actus peccati Deo erit inevitabilis: nam si voluntate Dei conditionata fit talis actus, tum habet esse antecedenter ad voluntatem, & sic Deus fato volet actum lege prohibitum. Non enim potest avertere, ut id quod est, non sit, & non potest non velle illum actum, quia ipsius voluntas, non potest non esse causa omnium actuum positivorum: Arminius hic Deum fato eximat. ȝ[?], Actus contingens à Deo definitus nullo sensu dicitur creaturae inevitabilis. Fit enim libere à creatura, quae libere id vult & aliud libere non vult, quam quod æterno Dei decreto est determinatum. Itaque commentitia illa inevitabilitas, si qua est, tam ortum habet à libertate creaturæ, quam à decreto Dei. 6. Deus ex absoluto suo dominio nulla lege nexus decernit efficere actus positivos libertatis tanquam prima causa, & creaturæ legi obnoxiæ libere eosdem actus efficiunt contra legem & dictamen conscientiæ, ideoque hic illæ peccant, Deus vero nullo modo transgreditur,
units.tr: 4. The act of sin will be inevitable for God. For if such an act comes about through God's conditional will, then it has being antecedently to the will, and so God would will by fate an act forbidden by law. For he cannot prevent what is from not being, and he cannot not will that act, since his will cannot fail to be the cause of all positive acts. Here Arminius frees God from fate. A contingent act defined by God is in no sense called inevitable for the creature. For it is done freely by the creature, who freely wills it and freely wills nothing other than what has been determined by the eternal decree of God. So that imagined inevitability, if there is any, arises as much from the freedom of the creature as from the decree of God. 6. God, from his absolute dominion and bound by no law, decrees to bring about the positive acts of freedom as first cause; and creatures, subject to law, freely perform those same acts against the law and the dictate of conscience. Therefore they sin, but God in no way transgresses.

units.la: 14. Ob. 8. Tertio (inquit Arminius) sequitur Deum homine peccatore & peccato indiguisse ad gloriam justitiæ & misericordiæ illustrandam. Resp. Expectabam ut audirem probationem consequentiæ, & Arminius obmutuit, satis habuit ponere non probare, quod ei solenne est, atqui dicemus nos Deum liberè gloriam justitiæ & misericordiæ declarare, potuit non declarasse, non est apud creaturas gloriæ indigus.
units.tr: 14. Objection 8. Thirdly (says Arminius), it follows that God needed a sinful man and sin in order to illustrate the glory of justice and mercy. Answer: I was expecting to hear the proof of the consequence, but Arminius fell silent. He was content to lay down his claim without proving it, which is his habit. We, however, say that God freely declares the glory of justice and mercy; he could have not declared it. He does not lack glory from creatures.

units.la: 2. Hoc posito quod Deus gloriam decreverit illustrare, libere decrevit peccati permissione eam patefacere, non indigus vel peccati vel peccatoris, sed libero decreto permittere volens. At vult Arminius nos docere Deum non potuisse alio modo quam peccato gloriam declarare. Resp. medium in hoc divinæ sapientiæ, cujus nulla est homuncionibus investigatio, credimus nos esse convenientissimum, ex hypothesi, quod Deus decreverit gloriam justitiæ vindicatricis & misericordiæ parcentis creaturis patefacere: illi spirispiritum Iehovæ instruant, nos adoramus & credimus, infinitæ Dei sapientiæ relinquimus innumera possibilia, quibus fines suos posset fortiter attingere.
units.tr: 2. Granting that God decreed to display his glory, he freely decreed to reveal it by the permission of sin, needing neither sin nor sinner, but willing to permit it by a free decree. Yet Arminius wants to teach us that God could not declare his glory in any other way than through sin. Answer: we believe that the means in this matter, a part of divine wisdom into which mortals have no investigation, is most fitting, given the hypothesis that God decreed to reveal the glory of avenging justice and of mercy sparing creatures. "Who has known the mind of the Spirit of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?" We adore and believe, and we leave to the infinite wisdom of God the countless possibilities by which it could strongly reach its ends.

units.la: Ob. 9. Sequitur ex decreto absoluto contingentium, peccatum non esse peccatum. Resp. Facile est Arminio quatuor verba ponere, at tam facile est mihi reponere, ex hoc decreto optime sequitur peccatum esse peccatum: nulla enim est hic necessitas, quæ libertatem evertat.
units.tr: Ob. 9. It follows from the absolute decree concerning contingent things that sin is not sin. Resp. It is easy for Arminius to set down four words, but it is just as easy for me to reply that from this decree it follows very well that sin is sin. For there is no necessity here that overturns liberty.

units.la: 15. Ad Suarezium accedo. Voluntas creata decreto subjacens non magis potest aliud velle, quam determinatum est illo decreto, quam Dei decretum rescindi potest. 'Sed non est satis (inquit Suarez.) si dicamus manere potestatem, posita necessitate ex suppositione, quoniam ex tali suppositione, est sopita & impedita, quoad alia omnia præter illud unum, quod eligitur, & ideo est tantum potentia remota ad plura, non vero propinqua, qualis requiritur ad usum libertatis. Resp. (voluntas non potest aliud velle, quam quod decernitur à Deo) distingui debet. Nam illud (non potest) vel notat impotentiam in voluntate, quasi per decretum esset constricta, & fataliter torta, vel (non potest) est libertatis non potentia electiva, & idem est quod libere non potest, vel non vult, quippe si (non potest) in latissimo sensu accipiatur, quoties vult hoc, non potest hoc non velle, at vero ut decreto subest, libere non potest aliud velle, quam vult, & decretum est, non ex impotentia, quasi decretum removeret, vel judicium rationis, vel vim electivam, vel imperialem illam propensionem voluntatis, imo haec omnia ponit, quia haec non-potentia aeque est ab ipsa libertate, sed dependenter & subordinatè, atque à Dei decreto principaliter. Hæ (voluntas decreto subjacens, non potest aliud velle quam quod decretum erat a Deo) & (voluntas non potest aliud velle quam actn vult) sunt una & eadem non-potentia quoad objectum & terminum, quoniam decretum Dei ad eundem terminum flectit mediante potentia, ad quam se libere flectit ipsa voluntas. jam vero voluntas libere volens hoc, non potest non velle hoc, idcoque haec non-potentia est libera, non sequitur ex hoc (non potest) vel laesio libertatis, vel usus.
units.tr: 15. I come now to Suarez. A created will subject to a decree cannot will anything other than what that decree determines, just as the decree of God cannot be rescinded. 'But it is not enough (says Suarez) to say that the power remains, the necessity being posited by supposition, since by such a supposition it is lulled and impeded in respect of all things except the one that is chosen; and so it is only a remote power to many things, not a proximate one, such as is required for the use of liberty. Answer. The statement that the will cannot will anything other than what God decrees must be distinguished. For that "cannot" either signifies an impotence in the will, as if it were constrained by the decree and fatally turned aside, or it is the non-power of liberty, the power of choice, and means the same as "freely cannot" or "does not will." For if "cannot" is taken in the widest sense, then whenever it wills this, it cannot not will this. But insofar as it is subject to the decree, it freely cannot will anything other than what it wills, and this is not from an impotence, as if the decree removed the judgment of reason, or the elective power, or that imperial propensity of the will. Indeed, it posits all these, because this non-power comes equally from liberty itself, but dependently and subordinately, and principally from God's decree. These two statements, (the will subject to the decree cannot will anything other than what God decreed) and (the will cannot will anything other than what it wills), are one and the same non-power as regards object and term, since the decree of God bends to the same term by means of the power to which the will itself freely bends. Now the will, freely willing this, cannot not will this, and therefore this non-power is free. From this "cannot" it does not follow either an injury to liberty or a failure of its use.

units.la: 2. Ita ait Alvar. ut homo (inquit) vere potuit velle aliquod objectum, non requiritur quod ex æternitate præcesserit in Deo absolutum & efficax decretum prædeterminans ejus liberum arbitrium ad volendum idem objectum, quamvis id requiratur ut illud aliu velit. unde ex hoc, quod in Deo non fuerit ejusmodi decretum, non sequitur quod homo non potuit velle tale objectum absolute loquendo, sed solum sequitur quod de facto non velit illud.
units.tr: 2. Thus Alvarez says: "A man (he says) can truly will some object. It is not required that there should have preceded from eternity in God an absolute and efficacious decree predetermining his free will to will that same object, although this is required in order that he should will it. Whence it does not follow from the fact that there was no such decree in God that man could not will such an object, speaking absolutely, but it follows only that in fact he does not will it."

units.la: Hinc recte infero, quamvis homo actu libere velit id solum ad quod decretum libertatem determinat mediante potentia, tamen, sive Deus tale decretum habuerit, sive non, potest voluntas contrarium velle. Nam ad posse velle non requiritur decretum absolutum, sed ad ꝓ velle. Ideoque posito decreto absoluto manet potentia aliud volendo, ideoque libertas, quod & annotavit Aquinas. 3. Manet (inquit Suarez) sed sopita & impedita sub Dei decreto, at vero quis sopor est Iesuita hoc allegare, non probare? Num lectorem sopore oppressum credit? Nam potentia hoc est non libere exerens suam potentiam aliud volendo, quam quod libere vult, & ad quod decretum absolutum voluntatem determinavit ut liberè vellet, hiccine sopor, an vero vigiliæ? nulla hic impeditio, quia libertas, si non hoc vellet, certe impediretur. Sed hæc res est, sopor est Iesuita, si libertas non ita solvatur à providentia, ut sopita providentia, possit libertas, absoluta indifferentia omnibus ad agendum requisitis positis, vel-le. vel non velle. Ideoque posita æterna suturitione volitionis, & non futuritione æterna nolitionis, tamen potest libertas non velle, & sic erat nolitio in tempore, quæ non futura erat ab æterno, quod Iesuita Vasquez jure merito rejicit. Sed memini quid Suarez alibi dicit potentia (inquit) solum in sensu divino (quam nempe nos libertati damus prout subest determinatio Dei) non potest immediate reduci in actu, sed oportet ut procedat aliqua dispositio aut mutatio, qua potentia reddatur proxima, vel acquirendo aliquid necessarium ad actum, vel tollendo impedimentum, & sic nisi potentia sit proxima ad agendum & non agendu [?] impeditur usus liber. Vt potestas quam habet album, ut fit nigrum non reducitur ad actum, nisi ablata albedine. R.1 Voluntas habitugratiae instructa subDei decreto est in potentia proxima ad non agendum in sensu divisio, si nempe removeatur decretum Dei, & ponatur contrarium. Nam neque decretum, tempus, aut locus, aut ejusmodi ponunt in voluntate, novam potentiae aut dispositionis accessionem. Nam oculus in tenebris, hoc modo, est in potentia proxima ad videndum, quoniam accessio luminis non addit novam potentiam visivam oculo, quam non habuit in tenebris. 2. Potentia albi, ut sit nigrum est potentia passiva: at voluntas sub Dei decreto habet potentiam electivam, vitalem, activam ad non agendum, si removeatur Dei decretum, & contrarium decretum poneretur. Neque decretum est impedimentum a-ctui contrario, tum quia repugnat voluntatem impediri in agendo, tum quoniam voluntas non potest contrarium actum tunc elicere, non-impotentia, sed voluntatis libera non-potentia & vi electiva. 3. Vis pandam mysterium hic Iesuiticum? vult libertatem omnibus ad agendum requisitis absolute posse agere & non agere, ita ut si velit, praecesserit in Deo decretum volendi; si nolit, uti absolute potest, fuerit in Deo decretum nolendi. Unde Deus nihil omnino absolute determinavit de actibus liberis, sed voluntas Dei hodie est suspensa, & ab aeterno fuit suspensa tam ad Petri volitionem quam nolitionem approbandam, ideoque decretum Dei certum & fixum de hac potius volitione Petri quam de illa, vel de nolitione, tum oritur de novo in Deo, quando Petrus ult: aliqui potentia libera non erit immediate & proxime indifferens ad agendum vel non agendum. Certe decretum Dei non magis est causa vastationis Chaldaeorum, quam non vastationis, & objectum decreti est possibile, quaero de consequentia Dei a decretis, id quod Arminius testatur, Certa eventus contingentium futuritio necessitatem non includit. At quid hoc aliud est, quam Deum nihil certo scire, nihil voluntate decernere de futuris contingentibus, donec actu evenianr? & scientiam Dei in tempore incipere, ut & omnes volitiones? ut taceam quam fit absurdum futuritionem rei non esse necessariam. Nam fi est futuritio & è statu poffibilitatis extracta, tam necessaria est, quam necesse est idem fit idem, futurum fit futurum. Imo futurum necessitatem non includere est futurum posse esse non futurum.
units.tr: Hence I rightly infer that, although a man in act freely wills only that to which the decree determines his liberty by means of power, nevertheless, whether God had such a decree or not, the will can will the contrary. For to be able to will, an absolute decree is not required; it is required only for willing. Therefore, with an absolute decree posited, the power of willing otherwise remains, and so does liberty, as Aquinas also observed. 3. The power remains (says Suarez), but lulled and impeded under God's decree. But what a sleep it is for a Jesuit to allege this instead of proving it! Does he think the reader is weighed down by sleep? For the power not freely exercising itself to will otherwise than what it freely wills, and to which the absolute decree determined the will so that it would will freely: is this sleep, or is it wakefulness? There is no impediment here, since liberty, if it did not will this, would certainly be impeded. But here is the point: it is a Jesuit's sleep if liberty is not so released from providence that, with providence lulled, liberty could, with absolute indifference and with all things required for acting posited, will or not will. And therefore, with the eternal futurition of the volition posited, and no eternal futurition of the nolition, liberty could still not will, and so there would be a nolition in time which was not future from eternity, which the Jesuit Vasquez rightly rejects. But I remember what Suarez says elsewhere: "power (he says), only in the divine sense (which we grant to liberty insofar as it is subject to God's determination), cannot be immediately reduced to act, but some disposition or change must come before, by which the power is made proximate, either by acquiring something necessary for the act or by removing an impediment; and so unless the power is proximate to acting and not acting, free use is impeded. Just as the power a thing has to be white, when it becomes black, is not reduced to act unless the whiteness is removed." Answer 1: The will, endowed with grace and subject to God's decree, is in proximate power to not acting in the divided sense, namely if God's decree were removed and the contrary posited. For neither the decree, nor time, nor place, nor anything of the kind puts into the will any new addition of power or disposition. Thus the eye in darkness is in proximate power to seeing, since the coming of light adds no new visual power to the eye which it did not have in darkness. 2. The power of white to become black is a passive power, but the will under God's decree has an elective, vital, active power to not act, if God's decree were removed and the contrary decree posited. Nor is the decree an impediment to the contrary act, both because it is repugnant for the will to be impeded in acting, and because the will could not then elicit the contrary act. This is not an impotence but a free non-power of the will and an elective force. 3. Shall I unfold here the Jesuit mystery? It wills that liberty, with all things required for acting absolutely posited, can absolutely act and not act, so that if it wills, a decree of willing will have preceded in God; if it does not will, which it can absolutely do, there will have been in God a decree of not willing. Whence God has absolutely determined nothing at all about free acts; rather, the will of God is today suspended, and from eternity was suspended, both as regards approving Peter's volition and as regards approving his nolition. Therefore the certain and fixed decree of God about this volition of Peter rather than that one, or about the nolition, then arises anew in God, when Peter wills. [Some part of the free power will not be immediately and proximately indifferent to acting or not acting.] Certainly the decree of God is no more the cause of the devastation of the Chaldeans than of their non-devastation, and the object of the decree is possible. I ask about the consequence of God's decrees, which Arminius attests: "The certain futurition of contingent events does not include necessity." But what is this other than saying that God knows nothing with certainty, decrees nothing by his will concerning future contingents until they actually come to pass, and that God's knowledge, like all volitions, begins in time? Not to mention how absurd it is to say that the futurition of a thing is not necessary. For if there is futurition, and it is drawn out of the state of possibility, it is as necessary as it is necessary that the same be the same and that what is future be future. Indeed, to say that futurition does not include necessity is to say that what is future can be not future.

units.la: 10. 2. Ob. Suar. Si suppositio ita antecedit voluntatem ut non fit in potestate ejus, illam ponere vel tollere, & ex tali suppositione neceffario sequitur actus, talis actus non potest esse liber. Hinc formatur argument. Decretum absolutum pugnat cum Dei justitia, quia praemia & poenae non jure irrogantur hisce qui in sua potestate non habent, quae faciunt, atqui posito tali decreto, non habent homines in sua potestate, quae faciunt. Ergo &c. Prob. minor. Illud in potestate, homines non habent, cujus necessarium antecedenter requifi-tum tum in sua potestate non habent, atqui non habent homines necessarium antecedenter requisitum in sua potestate. Non enim in sua potestate habent Dei absolutum decretum, neque determinationem Dei physicam. Hinc Re-monstrant. ut quis liber dicatur, volunt eum habere debere in sua potestate omnem circumstantiam, cum qua componatur agere vel non agere. Hoc argumentum urgent. Vasquez, Molina, Fonseca, Lessius.
units.tr: 10. Second objection, from Suarez: If a supposition so precedes the will that it is not in the will's power to posit or remove it, and a given act necessarily follows from such a supposition, then that act cannot be free. From this the argument is formed: an absolute decree conflicts with the justice of God, because rewards and punishments are not justly inflicted on those who do not have in their power what they do. But once such a decree is posited, men do not have in their power what they do. Therefore, etc. Proof of the minor: men do not have in their power that whose necessary antecedent requisite they do not have in their power. But men do not have in their power the necessary antecedent requisite. For they do not have in their power God's absolute decree, nor God's physical determination. Hence the Remonstrants hold that, for someone to be called free, he must have in his power every circumstance with which he would be combined to act or not to act. Vasquez, Molina, Fonseca and Lessius press this argument.

units.la: 11. Quoniam hoc unico argumento tantum non triumphant Iesuitæ & Arminiani, quanti fit videamus. Resp. Eo inclinat argumentum hoc ut dicant homines habere in sua potestate Dei decreta, ut sic homines electionis & reprobationis suae fabros faciant, Deum dominio in creaturas, & libertate in eligendo & reprobando, spolient. Quo nomine Deus figulo terreno dignitate cedet, & terrenis iudicibus, qui sua decreta & statuta, subditorum arbitrio aegerrime indulgent; sic hic videant quaeri, utrum Deo, an hominibus competat absoluta libertas. Sed si homines efficiant, ut Deus talia vel talia decreta formet, sequi humanam voluntatem esse divinae volitionis occasionem vel causam, id quod diserte affirmat Arminius, ideoque Dei causam dari posse, vel voluntatem non esse essentiam Dei, quod est Deum non esse Deum. 2. Quia est in omnium arbitrio ad finem credere, habent homines in suo arbitrio decretum universale electionis, & in omnium arbitrio est nunquam credere, habent homines in suo arbitrio universalem reprobationem. 3. Neque Deus quorum vult miserebitur, sed ex debito flectetur voluntas miserendi: atqui Arminiani suam gratiam efficacem administratam decreto prædestinationis à decreto providentiæ distinćto, uti fabulatur Arminius, & Iesuitæ, motionem congruam hominum arbitrio non subjicient: qui igitur habent homines in suo arbitrio omnia antecedentia ad liberum actum requisita? 2. Illud (in potestate, id homines non habent, cujus necessarium antecedenter requisitum, in potestate non habent) est multis nominibus aperte falsum. Nam erat in Adami arbitrio, legem præstare, & non comedere de fructu vetito: at vero non erat in Adami, sed infolius Dei arbitrio, interdicere esu illius arboris, quod erat tamen antecedens requisitum ad obedientiam Adami. Electi per gratiam Dei habent in sua potestate, ut credant promissionibus Dei:at vero solius Dei est promissiones proponere, quod antecedenter requiritur ad fidem. Subditi & servi, in potestate sua habent, ut obediant legislatoribus, & heris justa imperantibus: at in potestate non habent, ut legislatores & Domini imperent hæc, vel non. Congrue vocati habent in sua potestate, ex placitis Iesuitarum, ut obediant Deo congrue vocanti: at vero in potestate sua non habent, ut congrue vocet vel non.
units.tr: 11. Since the Jesuits and Arminians scarcely triumph on this one argument alone, let us see how great it is. Answer: this argument tends to say that men have God's decrees in their power, so that men make themselves the authors of their own election and reprobation, and despoil God of dominion over creatures and of liberty in electing and reprobating. By this reasoning God would yield in dignity to the earthly potter and to earthly judges, who very grudgingly grant their decrees and statutes to the choice of their subjects. Thus it seems that the question here is whether absolute liberty belongs to God or to men. But if men bring it about that God forms this or that decree, it follows that the human will is the occasion or cause of the divine volition, which Arminius expressly affirms; and so a cause could be given to God, or the will would not be the essence of God, which is for God not to be God. 2. Because it is in everyone's power to believe to the end, men have in their power the universal decree of election; and because it is in everyone's power never to believe, men have in their power universal reprobation. 3. Nor will God have mercy on whom he wills; rather, his will to show mercy will be bent by what is owed. Yet the Arminians and the Jesuits, who fabricate their efficacious grace administered by a decree of predestination distinct from the decree of providence, as Arminius and the Jesuits invent, will not subject it to a congruous motion of the human will. Who then has men in their power, so that all things antecedent are required for a free act? 2. The principle (what men do not have in their power, they do not have in their power whose necessary antecedent requisite they do not have in their power) is clearly false in many respects. For it was in Adam's power to keep the law and not to eat the forbidden fruit; yet it was not in Adam's power, but in God's alone, to forbid eating of that tree, which was nonetheless an antecedent requisite for Adam's obedience. The elect, by the grace of God, have in their power to believe God's promises; but to set forth the promises belongs to God alone, and this is antecedently required for faith. Subjects and servants have in their power to obey lawgivers and masters who command justly; but it is not in their power whether lawgivers and masters command these things or not. The congruously called have in their power, according to the Jesuits' opinions, to obey God when he calls congruously; but it is not in their power whether he calls congruously or not.

units.la: 3. Respondet Alvarez. Si suppositio (inquit) ita antecedit voluntatem, ut teneat fe ex parte causæ creatæ distinćtæ ab ipsa voluntate humana, tum propositio est vera: at vera non est, si se teneat ex parte primæ & universalissimæ causæ. Ratio, quia sola prima causa potest immutare voluntatem humanam efficaciter, ut ipsa servet ordinem naturalem operandi, huic responso illudere satagit Suarez. 16. ad fig. 12. sed revera petit principium. 4. Illud assertum optime distingui potest. nam si illud antecedenter requisitum, vi & contra naturam arbitrii, fatali necessitate torqueret arbitrium, valeret argumentum. At hoc nos minime docemus. Sed si illud antecedenter requisitum suaviter determinet potentiam ad illud idem numero objectum, & non ad aliud, quod voluntas de facto libere eliget, tum actus liber est in voluntatis potestate, quamvis illud antecedenter requisitum non sit in nostra potestate, quoniam decretum conspirat in illud idem volitum cum libertate. 5. Distingui etiam potest minor. ( atqui Dei absolutum decretum, non est in potestate hominis) duobus enim modis Dei decretum est in potestate arbitrii, vel ut in causa, vel ut in effectu: ut in causa; quando ipsum decretum est in arbitrio nostro, & non necesse est hoc dicere, neque possibile est, ut actus in Deo immanens & æternus sit in potestate arbitrii nostri, quod in tempore operatur: at vero eo modo, decretum Dei est in potestate arbitrii, quo possibile est, & quo sufficit ad salvandam libertatem, nempe est in arbitrio nostro secundum effectum, quoniam, nempe, quod est a Deo determinatum in decreto absoluto, est in noftra potestate, huic qui libere non credit in effectu, & interpretative apponit sigillum decreto reprobationis, ut Prov. 8. 36. Qui me (inquit sapientia) odio habent, mortem diligunt; interpretative, & ita etiam decreta Dei in hoc sensu sunt in nostra potestate, quod nos talia non voluissemus, nisi Deus, ut vellemus talia, decrevisset. Hoc itaque sensu decretum est in nostra potestate, nempe quoniam essectus, objectum, & terminus decreti, nempe actus liber absolute a Deo decretus est in nostra potestate, & hoc sufficit ad salvandam libertatem. Ideoque hic est fanus & verus asserti illius sensus. Illud non est in nostra potestate, quod nec in causa sive in seipso, nec in effectu, interpretative, vel in objecto volito, est in nostra potestate, quo sensu vera est major, & minor est falsa. Et ratio hujus est plana, quia ratio obedientiae aut inobedientiae, meriti aut demeriti non est formaliter in hoc quod nos homunciones habeamus in nutu & potestate arbitrii nostri decretum antecedens actus nostros. Nulla enim lex mihi imperat ut vel habeam, vel non habeam Dei absolutum decretum in mea potestate; sed in eo est ratio obedientiae aut inobedientiae, quod id eligam, vel non, quod non tantum decreto absoluto decretum est, sed etiam quod lege Dei revelatur.
units.tr: 3. Alvarez replies. If a supposition (he says) so precedes the will that it holds itself on the side of a created cause distinct from the human will itself, then the proposition is true; but it is not true if it holds itself on the side of the first and most universal cause. The reason is that only the first cause can efficaciously change the human will so that it keeps its natural order of acting. Suarez labours to mock this answer in 16 ad fig. 12, but in fact he begs the question. 4. That assertion can be distinguished very well. For if that antecedent requisite were to press the power with force and against the nature of the will, with fatal necessity, the argument would hold. But we by no means teach this. If, however, that antecedent requisite sweetly determines the power to that same numerically identical object, and not to another, which the will in fact freely chooses, then the free act is in the power of the will, even though that antecedent requisite is not in our power, since the decree agrees with liberty in choosing that same object. 5. The minor can also be distinguished (but God's absolute decree is not in man's power). For God's decree is in the power of the will in two ways, either as in a cause or as in an effect. As in a cause, when the decree itself is in our will; and it is neither necessary to say this nor possible, for an act immanent and eternal in God, which works in time, to be in the power of our will. But God's decree is in the power of the will in the way that is possible and sufficient to save liberty, namely in our will according to its effect: since what God has determined in the absolute decree is in our power. This holds for the one who does not believe freely, and who, interpretatively, sets his seal to the decree of reprobation, as in Prov. 8. 36: "Those who hate me, love death," says Wisdom. This is interpretative, and in this sense God's decrees are also in our power, in that we would not have willed such things unless God had decreed that we should will them. In this sense, therefore, the decree is in our power, namely because the effect, object and term of the decree, that is, the free act absolutely decreed by God, is in our power; and this suffices to save liberty. Hence this is the sound and true sense of that assertion. That is not in our power which is in our power neither in its cause, that is in itself, nor in its effect (interpretatively), nor in the object willed. In this sense the major is true and the minor false. The reason is plain: the ground of obedience or disobedience, of merit or demerit, does not formally lie in our having, at the nod and power of our will, a decree antecedent to our acts. For no law commands me to have or not to have God's absolute decree in my power. Rather, the ground of obedience or disobedience lies in whether I choose this or not, which is decreed not only by the absolute decree but also revealed by the law of God.

units.la: Ob. 12. 3. Sic Suarez, Actus hominis non est liber per ordinem ad voluntatem Dei, sed per ordinem ad voluntatem hominis, sicut non est vitalis actus, quia procedit a Deo, sed quia procedit ab intrinseco principio vitae hominis: Ergo, ut actus sit liber homini, oportet, ut non sit necessarius eidem homini, per necessitatem antecedentem liberum influxum ejus. Resp. 1. Non est formaliter liber in ordine ad Dei voluntatem, est tamen liber causaliter ab eo, alioquin Iesuita non vult nos agere Deo gratias ob actus supernaturales fidei charitatis, spei, & refipiscentiae. 2. Non sequitur, quoniam quando Dei determinatio cadit in idem objectum, in quod libertas creata cadit, (quod hic fit,) idem actus est liber Deo independenter & principaliter, & homini dependenter & subordinate.
units.tr: Objection 12. 3. Thus Suarez: a human act is not free through its order to God's will, but through its order to the human will, just as it is not a vital act because it proceeds from God, but because it proceeds from the intrinsic principle of man's life. Therefore, for an act to be free to a man, it must not be necessary to the same man through a necessity antecedent to his free influence. Answer: 1. It is not formally free in relation to God's will, yet it is causally free from him; otherwise the Jesuit would not want us to give thanks to God for supernatural acts of faith, charity, hope and repentance. 2. It does not follow. When God's determination falls on the same object on which created liberty falls (as happens here), the same act is free independently and principally with respect to God, and dependently and subordinately with respect to man.

units.la: 14. Ob. 13. 4. Sic arguit, necessitas antecedens non est necessitas ex suppositione, quia non fundatur in illo principio, impossibile & idem esse, & non esse, sed in hoc impossibile est talem causam sic effectam esse, & ex illa non sequi effectum, est itaque necessitas ex causa, & Physica, ideoque destruit libertatem. Resp. 1. Fundatur in illo principio possibile est Deum movere libertatem, & illam non moveri. 2. Non fluit liber actus ex decreto causative, si proprie loquamur, sed fluit proprie, expositione decreti, mediante potentia. Nam decretum ponit voluntatem sese inclinaturam libere, & etiam necessario secundum quid. 3. Quamvis necessitas causalis repugnet libertati, tamen necessitas ex causa infinita, qualis est Deus, non repugnat, quia ea arte infinita potest movere libertatem, ciendo illam, potentiæ, quasi partem, quæ respicit objectum à se absolute determinatum, ut tamen & necessario & libere moveatur.
units.tr: 14. Objection. 13. 4. He argues thus: a antecedent necessity is not a necessity by supposition, because it is not founded on the principle that the impossible is both the same and not the same; but it is impossible that such a cause should be so effected and that the effect should not follow from it. Therefore it is a necessity from a cause, and a physical one, and so it destroys liberty. Answer. 1. It is founded on the principle that it is possible for God to move the will and for it not to be moved. 2. The free act does not flow from the decree causatively, if we speak properly, but flows properly from the exposition of the decree, through the power. For the decree posits that the will will incline itself freely, and also necessarily in a certain respect. 3. Although causal necessity is repugnant to liberty, necessity from an infinite cause, such as God is, is not repugnant, because by that infinite art he can move liberty by stirring it, as a part of the power, which regards an object absolutely determined by himself, so that it is moved both necessarily and freely.

units.la: 1 5. Obj. Quinto sic arguit; si suppositio decreti antecedat influxum libertatis, sicut in ejus positione non intervenit exercitium libertatis, nec in emanatione effectus à tali suppositione, quia suppositio non subditur domino libertatis, ac proinde nec ipsa potest talem emanationem impedire. Resp.
units.tr: 15. Objection. Fifthly he argues thus: if the supposition of the decree precedes the influence of liberty, then just as no exercise of liberty intervenes in its positing, so none intervenes in the emanation of the effect from such a supposition, because the supposition is not subject to the lord of liberty, and therefore it cannot itself prevent such an emanation. Answer.

units.la: 1. Supra probatum est consequens esse in arbitrio voluntatis, quamvis antecedens non sit.
units.tr: 1. It has been proved above that the consequent is in the power of the will, although the antecedent is not.

units.la: 2. Non potest impedire, quia liberè non potest, ideoque non vult, & tamen sequitur absolutum Dominium sui actus non competere libertati creatæ, quod haud indignanter largimur: id enim soli Deo competit.
units.tr: 2. It cannot prevent it, because it cannot do so freely, and therefore it does not will to; and yet it does not follow that absolute dominion over its own act does not belong to created liberty, which we freely grant. For that belongs to God alone.

units.la: Huc refer, quod habet Suarez. de decreto conditionato concurrendi hac hora & loco cum voluntate humana non determinatè ad agendum, sed ad coagendum, si arbitrium creatum coagere voluerit. Resp. Somniant vero salvari non posse libertatem nostram, nisi Deus tali decreto exponat se in bivio ad concurrendum, vel non, siquidem homo velit, vel non, sed. 1. ipse Suarez nullam admittit confusionem in decretis Dei: ait enim hoc sapere imperfectionem, sed voluntas concurrendi cum Petro, si velit, aut non concurrendi, si noluerit, est decretum confusum. Quid hic Suarez. ib. fig. 16. Dicitur (inquit) hoc decretum generale, non tamen confusum, quia per Illud non offertur concursus ad unum tantum actum, sed ad plures vel etiam ad omnes, quos liberum arbitrium circa obiectum sic propositum potest hic et nunc exercere, ad omnes (inquam) non in individuo possibiles, sed in specie, non tamen confuse, sed in particulari, ad determinatum et singularem actum sub speciebus singulis, it ad talem actum amoris, odii, consensus vel dissensus. Resp. 1. Ipse Suarez. ib. fig. 10, agnoscit decreta circa possibilia futura esse otiosa & a sapientia Dei aliena: atqui hoc decretum est concurrendi cum Petro, siquidem ipse cogere voluerit. Nempe si Iudas finaliter vult credere, decrevit Deus cum illo concurrere; & tamen Iudas nunquam est finaliter creditrus, quae vel hic sapientiae umbra; vel Suarezio judice? 2. Hoc decretum conditionatum vel innititur scientiae, vel non. Si non, est decretum caecum & irrationale. Si prius: insulse Deus decrevit concurrere cum actu, quem nunquam futurum praevidet: sic enim dici posset Deum decrevisse respiscentiam diabolorum, & fidem finalem omnium reproborum. 3. Quomodo hoc decretum fit generale, expositum omnibus actibus possibilibus, & tamen non confusum, est [illegible, ~8 letters]. 4. Per hoc decretum vult concursum offerri ad actus non in individuo, sed in specie possibiles, & tamen ad omnes, quos liberum arbitrium potest hic & nunc exercere, haec est contradictio, nempe offertur concursus ad omnes in individuo, & non ad omnes hic & nunc, hoc est, non ad omnes in individuo. §. Si Deus decernit mittere Ieremiam ad prophetandum, tali decreto quo exponit concursum suum ad prophetandum, vel non prophetandum, male arguit Deus a decreto ad necessitatem prophetandi. nam tali decreto Ieremias tam est non prophetaturus, quam prophetaturus. Et quis putaret, quando Deus exponit decretum de vastatione Assyriorum, Tyriorum, Chaldæorum per agentia libera & confirmet decretum, hoc asserto[?] (ego Ichova loquutus sum, & faciam) Deum tam velle hostes ipsos non vastare, quam vastare? Quia decreto plane affirmativo, se vastaturum ipsos affirmet. Aut quis sanus, nisi Iesuitico spiritu raptus, affirmationem exponeret disjunctivo sensu per affirmationem vel negationem, & ita per ita vel non.
units.tr: To this refer the words of Suarez about a conditional decree of concurring with the human will at this hour and place, not determinately to act, but to co-act, if it shall wish to co-act the created choice. Answer. They dream indeed that our liberty cannot be saved unless God by such a decree sets himself at a fork, to concur or not to concur, according as man wills or does not will. But: 1. Suarez himself admits no confusion in the decrees of God; for he says that this savours of imperfection; yet the will to concur with Peter if he wills, or not to concur if he does not will, is a confused decree. What does Suarez say here, in the same place, fig. 16? It is said (he says) that this decree is general, yet not confused, because through it concurrence is offered not to one act only, but to several, or even to all, which the free choice can exercise here and now with regard to the object so proposed; to all (I say) possible not in the individual but in the species, yet not confusedly, but in particular, to a determinate and singular act under each species, as to such an act of love, hatred, consent or dissent. Answer. 1. Suarez himself, in the same place, fig. 10, acknowledges that decrees concerning future possibles are idle and alien to the wisdom of God; but this decree is of concurring with Peter, if he himself shall will to co-act. Indeed, if Judas finally wills to believe, God has decreed to concur with him; and yet Judas was never going to believe finally. Is this not a shadow of wisdom, or is it one in the judgement of Suarez? 2. This conditional decree either rests on knowledge or it does not. If not, it is a blind and irrational decree. If the former: God foolishly decreed to concur with an act which he foresees will never come to be; for in that way one could say that God had decreed the repentance of the devils and the final faith of all the reprobate. 3. How this decree is general, extended to all possible acts, and yet not confused, is [illegible, about eight letters]. 4. By this decree he wills concurrence to be offered to acts possible not in the individual but in the species, and yet to all which the free choice can exercise here and now; this is a contradiction: namely, concurrence is offered to all in the individual, and not to all here and now, that is, not to all in the individual. §. If God decrees to send Jeremiah to prophesy, by such a decree whereby he exposes his concurrence to prophesying or not prophesying, he argues badly from the decree to the necessity of prophesying; for by such a decree Jeremiah is as much not going to prophesy as going to prophesy. And who would think, when God sets forth the decree concerning the desolation of the Assyrians, Tyrians and Chaldeans through free agents, and confirms the decree by this assertion (I, Jehovah, have spoken, and I will do it), that God wills the enemies themselves not to lay waste as much as to lay waste? Because by a plainly affirmative decree he affirms that he will lay them waste. Or who that is sound, unless carried away by a Jesuitical spirit, would explain an affirmation in a disjunctive sense, by affirmation or negation, and so by this or not this?

units.la: 6. Hoc etiam Vasquezio forte excidit. Quia (inquit) Deus in tempore non generatim, & confuse concurrit cum libero arbitrio, nec statuit ab æterno generatim & confuse concurrere. Hoc enim Pelagianos docuisse asserit ibid. Et revera si Deus modo illo indeterminato paratus est concurrere, ad tam nolle, quam velle Petri, quis hic confusum decretum tali modo ab æterno concurrendi, non videat? Nemo enim aliquid inter homines agit sub disjunctione, (si non hoc, tamen illud vel hoc, vel sin minus illud) in quo non est & ignorantia & confusa suspensio animi.
units.tr: 6. This perhaps also slipped from Vasquez. For (he says) God does not concur with free choice in time generally and confusedly, nor did he decide from eternity to concur generally and confusedly. For he asserts that the Pelagians taught this, in the same place. And indeed, if God is prepared with that indeterminate mode to concur so as not to will Peter's act as much as to will it, who here would not see a confused decree of concurring from eternity in such a way? For no one among men acts under a disjunction (if not this, yet that, or this, or if not that), in which there is not both ignorance and a confused suspension of the mind.

units.la: Septimo, ita Suarez, prædeterminatio ista est ita necessaria, ut sit essentialiter inhibita in concursu primæ causæ. Ergo si Deus absoluta voluntate sua determinat humanam voluntatem ad non prædeterminari. unum actum, & non ad alios, præbet suum concursum ad illum actum solum, & relinquit voluntatem & sine concursu ad alios, sed voluntas sine concursu primæ causæ non potest operari: Ergo alii actus non manent in potestate vera, proxima ac morali voluntatis. Resp. Quicunque non operatur, caret actuali concursu, & tamen non inde sit, qui sic non operatur, non posse operari. Replicat ibid. Suar. Aliud est non habere concursum in actu secundo, aliud non habere illum in potestate sua seu in actu primo, sed omnino esse denegatum a Deo, illud prius non dicit carentiam potestatis proximæ & expeditæ ad operandum, quamvis non tollat facultatem intrinsecam ad operandum. Resp. 1.
units.tr: Seventhly, thus Suarez: this predetermination is so necessary that it is essentially inhibited in the concurrence of the first cause. Therefore if God by his absolute will determines the human will not to be predetermined to one act and not to others, he offers his concurrence to that act alone, and leaves the will without concurrence to the others; but the will without the concurrence of the first cause cannot operate. Therefore the other acts do not remain in the true, proximate and moral power of the will. Answer. Whoever does not operate lacks actual concurrence, and yet it does not follow that one who thus does not operate cannot operate. Suarez replies in the same place: It is one thing not to have concurrence in the second act, another not to have it in one's power or in the first act, but to be wholly denied by God; the former does not mean lacking a proximate and ready power to operate, although it does not remove the intrinsic faculty of operating. Answer 1.

units.la: Quamvis voluntas humana haberet concursum Dei in sua potestate in actu primo, non tamen esset potentior ad agendum vel non agendum, quam quando eum habet tantum in actu secundo. Neque enim Dei concursus, quo est proprior, facit accessionem potentiæ novæ in libertate, sicut præsentia luminis, non addit novam potentiam realem visivam oculo, quæ non fuit ei dum in tenebris constitueretur, ideoque somnium est voluntatem non esse in proxima ad agendū potentia nisi habeat in potestate sua concursum Dei.2.Quando concursus ille Dei, quem nos dicimus voluntatem habere, non in sua potestate, sed in actu secundo, licet non in actu primo; in idem cadit objectum in quod cadit libertas electivè influens salvatur proxima libertatis potentia. 3. Negamus nos libertatis hanc esse naturam, ut possit, omnibus positis ad agendum requisitis, indifferenter agere vel non agere, & absurdum esse putamus, ut voluntas creata haberet in sua potestate ut Dei concursum traheret indifferenter ad hunc vel illum pro absoluto suo arbitrio actum in specie, quia hoc tolleret Dei libertatem & providentiam, tum etiam quia necesse foret, ut fuisset ab aeterno hujus & ejusdem actus liberi & futuritio, & non futuritio, quae est palpabilis contradictio. Nam positis omnibus requisitis posset hoc velle, & necessario procedere debuit aeterna futuritio hujus volitionis, & poterat etiam hoc non velle, & sic necefsario praecessit aeterna futuritio nolitionis, quod est absurdum. Ergo necessario dicendum unam tantum volitionem futuram fuisse in potentia illa, quam Suarez vocat proximam.
units.tr: Although the human will had God's concurrence in its power in the first act, it would not be any more powerful to act or not to act than when it has it only in the second act. For God's concurrence, by which he is nearer, does not add a new power to liberty, just as the presence of light does not add a new real visual power to the eye, which the eye did not have while it was situated in darkness; and so it is a dream that the will is not in proximate power to act unless it has God's concurrence in its power. 2. When that concurrence of God, which we say the will has not in its power but in the second act, though not in the first act, falls on the same object on which liberty falls as electively influencing, the proximate power of liberty is preserved. 3. We deny that liberty is of such a nature that, with all the things required for acting posited, it can act or not act indifferently; and we think it absurd that the created will should have it in its power to draw God's concurrence indifferently to this or that act in particular at its absolute choice; for this would destroy the liberty and providence of God, and also because it would be necessary that from eternity there should have been both a future and a non-future of this one and the same free act, which is a palpable contradiction. For with all the requisites posited, it could will this, and the eternal futurition of this volition must have necessarily followed; and it could also not will this, and so the eternal futurition of the nolition would necessarily have preceded, which is absurd. Therefore it must be said necessarily that only one volition would have been future in that power which Suarez calls proximate.

units.la: 18. ob. 8. Sic arguit Suarez, Constituamus (inquit) hominem cui hic & nunc proponitur hoc objectum amandum, v. g. Ingredi religionem, ita ut ex parte intellectus, habeat omnem considerationem & judicium necessarium, & in voluntate non habeat aliquid impedimentum, positive, contrarium, solumque illi deest voluntas divina efficax, qua velit Deus illum amare illud objectum. Quid quaeso ille homo faciet, ut amet illud objectum: Non movetur nec determinatur a Deo, non potest fingi aliquid in ejus potestate, quo a Deo determinetur, quia ad illam cogitationem necessaria esset illa praemotio efficax. Ergo non potest moraliter imputari tali homini, quod non amet tale objectum. R esp. 1° Homo cui proponitur hoc objectum amandum vel amat, vel amare cupit objectum, ad & amationem & amandi desiderium praecessit aeterna & efficax Dei volitio, ideoque in actu secundo habuit in sua potestate praedeterminationem Dei, nihil ergo aliud requiritur ab eo nisi ut amet objectum. 2. Si caret praedeterminatione Dei, caret ea libere saltem interpraetative, quia libere recusat amare objectum, & actus liber recusandi tendit objective in non-amationem, in quam tendit aeterna dei efficax voluntas, & decretum. Ideoque, & si careat Dei praedeterminatione, imputatur non-amatio in peccatum, quia libere non amat, ideoque consequenter subscribit carentiae praedestinationis. 3. Si intellectus habeat omnem considerationem, & judicium, & voluntas nullum impedimentum, non potest non praecessisse efficax volitio, & sic instantia est vana, utcunque se res habet, negamus dari non-amationem objecti ex sola carentia efficacis Dei volitionis, quia impossibile est componi simul carentiam efficacis volitionis Dei, & conatum sufficientem ex parte voluntatis quo propendet in amorem objecti, quod actu amare haud potest, ex sola carentia illius praedeterminationis, ideoque instantia est impossibilis eo rigido sensu, quo proponitur, quia semper in idem cadunt objectum, negatio efficacis volitionis Dei, & libera non-amatio objecti.
units.tr: 18. Objection 8. Suarez argues thus: Suarez, Constituamus (he says) let us suppose a man to whom here and now this object is proposed to be loved, for example, entering a religious order, so that on the side of the intellect he has every necessary consideration and judgment, and in the will has no positive contrary impediment, and only the efficacious will of God is lacking, by which God wills that he love that object. What, I ask, will that man do, so that he loves that object? He is not moved or determined by God; nothing can be imagined in his power by which he is determined by God, since for that thought that efficacious premotion would be necessary. Therefore he cannot morally be imputed with not loving such an object. Answer 1. A man to whom this object is proposed to be loved either loves it or desires to love it, and before both the loving and the desire to love there preceded an eternal and efficacious volition of God. Therefore in the second act he had in his power the predetermination of God, and nothing more is required of him than that he love the object. 2. If he lacks the predetermination of God, he lacks it freely, at least interpretatively, because he freely refuses to love the object, and a free act of refusing tends objectively toward non-love, which is the end toward which the eternal efficacious will and decree of God tends. Therefore, even if he lacks God's predetermination, his non-love is imputed to him as sin, because he does not love freely, and so he consequently subscribes to the lack of predestination. 3. If the intellect has every consideration and judgment, and the will no impediment, an efficacious volition cannot but have preceded, and so the instance is empty, however the matter stands. We deny that non-love of the object arises from the mere lack of the efficacious volition of God, because it is impossible for the lack of God's efficacious volition and a sufficient endeavour on the part of the will, by which it inclines toward love of the object it cannot actually love, to be combined merely by the lack of that predetermination. The instance is therefore impossible in the rigid sense in which it is put, because the same object always falls under both: the negation of God's efficacious volition and the free non-love of the object.

units.la: 14. Priusquam vero alias objectiones solvamus, quæritur an nullo sensu admitti possit decretum conditionatum. R. Decretum conditionatum est duplex: vel est ita conditionatum, ut conditio referatur ad Dei voluntatem, quasi quis diceret, Deum hoc decernere, & velle, si homo tale aliquid faceret: hoc modo pernegamus omne in Deo decretum conditionatum, quia Dei voluntas suspenditur à nulla conditione, causa aut occasione, qua voluntas ipsius moveatur ad decernendum, aut volendum. Decretum vero conditionatum dicitur tale ex parte non Dei volentis, sed objecti voliti, & poni possunt in Deo decreta conditionata, præsertim in essectis contingentibus conditionatis, hoc est, futuris ex positione decreti. Sic in decreto conditionato prædeterminante Deus vidit Tyrios refipiscentiam, si factæ fuissent illic virtutes & signa: & Relitas traditurus Davidem in manus Sauli, siquidem David apud ipsos permaneret, & exteras gentes audituras Ezechielem, siquidem apud ipsas vaticinatus esset Propheta Dei.
units.tr: 14. Before we answer the other objections, the question is whether a conditional decree can be admitted in any sense. Answer: a conditional decree is of two kinds. Either it is conditional in such a way that the condition refers to the will of God, as if someone were to say that God decrees and wills this if man does such a thing. In this way we utterly deny any conditional decree in God, because the will of God is not suspended on any condition, cause or occasion by which his will is moved to decree or to will. But a decree is called conditional in another way, not on the part of God who wills, but on the part of the object willed, and conditional decrees can be posited in God, especially concerning contingent effects that are conditional, that is, future upon the positing of the decree. Thus in the conditional predetermining decree God foresaw that the Tyrians would repent, if the powers and signs had been done there; and that Keilah would deliver David into the hands of Saul, if David remained among them; and that foreign nations would hear Ezekiel, if the prophet of God had prophesied among them.

units.la: Tria hic video à Suarezio Objici. 1. non posse talia cognosci in decreto conditionato prædeterminante. Quia (inquit) si Deus habuisset tale decretum conditionatum de prædeterminanda voluntate creata ad talem effectum, subsistente tali conditione, oportuisset ut ex vi talis decreti esset paratus ad illam prædeterminationem conferendam, alioqui vanum esset decretum. At Deus in eo casu non
units.tr: I see three objections raised here by Suarez. 1. Such things cannot be known in a conditional predetermining decree. Because (he says) if God had such a conditional decree concerning the predetermination of the created will to such an effect, the condition holding, it would have been necessary that by virtue of such a decree he be ready to confer that predetermination, otherwise the decree would be vain. But God in that case is not

units.la: Suarez. de gratia efficaci, lib. 2. de concurs. cap. 8. f. 13. non est paratus ad dandum tale auxilium, quia si effet paratus, daret illud cum ab homine non pendeat (nempe quod in Ty-rii signa fierent) sed a solo Deo, Ergo non habuit tale decretum. Resp. 1. Nego mai. conex. quia decretum hoc conditionatum, est tantum volitio Dei qua voluit ut Tyrii videntes signa resipiscerent: & libere, & recusavit ipsis signa, & libere recusavit ipsis dare refipiscentiam. Potest enim Deus decernere coexistentiam duorum extremorum connexorum ex hypothesi, & non decernere extrema. Nempe vult & decernit fidem reproborum, & vitam aeternam cohaerere, & tamen nec Iudae fidem, nec vitam aeternam decrevit, hoc est enim objectum decreti Dei, omnis credens habebit vitam aeternam. 2. Non est tale decretum vanum, habet enim in Deo graves causas, & potest Deus velle connexa ex hypothesi, quorum extrema non vult, & decretum tale est liberum. Hoc enim asserit scriptura, Deum voluisse ipsis dare refipiscentiam, siquidem signa vidissent. 3. Nec sequitur Deum non esse paratum ad dandum illis tale auxilium, & quia libere dat & dedisset siquidem signa vidissent: at vero signa libere recusavit, quamvis haud negem non proprie esse decretum conditionatum, sed potius absoluta est volitio qua coexistentiam vult duorum conditionatè cohaerentium.
units.tr: Suarez, On Efficacious Grace, book 2, On Concurrence, ch. 8, f. 13. ready to give such help, because if he were ready he would give it, since it does not depend on man (namely, that the signs would be done among the Tyrians) but on God alone. Therefore he did not have such a decree. Answer 1. I deny the major premise, because this conditional decree is only a volition of God by which he willed that the Tyrians, seeing the signs, would repent; and he freely refused them the signs, and freely refused to give them repentance. For God can decree the coexistence of two connected extremes on a hypothesis without decreeing the extremes. Namely, he wills and decrees that the faith of the reprobate and eternal life cohere, and yet he decreed neither the faith of Judas nor eternal life for him; for this is the object of God's decree: every believer will have eternal life. 2. Such a decree is not vain; it has grave causes in God, and God can will connected things on a hypothesis, whose extremes he does not will, and such a decree is free. For Scripture asserts this: that God willed to give them repentance, if they had seen the signs. 3. Nor does it follow that God is not ready to give them such help, since he gives freely and would have given it if they had seen the signs; but in fact they freely refused the signs. Although I do not deny that this is not properly a conditional decree, but rather an absolute volition by which he wills the coexistence of two things that cohere conditionally.

units.la: 2. Ob. Suarez: Conditio illa (inquit) ut supponitur, pendet ex sola voluntate Dei, alioqui Deus ex se decrevit non ponere talem conditionem, quia supposupponitur nunquam futura: ergo non potest paratus esse ad dandum tale auxilium, quod illam conditionem impletam necessario requirit. Resp. Neg. consequens; decernit enim, ut credentes salventur, nunquam tamen decernit, ut Iudas crederet.
