Itaque non necesse est ut mutatio realis in creaturis sequatur ex decreto conditionato ex parte objecti. Dicit enim expresse exteras gentes audituras Ezechielem, si ad ipsas missus foret, & tamen noluit Ezechielem ad ipsas mittere.
units.tr: 2. Objection of Suarez: That condition (he says) as supposed depends solely on the will of God; otherwise God would have decreed of himself not to posit such a condition, since it is supposed never to be future. Therefore he cannot be ready to give such help, which necessarily requires that condition to be fulfilled. Answer: I deny the consequence. For he decrees that believers be saved, yet he never decrees that Judas would believe. Therefore it is not necessary that a real change in creatures follow from a conditional decree on the part of the object. For he expressly says that foreign nations would hear Ezekiel, if he had been sent to them, and yet he was unwilling to send Ezekiel to them.

units.la: 3. Ob, Conditio sub qua prædicta fuit Tyriorum pœnitentia, fuit, si tales virtutes factæ fuissent in te, & per absolutum decretum, præscinitum fuit, ut tales virtutes iis nunquam fierent. Erg. Non habuit tale decretum conditionatum. Prob. conseq. Quia tale decretum fuisset de re pendente a sola voluntate Dei, & sub conditione ab eadem sola voluntate pendente, & ex decreto ejusdem voluntas absoluto numquam implenda; tale autem decretum conditionatum est prorsus otiosum & frustraneum, quia per illud revera Deus nihil contulit Tyriis, nec paratus fuit conferre, nec continet promissionem ullam, nec sub ulla generalitate divinæ providentiæ, nec ad [illegible, ~1 word] quid confert. Resp. 1. Posito illo antecedente, non seq. consequens. Nam non est decretum frustraneum, quo Deus, sicut decreto libero voluit entia in actu cohærere, ut fidem electorum & salutem, transitum populi sui per mare rubrum, & submersionem Ægyptiorum, & multa alia quæ ex se contingenter connexa sunt, ita eodem libero decreto æquum est ad perfectionem infinitæ & altissimæ providentiæ ut connectantur etiam futura conditionata, & quid ni ad astruendam Dei libertatem inserviret? ut videamus in Dei decreto absoluto connexiones rerum tantum possibilium quamvis ipsæ res non sint futuræ: hoc docet nos ne res quidem possibiles effugere providentiam, & docet nos humillime nosmet Deo subjicere & abyssum judiciorum Dei adorare, qui voluit mittere Ezechielem ad non auditurum populum, & noluit ad auditurum mittere, idque ex solo beneplacito suo, ut videamus Deum non ex indigentia vocare hos, cum posset alios obsequentiores vocare, & ex mera gratia vocare, & ex absoluto arbitrio rerum etiam possibilium combinationes determinare.
units.tr: 3. Objection: The condition under which the repentance of the Tyrians was foretold was: if such powers had been done in you; and by an absolute decree it was foreseen that such powers would never be done for them. Therefore he did not have such a conditional decree. Proof of the consequence: because such a decree would concern a thing depending solely on the will of God, and under a condition depending on that same sole will, and by the absolute decree of that same will never to be fulfilled. But such a conditional decree is utterly idle and futile, because by it God really conferred nothing on the Tyrians, nor was he ready to confer anything, nor does it contain any promise, nor is it under any generality of divine providence, nor [illegible, about one word] does it confer anything. Answer 1. Granting that antecedent, the consequence does not follow. For it is not a futile decree, by which God, by a free decree, willed entities to cohere in act, such as the faith and salvation of the elect, the passage of his people through the Red Sea, and the drowning of the Egyptians, and many other things that are contingently connected in themselves. So by the same free decree it befits the perfection of infinite and most high providence that even conditional future things be connected. And why should it not serve to establish God's liberty? So that we may see in God's absolute decree connections of things that are only possible, although the things themselves will not be future. This teaches us that not even possible things escape providence, and it teaches us most humbly to submit ourselves to God and to adore the abyss of God's judgments, who willed to send Ezekiel to a people who would not hear, and was unwilling to send him to one who would hear, and this from his mere good pleasure. So we may see that God calls these not from need, when he could call others more obedient, and calls from mere grace, and from absolute arbitrium determines combinations even of possible things.

units.la: 2. Non tantum decretum hoc non est otiosum, sed necesse est fit in Deo, quia Dei voluntas non potest esse suspensa & indeterminata circa entia in actu, sed nec circa entia in potestate. Quia vero miraculorum visio & Tyriorum fides, quoad coexistentiam sunt possibilia, vel horum duorum coexistentia in se fit possibilis [?], & etiam futura ex hypothesi Deus eam coexistentiam vel decernit & vult, vel non decernit & non vult. Deum illam coexistentiam ex hypothesi non voluisse, haud possumus tuto affirmare, quia scriptura dicit, visis miraculis convertendos fuisse Tyrios: at vero si conversio illa antevertisset Dei decretum, homines nulla providentia, nullo Dei voluntatis actu praevio, ac proinde, nec praeeunte gratia, & gratuito Dei favore convertuntur, quam theologiam sacra oracula explodunt. Itaque sicut est voluntas approbans & simplex complacentiae, quae revelatur in scripturis, de re nunquam futura, qualis est obedientia reproborum, & voluntas beneplaciti de re, quamDeus indeclinabiliter est effecturus,ita est decretum absolutum in Deo de rebus vere suturis, & decretum simplicis complacentiae seu approbationis de multis possibilibus nunquam futuris, sed ponendis ex hypothesi. At objici potest me hoc argumento rejecisse decretum Dei conditionatum de concursu Dei cum actibus libertatis possibilibus nunquam futuris, quia alienum est a Dei sapientia ut illud decernat fore quod praescit nunquam suturum esse. Id enim non est viri prudentis: nulla enim provida mater praeparat tunicam foetui, quem certo scit in ventre enecatum. Ergo alienum est a sapientia, ut Deus decernat Tyriorum conversionem ex hypothesi, quod miracula illis fierent, quando & praescit & decrevit hypothesin illam nunquam ponere. R. Non jam hoc argumneto a nunquam rei futuritione, decretum conditionatum rejicio, quam quia Dei voluntas fixa & rata fit (alioqui non est decretum) circa rem nunquam futuram & quoniam Dei voluntas sit, quasi intellectus nihil praesciret, suspenderetur a voluntate humana: at vero hic quamvis Deus praescit extrema conditionati connexi nunquam futura, tamen praescit connexionem esse veram & realitatem habere in sua voluntate. Ideoque non decernit Deus non ens: nam in Dei decreto vere coexistunt visio miraculorum & Tyriorum resipiscentia: quamvis nec miracula illa, nec resipiscentia seorsim & separatim existunt: at vero per decretum conditionatum Suarezij quod ego rejeci, statuitur Deus id intendere & decernere, quod videt esse plane non ens, & id decernitur a Deo actu futurum, quod præscit nunquam esse futurum, & præscit in sua voluntate determinante nullum omnino esse habere: in hoc enim decreto conditionato,non decernitur,ut res nunquā futura,fit futura;nam revera conversioTyriorum visis signis,est ens vere volitum & decretum a Deo. 2. Non nego hoc decretum admodum improprie dici conditionatum, quia conditio pendet ab absoluta Dei voluntate, sicut & conditionatum, imo est simplex & absoluta volitio, ut duæ res cohæreant inter se, nempe visio signorum & conversio Tyriorum. At vero in decreto conditionato quod ego rejicio, Deus vult aliquid, quod scit nunquam esse futurum ex hypothesi[?] quam scit nunquam esse ponendam, ut decernit Deus ut Iudas crederet, & concurrere cum eo, siquidem vult credere, & scit & eum nunquam crediturum, & se nunquam concursurū. At vero dicimus Deum neq; velle, neque præscire vel miracula Tyrii visa vel ipsorum conversione, sed tantum simpliciter Deo complacere in coexistentia horum duorum sicut Deus complacet in obedientia Iudæ nunquam futura.
units.tr: 2. This decree is not idle. It must exist in God, because the will of God cannot be suspended or undetermined with respect to things that are actual, nor even with respect to things that are merely possible. Now the seeing of the miracles and the faith of the Tyriorum are possible as to their coexistence, or the coexistence of these two is itself made possible, and even if they are future on the hypothesis, God either decrees and wills that coexistence or does not decree it and does not will it. We cannot safely affirm that God did not will that coexistence on the hypothesis, because Scripture says that the Tyrios were to be converted once the miracles had been seen. But if that conversion had come before the decree of God, men would be converted without any providence, without any prior act of the will of God, and therefore without grace going before and without God's free favour, and the sacred oracles reject that theology. So, just as there is a will of approval and of simple complacency, which is revealed in the Scriptures, concerning a thing that will never be, such as the obedience of the reprobate, and a will of good pleasure concerning a thing that God will infallibly bring to pass, so in God there is an absolute decree concerning things that will truly be, and a decree of simple complacency or approval concerning many possibles that will never be, but are to be posited on the hypothesis. But it may be objected that by this argument I have rejected God's conditional decree concerning the concurrence of God with possible acts of freedom that will never be, because it is foreign to the wisdom of God to decree that what he foreknows will never be shall come to pass. For this is not the part of a prudent man: no provident mother prepares a little coat for a foetus which she knows for certain has been killed in the womb. Therefore it is foreign to wisdom that God should decree, on the hypothesis that miracles were done for them, the conversion of the Tyriorum, when he both foreknows and has decreed never to posit that hypothesis. Answer: I do not reject the conditional decree on the ground that the thing will never be future; I reject it because the will of God is fixed and settled (otherwise it is not a decree) concerning a thing that will never be future, and because, if the will of God were as it were ignorant of nothing, it would be suspended upon the human will. Rather, although God foreknows that the terms of the conditional connection will never be future, he foreknows that the connection is true and has its reality in his will. Therefore God does not decree a non-being, for in God's decree the seeing of the miracles and the repentance of the Tyriorum truly coexist, although neither those miracles nor that repentance exist separately and apart. But by the conditional decree of Suarezius, which I have rejected, God is held to intend and decree what he sees is plainly a non-being, and that is decreed by God to be actually future which he foreknows will never be, and he foreknows that in his determining will it has no being at all. For in this conditional decree it is not decreed that a thing which will never be shall be; for in truth the conversion of the Tyriorum, once the signs were seen, is a being truly willed and decreed by God. 2. I do not deny that this decree is very improperly called conditional, since the condition depends upon the absolute will of God; it is rather a simple and absolute volition that two things cohere with one another, namely the seeing of the signs and the conversion of the Tyriorum. But in the conditional decree which I reject, God wills something which he knows will never be future on a hypothesis which he knows will never be posited; thus God decrees that Judas should believe, and concur with him, if indeed he wills to believe, and yet he knows that he will never believe and that he will never concur. But we say that God neither wills nor foreknows either the miracles seen by the Tyrii or their conversion, but only that he is simply pleased with the coexistence of these two, just as God is pleased with the obedience of Judas, which will never be.

units.la: 18. Ob. 15. Pergo jam ad reliquas objectiones. Pauca habent Vasquez. & Molina quae apud Suarezium non sunt, & a nobis examinata, ita Vasquez. Quamvis decretum extrinsece, & non intrinsece & physice immutat & necessitat voluntatem, tamen tollitur libertas, quia sub suppositione decreti, non potest non agere, ideoque actus non est possibilis: possibile enim est quo posito nihil absurdi sequitur ut habet Philosf.[?] R.nō[?] recte exponit Jesuita axioma illud. Nam possibile est illud quo actu posito, dependenter & subordinate ad motionem primae causae, nihil absurdi sequitur. 2. Absurdum sequitur, si removeatur actus a libertate, a Dei decreto ad agendum, determinata, quia Dei decretum ponit libertatem in eo situ vitali, in quo libere agit hoc quod determinatum est a decreto, ideoque si hoc non ageret, libertas lederetur, quod est absurdum.
units.tr: 18. Objection 15. I now proceed to the remaining objections. Vasquez and Molina have a few points which are not in Suarez, and which we have examined. Thus Vasquez: "Although the decree changes and necessitates the will extrinsically and not intrinsically and physically, freedom is nevertheless taken away, because under the supposition of the decree it cannot but act, and so the act is not possible; for that is possible which, once posited, nothing absurd follows, as the Philosopher holds." Answer: the Jesuit rightly explains that axiom. For that is possible which, once the act is posited, dependently and subordinately upon the motion of the first cause, nothing absurd follows. 2. Absurdity would follow if the act were removed from freedom, determined by God's decree to act, because God's decree places freedom in that vital situation in which it acts freely what has been determined by the decree; therefore if it did not act, freedom would be injured, which is absurd.

units.la: 19. Ob, 16. Ob quam ratione rejicitur fatum Stoicorum, ob eandem rejici debet decretum absolutum: sed ab antiquitate hoc fatum rejiciebatur, quia per illud homines non plus boni facere, aut plus mali, aut minus omittere possunt, quam faciunt, & omittunt, sed hoc etiam sequitur ex decreto absoluto. Ergo. Et ita Molina, Leffius, Remonstrantes.
units.tr: 19. Objection 16. By the same reasoning by which the fate of the Stoics is rejected, the absolute decree must also be rejected. But from antiquity this fate was rejected, because through it men could not do more good, or more evil, or omit less than they do and omit; but this also follows from the absolute decree. Therefore. And so Molina, Leffius, and the Remonstrants.

units.la: Resp. 1. Neg. maj. Nam rejicitur fatum Stoicorum, quoniam per id creaturae rationales non possunt plus minusve boni aut mali facere, eo quod constellatio aut creatura determinet libertatem & in ipsam agat, quod nulla creatura præstare potest, illibatâ manente libertate: solus enim Iehova quocunque vult, voluntatem inflectit. Prov. 21. Concedimus quidem, si causa creata, ita flecteret voluntatem, tolli libertatem, At vero Deus potest determinare voluntatem, & non evertere. 2. Factum rejicitur, quia ipsum Deum rectorem actuum liberorum fato Stoici alligabant, unde Iupiter Homerianus Sapedonis filii sui, fato mortui necem deflet & Neptunus, quod Vlissis reditum in patriam, contra fatales leges, nequeat prohibere. Quod vero Grevinchovius nugetur, fati assertores, ut Cleanthen, Iovem precibus solicitasse, sicut & nos Iehovam, nihil est contra nos: nam fato se orare, & fato Iovem audire dictitabant. Ideoque Plutarchus in fatalibus, agnoscit divinam dispositionem, sed fatalem, quo nomine merito Stoici vapulant à patribus, Augustino & aliis. 3. Iesuitas & Arminianos Deum fato alligare certissimum est. Ordo prioris & posterioris (inquit Vasquez) inter decreta divinæ voluntatis, non ex solo Dei beneplacito (en fatum fatalissimum) sed ex vario rerum ordine, quæ à Deo prædestinantur. Itaque sicut Deus non prius concurrit ad calefaciendum, quam ignis cooperetur, sic non prius prædefinit concurrere, quam videat ignis determinationem. Sed ut hoc obiter doceam, Vasquez ipse hic suum decretum concomitans convellit, quando vult determinationem causæ secundæ prius à Deo scitam ac proinde prius esse, quam ipse aliquid prædefiniat. Quo pacto Deus ordinem, situm, dispositionem, intentionem, aut remissionem, aut modum in operando in causis fecundis, & esse effectuum contingentium non aliter determinare potest, quam sint praedeterminata ab ipsis causis fecundis antecedenter ad voluntatem Dei, magis quam efficere potest, ut quod jam est, non fit, quod est simpliciter impossibile, Deumque fato involvit.
units.tr: Answer. 1. I deny the major premise. For the fate of the Stoics is rejected because through it rational creatures cannot do more or less good or evil, since the constellation or the creature determines the freedom and acts upon it, which no creature can accomplish with freedom remaining unimpaired; for Jehovah alone turns the will whichever way he wills. Prov. 21. We concede indeed that if a created cause were so to bend the will, freedom would be abolished. But God can determine the will without overthrowing it. 2. The fate of the Stoics is also rejected because they bound God himself, the ruler of free acts, to fate; whence Homer's Jupiter bewails the death of his son Sarpedon, who had died by fate, and Neptune, who could not prevent Ulysses' return to his homeland against the fatal laws. As for Grevinchovius' trifling that the advocates of fate, such as Cleanthes, solicited Jupiter with prayers, just as we do Jehovah, this is nothing against us; for they used to say that they prayed by fate and heard Jupiter by fate. Therefore Plutarch, in his book on fate, acknowledges a divine disposition, but a fatal one, for which reason the Stoics are rightly scourged by the Fathers, Augustine and others. 3. It is most certain that the Jesuits and the Arminians bind God to fate. "The order of the prior and the posterior (says Vasquez) among the decrees of the divine will is not from the mere good pleasure of God (behold most fatal fate), but from the varied order of things which are predestined by God." Thus just as God does not concur to heating before the fire cooperates, so he does not predefine to concur before he sees the fire's determination. But to teach this incidentally: Vasquez himself here overthrows his own concomitant decree, when he wants the determination of the second cause, known to God beforehand, and therefore prior, to be prior to God's predefining anything. By what means can God determine the order, position, disposition, intention, or remission, or the mode of operating, in second causes, and the being of contingent effects, otherwise than they have been predetermined by the second causes themselves, antecedently to the will of God, any more than he can bring it about that what already is does not come to be, which is simply impossible, and thus he involves God in fate?

units.la: 20. Ob.i7[?]. Si omnia hoc decreto fixa sunt; tum necesse est iidem homines ad eandem gloriam in Christo per remissionem eorundem peccatorum pervenirent; necesse effet iisdem hominibus, sacrilegis, adulteris &c. nascerentur; eodem cibo, la&te, pane, ut herbis vescerentur, eadem facerent opera meritoria &c. Ita ait Leffius, Resp. Puerili hoc argumento evincitur omnia necessitate hypothetica fieri, quod concedimus, si Deus voluisset omnia hisce contraria statuere. Quid ni statuisse poterat?
units.tr: 20. Objection 17. If all things are fixed by this decree, then necessarily the same men would attain the same glory in Christ through the remission of the same sins; it would be necessary that the same men be born sacrilegious, adulterers, and so on; that they feed on the same food, milk, bread, or herbs, that they do the same meritorious works, and so on. So Leffius says. Answer. By this puerile argument it is shown that all things come to pass by hypothetical necessity, which we concede, if God had willed to establish all things contrary to these. Why could he not have established them?

units.la: 21. Ob.18. Si actus liberi sunt necessarii respectu decreti Dei, tum respectu decreti non sunt contingentes, quia sic respectu ejusdem & secundum idem essent necessarii, & non necessarii, & sic etiam actus contingentes Deo non sunt contingentes, quod absurdum. Nam Deus decrevit & entia & modos entium; hoc ex Fonseca colligitur, & non refert (inquiunt Remonstrantes) an quis externa vi, an interna operatione, vel cessatione ab operatione peccet ac pareat, si peccare eum ac parere necesse cesse cesse est. Resp. 1. Fallunt hic adversarii: nam necessitas non est proprie à decreto, sed à positione decreti, neque est proprie necessitas interna, qualis rebus convenit: sed est quid commune necessario & contingenti. Nam efficacia voluntatis divinæ fit, ut statuatur futuritio omnium entium & necesseriorum & contingentium, ideoque sicut effectus naturales non possunt non esse necessitate interna, respectu causarum naturalium, & tamen possunt esse, vel non esse, necessitate externa respectu decreti divini, in habitudine ad quod omnia maximè alioqui necessaria, ut ortus solis, eclipsis, motus corporum cælestium, possunt esse, vel non esse; ita pari jure, efsectus contingentes internæ contingentiæ à causis secundis respectu, possunt esse vel non esse, & necessitate externa, in relatione ad Dei voluntatem non possunt non esse, ideoque contingentia esse Deo contingentia dupliciter intelligitur. 1. Quasi non obstante positione decreti, possunt esse vel non esse absolute, & hoc non est dicendum: nam Deo decernente non possunt non esse. 2. Sunt contingentia respectu decreti hoc sensu, quod decretum ponat in iis contingentem, adeoque futuritionem liberam in habitudine ad naturalem modû agendi in causa secunda, & quid impedit quo minus Deus effectus contingentes consideret, & in habitudine ad suum decretû, & in habitudine ad causas secundas ? Nam omnia evenire necessariò in habitudine ad Dei decretum, tripliciter etiam intelligitur. 1. Itâ ut necessitas componatur cum rebus à Deo volitis. Hoc non docemus: decrevit enim Deus ut effectus contingentes fierent contingenter non necessario, ideoque & entia & modos entium decrevit. 1. [?] Ita ut vox necessitatis cum Dei voluntate componatur, neque sic Deus necessario, sed liberrimè decrevit ut omnia fierent, vel contingenter, vel necessario, vel 3. ut necessitas referatur ad futuritionem entium contingentium, & sic contingentia sunt Deo necessaria respectu sui decreti, & nullo modo sequitur. Ergo non sunt Deo contingentia. 3. Multum refert, contra quod sentiunt Remonstrantes, utrum necessitas externa sit, an vero interna. Nam quia necessitas est externa & à Deo omnipotente, cujus est ex infinita sapientia sua libertatem determinare manente illæsa indifferentia naturali, ideo illa necessitas non aufert nativam libertatem.
units.tr: 21. Obj. 18. If free acts are necessary with respect to God's decree, then with respect to the decree they are not contingent. In that case the same things would be both necessary and not necessary in respect of the same thing, and so acts that are contingent to God would not be contingent, which is absurd. For God has decreed both beings and the modes of beings; this is gathered from Fonseca. And, say the Remonstrants, it makes no difference whether a man sins and obeys by external force, or by internal operation, or by ceasing from operation, if it is necessary that he sin and obey. Answer, 1. Here the adversaries are mistaken. Necessity does not properly come from the decree but from the positing of the decree, and it is not properly internal necessity, the kind that belongs to things. It is something common to the necessary and the contingent. For the efficacy of the divine will brings it about that the future existence of all beings, both necessary and contingent, is established. Therefore, just as natural effects cannot but be by internal necessity with respect to natural causes, and yet can be or not be by external necessity with respect to the divine decree (in relation to which even the most necessary things otherwise, such as the rising of the sun, an eclipse, or the motions of the heavenly bodies, can be or not be), so by the same right effects that are contingent by internal contingency with respect to secondary causes can be or not be, and by external necessity, in relation to the will of God, cannot not be. So that they are contingent to God is understood in two ways. 1. As if, notwithstanding the positing of the decree, they could be or not be absolutely. This is not to be said, for when God has decreed, they cannot not be. 2. They are contingent with respect to the decree in this sense: the decree posits them as contingent, and so a free future existence in relation to the natural mode of acting in the secondary cause. And what prevents God from considering contingent effects both in relation to his decree and in relation to secondary causes? That all things happen necessarily in relation to God's decree is also understood in three ways. 1. So that necessity is joined with the things willed by God. This we do not teach, for God decreed that contingent effects should come about contingently and not necessarily, and so he decreed both beings and modes of beings. 1. [?] So that the word necessity is joined with the will of God: thus God does not decree necessarily, but most freely, that all things should happen either contingently or necessarily. 3. That necessity is referred to the future existence of contingent beings, so that contingent things are necessary to God with respect to his decree. In no way does it follow from this that they are not contingent to God. 3. It matters a great deal, contrary to what the Remonstrants think, whether the necessity is external or internal. For the necessity is external and comes from almighty God, whose office it is, from his infinite wisdom, to determine freedom while natural indifference remains unharmed. Therefore that necessity does not take away native freedom.

units.la: 22. Ob. 19. Voluntas sub determinatione divina vel agit necessario, aut minime. Resp.: Et necessario & libere, verum ea necessitas cum libertate consspirat, ut dictum.
units.tr: 22. Obj. 19. The will under divine determination either acts necessarily or not at all. Answer: it acts both necessarily and freely; but that necessity agrees with freedom, as has been said.

units.la: 23. Ob. 20. Si omnia sunt decreta absolute, tum quaerenti cur hodie decem opera facias, non plura non pauciora, respondendum, quia Deus decrevit, & decretum esset causa omnium, & ad tot actus opus esset admiranda providentia.R. Decretum & voluntatem Dei esse omnium causam, si neget, scripturæ Rom. 11. 36. Apoc. 4. 11. Matth. 10. 29. contra-dicit: quia vero est prima & communis causa omnium, in qua mens non acquiescit, per hanc male responderetur omnibus quæsitis, 2. Nos admirandam providentiam adoramus, cujus viæ sunt impervestigabiles Rom. 12. rideat, siquidem volet, Iesuita.
units.tr: 23. Obj. 20. If all things are decreed absolutely, then to one who asks why you do ten works today, and not more or fewer, the answer must be: because God so decreed; the decree would be the cause of all, and for so many acts there would be need of admirable providence. Answer, 1. If someone denies that the decree and will of God is the cause of all, he contradicts Scripture: Rom. 11. 36; Rev. 4. 11; Matt. 10. 29. But since it is the first and common cause of all, in which the mind does not rest, by this line of reasoning all questions would be answered badly. 2. We adore admirable providence, whose ways are unsearchable (Rom. 12). Let the Jesuit laugh, if he wishes.

units.la: 24. Ob. 21. Si Deus omnia absolute determinavit præcise ad unam partem, tum perit Dei libertas, aliter disponendi res quam sunt dispositæ: ita Vorstius. Deus nullum statutum (inquit Lacksonus) ponit quod absolutæ & æternæ suæ dominij potestati adversetur. Et strictâ (inquit) nimis obligatio legibus positivis, vel decreta immutabilia, & legislatores & alios nativa sua libertate & bene agendi opportunitate spoliant. Resp. 1. Crasso & modo plane anthropomorphetico (in quod delirium semper inclinat ferum & agreste cerebrum hujus novatoris) metuit Dei libertatem, quasi determinando suam voluntatem, libertatem sic profunderet & exhauriret: sed dic, novator, an post decretum creandi mundum; & redimendi genus humanum, & resuscitandi filium Dei a mortuis, quæ decreta jam sunt completa, an Deus aliquid libertatis absolutæ perdidit? Ergo Deus est minus liber, nunc quam ante mundum conditum. quid? fare, quæso: an homo quo plures actus liberos exerceat minus est liber? non dices, nisi te tam heterodoxa scribendo, libertatem scribendi saniora dixeris, quod certe ego verissimum esse arbitror. 2. Per decreta absoluta nihil Deo libertatis decedit, quia non oritur in Deo novum judicium, aut scientia nova, quâ quædam hodie incipit scire, quæ ab æterno ignoravit, quo casu necesse fuit ei, inconsulta vel mutare, vel nunquam fecisse. 3. Vult longè satius esse Deo, ut decreta ipsius alterabilia sint, ut sic retineat libertatem bene agendi: itaque Jacksono, Deus per immutabilia decreta amittit opportunitatem bene agendi, ideoque satius esset singere Deum mutabilem, ut posset esset liber. An absoluta libertas & immutabilitas in Deo simul esse non possunt? 4, Quia Deus est infinite sapiens & infinite justus, ideo ipsius decreta sunt mutabilia: ait enim, Papam, siquidem sapientia & justitia in eo dignitati & potestati pares forent, longe tutius decreta & facta, cum spiritus inspiratione vel exspiratione rescindere, ideoque decreta Dei debent esse mutabilia, quia Dei justitia & sapientia est infinita, ideoque justitia & libertas in Deo adversis frontibus pugnant. §. Confundit Jacksonus, ut optime annotavit doctissimus vir G. Tuissius, libertatem naturae æqualiter communem omnibus, cum libertate conditionis seu[?] authoritatis, quæ major est in principe, quam in subdito, ideoque princeps post latam legem irrevocabilem, habet naturae libertatem, sicut ante latam legem habuit: non tamen habet libertatem conditionis, ita ut sine inconstantiæ notâ mutare possit decreta sua. Deus post decreta est liberrimus naturæ libertate, sicut fuit ante positum decretum, sed post latum decretum, non potest esse Deus, si decreta rescinderet, & tamen liberrime decreta sua exequitur: nullam enim videt, aut videre potest rationem, cur rescinderet decreta. 6. Sicut per decreta, ita per promissiones pari ratione Deus amitteret opportunitatem bene agendi, ergo Deus promissiones etiam violare potest. 7. Notum est Vorstium Deo corporeitatem, poenitentiam & multas passiones humanas, blasphemiae, adfinxisse: ita hic vult, Deum posse decreta sua mutare, ne periret libertas decernendi.
units.tr: 24. Obj. 21. If God has determined all things absolutely to one side, then God's freedom perishes, since he could not dispose things otherwise than they are disposed. So Vorstius. God establishes no statute (says Jackson) which would be opposed to the power of his absolute and eternal dominion. And too strict (he says) an obligation to positive laws, or immutable decrees, strips legislators and others of their native freedom and their opportunity to act well. Answer. 1. With a crude and plainly anthropomorphic notion (into which the wild and rustic brain of this innovator always tends to fall), he fears for God's freedom, as if by determining his will he would squander and exhaust his freedom. But tell me, innovator: after the decrees to create the world, to redeem the human race, and to raise the Son of God from the dead, which decrees are now completed, has God lost any absolute freedom? Therefore God is now less free than he was before the world was made. Well? Tell me, I beg you: does a man who exercises more free acts become less free? You will not say so, unless by writing so heterodoxly you have made yourself say saner things about freedom in writing, which I myself think most true. 2. Nothing of God's freedom is lost through absolute decrees, because no new judgment arises in God, nor new knowledge by which he begins today to know what he did not know from eternity. In that case it would have been necessary for him either to change, having been ill-advised, or never to have done it. 3. He would have it far better for God that his decrees be alterable, so that he may retain the freedom of acting well. Thus, according to Jackson, God through immutable decrees loses the opportunity of acting well, and therefore it would be better to feign God mutable so that he could be free. Can absolute freedom and immutability not be together in God? 4. Because God is infinitely wise and infinitely just, therefore his decrees are mutable. For he says that the Pope, if his wisdom and justice were equal in him to his dignity and power, would far more safely rescind decrees and deeds with the inspiration or expiration of a breath. Therefore God's decrees must be mutable, because God's justice and wisdom are infinite, and so justice and freedom in God fight with opposed foreheads. §. Jackson confuses, as the most learned man G. Tuissius has well noted, the freedom of nature, which is equally common to all, with the freedom of condition or authority, which is greater in a prince than in a subject. Therefore a prince, after a law has been issued irrevocably, has the freedom of nature just as he had it before the law was issued; yet he does not have freedom of condition, so that he could change his decrees without a mark of inconstancy. After decrees, God is most free with the freedom of nature, just as he was before the decree was posited. But once a decree has been issued, he cannot be God if he rescinded it; and yet he carries out his decrees most freely, for he sees, or can see, no reason why he should rescind them. 6. Just as through decrees, so by the same reasoning through promises God would lose the opportunity of acting well. Therefore God can also violate promises. 7. It is well known that Vorstius attributed to God corporeality, repentance, many human passions and blasphemies. So here he wants God to be able to change his decrees, lest the freedom of decreeing perish.

units.la: 25. Ob. 22. Ita objicit Iackson. Quod (inquit) unicuiusque vitae cursus & sententiae finales unicuique destinatae immutabiles esse debeant, quia sunt praedeterminatae ab immutabili omnipotente decreto, nihilo majorem veritatis colorem habet, quam si diceremus, oportere Deum esse nigrum, quoniam nigros facit Corvos &c. Resp. Praeter Iacksonum nemo ita disserit: quia Deus fecit Corvos. Ergo dic Deum tuum Arminianum esse Corvum: nam mutabilem statuisse eum. 2. Nemo asserit, decreta Dei facere res decretas immutabiles, sic faceret creaturas non creaturas. 3. Decretum esse immutabile, & res decretas in relatione ad decretum esse mutabiles, est contradictio. Nam si Deus decernit, ut Petrus crederet, non potest fieri necessitate modali, ut non credat: eo enim modo statuit decreta Dei esse immutabilia, quo decreta Persarum. p. 123. At si res a Persis decretae, quatenus sunt decretæ, revocari & mutari possunt, an non decretum erat revocabile? Definiat nobis decretum immutabile: an relinquet res decretas, ut possint esse vel non esse? scilicet hoc est decretum disjunctivum, atque sublato omni in Deo, decreto, necesse est Iudas ut credat vel non credat, vel damnetur vel non damnetur, nec opus est, imo ridiculum est, ut Deus hoc decernat. 4. Sententiæ de morte vel vita hominum, sunt actiones Dei, at si eæ fuut [?] mutabiles,tum actus Dei sunt mutabiles,& volitiones. 5. Quod mors & vita hominum sic sunt Deo in æquilibrio, sapit Deum ignorantem, mutabilem, suspensum, pendulum & minime infinitum, qui expectat creatas volitiones, nè vel aliquid statuat, vel certi quicquam cognoscat.
units.tr: 25. Obj. 22. Thus objects Jackson: that the course of each person's life and the final sentences destined for each should be immutable, because they are predetermined by an immutable almighty decree, has no more colour of truth than if we said that God ought to be black, since he makes black crows, etc. Answer, 1. Apart from Jackson, no one argues thus: "because God made crows." So say that your Arminian God is a crow, for you make him mutable. 2. No one asserts that God's decrees make the decreed things immutable; in that way they would make creatures not creatures. 3. That a decree is immutable while the things decreed are mutable in relation to the decree is a contradiction. For if God decrees that Peter should believe, it cannot happen by modal necessity that he does not believe. For in that way he establishes that the decrees of God are immutable, in the same way as the decrees of the Persians (p. 123). But if things decreed by the Persians, insofar as they are decreed, can be revoked and changed, was not the decree itself revocable? Let him define for us an immutable decree. Will he leave the decreed things so that they may be or not be? Clearly this is a disjunctive decree, and with every decree in God removed, it is necessary that Judas believe or not believe, be damned or not damned. Nor is there any need, indeed it is ridiculous, for God to decree this. 4. Sentences of death or life pronounced on men are actions of God. But if these were mutable, then God's actions and volitions would be mutable. 5. That the death and life of men stand thus in equilibrium with God savours of a God who is ignorant, mutable, suspended, hanging in the balance, and by no means infinite, who waits for created volitions, lest he either decide anything or know anything for certain.

units.la: 26. Ob. 23. Pater meus hodie operatur Ioh. 5. Ergo (inquit) Deus hodie decernit, omnia facit secundum consilium voluntatis. Ergo: & ita Iackfo. Resp. confundit decretum cum decreti executione. 2. Ergo aliquid facit in tempore, quod ab æterno se facturum non decrevit, & incipiunt novæ in Deo volitiones hodie, aliæ cras. Absurda omnia, hodie decernet creationem,
units.tr: 26. Obj. 23. My Father works hitherto, John 5. Therefore (he says) God decrees today, and does all things according to the counsel of his will. Therefore, and so Jackson. Answer: he confuses the decree with the execution of the decree. 2. Therefore he does something in time which he did not decree from eternity that he would do, and new volitions arise in God today, others tomorrow. All absurd: he will decree the creation today.

units.la: 27. Ob. 24. Sequitur justitiæ actus omitti, quia Deus decrevit absolute & simpliciter ne fierent, ideoque Deus erit impeditor justitiæ & bonorum actum. Resp. 1. Clarissimus D. Tuiff. voluntas omittendi bonum erit a Deo decreta, neque alia actio fingi potest. Nempe Placet Arminio decrevisse Deum, ut actus justitiæ omitterentur ab hominibus, si modo vellent. Deus ergo decrevit illam voluntatem omittendi, voluntate absoluta, aut respectiva; si absoluta, habetur institutum: si respectiva, nempe decrevit, ut creaturæ vellent omittere actus justitiæ, modo vellent. 2. An non Deus multos credentes operaturos, siquidem satis superesset, multos actus justitiæ ex hac vita in beatitudinem vindicat? & tum actus justitiæ impedit Deus. Resipuissent Tyrii, si Deus signa adhibuisset, audiissent exteræ gentes Ezechielem, siquidem Deus ipsum ad vaticinandum misisset. At noluit Tyriis signa, noluit nationibus prophetas indulgere: Item Esai.63.17. 1.Sam.2.2 5. 3. Impeditor proprie est justitiæ, qui creaturam propendentem in actus justitiæ violentia alio torquet & avocat: at vero qui libere actus justitiæ omittunt, & eosdem actus qui ut omitterentur, absolute Deus decrevit, sese libere impediunt, quo minus juste operentur, ideoque libere actus omittunt, & etiam necessitate decreti divini.
units.tr: 27. Obj. 24. It follows that acts of justice are omitted, because God decreed absolutely and simply that they should not happen, and so God will be the hinderer of justice and of good works. Answer 1. The most distinguished Mr. Twisse: the will to omit good will be decreed by God, and no other act can be imagined. Indeed Arminius holds that God decreed that acts of justice should be omitted by men, if only they should wish it. God therefore decreed that will to omit, by an absolute or a respective will. If absolute, the thing is established as an ordinance; if respective, namely, he decreed that creatures should wish to omit acts of justice, provided they wished it. 2. Does not God, who claims for himself many believers from this life into blessedness, if indeed enough remained, also claim many acts of justice? And then God hinders acts of justice. The Tyrians would have repented, if God had employed signs; the foreign nations would have heard Ezekiel, if God had sent him to prophesy. But he did not will signs for the Tyrians, did not will to grant prophets to the nations. Likewise Isaiah 63:17; 1 Sam. 2:25. 3. A hinderer, properly speaking, is one who by violence turns and calls away a creature inclined to acts of justice; but those who freely omit acts of justice, and whose very acts God absolutely decreed should be omitted, freely hinder themselves from acting justly, and therefore they omit the acts freely, and also by the necessity of the divine decree.

units.la: 28. Non genio meo admodum arridet coacervare testimonia humana, huic sæculo ostentationibus delectanti unice placet, quædam tamen addo. August. 1. Si propterea quisquam res humanas tato Dei [?] (ut causæ, vide textum patris) tribuit, quia ipsam Dei voluntatem fati nomine appellat, sententiam teneat, & linguam corrigat. Et Enchrid. Nullus fit salvus nisi ille velit, & ideo rogandus est, ut velit, quia si ille velit, necesse est fieri. Et Deus vult nos velle, nos vero ad volendum eum movere non possumus. Et in Soliloq. Velle quod bonum est non possum, nisi tu velis. Fulgentius: Hoc praedestinavit Deus, quod erat ipse facturus, aut quod fuerat largiturus. Hieronymus: Reprobat enim (Deus) cogitationes populorum, hoc est, Judaeorum consilia, quia non potuerunt illa facere, nisi quantum a Deo praedefinitum erat. Athanasius, vel ut alii voluntatis, Theophylact. Ephes. c. 1. Bona opera nostra sunt a Deo praeparata, & praedefinita. Theodoret. Nostram precationem praeconstituit, ut nos filiorum adoptionis donum perciperemus secundum propositum voluntatis suae. Damascenus: Omnia a Deo (inquit) praefinita, & fine ulla commutatione futura, in ejus consilio non aliter, antequam fierent, erant expressa, quam si quis velit domum aedificare, prius imaginem ac formam ipsius in animo effingit &c. Anselmus: quoniam enim quod Deus vult, non potest non esse, cum vult hominis voluntate nulla cogi vel prohiberi necessitate ad volendum, vel non ad volendum, & vult effectum sequi voluntatem, tunc necesse est, voluntatem esse liberam, & esse quod vult. Leo: Quod homines per crucem salvarentur, erat commune Patris & Filii consilium, nec ulla potetat ratione turbari, quod ante aeterna saecula, & misericorditer erat dispositum, & incommutabiliter praefinitum. Prosper: Nec aliter (inquit) quidquam procedere potest: quam omnipotentis voluntate dispositum est. Petrus Diaconus: Dona, Domine, virtutem ac tutimentum, malos quæfumus, bonos facito, bonos in bonitate conserva, omnia enim potes, & non est, qui contradicet tibi: Cum enim volueris, salvas, non est qui resistat tibi. Hæc verba è diametro pugnant cum voluntate Dei conditionatâ ex præscientiâ media liberæ cooperationis arbitrii humani.
units.tr: 28. It does not greatly please my disposition to heap up human testimonies; this age, delighting in display, alone is pleased by them. Still, I add some. Augustine, On the Trinity 1. If anyone attributes human affairs to God's causality (see the author's text) because he calls the very will of God by the name of fate, let him keep the opinion and correct the language. And in the Enchiridion: No one is saved unless he wills it, and therefore he must be asked to will it, because if he wills it, it must happen. And God wills that we will, yet we cannot move him to will. And in the Soliloquies: I cannot will what is good, unless you will it. Fulgentius: God predestined that which he himself was going to do, or which he had been going to bestow. Jerome: For God rejects the thoughts of the peoples, that is, the counsels of the Jews, because they could not do those things except so far as they had been predefined by God. Athanasius, or as others read, of the will; Theophylact on Ephesians chapter 1: Our good works were prepared and predefined by God. Theodoret: He prearranged our prayer, so that we might receive the gift of adoption as sons according to the purpose of his will. Damascene: All things (he says) were predetermined by God, and were to come about without any change; in his counsel they were expressed, before they happened, in no other way than if someone wishes to build a house, and first forms in his mind the image and plan of it, etc. Anselm: For since what God wills cannot not be, when he wills, the human will is compelled by no necessity to will or not to will, and he wills that the effect follow the will; then it is necessary that the will be free and be what he wills. Leo: That men should be saved through the cross was the common counsel of the Father and the Son, and it could not be disturbed by any reason, since it had been arranged before the eternal ages, and mercifully, and predetermined unchangeably. Prosper: Nor (he says) can anything proceed otherwise than as it has been disposed by the will of the Almighty. Peter the Deacon: Grant, Lord, virtue and steadfastness; we ask you, make the wicked good, keep the good in goodness, for you can do all things, and there is no one who can contradict you: for when you will, you save, and no one resists you. These words fight directly against a conditional will of God, grounded in middle knowledge, and in the free cooperation of the human will.

units.la: Scholastici hic nobis unicè favent. Schola Parifiens damnaviteos, qui dixerunt, Deum velle aut decernere, quia nos prius volumus. Aquinas: Fieri non potest, ut Deus aliqua faciat, quæ non præsciverit & præordinaverit, se facturum & 1. par. [?]16. ar.1. Contingit aliquid esse casuale & fortuitum ad res inferiores relatum, quod tamen, relatum ad primam causam, fit per se intentum. Et 1. par. q. 23. concl. Deum ordinare (ait) omnes causas ad determinatos effectus. Aquinas: Quamvis (inquit) voluntas Dei fit immutabilis & invincibilis, non tamen sequitur, quod omnis ejus effectus fit necessarius necessitate absolutâ, quam habet res a causa suâ proximâ, sed solum necessitate conditionatâ, sicut de præscientiâ dictum est. Durand. Stante suppositione, quod omnia sunt volita à Deo, non possunt non evenire. Bonavent. Voluntas Dei absoluta connotat eventum rei, & ideo est ibi necessitas consequentiæ, sed non consequentis, quia non mutat eventum rei, imo vult Deus quod eveniat consequens contingens. Et hanc esse Scholafticorum sententiam unanimem, docet ipse Je-fuita Gregor. de Valent. Communiter (inquit) theologi dicunt effectum contingentem, quatenus est quidem a Deo provisus, esse inevitabibilem (seu necessarium fecundum quid, nimimirum ex ea hypothesi divinae providentiae. Simpliciter autem & absolute evitabilem propter conditionem nimirum proximae causae illius, quae est contingens. Et Cajetanus, Omnes (inquit) Doctores affirmant hoc. Idem doceri a Trigofio docet Guil, Tuiffus in fcholasticorum scriptis vir non mediocriter versatus. Braduard, Illum (inquit) pro Deo noftro nolo habere, qui non fit omnipotens in agendo, qui non habeat omnipotentiffimum dominatum supra meam debilem voluntatem, qui non posset omnipotentiffime facere me velle; & facere quicquid vellet, qui non habeat voluntem universaliter efficacem, infrustrabilem, indefectibilem & necessariam in causando; imo cujus voluntas, non fit mihi necessitas, cujus sanctissimam voluntatem ego peccator, velut mulierculam debilem facillime possum opprimere & neceffitare ad horribilem actum peccati, &c. Haec eadem citat & Tuiffius. Scotus, Contra (inquit) naturam voluntatis est determinari a causa inferiori quia hoc ipso non effet superior, non est autem contra eam determinari a causa superiore. Id docent Capreolus, & Ferrariensis. Alvarez de auxil. d, 22. Probat quod Deus absoluto decreto, vere efficienter sive ad modum causæ physicæ prædeterminet omnes causas secundas, & ex gent. Thoma affert expositiones locorum Damasceni & aliorum qui videntur contrariæ sententiæ favere. Et Do. Bannes. Neque (inquit) essectus divinæ voluntatis impediri potest à voluntate nostra, sed necesse est necessitate consequentiæ & suppositionis, quod voluntas nostra sequatur efficacem Dei directionem & concursum. Gul. Estius, Sequitur (inquit) rem necessario fore in tempore, quia Deus eam prædeterminavit ab æterno fore.
units.tr: The Scholastics here favour us alone. The Paris school condemned those who said that God wills or decrees because we first will. Aquinas: It cannot be that God does anything which he has not foreknown and foreordained that he would do; and in the first part, question 16, article 1: Something is said to be chance and fortuitous as related to inferior things, which nevertheless, related to the first cause, is intended per se. And in the first part, question 23, conclusion: God (he says) orders all causes to determinate effects. Aquinas: Although (he says) the will of God is immutable and invincible, it does not follow that all its effects are necessary with an absolute necessity, which a thing has from its proximate cause, but only with a conditional necessity, as has been said about foreknowledge. Durandus: Given the supposition that all things are willed by God, they cannot fail to happen. Bonaventure: The absolute will of God connotes the event of the thing, and therefore there is a necessity of consequence there, but not of the consequent, because it does not change the event of the thing; rather God wills that the contingent consequent should come about. And that this is the unanimous opinion of the Scholastics the Jesuit Gregory of Valencia himself teaches. Commonly (he says) theologians say that a contingent effect, insofar as it is indeed foreseen by God, is unavoidable (or necessary in a certain respect, namely from that hypothesis of divine providence); but simply and absolutely avoidable, on account of the condition of its proximate cause, which is contingent. And Cajetan: All the Doctors affirm this. William Twisse, a man well versed in the writings of the Schoolmen, shows that Trigosius teaches the same. Bradwardine: I do not want to have as our God one who is not omnipotent in acting, who does not have the most omnipotent dominion over my weak will, who could not most omnipotently make me will, and make whatever he willed, who does not have a will universally efficacious, unfrustrable, indefectible and necessary in causing; indeed, whose will is not a necessity to me, whose most holy will I, a sinner, can very easily overpower and compel, like a weak little woman, to the horrible act of sin, etc. Twisse also cites these same words. Scotus: It is contrary to the nature of the will to be determined by an inferior cause, because by that very fact it would not be superior; but it is not contrary to it to be determined by a superior cause. Capreolus and Ferrariensis teach this. Alvarez, On Auxilium, disputation 22, proves that God, by an absolute decree, truly predetermines all secondary causes efficiently, or in the manner of a physical cause, and from Thomas's Gentiles he brings forward explanations of the passages of Damascene and others which seem to favour the contrary opinion. And Domingo Báñez: Neither (he says) can the effect of the divine will be impeded by our will, but it is necessary, by a necessity of consequence and of supposition, that our will follow God's efficacious direction and concurrence. William Estius: It follows that the thing will necessarily happen in time, because God predetermined from eternity that it would happen.

units.la: 29. Hisce testimoniis & veritate convictus Fr. Suarez. Concedit prædefinitionem quandam immanentem, non transeuntem, eamque efficacem & absolutam actuum supernaturalium. Hinc infero, quia actus supernaturales sunt actus vere liberi, & quoad potentiam & usum, decretum nostrum absolutum optime consistere cum libertate arbitrii, & quoad potentiam & exercitium potentiæ etiam juxta doctrinam Suarezij. Fundamenta ipsius an sint valida examini subjiciantur, necesse est 1. actus supernaturalis est honestus. Ergo ex hac parte non repugnat, quod Deus illum afoblute velit & amet. Resp. 1. Si non fit actus liber, non proprie est honestus, at ex placitis Jesuitæ non potest dari actus liber ex absoluta prædefinitione. Ergo: &c. addit Suarez, deinde præcognovit Deus talem vocationem vel auxilium (de congruo loquitur) esse accommodatum medium, ut per illud voluntas humana de facto incline-turtur ad talem actum eliciendum. Ergo potest Deus unico actu simplicissimo suae voluntatis velle, quod creata voluntas eliciat talem actum &c. Resp. 1. PræcognoscitDeus consilium congruum de facto accommodatè ad naturam libertatis inclinaturam voluntatè ad actumsupernaturalem, scientia non simplicis intelligentiæ, sed media, quæ præsupponit actum supernaturalem liberum antecedenter ad omnem actum divinæ voluntatis: Ergo Deus potest talem actum absolutè decernere, nullo modo sequitur.Nam absolutum decretum non antecedit futuritio actus liberi, sed sequitur, ut effectus causam: lectorem itaque Jesuita vaferrime ludificatur.
units.tr: 29. Convinced by these testimonies and by the truth, Fr. Suarez concedes a certain immanent, not transeunt, predefinition, and one that is efficacious and absolute, of supernatural acts. From this I infer that, because supernatural acts are truly free acts, and as regards power and use, our absolute decree can very well consist with freedom of the will, and as regards power and the exercise of power, also according to the doctrine of Suarez. It is necessary to subject his foundations to examination, to see whether they are valid. 1. A supernatural act is honest. Therefore, on this side, there is nothing repugnant in God absolutely willing and loving it. Answer 1. If it is not a free act, it is not properly honest; but according to the opinions of the Jesuits, no free act can exist from an absolute predefinition. Therefore, etc. Suarez adds: then God, having foreknown that such a calling or help (he speaks of congruous grace) is a suitable means by which the human will is in fact inclined to elicit such an act. Therefore God can by a single most simple act of his will will that the created will elicit such an act, etc. Answer 1. God foreknows by a congruous counsel, in fact adapted to the nature of freedom which inclines the will to a supernatural act, a knowledge not of simple understanding but of middle knowledge, which presupposes a free supernatural act antecedently to every act of the divine will. Therefore it does not at all follow that God can absolutely decree such an act. For an absolute decree does not precede the futurition of a free act, but follows it, as an effect follows its cause; so the Jesuit most craftily deceives the reader. 2. Therefore he cannot absolutely will a free act, but only conditionally; for here God wills a free act on the hypothesis that it is already being produced through congruous help. 3. By the same reasoning all contingent acts are determined by an immanent predefinition, though not a transeunt one, because they come about…

units.la: 2. Ergo non potest absolute velle actum liberum, sed conditionate: nam Deus hic vult actum liberum, ex hypothesi, quod jam fit per auxilium congruum productus. 3. Pari ratione omnes actus contingentes sunt determinati immanente prædefinitione, licet non transeunte, quia fiunt omnes actus contingentes vel motione congrua vel incongrua, eo quod fiant scientia media, qua cognoscit Deus, utrum motio sic accommodata, ut de facto inclinet causam secundam, vel non inclinet.
units.tr: 2. Therefore he cannot will a free act absolutely, but only conditionally: for God here wills the free act on the hypothesis that it is now being produced through the congruous aid. 3. By the same reasoning, all contingent acts are determined by an immanent predefinition, though not a transient one, since all contingent acts come about either through a congruous or an incongruous motion, because they are made by middle knowledge, by which God knows whether a motion so adapted will in fact incline the secondary cause, or will not incline it.

units.la: Addit Jesuita: Quod vero (inquit) in hoc decreto nihil fit repugnans libertati gratiæ, patet, quia per tale decretum vult Deus actum illum in ordine ad causam, & ad medium, per quæ libere futurus est, & ex vi talis decreti nullam aliam causam adhibet ad talem effectum. Non ergo ledit libertatem, quia directè vult ipsum actum creaturæ & liberum & ex vi ejus ordinat medium aptum ad liberam determinationem causandam. Refp. 1. Admiror Jesuitae versatile & vafrum ingenium. Nam vult Deus actum liberum, qui in ordine ad causam est libere futurus, vel antecedenter & absolute priusquam fit futurus liber actus, & sic perit scientia media, quae statuit actus liberos futuros esse antecedenter ad voluntatis decretum, & sic antecedens necessitas optime etiam stat cum libertate, quod totis viribus Jesuita profligare satagit, imo unice in hoc vires ingenii intendit: vel vult illum actum libere futurum conditionate, & sic ludit nos; nam praefinitio haec tum est conditionata: vel denique det Jesuita voluntatem Dei, quae nec fit absoluta nec conditionata, quod certe dari non potest, quoniam contradictorie opponuntur. 2. Directe vult ipsum actum creaturae, pro voce (directe) suppone, quaso, vocem (antecedenter & absolute) secus causam tuam non promovebis, & sic videbis causae tuae ruinam, nempe Deum velle absolute actum creaturae ut liberum. 3. Ordinat (inquit) medium aptum (dic congruum) ad liberam determinationem causandam. Atqui congrua causatio & motio includit praescientiam, & praescientia objectum non facit, sed praesupponit jam factum, ergo ordinat volitionem congruam, quae jam antecedenter ad ordinationem est, ubi jam Jesuita, praedefinitio tua absoluta; Viden' praefinitionem conditionatam, quae objectum esse praesupponit? Proh dolor! non e-rubuit rubuit Iesuita & chartam albam haud erubuisse admiror.
units.tr: The Jesuit adds: But that nothing repugnant to the liberty of grace is done in this decree is clear, because by such a decree God wills that act in relation to the cause and to the means by which it is to be future freely, and by the force of such a decree he applies no other cause to such an effect. Therefore he does not injure liberty, because he directly wills the act itself, both created and free, and by its force he orders the means apt for causing a free determination. Answer: 1. I marvel at the versatile and crafty wit of the Jesuit. For either God wills a free act, which in relation to the cause is to be future freely, antecedently and absolutely before the act is future as free; and then middle knowledge perishes, which holds that free acts are future antecedently to the decree of the will, and then antecedent necessity agrees very well even with liberty, which the Jesuit strives with all his might to overthrow, indeed he directs the whole force of his wit to this alone. Or he wills that act to be future freely only conditionally, and then he mocks us, for this predefinition is then conditional. Or finally, let the Jesuit give a will of God that is neither absolute nor conditional, which certainly cannot be given, since these are contradictory opposites. 2. He directly wills the act of the creature itself. I beg you, in place of the word (directly) suppose the words (antecedently and absolutely); otherwise you will not advance your cause, and so you will see the ruin of your cause, namely that God absolutely wills the act of the creature as free. 3. He orders (he says) a means apt (say, congruous) for causing a free determination. But congruous causation and motion includes foreknowledge, and foreknowledge does not make the object but presupposes it as already done. Therefore he orders a congruous volition, which is already antecedent to the ordering; here, Jesuit, is your absolute predefinition. Do you see a conditional predefinition, which presupposes that the object is? Alas! The Jesuit has not blushed, and I marvel that the white paper did not blush.

units.la: 22. Perge Iesuita. Talis voluntas est absoluta & efficax. Nam decretum quo statuit Deus dare hominem talem vocationem congruam, ut credat, est praedefinitio respectu talis vocationis, quia simpliciter vult dare illam antequam praesciat absolute futuram, quamvis non velit eam dare nisi propter talem finem vel actum: Ergo & e contrario decretum de actu ipso erit praedefinitio ejus, quamvis non fit volitus nisi per tale medium, tandem ille actus non comparatur ad nostram voluntatem ut determinandam solum concomitanter, sed antecedenter & causaliter, quia per illum Deus vult non tantum concurrere, si voluntas consenserit, sed vult ut consentiat, idque non per velleitatem simplicem affectum, sed absoluto & efficaci decreto, quale est illud de quo Augusti. Deo volenti salvum facere nullum humanum resistit arbitrium.
units.tr: 22. Go on, Jesuit. Such a will is absolute and efficacious. For the decree by which God determines to give a man such a congruous calling that he believes is a predefinition with respect to such a calling, because he simply wills to give it before he foreknows absolutely that it will be future, although he does not will to give it except for such an end or act. Therefore, conversely, the decree about the act itself will be a predefinition of it, although it is not willed except through such a means. Finally, that act is not compared to our will as determining it only concomitantly, but antecedently and causally, because through it God wills not only to concur if the will consents, but wills that it consent, and this not by a mere velleity or simple affection, but by an absolute and efficacious decree, such as that of which Augustine speaks: "God willing to save, no human will resists."

units.la: Resp. Quid hoc est? Deus simpliciter vult dare vocationem congruam antequam praesciat absolutam futuram, nempe vocationem congruam: quid hoc ad praedefinitionem absolutam actus liberi? quaeritur an velit dare vocationem congruam, priusquam natura praesciat, hominem actu libero obediturum tali vocationi: hoc nisi dixeris, nunquam probabis praedefinitionem absolutam.
units.tr: Answer. What is this? God simply wills to give a congruous calling before he foreknows that the absolutely future one, namely the congruous calling, will be future. What has this to do with the absolute predefinition of a free act? The question is whether he wills to give a congruous calling before he foreknows that the man will obey such a calling by a free act. Unless you say this, you will never prove an absolute predefinition.

units.la: 2. Ergo decretum de actu libero erit praedefinitio, non sequitur, quia vel praescit illum actum absolute futurum priusquam velit dare vocationem congruam, vel non praescit: si prius, adhuc praefinitio erit conditionata, non absoluta: si Posterius, quo evanuit scientia media, imo fieri potest ut voluntas dissentiat. 4. Si Deus vult antecedenter, ut voluntas consentiat, & non vult actum fi consentiat, profecto efficax Dei decretum antecedet actum liberum, & sic actus liber erit necessarius necessitate antecedente, quod non ferent aures Jesuiticæ; vel posito efficaci Dei decreto de actu libero, poteft ille actus liber non fieri: ita enim Jesuita libertatem definit, quæ possit, omnibus ad agendum requisitis positis, agere vel non agere. Ergo potest resisti absoluto decreto, quod est absurdum. 4. Si ille actus comparatur ad voluntatem nostram ut determinandam antecedenter & causaliter respectu decreti divini, dabitur futuritio determinationis liberæ antecedenter ad Dei decretum, & sic tollitur decretum absolutum: si consequenter ad decretum, necesse est ponat antecedentem necessitatem & actus liberos, quod Jesuitis est absurdum. 5. Aquo est determinanda voluntas antecedenter & causaliter, an a Deo? Hoc pernegat Jesuita, ab ipsa voluntate, tum Deus vult antecedenter voluntatem se determinare, & sic adhuc antecedens necessitas & liber actus componentur & se invicem compatientur, quæ nostra est sententia. 6. Ipse Jesuita nodum solvit, & suam causam jugulat. Ibid. ad figur. 10. Ut providentia (inquit) fit perfecta & sufficiens ad effectum prædefinitum, necesse est ut & permissio fit particularis de actu cum omnibus circumstantiis ejus, quæ necessariæ sunt ad effectum præfinitum, & ut fiat fit actus permissus infallibiliter futurus, si permittatur, quod nullo modo esse aut intelligi posset, nisi suppositā conditionatā scientiā ante praedefinitionem talis effectus. Eadem ergo supponenda est, quando liber actus, per quem fit effectus a Deo praedefinitus, est bonus & supernaturalis. Quid multis? vult scientiam conditionatam supponi absolutae praedefinitioni actuum supernaturalium; atqui futuritio actuum supernaturalium supponitur scientiae conditionatae, quia objectum scientiae est prius ipsa scientia. Ergo multo magis ipsi actus supernaturales erunt priores absoluta praedefinitione hac Jesuitica, & eo redit; quae habet hic Jesuita, Deus absolute decernit actus supernaturales, ex hypothesi, quod jam sint: quis hic non rideret acumen Jesuiticum, aut potius caput vertiginosum? At veritas Jesuitae cedit veritati, Lib. 1. de concurs. Dei cum volunt. Et sane (inquit) videtur per se incredibile, & indignum Deo dicere, quod non potuit absoluto decreto suae voluntatis aliquid faciendum statuere, si per voluntatem creatam liberam faciendum fit, nisi prius videat tales effectus absolute futuros: Sic enim & potestas Dei in actum humanae voluntatis, nimis esset contracta & limitata: & omnes effectus liberi, licet non essent praeter scientiam Dei, necessario tamen essent praeter intentionem ejus efficacem, vel sine illa, quod est praeter omnem rationem. Hinc infero esse praeter omnem rationem, ut actus liberi non sint vere liberi, etiam prout subsunt decreto Dei absoluto, antecedenti praescientiam absolutae futurionis actuum liberorum[?]. 2. Est praeter omnem rationem, ut libertas sit essentialiter talis potentia, quae positis omnibus ad agendum requisitis possit agere, vel non agere. At vero audiat quaeso lector modum, quo Jesuita salvet libertatem sub praedefinitione hac immanente Ibid ad f.
units.tr: 2. Therefore the decree about a free act will be a predefinition. It does not follow: for either he foreknows that act as absolutely future before he wills to give the congruous calling, or he does not foreknow it. If before, the predefinition will still be conditional, not absolute; if after, middle knowledge has vanished, and indeed it may happen that the will dissents. 4. If God wills antecedently that the will consent, and does not will the act if it does not consent, then surely the efficacious decree of God precedes the free act, and so the free act will be necessary with an antecedent necessity, which Jesuitical ears will not bear. Or, with the efficacious decree of God about the free act posited, that act may not come to be; for thus the Jesuit defines liberty, as that which, all things required for acting being posited, can act or not act. Therefore it can be resisted by an absolute decree, which is absurd. 4. If that act is compared to our will as determining it antecedently and causally with respect to the divine decree, there will be a futurity of free determination antecedent to God's decree, and so the absolute decree is abolished; if it is consequent to the decree, he must posit an antecedent necessity and free acts, which is absurd for the Jesuits. 5. By what is the will to be determined antecedently and causally: is it by God? The Jesuit denies this, saying it is by the will itself. Then God wills that the will determine itself antecedently, and so antecedent necessity and free act are still combined and mutually agree, which is our opinion. 6. The Jesuit himself unties the knot and cuts the throat of his own cause. In the same place, on figure 10: That providence (he says) may be perfect and sufficient for the predefined effect, it is necessary that the permission also be particular concerning the act with all its circumstances, which are necessary for the predefined effect, and that it be an act permitted to be infallibly future if it is permitted, which could in no way be, or be understood, unless a conditional knowledge is supposed before the predefinition of such an effect. Therefore the same must be supposed when the free act, through which the effect predefined by God comes about, is good and supernatural. To say more: he wants conditional knowledge to be supposed to the absolute predefinition of supernatural acts. But the futurity of supernatural acts is supposed to conditional knowledge, because the object of knowledge is prior to the knowledge itself. Therefore the supernatural acts themselves will be far prior to this Jesuitical absolute predefinition, and it comes back to what the Jesuit here holds: God absolutely decrees supernatural acts on the hypothesis that they already are. Who here would not laugh at Jesuitical acumen, or rather at a dizzy head? But the truth of the Jesuit yields to the truth: Book 1, On the Concurrence of God with the Will. And indeed (he says) it seems in itself incredible and unworthy of God to say that he could not determine by an absolute decree of his will that something is to be done, if it is to be done through a free created will, unless he first sees such effects as absolutely future. For thus the power of God over the act of the human will would be too narrow and limited; and all free effects, although they would not be outside the knowledge of God, would nonetheless be outside his efficacious intention, or without it, which is beyond all reason. Hence I infer that it is beyond all reason that free acts should not be truly free, even as they fall under God's absolute decree, which is antecedent to the foreknowledge of the absolute futurity of free acts. 2. It is beyond all reason that liberty should be essentially such a power that, all things required for acting being posited, it can act or not act. But let the reader hear, I beg, the manner in which the Jesuit saves liberty under this immanent predefinition. Ibid. ad f.

units.la: 8. Quamvis (inquit) hoc decretum sit in se efficax & absolutum, tamen non per se immediate immutat voluntatem, aut ad agendum determinat, neque extrahit eam a suo connaturali modo agendi, sed tantum adhibet, & applicat media consentanea & aptissima, ut eo modo, quo praedefinitus est, infallibiliter fiat: ad infallibilitatem vero effectus, ait, sufficere aliam motionem moralem cum communi concursu, adjuncta conditionata scientia, qua Deus praevidit fore, ut his positis, voluntas humana libere consentiat in talem actum: nam hoc est medium infallibile, & efficax ut illa divina voluntas impleatur. Sed Resp. 1. Iesuita falsum & Dei perfectione indignum praesupponit, nempe Dei decretum absolutum, quo voluntas Physice praedeterminatur, extrahere ipsam a naturali agendi modo, hoccine nos docemus? Evince si potes argumento, & Deum non posse indeclinabiliter, & tamen modo connaturalissimo[?] voluntatem flectere Deo imperfectionem aspergit, & dominium in actus liberos non mediocriter labefactar. 2 Praedeterminatio Physica etiam ponit medium morale aptissimum, quippe voluntas est agens vere ethicum & morale, etiam Dei determinatione, & propter moralem suasionem etiam libere secedit & donat determinationi physicæ. 3. Falso salsius est sufficere ad infallibilitatem effectus, motionem moralem cum generali concursu, & conditionata præscientiâ. Nam conditionata præscientia vel præscit Deus voluntatem assensum præbituram morali motioni antecedenter ad efficax & absolutum decretum, vel consequenter: si antecedenter, ludit Iesuita; nam tum non absolute decernit, & prædefinit actum libertum, sed ex hypothesi & consequenter: age itaque sic argumento, Deus, ex Iesuita, absolute decrevit omnes actus bonos & supernaturales; necesse est itaque actus illos fore, hic necessitas antecedens stat cum libertatis exercitio, quod sæpe pernegavit Iesuita, ut supra vidimus, sed adhuc urgeo: posito illo decreto Petrus libere credit. Ergo potest nunquam credere ex doctrina Iesuitica, si Petrus potest nunquam credere, etiam adhibita morali motione & concursu generali (nam neutrum ex hisce indeclinabiliter determinat voluntatem, ut docent Iesuitæ) Ergo Deus non potest præscire medium congruum, quo infallibiliter moveatur voluntas Petri ad credendum. Nam non potest Deus id præscire futurum, quod nunquam est futurum, quid hic cogitari potest à Iesuita, quo satisfaciat argumento? hoc unicum restat asylum, nempe, Deus in infinita sua sapientia præscit omnium hominum voluntates, si hisce & talibus suasionibus moveantur, talibus positis conditionibus, infallibili-ter ter tamen cessuras esse & persuadendas fore.
units.tr: 8. "Although (he says) this decree is in itself efficacious and absolute, it does not of itself immediately change the will or determine it to act, nor does it draw the will away from its connatural mode of acting. It only employs and applies means that are suitable and most apt, so that the thing comes to pass infallibly in the manner in which it was predefined. For the infallibility of the effect, he says, another moral motion together with general concurrence is sufficient, joined with conditional foreknowledge, by which God foresaw that, these things being posited, the human will would freely consent to such an act. For this is an infallible and efficacious means by which that divine will is fulfilled." But the response is: (1) The Jesuit presupposes something false and unworthy of God's perfection, namely that God's absolute decree, by which the will is physically predetermined, draws the will away from its natural mode of acting. Do we teach this? Prove it by argument if you can, namely that God cannot bend the will indeclinably and yet in a most connatural mode. To deny this attributes imperfection to God and considerably undermines his dominion over free acts. (2) Physical predetermination also posits a most apt moral means, since the will is a truly ethical and moral agent even under God's determination, and because of moral persuasion it freely yields and submits to physical determination. (3) It is still falser to say that a moral motion with general concurrence and conditional foreknowledge is sufficient for the infallibility of the effect. For conditional foreknowledge either foresees that the will will give assent to the moral motion antecedently to the efficacious and absolute decree, or consequently. If antecedently, the Jesuit is trifling, for then God does not absolutely decree and predefine the free act, but only by hypothesis and consequently. Let us then argue from the Jesuit's own premises. God has absolutely decreed all good and supernatural acts; it is necessary, therefore, that those acts will come to be. This antecedent necessity is compatible with the exercise of liberty, though the Jesuit has often denied it, as we saw above. But I press further: given that decree, Peter freely believes. Therefore, by Jesuit doctrine, he can never believe, if Peter can never believe even when the moral motion and general concurrence are applied. For neither of these indeclinably determines the will, as the Jesuits teach. Therefore God cannot foreknow a congruous means by which the will of Peter is infallibly moved to believe. For God cannot foreknow as future what never will be future. What can the Jesuit think of here to satisfy the argument? Only one refuge remains: that God, in his infinite wisdom, foreknows that men's wills, if moved by such and such persuasions under such and such conditions, will infallibly yield and be persuaded.

units.la: Sed age, sic diluo facillime hoc, voluntas sub omnibus conditionibus & suasionibus libere credit, ac proinde potest non credere. Nam nullæ circumstantiæ, nullæ conditiones, nulla denique suasio determinat voluntatem, ex Iesuitis: ergo non potest infinita Dei scientia præscire Petrum crediturum infallibiliter, quando nunquam est crediturus, imo sic Dei præscientia non esset infinita, sed fallax & conjecturalis, quod est blasphemum: si dixerit Iesuita, Deum non absolute prædefinire actum credendi in Petro, donec præsciat prius scientia conditionata, voluntatem talibus congruis suasionibus cessuram. Tum ecce adhuc Deus absoluta prædefinitione hac immanente prædefinit actus liberos, postquam sunt futuri; certe hic impossibile est Iesuitam non capi, & hærere limo argumento hoc Achilleo.
units.tr: But come, I dissolve this very easily as follows. The will, under all conditions and persuasions, believes freely, and therefore can also not believe. For, according to the Jesuits, no circumstances, no conditions, and finally no persuasion determine the will. Therefore God's infinite knowledge cannot infallibly foreknow that Peter will believe, when he never will believe. Indeed, God's foreknowledge would then not be infinite but deceptive and conjectural, which is blasphemous. If the Jesuit says that God does not absolutely predefine the act of believing in Peter until he first foreknows, by conditional knowledge, that the will will yield to such fitting persuasions, then behold, God still predefines free acts by this immanent absolute predefinition after they are already future. Certainly here it is impossible that the Jesuit is not caught, and that he does not stick fast in the mire of this Achillean argument.

units.la: 23. Vide vero ibid.f. 10. quas differentias ponat Iesuita inter prædefinitionem immanentem prædefinientem actus liberos ad intra, & prædeterminantem ad extra, 1.diff. Prior voli-ntas habet conjunctam voluntatem, vel potius simul est voluntas talis medii, quod non determinet liberum arbitrium, sed contingenter illud moveat quantum in ipso est, infallibiliter autem ex præscientia. Posterior, prædeterminans non requirit aliud medium, quam suam efficacitatem, qua secum rapit voluntatem, determinando illam. Resp. 1. Medium infallibiliter ex præscientia movere voluntatem humahumanam, falsum est: omnis enim infallibilitas fundatur in necessitate entitativa: atqui hic nulla est necessitas omnino inter motionem moralem medii, & actum liberum, sed omnino tam possunt simul non esse, quam simul esse. 2. Decretum praedeterminans nullum medium requirere, est plane falsum: illo enim decreto statuitur medium quod movet voluntatem modo connaturali, neque sua efficacitate rapit, sed suaviter determinat & flectit voluntatem. 2. Diff. Prior (inquit) voluntas praedefinit actum cum habitudine ad modum operandi causae secundae, unde in objecto suo includit actum ut faciendum ex determinatione ipsiusmet liberi arbitrii, modo congruo. Posterior habet pro objecto non solum actum, sed etiam modum seu praedeterminationem physicam per efficacem Dei motionem. Resp. Repugnantis in adjecto est, absolute praedefinire actum liberum faciendum ex determinatione ipsius liberi arbitrii, quod, positis omnibus motionibus congruis, potest agere vel non agere,ut docet Jesuita: nam posito decreto praedefiniente, non potest non agere.
