Tertio, hinc fit, (inquit Jesuita) ut prior praedefinitio obstracte[?] concepta, ut praescindit ab effectione seu applicatione medii accommodati, non fit immediate activa ad extra, nec applicativa potentia divina, donec intelligatur determinata ad tale medium; altera est applicativa potentia divina ad vim seu necessitatem aut praedeterminationem inferendam voluntati creatae. Resp. 1. Quamvis praedefiniens illa voluntas non fit immediate applicativa potentiæ vel medii accommodati ad movendam voluntatem, tamen ea posita, non potest non voluntas mota permoveri: hæc vero, Iesuitico sensu, vis est evertens libertatem, alioqui posita prædefinitione, si potest voluntas non permoveri, tum nulla est hic prædefinitio absoluta. 2. Falsum est vim inferri voluntati per decretum transiens: ita enim applicat potentiam divinam ut ipse ferat secum libertatem in illud objectum, in quod ipse se libere inclinat. Quarto (ait) ex vi prædefinitionis prioris non variatur concursus Dei concomitans, quo Deus concurrit cum voluntate, sed solum ita dirigitur & guberuatur voluntas, ut infallibiliter eo utatur, ut illi se accommodet. At vero ex vi alterius voluntatem prædeterminantis, necesse est variari concursum Dei, talemque præstari, ut ille potius voluntate utatur, quam voluntas illo, nec voluntas illi se accommodet, sed potius ille voluntatem secum operari compellat, nec sit indifferens talis concursus, sed determinatus ad unum. Resp. 1. Ex vi prædefinitionis absolutæ concursus Dei est determinatus ad actum assentiendi prædefinitum absolute, ita ut si poneretur actus dissentiendi, & prædefinitus esset actus assentiendi, fallibilis esset Dei scientia, prædefinitio non esset efficax, quod est grave absurdum. 2. Ad laudem gloriæ divinæ toto corde nos profitemur Deum uti voluntate creata in omnibus actibus suis: alioqui non posset ad finem pervenire intentum per talia media, nec Deo constaret dominium in creaturas, aut providentia in omnibus, nisi hoc dicādicamus, & tamen voluntatem non compellit, quia lubens sequitur, & libere etiam Dei voluntatem, & tam libere quam si poneremus non esse in Deo decretum. 3.Si voluntas creata Dei concursu uteretur pro libitu, tum creatura necessitaret Deum ad concurrendum ad actus peccaminosos, ad actus bonos, imo ad omnes actus morales, & sic Deo honos & gloria bonorum actuum non constaret, & libertate concurrendi spoliaretur.
units.tr: 23. See indeed ibid. p. 10 what differences the Jesuit lays down between the immanent predefinition, which predefines free acts ad intra, and the predetermining predefinition, which acts ad extra. 1st difference. The former will has a conjoined will, or rather is at the same time the will of such a means, which does not determine the free will but moves it contingently as far as in itself lies, yet infallibly from foreknowledge. The latter, the predetermining, requires no other means than its own efficacy, by which it sweeps the will along with it, determining it. Response: (1) That the means moves the human will infallibly from foreknowledge is false. For all infallibility is founded on entitative necessity, but here there is no necessity at all between the moral motion of the means and the free act; they can just as well not be together as be together. (2) That a predetermining decree requires no means is plainly false. For by that decree a means is established which moves the will in a connatural mode, not carrying it off by its efficacy, but sweetly determining and bending the will. 2nd difference. The former (he says) predefines the act in relation to the mode of operating of a secondary cause, whence it includes in its object the act as to be done by the determination of free will itself, in a fitting mode. The latter has as its object not only the act but also the mode, or physical predetermination through the efficacious motion of God. Response: It is a contradiction in terms to predefine absolutely a free act to be done by the determination of free will itself, which, all congruous motions being posited, can act or not act, as the Jesuit teaches. For, given the predefining decree, it cannot not act. Third: hence it follows (says the Jesuit) that the former predefinition, conceived abstractly, insofar as it abstracts from the effecting or application of a fitting means, does not become immediately active ad extra, nor an applying divine power, until it is understood as determined to such a means. The other is a divine power applying itself to bring force or necessity or predetermination to the created will. Response: (1) Although that predefining will does not become immediately an applying power or applying of a fitting means to move the will, nevertheless, once that is posited, the moved will cannot but be moved. And this, in the Jesuit's sense, is a force subverting liberty. Otherwise, given the predefinition, if the will could not be moved, then there is no absolute predefinition here. (2) It is false that force is brought to bear on the will by a transient decree. For it applies the divine power in such a way that it itself carries liberty with it into that object towards which it freely inclines itself. Fourth, he says: from the force of the former predefinition, God's concomitant concurrence, by which God concurs with the will, is not varied, but the will is only so directed and governed that it infallibly makes use of it, so that it accommodates itself to it. But from the force of the other, which predetermines the will, it is necessary that God's concurrence be varied and so given that he rather makes use of the will than the will of him, nor does the will accommodate itself to him, but rather he compels the will to work along with him; nor is such concurrence indifferent, but determined to one. Response: (1) From the force of absolute predefinition, God's concurrence is determined to the act of assenting, predefined absolutely. So if the act of dissenting were posited, and the act of assenting were predefined, God's knowledge would be fallible and the predefinition would not be efficacious, which is a grave absurdity. (2) For the praise of divine glory we profess with our whole heart that God uses the created will in all his acts. Otherwise he could not reach the end intended through such means, nor would dominion over creatures, or providence over all things, belong to God, unless we say this. And yet he does not compel the will, because it follows willingly, and freely also God's will, and as freely as if we held that there was no decree in God. (3) If the created will used God's concurrence at its pleasure, then the creature would necessitate God to concur in sinful acts, in good acts, and indeed in all moral acts. Thus honour and glory for good acts would not belong to God, and he would be stripped of the freedom to concur.

units.la: 24. Tandem miserrime Iesuita ib. ad fig. 12. hanc prædefinitionem non-prædefinitionem absolutam facit. Prædefinitio (inquit) hæc non est simpliciter antecedens usum libertatis, quia supponit præscientiam ejus saltem ut futuri sub tali conditione. Ergo absolute Deus prædefinit actus liberos, ex hypothesi quod sint actus liberi: at quis negaret omnes morales bonos actus, malos, naturales, supernaturales a Deo definiri, postquam sint? at sic a nobis, ab angelis definiuntur. 2. Quid non potest esse absolutum ex hypothesi, quod jam sit? putat Iesuita se Deo gratificari in hac prædefinitione, quam ille ib.f. 15. putat necessariam esse, non propter dependentiam effectuum contingentium ex causa prima, sed ex parte Dei ut convenienti modo prævideat & præordinet ea, quæ sub ejus voluntatem & actionem cadunt. Sed dic, Iesuita, quare Deus non omnes actus hac prædefinitione immanente prædefiniat. Causa patet, in quibusdam Deus prætordinat ea, quæ cadunt sub voluntatem & actionem[?] ipsius convenienti modo, in aliis, modo non convenienti, in quibusdam sapienter & ex infinita scientia sua, in aliis nulla providentia. Hoccine est Deo dignum philosophari?
units.tr: 24. Finally, the most wretched Jesuit (ib., ad fig. 12) makes this predefinition a non-predefinition, an absolute one. "This predefinition," he says, "is not simply antecedent to the use of freedom, because it presupposes foreknowledge of that use at least as future under such a condition." Therefore God absolutely predefines free acts, on the hypothesis that they are free acts. But who would deny that all morally good acts, evil acts, natural and supernatural acts are defined by God after they have occurred? And in this way they are defined by us and by angels. 2. What cannot be absolute on the hypothesis that it already is? The Jesuit thinks he pleases God in this predefinition, which he (ib., f. 15) thinks necessary, not because of the dependence of contingent effects on the first cause, but on God's part, so that God may foresee and predetermine in a fitting manner those things which fall under his will and action. But tell me, Jesuit, why God does not predefine all acts by this immanent predefinition. The reason is plain: in some cases God predetermines, in a fitting manner, those things which fall under his will and action; in others, not in a fitting manner. In some he does so wisely and from his infinite knowledge; in others, with no providence at all. Is this philosophizing worthy of God?

units.la: 25.[?] Pergo ad alia quæ habet Iesuita, super hac re, ait actiones necessarias vel de facto ordinaras ad finem aliquem particularem intentum efficaciter à Deo ac præfinitum à Deo prædefinitione absoluta, determinari, cujusmodi sunt consensus Josephi & Mariæ in matrimonium. Dic Iesuita, rationem, quia specialis est hic providentia circa media fini ultimo necessaria: at vero omnia Iehova fecit propter seipsum Prov. 16. & ex hypothesi divini decreti, sunt media gloriæ Dei illustrandæ necessaria, & specialis providentia in minimis refulget. Altera pars distinctionis est hæc.
units.tr: 25. I proceed to the other things the Jesuit says on this matter. He says that actions which are necessary, or which are in fact ordained to some particular end, are efficaciously intended by God and determined by God through absolute predefinition. Examples are the consents of Joseph and Mary to marriage. Tell me, Jesuit, the reason. It is because a special providence is here necessary for the means to the ultimate end. But indeed Jehovah made all things for himself (Prov. 16), and on the hypothesis of the divine decree they are means necessary for displaying the glory of God, and special providence shines forth even in the smallest things. The second part of the distinction is this.

units.la: Quando actus humani (inquit ibid. fig. 12.) etiam moraliter boni, non sunt ordinati à Deo ex efficaci intentione alicujus finis specialis, sed ab humana voluntate cum generali concursu ac providentia oriuntur, non oportet ut à speciali Dei voluntate præscriente procedant, nec est ulla sufficiens ratio ad id credendum: & hujusmodi sunt majore ex parte actus morales omnes, quia ita ab hominibus fiunt, ut nihil iis ad vitam æternam consequendam prosint, nec Deo specialiter deservant ad aliquem finem peculiarem providentiæ ejus. Proba. quia ea proprie dicuntur esse à Deo præfinita, quæ vel ut fines vel ut media sunt ab ipso peculiariter intenta, aut electa, vel volita. Ergo, quæ hoc modo non cadunt sub divinam voluntatem, & alioqui sequuntur ex generali ordine causarum secundarum cum generali concursu non oportet esse praefinita. Resp. efficax & specialis Dei intentio in omnibus quae vult & facit (omnia autem bona vult & facit) est ut ipse glorificetur, ut expresse ait scriptura Prov. 16.4. Rom. 11.36. Apoc. 4.11. Ergo omnia sunt a Deo praefinita. 2 Quaedam esse entia, quae Deo non deserviant, ad aliquem peculiarem finem providentiae, est Deum multa facere ob nullum finem, & sic non erit Deus agens intellectuale, quod est blasphemum, quippe multa faciet extra se vel naturae sive impetu, uti guttulae pluviales decidunt, sive instinctu naturae, ut aves nidos conficiunt: at vero quae sic agunt, ab intelligente superiore ordinantur: at quis superior spiritum Iehovae[?] dirigit? quis ei consilium dedit? 1. Cor. 2. 16. Rom. 11. 34.
units.tr: "When human acts (he says, ibid., fig. 12) are good even morally, but are not ordained by God through an efficacious intention towards some special end, and arise from the human will with general concurrence and providence, it is not necessary that they proceed from a special, foreknowing will of God, nor is there any sufficient reason to believe it. And of this kind are for the most part all moral acts, because they are done by men in such a way that they contribute nothing to the attainment of eternal life, nor do they specially serve God for some particular end of his providence. Proof: because those things are properly said to be predetermined by God which are intended, chosen or willed by him in particular, either as ends or as means. Therefore, those things which do not fall under the divine will in this way, and which otherwise follow from the general order of secondary causes with general concurrence, need not be predetermined." Reply: God's efficacious and special intention in all that he wills and does (and he wills and does all good things) is that he himself may be glorified, as Scripture expressly says (Prov. 16:4; Rom. 11:36; Rev. 4:11). Therefore all things are predetermined by God. 2. That there are certain beings which do not serve God for some particular end of providence means that God does many things for no end, and so he will not be an intellectual agent, which is blasphemous. For he will do many things outside himself by the force of nature, as drops of rain fall, or by the instinct of nature, as birds build their nests. But those things which act in this way are ordered by a superior intelligence. And what superior directs the Spirit of Jehovah? Who gave him counsel? (1 Cor. 2:16; Rom. 11:34).

units.la: At vult Iesuita Deum intendere illos actus bonos ob finem communem, nempe bonum in communi, vel hoc, vel illud: at vero confusa talis in Deo intentio, alibi a Iesuita rejicitur, utpote quae imperfectionem sapiat: 3. Ipsa scriptura diserte ait minima quaeque, ut passerum volatus, capillorum casus, a Deo intendi & curari, Deumque illa specialiter velle Mat. 10. 29. Deum responsa linguae dirigere Prov. 16. 1. egressum fortium e gremio Prov. 16. 33. occisionem viri, ut videtur, casu occisi Exod. 21.13. proiectum sagittae in Achabum 1. Reg. 22. 34. Deum facere divitem & pauperem Prov. 22. 2, extollere & deprimere quem vult. Psal. 75. 78. Quis diceret Deum ita ista velle, nempe ex hypothesi quod sint, & posita Dei voluntate, aut actione posse haec fieri vel non fieri? hoccine est Deum horum, facere cum scripturis, autorem? Aut quis diceret Deum haec velle ob finem conditionate aut inefficaciter intentum, quia nempe Deo etiam volente, haec possunt non fieri, ac proinde excidere fine ad quem haec tendunt, ut medio, & alium tunc finem Deum assequi, excussum a fortuna, hoc fine? At vero dici non potest haec praecise inservire ad vitam aeternam consequendam, potest enim Ionah vel Matthias vitam consequi aeternam, sive sors ipsis obtigerit, sive non. 4. Si non fiant haec praefinitione illa saltem immanente, tum oparabitur Deus ad productionem horum effectuum, nec operatione congrua, qua scit illa non fore, ac proinde, nulla scientia ideoque nec providentia: nam vel intendit, ut haec sors obtingat alicui, vel non: ideoque fortes exeunt praeter Dei intentionem, quod Iesuita dixit esse praeter rationem: si intendit, vel absolute intendit, vel conditionate: si absolute, habemus quod volumus: si conditionate; tum ex praescientia: atqui haec praescientia vel adhibet media congrua, vel non; quicquid dixerit, sequitur eodem modo praefiniri, quo ea, quae praedestinationi inserviant, ut media necessaria; ideoque vana est Iesuitae distinctio. Ad haec omnia (ait Iesuita) Deum per se intendere, essentialem mundi perfectionem, & conservationem, donec numerus electorum compleatur qui est maxime perse intentus. Quia vero est per accidens sæpe ad hunc finem & essentialem mundi perfectionem, ut sint tot vel plura, ideo oportet esse à Deo præfinita, neque ut finem, neque ut media, sed tantum præcognita, ut consequenda & futura ex instituto causarum ordine, & permissa vel admissa ac effecta per Dei voluntatem volentem suum in suo influxum impendere. Resp.
units.tr: But the Jesuit wills that God intends those good acts for a common end, namely the good in general, this or that. But such a confused intention in God is rejected elsewhere by the Jesuit himself, as savouring of imperfection. 3. Scripture itself plainly says that even the smallest things, such as the flight of sparrows and the falling of hairs, are intended and cared for by God, and that God wills them specially (Matt. 10:29). It says that God directs the answers of the tongue (Prov. 16:1); that the lot is cast into the lap, but its whole disposition is from the Lord (Prov. 16:33); that a man is slain, as it seems, by chance (Exod. 21:13); that an arrow shot at random struck Ahab (1 Kings 22:34); that God makes rich and poor (Prov. 22:2), and that he exalts and humbles whom he wills (Ps. 75:7; 78). Who would say that God wills these things in such a way, namely on the hypothesis that they are, and that, given God's will or action, they could either happen or not happen? Is this to make God the author of these things, as Scripture does? Or who would say that God wills these things for an end intended conditionally or inefficaciously, because even though God wills them, they may not happen, and so the end to which they are directed would fall away as a means, and God would then attain some other end, one shaken loose from fortune? But indeed it cannot be said that these things serve precisely to attain eternal life, for Jonah or Matthias could attain eternal life whether the lot fell to them or not. 4. If these things do not happen by that predefinition, at least the immanent one, then God will work towards the production of these effects without a congruous operation by which he knows they will not come about; and so there will be no knowledge and therefore no providence. For either he intends that this lot should fall to someone or he does not. So the lots would come forth beyond God's intention, which the Jesuit said is beyond reason. If he intends it, he intends it either absolutely or conditionally. If absolutely, we have what we want. If conditionally, then it is from foreknowledge. But this foreknowledge either applies congruous means or it does not. Whatever he says, it follows that these things are predefined in the same way as those which serve predestination, as necessary means. So the Jesuit's distinction is empty. "To all these things" (says the Jesuit) "God intends by himself the essential perfection and preservation of the world, until the number of the elect is complete, which is the thing most of all intended in itself. But since it often happens per accidens that there are so many or more for this end, and for the essential perfection of the world, these things need not be predetermined by God, neither as ends nor as means, but only foreknown, as things to be attained and future from the established order of causes, and permitted or admitted and brought about through God's will, which bestows its influence on his own creatures." Reply.

units.la: 1. Ante Bellarminum idem docuit atheos Averroes, qui particularem Dei providentiam negavit. 2. Quicquid Deus facit, illud vult, alioqui facit multa invitus: atqui Deum actus bonos particulares facere, non negat Iesuita. Ergo hæc vult. Sed quicquid Deus vult, vel sunt fines, vel media, quia quicquid vult, vel vult propter aliud, ut omnia entia creata, vel propter se, uti vult suam gloriam. Omne volitum est vel medium, vel finis; est axioma, quod ad hunc usque diem apud omnes Philosophos, obtinuit. 3. Quis hanc theologiam ferret, egressus fortium est à Deo, volatus passerum, responsu linguæ, sed hæc non sunt volita a Deo, vel ut media, vel finis, tum certe ob nullum finem fient à Deo & Deus in hisce non erit agens intellectuale. 4. Scriptura dicit Deum decrevisse Achitophelis consilium evertere, à Deo esse quod decem tribus deficerent à Domo Davidis, & tamen ita habuerint se accidentaliter ad prædestinationem Davidis, & Ianctorum[?] in Israele. Blasphemia itaque est hæc distinctio.
units.tr: 1. Before Bellarmine, Averroes, who denied God's particular providence, taught the same thing, and he was an atheist. 2. Whatever God does, he wills; otherwise he would do many things unwillingly. But the Jesuit does not deny that God does particular good acts. Therefore he wills these things. But whatever God wills is either an end or a means, because whatever he wills, he wills either for the sake of something else, as all created beings are willed, or for its own sake, as he wills his own glory. Every thing willed is either a means or an end. This is an axiom which has held among all philosophers until this day. 3. Who would endure this theology? The going forth of the brave is from God, the flight of sparrows, the answer of the tongue. But these are not willed by God either as means or as ends. Then certainly they happen for no end, and God in these matters will not be an intellectual agent. 4. Scripture says that God decreed to overturn the counsel of Ahithophel, and that it was from God that the ten tribes should fall away from the house of David (2 Sam. 17:14; 1 Kings 11:31). Yet they stood in an accidental relation to the predestination of David and of the saints in Israel. Therefore this distinction is blasphemy.

units.la: 26. Quoniam Deus permissione sola actus bonos facit, neque magis erint à Dei voluntate & providentia, quam actus mali. Resp. Suarez. ib. Non sequi, quia Deus actus bonos intendit, & vult, malos non vult aut intendit, excitat & moraliter inclinat ad bonos, non sic ad malos. Resp. At si Deus actus omnes bonos vult & intendit, vel vult illa ut media, vel ut fines, quod supra negavit. 2. Sic providentia Dei occasiones & argumenta ad malum objiciuntur, licet non secundum voluntatem revelatam. 3. Non video, qui Deus non intendat hosce actus, an absolute, & sic revera praedefinita sunt, an conditionate, ex hypothesi quod sint: at absurda est intentio, illud intendere ut sit, quod jam est. 4. Si loquamur de concursu Physice requisito ad entitatem actus, non majore influentia reali fiunt actus boni quam mali, quod absurdum rotunde concedit Jesuita, ideoque nulla est physica gratiae influentia in actus bonos, potius quam in malos? Sola differentia stat in suasione pelagiana per excitationem ethicam. 6. Quo fine intendit Deus actus hosce bonos, an propter suam gloriam, propter quam facit omnia, uti dicit scriptura, vel non? Si prius, non possunt non omnia media gloriae illustrandae praedefiniri, quippe Deo inserviunt ad peculiarem finem providentiae, uti supra fassus est; at dicit hos actus non specialiter inservire gloriae Dei declarandae, sed per accidens se habere ad hunc finem, ideoque non praefiniri: at si haec ratio (inquam ego) valeret, nulla à Deo praedefinirentur: posset enim gloriam suam aliis mediis declarere, quam per haec media praedefinita, alioqui non est infinite sapiens.
units.tr: 26. Since God makes good acts by permission alone, they will be no more from the will and providence of God than evil acts. Answer (Suarez, ib.): It does not follow, because God intends and wills good acts, but does not will or intend evil ones; he excites and morally inclines people to good, not to evil. Reply: But if God wills and intends all good acts, he wills them either as means or as ends, which he denied above. 2. So the providence of God is set before occasions and arguments to evil, although not according to his revealed will. 3. I do not see how God does not intend these acts. Either he intends them absolutely, and so they are really predefined, or he intends them conditionally, on the hypothesis that they will be; but it is absurd to intend that something should be, when it already is. 4. If we speak of the concurrence physically required for the being of an act, good acts are not made by any greater real influence than evil ones. The Jesuit flatly concedes this, which is absurd. Is there then no physical influence of grace on good acts rather than on evil ones? The sole difference lies in Pelagian persuasion through ethical excitation. 6. For what end does God intend these good acts? Is it for his own glory, for which he makes all things, as Scripture says, or not? If the former, then all means of illustrating his glory must necessarily be predefined, since they serve God for his particular end of providence, as he has admitted above. But he says these acts do not serve specially to declare the glory of God, but relate to this end only by accident, and so are not predefined. Yet if this reasoning (I say) held, God would predefine nothing at all. For he could declare his glory by other means than these predefined ones; otherwise he is not infinitely wise.

units.la: 27. Aliqui videntes indignum esse Deo adimere absolutam praedefinitionem, ideoque dixerunt Deum finem indeclinabiliter intentum adsequi, seu potius ad eum pervenire, per contingentia media, ita, ut si hoc deficiat, illud arrepturus sit, ut intendit (inquit Lacksonus) apprehendere latronem per centum media, deficientibus mediis nonaginta, ultimum quasi forte indeclinabiliter finem producet. Sed turpiter hic hallucinantur. Nam deficientibus 99. potest ultimum medium, quando contingenter operatur, non minus deficere, quam 99. defecerunt, imo poterat hoc ultimum fuisse ordine primum, et sic defecisse: quod vero nugator dicit hoc ultimum, quasi forte operari necessario, ad finis productionem, si per fortem, fortunam intelligit, plane evertetur providentia Dei: an potius velit hoc ultimum per adhibitam infinitam potentiam, aut sapientiam Dei agere, ne forte Deus fine intento excideret, tum ex horum doctorum placitis Deus praecise per hoc medium irrefistibiliter et necessario agens, ad finem pervenit: at cur non hoc in aliis mediis deficientibus fecit, et tum etiam hoc ultimum medium contra ipsorum hypothesin, non erit contingens. 2. Deinde quis credat (inquit Suarez) Deum dum hoc vel illo modo vocat hominem nescire an consensurus sit nec ne? ideoque quasi tentando incedere, ut si nunc non consenserit[?] homo, eum iterum vocet vel alio modo &c. 3. Sic providentia erit incerta & non infallibilis ex sola mediorum multitudine: nam unum hoc deficit, deficere possunt duo, & omnia. 4. Confusa & suspensa erit Dei voluntas tali praedefinitione.
units.tr: 27. Some, seeing that it is unworthy of God to take away absolute predefinition, have therefore said that God attains the end he has indeclinably intended, or rather reaches it, through contingent means, so that if one means fails, he will take up another, as he intends. (Lackson says:) to catch a thief by a hundred means, and if ninety of the means fail, the last one will, as if by chance, indeclinably produce the end. But these men wander shamefully here. For when ninety-nine means have failed, the last means, when it operates contingently, can fail no less than the ninety-nine did; indeed this last means could have been first in order and so have failed. But when the trifler says that this last means acts necessarily, as if by chance, to produce the end, if by "chance" he means fortune, then the providence of God is plainly overthrown. Or does he wish this last means to act through the infinite power or wisdom of God, lest God perhaps fall short of the end he intended? Then, by the views of these teachers, God acts irresistibly and necessarily through this one means alone and so reaches the end. But why did he not do this with the other means that failed? And then this last means too, contrary to their own hypothesis, will not be contingent. 2. Next, who would believe (says Suarez) that God, while calling a man in this or that way, does not know whether he will consent or not, and so proceeds as if by trial, so that if the man does not now consent, he calls him again, or in another way, etc.? 3. So providence will be uncertain and not infallible, depending on the mere multitude of means: for this one may fail, two may fail, and all may fail. 4. By such predefinition the will of God will be confused and suspended.

units.la: Habes hic lector nostram sententiam de decreto disjunctivo. 2. Conditionato. 3. De praefinitivo decreto immanente, quae omnia nobis sunt Chymerae Iesuiticae.
units.tr: Here, reader, you have our opinion on (1) the disjunctive decree, (2) the conditional decree, and (3) the predefinitive immanent decree. All of these are, to us, Jesuitical chimaeras.

units.la: CAP. V. Suarezii, Fonseca, & Arminianorum de nova Dei scientia, quam conditionatam, seu mediam vocant, rationes examini sub- jiciuntur.
units.tr: Chapter 5: The new knowledge of God, which they call conditional or middle knowledge, as held by Suárez, Fonseca and the Arminians, is subjected to examination.

units.la: AD alia festinanti, obviam se mihi dat scientia media, contradistincta à scientia simplicis intelligentiae, & scientia visionis, quae est partim naturalis, ut dicunt, quia volunt talem scientiam non posse, non esse in Deo; partim libera, nempe ab objecto, quia liberum est Deo scibilia creare, vel non creare: estque haec scientia qua Deus ex altitudine scientiae suae, ut ait Fonseca, effectus omnes contingentes antecedenter ad actum decreti sui praescit, ut habet Lod. Molina, si causae in hisce, vel illis circumstantiis collocentur. Sed contra 1. sic arguo. vana est illa scientia, cujus objectum est non-scibile, non-verum, & non-ens: atqui objectum hujus scientiae, quum sit ens habens esse & veritatem antecedenter ad suam causam, nempe Dei decretum, est non-scibile, & non-verum. Erg. Prob. minor.
units.tr: Hastening on to other matters, I meet middle knowledge, which is set apart from the knowledge of simple intelligence and from the knowledge of vision. It is partly natural, as they say, because they hold that such knowledge cannot exist in God; and partly free, namely in respect of its object, because it is free for God to create or not to create the things that can be known. This is the knowledge by which God, from the height of his knowledge, as Fonseca puts it, foreknows all contingent effects before the act of his decree, as Lod. Molina holds, if the causes are placed in these or those circumstances. But against this I argue first as follows. That knowledge is empty whose object is unknowable, untrue and non-existent. But the object of this knowledge, since it is a being that has existence and truth prior to its cause, namely God's decree, is unknowable and untrue. Therefore it is empty. I prove the minor.

units.la: Futuris contingentibus ex hypothesi, non convenit aliqua veritas realis ab aeterno in se: hoc enim est solius Dei proprium. Nec iis potest convenire aliqua realitas ratione efficientis, nempe Dei decretum. Refp. Suarez, Objectum hujus scientiae non esse omnino independens a decreto Dei, quoniam includitur concomitanter Dei decretum in objecto ad modum possibilis, quamvis decretum nullum sit antecedens, & modo cognoscendi & loquendi nostro prior sit praescientia quam decretum.
units.tr: Of contingent future things, on a hypothesis, no real truth belongs to them from eternity in themselves; for this belongs to God alone. Nor can any reality belong to them by reason of an efficient cause, namely God's decree. Suárez replies: the object of this knowledge is not wholly independent of God's decree, since God's decree is included concomitantly in the object, in the manner of a possible, although no decree is antecedent, and in our mode of knowing and speaking foreknowledge is prior to the decree.

units.la: Refp. 1. Si Dei decretum sit causa objecti scientiae mediae, non comitatur sed antecedit objectum. 2. Qui docent necessitatem ex decreto esse consequentem, non minus, quam est necessitas ex Dei scientia, ne illi nimis lincei sunt, qui velint concomitanter includi decretum in objecto. 3. Observa quomodo loquatur sophista, quam timide quam fraudulenter: (objectum non est omnino independens a decreto) at si est aliquo modo dependens, an sit causativa dependentia, exprimere debebat, sed in dumetis & vepribus anguis latitare cupit. 4. Includitur decretum in objecto ad modum possibilis: at si objectum sit determinate suturum, uti fatetur, an decretum tantum est possibile? Ergo decretum potest non esse; atqui futurum contingens determinate est futurum: vin' igitur sophista nobis demonstrare quomodo objectum hujus scientiae non fit omninò independens à decreto, quando fit absque omni decreto. 5. Si nullum decretum fit antecedens, num prius dependet à posteriore? & id quod habet esse antecedenter ad decretum, ullo modo est dependens à decreto in esse, ac proinde in veritate essendi? Dic libere, nec frontem perfrices, oro. 6. Modo loquendi & cognoscendi nostro (ais) prior est praescientia quam decretum, sed dic ex tuis somniis, an tantum modo cognoscendi nostro, an non est etiam prior natura? Et prior modo cognoscendi in Deo? Imo est, si vobis credimus.
units.tr: Reply 1. If God's decree is the cause of the object of middle knowledge, it does not accompany the object but precedes it. 2. "Those who teach that the necessity arising from the decree is consequent, no less than the necessity arising from God's knowledge, are too lynx-eyed, who want the decree to be included concomitantly in the object." 3. Note how the sophist speaks, how timidly and how deceitfully: "the object is not wholly independent of the decree." But if it is dependent in some way, he ought to have said whether the dependence is causative; yet he wants to lie hidden like a snake in the brambles and thorns. 4. "The decree is included in the object in the manner of a possibility." But if the object is to be determinately future, as he admits, is the decree only possible? Therefore the decree can fail to be; yet a contingent future is determinately future. Will the sophist therefore show us how the object of this knowledge is not wholly independent of the decree, when it exists without any decree at all? 5. If no decree is antecedent, does the prior depend on the posterior? And does that which has being antecedently to the decree depend in any way on the decree for its being, and so for its truth of being? Answer freely, I beg you, and do not rub your forehead. 6. "By our mode of knowing," he says, "foreknowledge is prior to the decree." But tell us, from your dreams, whether it is prior only in our mode of knowing, or whether it is not also prior in nature? And is it prior in God's mode of knowing? Indeed it is, if we believe you. 7. For the object of this knowledge to be a being and knowable, it must have a cause; but if the decree is posterior to it, it cannot be its cause. Give a cause, then. Where has the accompanying decree now vanished?

units.la: 7. Ut objectum hujus scientiae fit ens & scibile, necesse est habeat causam: at si decretum est posterius eo, non potest esse ipsius causa. Da causam igitur. En quo evanuit jam decretum concomitans?
units.tr: 7. For the object of this knowledge to be a being and knowable, it must have a cause. But if the decree is posterior to it, it cannot be its cause. Name the cause, then. Where has the accompanying decree now vanished to?

units.la: 2. Rat. 2. Illa scientia explodenda est, cujus objectum est tale, ut eo posito effectus reducatur in arbitrium creatum, ut in primum determinans: nam solus Deus est primum determinans: atque si decretum fit posterius objecto scientiae mediae, objectum hoc ultimatè resolvetur in arbitrium creatum: non enim potest resolvi in Dei decretum ut in primum determinans, quia decretum est eo posterius.
units.tr: 2. Argument 2. That knowledge must be rejected whose object is such that, once it is posited, the effect is traced back to the created will as the first determining cause. For God alone is the first determining cause. And if the decree comes after the object of middle knowledge, this object will ultimately be resolved into the created will, since it cannot be resolved into God's decree as the first determining cause, because the decree is posterior to it.

units.la: Respondet Suarez. ib. f. 7. Non esse hoc contra Dei omnipotentiam, vel absolutum dominium, quia nullus effectus non est futurus sine influxu omnipotentiae Dei, qua vult & voluntatem creatam sinere liberè operari, & cum illa concurrere, possetque, si vellet vellet, illum actum impedire aliter se habendo cum voluntate, si autem vult illam indifferentem sinere, necesse est quod voluerit, ipsa operetur. Refp. si non sit contra Dei dominium, sed penes arbitrium creatum ut primum determinans in cujus potestate est ut sint vel non sint effectus contingentes, male Iacobus arguit, si dominus voluerit, & si permiserit hoc, vel illud; faciemus: si enim voluntas humana sit primum determinans, est ab homine non a Deo, quod ex multis itineribus possibilibus, hoc potius quam illud iter faciamus. 2. Quod dicit Deum posse impedire actus liberos, dilute nimis & ἀλόγως[?] dictum est. Nam si ego hoc non illud velim antecedenter; ad Dei decretum, & etiam ad scientiam mediam, uti fatetur Jesuita; non potest Deus liberos actus impedire: nam quod jam est, & quod Deus infallibiliter praescit futurum esse, infallibiliter futurum est; sed dicat Jesuita, an omnipotentiae divinae locus sit ut impediat, quo minus, propositio identica sit vera. 3. Non est effectus contingens (inquit) futurus sine voluntate Dei; sed qualem vis sophistam voluntatem? consequentem & non antecedentem neque potentiam actu applicantem, nisi humanum arbitrium coagere vult? & sic eripitur Deo dominium, & transfertur in voluntatem creatam.
units.tr: Suárez replies, in the same work, folio 7: this is not contrary to God's omnipotence or absolute dominion, since no effect will be future without the influence of God's omnipotence, by which he wills to let the created will act freely and concur with it, and he could, if he wished, prevent that act by acting otherwise with the will; but if he wills to let it be indifferent, it is necessary that it operate as it has willed. Reply: if it is not against God's dominion but lies with the creature's will as the first determining cause, in whose power it is that contingent effects should be or not be, then James argues badly: "If the Lord wills, and if he permits this or that, we shall do it." For if the human will is the first determining cause, it is from man and not from God that we take this route rather than that one out of many possible routes. (2) What he says, that God can prevent free acts, is said too loosely and irrationally [ἀλόγως]. For if I antecedently will this and not that, then, according to the decree and also to middle knowledge, as the Jesuit admits, God cannot prevent free acts; for what already is, and what God infallibly foreknows will be, will infallibly be. But let the Jesuit say whether there is room for divine omnipotence to prevent it, so that the identical proposition is not true. (3) The effect, he says, is not future without the will of God; but what sort of will does this sophist mean? A consequent will and not an antecedent one, nor one that applies its power in act, unless he wants to compel the human choice? And so dominion is snatched from God and transferred to the created will.

units.la: 4.Voluntatem vult Jesuita concurrendi Physice generalem, qualiter cum porcis manducantibus & passeribus volitantibus concurrit. Digna certe hostibus gratiae dominatio & gratia præpræpotens. 5. Tandem Jesuita victus dat manus: si vult sinere voluntatem indifferentem, necesse est operetur, quod voluerit. Ergo necesse est Deus suam voluntatem & concursum contemperet nutui libertatis creatæ; & Deus facto victus non potest reconcurrere, & velle quod voluntas creata primum determinans voluerit. Quale jam est objectum hujus scientiæ? 6. Potest Deus voluntatem (inquit) impedire, at quomodo? vel non creando voluntatem, vel annihilando, vel necessitando. At sic recedit a quæstione, quæ non est de Dei dominio in voluntatem, sed de Dei dominio in voluntatem quatenus est agens liberum: dicimus enim per hanc scientiam poni actus contingentes præter & contra dominium creatoris, qui nodus ut a Jesuitis diffringatur, vereor.
units.tr: (4) The Jesuit wishes for a concurrence with the will that is physically general, such as he has with pigs eating and sparrows flying. Surely a dominion worthy of the enemies of grace, and a grace most powerfully preeminent! (5) At last the Jesuit, beaten, gives up: if God wills to let the will be indifferent, it is necessary that it operate as it has willed. Therefore God must adjust his will and concurrence to the nod of created liberty; and God, having done this, when beaten cannot concur again and will what the created will, the first determining cause, has willed. What sort of object is this of the knowledge in question now? (6) God can prevent the will, he says; but how? Either by not creating the will, or by annihilating it, or by necessitating it. But in this way he withdraws from the question, which is not about God's dominion over the will, but about God's dominion over the will as a free agent. For we say that by this knowledge contingent acts are posited beside and against the dominion of the Creator. I fear this knot will not be untied by the Jesuits.

units.la: 3. Rat. 5. Objectum omnis scientiæ infallibilis est necessarium: atqui contingentia sutura antecedenter ad Dei decretum, non sunt necessaria. Ergo non datur objectum hujus scientiæ. Major est certa, quia omnis infallibilitas scientiæ fundatur in necessitate objectiva.
units.tr: Third argument: The object of all infallible knowledge is necessary; but contingent things that would be future antecedently to God's decree are not necessary. Therefore there is no object of this knowledge. The major is certain, because all infallibility of knowledge is grounded in objective necessity.

units.la: Neque dari posse certitudinem mentis seu subjectivam citra omnem certitudinem entis, seu objectivam, omnes uno ore clamitant metaphysici. Proba. minor. Antecedenter ad Dei decretum & ex se, Tyrij vilis signis, tam possunt non credere & respipiscere, quam credere & respipiscere, ex se Keilitæ[?] tam Davidem permanentem poterant non tradere in manus Sauli quam tradere. Nam hæc est illis libertatis natura, ut positis omnibus ad agendum requisitis, possint agere vel non agere.
units.tr: That a certainty of the mind, or subjective certainty, can exist without all certainty of being, or objective certainty, all the metaphysicians cry with one voice. I prove the minor. Antecedently to God's decree and of themselves, the Tyrians, by base signs, could as well not believe and repent as believe and repent; of themselves the men of Keilah could as well not hand David over into the hands of Saul, who was remaining with them, as hand him over. For this is the nature of their liberty: that, all the things required for acting being posited, they can act or not act.

units.la: 4. Advetfarii nullum non saxum volvunt, ut hoc argumentum amoliantur, sed frustra. Nam 1. Suarez. ait duplicem esse in futuris contingentibus determinationem, aliam in sua causa, seu in actu primo, aliam in se seu in actu secundo: hanc posteriorem vult Deum videre, ita ac si jam existeret, & objici divinæ scientiæ, ex cujus efficacia intuetur non solum quid voluntas humana operari possit, sed etiam quid operetur. Resp. Petit principium: nam determinationem causæ contingentis objici infinitæ Dei scientiæ nos credimus: at vero quæstio remanet in qua ratione objectivaDeus videat hanc determinationem. Nam vel videt ipsam in se præsentem: at vero objectiva non realis est hæc præsentia (res enim ab æterno non realiter coexistebant cum Deo) at non est præsentia hæc realis in se, neque est realis in sua causa nempe in Dei decreto: nam volunt illi objectum hoc antecedenter decretum, & tamen aliam causam quam decretum Dei dare non possunt, 2. Resp. Leffius, Deum ista præscire in determinata ipsorum existentia quam habitura sunt, si hoc vel illud ponatur: sed adhuc quæstio est, qui Deus talem existentiam cognoscat: non in inclinatione causæ contingentis. Nam Aquinas, Valentia, Suarez, Durandus, Vasquez dicunt hanc cognitionem esse conjecturalem, nec posse Deo attibui. 3. Respond. Valentia Deum ista videre non in sese, sed in causa contingente qua contingens est determinata a sese ad agendum. Resp. Infinities redibit argumentum quae sit ratio objectiva in qua Deus praescit istam liberam determinationem, vel in alia causa libera, & sic revivicit argumentum, vel in alia causa necessaria, & haec non est alia quam Dei decretum.
units.tr: (4) The adversaries turn over every stone to remove this argument, but in vain. For (1) Suárez says that there is a twofold determination in future contingents: one in their cause, or in the first act, the other in themselves, or in the second act. He wants God to see this latter as if it already existed, and to be presented to divine knowledge, from whose efficacy he sees not only what the human will can do but also what it will do. Reply: this begs the question. For we believe that the determination of a contingent cause is presented to God's infinite knowledge; but the question remains by what reason God sees this determination objectively. For either he sees it as present in itself; but this presence is objective and not real (for things did not really coexist with God from eternity); and this presence is not real in itself, nor is it real in its cause, namely in God's decree; for they want this object to be antecedent to the decree, and yet they cannot give any cause other than God's decree. (2) Reply of Lessius: God foreknows these things in the determinate existence they will have if this or that is posited; but the question still remains which God knows this existence, not in the inclination of a contingent cause. For Aquinas, Valentia, Suárez, Durandus and Vásquez say that this knowledge is conjectural and cannot be attributed to God. (3) Reply of Valentia: God sees these things not in himself but in the contingent cause, which is determined by itself to act. Reply: the argument will return endlessly, asking what the objective reason is by which God foreknows this free determination, whether in another free cause, and so the argument revives, or in another necessary cause, and this is nothing other than God's decree.

units.la: 4. Iacksonus ait Deum ista omnia videre in essentia sua, alii in ideis, alii in altitudine infinitae scientiae. Sed Resp. 1. Res in Dei essentia sunt possibiles, non vero futurae, nisi per liberum Dei decretum: si sunt necessariae in Dei essentia, tum antecedens necessitas & contingentia optime consociantur. At vero, ut recte annotavit Scotus, tum Dei essentia, tum ideae praecedunt omnem actum voluntatis divinae, & naturaliter res repraesentant sub esse possibili. Ergo non repraesentant eas in essentia, ut futuras determinate, imo nos possibilia contingentia sub esse possibili cognoscimus. 2. Infinitas essentiae Dei & scientiae est ei ratio ex parte cognoscentis, quare omnia cognoscat; non vero est ratio objectiva ex parte objecti cogniti: ideoque hic recedunt a statu quaestionis, quae est an ulla sit ratio objectiva infallibilis futuritionis contingentium antecedenter ad Dei decretum. Id nos pernegamus.
units.tr: 4. Jackson says that God sees all these things in his essence; others say in ideas; others in the height of his infinite knowledge. But I reply: (1) Things in the essence of God are possible, but they are not future, except through God's free decree. If they are necessary in the essence of God, then antecedent necessity and contingency agree perfectly. But as Scotus rightly observed, both the essence of God and the ideas precede every act of the divine will, and they naturally represent things under possible being. Therefore they do not represent them in the essence as determinately future. Indeed, we know possible contingent things under possible being. (2) The infinity of God's essence and knowledge is a reason on the side of the knower why he knows all things; it is not an objective reason on the side of the known object. So these men depart from the state of the question, which is whether there is any objective and infallible reason for the futurition of contingent things antecedent to God's decree. We flatly deny this.

units.la: 5. Argum. 4. Deus invicta ratiocinatur 1. Sam. 23. Si David permanserit, tum Keilitae ipsum tradent Saulo, & si Tyrij vidissent signa, tum resipuissent; hæ conditiones sunt syllogisticæ, & Deo notæ; consequentia autem bona, semper est bona, & semper necessaria erit hæc. Tyrii vident signa: Ergo resipiscunt. At si sit veritas in hisce antecedenter ad Dei decretum, illo decreto nondum posito, ut docent adversarii, mala & impossibilis, & falsa est hæc consequentia, Tyrij vident signa, ergo resipiscunt. Imo æque firma est hæc consequentia, Tyrij vident signa, ergo non resipiscunt: nulla enim necessaria, sed plane contingens & indifferens connexio inter visionem signorum & Tyriorum resipiscentiam. Resp. Fonseca, Suarez. & declamator Grevinchovius, qui Jesuitis nihil non debet, Deum non cognosce-re consequens ex illo antecedente, sed Deum ista sci-re per modum simplicis coexistentiæ atque affirmatio-nis unius de alio, sub tali conditione, hoc est, non in connexione illativa, sed obje-ctorum utriusque partis enunciationis, vel in idem tempus, vel in promissionis divinæ aut prædictionis certitudinem. Resp. 1. Misera est hæc logica. Nam argumentatio hæc est Dei, qui logicam excogitavit. Keylitæ, te tradent in manus Sauli: Ergo fuge: imo (inquiunt) falsa, bone Deus, consequentia: ergo non est quod fugias. Nam esto quod permaneat David, Keilitæ hic sunt agentes liberi, ac proinde tam possunt non tradere, quam tradere. 2. Obtrudunt nobis propositiones connexas, quæ in argumentativas resolvi nequeunt, quod est concedere totum & negare partes, & negare totum partibus suis constare, in quo nullos non logicae peritos, Aristotelem, Ramum, & quos non? judices appellamus; aut dies est, aut nox. Semper ante hoc tempus continebat connexionem syllogisticam, Non est dies: Ergo est nox. Sic hic dant novas propositiones connexas, cum nova scientia.
units.tr: 5. Argument 4. God reasons invincibly from 1 Sam. 23: "If David remains, then the Keilites will deliver him to Saul; and if the Tyrians had seen the signs, they would have repented." These conditions are syllogistic and known to God, and a good consequence is always good, and this will always be necessary. The Tyrians see the signs; therefore they repent. But if this is true antecedent to God's decree, the decree not yet having been made, as our opponents teach, then this consequence is bad and impossible and false: "The Tyrians see the signs; therefore they repent." Indeed the opposite consequence is equally firm: "The Tyrians see the signs; therefore they do not repent," for there is no necessary but only a plainly contingent and indifferent connection between the seeing of the signs and the repentance of the Tyrians. I reply: Fonseca, Suarez, and the declaimer Grevinchovius, who owes the Jesuits everything, say that God does not know the consequent from that antecedent, but that God knows these things by way of a simple coexistence and the affirmation of one thing of another under such a condition: that is, not in an inferential connection, but in the objects of each part of the proposition, either at the same time or in the certainty of the divine promise or prediction. I reply: (1) This logic is wretched. For this argument is that of God, who devised logic: "Keilites, they will deliver you into the hands of Saul; therefore flee." Nay, they say, good God, the consequence is false; therefore there is no reason for you to flee. For suppose David remains: the Keilites here are free agents, and therefore they can deliver him or not deliver him. (2) They thrust upon us connected propositions which cannot be resolved into arguments. This is to concede the whole and deny the parts, and to deny that the whole consists of its parts. In this matter we appeal to all who are skilled in logic, to Aristotle, to Ramus, and to whom not? "It is day or it is night." Until this time there was a syllogistic connection in "It is not day; therefore it is night." So here they give new connected propositions along with a new knowledge.

units.la: 3. Conficta plane & falsa est haec simplex coexistentia: nam visio signorum & resipiscentia Tyriorum tam contingenter inter se cohaerent, quam Socratis ambulatio hora decima & solis resplendentia & fulguratio: imo antecedenter ad decretum Dei, vel necessario vel contingenter cohaerent. Nam necessarium & contingens dividunt totam entis amplitudinem, & contradictorie opponuntur, ait Arminius: at novi hi logici negant omne ens esse necessarium vel contingens, dant medium inter contradictorie opposita, quae principia, omnibus vel metaphysicae candidatis fatentibus, inconcussa steterunt. Si cohaerent contingenter, non sunt scibilia: si necessario, flagitamus causam necessitatis aliam praeterquam decretum Dei.
units.tr: 3. This simple coexistence is plainly invented and false. For the seeing of the signs and the repentance of the Tyrians cohere as contingently as Socrates' walking at the tenth hour and the shining and flashing of the sun. Indeed, antecedent to God's decree, they cohere either necessarily or contingently. For the necessary and the contingent divide the whole extent of being and are contradictorily opposed, as Arminius says. But these new logicians deny that every being is either necessary or contingent; they admit a middle between contradictories. These principles have stood unshaken, with all candidates in metaphysics agreeing. If they cohere contingently, they are not knowable; if necessarily, we demand a cause of the necessity other than God's decree.

units.la: 4. Deus ista videt in simplici coexistentia: at hoc est petere principium: coexistentia illa est contingens, ergo ne quidem infinitae scientiae visibilis, nisi aliquo modo necessitetur.
units.tr: 4. God sees these things in simple coexistence. But this is to beg the question: that coexistence is contingent, so it cannot even be seen by infinite knowledge unless it is necessitated in some way.

units.la: 5. Omnes Dei promissiones sunt nobis in scriptura argumentativae: alioqui Deus sophisticaretur in scripturali hac consequentia Ego promisi, Ergo hic contingens effectus indeclinabiliter fiet. Ier. 32. 40. Ezech. 36. 27, Deut. 30. 6. Genef. 17. 8. Zach. 12. 10. Ioel. 2. 28. Mal. 1. 11.
units.tr: 5. All God's promises are argumentative in Scripture; otherwise God would be sophistical in this scriptural consequence: "I have promised; therefore this contingent effect will certainly come to pass." Jer. 32. 40. Ezek. 36. 27. Deut. 30. 6. Gen. 17. 8. Zech. 12. 10. Joel 2. 28. Mal. 1. 11.

units.la: 5. Si resolvitur coexistentia horum in Dei voluntatem promittentem, vel haec voluntas promittens est consequens vel antecedens rem promissam. Si consequens, Deus promittit Ezech. 36. 27. se effecturum, ut in viis ipsius ambulemus, posterius natura quam efficit ut in viis ipsius ambulemus. En ridiculae propositiones promissoriae. Si antecedens fit voluntas respectu rei promissae & Dei promissio det esse rebus promissis uti revera causa dat esse effecto, tum antecedens voluntas efficax& essectus contingens (saepe enim Deus effectus contingentes promittit) optime consociantur.
units.tr: 5. If the coexistence of these things is resolved into God's promising will, then this promising will is either consequent upon or antecedent to the thing promised. If consequent, then God promises in Ezek. 36. 27 that he will bring it about that we walk in his ways; the promise is posterior in nature to his bringing it about that we walk in his ways. Behold the ridiculous promissory propositions! If the will is antecedent to the thing promised, and God's promise gives being to the promised things just as a real cause gives being to its effect, then an antecedent efficacious will and a contingent effect (for God often promises contingent effects) agree perfectly.

units.la: 6. Coexistentia haec pendet illis à certitudine praedi-ctionis divinae: age itaque: unde quaeso pendet coexistentia abnegationis Petri & tentationis qua impetebatur in aula praetoris? nempe ex praedictione Salvatoris. Itaque vero Christus Petrum se abnegaturum si tentaretur, praedixit, & certa fuit praedictio, quia res prius in se certa erat, non contra. Ideo Petrus abnegavit salvatorem quia salvator eum abnegaturum praedixit, ut omnes norunt: an non hi davi in ecclesia omnia turbent, theologiam, logicam communes etiam naturae ἐφνοίας[?]?
units.tr: 6. This coexistence depends on the certainty of divine prediction. Come then: on what, I ask, does the coexistence of Peter's denial depend, and of the temptation by which he was assailed in the hall of the governor? Surely on the prediction of the Saviour. Christ predicted that Peter would deny him if he were tempted, and the prediction was certain because the thing was first certain in itself, not the reverse. Peter denied the Saviour because the Saviour predicted that he would deny him, as everyone knows. Do these men not throw everything into confusion in the Church: theology, logic, and even the common notions of nature?

units.la: 6. Dicunt Deum hanc coexistentiam praescire ex hypothesi: hypothesin scire difcupio; videt Tyrios poenitentiam acturos, si signa vidissent: at mera cyphra est haec hypothesis: nam visis signis possunt non resipiscere. Quid hic Grevinchovius? Deus (inquit) hic videt veritatem, non necessitatem. At an homini satis sana mens est? Videt Deus veritatem infallibiliter, Ergo necessitas est in ea veritate: alioqui idem est, ac si diceret, Deum infallibiliter scire id quod est fallibile, ac si diceret hominem videre non visibile, audire non audibile, Deum scire non scibile.
units.tr: 6. They say God foreknows this coexistence from a hypothesis. I want to know this hypothesis. God sees that the Tyrians would have repented if they had seen the signs. But this hypothesis is a mere cipher: for, the signs having been seen, they might still not repent. What does Grevinchovius say here? God (he says) sees here the truth, not the necessity. But is this man of sound mind? God sees the truth infallibly; therefore there is necessity in that truth. Otherwise it is the same as if he said that God knows infallibly what is fallible, or as if he said that a man sees what is not visible, hears what is not audible, or that God knows what is not knowable.

units.la: 6. Arg. §. Si objectum hujusce scientiæ præcedit liberum Dei decretum, tum omnia contingentia antevertunt Dei libertatem, nec poterit misereri quorum vult, Christum revelare, quibus vult, neque aliter disponere contingentia, quam sese disposuerunt antecedenter ad Dei decretum, & Deus fatali necessitate omnia velle cogetur. Nam si contingentia præcedunt scientiam mediam, & præscientia præcedit decretum, multo magis contingentia omnia, quoad realem ipsorum futuritionem, antecedunt Dei decretum. Hoc autem est absurdum. Ergo absurdum est objectum hujus scientiæ. Resp. Suarez. Licet illa scientia non supponit aliquod decretum liberum quasi præexistens in Deo, includit in ipsa hypothesi decretum ponendum in re, ut ab illo esse possit effectus. Resp. 1. Si non supponit hæc scientia decretum, quasi præexistens in Deo, cognoscit effectum priusquam est ens & verum & scibile: nam nihil habet esse aut essendi veritatem, nisi præsupposita causa sua. 2. Includit in ipsa hypothesi decretum ponendum, ac cur non positum? an posito effectu causa est tantum ponenda non posita? Qualis est hæc logica? 3. Si ponendum est decretum positâ scientiâ mediâ, adeoque posita futuritione contingentis, vel est hoc decretum ponendum libere, vel non: si libere, potest non poni decretum, & sic dari possunt omnia futura contingentia, adeoque ipso actu, per eandem rationem existere possunt, citra omne Dei decretum: sed si decretum Dei est ponendum non liberè, Deus non est liber in decretis suis ponendis, quod est prorsus ἀντιλογία[?]. Ideoque fato & necessitate Deus non potest decernere, quod jam est. 4. Hoc decretum est tantum approbatio rei jam futuræ antecedenter ad Dei volitionem, non decretum: quicquid enim aliquis decernit, id habet esse per decretum. decretum enim facit & dat esse rei decretæ, sicut scientia supponit fuû objectum: at vero approbatio est rei jam præexistentis, ideoque non est causa rei, sed rem in suo esse jam existentem supponit. 5. Includitur decretû in hypothesi quasi ponendum: ut ab illo esse possit effectus, absurdè, inconcinnè, & inepte omnia. Si præscientia media jam est, jam objectum ejus est, imo objectum prius natura est quam scientia. At si quando objectum est, ponendum est decretum ut ab illo objectum posset esse, tum quod jam est, potest esse, & sic nondum est, quod est: quali vero homo qui est actu homo, fit in potentia ut possit esse homo, & futuritio quæ jam est actu, fit in potentia ut possit esse actu, quis magnum & clatum[?] Iesuitam, qui sacræ theologiæ volumina sedecim typis mandavit, ita differentem fustineret? 6. Objectum scientiae mediae est prius ipsa scientia, ac proinde cum haec scientia sit prior decreto Dei libero, sequitur futura contingentia esse vere futura antecedenter ad actus omnipotentiae: nam omnipotentia nihil agit in Deo nisi qua determinata per actus liberae voluntatis, & sic omnia futura contingentia sunt futura ante omnes actus divinae omnipotentiae, intellectus, vel voluntatis, ideoque ante omnem actum providentiae. O providentiam Jesuitico-Arminianam! Anima mea in horum secreta ne ingrediaris.
units.tr: 6. Argument. If the object of this knowledge precedes God's free decree, then all contingent things precede God's liberty. Then he cannot have mercy on whom he wills, reveal Christ to whom he wills, or dispose contingent things otherwise than they have disposed themselves antecedent to God's decree, and God will be compelled by fatal necessity to will all things. For if contingent things precede middle knowledge, and foreknowledge precedes the decree, then much more all contingent things, as to their real futurition, precede God's decree. But this is absurd. Therefore the object of this knowledge is absurd. I reply, with Suarez: Although that knowledge does not presuppose any free decree as if pre-existing in God, it includes in the hypothesis itself a decree to be posited in reality, so that the effect may be able to come from it. I reply: (1) If this knowledge does not presuppose a decree as pre-existing in God, it knows the effect before it is a being, and true, and knowable; for nothing has being or the truth of being unless its cause is presupposed. (2) It includes in the hypothesis itself a decree to be posited. But why is it not posited? When the effect is given, is the cause only to be posited, not posited? What kind of logic is this? (3) If the decree is to be posited when middle knowledge is posited, and so when the futurition of the contingent is posited, then either this decree is to be posited freely or not. If freely, the decree can fail to be posited, and so all future contingent things could exist, and by the same reasoning exist in act, without any decree of God. But if God's decree is to be posited not freely, then God is not free in positing his decrees, which is plainly a contradiction [ἀντιλογία]. So God cannot decree by fate and necessity what already is. (4) This decree is only an approval of a thing already future, antecedent to God's volition, not a decree. For whatever someone decrees has its being through the decree. A decree makes and gives being to the decreed thing, just as knowledge presupposes its object. But approval concerns a thing already pre-existing, and so it is not the cause of the thing but presupposes the thing already existing in its being. (5) The decree is included in the hypothesis as if it were to be posited, so that the effect could come from it: all of this is absurd, incoherent, and inept. If middle knowledge already is, then its object already is; indeed the object is prior in nature to the knowledge. But if at some time the object is, then the decree is to be posited so that the object could be from it. Then what already is, can be; and so what is not yet, is. Just as a man who is actually a man becomes in potency able to be a man, and a futurition which is already actual becomes in potency able to be actual, who would endure such nonsense from a famous Jesuit who has published sixteen volumes of sacred theology in print? (6) The object of middle knowledge is prior to that knowledge itself. Hence, since this knowledge is prior to God's free decree, it follows that future contingent things are truly future antecedent to the acts of omnipotence. For omnipotence acts in God only as determined through the acts of his free will; thus all future contingent things are future before all acts of divine omnipotence, intellect, or will, and therefore before every act of providence. O Jesuitical-Arminian providence! "O my soul, do not enter into their secrets."

units.la: 7. Huic argumento aliter occurrit Petr. Fonseca : Non inde (inquit) sequitur hujusmodi scientiam Deo quicquam libertatis ademisse ad volendum aut permittendum oppositum ejus quod voluntas creata facit. Id doce Jesuita. Scivit enim etiam certo illam, si in quibusdam aliis occasionibus ponerentur, oppositum esse facturam: ut postquam per scientiam conditionatam intellexit, quid illa in his vel illis circumstantiis collocata, factura esset, idque absoluta voluntate fieri aut permittere voluit, jam repugnaret hypothesi oppositum, fieri velle aut permittere, alioqui in Dei voluntate mutatio admitteretur. Ref. 1. Ratio quam adfert Jesuita, non est hili[?]: nam si antecedenter & ad Dei scientiam & decretum scivit, voluntatem in hisce non in aliis circumstantiis collocandam & hoc volituram: non potuit vel scire, vel velle, vel per omnipotentiam efficere, ut ullo modo aliud vellet, quam voluit. Non diffiteor, voluntatem aliud potuisse velle, sed argumento non hoc contendo: sed si Deus videt antecedenter ad ipsius scientiam & voluntatem, voluntatem creatam hoc non illud velle, non potuit efficere, ut aliud non vellet. At inquit Iesuita, potuit in aliis circumstantiis voluntatem collocasse, in quibus contrarium voluisset creata voluntas: at dico, in hisce circumstantiis voluntatem fuisse libere à Deo collocatam, & ex Iesuitæ doctrina ib. refpo. ad argum. 4. Deus præscit scientia media suos liberos actus, & ideo antecedenter ad ipsius voluntatem, fuit illa libera collocatio voluntatis creatæ in hisce, non in aliis circumstantiis, ideoque non potuit aliter collocare voluntatem quam se collocaturum præscivit scientia media. 2. Postulo, ut probet Iesuita, voluntatem creatam in aliis circumstantiis quam in hisce sub quibus hoc vult, quod vult, acturam fuisse oppositum ejus quod jam facit; imo poterat sub omnibus possibilibus circumstantiis illud idem agere quod jam agit. Nam indifferens est ad agendum vel non agendum, sub omnibus circumstantiis: neque enim illæ circumstantiæ determinassent voluntatem ad oppositum agendum: ideoque hoc pro suo more dictitat, non probat, ejusque probatio non parvi est, ad argumentum hoc corroborandum. 3. Præscientia media Deus præscivit, voluntatem creatam hoc volituram, non & hoc, & oppositum de facto: atqui futuritio volitionis hujus non oppositi, ex Iesuita præpræcessit omnes actus tum scientiæ tum voluntatis liberæ: Dei, ac proinde non potuit non absolutè velle hos actus liberos, qui fiunt, non alios; ideoque hujusmodi scientia omnem Deo libertatem adimit: an non longe tutius Hilarius? Quæ Deus facere decrevit, ea in sua voluntate cognoscit.
units.tr: 7. Fonseca answers this argument in another way: "It does not follow from this," he says, "that such knowledge has taken from God any freedom to will or to permit the opposite of what the created will does." The Jesuit teaches this. "For he knew with certainty that, if the creature were placed in certain other circumstances, it would do the opposite. So once, through middle knowledge, he understood what it would do when placed in these or those circumstances, and willed or permitted that this be done absolutely, it would now contradict the hypothesis for him to will or permit the opposite, or else change would be admitted into God's will." Reply 1. The reasoning the Jesuit brings is not trivial. If God knew antecedently to his knowledge and decree that the will would be placed in these circumstances and not in others, and would will this, then he could neither know, nor will, nor by omnipotence bring it about, that it should will in any way other than it wills. I do not deny that the will could have willed otherwise, but that is not what I am contending in this argument. If God sees, antecedently to his knowledge and will, that the created will wills this and not that, he could not bring it about that it would not will otherwise. But the Jesuit says that God could have placed the will in other circumstances, in which the created will would have willed the contrary. I say that in these circumstances the will was placed freely by God, and by the Jesuit's own doctrine (see his reply to the fourth argument), God foreknows his free acts by middle knowledge. So, antecedently to his will, this free placing of the created will in these circumstances rather than others was made. Therefore he could not place the will otherwise than he foresaw by middle knowledge he would place it. 2. I demand that the Jesuit prove that the created will, in circumstances other than those under which it wills this, would have done the opposite of what it now does. Indeed, under all possible circumstances it could have done the very same thing it now does, for it is indifferent to acting or not acting under all circumstances. Those circumstances would not have determined the will to act the opposite. So he asserts this in his usual way and does not prove it, and his proof would be of no small help in strengthening this argument. 3. God foreknew by middle knowledge that the created will would will this, not both this and its opposite in fact. But, according to the Jesuit, the futurition of this volition, and not of its opposite, preceded all the acts of God's knowledge and free will, and therefore God could not but absolutely will these free acts which occur, and not others. So this kind of knowledge takes away all freedom from God. Is not Hilary much safer? "What God has decided to do, he knows in his own will."

units.la: 8. Nullius sunt momenti quæ pro hac scientia adferunt adversarii. Nam 1. Deus Keylitas[?] Davidem in manus Sauli traditurus, siquidem permanserit, & Tyrios actūros pœnitentiam, si signa vidissent, & ejusmodi cognovit scientia libera in decreto prædeterminante, quo concatenationem entium omnium possibilium absolutè prædefinivit: quod certe spectat ad admirandam Dei providentiam, cujus voluntas ad nulla entia vel quæ actu, vel quæ possibilia sunt, est indeterminata & suspensa: & sic exponenda sunt dicta Patrum & Scholasticorum, quæ prolixè nimis accumulat Franc. Suarez[?] pro hac scientia: poterat gratis Jesuita se hoc onere scribendi facile levasse.
units.tr: 8. The arguments the adversaries bring for this knowledge are of no weight. For 1. God knew that the men of Keilah would hand David over into the hands of Saul, if he remained there, and that the Tyrians would repent if they had seen the signs. He knew this by a free knowledge within a predetermining decree, by which he absolutely predefined the concatenation of all possible beings. This certainly belongs to the admirable providence of God, whose will is indeterminate and suspended with regard to no beings, whether actual or possible. So the sayings of the Fathers and the Scholastics, which Francis Suarez heaps up too profusely in favour of this knowledge, must be explained in this way. The Jesuit could easily have spared himself the labour of writing all that for nothing.

units.la: 9. 2. Objiciunt: datur medium inter absolute futurum & possibiliter futurum, nempe conditionaliter futurum. Ergo inter scientiam naturalem, qua Deus possibilia cognoscit, & liberam, qua quæ absolute futura sunt & existunt, datur media scientia. Resp. Sententia libera: Deus cognoscit futura conditionata, ideoque media hæc est vana, quia ex sola Dei voluntate necessario connectuntur interse Tyriorum resipiscentia & visio signorum. At quando antecedens & consequens effentialiter connectuntur, ut si Petrus est homo: Ergo est animal; citra omne decretum naturaliter Deus cognoscit ejusmodi: habent enim esse antecedenter ad Dei decretum.
units.tr: 9. 2. They object: there is a middle between what is absolutely future and what is possibly future, namely what is conditionally future. Therefore between natural knowledge, by which God knows possibles, and free knowledge, by which he knows what is absolutely future and actually exists, there is a middle knowledge. Reply: On the free view, God knows future conditionals, and so this middle is empty, because the repentance of the Tyrians and the seeing of the signs are connected with each other necessarily by God's will alone. But when antecedent and consequent are connected essentially, as in: if Peter is a man, therefore he is an animal, God knows such things naturally, without any decree, for they have being antecedently to God's decree.

units.la: 10. Ob. 3. Ante omne decretum hæ duæ sunt contradictoriæ: si Petrus in tali ordine collocetur, peccabit; si in tali ordine, non peccabit. Contradicentium altera est vera, altera falsa. Ergo veritas alterius determinatè cognoscitur à Deo, sed non scientia libera, quæ decretum supponit: hæc enim est scientia de rebus antecedentibus decretum, neque naturaliter, ut mere possibilia hæc cognoscit: nam hic aliquid est futurum conditionate.
units.tr: 10. Objection 3. Before any decree, these two are contradictories: if Peter is placed in such an order, he will sin; if he is placed in such an order, he will not sin. One of two contradictories is true and the other false. Therefore the truth of one of them is determinately known by God, but not by free knowledge, which presupposes the decree. For this is knowledge of things antecedent to the decree, and it is not natural knowledge, by which he knows merely possibles, for here something is future conditionally.

units.la: Resp. 1. Contradicentium in materia contingenti, si una est vera, altera necessario erit falsa. At vero hæc, Petrus si in tali rerum ordine collocetur, peccabit, ante Dei decretum; non est vera: at non est necesse ut una sit determinate vera antecedenter ad causam connectentem inter se extrema: hoc est, ante Dei voluntatem permittentem, fieri non potest ut Petrus peccet, etiam si ita constitueretur, 2. De ente vere futuro, neutra pars ante Dei decretum, est vel vera, vel falsa proprie, quia extrema propositionis nempe (Petrus) (constitutio in tali ordine) & (peccatum) sunt non entia, ideoque non vera, non scibilia, ac proinde eorum connexio est non ens & non verum, sed indifferens ad veritatem & falsitatem. Nec enim necesse est ut quavis posita hypothesi contradicentium altera sit vera, altera falsa, nam poni potest conditio, qua desinant esse contradicentes: neque enim hypotheses quaelibet sunt nobis liberae, nec est necesse ut in quolibet rationis signo, contradicentium altera sit vera, uti post Didacum Alvarez. observavit doctissimus vir, & de ecclesia Dei, si quis alius, praeclare meritus, Guliel. Amesius in rescript. ad Grevinch. 3. Ipse Suarez. agnoscit nulla entia esse, nisi decretum, saltem ad modum possibilis, supponatur, ideoque illos adversarios tanget hoc argumentum. Nam veritas & falsitas sunt affectiones entis veri & realis: at nullum est ens vere & reale antecedenter ad suam causam.
units.tr: Reply 1. In a contingent matter, if one of two contradictories is true, the other must necessarily be false. But this proposition, that Peter, if placed in such an order of things, will sin, is not true before God's decree. Nor is it necessary that one of them be determinately true antecedently to the cause that connects the extremes. That is, before God's permissive will, it cannot happen that Peter sins, even if he were so placed. 2. Concerning a being that is truly future, neither part is properly true or false before God's decree, because the extremes of the proposition, namely (Peter), (placement in such an order) and (sin), are non-beings. Therefore they are not true, not knowable, and so their connection is a non-being and not true, but indifferent to truth and falsity. Nor is it necessary that, under any given hypothesis, one of two contradictories be true and the other false, for a condition can be posited by which they cease to be contradictories. Not every hypothesis is open to us, nor is it necessary that at every point of reason one of the contradictories be true. The most learned man observed this after Diego Alvarez, and William Ames, who deserved as well as anyone of the Church of God, excellently noted it in his reply to Grevinchovius. 3. Suarez himself acknowledges that there are no beings unless a decree is supposed, at least in the mode of possibility. So this argument touches those adversaries. For truth and falsity are affections of a true and real being, but no being is truly and really antecedent to its cause.

units.la: 11. Ob. 4. Nullus sapiens aliquid absolute decernit nisi praescit deliberate quid sit ex hoc vel illo sequuturum. Ergo alienum est a sapientia Dei, ut decernat futura contingentia priusquam praescit illa: alioqui temere decernit.
units.tr: 11. Objection 4. No wise man decides anything absolutely unless he foreknows deliberately what will follow from this or that. Therefore it is foreign to the wisdom of God to decree future contingents before he foreknows them; otherwise he decides rashly.

units.la: Ita Fonseca, Suarez, Lackfonus, ne jejunae & macilentae forent ipsius meditationes, ex hisce talia hausit. Resp. Argumentum praesumit in hoc eminere Dei sapientiam, quod faciendae & decernenda praesciat. At hoc in omnes moriones & idiotas cadit, ut ipsorum facta & decreta praecedat aliqualis factorum & determinandorum cognitio. 2. Scientiam simplicis intelligentiae qua Deus novit quid sit possibile, quid facto expediens, quidnon, praecedere dicimus omnia Dei decreta, & scientiam visionis seu libera decreta subsequi: & & sic Deus ex infinita sua sapientia & scientia & nullo modo temerè decernit, quasi vero temeritas decernendi in Deum caderet, nisi videret ante decretum suum omnia possibilia ut futura necessario, id quod implicat contradictionem. 3. Detur ergo scientia media antecedens omnia Dei decreta, & videbimus qualem Deo sapientiam tribuant. Ego {inquit Deus} praescio scientia media, priusquam decernam, ut Petrus crederet, Petrum certissime crediturum: ideo decerno ut credat. Ego praescio antecedenter ad decretum permittens Iudam proditurum Salvatorem, Pilatum condemnaturum, & milites crucifixuros ipsum: ideo ego permittere haec decerno. Hæccine est sapientia Iesuitica quam Deo affingunt? Decernit liberè hoc fore, postquam est: quae providentia esset haec? Nauclerus certissime praescit navem naufragium subituram, & tum naufragium decernit: Petrus suam Domini abnegationem praevidit & praescivit in Christi praedi-ctione, & voluit. Ergo Petrus decrevit suam Domini abnegationem. 4.
