Sapientes viri ex scientia media vellent decernere ne forte errent, decernendo media fini non idonea: at non est quod Iesuitae vereantur ne media a Deo volita sint inepta fini, quem intendit: quia enim Deus voluit talia media, ideo sunt idonea: at non sic inter homines se res habet: dabimus ergo fortè hominibus scientiam quandam mediam, ne forte errent, an Deo etiâ dabimus ex periculo errandi? Apage nugas.
units.tr: Thus Fonseca, Suarez, Lackfonus, so that their meditations should not be dry and meagre, drew such things from these premises. Reply: The argument presumes that God's wisdom stands out in this, that he foreknows what is to be done and decreed. But this applies to every fool and simpleton: their deeds and decrees are preceded by some knowledge of the things to be done and determined. 2. We say that the knowledge of simple understanding, by which God knows what is possible and what is expedient or not expedient for the deed, precedes all of God's decrees, and that the knowledge of vision, or free decrees, follow. And so God, from his infinite wisdom and knowledge, in no way decrees rashly. As if rashness in decreeing could fall upon God, unless he saw all possibles before his decree as necessarily future, which implies a contradiction! 3. Let there then be a middle knowledge antecedent to all God's decrees, and we shall see what wisdom they attribute to God. "I," says God, "by middle knowledge foreknow, before I decree, that Peter would believe, and that he would most certainly believe. Therefore I decree that he believes. I foreknow, antecedently to my permissive decree, that Judas will betray the Saviour, that Pilate will condemn him, and that the soldiers will crucify him. Therefore I decree to permit these things." Is this the Jesuitical wisdom they ascribe to God? He decides freely that a thing will be, after it is? What providence would that be? A ship's captain foreknows most certainly that his ship will suffer shipwreck, and then decrees the shipwreck. Peter foresaw and foreknew his denial of the Lord in Christ's prediction, and willed it. Therefore Peter decreed his denial of the Lord. 4. Wise men would wish, by means of middle knowledge, to decree so that they do not perhaps err by decreeing means unsuited to the end. But the Jesuits need not fear that the means willed by God are unfit for the end he intends. For because God willed such means, they are suitable. But it is not so among men. Shall we then perhaps give men some middle knowledge, lest they err, and give it to God too, from danger of error? Away with such trifles!

units.la: 12. Ob. 5.[?] Sicut in absolutis (inquit Suarez) de causa existente vel praesente in intuitu Dei, ut existens vere affirmatur in eadem mente Dei tale essectum esse libere dimanaturum ab illa, non quia in virtute causae hoc videat Deus, sed quia intuitu suo videt causam illam, tametsi liberam, tanquam influentem in illum effectum, ita in hac conditionata de causa ex hypothesi concepta, ut praesenti sub tali existentia possibili potest vere affirmari & cognosci in mente Dei, hunc determinatum effectum esse dimanaturum ab illa causa libera ex eadem hypothesi, non quia in virtute causae talis effectus determinate cognoscitur, sed quia vere in se & actu secundo effet ad actum illum determinanda. R. Audis, lector, regia dictata, sic volo, sic jubeo, sed nihil probat.
units.tr: 12. Objection 5[?] Just as in absolute matters (says Suarez), when a cause is existing or present to the view of God, it is truly affirmed as existing in the same mind of God that such an effect will freely flow from it. This is not because God sees it in the power of the cause, but because by his own view he sees that cause, although free, as flowing into that effect. So in this conditional matter, concerning a cause conceived under a hypothesis, the determinate effect can be truly affirmed and known in the mind of God, as present under such possible existence, to flow from that free cause under the same hypothesis. This is not because the determinate effect is known in the power of the cause, but because it would truly be, in itself and in actual second act, determined to that act. Reply: You hear, reader, royal decrees: "So I will, so I command." But it proves nothing.

units.la: Hoc onere se levat. 1. Nam fabula est, effectum secundum in se determinandum: & a nullo causa determinandum: quid? an erit Deus habens esse a nulla causa? si indifferens causa se determinat, sibi dat esse determinatum. 2. Si effectus contingens habet esse determinatum a Dei voluntate, quod negari non potest; an Deus videt hoc esse determinatum, priusquam ipsius voluntas dederit esse determinatum? Tum videt non ens, quod est non visibile: nihil enim est habens esse & scibile priusquam esse acceperit, & est scibile: esse autem est scibilitatis fundamentum. 3. Libera determinatio prout in se futura (inquit) est praefens ex hypothesi, aeterno Dei intuitui, sed an est praesens antecedenter ad Dei decreto divino intuitui, hoc tu proba, imo nullis ingeniorum machinis hoc effectu dabis. 4. Deus (inquit) videt effectum determinandum, non in virtute causæ, nempe contingentis, sed in se & in actu secundo. Sed tum dico Deum non videre effectum contingentem qua contingentem, sed qua necessarium, quod nobis vitio dant adversarii: & sic Deus non cognoscit contingentia qua contingentia. §. [?] Quæro an effectus contingens sit cognoscibilis in suâ causâ, an non. Dicent non, quia propensio causæ contingentis est ad utramque partem indifferens: at quid tum? est (inquam ego) indifferens disjunctive non copulative: sed hi malunt ipsam Dei scientiam in jus vocari, quam vel contingentiæ suæ tantillum detrahi patiantur. Sed adhuc audite Jesuitam fortunæ causam agentem. Negat enim rationem futuritionis contingentis effectus sumendam esse à causa.
units.tr: He relieves himself of this burden in the following ways. 1. For it is a fable that an effect is to be determined in itself, and determined by no cause. What then? Will God have being from no cause? If an indifferent cause determines itself, it gives itself determinate being. 2. If a contingent effect has determinate being from the will of God, which cannot be denied, does God see this as determinate before his will has given it determinate being? Then he sees a non-being, which is not visible. For nothing that has being and is knowable is knowable before it has received being; but being is the foundation of knowability. 3. A free determination, as it is future in itself, is (he says) present under the hypothesis to the eternal intuition of God. But whether it is present antecedently to the divine decree in God's intuition, you must prove this; indeed, by no machinery of wit will you bring this about. 4. God (he says) sees the effect to be determined not in the power of the cause, namely a contingent one, but in itself and in actual second act. But then I say that God does not see a contingent effect as contingent, but as necessary, which our opponents charge us with; and thus God does not know contingent things as contingent. §. [?] I ask whether a contingent effect is knowable in its cause or not. They will say no, because the tendency of a contingent cause is indifferent to either side. But what then? It is indifferent (I reply) disjunctively, not conjunctively. But they would rather put God's own knowledge on trial than allow the least detraction from its contingency. But still hear the Jesuit pleading the cause of Fortune. For he denies that the reason for the futurity of a contingent effect is to be taken from the cause.

units.la: Forma (inquit) illa à quâ esse possibile in causa denominatur futurum, non est causa ipsa, vel determinatio ejus, ut (inquit) à nobis Calvini sectatoribus (ut vocat) contenditur. Nam hoc est tollere (inquit ille) contingentiam effectuum & libertatem causarum secundarum: est ergo habitudo quædam quam res prout est in causa habet ad seipsam, ut erit præsens in suo tempore, qui ordo in mente Dei est objectiva præsentia, quam illud esse habet in æternitate, ratione cujus veritas illa per modum præsentis cognoscitur, quamvis in ordine ad nos denominatur futura. Resp. Subtilius Paulo illa dici fateor, sed nihil veri continent. Nam 1. posse denominari futurum à causa est ambiguum: nam à causa secunda non denominatur futurum simpliciter, sed à causa prima : nam futuritio est tendentia entis è statu possibilitatis ad statum actuationis per causam primam: nulla enim fuit causa ab æterno præter unicam Dei voluntatem, quæ hanc tendentiam caufaretur. 2. Si tollitur libertas, quoniam essectus contingens habet futuriritionem à causa sua , an habet futuritionem, antecedenter ad suam causam ? & sic nulla causa opus erit, quæ det futuritionem, si ipsam, antequam accedat causatio actualis, habent. 3. Si forma à quâ possibile denominatur futurum, fit habitudo sive ordo, quam res prout est in causa habet ad seipsam prout in tempore existit, ille ordo vel terminatur necessario ad rem in tempore existentem, vel contingenter : si necessario ; tûm res est necessario futura, & etiam contingens, quod Jesuita putat esse grave absurdum ; si terminatur contingenter ad rem prout in tempore existit, tum contingens futurum non est futurum, quod absurdû. Nam omne futurum sive contingens , sive necessarium , imò etiam possibile futurum est necessario, & non potest non esse futurum : nam futurum non est terminus diminuens. 4. Quæro quam causam intelligit quando dicit futurum esse habitudinem rei in sua causa ad rem actu existentem. Nam vel intelligit Dei voluntatem, primam causam, vel intelligit causam contingentem : si sic, tum vel intellit causam contingentem, qua talem, vel qua determinatam : si primum, futuritio non est habitudo rei in causa contingente qua est contingens. Nam causa contingens qua talis, est causa rei tantum possibilis, non futurae. Si vero intelligit causam contingentem qua determinatam, vel intelligit determinatam a Dei voluntate, & sic habemus institutum, vel ab ipsa causa secunda contingente, quatenus est determinata a seipsa. At vero non potest ratio futuritionis aeternae sumi a temporali determinatione facta a causa contingente. Si vero velit futuritionem esse habitudinem rei prout est in prima causa, hoc doceat. Nam prima haec causa est Deus qua libere agit, & sic adhuc habeo institutum.
units.tr: That form (he says) from which the possible is denominated future in the cause is not the cause itself, or its determination, as is contended by us followers of Calvin (as he calls us). For this (he says) is to remove the contingency of effects and the freedom of secondary causes. There is therefore a certain relation which a thing, as it is in the cause, has to itself, insofar as it will be present in its own time. This order is, in the mind of God, objective presence, which that thing has in eternity, by reason of which that truth is known in the manner of the present, although in relation to us it is denominated future. Reply: I grant that these things are put more subtly than Paul's, but they contain nothing true. For 1. to be denominated future by a cause is ambiguous. For it is not denominated future simply by a secondary cause, but by the first cause. Futurity is the tending of a being from the state of possibility to the state of actuality through the first cause; for there was no cause from eternity except the sole will of God, which would cause this tendency. 2. If freedom is removed, since a contingent effect has futurity from its cause, does it have futurity antecedently to its cause? And so no cause will be needed to give futurity, if they have it before actual causation arrives. 3. If the form from which the possible is denominated future becomes a relation or order which a thing has to itself, as it is in the cause and as it exists in time, then that order is either necessarily terminated in the thing existing in time, or contingently. If necessarily, then the thing is necessarily future, and also contingent, which the Jesuit thinks a grave absurdity. If it terminates contingently in the thing as it exists in time, then the contingent future is not future, which is absurd. For every future, whether contingent or necessary, indeed even every possible future, is necessarily future and cannot not be future; for future is not a diminishing term. 4. I ask what cause he understands when he says that futurity is the relation of a thing in its cause to the thing actually existing. For he understands either the will of God, the first cause, or a contingent cause. If the latter, then he understands either a contingent cause as such, or as determined. If the first: futurition is not a relation of a thing to a contingent cause as it is contingent, for a contingent cause as such is the cause of what is merely possible, not of what is future. But if he understands a contingent cause as determined, he understands either as determined by the will of God, and so we have the point at issue, or by the secondary contingent cause itself, insofar as it is determined by itself. But the reason for eternal futurity cannot be taken from a temporal determination made by a contingent cause. If he wishes futurity to be a relation of a thing as it is in the first cause, let him show this. For this first cause is God, who acts freely, and so I still have the point at issue.

units.la: 5. Si futuritio est habitudo rei prout est in causa ad seipsam, ille ordo est quid determinatum: nam futurum superaddit aliquid determinatum tum possibili, tum contingenti. At si fit determinatum, manet quaestio unde est illa determinatio? non aliunde quam vel a fortuna, vel a constellatione, quod non est dicendum, vel a Dei voluntate; quod necessario est admittendum. 6. Semper efuita petit principium: nam unde est quod talis habitudo fit objectiva praesentia intuitui divino & scientiae subjecta. Haec enim praesentia vel est ab ipso effectu contingente, quod est absurdum, vel a Dei voluntate in qua Deus habitudinem hanc praesentem videt; vel in alia aliqua causa, quam dare non possunt.
units.tr: 5. If futurity is the relation of a thing, as it is in its cause, to itself, then that order is something determinate. For future adds something determinate both to the possible and to the contingent. But if it becomes determinate, the question remains: whence is that determination? Not from anything other than either chance or constellation, which is not to be said; or from the will of God, which must necessarily be admitted. 6. The Jesuit always begs the question. For whence is it that such a relation becomes objective presence to the divine intuition and subject to knowledge? For this presence is either from the contingent effect itself, which is absurd, or from the will of God, in which God sees this present relation, or from some other cause, which they cannot supply.

units.la: 13. Objecti. 6. Si Deus non nisi in decreto praedeterminante cognoscit futura contingentia, tum non cognoscit futura contingentia ut contingentia: in eo enim decreto sunt necessaria, non contingentia. Ita Suarez, ib. f. 5. Nec aliter cognoscere potest haec, quam cognoscit possibilia (inquiunt Remonstrantes) vid. scientia indeterminata seu simplicis intelligentiae, sub ratione possibilis existentiae. Resp. scilicet grave incommodum; quod nos haud gravate concedimus. Vide quid hic princeps Scholasticorum Thomas Aquinas pro nobis loquatur: Contingens ut nondum determinatum ad unum non subditur per certitudinem alicui cognitioni. Vult contingens qua contingens non posse determinatè cognosci ut futurum, imo contingens, uti antecedit decretum, vel ut mente consideratur contradistinctum a decreto tantum est possibile, & Deus cognoscit exactissimè contingentia, & eorum naturam hanc esse, quod possunt esse vel non esse nempe scientia naturali, & sub esse possibili: at vero futurum aliquid superaddit contingenti. Nam contingens aliud est possibile, aliud futurum; & Deum cognoscere contingentia futura qua futura, nisi in decreto suo putamus esse impossibile, neque desinunt esse contingentia, quando per decretum incipiunt esse futura, non magis qua necessaria desinunt esse necessaria, quia libere à Deo sunt volita, & in relatione ad Dei voluntatem necessaria sunt contingentia, quia possunt non esse, siquidem Deo ita visum; ita contingentia in relatione ad Dei decretū determinans sunt necessariafecundum quid, nec desinunt esse contingentia.2. Nihil prius est nobis in votis, quam ut hi doctores nobis ostendant contingentia, qua contingentia & nullam omnino necessitatem habentia, sint fundamentum scientiæ infallibilis: clamant nobis hic Deum videre veritatem non necessitatem, sed, Deus bone, quam exoptamus ut id omni quo possunt apparatu Rhetorico, nobis demonstrent; Sed audimus meras affirmationes.
units.tr: 13. Objection 6. If God knows future contingents only in a predetermining decree, then he does not know future contingents as contingent, for in that decree they are necessary, not contingent. Thus Suarez, ib. f. 5. Nor can he know these otherwise than he knows possibles (say the Remonstrants), namely by indeterminate knowledge or simple intelligence, under the aspect of possible existence. Reply: Certainly a grave inconvenience, which we do not hesitate to concede. See what the prince of the Schoolmen, Thomas Aquinas, says on our side: "A contingent thing, as not yet determined to one, is not subject to certainty by any knowledge." He wants the contingent as contingent not to be determinately knowable as future. Indeed the contingent, as it precedes the decree or is considered in the mind distinct from the decree, is only possible; and God knows contingent things most exactly, and knows that their nature is this, that they can be or not be, namely by natural knowledge and under possible being. But the future adds something to the contingent. For the contingent is one thing as possible, and another as future. We think it is impossible for God to know future contingents as future, except in his decree; and they do not cease to be contingent when through the decree they begin to be future, any more than the necessary ceases to be necessary because it is freely willed by God. In relation to the will of God, contingent things that determine are necessary in a certain respect, yet they do not cease to be contingent. 2. Nothing is nearer our wishes than that these teachers should show us contingent things, as contingent and having no necessity at all, to be the foundation of infallible knowledge. They cry out here that God sees truth, not necessity. But, good God, what we long for is that they demonstrate this to us with every rhetorical apparatus they can muster. Instead we hear mere assertions.

units.la: 12. Quamvis autem Petrus Fonseca, Jesuita accuratioris philosophiæ nomine cum primis nobilis, hanc scientiam mediam pro aris tanquam & focis propugnet, & se parentem ipsius glorietur, qui hoc viva voce docuit an. 1569. (licet Lod. Molina scriptis illud miserrimum mandarit anno 1588.) tamen argumentis non contemnendis contendit contingentia, quæ re vera aliquando futura sunt, si in statu quidem absoluto sumantur, non cognosci nisi in actu approbativo, aut permissio divinæ voluntatis; quod mysterium Jesuiticum mihi admiratione omni majus apparet. Nam vult enunciationes de futuris contingentibus ante omnem divinæ voluntatis actum esse determinatè veras aut falsas: attamen quia libera Dei voluntas est prima radix & causa omnis contingentiæ & libertatis, vult contingentia absolutè futura non cognosci, nisi in Dei voluntate approbante vel promittente: quare hoc Jesuita? Quia enim (inquis) res est, aut non est, oratio est vera vel falsa. Ut igitur Deus certo sciat, quid sit eventurum contingenter, necesse est ut intelligat actum voluntatis suæ, ex cujus concursu illud pendebit. Resp. Tum dico vanam esse tuam scientiam mediam, qua cognoscit Deus antecedenter ad suam voluntatem futura contingentia, quia ad certitudinem scientiae necesse est prius intelligat actum voluntatis suae: haec Iesuita sic emollire vult. Quapropter (inquit) diligenter notandum est, non esse negandum futura contingentia certo praescii a Deo in priori signo rationis, quam fit illud, in quo voluntas divina se determinet ad haec vel illa efficienda. Hoc enim non dicimus; sed hoc asserimus, non prius Deum considerari, ut scientem futura contingentia, quatenus futura sunt, quam consideretur scire suam voluntatem de iis approbandis, libere se determinaturam ad alteram oppositionis partem: quae voluntas, si in posteriore consideratione signo in quo se determinat, non esset libere determinanda, neque in priore illo, talia contingentia a divino intellectu certo scirentur futura. Hinc certum est Iesuitam concedere nobis quod postulamus, ac proinde scientia media cognoscere Deum futura contingentia tantum ut possibilia antecedenter ad suam determinationem liberam, non vero ut futura: atqui haec scientia est simplicis intelligentiae, quam nos non gravate concedimus, non vero scientia media. 2. Quoniam Iesuita expresse ait ibid. ab actibus liberis divinae voluntatis pendere futura contingentia & eorum certam cognitionem: patet funditus sic everti scientiam mediam quam ille vult infallibilem esse antecedenter ad actus divinae voluntatis, a quibus pendet futuritio actuum liberorum, quod & ipse Vasquez. concedit: Creatura (inquit) nondum futura est, 4· donec decretum voluntatis (Dei) esse intelligatur, ex quo ut ex causa futura est. Idem ait Durand. 3. Mihi videtur omnino ἀκαταλήπτως[?] quomodo res non est futura nisi per divinam voluntatem, tanquam causa futuritionis, & tamen libere fiat ex principiis Jesuitae, item quomodo res est futura prius libere, quam a Deo praedefiniatur, quando praedefinitio sit causa rei liberè futurae.4. Admirabile est mysterium ejusdem Jesuitae negantis sutura contingentia certo cognosci a Deo, nisi in actu approbativo suae voluntatis, non quidem elicito in illo rationis signo, quo contingentia sunt futura, sed eliciendo in alio signo rationis subsequuturo futuritionem ipsorum. Nam in illo signo, in quo contingentia sunt futura, actus liber Dei de eorum futuritione est nondum elicitus, sed eliciendus; sed vel est eliciendus a Deo necessario, & sic non est actus liber, vel libere: si libere, potest non elici talis actus, ex ipsorum principiis, & sic datur futuritio rei contingentis sine omni actu divinae voluntatis, quod est impossibile. Item fatetur Fonseca ibid. arg. 2. Liberam Dei voluntatem esse primam radicem & causam omnis contingentiae, & essectus contingentes pendere ab actu libero Dei. Atqui si futuritio contingentium est antequam eliciatur actus liber Dei, actus liber non est causa illius futuritionis, & contingentia aliqua particularis est prior sua radice & causa. 3. Ait etiam ibid. Jesuita: Si omnis certitudo actuum futurorum contingentium pendeat ex solis decretis divinis, qui fieri potest, ut ea decreta non necessitent volumvoluntates ad omnes actus suos? Sed quaero, an sit certitudo actuum liberorum futurorum antecedenter ad decreta Dei? Si sit, tum etiam est necessitas fundamentalis & entitativa in iis antecedenter ad Dei decreta: Erg. Deus non habet in sua potestate aliter decernere actus liberos, quam sunt antecedenter ad Dei decreta. Eligat jam Iesuita utrum Deum, an homines velit necessitari ad actus liberos. 2. Videtur sequi hinc duas esse necessitates actuum liberorum, unam antecedenter, aliam consequenter ad Dei decreta: at quid opus est Deus praescire in actu approbativo & permissivo suturos actus liberos, si jam sunt illi actus Deo certissimi ante omnes Dei voluntatis approbativos & permissivos actus? Sed nos Arrianis primis hujus scientiae authoribus, ut observat Did. Alvarez, & novatoribus hisce relinquamus hoc mysterium pudendum.
units.tr: 12. Although Peter Fonseca, a Jesuit and among the most distinguished of those who pride themselves on a more exact philosophy, defends this middle knowledge as if it were the altar and hearth itself, and boasts that he is its parent, since he taught it orally in 1569 (though Luis Molina committed it to writing in 1588, a most wretched act), he nevertheless contends, with arguments not to be despised, that contingent things which in fact will come to pass, taken in their absolute state, are not known except in the act of approval or permission of the divine will. This Jesuit mystery seems to me more wonderful than any other. For he holds that propositions about future contingents are determinately true or false before any act of the divine will; yet since the free will of God is the first root and cause of all contingency and freedom, he holds that absolutely future contingents are not known except in God's approving or promising will. Why does the Jesuit do this? Because (you say) a thing either is or is not, and the statement is therefore true or false. So that God may know with certainty what will happen contingently, it is necessary that he understand the act of his own will, from whose concurrence it will depend. I reply: then I say that your middle knowledge, by which God knows future contingents antecedently to his will, is vain, because for certainty of knowledge he must first understand the act of his will. The Jesuit wishes to soften this in the following way: Therefore (he says) it must be carefully noted that it is not to be denied that future contingents are foreknown by God with certainty in the first moment of reason, before that moment in which the divine will determines itself to effect this or that. For we do not say this; we assert rather that God is not first considered as knowing future contingents, insofar as they are future, than he is considered to know his own will to approve them, freely determining itself to the one side of the opposition. If that will, at the later moment of reason in which it determines itself, were not to be freely determined, then neither in that earlier moment would such contingents be known with certainty as future by the divine intellect. Hence it is certain that the Jesuit concedes to us what we demand, and consequently that middle knowledge knows future contingents only as possible, antecedently to his free determination, and not as future. But this is knowledge of simple intelligence, which we readily concede, and not middle knowledge. 2. Since the Jesuit expressly says in the same place that future contingents and their certain knowledge depend on the free acts of the divine will, it is plain that the middle knowledge which he wants to be infallible antecedently to the acts of the divine will, on which the futurition of free acts depends, is utterly overturned. Vasquez also concedes this: a creature (he says) is not yet future until the decree of the (divine) will is understood, from which it is future as from its cause. Durand says the same. To me it seems altogether [ἀκαταλήπτως] incomprehensible how a thing is not future except through the divine will as the cause of its futurition, and yet comes about freely according to the Jesuit's principles; likewise how a thing is future freely before it is predefined by God, when the predefinition is the cause of a freely future thing. 4. Admirable is the mystery of this same Jesuit, who denies that future contingents are known with certainty by God except in the approving act of his will; not indeed as elicited in that moment of reason in which the contingents are future, but as elicited in another moment of reason that follows their futurition. For in that moment in which the contingents are future, the free act of God concerning their futurition has not yet been elicited, but is to be elicited. Now either it is to be elicited by God necessarily, and so it is not a free act, or freely. If freely, such an act may not be elicited, according to their own principles, and so there is futurition of a contingent thing without any act of the divine will, which is impossible. Likewise Fonseca himself, in the same place, under the second argument, admits that the free will of God is the first root and cause of all contingency, and that contingent effects depend on a free act of God. But if the futurition of contingents comes before the free act of God is elicited, then the free act is not the cause of that futurition, and some particular contingent thing is prior to its own root and cause. 3. The Jesuit also says in the same place: If all certainty of future contingent acts depends on the divine decrees alone, how can it be that those decrees do not necessitate the wills to all their acts? But I ask whether there is a certainty of future free acts antecedently to God's decrees. If there is, then there is also a fundamental and entitative necessity in them antecedently to God's decrees. Therefore God does not have it in his power to decree free acts otherwise than as they are antecedently to his decrees. Let the Jesuit now choose whether he wants God, or men, to be necessitated with regard to free acts. 2. It seems to follow from this that there are two necessities of free acts, one antecedent and the other consequent to God's decrees. But what need is there for God to foreknow in an approving and permissive act that free acts will come to pass, if those acts are already most certain to God before all his approving and permissive acts of will? But we shall leave this shameful mystery to the Arians, the first authors of this knowledge, as Didacus Alvarez observes, and to these novelty-mongers.

units.tr: Concerning the notions of the divine will.

units.tr: On the will of sign and of good pleasure.

units.la: AGnoscunt unanimiter Scholastici hanc distinctionem: circa objectum ipsius non nihil discrepant. D. Bannes ait, probabile esse Alexan. 1. quod fit in Deo formaliter actus volendi bonum, qui non compleatur. Alexander Halensis, Cajetanus, Driedo, & alii agnoscunt non esse Dei
units.tr: The Scholastics unanimously acknowledge this distinction, though they differ somewhat about its object. D. Bannes says it is probable that Alexan. 1. there is in God, formally, an act of willing the good which is not fulfilled. Alexander of Hales, Cajetan, Driedo, and others acknowledge that it is not the good pleasure of God that all should obey and be saved.

units.la: [?] Note marks and references are printed in the margin; see the notes below. Dei beneplacitum ut omnes obediant & salventur. Ita Gul. Estius, Alvarez & Dominicanæ familiæ scholastici cum primis nobiles.
units.tr: Thus Gul. Estius, Alvarez, and the scholastics of the Dominican family, the most distinguished of all.

units.la: At vero Vasquez, Suarez, Arminius ejusque asseclæ, Corvinus, Schaafman, volunt Deum decernere voluntate beneplaciti ut omnes vocati obediant & salventur.
units.tr: But Vasquez, Suarez, Arminius and his followers, Corvinus, and Schaafman hold that God decrees, by the will of good pleasure, that all who are called should obey and be saved.

units.la: 2. Voluntas signi, seu illa, quæ alio nomine est revelata & approbans seu præcipiens, consideratur bifariam. 1. Ut objectum ipsius est à Deo decretum ab æterno ut actu existeret: nam uti Deus voluntare signi imperat electis ut sibi faciant cor novum, ita hoc in iis operari ab æterno decrevit, & in tempore promittit Ezechiel. 36. vers. 26, 27. sic voluntas revelata quoad objectum cum voluntate occulta seu decernente, seu efficiente coincidit, neque de eo hic proprie disputatio admodum est intricata. 2. Contradistinguitur hæc voluntas signi à voluntate beneplaciti, hoc modo: Deus revelat creaturæ rem bonam & sanctam, quæ ipsam ad obedientiam obliget, sive obedientia illa actu existat, sive non. Nam hoc diligenter notandum, actualem obedientiam vel non obedientiam, ut à Deo volitam vel nolitam, esse accidentale;plane quid voluntati signi: sive enim actu fiat, sive non, quod Deus in verbo revelat, salvatur essentia voluntatis signi, ideoque res revelata qua volita, hoc est, approbata est objectum voluntatis signi; & eadem res quatenus existit actu vel non existit fit[?] in natura, est objectum voluntatis beneplaciti. 3. Hinc est quod Aquinas, Valentia, Durandus & Suarez velint voluntatem Dei hic divisam, improprie esse voluntatem, & divisionem esse homonymam in homonymata, eo quod voluntas signi sit improprie voluntas. Ita Durand. ad f. 13. Praeceptum enim (inquit) non est directe & semper signum quod praecipiens velit rem praeceptam fieri, sed solum quod velit subditum obligare. Et Aquinas vult esse voluntatis fignum improprie, sicut punitio est irae signum, quando ira formaliter in Deo nulla est: sed quia nos irascimur quando punimus, ideo punitio est signum irae, ideoque Deus (dicerent illi) in voluntate sua revelata potius habeat se ad modum volentis, quam velit: & ingeniorum flos ille illibatus Gul. Tuissius vult Dei voluntatem non transire in rem praeceptam, sed potius in suam praeceptionem, quod certe est verissimum hoc sensu, respectu boni voliti ad extra. Nam ex voluntate signi, non est proprie, quod res volita existat vel non existat, Deus enim multa sic vult, ut obedientiam reproborum, quae actu existere non vult; hoc tamen non est praeterendum, quod voluntas signi respectu sui obiecti est propriissime voluntas. Nam quod Deus praecipit, vult & approbat ut rem bonam & sanctam; quod vetat, improbat ut malum: & ab aeterno decrevit ut illa res sit bona etiam voluntate beneplaciti & decernente, ideoque obiectum omne voluntatis signi, est volitum voluntate beneplaciti, at non continuo objectum omnis voluntatis beneplaciti est à Deo decretum & volitum voluntate signi, sed id tantum quod verbo revelatur, ut justum aut injustum; & hoc sensu voluntas signi & in præceptionem & prohibitionem, & in rem præceptam & prohibitam terminatur & transit.
units.tr: 2. The will of sign, or that which is revealed under another name and approves or commands, is considered in two ways. 1. As to its object, it is what God has decreed from eternity that it should actually exist. For just as God commands the elect by the will of sign to make themselves a new heart, so from eternity he decreed that this should be worked in them, and in time he promises it (Ezekiel 36.26, 27). Thus the revealed will, as to its object, coincides with the hidden will, whether decreeing or effecting, and the dispute about this is not really very intricate. 2. This will of sign is distinguished from the will of good pleasure in the following way: God reveals to the creature a good and holy thing, which binds it to obedience, whether that obedience actually exists or not. For it must be carefully noted that actual obedience or disobedience, as willed or unwilled by God, is accidental to the will of sign. For whether it actually happens or not, what God reveals in his Word, the essence of the will of sign is preserved. Therefore the thing revealed, as willed, that is, as approved, is the object of the will of sign; and the same thing, insofar as it exists or does not exist in nature, is the object of the will of good pleasure. 3. Hence Aquinas, Valentia, Durandus, and Suarez want this division of God's will to be improper, and the division to be one of homonyms into homonyms, because the will of sign is improperly a will. So Durand. ad f. 13. For a precept (he says) is not directly and always a sign that the one commanding wills the commanded thing to be done, but only that he wills to bind the subject. And Aquinas holds that it is a sign of the will improperly, just as punishment is a sign of anger when anger is not formally in God; but because we are angry when we punish, therefore punishment is a sign of anger. Hence God (they would say) in his revealed will stands rather in the manner of one willing than wills. And that unblemished flower of talents, Gul. Tuissius, holds that God's will does not pass into the thing commanded, but rather into his own command; which is certainly most true in this sense, with respect to the good willed outside God. For it is not properly from the will of sign that the willed thing exists or does not exist, since God wills many things in this way, such as the obedience of the reprobate, which he does not will to exist in act. Yet this must not be passed over: the will of sign, with respect to its own object, is most properly a will. For what God commands, he wills and approves as a good and holy thing; what he forbids, he disapproves as evil. And from eternity he decreed that this thing should be good, also by the will of good pleasure and decreeing. Therefore every object of the will of sign is willed by the will of good pleasure; but the object of every will of good pleasure is not continually decreed and willed by God by the will of sign, but only that which is revealed in the Word, as just or unjust. And in this sense the will of sign terminates and passes both into the command and prohibition, and into the thing commanded and forbidden.

units.la: 4. Quæres igitur, quid voluntas signi nobis exprimat? Resp. exprimere. 1. Hanc esse verbi naturam, ut fidem & bona opera instanter urgeat & persuadeat. 2. Revelare legem & euangelium, nempe sapiens & sanctissimum Dei decretum & beneplacitum de præmiandis obedientibus, & plectendis immorigeris, Micha. 6.8. Indicavit tibi o homo quid sit bonum. Rom. 12. 2, 3. Revelat nobis omnium ossicium esse & obligationem ut obediant. Obad. 13. Non debebas aspexisse in diem fratris tui. 4. Exprimat denique nobis, Deum simpliciter approbare actuque complacentiæ velle obedientiam hominum, sive actu obediunt, sive non.
units.tr: 4. You will ask, then, what the will of sign expresses to us? I answer that it expresses: 1. That it is the nature of the Word to urge and persuade faith and good works earnestly. 2. That it reveals the law and the gospel, namely the wise and most holy decree and good pleasure of God concerning the rewarding of the obedient and the punishing of the disobedient (Micah 6.8: He has shown you, O man, what is good. Romans 12.2, 3.). It reveals to us that it is the duty and obligation of all to obey (Obadiah 13: You ought not to have looked on the day of your brother). 5. Finally, it expresses to us that God simply approves, and by an act of complacency wills the obedience of men, whether they obey in act or not.

units.la: 1. Sam. 15.20, 21, 22. At vero quod ad actualem obedientiam, voluntas signi formaliter ipsam non vult, hoc est, non hac voluntate intenditur, & sic hæc Deum virtualiter & eminenter velle, quæ jubet, observavit gravis & eruditus Vir Doct. Gulielmus Ame-tic. 1. Bnd. [illegible, ~8 letters]
units.tr: 1 Sam. 15.20, 21, 22. But as to actual obedience, the will of sign does not formally will it; that is, it is not intended by this will. And that God wills virtually and eminently what he commands, a grave and learned man, Dr. Guilielmus Ame-tic. 1. Bnd. [illegible, ~8 letters]

units.la: 5. Hinc multis nominibus differunt voluntas signi & beneplaciti. 1. Differunt ipsis actibus. Nam voluntas beneplaciti est Dei decretum & æterna determinatio de re fienda vel non : voluntas signi est actus divinae complacentiae de re non facienda, sed simplex amatio rei, sive fiat sive non. 2. Differunt objectis. Objectum voluntatis approbantis est bonum qua bonum: quatenus vetat, est malum morale, hoc est, bonum aut malum, quatenus legi vel evangelio convenit, vel non, sed tale bonum morale, quod de se abstrahit ab actuali existentia rei mandatae vel veritæ. At objectum decreti est non bonum morale qua tale, sed bonum, vel id quod habet rationem expedientiæ & conducibilitatis in relatione ad sapientissimam Dei libertatem, & quidem non abstrahens ab existentia, sed quatenus indeclinabiliter est actu extituram per decretum Dei vel non. Hinc Deus quædam approbat, ut obedientiam Iudæ & Pharaonis, quæ tamen quoad realem existentiam, nunquam fieri decrevit, & quædam sub ratione conducibilis boni, licet non sub ratione honesti, decrevit, ut venditionem Iosephi, occisionem Salvatoris a truculentis & feris sicariis, quæ nullo modo approbat ullo complacentiæ actu. Hinc 3. objectum voluntatis approbantis est multo arctius & angustius objecto decreti. Nam objectum voluntatis approbantis est bonum & malum morale, quatenus præceptione & inhibitione legali nos obliget: at objectum decreti est hoc, & insuper id quod Deus non ex officio aut debito, sed ex sapientissima libertate tanquam universalis & supremus omnium Dominus &c nus & rerum moderator fieri statuit & decernit, & non tantum quae decernit tanquam legislator. Hoc itaque observandum est, Dei decreta non coarctari aut limitari quoad aequitatem ipsorum à voluntate approbante: sed contra, voluntas approbans limitatur & determinatur à libero Dei decreto: ideoque non ex officio tenetur Deus, aut ulla lege astringitur aut regulatur aliunde quam à solo suo beneplacito in decretis suis liberis faciendis: neque haec res est Deo bona, & objectum congruum decreti, quia est approbanti voluntati consentanea & justa, quasi Deus injusta faceret, si contrarium decerneret. Sic enim non posset decernere jure, nisi quae lege aut euangelio jubentur, & ex necessitate justitiae teneretur[?], lege aut euangelio prohibita non decernere: id quod est aperte falsum. Dicant enim mihi adversarii, num lege aut euangelio scriptum sit, ut Deus vel permitteret peccatum, vel non permitteret ullo debito aut ex aequo? ubi scripturarum jubetur Deus uni facere gratiae efficacis copiam, alteri denegare eandem, hunc eligere, illum reprobare, huic genti euangelii lucem indulgere, & etiam genti meliori eandem negare, etiam ex consessione Arminianorum? Ita docent post ipsum Arminium, Remonstr. in scriptis synodi Dordrac. ita Corvinus. Ac proinde Deus quamvis contrarium voluntati nequeat decernere (sic enim sibi ipsi contradiceret) attamen non ab ea regulatur in decretis: at vero voluntas approbans regulatur à decreto libero: ideo enim hoc lege & euangelio approbat, illud improbat, quia ita sapienti sua libertate voluit. Et quis ignorat Deum posse vetare multa, quae imperat, & imperare quae vetuit? Næ illi itaque somniant qui decretū praedestinationis proprie iustum appellent: est proprie liberum. At iustitia illa Dei, scripturis nobis revelata, est posterior natura decreto praedestinationis in signo rationis: ideo enim eligit aut reprobat, non proprie quia est æquum & iustum, quasi ex iustitia ut à principio formali hi actus fluerent. Sic e. iniustum esset, si alii vel plures, vel pauciores electi aut reprobati forent, quam qui electi aut reprobati jam sunt, sed quia ita sapienti sua libertate & dominio decrevit. 4. Hinc ex voluntate approbante, sequitur hanc rem esse iustam aut iniustam, sed non hoc actu exiturum vel non, qua tali: ex decreto vero non sequitur legalitas aut æquitas aut iniquitas rei, sed tantū existentia ipsius necessaria tandē aliquando præscripto à Deo tempore. Nam voluntas signi respicit ποῖόν τι[?] nempe qualitatem & naturam facti, quod reprobi ex officio præstare tenentur, sicut & electi, præcisa consideratione efficientiæ aut actualis existentiæ rei mandatæ aut prohibitæ: at vero decretum respicit, non ποῖον[?] sed τὸ ὄν[?] nempe quod res sit tandem indeclinabiliter sutura & extitura actu, sive sit æqua aut iniqua.
units.tr: 5. Hence the will of sign and the will of good pleasure differ in many respects. 1. They differ in their acts. For the will of good pleasure is God's decree and eternal determination concerning a thing to be done or not done; the will of sign is an act of divine complacency concerning a thing not to be done, but a simple love of the thing, whether it is done or not. 2. They differ in their objects. The object of the approving will is the good as good; insofar as it forbids, it is moral evil, that is, good or evil insofar as it agrees or does not agree with the law or gospel; but it is such a moral good as abstracts from the actual existence of the commanded or forbidden thing. But the object of the decree is not the moral good as such, but the good, or that which has the character of expediency and advantage in relation to God's most wise liberty; and indeed not abstracting from existence, but insofar as by God's decree it will inevitably exist in act or not. Hence God approves certain things, such as the obedience of Judah and of Pharaoh, which yet he never decreed to exist in reality; and he decreed certain things under the aspect of a useful good, though not under the aspect of the honourable, such as the selling of Joseph, and the killing of the Saviour by savage and wild assassins, which he in no way approves by any act of complacency. Hence 3. the object of the approving will is much narrower and more restricted than the object of the decree. For the object of the approving will is moral good and evil, insofar as it binds us by legal command and prohibition; but the object of the decree is this, and in addition that which God decides and determines to be done not from duty or obligation, but from his most wise liberty, as the universal and supreme Lord of all and ruler of things, and not only what he decrees as lawgiver. Therefore it must be observed that God's decrees are not restricted or limited as to their equity by the approving will; rather, on the contrary, the approving will is limited and determined by God's free decree. Therefore God is not bound by duty, nor constrained by any law, nor regulated from any source other than his own good pleasure in making his free decrees; nor is this matter good for God, and a fitting object of the decree, because it agrees with the approving will and is just. It would be as if God acted unjustly if he decreed the contrary. For thus he could decree lawfully only what is commanded by law or gospel, and by the necessity of justice he would be bound not to decree what is forbidden by law or gospel; which is plainly false. For let my opponents tell me: is it written in law or gospel that God should either permit sin, or not permit it, by any debt or equity? Where in the Scriptures is God commanded to grant the supply of efficacious grace to one and deny it to another, to choose this one and reprobate that one, to grant the light of the gospel to this nation and deny the same to a better nation? Even by the confession of the Arminians, is this so? Thus Arminius himself taught, and after him the Remonstrants in the writings of the Synod of Dort, and thus Corvinus. And therefore God, although he cannot decree the contrary of what the will approves (for thus he would contradict himself), is nevertheless not regulated by it in his decrees. But the approving will is regulated by the free decree; for he approves this by law and gospel and disapproves that because he willed it so by his wise liberty. And who does not know that God can forbid many things which he commands, and command what he has forbidden? Those therefore dream who call the decree of predestination properly just: it is properly free. But that justice of God, revealed to us in the Scriptures, is in the order of reason posterior in nature to the decree of predestination. For he chooses or reprobates not properly because it is equal and just, as if these acts flowed from justice as from their formal principle. Thus it would be unjust if more or fewer were elected or reprobated than those who are now elected or reprobated; but he decreed it so by his wise liberty and dominion. 4. Hence from the approving will it follows that this thing is just or unjust, but not that it will or will not exist in act as such; but from the decree it does not follow that the thing is lawful, equitable, or iniquitous, but only that its existence is necessary, to be brought about at some time appointed by God. For the will of sign regards the what-kind (ποῖόν τι), namely the quality and nature of the deed, which the reprobate are bound to perform by duty, just as the elect are, setting aside the consideration of efficacy or of the actual existence of the thing commanded or forbidden; but the decree regards not the what-kind but the being (τὸ ὄν), namely that the thing will at last inevitably be and exist in act, whether it is equitable or iniquitous.

units.la: 5. Voluntas approbans non revelat nobis intentionem aut decretum Dei: hæc enim & similia, (Cain, Saule, Pharaoh, Iuda, obedite, & credite, ) non habent hoc pro re significatâ aut volirâ à Deo, mea hæc est intentio, & decretum est apud me ab æterno,ut vos obediretis. Si enim hoc Deus verbis exprimeret[?], procul dubio qui ponunt in Deo voluntatem signi & beneplaciti hoc sensu faterentur necefse effet, esse in Deo contradictorias voluntates circa unum & idem objectum uniforme. Id nobis Arminiani vel ex ignorantiâ vel solâ libidine calumniandi salsissime imputant: sed tantum dicit Deus hoc præcepto Cajino, Saulo & Pharaoni propósito; ego indico, & præcepto vobis revelo, mihi gratam & acceptam esse obedientiam, ad quam præstandam vos ex lege & debito obligati estis creatori vestro, siquidem ei accepti esse velitis, sive actu obediatis, sive non: jam illi non obediunt: nulla hic vel umbra contradictionis. Non enim dicit Deus, volo ut obediatis, & interim apud me decerno & volo ut non obediatis, sed tantum voluntas mea vestram obedientiam approbat, & amat actu simplicis complacentiæ, quo bonum amo, malum aversor, & volo etiam & decerno, ut nunquam actu obediatis. Quid enim impedit, quo minus Deus multa approbet, ut entia juxta omnipotentiam possibilia, ut plures mundos, & plures angelos bonos, & obedientiam angelorum bonorum, qui nunquam sunt creandi, etsi illa non fore decernat aut intendat? Dicet aliquis, euangelium sæpe, ut & legem revelare ipfamDei intentionem & decretum, quod ipse exequitur, ut quando promittit se effecturum cor novum in electis, se reprobos induraturum, & immorigeros æterno exitio devoturum. Resp. Neque hoc potest negari, voluntatem signi interdum revelare Dei decretum: tum enim ipsum decretum transit per illam revelationem in voluntatem signi, ut patet in allatis exemplis, sed instituta est præfens hæc διατάξις[?] præcipue de voluntate signi, qua Deus revelat creaturis, quid ipsæ teneantur facere, sive faciant sive non, & prout contradistinguitur a voluntate beneplaciti, qua Deus quod ipse facturus est, vel per seipsum immediate, vel interventu creaturarum, libere decernit: & dico voluntatem signi in hac restrictione nullo modo revelare Dei intentionem, quod nimirum ipse intendit efficere, quod præcepto revelat, vel avertere aut impedire, quod prohibet. 6. Quod Deus decernit illud libere decernit & vult, & potest non velle: at vero voluntas approbans necessario bonum amat, nempe necessitate hypothetica, quoniam hæc voluntas præfupponit liberum & sapiens Dei decretum, quo statuit hoc esse bonum; & tum Deus id non potest non velle, hoc est, amare & approbare actu simplicis complacentiæ, quamvis forte decreverit ut nunquam fieret. Inde est quod Deus approbet bonum secundum essentiam, etiam ut non existit, uti aprobat obedientiam omnium, tum electorum tum reproborum. At quæri potest causa, quare Deus possit approbare bonum, quod nunquam actu existit: at vero non potest decernere illud. Resp. Potest decernere quicquid approbat, sed non vult, quia libere decernit, quicquid decernit: at vero non approbare non potest bonum ex hypothesi. quod jam boni essentiam habeat per liberum decretum. Et ratio est duplex. 1. Quia bonum est affectio entis quod comitatur ens non tantum prout actu exsistit, sed etiam secundum essentiam ei convenit. Hinc est quod bonum quoad essentiam potest movere appetitum creaturarum, & terminare appetitum Dei, etsi actu nunquam exsistat. 2. Quod Deus decreto libero bonum esse voluit, nempe ut homines colant Deum, seniores revereantur, Deus nOn potest non amare & approbare in omnibus, etsi omnes hoc actu non faciant, quia quod Deus voluit in decreto, non post non velle. Hisce adde, quod approbatio est simplex complacentia voluntatis, qua consentit bono quod sit bonum, ideoque non approbari non potest a Deo bonum secundum essentiam: at vero decretio rei est Dei libera volitio, ut actu fit, in aliqua differentia temporis. Hinc patet Deum posse voluntate consentire rei ut bonae, & tamen velle potest ut nunquam actu exsistat, alioqui necesse foret ut ut Deus decerneret, adeoque ut efficeret ut omnia bona possibilia actu exsisterent, nempe millies milleni mundi, angeli, homines, actus obedientiae creaturarum intelligentium quae Deo sunt possibilia, quod absurdum est.
units.tr: 5. An approving will does not reveal God's intention or decree to us. Such statements as these, addressed to Cain, Saul, Pharaoh, Judah (obey, and believe), do not present as a thing signified or willed by God, "this is my intention, and it has been my decree from eternity that you should obey." For if God expressed this in words, then, without doubt, those who posit in God a will of sign and a will of good pleasure in this sense would have to admit that there are contradictory wills in God concerning one and the same object. Our Arminians very wittily impute this to us, either out of ignorance or from sheer appetite for slander. But God says only this, by the precept, to Cain, to Saul and to Pharaoh; I point it out and reveal it to you by the precept: my obedience is pleasing and acceptable to me, and you are bound by law and duty to render it to your Creator, if you wish to be acceptable to him, whether you actually obey or not. Now they do not obey, and here there is not even a shadow of contradiction. For God does not say, "I wish you to obey, and meanwhile I decree and will that you not obey"; rather, my will approves your obedience and loves it with the act of simple complacency, by which I love the good and turn from evil, and I also will and decree that you never actually obey. For what prevents God from approving many things that are possible according to his omnipotence, such as more worlds, more good angels, and the obedience of good angels who are never to be created, even though he does not decree or intend that these shall come about? Someone will say that the gospel, like the law, often reveals God's own intention and decree, which he carries out, as when he promises that he will effect a new heart in the elect, that he will harden the reprobate, and that he will devote the disobedient to eternal destruction. I reply: this cannot be denied, that the will of sign sometimes reveals God's decree; for then the decree itself passes through that revelation into the will of sign, as is clear from the examples cited. But this present distinction is set up chiefly concerning the will of sign, by which God reveals to creatures what they themselves are bound to do, whether they do it or not, and insofar as it is distinguished from the will of good pleasure, by which God freely decrees what he himself is going to do, either immediately through himself or through the intervention of creatures. And I say that the will of sign, in this restriction, in no way reveals God's intention, namely what he himself intends to bring about, which he reveals by precept, or what he intends to avert or prevent, which he forbids. 6. What God decrees, he decrees and wills freely, and he is able not to will it. But the approving will necessarily loves the good, namely by hypothetical necessity, since this will presupposes the free and wise decree of God by which he establishes this to be good; and then God cannot not will it, that is, love and approve it with the act of simple complacency, although perhaps he has decreed that it should never come to pass. Hence it is that God approves the good according to its essence, even as it does not exist, just as he approves the obedience of all, both of the elect and of the reprobate. But it may be asked why God can approve a good that never actually exists, yet cannot decree it. I reply: he can decree whatever he approves, but he does not will to, because whatever he decrees he decrees freely; whereas, once the good has its essence through a free decree, it is not possible, on that supposition, for him not to approve it. And the reason is twofold. 1. Because the good is an affection of being which accompanies being not only as it actually exists, but which also belongs to it according to its essence. Hence the good, as to its essence, can move the appetite of creatures and terminate the appetite of God, even though it never actually exists. 2. Because God, by a free decree, willed that the good should be, namely that men should worship God and that elders should be reverenced, God cannot not love and approve it in all cases, even if all do not actually do it, because what God willed in his decree he cannot not will. To these add that approval is the simple complacency of the will, by which it consents that a thing is good; so the good according to its essence cannot but be approved by God. But the decreeing of a thing is God's free volition that it should come to pass actually, at some point in time. Hence it is plain that God can consent by his will to a thing as good, and yet can will that it never actually exists; otherwise it would be necessary, whatever God decreed, that he should bring about that all possible goods actually existed, namely a thousand thousand worlds, angels, men, and acts of obedience of intelligent creatures, which are possible to God; and this is absurd.

units.la: 7. Voluntas signi verbo revelatur, & eam fide apprehendere tenemur: Deus enim legi & testimonio nos astringit Efai. 8. At decreta Dei, prout ab hac voluntate contradiftinguuntur, eventu patefiunt, non proprie verbo, nisi quatenus decretum transit in voluntatem signi, ideoque quando Deus jussit Abrahamum immolare filium, non tenebatur Abrahamus credere immolationem Isaci, esse decretam & intentam a Deo, sed fui esse officii ut immolaret Isaacum. Si Deus expresse dicit se hoc facturum, tum quidem credendum est ipsum decretum, sed eventu decreta proprie revelantur, si ego credo, tum constat Deum fidem meam decrevisse: si nunquam credat aliquis, constat Deum nunquam decrevisse, ut iste[?] crederet. Hinc patet, Arminianos arenosas nobis nectere consequentias, nempe Deus jubet omnes in visibili ecclesia credere: Ergo decrevit conditionate, vel voluntate antecedenter ut omnes crederent. Negamus sequelam, nam quod Deus vult fieri, id non potest non fieri, neque est scripta talis intentio de me aut te nominatim, sed eventu patefit decretum. Iubent itaque hi boni viri homines credere falsum, quod nobis invidiose ascribunt: haec nostra est super hac distinctione sententia.
units.tr: 7. The will of sign is revealed by the Word, and we are bound to apprehend it by faith; for God binds us to the law and the testimony, Isaiah 8. But the decrees of God, insofar as they are distinguished from this will, are made manifest by the event, not properly by the Word, except insofar as a decree passes over into the will of sign. Therefore, when God commanded Abraham to sacrifice his son, Abraham was not bound to believe that the sacrifice of Isaac was decreed and intended by God, but it was his duty to sacrifice Isaac. If God expressly says that he will do this, then indeed the decree itself must be believed; but decrees are properly revealed by the event. If I believe, then it is established that God decreed my faith; if no one ever believes, it is established that God never decreed that this man should believe. Hence it is plain that the Arminians weave sandy consequences against us: God commands all in the visible Church to believe; therefore he decreed conditionally, or by an antecedent will, that all should believe. We deny the consequence, for what God wills to come about cannot but come about, and no such intention is written concerning me or you by name, but the decree is made manifest by the event. These good men therefore bid men believe what is false, which they invidiously ascribe to us; this is our opinion concerning this distinction.

units.la: 6. Hinc hanc thesin probo.
units.tr: 6. From this I prove the following thesis.

units.la: Deus multa verbo præcipit, quæ fieri non vovoluit, hoc est, nunquam decrevit aut intendit, ut actu existerent.
units.tr: God commands many things in the Word which he has not willed to be done, that is, he has never decreed or intended that they should actually come to pass.

units.la: Adversariorum causa liceat mihi incipere, ab ipsorum confessione. Ita Vorstius: Etsi igitur Deus non tam subito populum suum ( a Pharaone ) dimitti fortasse voluit, postquam ipsius malitiam omnino punire ac traducere decrevisset, vere tamen praestari ab eo tandem voluit quod saepius illi praeceperat. Ita Corvinus: Voluit Deus inobedientiam (Pharaonis) extare continuam ac diuturnam, ut tanto justior esset punitio. Hinc sequitur Deum praecepisse Pharaoni, quae fieri noluit: Corvinus mollire-satagens Vorstij verba, ait Vorstij velle idem hic esse ac permittere, itane vero? Reclamant ipsius verba. 1. Utitur voce dubitativa (fortasse) ut ipse Corvinus notat: creditne quaeso Vorstius Deum fortasse permittere, Pharaonem non dimittere populum? Atqui non fortasse, sed procul dubio permisit, ex Vorstio: corrumpit ergo mentem & verba Vorstij. 2. Ait Vorstius (vere tamen praestari ab eo tandem voluit, quod saepius illi praeceperat) quaero ex Vorstio, an non secundum ipsius doctrinam, non tantum tandem, sed semper etiam quando Deus praecepit Pharaoni dimissionem, voluit vere dimissionem, an tantum vere voluit tandem, hoc est post inflictam decimam plagam: quicquid dixerit, capietur: si non vere voluit post primam, post secundam, post tertiam plagam, ergo praecepit aliquid quod non vere voluit: at hoc est ponere in Deo, ipsis fatentibus, voluntates contradictorias & hypocrisin, & certe illud (vere voluit) idem est ac si dixisset, antea non vere voluit sed simulate. Si vero vere voluit ab initio & semper dimisfionem, quorsum sunt illa verba (vere voluit tandem:) & falso (fortasse non tam subito dimitti voluit) dixit? Deinde Corvinus concedit & certe consentanee admodum & convenienter Arminij Palato: Postquam Pharaoh inobediens esse cœpit, Deum voluisse inobedientiam ejus extare diuturnam ac continuam. Assumo ego, atqui postquam Pharaoh cœpit esse inobediens, Deus dixit Pharaoni multoties, dimitte populum meum, uti testatur sacra historia: ergo Deus Pharaonem saltem inobedientem hypocritice & malo dolo allocutus est. Major est Corvini & Vorstij & Arminij. Assumtio est sacræ scripturæ: conclusio igitur sua vi valebit. Hæc est hypocrisis (ait Corvinus) si Deus præcepto significet, velle se ut homo aliquid agat (ut Pharaoh jam inobediens & contumax dimitteret populum, ut ait Corvinus) intus vero, & apud se, nollet, ut id ipsum agat. Addo ego, ut Deus intus & apud se velit inobedientis Pharaonis inobedientiam extare continuam, ut tanto justior effet punitio. jam arrigite aures vestras Arminani, ita Iehova Pharaonem affatur: quamvis intus & apud me voluerim & decreverim, ut post secundam, & tertiam plagam populum meum dimitteres, idque præcepto (dimitte, inobediens Pharaoh, populum meum) significaverim, tamen revera apud me volo & decerno ut diuturna & continua extet tua inobedientia, ut tanto justius puniaris. Et hoc est revera Deum habere erga præfractos & propter malitiam voluntariam incorrigibiles, ut citato loco habet Arminius, contradictorias & contrarias circa unum & idem objectum voluntates. Quid hic Corvinus? postquam Pharaoh est (inquit) inobediens potest urgere praeceptum in finem contrarium priori fini primitus intento, nempe ut justius puniatur tyrannus, at valebit hoc per nos. Huc ergo tendunt: potest Deus aliud loqui, aliud velle & hypocritice & malo dolo agere cum Pharone jam inobediente; non potest sic agere cum obediente: quid? quia homo peccat, Deus jure potest veteratorem agere & peccare, eo fine ut justius puniantur praefracti? Itane? an peccatum hominis laxat habenas Iehovae, ut possit peccare? o theologiam prodigiosam! neque finis bonus malum factum, cujusmodi est hypocrisis, excusare potest, ut vult Jacob. Arminius. Hic necesse est ad nos accedant, vel in aeternum haerebunt, vel haec erunt thesis Arminianae.
units.tr: Let me begin with my opponents, from their own confession. Thus Vorstius: Although God perhaps did not wish his people to be dismissed by Pharaoh so suddenly, after he had decided utterly to punish and bring down his wickedness, yet at last he truly wished to bring about what he had often commanded him. Thus Corvinus: God willed that Pharaoh's disobedience should continue and endure for a long time, so that the punishment might be all the more just. From this it follows that God commanded Pharaoh what he was unwilling to have done. Corvinus, labouring to soften the words of Vorstius, says that for Vorstius to will is here the same as to permit. Really so? His own words protest against this. (1) He uses the doubtful word (perhaps), as Corvinus himself notes: does Vorstius, I ask, believe that God perhaps permitted Pharaoh not to dismiss the people? But on Vorstius's account it was not perhaps but beyond doubt that he permitted it; so Corvinus corrupts the mind and words of Vorstius. (2) Vorstius says (that at last he truly wished to bring about what he had often commanded him). I ask Vorstius whether, according to his teaching, God not only at last but always, whenever he commanded Pharaoh to dismiss the people, truly willed the dismissal, or only truly willed it at last, that is, after the tenth plague was inflicted. Whatever he says, he will be caught: if he did not truly will it after the first, second and third plagues, then he commanded something he did not truly will. But this is to attribute to God, as they themselves confess, contradictory wills and hypocrisy; and surely (truly willed) is the same as saying that before he did not will it truly but feigned. If indeed from the beginning and always he truly willed the dismissal, why did he use those words (truly willed at last) and falsely (perhaps he did not wish the people dismissed so suddenly)? Then Corvinus concedes, and surely very consistently and agreeably with the taste of Arminius: after Pharaoh began to be disobedient, God willed that his disobedience should continue long and unbroken. I assume: but after Pharaoh began to be disobedient, God told Pharaoh many times, let my people go, as sacred history testifies. Therefore God addressed Pharaoh, at least when he was disobedient, with hypocrisy and evil deceit. The major premise belongs to Corvinus, Vorstius and Arminius; the assumption is from Holy Scripture; the conclusion will therefore hold by its own force. This is hypocrisy (says Corvinus), if God by his command signifies that he wills a man to do something (as Pharaoh, already disobedient and obstinate, should dismiss the people, as Corvinus says), but inwardly and in himself he is unwilling that he should do it. I add: that God, inwardly and in himself, wills the disobedience of the disobedient Pharaoh to continue, so that the punishment might be all the more just. Now prick up your ears, Arminians. Thus Jehovah speaks to Pharaoh: although inwardly and with myself I have willed and decreed that after the second and third plagues you should dismiss my people, and have signified this by a command (dismiss, disobedient Pharaoh, my people), nevertheless in truth, with myself, I will and decree that your disobedience should continue and endure, so that you may be punished all the more justly. And this is indeed for God to have, toward the obstinate and those incorrigible through voluntary wickedness, as Arminius holds in the passage cited, contradictory and contrary wills about one and the same object. What does Corvinus say here? After Pharaoh is (he says) disobedient, the command can urge toward an end contrary to the end first intended, namely that the tyrant be more justly punished; but this, he says, will hold for us. So they tend to this: God can say one thing, will another, and act with hypocrisy and evil deceit toward Pharaoh, already disobedient; he cannot so act toward an obedient man. What? Because a man sins, can God rightly act as a deceiver and sin, with the end that the obstinate may be punished more justly? Is that so? Or does the sin of man loosen the reins of Jehovah, so that he may sin? O prodigious theology! Nor can a good end excuse an evil deed, such as hypocrisy, as Jacob Arminius wants. Here it is necessary that they come over to us, or they will stick fast forever; or these will be the Arminian theses:

units.la: 1. Duae contrariae voluntates sint in Deo.
units.tr: 1. There are two contrary wills in God.

units.la: 2. Deus hypocritice & malo dolo agit cum praefractis.
units.tr: 2. God acts with hypocrisy and evil deceit toward the obstinate.

units.la: 3. Praefracti tenentur credere falsa & contradicentia Deum loqui.
units.tr: 3. The obstinate are bound to believe that God speaks falsehoods and contradictions.

units.la: 7. Sed ago Scripturis[?] Exod. 7. v. 2. Deus alloquitur Pharaonem ut dimittat filios Israelis e terra sua. 3. Ego vero obdurabo cor Pharaonis, ut multiplicem signa mea & prodigia in terra Ægyptiaca. 10. 1,2. ad Pharaonem. Nam ego aggravavi cor ejus &c. ut enarres filio tuo, quae praeclare gessero in Ægyptios. Hinc arguo: si Deus dicit Pharaoni (dimitte populum meum) ut patefiat gloria justitiæ, & longanimitatis, & potentiæ, & eo fine aggravet cor Pharaonis, ut posteris innotefcat talis gloria, tum non ea intentione aut voluntate præcipit ut Pharaoh obediat & salvetur, neque revera vult, ut obediat & salvetur: sed prius exprelse habetur in textu Exod. 9. 13, 14, 15. Rom. 9. 17. vide etiam Ezech. 28. 22. & c. 27. 17. Ergo verum consequens. Prob. major. Quoniam de fine Arminiano nempe ut Pharaoh obediat & salvetur nusquam scriptura vel syllabam vel jota unum habet: at vero finis hic assignatus, nempe ut Deus edat signa, ut declaretur nomen & potentia Dei, ut patefiat ira, expresse habetur; at vero non non potest Deus & intendere ut obediat, & non patefiat gloria justitiæ, & ut non obediat & patefiat gloria misericordiæ. Nam sic efsent in Deo contrariæ volitiones, neque dici potest Deum vel intendere gloriam misericordiæ, vel sin [?] minus, gloriam justitiæ, quia sic Deus non aliter quam terrenus judex penderet intentione ancipite & pendula inter contrarios fines, & id intenderet, quod præscit nunquam futurum fore, quod est absurdum. Item Deus alloquens Pharaonem vel considerat eum ut obedientem, vel non obedientem: non ut obedientem, quia sic ex placitis Arminianis non potest aggravare cor Pharaonis morigeri, neque eam aggravationem intendere. Id enim volunt illi alienum esse à Dei justitia: at vero post quintam aut sextam plagam inflictam, non potest Pharaoh considerari ut obediens sed ut jam meritus aggravationem, in quo statu Deus ei praecipiens, ut dimitteret populum, revera nec voluit nec intendit populi dimissionem, sed additionem plurium signorum, ut patefieret Dei nomen posteris, id quod Arminiani non diffitentur. Quid ad haec Jacksonus; videat quaeso Lector? Ait ille exemplum Pharaonis esse extraordinarium, & proponi eo fine ut caveamus a desperatis cum Deo colludandi principiis. Et ibid. ait, post septimam plagam inflictam, non fuisse Dei voluntatem, ut populum dimitteret, & tamen (inquit) postquam ipsius cor ita obduratum effet, ut resipiscere non posset, Deus ita punivit illum, ac si liberum & possibile ei foret resipiscere, & amicam populo suo egressum indulgere. Sed huc redit rudis ille novator: nempe Deus non ordinarie, bene tamen casu quodam extraordinario potest malo dolo & aequi vocatione lefuitica cum hominibus uti. Nam Deus post 7. plagam Exod. 9. 13. jussit Pharaonem dimittere populum suum, & recusanti plagam octavam inflixit. Ita ergo Deus Pharaonem alloquitur post septimam plagam: jubeo dimittas populum meum; id enim ego volo & decerno, sed quando jam rebellis evaseris, jubeo dimittas; volo tamen & decerno ut non dimittas. Estne hoc contradicentia Deum loqui? Bene est, extraordinarie tantum hoc facit. 2. Saepius Arminiani nos incusant, quod faciamus Deum ultorem peccatorum neceffitare commissorum: habemus hic reum confitentem, Deum punire Pharaonem post septimam plagam, quando jam non posset resipiscere, & hic etiam Deus erit injustus, fuccenset rei quam esse vult & decernit, id quod hic bonus vir p. 170. ait non cadere in habitatores gehennæ: sed salva res est per distinctiunculam, Deus ordinarie est justus: extraordinarie tamen injustus, & facit Pharaoni, quod nemo ex habitatoribus gehennæ jure facere posset.3. Neque ita extraordinarium est Pharaonis exemplum, quia Rom. 9. 17. est exemplar omnium qui sese indurant, & a Deo indurantur.
units.tr: 7. But come, let us go to Scripture. Exod. 7. v. 2: God addresses Pharaoh that he should let the sons of Israel go out of his land. 3: But I will harden the heart of Pharaoh, that I may multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt. 10. 1, 2: to Pharaoh: For I have hardened his heart etc., that you may tell your son what I have wonderfully done against the Egyptians. Hence I argue: if God says to Pharaoh, let my people go, so that the glory of his justice, long-suffering and power may be made manifest, and to that end hardens Pharaoh's heart, so that such glory may become known to posterity, then he does not command with the intention or will that Pharaoh should obey and be saved, nor does he truly will that he should obey and be saved. This is expressly stated in the text: Exod. 9. 13, 14, 15; Rom. 9. 17; see also Ezek. 28. 22 and c. 27. 17. Therefore the consequent is true. Proof of the major: concerning the Arminian end, namely that Pharaoh should obey and be saved, Scripture nowhere has a syllable or a jot; but the end here assigned, namely that God should work signs, that the name and power of God should be declared, that wrath should be made manifest, is expressly stated. Yet God cannot both intend that he obey, and the glory of justice not be made manifest, and that he not obey and the glory of mercy be made manifest. For thus there would be contrary volitions in God, nor can it be said that God intends either the glory of mercy or, if not that, the glory of justice; for thus God would hang, no differently from an earthly judge, in a wavering intention poised between contrary ends, and would intend what he foreknows will never come to be, which is absurd. Likewise, God addressing Pharaoh either regards him as obedient or as not obedient. Not as obedient, for then, by Arminian principles, he cannot harden the heart of a compliant Pharaoh, nor intend that hardening; for they hold that this is alien to God's justice. But after the fifth or sixth plague has been inflicted, Pharaoh cannot be regarded as obedient but as one who has already deserved hardening; and in that state God, commanding him to dismiss the people, neither truly willed nor intended the people's dismissal, but the addition of more signs, so that the name of God might be made manifest to posterity; which the Arminians do not deny. What does Jackson say to this? Let the reader please see. He says that the example of Pharaoh is extraordinary, and is set forth so that we may beware of the desperate principle of colluding with God. And in the same place he says that after the seventh plague had been inflicted it was not God's will that Pharaoh should dismiss the people; yet (he says) after his heart had been so hardened that he could not repent, God punished him as if it were free and possible for him to repent and to grant his people a friendly departure. But that crude innovator comes back to this: namely, that God, not ordinarily but yet by some extraordinary chance, can use evil deceit and the Jesuitical calling of equity with men. For God, after the seventh plague (Exod. 9. 13), commanded Pharaoh to dismiss his people, and when he refused, inflicted the eighth plague. So God addresses Pharaoh after the seventh plague: I command you to dismiss my people; for this is what I will and decree; but since you have now become rebellious, I command you to dismiss them; yet I will and decree that you do not dismiss them. Is this making God speak contradictions? Well, he does this only extraordinarily. (2) Often the Arminians accuse us of making God the necessitating author of the sins committed. Here we have the guilty man confessing that God punishes Pharaoh after the seventh plague, when he could no longer repent; and here too God will be unjust, angry at the thing he wills and decrees, which this good man, at p. 170, says does not befall the inhabitants of hell. But the matter is saved by a little distinction: God is ordinarily just, yet extraordinarily unjust, and does to Pharaoh what no one of the inhabitants of hell could rightly be made to suffer. (3) Nor is Pharaoh's example so extraordinary, because Rom. 9. 17 is the pattern of all who harden themselves and are hardened by God.

units.la: 8. Deut.2.27. Loquitur Deus Sihoni per populum suum, & orat populo suo amicum transitum. Quaero, an Deus intendat, ut Sihon obediat, & terram suam sibi ipsi servet? Nihil minus. v.30. Noluit transitum permittere. Quare? Quia obduravit Iehova spiritum ejus, nempe ut traderet terram populo, quam Abrahamo ejusque semini juramento se daturum astrinxerat. Non dicent in Deo hic contrarios fines fuisse, nempe Deum alloquentem Sihonem perblandis verbis intendisse & ut Sihon obediret, & terram promissionis sibi servaret, & ut non obediret, & terram illam daret Abrahami posteris. Sic Ioh.11.19. nulla civitas pacem fecit cum I-sraelitis præter Chivæos. At quare hoc? Deus enim pacem ipsis obtulit, sed an eo animo & voluntate ut oblata amplecterentur, ut somniant Arminiani? Nihil minus. Jehova enim fuit quod obfirmarent cor suum, ut populo resisterent, ut Deus internecioni devoveret illas propter abo-
units.tr: 8. Deut. 2. 27. God speaks to Sihon through his people and asks for a friendly passage for his people. I ask whether God intends that Sihon should obey and keep his land for himself. Quite the contrary. v. 30: Sihon was not willing to allow the passage. Why? Because the LORD hardened his spirit, namely so that he would hand over the land to the people, which he had bound himself by oath to give to Abraham and his seed. Here no one can say that there were contrary purposes in God, namely that God, speaking to Sihon with gentle words, intended both that Sihon should obey and keep the land of promise for himself, and that he should not obey and should give that land to the posterity of Abraham. So in Josh. 11. 19, no city made peace with the Israelites except the Hivites. But why was this? God indeed offered them peace, but was it with the intention and will that they should accept what was offered, as the Arminians dream? Quite the contrary. For Jehovah it was who hardened their hearts so that they would resist the people, so that God might devote those cities to destruction because of the abominations with which they had polluted the land.

units.la: 2 minationes, quibus terram polluissent. 2. Samuel. 12. 11. Comminatur Deus pollutionem tori Davidici, per incestum Absalomi, idque coram sole, an non eam pollutionem ut pœnam Davidis intendat? Si non intendit Davidi in illa comminatione, aliud loquitur, aliud intendit, quod est hypocritam agere. Et interim conscientiae Absalomi dicit in lege, non pollues torum patris tui: si hoc loquitur Absalomo ea voluntate & intentione, ut Absalomus obediat, & non polluat torum patris sui, tum Davidi dixerat in comminatione, id quod non intendebat, quod adhuc est absurdum. Ac proinde illa interdictione (Non pollues torum patris tui) proposita conscientiae Absolomi: non voluit neque intendit, ut Absalomus obediret. Hic itaque Arminiani haereant, necesse est.
units.tr: 2 comminations, by which they had polluted the land. 2. Samuel 12. 11. God threatens the pollution of David's bed through the incest of Absalom, and that openly, in the sight of the sun. Does He not intend that pollution as the punishment of David? If He does not intend it in that threat to David, He says one thing and intends another, which is to play the hypocrite.
