Meanwhile, He says to Absalom's conscience in the law, "You shall not defile your father's bed." If He says this to Absalom with the purpose and intention that Absalom should obey and not defile his father's bed, then in the threat He had said to David what He did not intend, and that is still absurd. Accordingly, when that prohibition ("You shall not defile your father's bed") is set before Absalom's conscience, He neither wished nor intended that Absalom should obey. Here the Arminians are necessarily stuck.

units.la: 9. Deus iussit Abrahamum immolare filium, sed nec voluit nec intendit Isaaci immolationem, sed decrevit ut viveret & filius promissionis foret. Ergo Deus non semper vult, quod praecipit. Arminiani dicunt fuisse tentationem, seu mandatum exploratorium, non officii praeceptionem. Resp. 1. Exploratio est mandati finis Deo propositus, at vero quocunque fine Deus non potest aliud loqui, aliud velle, aut bono fine malo dolo agere cum creatura: fine enim bono non potest Deus peccare, quoniam finis extrinsece se habet ad actum. 2. Mandatum hoc non fuisse officii est falsum: tum enim iussisset Deus aliquid legi contrarium: atqui hoc ipso quod Deus ju-
units.tr: 9. God commanded Abraham to sacrifice his son, yet he neither willed nor intended Isaac's sacrifice, but decreed that he should live and be the son of promise. Therefore God does not always will what he commands. The Arminians say that it was a trial, or a command for testing, and not a precept of duty. Answer: (1) Testing is an end proposed by God for the command; but whatever the end, God cannot say one thing and will another, or act with a creature with good purpose and bad deceit. For God cannot sin with a good end, since an end stands outside the act itself. (2) That this command was not a matter of duty is false: for then God would have commanded something contrary to the law. But by the very fact that God commands something, it is just and holy; indeed, if Abraham had refused the sacrifice, he would have grievously sinned against the sum of the whole decalogue, since he would have loved his son more than God. Nor can it happen that God, by testing, commands what the creature is under no duty to do. And granting that Abraham had refused obedience (which the Arminians allow to be possible), I ask whether Abraham would have sinned against God's decree and eternal intention concerning the sacrifice of Isaac. Believe me, they will fall silent here: for nothing of the kind was ever decreed or intended by God. But it cannot be denied that Abraham would have sinned grievously here against the will of the sign. Therefore someone can sin against the will of the sign by doing the very thing which is wholly consonant with the decree and the will of good pleasure. Therefore God commands something which he does not will to be done.

units.la: beret aliquid, est æquum & sanctum, quin imo, si Abrahamus recusasset immolationem, in summam totius decalogi graviter deliquisset, quippe filium suum Deo impensius dilexisset: neque fieri potest, ut Deus tentando id jubeat, quod creaturæ ex officio non incumbat faciendum: & hoc dato quod Abrahamus detrectasset obedientiam (quod Arminiani est possibile) quæro an Abrahamus peccasset in Dei decretum & æternam intentionem de immolando Isaaco: crede hic mihi obmutescent: nihil enim tale unquam Deo vel decretum vel intentum fuit: at vero negari non potest, quin Abrahamus hic graviter peccasset in voluntatem signi. Ergo potest quis peccare in voluntatem signi, qui illud idem faciat, quod apprime consonum est decreto & voluntati beneplaciti. Ergo Deus aliquid mandat, quod fieri non vult.
units.tr: by the very fact that God commands something, it is fair and holy. Indeed, if Abraham had refused the sacrifice, he would have grievously sinned against the sum of the whole Decalogue, since he would have loved his son more than God. Nor can it be that God, in testing, commands what the creature is not bound by duty to do. And granting that Abraham had refused obedience (which is possible, as the Arminians hold), I ask whether Abraham would have sinned against God's decree and eternal intention concerning the sacrifice of Isaac. Believe me, here they will fall silent, for nothing of the kind was ever decreed or intended by God. But it cannot be denied that Abraham would here have grievously sinned against the will of the sign. Therefore one can sin against the will of the sign by doing that very thing which is wholly in harmony with the decree and the will of good pleasure. Therefore God commands something which he does not will to be done.

units.la: 10. Deus etiam per Paulum Theffalonicenses, 1. Theff. 5. 4, 5, 6. & per Petrum sanctos, 2. Pet. 13.12[?]. horratur, ut exspectent diem secundi adventus Christi, & tamen non decrevit ut ipsis superstitibus dies ille adveniret: quin imo Paulus contrarium docet, 2. Thes. 2. 2,3. Ergo Deus sæpe præcepto proponit, quod fieri non decrevit, & id tantum vult, quod sibi approbatum est & acceptum, & nostri est ossicii, & debitæ obligationis.
units.tr: 10. God also exhorts the Thessalonians through Paul, 1 Thess. 5.4, 5, 6, and the saints through Peter, 2 Pet. 13.12[?], to await the day of Christ's second coming. Yet he has not decreed that that day should arrive while they themselves are still alive. Indeed Paul teaches the contrary, 2 Thess. 2.2, 3. Therefore God often sets before us by precept what he has not decreed to be done, and he wills only what has been approved and accepted by him, and what belongs to our duty and binding obligation.

units.la: 11. Hinc liquet, eos qui voluntatem signi per Dei intentionem, propositum, decretum, aut prædefinitionem de hoc vel illo faciendo, exponant, quod facit Thomas Iacksonus cum Arminianis, nunquam hanc distinctionem intellexisse, vel saltem mentem theologorum nostrorum vaferrime dissimulasse. Nam voluntas approbationis qua talis, non ponit ullam in Deo efficientiam, ne quidem executive: sive efsective at vero decretum & voluntas beneplaciti, quamvis sit actus in Deo immanes, non minus quam voluntas approbationis, attamen in executione ponit Deum actu effecturum, quod efficere decrevit, quod voluntas approbans nullo modo ponit, qua talis. Hinc assata ista ponimus.
units.tr: 11. From this it is clear that those who explain the will of the sign by God's intention, purpose, decree, or predefinition about this or that being done, as Thomas Jackson does together with the Arminians, have never understood this distinction, or at least have very cunningly concealed the mind of our theologians. For the will of approval, as such, places no efficiency in God, not even executive or effective. But the decree and the will of good pleasure, although it is an act immanent in God no less than the will of approval, nevertheless places God in the act of executing what He has decreed to effect, which the approving will, as such, in no way does. Hence we set forth these matters.

units.la: 1. Deus serió vult, hoc est, amat, approbat, actuque complacentiæ fertur in obedientiam reproborum, quatenus est res bona & sancta, sive actu existat illa obedientia, sive non.
units.tr: 1. God seriously wills, that is, He loves and approves, and by an act of complacency He is directed towards the obedience of the reprobate, insofar as it is a good and holy thing, whether or not that obedience actually exists.

units.la: 2. Nulla est in Deo voluntas huic contraria, & postquam decrevit ut hæc res, non illa fit moralis obedientia, non potest Deus non serio velle & approbare talem rem.
units.tr: 3. To have decreed from eternity, or to have intended by exhortations and threats, that the reprobate should obey and believe, and yet in the meantime to have reprobated them and denied them the efficacious grace by which they would believe, would be to posit contradictory wills in God.

units.la: 3. Deum decrevisse aut hortationibus & minis intendisse ab æterno, ut reprobi obedirent & crederent, & interim ipsos reprobasse, & gratiam efficacem, quâ crederent ipsis negasse tali decreto, esset ponere in Deo contradictorias voluntates.
units.tr: 3. For God to have decreed from eternity, or to have intended by exhortations and threats, that the reprobate should obey and believe, while at the same time having reprobated them and denied them the efficacious grace by which they would believe, would be to posit contradictory wills in God.

units.la: 4. Deum velle voluntate signi homines obedire euangelio, & interim iisdem nolle euangelium revelare, est contradictorium.
units.tr: 4. For God to will by the will of the sign that men obey the gospel, and at the same time to be unwilling to reveal the gospel to those same men, is a contradiction.

units.la: 4. Deum intendere & decernere mortem peccatoris, & Deum non delectari morte peccatoris, ut jurat Ezech. 33. 11. nullo modo sunt contradicentia : quippe terrenus judex sine contradictione (modo voluntates subditorum justissimè determinare possit) statuit justitiam suam patefacere, & tamen non laetatur morte bonorum. Nam Deum decernere interitum reproborum certissimum est, idque voluntate absoluta. Rom. 9. 11, 12, 13. Ut tamen Ezech. 33. non delectatur morte peccatoris eo sensu, quo Deo objiciebant blasphemi Judæi, qui v. 10 arripiebant ansam ex ca. 24. v. 23. Prophetas frustra ipsis vitam promittere, quoniam Deus ipsos in suis peccatis consumendos fore dixerat, adeo ut hanc Dei complacentiae voluntatem dicerent; fieri non posse ut viverent, etiam hoc dato quod à viis suis resipuissent. Imo (inquit Deus) haec mea est voluntas complacentiae, ut homines non morerentur, sed resipiscentes viverent, non resipiscentes morerentur, adeo ut eo loco contra multorum opinionem, non juret Deus se non simpliciter delectari morte peccatoris, sed tantum secundum quid, & sensu blasphemo Judæorum iniquitatem viarum Iehovæ protervè exprobrantium. Est itaque sophisma transparens à [illegible, ~5 letters] ad ἁπλῶς[?]. Ex textu enim nemini non patere poterit, Deum non verba facere de decreto suo, sed de voluntate approbante & revelata. Nam ait illic, se delectari, eo quod improbus à via sua resipiscat, & haec ipsissima est voluntas revelata, & ex hac reprehenfione (siquidem Deus non reprehendit nisi delinquentes) patet Iudæos credidisse Deum, ne quidem resipiscentium vita & salute delectari, sed tam legaliter & duriter cum ipsis agere, ut vellet ipsos in peccatis tabescere, non obstante eo, quod per prophetas vitam ipsis promittere constituerat, & præfecerat nomine tanquam vigiles: & Deus asseverat, interposito sancti juramenti solenni sacramento, se non hoc modo velle aut delectari interitu peccatorum. Si vero Deus vult omnium salutem & nullius interitum, donec flagitiofiffimus evaserit, sequitur amorem & voluntatem salvandi tum demum desinere, quando incipiunt actus flagitiosi, & mutari voluntatem Dei. Quid hic Lacksonus[?]? Non (inquit) mutatur voluntas aut decretum, sed objectum decreti: sed quæro an Deus decernat vitam Pharaoni, Saulo, Iudæ, donec incidant in gravissima peccata, & tum incipiat decernere ipsorum interitum? sed quæro rationem justitiæ decreti illius, quo decernit nunquam credentium vitam: Pharaoh enim nunquam credidit. At decretum electionis Arminiani non volunt vacare justitia. At amat (inquiunt illi) naturali & antecedente amore salutem omnium quatenus sunt homines. Itane? at vero amor quoad effectum, non quoad affectum est in Deo: quoad vero affectum non est salutem nisi actus divinæ voluntatis, quo vult bonum creaturæ: at an velit Deus homini, quatenus est creatura, vitam æternam? An justus est amor, velle coronam ei qui nondum certamen est ingressus? homo enim qua homo aut qua creatura, non credit: hic amor, ex Arminianis, justitiæ Dei adversatur.
units.tr: 4. God's intending and decreeing the death of the sinner, and God's not delighting in the death of the sinner, as He swears in Ezekiel 33. 11, are in no way contradictory. For an earthly judge, without contradiction (provided he can most justly determine the wills of his subjects), resolves to make his justice manifest, and yet does not rejoice in the death of the good. For it is most certain that God decrees the destruction of the reprobate, and this by an absolute will (Rom. 9. 11, 12, 13). Yet He does not delight in the death of the sinner in Ezekiel 33 in the sense in which the blaspheming Jews objected to God, who (v. 10) seized on an occasion from chapter 24, verse 23, claiming that the prophets promised them life in vain, since God had said they would be consumed in their sins; so that they described this as God's will of complacency, that they could not live even granting that they had turned from their ways. On the contrary (says God), this is my will of complacency, that men should not die but live when they repent, and that those who do not repent should die. So in that place, contrary to the opinion of many, God does not swear that He does not simply delight in the death of the sinner, but only in a certain respect, and in the blasphemous sense of the Jews who shamelessly reproached Jehovah for the iniquity of His ways. It is therefore a transparent sophism, from [illegible] to absolutely [ἁπλῶς]. For from the text it will be plain to anyone that God is not speaking of His decree, but of His approving and revealed will. For He says there that He delights in the wicked man's turning from his way, and this is precisely His revealed will; and from this reproof (since God reproves only offenders) it is evident that the Jews believed God took no delight even in the life and salvation of those who repent, but dealt with them so legally and harshly that He wished them to waste away in their sins, notwithstanding that He had determined through the prophets to promise them life, and had set them over as watchmen. And God affirms, with the solemn sacrament of an oath interposed, that He does not will or delight in the destruction of sinners in this way. But if God wills the salvation of all and the destruction of none, until they have become most wicked, it follows that His love and will to save then cease, at the moment when shameful acts begin, and God's will is changed. What does Jackson say to this? That the will or decree is not changed, but the object of the decree. But I ask whether God decrees life for Pharaoh, Saul, and Judas until they fall into the gravest sins, and then begins to decree their destruction? But I ask for the reason of the justice of that decree by which He decrees the life of those who never believe; for Pharaoh never believed. But the Arminians do not want the decree of election to be void of justice. Yet they say that He loves the salvation of all by a natural and antecedent love, insofar as they are men. Really? But love exists in God as to its effect, not as to its affection; and as to its affection, salvation is nothing but an act of the divine will by which He wills the good of the creature. But does God will eternal life for a man insofar as he is a creature? Is it just love to will the crown for one who has not yet entered the contest? For a man, as man or as creature, does not believe. This love, according to the Arminians, is opposed to the justice of God.

units.la: 12. Fateor durum admodum humanæ rationi videri, Deum approbare, & verbo mandare id quoad essentiam, quod quoad existentiam neque vult neque unquam fore decernit. At dices, ideo plectuntur Hierofolymitani, quoniam ipsorum actualis aggregatio ad Christum actu non existit. Nam illi voluntate approbante voluerunt suam ad filium Dei aggregationem quoad essentiam, & Deo se debere obedientiam ex officio & obligatione non diffitebantur, & sic eorum voluntas approbanti Dei voluntati conformis erat: at vero nolebant suam ipsorum aggregationem quoad existentiam, & sic Deus, quoad existentiam, illam congregationem noluit, ac proinde etiam decreto Dei ipsorum voluntas erat conformis. Quorsum ergo puniti sunt, qui volebant omni modo, id quod Deus volebat? Resp.
units.tr: 12. I admit it seems very hard to human reason that God approves and commands by his word what in existence he neither wills nor ever decrees to be. But you will say that the Jerusalemites are punished because their actual gathering to Christ does not actually exist. For by an approving will they willed their gathering to the Son of God as to essence, and they did not deny that they owed God obedience from duty and obligation, so their will was conformed to the approving will of God. But they were unwilling that their own gathering should exist, and so God, as to existence, did not will that gathering, and consequently their will was also conformed to the decree of God. Why then were they punished, when they wished in every way what God wished? Answer.

units.la: 1. Voluntas Dei approbans approbat etiam obedientiam existentem, quamvis salvetur essentia ipsius in simplici amatione obedientiæ, sive existentis sive non existentis. 2. Officium est reproborum & velle & actu præstare, ut actu existat ipsorum obedientia, & Deus vult hoc esse officii reproborum, ut actu & velint & præstent obedientiam, quamvis ipse existentiam obedientiæ non ab æterno decreverit, quod quoniam liberrime reprobi non præstant, jure plectuntur. Dices ergo: non adhuc impletur voluntas Dei approbans, quoniam reprobi id officii non actu præstant, quod Deus approbat quoad existentiam: at absurdum est Dei voluntatem non impleri. R. Approbatio Dei ut sic & formaliter non terminatur in existentiam obedientiæ, quatenus Deus illam existentiam actu causare decreverit, sed tantum applaudit voluntas approbans obedientiæ vel existenti, vel non existenti, tanquam rei bonæ & justæ: & quoniam reprobi non possunt efficere, ut hæc res Deo approbanti grata, non fit grata & accepta, ideo non contraveniunt, neque contravenire possunt voluntati Dei approbanti. Neque satis est quod reprobi approbent bonum, quod Deus approbat: nam Deo licet approbare rem quam efficere non tenetur, absque officii sui violatione, quoniam Deus legi non subest: neque lex flagitat à Deo efficientiam boni, quod approbat: at flagitat lex ab homine, ut & approbet, & actu efficiat bonum.
units.tr: 1. The approving will of God also approves the obedience that exists, although its essence is preserved in the simple loving of obedience, whether it exists or not. 2. It is the duty of the reprobate both to will and actually to perform, so that their obedience actually exists. God wills this to be the duty of the reprobate, that they both will and actually perform obedience, although he himself has not from eternity decreed that obedience should exist. Since the reprobate freely do not perform it, they are justly punished. You will say, then, that the approving will of God is not yet fulfilled, since the reprobate do not actually perform the duty which God approves as to existence; but it is absurd that the will of God should not be fulfilled. Answer: the approval of God, as such and formally, does not terminate in the existence of obedience, insofar as God has decreed actually to cause that existence. It only applauds obedience, whether existing or not, as a good and just thing. And since the reprobate cannot bring it about that this thing is pleasing to God in his approving, it is not made pleasing and acceptable, and so they do not contravene, nor can they contravene, the approving will of God. Nor is it enough that the reprobate approve the good which God approves. For God may approve a thing which he is not bound to effect, without violating his duty, since God is not subject to the law. Nor does the law demand from God the bringing about of the good which he approves; but the law demands from man that he both approve and actually effect the good.

units.la: 13. Quamvis homo servo suo imperaret, quæ fieri non decreverat, si id insidias struendi animo haud faceret, non dicendus esset malo dolo agere. Non ergo jure Schaafmannes dixit, Deum hic malo dolo agere. At quare? quoniam (inquit ille) verbis perblandis præ se fert, se bene velle iis, quibus occultè, & inevitabili decreto æternum male cupit; At nihil dicit. Nam Deus reprobis nullam aliam exprimit benevolentiam, quam illam ipsam quam habuit intus apud se erga electos, nempe approbationem obedientiæ.
units.tr: 13. Although a man might command his servant to do what he had not decreed should be done, if he did not do so with the intent of laying snares, he should not be said to act with evil deceit. Therefore Schaafmannes was not right to say that God here acts with evil deceit. But why? Because, he says, by very flattering words God professes that he wishes well to those whom he secretly and by an unavoidable decree eternally desires ill. But this says nothing. For God expresses to the reprobate no other benevolence than the very benevolence which he had within himself toward the elect, namely the approval of obedience.

units.la: 14. Deinde quamvis homines legi subsint, in conceptibus suis enarrandis, ita ut aliter loqui non possint, quam verba quatenus sunt mentis symbola ordinaria, ferant sine nota mali doli, tamen quæ audacia est, Iehovam talibus legibus astringere? Ideoque causam ipsorum non juvat, quod citant ex Psal. 81. Utinam populus meus obediisset. Resp. Sensus est, verbis revelo tam impense charam esse voluntari meæ approbanti obedientiam populi mei, quam homines ea volunt, quæ totis desiderii optant. 2. Si optationes proprie sunt in Deo, cur non etiam agitatio viscerum, Ier. 31. 30. defatigatio, Esai. 1.24. animæ depressio, Iud. 10. 16? sed eo tendunt Arminiana dogmata, ut Deum cum Anthropomorphitis humanum, Epicureum, mutabilem, passionibus obnoxium nobis fingant. 3. Quæro an sit aliquid involuntarium in illis optationibus frustraneis, quas Deo affingunt? si sit, certè Deo non mediocrem imperfectionem ascribant, necesse est, nempe id fieri, cujus contrarium Deus fieri vult, id quod Suarez evitare, sed frustrà, obnixè contendit: si vero non sit aliquid involuntarium in Deo, optationes illæ non ponunt Deum velle & optare quod non fit. At vero Matth. 23. Quoties voluit congregare &c. Est quoties approbavi, amavi, & testimonio meo & Prophetarum mihi complacere testatissimum feci, vestri esse officii ut congregemini ad me. Nam si quis Christum assimilet gallinæ & Hierofolymitanos pullis infcienter se vulturibus exponentibus, & nolentibus contra matris suæ tenellum deliderium alis circumvolvi & protegi, is Christum Deum faciat non Deum. 2. Sit (quoties volui,) idem quod, (quoties decrevi,) tum decreta Dei cæterorum æterna indies iterari & reiterari, quoties prophetæ prædicabant, necesse foret, quod est absurdum. Prov. 1. Vocavi & renuistis, non decrevi ut veniretis: nam illa vocatio reiteratur per multos annos in competis[?], in foris, at decretum Dei unicum & æternum est, ideoque vocavi idem est, quod verbo invitavi & testatum feci, mihi complacere vestram obedientiam, ne iota habet de Dei decreto.
units.tr: 14. Further, although men are subject to the law in declaring their concepts, so that they cannot speak otherwise than with words as the ordinary symbols of the mind, and such words carry no mark of evil deceit, yet what audacity is it to bind Jehovah by such laws? Therefore it does not help their cause that they cite Psalm 81: "Oh that my people had obeyed." Answer: the sense is that by words I reveal that the obedience of my people is as dear to my approving will as men wish those things which they desire with their whole longing. 2. If desires are properly in God, why not also the agitation of the bowels (Jer. 31. 30), weariness (Isa. 1. 24), depression of soul (Judg. 10. 16)? But the Arminian dogmas tend to this, that they feign God to be human, like the Anthropomorphites: Epicurean, changeable, and subject to passions as we are. 3. I ask whether there is anything involuntary in those vain desires which they ascribe to God. If there is, they necessarily ascribe to God no small imperfection, namely that something should happen whose contrary God wills to happen, which Suarez strenuously but in vain tries to avoid. But if there is nothing involuntary in God, those desires do not imply that God wills and desires what does not come to pass. But indeed Matt. 23: "How often would I have gathered..." means: how often I approved and loved, and by my testimony and that of the Prophets have most fully shown that I am pleased, that it is your duty to gather to me. For if someone likens Christ to a hen, and the Jerusalemites to chicks unwittingly exposing themselves to vultures, and unwilling to be wrapped and protected under their mother's wings from her tender longing, he makes Christ a God who is not God. 2. Suppose "how often I willed" were the same as "how often I decreed": then the eternal decrees of God would have to be repeated and reiterated day after day, as often as the prophets preached, which is absurd. Prov. 1: "I called and you refused; I did not decree that you should come." For that calling is repeated over many years at the crossroads and in the streets, but the decree of God is single and eternal. Therefore "I called" is the same as "I invited by word and testified that your obedience pleases me," and it has not a jot of God's decree in it.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CAP. II.

units.la: Solvitur illud, quod unusquisque tenetur cre- dere, id est verum &c. 2. Quomodo Deum fidem exigat a reprobis. 3. De promis- sis Euangelij.
units.tr: The objection is answered, that everyone is bound to believe what is true, etc. 2. How God requires faith from the reprobate. 3. Concerning the promises of the Gospel.

units.la: NOn parum lucis huic disputationi fæneratur solutio illius objectionis, quam solam potentem esse nostram sententiam convellere dixit Arminius satis pro suo more Thrafonice. Ea hæc est.
units.tr: THE solution of that objection, which Arminius, in his usual Thracian fashion, said alone was able to overthrow our opinion, sheds no little light on this dispute. It is this.

units.la: Quod unusquisque tenetur credere, id est verum.
units.tr: Everyone is bound to believe what is true.

units.la: Atqui unusquisque tenetur credere Christum pro se mortuum esse.
units.tr: But everyone is bound to believe that Christ died for him.

units.la: Ergo Christum pro unoquoque mortuum esse, est verum.
units.tr: Therefore, that Christ died for each one is true.

units.la: Respondet Ioannes Camero. Distinguendo majorem. Quod unusquisque tenetur credere, id est verum, vel quomodo vera sunt, quæ narrantur, vel quomodo vera sunt quæ prædicantur, vel ut promittuntur: primo & secundo modo verum non est, narrata & prædicta sunt vera sive credideris, sive non. At quæ vera sunt ut promissa ea nihil necesse est esse, nisi credideris, imo necesse est ea non esse, si non credideris. Hoc ideo docet quia salsissimè, & nullo fundamento vult Christum mortuum esse pro omnibus conditionatè, sive electi, sive reprobi fuerint; pro electis vero absolutè, quæ sententia hæresi affinis mihi videtur. Nam fides non facit objectum, neque dat veritatem promissis divinis nostra obedientia, imo hominum infidelitas Dei fidem sic abrogaret.
units.tr: John Cameron replies by distinguishing the major premise. "What everyone is bound to believe is true" may mean either how things that are related are true, or how things that are preached are true, or how they are true as promised. In the first and second sense it is not true: things related and things preached are true whether you believe them or not. But things that are true as promised need not be so unless you believe them; indeed, if you do not believe them, they are not so. He teaches this because he holds, most foolishly and on no foundation, that Christ died for all conditionally, whether they are elect or reprobate, and for the elect absolutely. This opinion seems to me akin to heresy. For faith does not make the object, nor does our obedience give truth to the divine promises; rather, the unbelief of men would thus abolish the faithfulness of God.

units.la: 2. Potest Camero citra omnem distinctionem totum argumentum concedere, ut pote ipsius errori unice subridens. Ergo omnes mortales tenentur credere Christum pro se, conditionate, mortuum esse, & stat inconcussum id Arminianorum, gratiam redemptionis universalem & communem esse & electis & reprobis. Ergo pœnas reprobis debitas Christus luebat. Ordine itaque justitiæ omnes reprobi immunes sunt à pœna æterna. O Carneadeam subtilitatem, sed de hisce alibi.
units.tr: 2. Cameron could concede the whole argument without any distinction, since he simply mocks its error. Therefore all mortals are bound to believe that Christ died for them, conditionally; and the Arminian position stands unshaken, that the universal grace of redemption is common both to the elect and to the reprobate. Therefore Christ bore the punishments due to the reprobate. In the order of justice, then, all the reprobate are exempt from eternal punishment. O Carneadean subtlety! But of these matters elsewhere.

units.la: 2. Respondet gravissimus & clarissimus vir Ioannes Piscator, & alius quidam non mediocris theologus, quem honoris causa tacebo, majorem simpliciter esse falsam. Imo (inquiunt) homines obligari, ad credendum Deum intendere seu velle fieri, id quod nobis præcipit: quamvis forsitan quoad eventum verum, non fuerit, Deum illud intendere, quippe nunquam forsitan eventurum, imo afferunt objectum fidei esse interdum falsum id quod nec theologia nostra, nec veritas patitur. Nam 1. Fides nititur veritati divinæ, cui nihil salfi subesse potest. Ergo ejus objectum nullo modo est falsum. Antedens est Heb. ii. ii. Tit. 1. 2. Imo ut rede[?] observavit Gul. Tuissius flos ille illibatus ingeniorum scholasticorum, intentio Dei non proprie revelatur & infallibiliter, sed colligitur ex mandato, quæ fuerit intentio Dei. 2. Credendum foret Deum loqui id quod falsum esse potest, & Deum nos velle credere falsa, quod est absurdum. Tenemur enim credere rem ita fe habere prout;Deus loquitur: atqui Deum intendere ut Iudas crederet, non est tale in rerum natura. 3. Fides ultimate resolvitur in hoc (sic ait Iehova) atque quod Deus intendat obedientiam omnium vocatorum, non est Iehovæ dictum, neque potest in falsum resolvi verum. 4. Si ex hortationibus evangelicis teneantur omnes in visibili ecclesia Deum ipsorum obedientiam intendere, tum tenerentur etiam credere ipsos ad æternam gloriam à Deo destinatos, & Christum ex suo & æterno Patris consilio ipsorum in cruce peccata expiasse, at posterius est absurdum: Ergo etiam prius, Prob. major. Si tenerentur credere Deum in præceptis suis ipsorum fidem intendere, quod est medium, tenerentur credere Deum etiam finem intendisse: vel credere tenerentur Deum intendere medium, & non finem, quod contradicit scripturæ. Nam quos vocavit, glorificavit, Rom. 8. Ergo quos intendit vocare, eosdem intendit glorificare: sed quod omnes in visibili ecclesia non teneantur credere, Deum ipsos ad gloriam destinasse, patet, quia si omnes hoc tenerentur credere, tenerentur omnes credere se electos esse, & sic non esse in ecclesia visibili reprobos & electos, oves & hædos, paleam & frumentum, zizania & bonas fruges contra scripturas, Matth. 22. 14. Matth. 3. 12. & 13.27. & Deum omnes vocatos externa vocatione, gratia universali completi, & Deum falsa in scripturis dictitare & contradictoria, quo nihil absurdius. Neque fieri potest ut hic & ille teneatur credere, Deum intendere suam ipsius salutem, & etiam credere teneretur Deum multorum obedientiam & salutem non intendere.
units.tr: 2. The most grave and most distinguished man John Piscator, and another theologian of no small standing whom I will not name out of respect, reply that the major premise is simply false. Indeed, they say, men are bound to believe that God intends, or wills, what he commands us to do, although perhaps as regards the outcome it may not be true that God intends it, since it may never come about. They even assert that the object of faith is sometimes false, which neither our theology nor the truth allows. For: 1. Faith rests on divine truth, to which nothing false can be subject. Therefore its object is in no way false. The antecedent is Heb. ii. ii. Tit. 1. 2. Indeed, as the notable William Twisse, that unblemished flower of the scholastic minds, has observed, God's intention is not properly and infallibly revealed, but is gathered from the command as to what God's intention is. 2. It would have to be believed that God speaks what can be false, and that God wishes us to believe falsehoods, which is absurd. For we are bound to believe a thing to be as God speaks it; but that God intends Judas to believe is not such a thing in the nature of things. 3. Faith is ultimately resolved into this (so Jehovah says), and that God intends the obedience of all who are called is not a saying of Jehovah, nor can the true be resolved into the false. 4. If from the evangelical exhortations all in the visible Church are bound to hold that God intends their obedience, then they would also be bound to believe that they were destined by God for eternal glory, and that Christ, by the eternal counsel of himself and the Father, expiated their sins on the cross; but the latter is absurd, therefore the former also. Proof of the major: if they were bound to believe that God intends their faith in his precepts, which is the means, they would be bound to believe that God also intended the end; or else they would be bound to believe that God intends the means and not the end, which contradicts Scripture. For Rom. 8. "whom he called, them he also glorified." Therefore whom he intends to call, those he intends to glorify. But that all in the visible Church are not bound to believe that God has destined them to glory is plain, because if all were bound to believe this, they would all be bound to believe themselves elect; and so there would be no reprobates and elect, sheep and goats, chaff and wheat, tares and good fruit, within the visible Church, against the Scriptures, Matth. 22. 14. Matth. 3. 12. & 13. 27.; and God would have called all by external calling, filled all with universal grace, and God would be saying false and contradictory things in the Scriptures, than which nothing is more absurd. Nor can it be that one is bound to believe that God intends his own salvation, and yet is also bound to believe that God does not intend the obedience and salvation of many.

units.la: 5. Tenerentur omnes indurati credere Deum ipsorum indurationem in hortationibus euangelicis non intendere, sed obedientiam: & scripturas hasce & similes Esai. 6. 9, 10. Matth. 13.14, 15. Actor. 28. Ioh. 12. falsa dicere.
units.tr: 5. All the hardened would be bound to believe that God does not intend their hardening in the evangelical exhortations, but their obedience; and they would be bound to hold that these Scriptures and similar ones, Isaiah 6. 9, 10; Matt. 13. 14, 15; Acts 28; John 12, are false.

units.la: 6. Tenebatur Petrus in Prætorio credere, Christum intendisse illo di-cto (qui[?] {?}to[?] (qui me confitebitur coram hominibus, hunc etiam confitebor coram patre meo & angelis &c.) ut Petrus obediret & confiteretur se coram hostibus Christi. Ergo quo animo dixerat Christus ipsum abnegaturum se ter? tenebatur Petrus credere Christum falsum praedixisse, vel non intendisse Christum illo dicto (qui me confitebitur &c.) ut Petrus obediret. Atqui Christum falsa dicere Petrus non tenebatur credere. 7.
units.tr: 6. Peter in the Praetorium was bound to believe that Christ intended by that saying (whoever shall confess me before men, him also will I confess before my Father and the angels, etc.) that Peter should obey and confess himself before Christ's enemies. Therefore, with what purpose Christ had said that he would deny him three times, Peter would be bound either to believe that Christ had predicted falsely, or to believe that Christ did not intend by that saying (whoever shall confess me, etc.) that Peter should obey. But Peter was not bound to believe that Christ spoke falsely. 7.

units.la: Lex dicit omnibus etiam post lapsum, hoc fac & vives. An igitur tenebimur credere, Deum illo mandato legali intendere, ut nos legem & foedus operum praestemus? Hoc aperte etiam scripturis contradicit, 8. Quoniam tenentur omnes credere Deum omnipotentem sua intentione excidere non posse, utpote, qui ipsam vi irresistibili impleat, tenerentur omnes credere Deum externae vocationi semper additurum internam gratiam electorum, atque ita regenerationis gratiam fore omnium communem: at hoc scripturis adversatur. 9.
units.tr: The law says to all, even after the fall, Do this and you shall live. Shall we then be bound to believe that God intends by that legal command that we should perform the law and the covenant of works? This too clearly contradicts Scripture. 8. Since all are bound to believe that God omnipotent cannot fail of his intention, inasmuch as he fulfils it by irresistible power, all would be bound to believe that God would always add the internal grace of the elect to the external calling, and thus that the grace of regeneration would be common to all; but this is opposed to Scripture. 9.

units.la: Si tenerentur omnes posteri Adami lege cordi insculpta & verbo evangelico revelato Deum velle & intendere omnium obedientiam, tum non tenerentur Deum intendere, aut velle peccati permissionem: sic enim credere tenerentur Deum intendere peccati permissionem, & ipsam non intendere, sed intendere obedientiam, & sic fides fidei contradiceret, quod absurdum. Atque ex scripturis & experientia plusquam quotidiana scimus Deum velle & intendere peccati permissionem: haec autem volitio illius permissionis non potest stare cum intentione obedientiae: Ergo neq; fides hujus cum fide illius consistet. 10. Ille actus credendi Deus intendere nostram obedientiam, si sit fidei actus, ut vult Piscator, erit supernaturalis: Ergo proveniet à gratia spiritus sancti, ut à principio quo: at gratiam esse principium quo & immediatum credendi falsum, quis crederet?
units.tr: If all the posterity of Adam were bound, by the law written on the heart and by the revealed evangelical word, to believe that God wills and intends the obedience of all, then they would not be bound to believe that God intends or wills the permission of sin. For they would then have to believe that God intends the permission of sin and does not intend it, but intends obedience; and so faith would contradict faith, which is absurd. From Scripture and experience, more than daily, we know that God wills and intends the permission of sin; but this volition of that permission cannot stand with the intention of obedience. Therefore neither will faith in the one be consistent with faith in the other. 10. That act of believing that God intends our obedience, if it is an act of faith, as Piscator wills, will be supernatural; therefore it will proceed from the grace of the Holy Spirit as its principle by which. But to hold that grace is the immediate principle by which we believe is false; who would believe it?

units.la: 3. Audiamus argumenta Piscatoris & aliorum. 1. Arg. Deus jussit Abrahamum immolare filium. Ergo Abrahamus tenebatur credere Deum intendisse immolationem ipsius, ac proinde falsum credere tenebatur: nam nihil tale intendebat Deus. Resp. Abrahamus tenebatur ad immolationem se accingere, & tenebatur credere se obligari ad filium mactandum, & esse rem Deo gratam & acceptam, quod vero ad intentionem Dei vel non intentionem de actuali immolatione Abrahami fides neutram contradictionis partem attingere tenebatur: nam nec Dei intentio, nec non intentio eo casu revelabatur. At instat Paul. Baines theologus insignis eruditionis, Abrahami fidem innixam fuisse huic, quod Deus Isaacum à mortuis resuscitare potuerit, ut est Heb. 11. Ergo vere credidit Deum intendisse Isaaci immolationem. Resp. 1. salvo tanti viri honore, liceat mihi negare consequentiam. Nam Heb. 11 v. 19. dicitur Abrahamum credidisse Deo fuisse facultatem resuscitandi Isaacum mortuum, ex hypothesi quod immolatus fuisset: at vero in textu non dicitur Abrahamum credidisse Deum intendisse immolationem ipsius: hæc enim toto cœlo distant. At quatenus fides Patriarchæ innixa est omnipotentiæ divinæ, non gravate concedo veram fuisse fidem: at quatenus attingebat intentionem Dei de immolatione Isaaci, eatenus conjectura, non fides est, exemplum esto Maria Magdalena incidit in hortulanum, opinatur (uti suppono) esse salvatorem, ipsum devoluta in genua supplex adorat. Adoratio quatenus terminatur in objectum materiale, nempe in creaturam idolatria est, non adoratio: quatenus vero in illud idem, non sub ratione creaturæ, sed quatenus est salvator, adoratio dici potest. 2.
units.tr: 3. Let us hear the arguments of Piscator and the others. 1. Arg. God commanded Abraham to sacrifice his son. Therefore Abraham was bound to believe that God intended his immolation, and so was bound to believe what is false, for God intended nothing of the kind. Reply: Abraham was bound to prepare himself for the immolation, and was bound to believe that he was obliged to slay his son, and that the deed was pleasing and acceptable to God; but as to God's intention, or non-intention, regarding Abraham's actual immolation, faith was not bound to touch either side of the contradiction, for neither God's intention nor his non-intention was revealed in that case. But the distinguished theologian Paul Baynes, a man of great learning, insists that the faith of Abraham rested on this, that God could raise Isaac from the dead, as is said in Heb. 11. Therefore Abraham truly believed that God intended the immolation of Isaac. Reply 1: saving the honour of so great a man, let me be allowed to deny the consequence. For Heb. 11 v. 19 says that Abraham believed God had the power to raise Isaac from the dead, on the supposition that he had been sacrificed; but in the text it is not said that Abraham believed God intended his immolation, for these things are as far apart as the heavens. But insofar as the faith of the Patriarch rested on divine omnipotence, I do not hesitate to concede that it was true faith; but insofar as it touched God's intention concerning the immolation of Isaac, so far it was conjecture, not faith. Let the example be Maria Magdalena, who, having fallen in with the gardener, supposes (as I assume) that he is the Saviour and, throwing herself at his feet, worships him as a suppliant. Worship, insofar as it terminates on the material object, namely the creature, is idolatry, not worship; but insofar as it terminates on that same object, not under the aspect of a creature but as Saviour, it can be called worship. 2.

units.la: Arg. Unusquisque obligatur illud credere, quod dictante conscientia judicaverit esse sensum cujuslibet loci sacrarum literarum, cum tamen interim fieri potest, ut a vera loci sententia non nihil aberret: hoc suppositio illud credere tenebitur tanquam verum, quod revera est falsum. Resp. Docent recte theologi conscientiam erroneam ligare, non vero obligare: ligat quatenus non potest quis sine peccato credere, contra id quod conscientia erronea dictat: peccat enim tum contra conscientiam: sed nemo obligatur sequi ductum erroneæ conscientiæ, sed assensum suspendere & erroneam conscientiam deponere, & veritatem humillime indagare: alioqui qui ex defectu sani judicii credit hæresin esse fidei articulum, teneretur errare. At ad peccatum non est obligatio. 4. Dicet quispiam, quando quidem Deus gratuitâ electione paucos tantum complexus sit, quomodo fiat, ut in hortationibus & promissis evangelicis indefinite propositis mea vacillans conscientia consolationes inde hauriat, nisi ex Dei intentione & decreto teneat credere promissa mihi esse facta nominatim? Resp. Consolatio vana erit, si credideris falsa: Longe tutius est, ut unusquisque se & suam conscientiam scrutetur, quam arcanam Dei intentionem nondum revelatam, sed eventu, & signis revelandam. Sic illustro: Rex in turbam egenorum auri copiam spargit eo animo, ut ditentur quidam quos prae aliis diligit, non omnium gratia indiscriminatim: si quis sic argutaretur; nolo ego sparsum aurum colligere, donec mihi constet de propenso & benevolo regis erga me amore, an non indignus esset argutator tali munificentia regia? Porrigit nauclerus etiam viginti hominibus in profundum submersis funem, apprehendere jubet omnes, an non male sana & importuna esset illius dialectica, qui in undis volutabundus, & tantum non spiritum reddens, sic apud se statueret? nolo ego demissam funem apprehendere, donec me nominatim compellat nauclerus, ipsiusque intentionem mihi aperiat. Quid an non tutius est nobis mendicis regis nostri aurum colligere, & funem demissam praecipitatis cum diabolis in condemnationem suppliciter apprehendere & consciis[?] miseriæ oblatum Christum nobis attrahere? quod si fecerimus, tum licebit colligere, gratiosam fuisse erga nos, & erga me nominatim Dei intentionem & æternum decretum.
units.tr: Arg. Everyone is bound to believe what, as his conscience judges, is the sense of any passage of Holy Scripture, although it can happen that he strays somewhat from the true meaning of the passage. So by this supposition he will be bound to believe as true what is in fact false. Resp. Theologians rightly teach that an erroneous conscience binds but does not oblige. It binds in the sense that a person cannot believe without sin against what his erroneous conscience dictates, for he sins against his conscience if he does so. But no one is obliged to follow the lead of an erroneous conscience. Rather he ought to suspend his assent, lay aside the erroneous conscience, and search out the truth with the utmost humility. Otherwise, someone who through a defect of sound judgement believes heresy to be an article of faith would be bound to err. But there is no obligation to sin. 4. Someone will say: since God, by free election, has embraced only a few, how does it happen that my wavering conscience draws consolation from the evangelical exhortations and promises, which are proposed indefinitely, unless by God's intention and decree I hold that the promises have been made to me by name? Resp. The consolation will be empty if you believe falsehoods. It is far safer for each person to examine himself and his own conscience than to examine God's secret intention, which is not yet revealed but is to be revealed by the outcome and by signs. I illustrate: a king scatters a store of gold among a crowd of the needy, with the purpose that certain men whom he loves above the rest should be enriched, not that all should benefit indiscriminately. If someone reasoned thus: "I will not gather the scattered gold until it is certain to me that the king has a favourable and kindly love toward me," would the reasoner not be unworthy of such royal generosity? Or again, a shipmaster lets down a rope to twenty men sunk in the deep and bids them all take hold of it. Would not the argument of a man tossing in the waves, barely drawing breath, be a foolish and unseasonable one, if he reasoned to himself thus: "I will not take hold of the lowered rope until the shipmaster calls me by name and makes his intention known to me"? Is it not safer for us, beggars of our king, to gather the gold, and humbly to lay hold of the rope let down to us, lest we fall headlong with the devils into condemnation, and to draw to ourselves Christ offered to us, we who are conscious of our misery? If we do so, then we may gather that God's intention and eternal decree toward us, and toward me by name, was gracious.

units.la: Resp. 1. Quod unusquisque tenetur credere, id est verum, esse captionem ab homonymia vocis, Credere, quod aliter in propositione, aliter in assumptione sumitur. Nam τὸ Credere tribus modis sumitur. 1. pro τῷ[?] assentiri omni Dei verbo, & sic verbum Dei revelatum est fidei objectum: hinc sic formo.
units.tr: Resp. 1. That everyone is bound to believe what is true is a fallacy arising from the ambiguity of the word to believe, which is taken in one sense in the major premise and in another in the minor. For "to believe" is taken in three ways. 1. As assenting to every word of God; and so the revealed word of God is the object of faith. Hence I frame the argument thus:

units.la: Illud est verum cui unusquisque tenetur assentiri, tanquam Dei verbo revelato, Erg. Major est vera, & minor falsa. Nam non est Dei verbum Christum pro me nominatim mortuum esse, ea intentione & decreto ut me salvet: verbum enim Dei revelat Dei complacentiam & approbationem, non vero proprie intentionem & decretum Dei de hoc vel illo homine salvando, nisi excipiemus quosdam Patriarchas, Apostolos, qui nominantur in scripturis, & electos qui non per nomina, sed per alias conditiones communiores designantur, & sic voluntas signi aperit decretum, sed non qua voluntas signi contradistincta à voluntate beneplaciti. At vero quæ fuerit intentio Dei de unoquoque nominatim, colligitur ex applicatione cujuslibet hominis conscientiæ, ex certis signis accommodatis generalibus verbi promissionibus. Arminiani vero inclinant in universalem & conditionalem omnium electionem & reprobationem, sicut promissiones & comminationes euangelicæ sunt universales. Imo (inquit Corvinus) promissiones & minæ sunt ipsum Dei decretum quâ verbo patefactum. At vero decretum esse, quis negat, sed quale? Prædestinationisne? Nihil minus. Prædestinatio enim est pars & articulus Euangelii non totum Euangelium, sic enim Euangelium esset arcanus ille vitæ liber, cui electorum nomina sunt inscripta. At vero iste liber est scriptus in cœlis, si scripturis credimus, nec extant nomina electorum in euangelio: dic ubi legeris?
units.tr: What everyone is bound to assent to, as the revealed word of God, is true. Therefore the major is true, and the minor false. For it is not the word of God that Christ died for me by name, with the intention and decree that he should save me. For the word of God reveals God's good pleasure and approval, not properly his intention and decree concerning the saving of this or that man, unless we except certain patriarchs and apostles who are named in Scripture, and the elect who are designated not by names but by other, more general conditions. In that case the will of the sign reveals the decree, but not as the will of the sign distinguished from the will of good pleasure. But what God's intention is toward each person by name is gathered from the application of each man's conscience, by certain signs fitted to the general promises of the word. The Arminians, however, incline toward a universal and conditional election and reprobation of all, just as the evangelical promises and threats are universal. Indeed (says Corvinus) the promises and threats are God's own decree as revealed in the word. But who denies that they are a decree? The question is, of what kind? Of predestination? By no means. For predestination is a part and article of the Gospel, not the whole Gospel; otherwise the Gospel would be that secret book of life in which the names of the elect are written. But that book is written in heaven, if we believe the Scriptures, and the names of the elect do not stand in the Gospel. Tell me, where have you read it?

units.la: 2. Τὸ [?] Credere est actu fiduciali cordis in Christum ut sufficientem salvatorem recumbere, & sic major,
units.tr: 2. To believe is a fiducial act of the heart resting on Christ as a sufficient Saviour; and so the major premise

units.la: Quod unusquisque tenetur credere, id est verum, est falsa. Nam nec est verum nec falsum, sed bonum & salutare Dei donum, quod cor & assectus apprehendunt, & nullo modo mentis objectum, & sic adhuc non sequitur conclusio.
units.tr: "What everyone is bound to believe is true" is false. For this is neither true nor false, but a good and saving gift of God, which the heart and affections lay hold of, and in no way an object of the mind. And so the conclusion still does not follow.

units.la: 3. Τὸ [?] Credere est sensu & ex consequente apprehendere, & sic quod unusquisque tenetur credere, hoc est, fidei sensu, & ex fidei actu fiduciali, tanquam ex causa colligere id est verum: valeat jam major. Assumo: atqui unusquisque tenetur credere, nempe non formali fidei actu fiduciali, aut mentis assensu, sed fidei sensu, & collectione evidenti ex causa concludere Christum ex sua & Dei Patris intentione & consilio pro se mortuum esse: Minor jam est aperte falsa.
units.tr: 3. To believe is to apprehend by sense and by consequence; and so what everyone is bound to believe, that is, by the sense of faith and from the fiducial act of faith, is gathered as true from its cause. Let the major stand. I assume: but everyone is bound to believe, namely not by a formal fiducial act of faith or by assent of the mind, but by the sense of faith and by an evident collection from a cause, that Christ has died for him by the intention and counsel of himself and of God the Father. The minor is now plainly false.

units.la: Soli enim credentes tenentur tali sensu Dei intentionem & æternum decretum circa se nominatim colligere: reliqui enim non tenentur id credere, hoc est colligere, imo sic obligarentur alere inanem & evanidam præsumptionem & conjecturam umbratilem & Chymericam. Itaque major procedit de fidei actu, tum mentis in assentiendo, tum fiduciali cordis amplexu, quæ proprie est fides: minor vero de sensu fidei, & collectione quadam practica, quæ est improprie fides. Sunt itaque quatuor termini in syllogismo: si enim verbum omnibus revelaret Dei esse intentionem & decretum, ut unusquisque crederet se id intendere & decernere quod mandat, revelaret aperte falsa & contradictoria.
units.tr: For only believers are bound with such a sense to gather God's intention and eternal decree concerning themselves by name. The rest are not bound to believe this, that is, to gather it. Indeed, they would thus be bound to nourish an empty and vain presumption, a shadowy conjecture and a chimera. Therefore the major proceeds of the act of faith, both of the mind in assenting and of the fiducial embrace of the heart, which is properly faith; but the minor proceeds of the sense of faith and of a certain practical collection, which is faith only improperly. There are therefore four terms in the syllogism. For if the word revealed to all that it is God's intention and decree that each should believe that he intends and decrees what he commands, it would reveal things plainly false and contradictory.

units.la: 4. 2. Resp. Distinguo vocem (verum) quod unusquisque tenetur credere, id est verum, metaphysice & fundamentaliter in se & quoad eventum, concedo majorem, & tum minorem pernego. Christum enim pro unoquoque mortuum esse in se fundamentaliter & metaphysice, non est verum, sed falsum. 2. Quod unusquisque tenetur credere id est verû, non tantum metaphysice, sed etiam moraliter & theologice, utpote credenti revelatum per Dei verbum, vel per evidens aliquod in conscientia πληροφορίαν[?], & sic vera major, & adhuc falsa minor. Nam Christum pro unoquoque esse mortuum, non est verum theologice, nec unicuique revelatum, sed tantum electio & quidem credenti, hoc est, actu fiduciali recumbenti in Christum salvatorem. Iam sic syllogismus struatur, & vanitas Arminiana apparebit statim.
units.tr: 4. 2. Resp. I distinguish the word (true) in "what everyone is bound to believe is true": metaphysically and fundamentally, in itself and as to the outcome, I grant the major and deny the minor. For that Christ died for each person is not true in itself, fundamentally and metaphysically, but false. 2. What everyone is bound to believe is true not only metaphysically but also morally and theologically, as revealed to the believer through the word of God, or through some evident full assurance (plerophoria) in the conscience. So the major is true, and the minor is still false. For that Christ died for each person is not theologically true, nor revealed to each person; it is revealed only to the elect, and indeed to the believer, that is, to the one who by a fiducial act rests on Christ as Saviour. Now let the syllogism be framed thus, and the Arminian vanity will appear at once:

units.la: Quod unusquisque tenetur credere, id est verum, nempe metaphysice & etiam theologice revelatum, nimirum, cuique recumbenti toto corde in Christum.
units.tr: What everyone is bound to believe is true, namely, revealed both metaphysically and theologically, that is, to each one who rests with his whole heart on Christ.

units.la: Atqui Christum pro unoquoque esse mortuum est verum Metaphysice & etiam Theologice revelatum, nempe unicuique credenti & recumbenti toto corde in Christum.
units.tr: But that Christ died for each person is true, metaphysically and also theologically revealed, namely to each believer who rests with his whole heart on Christ.

units.la: Ergo.
units.tr: Therefore.

units.la: Conclusio conceditur à nobis, nempè, Ergo Christus pro unoquoque credente est mortuus.
units.tr: We grant the conclusion: therefore Christ died for each believer.

units.la: §. 3. Sic etiam respondeo, distinguendo & limitando vocem (unusquisque) quod unusquisque nempe oneratus & pondere peccatorum gravatus tenetur credere, id est verum, quod unusquisque sese & suam justitiam deferens & auxilium omne creatum ex humili desiderio salutis id est verum. Jam nemo non videt, non omnes sed onustos pondere peccatorum tantum teneri credere Christum pro se mortuum, & hoc scripturis consentaneum est. Venire ad Christum est credere: atqui tantum onerati & fatigati jubentur venire ad Christum. Matth. 11. 28, 29. Ad quas invitantur tantum sitientes & suæ ariditatis conscii Esai. 55. 1. Joh. 7. 37. Apocal. 21 6 7. tantum onusti peccatis immediate invitantur ad Christum. Object[?], Ergone in mandatis evangelicis reliqui mandencur præsumere, non credere: omnes enim jubentur credere. Resp. Omnes jubentur credere, sed tamen certo ordine. Dici forte poteft, me applicationem fidei effentiâ non includere, contra theologorum orthodoxorum sententias. Resp. me opinari esse effectum inseparabiliter fidem comitantem, non actum formalem, neque puto me habere profundiores theologos reluctantes. Neque assensus generalis erit fides justificans, nec ut vult Dounamus, assensus liber, vivus, verus, efficax, sed Paulus 1. Tim. 1. 15. mihi videtur tria hæc distinguere. 1. Assensum, ratione cujus evangelium dicitur fidus sermo. 2. Fiduciam, cordis acquiescentiam & innixum in Christum, ut in fiduciæ objectum, quod & in promissiones ut objectum quo, ratione cujus, dicit esse λόγ[?]ος ἄξιον πάσης ἀποδοχῆς [?] dignum sermonem qui toto cordis amplexu recipiatur, estque hæc formalis fidei ratio. Hinc Hebræis exprimitur [illegible, ~2 letters] & [illegible, ~3 letters] Prov. 3. 5. Esai. 50. 10. Psal. 71. 6. Hinc εἰς τὸν Θεόν [?], & expressius Hebræi per verbum [illegible, ~3 letters] devolvere Psal. 22. 8. [illegible, ~4 letters] Psal. 37. v. 5.
units.tr: §. 3. I answer in the same way, distinguishing and limiting the word (everyone): everyone, namely one burdened and weighed down by the weight of sins, is bound to believe what is true, that everyone who renounces himself and his own righteousness, and all created help, from a humble desire of salvation, is in truth. Now no one fails to see that not all, but only those laden with the weight of sins, are bound to believe that Christ died for them, and this agrees with Scripture. To come to Christ is to believe; but only the burdened and weary are bidden to come to Christ. Matth. 11. 28, 29. Only the thirsty and those conscious of their dryness are invited, Esai. 55. 1; John 7. 37; Apoc. 21. 6, 7. Only those laden with sins are invited immediately to Christ. Objection: are the rest, then, commanded in the evangelical precepts to presume and not to believe? For all are commanded to believe. Resp. All are commanded to believe, but yet in a certain order. Perhaps someone will say that I do not include application in the essence of faith, contrary to the opinions of the orthodox theologians. Resp. I hold that it is an effect inseparably accompanying faith, not a formal act; and I do not think that I have more profound theologians opposing me. Nor will a general assent be justifying faith, nor, as Dounam wishes, a free, living, true and effective assent. But I think Paul, at 1 Tim. 1. 15, distinguishes three things here. 1. The assent, by reason of which the gospel is called a faithful saying. 2. Fiducia, the heart's acquiescence and leaning on Christ as the object of trust, which, as to the promises, is the object by which, and by reason of which, it is called a word worthy of all acceptance, to be received with the whole embrace of the heart; and this is the formal ground of faith. Hence the Hebrews express it by [illegible, ~2 letters] and [illegible, ~3 letters], Prov. 3. 5; Esai. 50. 10; Psal. 71. 6. Hence "unto God", and more expressly the Hebrews by the verb [illegible, ~3 letters] to roll oneself upon, Psal. 22. 8; [illegible, ~4 letters], Psal. 37. 5.

units.la: 3. Paulus addit applicationem, qua credit Christum venisse ad salvandum se præcipuum ex peccatoribus.
units.tr: 3. Paul adds an application, by which he believes that Christ came to save him, the chief of sinners.

units.la: 6. At dici potest, non posse me fiducia recumbere in Christum salvatorem in genere, nisi perspicuum sit mihi, eum meum esse salvatorem. Vel enim innitor Christo salvatori indefinite, sine respectu ad salvatos, quod absur-dum: abfur-dum: dum : ita relatum à correlato suo separaret; vel salvatori aliorum credentium, & hic applico eum aliis, non mihi, quod est absurdum, vel 3.[?] tanquam meo salvatori, & sic particularis applicatio clauditur in conceptu quidditativo fidei. Respondeo, me actu formali fidei fiducialiter recipere[?] in Christum, ut sufficientem salvatorem omnium credentium, neque est absurdum applicare Christum iis quibus Deus ipsum in verbo applicat: deinde fidei sensu credo eum esse meum salvatorem. Paulus n. ista distinguit. 1.Tim. 1.15.
units.tr: 6. But it can be said that I cannot rest in Christ as Saviour in general unless it is plain to me that he is my Saviour. For either I lean on Christ the Saviour indefinitely, without regard to those who are saved, which is absurd, since it would separate the relative from its correlate; or I lean on the Saviour of other believers, and then I apply him to others, not to myself, which is absurd; or I lean on him as my Saviour, and so particular application is enclosed within the quidditative concept of faith. I reply: in the formal act of faith I receive Christ fiducially as the sufficient Saviour of all believers, and it is not absurd to apply Christ to those to whom God applies him in the word. Then, by the sense of faith, I believe that he is my Saviour. Paul distinguishes these things. 1 Tim. 1.15.

units.la: 2. Necesse est prius recumbam in Christum tanquam sufficientem authorem salutis, qualis in verbo describitur potens salvare ad se venientes, clemens, misericors & gratiosus in omnes ad se confugientes, priusquam in eum recumbam ut in meum salvatorem, alioqui fides mea plane enthusiastica erit; nempe reclinans in eum erga me, de cujus gratiola natura erga genus humanum mihi nondum in verbo constat, & in hoc actu fiduciali esse applicationem illam à theologis nostris toties inculcatam, utpote, quæ opponatur generali aisenfui[?] adhibito Dei verbo à reprobis & diabolis, dici potest.
units.tr: 2. I must first rest in Christ as the sufficient author of salvation, such as he is described in the word: able to save those who come to him, merciful and gracious toward all who flee to him. Only then do I rest in him as my Saviour. Otherwise my faith will be plainly enthusiastic, leaning on him toward me while it is not yet established to me in the word what his kindly nature toward mankind is. And that application so often urged by our theologians, in this fiducial act, can be said to be what is opposed to the general assent given to the word of God by the reprobate and the devils.

units.la: 3. Quod fit mortuus ex intentione & æterno decreto, ut me salvet, non est fidei objectum, neque scriptum neque secundum consequentiam est in verbo, nisi accedat aliquod internum in conscientia mea προληπτικόν[?], ex quo præeunte, actu fiduciali fidei in verbum promissionis & Christum promissum & exhibitum, illud colligam. 4. Reus laesae majestatis prius principem clementem esse in omnes, iram ipsius supplicer deprecantes credit, quam erga se clementem esse confidit. Mendicus aspiciens auri summam prius affectu in id inclinat, tanquam in egestatis remedium, quam ad se cordis affectu id attrahat. §.[?] Prius natura Christus innotuit mihi salvator meus esse jure promissionis, eo quod in ipsum credam, quam salvatorem meum esse, persuasum habeam. Fides enim declarat mihi esse jus in Dei filium: at prius est me habere jus in rem, quam confidam illam ad me pertinere: fides enim qua sciam, nititur jure quo possideam, imo quia credo Christum pro me mortuum, ideo prius est verum eum fuisse pro me mortuum: atqui non constat pro me mortuum esse, nisi credidero in illum prius fiduciali cordis amplexu, ut in salvatorem sufficientem, & hic est fidei actus specificus.
units.tr: 3. That Christ died, by intention and eternal decree, so that he might save me is not an object of faith. It is neither written nor a necessary consequence in the word, unless there is added some internal thing in my conscience, a προληπτικόν [anticipation], from which, going before, I may infer by the fiducial act of faith that the promise in the word and the promised and offered Christ are mine. 4. A man guilty of treason first believes that the prince is merciful toward all who humbly beg him to lay aside his anger, and only then trusts that he is merciful toward himself. A beggar who sees a heap of gold is first inclined toward it by affection, as a remedy for his want, before he draws it to himself by an affection of the heart. §. Christ was first made known to me, by nature, as my Saviour by right of promise, because I believe in him, before I am persuaded that he is my Saviour. For faith declares to me that I have a right to the Son of God; but I must first have a right in the thing before I trust that it belongs to me. For faith by which I know rests on the right by which I possess. Indeed, because I believe that Christ died for me, it is first true that he died for me; yet it is not established that he died for me unless I have first believed in him with the fiducial embrace of the heart, as the sufficient Saviour. This is the specific act of faith.

units.la: 7. Quaerunt Arminiani cujusmodi fidem ex nostra sententia Deus exigat à reprobis, propter carentiam cujus, qui sunt in visibili ecclesia, rei sunt aeternae condemnationis. Resp. Exigere ab iis ut assentiantur omni Dei verbo & promissionibus, & ut recumbant actu fiduciali in Christum sufficientem salutis authorem, nullo vero modo tenentur credere Christum pro se mortuum esse. Quid hic Arminius? Ita insurgit: nemo potest se fateri affinem culpae, ut repudiatam promissionem verbo fallam, si mens dicenlicentis statuit illi promissionem non praestare, vel potius, si certo decreto statuerit, qui verbo promittit, ne promissio ad illum pertineat, aut pertinere possit. Resp. 1. ex Arminij itaque placitis, nemo poterit se fateri affinem culpae ob repudiatam promissionem: statuit enim ille. Deum vocare reprobos gratia inefficaci, quam effectum non sortituram praescit: ita ergo ipsos reprobos alloquitur. Volo, & decerno, & ab aeterno intendo, ut promissis euangelicis crederetis, & obediretis, & salvaremini, & tamen ab aeterno decrevi ex multis possibilibus vocationibus libertatem vestram minime laesuris, eam solam adhibere, quam adhibitam ab aeterno praescivi inutilem fore, & nunquam obediturros vos, sed graviores longe cruciatus nunquam finiendos vos incursuros, & eam solam vocationem negare, quae adhibita fieret, ut obediretis & salvaremini. An hic non Deo blasphemè veram hypocrisin, & contrarias voluntates affingant, aequos lectores judices & ipsorum conscientiam per Deum obtestamur: effari libere velint.
units.tr: 7. The Arminians ask what kind of faith, according to our opinion, God requires of the reprobate, for lack of which those who are in the visible Church are guilty of eternal condemnation. Answer: he requires of them that they assent to every word and promise of God, and that they rest by a fiducial act on Christ as the sufficient author of salvation; but they are in no way bound to believe that Christ died for them. What does Arminius say here? He rises up thus: no one can confess himself akin to guilt for rejecting a promise falsely made in the word, if the mind of the speaker has determined not to fulfil the promise to him, or rather, if he has decided by a certain decree that the promise should not pertain, or be able to pertain, to him. Answer 1: according to the tenets of Arminius himself, no one can confess himself akin to guilt on account of a rejected promise. For he holds that God calls the reprobate with an ineffectual grace, which he foreknows will not attain its effect; so he thus addresses the reprobate: "I will, and decree, and from eternity intend, that you believe and obey the gospel promises and be saved; and yet from eternity I have decided, out of many possible callings that would not harm your freedom, to use only that one which I foreknew from eternity would be useless, and you would never obey, but would incur far greater torments that would never end; and to deny that one calling alone which, if applied, would make you obey and be saved." Do they not here attribute to God a true hypocrisy and contrary wills? We call upon fair readers as judges, and upon their own conscience before God, to be willing to speak freely.

units.la: 2. Ut constet, qui promissiones universales sint: notari velim promissiones has bifariam considerari 1 Formaliter, ut sint significativae divinae voluntatis remunerantis vita aeterna credentes, & sic nihil aliud sunt, quam Dei voluntas sapiens, qua liberrimè statuit ita concatenare fidem & vitam aeternam, ut tam impense charam habeat fidem & obedientiam, ut eam vita aeterna remunerari velit: hanc concatenationem electis pariter & reprobis promissiones promulgatae revelant, & omnes in ecclesia visibili obligant ad assensum, actum fiduciale[?] m in Christum, & sedulam obedientiam, sive Deus statuit decreto suo aeterno bona promissa ad ipsos pertinere, sive non. Nihil itaque hoc salsius (neminem esse affinem culpae ob repudiatam promissionem, si promittens statuit certo decreto, ne promissio ad illum pertineat,) hoc dictitat Arminius, utinam probaret, sed regia est ipsius theologia & dictatoria. Quid? Quod Deus omnibus jam peccandi necessitate constrictis dicit (hoc fac & vives) & statuit certo decreto, ne vita aeterna reddita legali obedientiae ad nos mortales (si Salvatorem excipiemus) pertinet, nemo igitur reus erit ob violationem legis Dei: Deinde certum est Deum nunquam intendisse praemiare actualem Isaaci immolationem, sed nemo sanus diceret Abrahamum culpae affinem non fuisse, si immolare filium, Deo ita jubente detractasset. 3. Statuit hoc argumentum rationem formalem reatus consistere in hoc quod voluntas nostra non sit conformis intentioni Dei & decreto aeterno, nempe vult hominem non esse affinem culpae ob repudiatam promissionem, quae ad ipsum ex Dei intentione non spectat. Si ergo ex Dei intentione ad eum non spectat promissio repudiata, repudiantem nec scelere nec reatu obstringit. Excipe igitur, Iacobe, egregiam theologiam, voluntas Abrahami intendebat immolationem Isaaci: nihil enim certius, nihil firmius decretum erat Abrahamo: at Deus nunquam vel intendit vel decrevit immolationem Isaaci, est hic oppositio inter Abrahami & Dei intentionem. Ergo (inquam ego) Abrahamus intendendo filii mactationem reatui subderat & scelere se obstrinxit. Itane? Atqui in hoc Deus Abrahami obedientiam eximiam collocavit, quod decreverit pro creatore suo unigenitum filium immolare. 2. Promissiones sumuntur in concreto, ut sunt media praedestinationis, & divinam intentionem de promissis beneficiis gratificandis connotant, & sic non sunt nudae voluntatis approbantis signa, sed & connotant Dei decretum. Priore sensu affero, promissiones evangelicas non minus spectare ad reprobos, quam ad electos, posteriore sensu ad solos electos pertinent: soli enim electi dicuntur in scripturis foederati, filii, & haeredes promissionis, Rom.9.8. Et soli Christo principi & Antesignano haeredi fiunt promissiones. Gal. 3. 16. Psal. 89. 26, 27. in eo, femini ipsius & liberis ei a patre datis, Heb. 2. 13.
units.tr: 2. So that it may be clear which promises are universal, I would have it noted that these promises are considered in two ways. 1. Formally, as signifying the divine will which rewards believers with eternal life. In this sense they are nothing other than God's wise will, by which he most freely decided to link faith and eternal life together, holding faith and obedience so dear that he wishes to reward them with eternal life. The published promises reveal this linkage equally to the elect and the reprobate, and oblige all in the visible Church to assent, to the fiducial act in Christ, and to earnest obedience, whether or not God has determined by his eternal decree that the promised good things pertain to them. Nothing therefore is more insipid than the claim (that no one is akin to guilt on account of a rejected promise if the promiser has determined by a certain decree that the promise should not pertain to him), which Arminius keeps repeating. I wish he proved it, but his theology is royal and dictatorial. What then? God says to all men, already bound by the necessity of sinning, (do this and you will live), and decrees by a certain decree that eternal life, owed to legal obedience, does not pertain to us mortals (if we except the Saviour). Therefore no one will be guilty of violating God's law? Furthermore, it is certain that God never intended to reward the actual immolation of Isaac; yet no sane person would say that Abraham was not akin to guilt if he had refused to sacrifice his son when God so commanded. 3. This argument holds that the formal reason of guilt consists in this: that our will is not conformed to God's intention and eternal decree, namely when we will that a man should not be akin to guilt for rejecting a promise which, by God's intention, does not pertain to him. If therefore, by God's intention, the rejected promise does not pertain to him, the one rejecting it is bound by neither crime nor guilt. Take up then, Jacob, your excellent theology: the will of Abraham intended the immolation of Isaac, for nothing was more certain, nothing firmer, than the decree to Abraham; but God never either intended or decreed the immolation of Isaac. Here there is an opposition between the intention of Abraham and that of God. Therefore (I say) Abraham, by intending the slaughter of his son, subjected himself to guilt and bound himself by crime. Is that so? Yet in this God placed the singular obedience of Abraham, that he decided to sacrifice his only son for his Creator. 2. Promises are taken in the concrete, as they are means of predestination, and they connote the divine intention to bestow the promised benefits; so they are not merely signs of an approving will, but also connote God's decree. In the former sense I affirm that the evangelical promises pertain no less to the reprobate than to the elect. In the latter sense they pertain to the elect alone: for only the elect are called in Scripture covenanted, sons and heirs of the promise, Rom. 9.8. And the promises are made only to Christ, the prince and forerunner heir, Gal. 3.16; Ps. 89.26, 27, and in him to his seed and the children given him by the Father, Heb. 2.13.

units.la: 8. Imo ex intentione Dei ne quidem sub conditione offertur vita aeterna reprobis, nihilque salsius nova illa Ioannis Cameronis opinione, statuentis Christum mortuum esse pro omnibus pariter reprobis & electis ex conditione fidei, pro fidelibus vero solis absolute. Christus enim (inquit) pro te satisfecit, sed ea lege, si tu fit tu id factum credas, ut si captivum redimerem, pretio numerato, ita tamen ut nisi ille se redemtum agnoscat meo beneficio, habeatur pro non redemto. Contr. sic arguo. 1. Si Christus mortuus est pro reprobis conditionatè, pro ipsorum peccatis attritus fuit, & mortem æternam illis debitam in corpore & anima luisset, necesse est, at hoc posterius est absurdum. Ergo etiam prius. Major est manifesta: quid enim est Christum pro aliquo mori, nisi iram Dei ei debitam, pro quo moritur, sustinere. Prob. minor. Si Christus vel conditionatè mortem reprobis debitam sustinuit, reprobi etiam nunquam credentes non possunt ex ordine justitiæ divinæ mortem æternam in se sustinere, quod posterius palpabilis falsitatis damnant in nullâ fere non pagina sacra oracula. Dicet Camero Christum conditionatè satisfecisse pro reprobis, nempe si crediderint: at vero an non conditionatè satisfecit pro omnium reproborum peccatis? Credo neminem hoc negaturum, nisi quis, Christum pro solo peccato originali satisfecisse assereret, quod est contra scripturas, quæ nos sanguine Christi ab omnibus peccatis purgari volunt, 1. Joh. 1. 8. 1. Pet. 1. 18. 19. Esai. 53. 6. Si pro omnibus peccatis reproborum pœnam sustinuit, tum etiam pro finali infidelitate & impœnitentia reproborum, & sic ex ordine justitiæ non debent reprobi pœnas finalis infidelitatis in gehenna æternum lueri: justitia enim Dei pro eodem peccato non postulat satisfactiones binas. 2. Pro quibus Christus satisfecit, Deus ipsis peccata non imputat, 2.Cor.5.19. Atqui reprobis peccata imputat. Ergo &c. Non imputat (inquit Camero) Deus reprobis peccata, ex hypothesi quod credant: nugæ: imputatio est actus divinæ voluntatis immanens, atqui nulla in Deo volitio est conditionata aut pendet indeterminata à voluntate creata. 3. Si Christus intendit & suo & Patris consilio, satisfactionis pretium numerare conditionatè pro reprobis, tum ipsos etiam ad æternam gloriam destinat conditionatè: at vero quid hoc aliud est, quam universalis omnium, citra exceptionem, electio ex hypothesi fidei, à quo verbis saltem ipsi Arminiani se abhorrere profitentur. 3. Si Christus mortuus est pro reprobis, eos amore, quo major dari non potest, Ioh. 15. v.13. complexus est: atqui hoc dici non potest, nisi etiam fidei & regenerationis gratiam ipsis meritus esset, & pro iisdem Patrem precibus interpellet, quod ipse salvator negat, Ioh. 17. Non rogo pro mundo. Si enim Deus Filium pro ipsis in mortem tradidit, quomodo non cum eo omnia daret? Rom. 8. Atqui non dat ipsis fidem, nec eam ipsis meritus est. 4. Hæc est Pauli consequentia, Rom. 8. Christus est mortuus, ergo quis condemnet? quo innuit propositionem hanc connexam esse veram, non condemnantur ulli pro quibus Christus est mortuus, nempe pro quibus absolute mortuus est, ii non condemnantur: si vero non crediderint, condemnabuntur: at vero fides non-condemnationis non est causa meritoria, sola Christi satisfactio est non-condemnationis causa meritoria: fides vero nec scripturis, nec rationi convenienter est causa organica mortis Christi: quasi vero nos credendo efficeremus, ut Christus mortuus esset, aut quasi nos non credendo efficeremus, ut Christus nos pro non peccatoribus aestimet. §. [?] Numeratio pretii & mors Christi est absoluta: mortuus est enim pro multis nondum natis, nedum non credentibus: at vero numerari pretium & non redimi captivum, adversatur justitiae: dices non adversari justitiae, ubi ad actualem acceptationem numerati pretii requiritur fides nostra, ex speciali Dei mandato: sed sic diluo: Dei εὐδοκία[?] & complacentia & acceptatio peccatorum ubique Christi satisfactionis nomine Deo in scripturis tribuitur Mat. 3. 17. Ephes. 1 6. Col. 1. 21. 22. Rom. 5. 10. Neque dicitur Deo complacitum satisfactoriè esse, in fide nostra. 6.
