Christus moriens praescivit reprobos, nunquam crediturus, imo ne quidem credere posse, utpote qui absolute fidei gratiam ipsis non est commeritus, idem etiam Deus Pater ab aeterno praescivit: at absurdum est Christum mori, & Deum ipsius mortem acceptare, ex hypothesi conditionis, quam nunquam futuram fore praescit, neque fore posse: quasi vero Christus ita in evangelio reprobos alloqueretur: Ego pro vobis animam meam depono, quod amoris est intentissimi mei ergo vos, eo animo ut si credere velitis, salvaremini: certo tamen scio, vos nunquam credituroc, imo absoluta mea voluntate decrevi gratiam credendi nec vobis dare, nec promereri: atqui vir prudens ne quidem conditionatè intendit, quod præscit nunquam futurum esse. 7. Qui intendit finem, intendit etiam media ad finem: atqui Deus reprobis fidem,falutis medium non intendit. Ergo nec salutem morte Christi ipsis intendit. 8. Dici non potest Christum mortuum esse pro iis, qui ex absoluta Dei voluntate, ne fando, vel tenuissima rumoris aurâ, quicquam de morte ipsius audierunt. Quomodo enim tale beneficium mortalibus pareret, qui ipsos de beneficentia certiores absolute noluit facere?
units.tr: 8. Indeed, in God's intention eternal life is not offered to the reprobate even conditionally, and nothing is more false than that new opinion of John Cameron, who holds that Christ died for all alike, reprobate and elect, on condition of faith, but for believers alone absolutely. "Christ has satisfied for you," he says, "but on this condition: that you believe it done, so that if I redeemed a captive by paying the price, yet unless he acknowledges himself redeemed by my kindness, he is to be regarded as not redeemed." Against this I argue thus. (1) If Christ died for the reprobate conditionally, and was crushed for their sins, and had paid in body and soul the eternal death owed to them, then it must follow; but the latter is absurd; therefore the former too. The major is plain: for what is it for Christ to die for someone, except to bear the wrath of God due to the one for whom he dies? As to the minor: if Christ endured conditionally the death owed to the reprobate, then the reprobate, even if they never believe, cannot by the order of divine justice bear eternal death in themselves; yet the sacred oracles condemn this latter as a palpable falsehood on almost every page. Cameron will say that Christ satisfied conditionally for the reprobate, namely if they believe. But did he not satisfy conditionally for the sins of all the reprobate? I think no one will deny this, unless someone should assert that Christ satisfied only for original sin, which is contrary to Scripture, which wills that we are cleansed from all sins by the blood of Christ (1 John 1:8; 1 Pet. 1:18, 19; Isa. 53:6). If he bore the punishment for all the sins of the reprobate, then also for their final unbelief and impenitence; and so by the order of justice the reprobate ought not to pay in hell eternally the penalty of final unbelief, for the justice of God does not demand a double satisfaction for the same sin. (2) God does not impute sins to those for whom Christ satisfied (2 Cor. 5:19). But God imputes sins to the reprobate. Therefore etc. Cameron says God does not impute sins to the reprobate on the hypothesis that they believe: trifles! Imputation is an immanent act of the divine will, and no volition in God is conditional or depends on an indeterminate creaturely will. (3) If Christ intended, by his own and the Father's counsel, to pay the price of satisfaction conditionally for the reprobate, then he also destines them conditionally to eternal glory. But what is this other than a universal election of all, without exception, on the hypothesis of faith, which the Arminians at least in words profess to abhor? (4) If Christ died for the reprobate, he embraced them with the love than which no greater can be given (John 15:13). But this cannot be said unless he also merited for them the grace of faith and regeneration, and intercedes with the Father in prayer for them; which the Saviour himself denies: "I do not pray for the world" (John 17:9). For if God delivered his Son to death for them, how will he not with him also give them all things? (Rom. 8:32). But he does not give them faith, nor did he merit it for them. (5) This is Paul's inference in Romans 8: Christ died, therefore who shall condemn? By which he implies that this connected proposition is true: none for whom Christ died are condemned; namely, those for whom he died absolutely are not condemned; but if they do not believe, they will be condemned. Yet the non-condemnation of faith is not a meritorious cause; only Christ's satisfaction is the meritorious cause of non-condemnation; and faith is in agreement neither with Scripture nor with reason the organic cause of Christ's death. As if by believing we brought it about that Christ should die, or as if by not believing we brought it about that Christ should not regard us as non-sinners! §. [?] The payment of the price and the death of Christ are absolute: for he died for many not yet born, let alone unbelievers. But that the price be paid and the captive not be redeemed is contrary to justice. You will say it is not contrary to justice where our faith is required for the actual acceptance of the price paid, by a special command of God. But I answer thus: God's good pleasure, complacency and acceptance of sinners, in Christ's satisfaction, is everywhere in Scripture ascribed to God (Matt. 3:17; Eph. 1:6; Col. 1:21, 22; Rom. 5:10); nor is it said that God is satisfied in our faith. (6) Christ, dying, foresaw that the reprobate would never believe, nor even be able to believe, since he had not absolutely merited for them the grace of faith; the Father too foresaw this from eternity. But it is absurd that Christ should die, and God accept his death, on the hypothesis of a condition which God foresees will never come to pass and cannot come to pass: as if Christ addressed the reprobate in the gospel thus: "I lay down my life for you, out of my most intense love for you, with the mind that you would be saved if you were willing to believe; yet I know for certain that you will never believe, and by my absolute will I have decreed neither to give nor to merit for you the grace of believing." But a prudent man does not even conditionally intend what he foresees will never be. (7) He who intends the end intends also the means to the end; but God does not intend faith, the means of salvation, for the reprobate. Therefore neither does he intend their salvation by the death of Christ. (8) It cannot be said that Christ died for those who, by the absolute will of God, have not heard, not even by rumour or the faintest breath of report, anything of his death. For how would such a benefit profit mortals whom he absolutely refused to make certain of his kindness?

units.la: 9. Nullibi dicitur crede, & Christus pro te mortuus erit. Quid absurdius? Prius mortuus est pro nobis, quam credimus. Nec argumenta Cameronis sunt hili: ea enim prolixius, favente Numine, refutabimus alibi.
units.tr: 9. Nowhere is it said: "Believe, and Christ will die for you." What is more absurd? He died for us before we believed. Nor are Cameron's arguments nothing: God willing, we will refute them at greater length elsewhere.

units.la: 9. Dicunt alii Christum pro omnibus esse mortuum, hoc sensu, ut possit Deus omnium peccata remittere, sub qua scilicet conditione sibi visum fuerit, & frustra postulari fidem ab omnibus, nisi peccata omnium remittere potuisset Deus Pater, & ad hoc sufficiens fuerit mors Christi, ideoque mortuum esse pro omnibus & singulis, ita ut omnes & singuli salvatentur, modo in Christum crederent: atqui ego hæc etiam falsa esse credo. Longe enim differunt ista (vitam æternam omnibus offerri & singulis sub conditione fidei) (& omnibus & singulis offerri vitam ex Dei intentione dandi illis vitam si crediderint.) Nam prius est verum, sed tum oblatio vitæ, nihil est aliud quam revelatio divinæ voluntatis, qua fidei & vitæ æternæ concatenatio proponitur. Posterius est falsum. 1. Deus vel offert vitam reprobis impetratam morte Christi sub illa conditione, vel non impetratam, sed ex absoluta Dei libertate, citra Christi satisfactionem communicandam, siquidem crediderint: non priori modo fit oblatio vitæ. Diceret enim euangelium, sic reprobis afferri vitam impetratam morte Christi si crediderint, quæ non est morte Christi impetrata, & quæ vita aut remissio impetrata oferanturiis[?], sub conditione fidei in Christum impetrante hæc, qui hæc non impetraverit, mihi videretur ἀνεπιλήπτον[?]: nec posterius dici potest. Nam si remissio & vita non impetrata per Christi mortem reprobis offerrentur, daretur aliud sub cælo nomen, per quod oporteat homines salvari præter nomen Christi, quod absurdum est. 2. Pater dedit Filio potestatem dandi vitam datis sibi à Patre tantum, Iob. 17. Atqui reprobi non sunt dati Filio à Patre. Pater ergo non dedit Filio potestatem dandi vitam æternam reprobis. Ergo neque potest Filius ex sua & Patris intentione vitam & remissionem iis, offerre. Dici enim non potest à Patre acquisivisse potestatem absolutam remittendi peccata reprobo-rum: eam enim habuit communem cum Patre ab æterno. Potest enim Deus absolutâ potentiâ omnium condonare peccata, citra Christi satisfactionem, id quod solide, ut & omnia probat Gul. Tuissus. Si vero Christus potestatem ordinariam & judiciariam remittendi peccata reproborum morte sua acquisivit, ita ut non obstante justitia Dei potuisset iis omnia delicta condonare, tum Christum reproborum peccatis non posse non satisfecisse credo: atqui hoc est falsum: nec enim Christus reproborum personam in ara crucis gestavit, nec pro peccatis ipsorum satisfecit? tum enim ex ordine justitiæ non possunt ipsi suorum peccatorum pœnas luere. 3. Christus solis electis impetravit & potentiam remittendi & actualem remissionem, quia & potentia remittendi & actualis remissio oriuntur ex satisfactione præstita: sed forte qui contra sentiunt, intelligunt potentiam remotam, quæ fundatur in sola infinita sufficientia mortis meriti Christi; at neque dici potest in tali potentia fundari voluntatem Dei conditionatam conferendi reprobis salutem, quoniam salus conditionata euangelio promissa est à λύτρῳ[?] formali & actuali pro peccatis satisfactione, ut effectus ex causa meritoria: Et sic dicendum, Christum morte suæ vitam reprobis meritum esse. Dicentes ex hoc quod Christus λύτρῳ[?] infiniti valoris Deo obtulit, eum posse remittere reproborum peccata, si crediderint. Audio commentum inauditum: quorum nomine Christus λύτρον[?] obtulit? Reproborum ne? Ergo absolute ipsos redemredemit: nam pro ipsis pretium numeravit. Electorum ne? At fare quaesso? an quia Deus pretium numeravit solorum electorum nomine iustitiae divinae, dici posset eum posse, non obstante iustitia, reproborum peccata, pro quibus non satisfecit, condonare? Ego vero, quae mea est infantia, non video qui Christus posset eorum peccata condonare, pro quibus non satisfeci[?] iustitiae Dei. 4. Christum pro omnibus & singulis sufficienter mortuum esse, nusquam scriptura innuit. Nam (pro) notat intentionem morientis, nulla vero fuit in Christo intentio moriendi pro reprobis, neque ullo icnsu dici potest Deum decrevisse, ut mors Christi esset sufficiens omnibus redimendis: ea enim sufficientia & materialis causalitas inest morti Christi antecedenter ad Dei decretum, & ex intrinseca virtute citra omne decretum est infiniti valoris, ideoque non nego λύτρον[?] materialiter sumptum esse omnibus & singulis sufficiens: at non est formaliter λύτρον[?], nisi quatenus persolvitur nomine eorum, pro quorum peccatis Christus satisfecit, quibus nullo modo accensendi sunt reprobi. Hic obiter notari velim vanitatem ratiocinationum Remonstrantium, qui dicunt nos enervare omnem vim meriti Christi, ergo reprobos. Voluntas itaque (inquiunt) divina sola causa est, qua fit, ut vis meriti Christi, per se & in se aliquum sufficiens, non pertingat ad eos nulla propria aut vincibili eorum culpa. Sed Resp. 1. Statuimus & palam profitemur solam Dei voluntatem acceptantem satisfactionem ctionem Christi facere mortem Christi formaliter λύτρον: Pretium enim captivi redimendi est formaliter pretium, quatenus numeratur à persolvente, & acceptatur ab eo, cui persolvitur. Sit pretium sufficientissimum, si non & persolvatur nomine captivi, & acceptetur ab eo qui captivum detineat, non est formaliter λύτρον.
units.tr: 9. Others say that Christ died for all, in this sense: that God is able to forgive the sins of all, on whatever condition seemed good to Him, and that faith would be demanded of all in vain unless God the Father could forgive the sins of all, and the death of Christ was sufficient for this; therefore He died for all and each, so that all and each might be saved, provided they believed in Christ. But I think these claims are false too. For there is a great difference between these two statements: that eternal life is offered to all and to each under the condition of faith, and that life is offered to all and to each by God's intention of giving it to them if they believe. The former is true, for the offer of life is nothing other than the revelation of the divine will, by which the connection between faith and eternal life is set forth. The latter is false. 1. Either God offers life to the reprobate, obtained by the death of Christ on that condition, or He offers it not obtained by Christ but to be bestowed from His absolute freedom, without Christ's satisfaction, if they believe. In the first way there is no offer of life. For the gospel would then say that life obtained by the death of Christ is brought to the reprobate if they believe, when it is not obtained by the death of Christ; and I would think it inexcusable that remission and life, which have not been obtained, are offered under the condition of faith in Christ, who did not obtain them. Nor can the second be said. For if remission and life not obtained through Christ's death were offered to the reprobate, there would be "no other name under heaven by which men must be saved" besides the name of Christ, which is absurd. 2. The Father gave the Son power to give life to those given to Him by the Father only (John 17). But the reprobate were not given to the Son by the Father. Therefore the Father did not give the Son power to give eternal life to the reprobate. Therefore the Son cannot, by His own intention and the Father's, offer life and remission to them. For it cannot be said that by the Father He acquired the absolute power of forgiving the sins of the reprobate; for He had that power in common with the Father from eternity. God can, by His absolute power, forgive the sins of all without Christ's satisfaction, a point which Gulielmus Tuissus proves soundly, and indeed proves everything. But if Christ acquired by His death the ordinary and judicial power of forgiving the sins of the reprobate, so that, notwithstanding the justice of God, He could have pardoned all their offences, then I believe Christ must have satisfied for the sins of the reprobate; yet this is false. For Christ did not bear the person of the reprobate on the altar of the cross, nor did He make satisfaction for their sins; for then, by the order of justice, they could not pay the penalties of their own sins. 3. Christ obtained both the power of forgiving and actual remission for the elect alone, because both the power of forgiving and actual remission arise from the satisfaction rendered. But perhaps those who think otherwise mean a remote power, which rests only on the infinite sufficiency of the death and merit of Christ. Yet it cannot be said that God's conditional will to bestow salvation on the reprobate is grounded in such a power, since conditional salvation is promised in the gospel on the basis of a formal and actual ransom and satisfaction for sins, as an effect follows from its meritorious cause. And so it must be said that Christ by His death merited life for the reprobate. Those who say that because Christ offered to God a ransom of infinite value, He can forgive the sins of the reprobate if they believe, I hear an unheard-of fiction. In whose name did Christ offer the ransom? In the name of the reprobate? Then He absolutely redeemed them, for He paid the price on their behalf. In the name of the elect? But I ask, how so? Could it be said that, because God accepted the price in the name of the elect alone, in virtue of divine justice, He can, notwithstanding justice, pardon the sins of the reprobate, for whom He did not satisfy? As for me, whatever my own simplicity may be, I do not see how Christ could pardon the sins of those for whom He did not satisfy the justice of God. 4. Scripture nowhere implies that Christ died sufficiently for all and each. For "for" (pro) denotes the intention of the one dying, and Christ had no intention of dying for the reprobate. Nor can it be said in any sense that God decreed that the death of Christ should be sufficient for the redemption of all. For that sufficiency and material causality belong to the death of Christ prior to God's decree, and by its intrinsic virtue, apart from any decree, it is of infinite value; therefore I do not deny that the ransom, taken materially, is sufficient for all and each. But it is not a ransom formally, except insofar as it is paid in the name of those for whose sins Christ satisfied, and the reprobate by no means belong to these. Here I would like to note in passing the vanity of the reasoning of the Remonstrants, who say that we undermine all the force of Christ's merit, and therefore that of the reprobate. "The divine will, then," they say, "is the only cause why the power of Christ's merit, which in itself and of itself is something sufficient, does not reach them, through no proper or avoidable fault of their own." But I reply: 1. We maintain, and openly profess, that the will of God alone, accepting the satisfaction of Christ, makes the death of Christ formally a ransom. For the price of a captive's redemption is formally a price insofar as it is paid by the one who pays it and accepted by the one to whom it is paid. Let the price be most sufficient: if it is not paid in the name of the captive, and accepted by the one who holds the captive, it is not formally a ransom.

units.la: 2. Falsum est solam Dei voluntatem esse causam, cur vis meriti non pertingat ad reprobos: est enim sola causa prima & remota: at reproborum malitiosa rejectio Christi est causa proxima, quâ admirandâ consociatione ipsorum obstinatus animus libertate id respuat & amplecti nolit, quod absoluta Dei voluntas ad ipsos pertinere nollet, & quoniam libere indulgent infidelitati suæ, jure meritissimo plectuntur.
units.tr: 2. It is false that the will of God alone is the cause why the power of Christ's merit does not reach the reprobate. It is only the first and remote cause; the proximate cause is the malicious rejection of Christ by the reprobate, by which, in a wonderful combination, their obstinate mind freely refuses and is unwilling to embrace what the absolute will of God would not want to pertain to them. And since they freely indulge in their unbelief, they are punished most deservedly.

units.la: 3. Cupimus, ut nos doceant, quid commeritus sit Christus reprobis? Non fidem, non regenerationem: id enim ipsi respuunt p.95 [?]. c.8. nimirum commeritus est iis ut possint credere vel non credere, id quod ab instinctu humani arbitrii esse credunt, siquidem sincere agere didicissent.
units.tr: 3. We want them to teach us what Christ has merited for the reprobate. Not faith, not regeneration: for these they themselves reject (p. 95, c. 8). Clearly he merited for them only that they might be able to believe or not to believe, which they think comes from the impulse of human free will, provided they had learned to act sincerely.

units.la: 5. Proponatur à Deo, Iudæ, Simoni Mago, aliisque reprobis universal. promissio: Intendo & decerno vobis salutem, si credideritis in filium meum. Illud (Si) vel referatur ad Dei intellectum, vel ad Dei voluntatem decernentem. Si ad intellectum: dubia erit Dei scientia, quod absurdum. Si ad voluntatem, pendebit Dei voluntas in bivio à conditione præstanda, vel non præstanda: atqui voluntas Dei utpote infinita à nullo agente externo dependet, nec aliunde, quam à fe determinatur, id quod non d ffitentur [?] Remonstrantes. 6. Si strictè & proprie loquendum, ne quidem Dei voluntas conferendi electis salutem est conditionata. Ergo multo minus eam reprobis conditionatè vult. Prob. antecedens. Quia conditio fidei non proprie pendet ab electorum arbitrio, ut sit, vel non sit, sed ab absoluta Dei gratiosâ voluntate Ephes. 2. 1. Phil. 1. 23. Idcoque hoc (volo dare vitam æternam electis, siquidem crediderint) æquipollet huic (volo ex absoluta libertate dare electis vitam, siquidem voluero ex eadem meâ absoluta libertate dare fidem) at quid hoc aliud est, quam si Deus diceret: (volo electis dare vitam, siquidem voluero dare vitam) non est hæc voluntas conditionata, quando & conditionatum & conditio pendent absolutè ab unâ & eâdem Dei absolutâ voluntate: pari enim ratione mundi creatio est conditionata: nempe ex hypothesi quod creare decrevisset. Sic si pater filio cupienti hæreditatem, eam dare velit, ea conditione, ut centum talenta, quibus ipsam redimit, dare velit, quid hoc aliud esset quam patrem dare filio hæreditatem, ex hypothesi, quod eam dare velit, quam voluntatem conditionatam in rigore nemo appellaret. Conditio vero potestativa ad esse & non esse (ut loquuntur jurifconfulti) Deo nullo modo competit: promissiones in verbo vero proponuntur conditionate, ad ingenerandam in nobis piam folicitudinem ea præstandi officia, quæ Deus adipiscendæ salutis antecedanea esse voluit. Non igitur dicimus Deum velle dare vitam reprobis, ex hypothesi, quod fidem dare velit: Arminiani vero accerrime digladiantur & concertant nobiscum pro conditionibus, quæ Dei voluntatem determinant: eas enim conditiones volunt, quas ex humano arbitrio suspendunt. Ideoque clamitant promifsiones æternæ vitæ conditionatas non posse subordinari decreto absoluto, quod antea illud bonum erat absolute destinatum: quod esset verum, si tales essent in scriptuis conditiones Dei voluntatis determinativæ, quales illi somniant. Dicunt nostri, fidem non esse conditionem moventem Dei voluntatem, & tamen salutem nostram esse conditionatam, quod est verissimum. Nam Deus non vult nobis aliam vitam, quam quæ antecedaneam habet fidem, & tamen nullo modo movetur Dei voluntas à fide nostra. Hoc itaque sacræ theologiæ mysterium est, Deum offerre reprobis vitam æternam sub conditione fidei, & tamen eam vitam nec esse partam Christi meritis, nec Deum decrevisse ipsis fidem dare: neque dicendum Christum indefinite præstitisse infinitam satisfactionem pro omnibus & singulis hactenus, quatenus justitiæ pro omnibus satisfactum, ita ut liberum sit Deo omnium & singulorum peccata remittere, vel non remittere, quia Christus pro quibusdam nominatim satisfecit justitiæ Dei, & pro nullis aliis. At dicunt, frustra postulari fidem à reprobis, nisi ita pro illis mortuus est Christus, ut posit Deus, non obstante justitia, ipsorum peccata remittere. Sed nego consequentiam. Nam ex ipsorum doctrina, qui ita opinantur, pari ratione dici posset, frustra postulari fidem ex viribus gratiæ mediatoris sanguine commeritæ ab iis, quibus mediator nullam talem gratiam commeritus est. At ipsi docent, gratiam credendi meritis Christi, reprobis haudquaquam esse partam, & tamen ab iis fidem postulari jure merito. At vero si Deus postulando à reprobis fidem, mandato euangelico ipsius intentionem dandi fidem revelaret, consequentia majorem veritatis speciem haberet. At vero mandata & promissiones euangelicæ Dei intentionem, ut reprobi obedirent, reprobis non exprimunt, sed tantum iis revelant sanctam illam concatenationem, tum inter fidem & ipsorum credendi obligationem, tum inter fidem & vitam æternam: quæ quidem concatenatio abstrahit à Dei decreto & intentione de actuali efficientia obedientiæ mandatę, & ab omni Dei intentione terminata in actualem obedientiam reproborum, tantum revelat reprobis sanctam & æquam Dei complacentiam in fide reproborum, quam complacentiam Deo visum est revelare iis, partim mandatis, partim promissis, partim euangelicis minis. Non vero revelat reprobis intentionem ipsius esse, ut obediant: nihil enim tale intendit aut vult, ut sic admirando modo ita rei sint reprobi, ut Deus intentione excidere non dici queat.
units.tr: 5. Let the universal promise be put forward by God to Judas, to Simon Magus, and to the other reprobate: "I intend and decree salvation for you, if you believe in my Son." The word Illud (Si) ("if") must refer either to God's understanding or to His decreeing will. If it refers to His understanding, God's knowledge will be doubtful, which is absurd. If it refers to His will, the will of God will hang in the balance, depending on a condition that may or may not be fulfilled. But the will of God, being infinite, depends on no external agent and is determined by nothing but itself, which the Remonstrants do not deny. 6. Strictly and properly speaking, not even God's will to confer salvation on the elect is conditional. Much less, then, does He will it conditionally for the reprobate. I prove the antecedent: the condition of faith does not depend properly on the choice of the elect, so that it either is or is not, but on God's absolute and gracious will (Ephes. 2. 1; Phil. 1. 23). Hence this proposition, "I will to give eternal life to the elect, if they believe," is equivalent to this one, "I will by my absolute freedom to give eternal life to the elect, if I will by the same absolute freedom to give them faith." But what is this other than if God were to say, "I will to give life to the elect, if I will to give life"? That will is not conditional, since both the conditioned thing and the condition depend absolutely on one and the same absolute will of God. By the same reasoning the creation of the world would be conditional, namely on the hypothesis that He had decreed to create. So if a father, when his son desires an inheritance, is willing to give it on condition that he is willing to give it in return for a hundred talents by which he redeems it, this is nothing other than the father giving the son the inheritance on the hypothesis that he is willing to give it; and no one would strictly call that a conditional will. A potestative condition, as the jurists call a condition of being or not being, in no way belongs to God. The promises in the Word are, however, set forth conditionally, to stir up in us a pious anxiety to perform those duties which God willed to precede the attaining of salvation. We therefore do not say that God wills to give life to the reprobate on the hypothesis that He is willing to give them faith. The Arminians, however, contend most fiercely with us and strive for conditions which determine God's will; for they want those conditions which they make dependent on human choice. And so they cry out that conditional promises of eternal life cannot be subordinated to an absolute decree, since that good had been absolutely destined beforehand; which would be true if such conditions determining God's will were in the Scriptures as they dream of. Our people say that faith is not a condition moving God's will, and yet that our salvation is conditional, which is most true. For God does not will us any other life than that which has faith going before it, and yet God's will is in no way moved by our faith. This, then, is the mystery of sacred theology: that God offers eternal life to the reprobate under the condition of faith, and yet that this life was neither procured by the merits of Christ nor did God decree to give them faith. Nor must it be said that Christ has indefinitely rendered an infinite satisfaction for all and each, in so far as satisfaction has been made to justice for all, so that it is free for God to remit or not to remit the sins of each and all; because Christ has satisfied the justice of God for certain persons by name, and for no others. But they say that faith would be demanded of the reprobate in vain, unless Christ died for them in such a way that God, notwithstanding justice, could remit their sins. But I deny the consequence. For on the doctrine of those who hold this opinion, it could by the same reasoning be said that faith is demanded in vain from those to whom the Mediator has not merited any such grace, though the grace of believing has been merited by the blood of the Mediator. Yet they themselves teach that the grace of believing has by no means been procured for the reprobate by the merits of Christ, and yet faith is rightly and deservedly demanded of them. But if God, by demanding faith of the reprobate, revealed in His evangelical command His intention to give them faith, the consequence would have a greater appearance of truth. In fact, however, the evangelical commands and promises do not express to the reprobate God's intention that they should obey; they only reveal to them that holy chain, both between faith and their obligation to believe, and between faith and eternal life. This chain abstracts from God's decree and intention concerning the actual effecting of the obedience commanded, and from every intention of God directed to the actual obedience of the reprobate. It reveals to the reprobate only God's holy and just complacency in the faith of believers, a complacency which it has pleased God to reveal to them partly by commands, partly by promises, and partly by evangelical threats. But it does not reveal to the reprobate that it is His intention that they obey; for He intends or wills nothing of the kind, so that in a wonderful manner the reprobate are so guilty that God cannot be said to have failed in His intention.

units.la: 1o. At dicit Arminius, Deum postulando fidem à reprobis, præ se ferre, se posuisse ipsis Christum ipsorum salvatorem esse, quod est falsum: Ergo præ se fert, quod non vult. Resp. 1. Hoc (reprobi credite, & salvi eritis) præ se fert (reprobi, sancta mea voluntas fidem & salutem concatenavit, vos autem credere obligamini) at Deum hic præ se ferre, ipsius esse intentionem & decretum, ut reprobi credant & salventur, præ se fert insigne mendacium.
units.tr: 1o. But Arminius says that by demanding faith of the reprobate God shows that He has set Christ before them as their Saviour, which is false; therefore He shows what He does not will. Reply 1. This statement, "Reprobate, believe and you will be saved," shows this: "Reprobate, my holy will has joined faith and salvation together, but you are bound to believe." But that God here shows that it is His intention and decree that the reprobate should believe and be saved, is a notable falsehood.

units.la: 2. Quamvis Deus non posuerit Christum salvatorem omnium, etiam reproborum, tamen jure exigit, ut tota fiducia recumbant in salvatorem sufficientissimum omnibus credentibus; & jure rei sunt, quia nolunt se dedere Christo, quamvis Christus ipsos ampletti[?] ab æterno nunquam decreverit. Quid etiam absurdi rationi humanæ, invitare ad convivium Deum quam plurimos, quos venire non decrevit, & jubere ampletti[?] Christum salvatorem ipsis æterno Dei consilio nunquam destinatum? Abrahamo præcipit verbo immolationem Isaaci nunquam Dei decreto destinaram & volitam: dices eum verbo suo dissimulatorem agere, aliud loqui, aliud velle. Resp. Non sequitur. Nam vult obedientiam omnium externe vocatorum sibi complacere, etsi plerique non obediant: hoc eloquitur & nihil aliud, neque intentionem suam & decretum Deus sermone suo exprimere tenetur. Quisquam mortalium Iehovam loqui docuit? licetne ei, sensa mentis, pro ut vult, exprimere?
units.tr: 2. Although God has not set Christ forth as the Saviour of all, even of the reprobate, yet He rightly requires that they rest with their whole trust on the Saviour who is wholly sufficient for all who believe; and they are rightly guilty, because they are unwilling to surrender themselves to Christ, although Christ from eternity never decreed to embrace them. And what is there absurd to human reason in God inviting very many to the feast, whom He has not decreed to come, and in commanding them to embrace Christ as Saviour, who by the eternal counsel of God was never destined for them? He commanded Abraham by word to sacrifice Isaac, though by God's decree the sacrifice was never destined and willed; you will say that He is acting deceitfully in His word, saying one thing and willing another. Reply: It does not follow. For He wills that the obedience of all who are outwardly called should please Him, even though most do not obey; this He expresses, and nothing more, nor is God bound to express His intention and decree in His speech. Did anyone among mortals teach Jehovah how to speak? Is He not free to express the thoughts of His mind as He wills?

units.la: 11. At obloquitur infœlix ingenium Vorstij, si crederent reprobi, frustra esse: nam Christus pro ipsis non est mortuus, ideoque posita fide reproborum, ipsorum salus est impossibilis, quoniam iis nec vitam nec remissionem meritus est Christus. Resp. 1. Nec Arminiani audent dicere reprobis partam esse remissionem actualem, sed nescio quam potentiam, quæ per actum fidei compleatur, quasi vero fides nostra esset pars collateralis satisfactionis. 2. Deinde qualem remissionem Christus impetravit, talem communicat: at persectam & actualem impetravit, non potentialem. (Siquidem remissio in potentia, non est remissio) Col. 2. 14. 15. 3. Reprobum esse, & credere, sunt ἀνύπαρκτα[?], si crederent, decreta suisset eorum fides, & si decreta fides, etiam decreta & salus, ideoque ex impossibili suppositione nihil sequitur. Nam in Dei decreto, hæc reciprocantur) Christus mortuus est pro credentibus) & (soli sunt credentes, pro quibus Christus est mortuus,) & tandem aliquando, re ipsa hæc reciprocantur etiam & in idem coincidunt suo tempore.
units.tr: 11. But the unhappy wit of Vorstius objects that if the reprobate believed, it would be in vain, for Christ did not die for them, and therefore, faith of the reprobate being supposed, their salvation is impossible, since Christ has not merited for them either life or remission. Reply 1. Neither do the Arminians dare to say that actual remission has been procured for the reprobate, but some unknown power which is completed through the act of faith, as if our faith were a collateral part of the satisfaction. 2. Further, what kind of remission Christ has obtained, that kind He communicates; but He obtained a complete and actual remission, not a potential one. (For remission in potency is not remission.) Col. 2. 14, 15. 3. To be reprobate and to believe are [ἀνύπαρκτα], non-existent together; if they believed, their faith would have been decreed, and if faith were decreed, salvation too would be decreed; therefore nothing follows from an impossible supposition. For in God's decree these are reciprocal: "Christ died for believers," and "only those are believers for whom Christ died," and finally, at some time, in fact these reciprocate and coincide in the same thing in their proper time.

units.la: 12. Quomodo electi ignari non minus intentionis divinæ, quam reprobi, quando pri-mo mo audiunt promissiones, sciant se debere credere? Resp. Recumbendum est illis in Christum omnium credentium salvatorem, & tum constabit iis de intentione Dei. 2. Sicut agnus solo instinctu matrem internoscit ab aliis ovibus, ita nati a Deo instinctu supernaturali in Christum innituntur, quod reprobi tali instinctu destituti, non possunt facere. At dicunt non posse non solutum esse redemtionis pretium pro omnibus, quibus; offertur. Resp. Si sermo sit de oblatione ex divina intentione, negatur talem reprobis fieri oblationem; si sermo sit de oblatione evangelica, negatur connexio: nam non magis absurdum est verbo offerri Christum iis, pro quibus tale pretium non numeravit, quam Pharaoni praecipi, & Abrahamo, quae Deus fieri non decrevit.
units.tr: 12. How do the elect, who like the reprobate do not know the divine intention, know that they ought to believe when they first hear the promises? Answer: They must lean on Christ, the Saviour of all believers, and then the will of God will be clear to them. 2. As a lamb recognises its mother among the other sheep by instinct alone, so those born of God lean on Christ by a supernatural instinct, which the reprobate, lacking such instinct, cannot do. But they say that the price of redemption must have been paid for all to whom it is offered. Answer: If the talk is of an offer made according to the divine intention, we deny that such an offer is made to the reprobate; if the talk is of an evangelical offer, we deny the connection. For it is no more absurd that Christ be offered by the word to those for whom he did not pay such a price, than that Pharaoh and Abraham be commanded things which God did not decree should happen.

units.la: 13. Deum vero obedientiam reproborum intendere, & intento fine excidere, absque insigni, in Dei majestatem, contumelia, dici non potest. Sed quo fine (inquies) hortatur Deus in evangelio, quos nunquam obedituros praescit? Gul. PembcOxoniensis, Deum eo fine hortari, ut reprobis declaretur ipsorum officium, & quae sit grata & accepta Deo obedientia. Sed videtur vir eruditus finem non assequi: nam hortari est officium declarare. Ergo declarat reprobis officium, eo fine ut declaretur officium, atqui idem non est sui ipsius finis. Dicunt alii, reprobos non proprie, & per se hortari, sed per concomitantiam,
units.tr: 13. But that God intends the obedience of the reprobate and falls short of his end cannot be said without a notable insult to the majesty of God. But (you will object) with what end does God exhort in the gospel those whom he foreknows will never obey? William Pemble of Oxford says that God exhorts with this end: that their duty may be declared to the reprobate, and what obedience is pleasing and acceptable to God. But the learned man seems not to reach the end, for to exhort is to declare duty. Therefore he declares duty to the reprobate in order that duty may be declared; but the same thing is not its own end. Others say that the reprobate are not exhorted properly and in themselves, but by concomitance,

units.la: quatenus electis externa societate permiscentur, ideoque sicut natura pluviarum demissione fatorum, non rupium intendit irrigationem, ita Deum, ut electi praecipue obediant & salventur; hortari omnes in ecclesia, non reproborum causa: sed hi aliquid dicunt: verbum enim praecipue mittitur ad electos. Hinc epistolae Paulinae inscribuntur, sanctis, dilectis, vocatis, sanctificatis, fidelibus fratribus: Et si quis est coetus, in quo nemo est electus, videtur quod Christus candelam suam, qua aes amissum quaereret, non esset ibi accensurus. Sed hi omnem veritatem non assequuntur: non enim casu, sed certo fine, Deus semen curat spargendum in corda saxea: quaestio enim manet, quo fine Deus hortetur reprobos electis commixtos, nec enim casu hoc est factum, sed Dei consilio. Quid si hic pia ignorantia exclamaremus cum Paulo? O altitudo &c. Rom. 11. Ille enim illic disputat de externa Judæorum vocatione, inter quos soli electi assequuti sunt promissiones, reliqui occalluerunt.
units.tr: insofar as they are mixed with the elect in outward fellowship. And so, just as rain falls by the nature of things and does not aim to water rocks, God (so that the elect may above all obey and be saved) exhorts all in the Church, not for the sake of the reprobate. But these men say something, for the word is sent chiefly to the elect. Hence the epistles of Paul are addressed to the saints, the beloved, the called, the sanctified, the faithful brethren. And if there is any assembly in which no one is elect, it seems that Christ would not kindle there the candle with which he sought the lost coin. But these men do not grasp the whole truth: for God does not sow seed to be scattered on stony hearts by chance, but for a certain end. The question remains: with what end does God exhort the reprobate who are mixed with the elect? For this did not happen by chance, but by the counsel of God. What if here, in pious ignorance, we cry out with Paul: O the depth! etc. Rom. 11. For he there disputes of the external calling of the Jews, among whom only the elect attained the promises, while the rest were hardened.

units.la: 14. Satis nobis est, posthabito fine Arminiano, quod nempe Deus reproborum obedientiam intendat, cum scripturis dicere, Deum ipsos hortari, ut inexcusabiles sint, Act. 13, 46. Poni Christum ut sit signum contradictionis, Luc. 2. 34. Lapis & Petra offensionis 1. Pet. 2. 7, 8. ut sciant inter ipsos fuisse Prophetam, Ezech. 2. 5. ut sit iis in testimonium, Matt. 24. 14. ut judicentur secundum auditum euangelium Matt.14. 15. ut indurentur Esai 6. 9,10 Mat.13.14,15,16. ut declaretur gloria potentiae in vasis irae Rom.9.23. At de fine Arminiano ne syllabam vel jacta habet scriptura. Deū excidere fine intento non posse probatur. 1. Deus noster est in coelis, & facit quodcunq; vult. Ergo non excedit intento volito. Resp. Schaafmannus, Deum voluntate absoluta, qua mundum creavit, facere quodcunque vult, non vero conditionata: haec enim non armatur omnipotentia. Resp. 1. Deus voluntate, qua ecclesiam libere bellantem & hostes profligantem actu libero facit, quod vult. Nam Pfal. 115. est oratio ecclesiae triumphantis in Deo, de idolis gentium: atqui talis voluntas Schaafmanno est conditionata. Ergo nulla est ipsius distinctio. Quis enim ignorat ecclesiam gratias agere Deo eo psalmo de victoriis, quibus potiti sunt ministerio causarum contingenter operantium, ut patet ex v.2. 2. Hoc responso non separatur Deus ab idolis gentium, quae illi credebant agere, quodcunque volunt, conditionate, si forte Deus non obstitisset. 3. Pf. 135. Nota est haec divinitatis ratione cuius laudibus efferendus est, & Deus, quod nempe, quodcunque voluit in coelo, mari & terra faciat: at quatenus non faciat, quod vult in terris, eatenus non est omnipotens, non Deus, non laudibus esserendus: quid absurdius? Daniel. 4. 35. Quodcunque vult facit in exercitu coelesti, & habitatoribus terræ, neque manui ejus resisti potest. Arminiani libera agentia, quæ terram incolunt resistere voluntati Dei clamitant: At absoluta voluntate nihil agere per agentia libera. At contrarium clamat textus ille. Nam 1. vers. 23. Dat Deus regna hominum, quibus vult. at ibid. Dat per milites, duces, principes, qui liberrime pugnant, & eripiunt regna, & in hoc elucet Dei invictum in homines dominium, quod tyrannus ille Babylonicus agnoscere noluit, 2. v. 24. & 36. Acceptum fert absolutæ Dei voluntati (non conditionatæ, cui resisti potest) quod proceres ipsum requisierint, & solitis honoribus affecerint: at vero non necessario, sed liberrime proceres Tyrannum denuo honoribus affecerunt. 3. Ad thronum denu oevectus erat per bella liberrime pugnata, ut ex historiis constat. At v. 37. hoc nomine Deum cœli laudibus effert invictæ omnipotentiæ, quâ fastuosos dejicit. Ergo Deus per agentia libera quodcunque voluit, fecit, nec est agens liberum, quod ipsius potentiæ potest contraniti. Idem probarut luculentissime Esai. 14.24. Prout ego decrevi, ita fiet. Ibi probat Medos Chaldæos deleturos, ratione à decreto invincibili, ubi distinctio de voluntate absoluta-& conditionata ex textu dissipatur. Medi enim liberrimè Chaldæos vastarunt, & tamen voluntate Dei, cui resisti non potest, id factum est, aliqui Deus salsum eo loci juraret, quod est blasphemum.
units.tr: 14. It is enough for us, setting aside the Arminian end, to say with the Scriptures that God intends the obedience of the reprobate, namely that God exhorts them so that they may be inexcusable, Acts 13. 46. Christ is set so that he may be a sign of contradiction, Luke 2. 34. A stone and rock of offence, 1 Pet. 2. 7, 8. That they may know a prophet has been among them, Ezek. 2. 5. That it may be a testimony to them, Matt. 24. 14. That they may be judged according to the gospel heard, Matt. 14. 15; that they may be hardened, Esai 6. 9, 10; Matt. 13. 14, 15, 16; that the glory of power may be declared in vessels of wrath, Rom. 9. 23. But Scripture does not have a syllable about the Arminian end. That God cannot fall short of an intended end is proved thus. 1. Our God is in the heavens, and does whatever he wills. Therefore he does not fall short of the end willed. Answer: Schaafmann says that God does whatever he wills by his absolute will, by which he created the world, not by his conditional will, for this is not armed with omnipotence. Answer 1: God, by the will by which he makes his Church, which wars freely and overthrows its enemies, does what he wills by a free act. For Psalm 115 is the song of the triumphant Church in God, about the idols of the nations; but such a will is conditional for Schaafmann. Therefore his distinction is void. For who does not know that the Church gives thanks to God in that psalm for the victories it gained through the ministry of causes that operate contingently, as is clear from v. 2? 2. By this answer God is not separated from the idols of the nations, which they believed did whatever they wished, conditionally, if perhaps God had not stood in their way. 3. Psalm 135. This is noted as the ground of his divinity, the reason he is to be praised: that he does whatever he wills in heaven, sea and earth. But insofar as he does not do what he wills on earth, so far he is not omnipotent, not God, not to be extolled with praise. What could be more absurd? Daniel 4. 35: He does what he wills among the host of heaven and the inhabitants of the earth, and no one can resist his hand. The Arminians cry out that free agents who dwell on the earth resist the will of God, but by absolute will nothing is done through free agents. But that text cries out the contrary. For in v. 23 God gives the kingdoms of men to whomever he wills, and he does so through soldiers, leaders and princes who fight most freely, and seize kingdoms; and in this shines forth God's invincible dominion over men, which that Babylonian tyrant refused to acknowledge. In vv. 24 and 36 the nobles' seeking him and honouring him as usual is credited to the absolute will of God (not the conditional will, which can be resisted); yet the nobles restored the tyrant to honours not by necessity but most freely. 3. He had been raised again to the throne by wars fought most freely, as is established from the histories. But in v. 37 God is praised with the heavens for his invincible omnipotence, by which he casts down the proud. Therefore God, through free agents, has done whatever he willed, and no free agent is able to resist his power. The same is proved most clearly in Isaiah 14. 24: As I have decreed, so it shall be. There he proves that the Medes will destroy the Chaldeans, from the reason of an invincible decree, where the distinction between absolute and conditional will is dissolved by the text. For the Medes laid waste the Chaldeans most freely, and yet this was done by the will of God, which cannot be resisted, unless God there swore falsely, which is blasphemous.

units.la: 15. 2. Cuicunque prædicatur verbum, id assequitur, quod Deus intendit: nam non potest vacuum ad Deum reverti Esai.55. 11.[?] Ergo si Deus per verbum reproborum obedientiam intenderet, procul dubio obedirent. Non ergo Deus sine per verbum intento, excidere potest. Et Deus Ezech. 2. v. 7. aperte dicit Israelitas non obedituros, vult tamen Prophetam loqui; quasi vero Deus diceret eo loci, scio eos non obediturox, volo tamen & intendo ut obediant. Sed audiat lector mirum commentum Re-monstrantium, qui volunt, postquam Deus fine excidit, manere tamen hypotheticam intentionem in Deo. O prodigium! Deus etiam hodie habet intentionem conditionalem salvandi Judam: & Pharaonis obedientiam vult, intentione scilicet optativa, etiam postquam æternis pænis est adjudicatus.
units.tr: 15. 2. Whoever is preached the word attains what God intends: for it cannot return to God empty, Isa. 55. 11. Therefore if God intended the obedience of the reprobate through the word, without doubt they would obey. Therefore God cannot fall short of an end intended through the word. And God, in Ezek. 2. 7, plainly says that the Israelites will not obey, yet he wills the prophet to speak; as if God were saying there: I know they will not obey, yet I want and intend that they obey. But let the reader hear the strange invention of the Remonstrants, who want a hypothetical intention to remain in God after he has failed of his end. O portent! God even today has a conditional intention of saving Judas, and wills Pharaoh's obedience by an optative intention, namely even after he has been adjudged to eternal punishments.

units.la: 16. 3. Id Deo non competit, quod in scripturis habetur, pro gravi judicio & maledictione: at consilio & intento fine excidere est reproborum maledictio Ps. 2. 4. Psal. 33. v. 10. Esai. 8. v. 9. Esai. 29. v. 7. Jer. 19. v. 7. Job. 15. v. 12. 13. Sic vero Deo in cœlis ridenti irrita & vana hominum consilia, ii in terris scommatum talionem referre pos-sent.
units.tr: 16. 3. What Scripture records as a grave judgement and curse cannot belong to God; but to fall short of one's counsel and intended end is the curse of the reprobate: Ps. 2. 4; Ps. 33. 10; Isa. 8. 9; Isa. 29. 7; Jer. 19. 7; Job 15. 12, 13. Thus, while God laughs in heaven, men on earth could return the retaliation of scorn for the vain and empty counsels of men.

units.la: 4. Quod est divinæ perfectionis nota, ejus contrarium Deo affingi non potest. At ad finem intentum pervenire, est tale: Ergo &c. Minor est, Iob. 23. 12. Deus unum agit: quis revocet eum? quod animus ejus cupit, id efficit. An ergo animus Dei obnixè cupiet obedientiam reproborum, & id non efficiet? Sic enim perit id discriminis à scripturis assignatum Psal. 3 3[?]. v. 11. inter hominis consilia, quæ infringi possunt, & Dei consilia, quæ in omnes ætates consistunt.
units.tr: 4. What is a mark of divine perfection cannot be ascribed to God in its contrary. But to arrive at an intended end is of this kind; therefore etc. The minor is Job 23. 12. God does one thing: who can turn him? What his soul desires, that he does. Does then the soul of God earnestly desire the obedience of the reprobate, and not bring it about? For thus the distinction assigned by Scripture is lost, Psalm 33. v. 11, between the counsels of men, which can be broken, and the counsels of God, which stand for all ages.

units.la: §. Quod hominibus ut pars beatitudinis tribuitur, & nullam includit imperfectionem, id Deo detrahi non potest: at tale est ad finem intentum pervenire. Ergo. Minor est Iob. 22. 28 Quum primum decernes sermonem, præstabitur tibi. At non est (inquit Corvinus) ex defectu potentiæ quod Deus desideriis frustre-tur, sed ex modo & termino, quem ipsius potentiæ exercitio posuit sapientia, quia non tanquam alicujus rei indigus desiderat; ideoque si impleretur desiderium, nihil ad beatitudinem Dei conferret. Ibid. possetque, si vellet, iis desideriis impleri. Resp. 1. Non est ex Dei sapientia, quod Deus fine excidat. Nam non intendit finem ex scientia, Ergo nec ex sapientia: at vero sapientiam absque scientia fingere vanum est. 2. Quæro ex Arminianis, an aliquid divinæ beatitudini decederet, si fine absolute intento excideret? Credo non, & quando mundi creationem intendit, non id facit tanquam alicujus rei indigus, & tamen si Deus absoluta intentione excideret, non esset Deus. 3. Infinitæ Dei perfectionis est, quod voluntas non possit magis ferri in vo-litum. litum, quod facere non posset, quam quod intellectus posset ferri in falsum. 4. Creaturae saepe ex finibus allecutis non semper sunt feliciores; quin improbi hoc sunt miseriores, quod consilia prava executioni mandent, & tamen, quia fine excidunt, produnt se non esse αὐτάρκεις[?], quod de Deo dici non potest. Cujus voliriones sunt licitae[?]. 4. Si Deus posset desideria sua implere, cur non implet? Nempe reclamat & obstat sapientia & justitia; apage potentiam in Deo aliquid faciendi contra sapientiam & justitiam, quasi posset iniqui aliquid facere, quae vera est impotentia, & Deum in non Deum transformat, ideoque impossibile est Deo salvare reprobos.
units.tr: §. What is ascribed to men as a part of blessedness, and includes no imperfection, cannot be withheld from God. But to reach an intended end is of this kind. Therefore (it follows). The minor premise is Job 22:28: "When you shall decide on a matter, it shall be established for you." But (says Corvinus) it is not from a lack of power that God frustrates desires, but from the mode and limit which wisdom has set for the exercise of that power, since he does not desire as one in need of anything; so if the desire were fulfilled, it would add nothing to God's blessedness. And in the same place: he could, if he wished, be fulfilled in those desires. Reply. 1. It is not from God's wisdom that God falls short of his end. For he does not intend an end from knowledge, therefore neither from wisdom; but to imagine wisdom without knowledge is empty. 2. I ask the Arminians whether anything would be taken from the divine blessedness if he failed to achieve an end absolutely intended. I think not; and when he intends the creation of the world, he does not do so as one in need of anything. Yet if God fell short of an absolute intention, he would not be God. 3. It belongs to the infinite perfection of God that his will cannot be carried toward willing what it could not do, any more than the intellect can be carried toward what is false. 4. Creatures often are not happier for the ends they attain; indeed the wicked are more miserable for this, that they carry out wicked plans, and yet, because they fall short of their end, they show that they are not self-sufficient [αὐτάρκεις], which cannot be said of God. Whose wills are lawful? 4. If God could fulfil his desires, why does he not fulfil them? Surely wisdom and justice oppose and stand in the way. Away with the idea of power in God to do anything against wisdom and justice, as if he could do something unjust. That is true impotence, and it turns God into a non-God. Therefore it is impossible for God to save the reprobate.

units.la: 2. Resp. Corvin. Si desideria Dei confiderantur, quatenus a justitia moderantur, ac unum quodque desiderium, ac unaquaeque voluntas ex ob-jecto adaequato existimetur, tum certe quatenus Deus desiderat hominum salutem, eatenus id desiderium impletur, puta, quia eam non desiderat, nisi quatenus id justitia permittit: cum vero id dicimus non impleri, tum absolute confideramus, puta, quatenus simpliciter de divina bonitate est, quatenus damnantur saepe quos Deus salvos velit.
units.tr: 2. Reply. Corvinus: "If God's desires are considered as far as they are moderated by justice, and each desire and each will is judged by its adequate object, then certainly, insofar as God desires the salvation of men, that desire is fulfilled, namely because he does not desire it except insofar as justice permits. But when we say that it is not fulfilled, we consider it absolutely, that is, as it is simply a matter of divine goodness, insofar as those whom God wishes to be saved are often damned."

units.la: Resp. 1. Si Dei desideria spectentur, ut inscitia modificantur, semper implentur. Assumo: atqui ex Arminio disp. publ. 4. thes. 73.74.[?] & Corvino justitia Dei semper moderatur naturalia Dei desideria in usu & exercitio reproborum obedientiam & salutem. Ergo (inquam ego) inclinatione seu potentia tantum tendente in amorem iustitiae vult obedientiam & salutem reproborum, atqui inclinatione naturali iustitiae, pari ratione vult reproborum inobedientiam ad exitum. 2. Dicunt Arminiani, Pharisæos irritum fecisse Dei consilium Luc 7. Quæritur an rejecerint Dei consilium in actu & exercitio, an non? Si primum, non erat Dei consilium iustitiâ modificatum, ut Pharisæi obedirent & salvarentur. Nam tantum Pharisæorum obedientium sic vult obedientiam & salutem. Si rejecerunt Dei consilium, prout vacat omni iustitia, tum quoniam rejecerunt euangelium, quod est Dei decretum de salvandis fidelibus & damnandis infidelibus, sequitur euangelium vacare omni sapientia & iustitia Dei, quo quid absurdius? Cont[?]net enim euangelium Ephes 3.10. imperveltigabiles opes Christi & πολυποίκιλον σο-φίαν Θεοῦ[?], & declarat nobis Dei iustitiam Rom. 1-21, 22, 23. R. 7.12. Lex sancta, mandatum sanctum, justum bonum. 3. Reprobi contraveniunt actui Dei voluntatis in usu & exercitio: atqui sic voluntas Dei utpote determinata à sapientia & iustitia Dei vult tantum obedientiam & salutem electorum: non ergo est voluntas in Deo, cui reprobi contraveniunt. 4. Quæro quando non impleatur Dei desiderium, nempe quando vacat sapientia: at tum reprobi peccant non in Dei sapientiam & iustitiam, sed tantum in dein desiderium & inclinationem Dei naturalem, puta cognitionis expertem: ac graviter peccant reprobi in omnes Dei proprietates, inprimis in sapientiam Psal. 50. 21. & iustitiam & longanimitatem, Rom. 2. 4. 5. Deus tantum in exercitio vult homines obedire & salvari, quatenus iustitia permittit. Assumo: atqui iustitia permittit tantum obedientes salvari ex Arminio. Ergo non intendit ac vult Deus obedientiam reproborum.
units.tr: Reply. 1. If God's desires are regarded as modified by his wisdom, they are always fulfilled. I assume: but according to Arminius (public disputation 4, theses 73 and 74) and Corvinus, the justice of God always moderates the natural desires of God, so that in the use and exercise of them he wills the obedience and salvation of the reprobate. Therefore (I say) he wills the obedience and salvation of the reprobate only by an inclination or power tending toward the love of justice. But by a natural inclination toward justice, by the same reasoning, he wills the disobedience of the reprobate to its outcome. 2. The Arminians say that the Pharisees frustrated the counsel of God, Luke 7. The question is whether they rejected God's counsel in act and exercise or not. If the first, then it was not God's counsel modified by justice that the Pharisees should obey and be saved. For he wills the obedience and salvation of the obedient Pharisees only in this way. If they rejected God's counsel as it is wholly void of all justice, then, since they rejected the gospel, which is God's decree concerning the saving of believers and the damning of unbelievers, it follows that the gospel is void of all wisdom and justice of God. What could be more absurd? For the gospel contains the unsearchable riches of Christ and the manifold [πολυποίκιλον] wisdom of God, Eph. 3:10, and it declares to us the justice of God, Rom. 1:21–23. Rom. 7:12: the law is holy, the commandment holy, just and good. 3. The reprobate act against God's will in use and exercise; but thus God's will, determined as it is by the wisdom and justice of God, wills only the obedience and salvation of the elect. Therefore there is no will in God against which the reprobate act. 4. I ask when God's desire is not fulfilled: namely when wisdom is absent. But then the reprobate sin not against God's wisdom and justice, but only against his natural desire and inclination, which is destitute of knowledge. And the reprobate sin grievously against all the properties of God, especially against his wisdom, Ps. 50:21, and his justice and long-suffering, Rom. 2:4–5. God wills men to obey and be saved in exercise only insofar as justice permits. I assume: but justice permits, according to Arminius, only the obedient to be saved. Therefore God does not intend or will the obedience of the reprobate.

units.la: 6. Homines contraveniunt antecedenti Dei voluntati, non simpliciter, sed quatenus est in cerebro Arminiano, salva res est.
units.tr: 6. Men act against God's antecedent will not simply, but insofar as it exists in the Arminian brain; then the matter is safe.

units.la: 17. 7. Deus quorundam saltem reproborum obedientiam non intendit. Ergo à pari, nec omnium intendit. Prob. antecedens. Postquam Deus prædixerat fore, ut Absalomus patris eorum pollueret, Hazaël mulieres Israelis praegnantes diffunderet, non potuit Deus per legem naturae aut verbum ipsis prolatum intendere, ut obedirent. Deus n. sic & intenderet castigationem Davidis per incestū Absaloni & Israelis per crudelitatem barbaram & immanem Hazaëlis, & non intenderet, sed ut Absalomus & Hazaël abstinendo illis facinoribus obedirent, & sic in Deo essent duae contradictoriae intentiones, quod absurdum. Deinde, nec electorum obedientiam semper intendit: postquam enim per Zachariam praedictum erat cap. 13. ut discipuli salvatorem abnegarent, & derelinquerent (erat enim haec pars passionis salvatoris, quod à suis derelinqueretur, & prædicta, & à Deo decreta.) Quis crederet Deum intendere, ut discipuli ipsum coram hominibus confiterentur? Sic enim Deus & intendisset, ut non adhærerent (quod est contradictorium) salvatori, & ut adhærerent.
units.tr: 17. 7. God does not intend the obedience of at least some of the reprobate. Therefore, by parity, he does not intend it of all. I prove the antecedent. After God had foretold that Absalom would defile his father's concubines, and that Hazael would dash in pieces the pregnant women of Israel, God could not, by the law of nature or by the word spoken to them, intend that they should obey. For otherwise he would both intend David's chastisement through Absalom's incest and Israel's through Hazael's barbarous and savage cruelty, and would not intend it, but intend that Absalom and Hazael, by abstaining from those crimes, should obey. Thus there would be two contradictory intentions in God, which is absurd. Next, nor does he always intend the obedience of the elect. For after it had been foretold through Zechariah, chapter 13, that the disciples would deny and forsake the Saviour (for this was part of the Saviour's passion, that he would be forsaken by his own, and it was foretold and decreed by God), who would believe that God intended the disciples to confess him before men? For thus God would have intended both that they should not cleave to the Saviour (which is contradictory) and that they should cleave to him.

units.la: 18. 8. Quod Deus præscit nunquam fore, illud non intendit, nemo enim sapientem intentionem talem putaret: atqui Deus præscit fore ut reprobi nunquam obediant. Erg. Respond. Arminius, Deum non semper ex præscientia sibi finem intendere, sed tantum (inquit Corvinus) ex affectu & bonitate naturali. Resp.
units.tr: 18. 8. What God foreknows will never happen, that he does not intend; for no wise person would think such an intention. But God foreknows that the reprobate will never obey. Therefore (he does not intend it). Arminius replies that God does not always intend an end from foreknowledge, but only (says Corvinus) from affection and natural goodness. Reply.

units.la: 1. Si Deus nihil certi habet de futuritione vocatorum, sine ullo actu providentiæ vel voluntatis, vel scientiæ, ruunt in peccatum & æternum exitium omnes homines reprobi & spiritus tenebrarum, & sic providentia, quæ curat casus capillorum, & volatulos salacissimorum passerum, nec præscit, nec curat lapsus tot nobilissimarum creaturarum. Quin & Arminius ipse Antiperkinsius, ait gratiam sufficientem adhiberi decreto providentiæ, cum certa præscientia fore, ut rejiciatur à libero hominis arbitrio, quam sententiam ait esse Augustini & forte etiam scripturæ. At vero gratia sufficiens in visibili ecclesia non est separanda à verbo, imo si candidi sunt Arminiani, est tantum ipsum verbum; & qualis Deus Arminianus, Anthropomorphiticusne an Epicureus, qui nulla providentia spargit semen verbi? Hactenus semper à theologis omnibus creditum, Deum n[?]hil agere nisi certa providentia: at hoc mihi videtur mysterium. Praescit Deus possibile esse ut reprobi vocati pareant vel non pareant, quia tam praescientia quam voluntas antecedens destruit libertatem hominis, ideoque hic consultissimum ducunt, praescientiam Dei sepelire: ac certe hoc est Ciceronis non Christi euangelium. 2 Intentio est volitio finis: at vero fatetur Arminius, Deum nihil velle, nisi quod cognoscat. Ergo non potest velle reproborum obedientiam, nisi ipsam cognoscat: atqui sic haec Dei volitio erit appetitus brutus & bruto deterior, qualis est appetitus lapidis in centrum inclinantis, absque omni cognitione.
units.tr: 1. If God has nothing certain about the future response of those called, without any act of providence, or will, or knowledge, then all reprobate men and the spirits of darkness rush into sin and eternal destruction, and so providence, which cares for the falling of hairs and for the little sparrows of the most lustful kind, neither foreknows nor cares for the fall of so many most noble creatures. Indeed Arminius himself, the Anti-Perkinsian, says that sufficient grace is applied by a decree of providence, with the certain foreknowledge that it will be rejected by man's free will; he says this opinion is Augustine's and perhaps also Scripture's. But sufficient grace in the visible Church is not to be separated from the Word; indeed, if the Arminians are candid, it is only the Word itself. And what kind of God is the Arminian God: an anthropomorphite, or an Epicurean, who scatters the seed of the Word without any providence? Hitherto all theologians have believed that God does nothing except by certain providence; but this seems to me a mystery. God foreknows that it is possible for the called reprobate to obey or not to obey, because both foreknowledge and antecedent will destroy man's freedom; therefore they think it most prudent here to bury God's foreknowledge. And surely this is the gospel of Cicero, not of Christ. 2. Intention is the willing of an end. But Arminius confesses that God wills nothing except what he knows. Therefore he cannot will the obedience of the reprobate unless he knows it; but thus this volition of God will be a brute appetite, and worse than brute, like the appetite of a stone inclining toward the centre, without any knowledge.

units.la: Expers ergo erit rationis ille creator (horresco referens) qui animam rationemque in homine finxit. At, stulte, qui oculum formavit, nonne ipse videbit? Psal. 94. 3. Arminius ipse exercituum omnium affectuum in Deo, subjicit sapientiae, cujus est (inquit) singulis, objectum, modum, finem, circumstantiasque praefigere. Ergo sapientia modum, objectum, finem praescribit Dei intentioni, qua vult affectu naturali reproborum obedientiam, imo (inquiunt Davi) sapientia finem praescribit non scientiam. O sapientiam insipientem, quae scientia vacet.
units.tr: Therefore that creator will be without reason (I shudder to say it) who formed the soul and reason in man. But, fool, he who formed the eye, shall he not himself see? Psal. 94. 3. Arminius himself subjoins wisdom to the exercise of all the affections in God, whose office (he says) is to set before each affection its object, mode, end and circumstances. Therefore wisdom prescribes the mode, object and end to God's intention, by which he wills the obedience of the reprobate with a natural affection; nay, Davi say that wisdom prescribes the end, not knowledge. O foolish wisdom, which is empty of knowledge!

units.la: 4 Caute pro suo more dicit Deum (non semper) intendere finem juxta praescientiam: at dic, Iacobe, ex conscientia tua, quare Deus in naturalibus finem intendat ex praescientia, nempe quoniam credis Deum suturorum contingentium non esse præscium.
units.tr: 4. Cautiously, after his manner, he says that God intends the end according to foreknowledge (not always). But tell me, Jacobe, from your own conscience, why God in natural things intends the end from foreknowledge; namely, because you believe that God is not foreknowing of future contingent things.

units.la: 5. Forte dicit, non semper Deum intendere finem ex præscientia, quia vocat electos secundum decretum prædestinationis, quo præscit eos obedituros, non vero sic vocet reprobos, at quæ ratio vocationum tam disparium? fieri enim potest ut electi & reprobi, quoad præsentem conditionem æque sint boni & obsequentes: nulla causa hic est, nisi ad decretum prædestinationis absolutum recurret, ut discrimen inveniat: at hoc Jacobo Arminio displicet tanquam anguis aut serpens Epidaurius. 6. Scriptura ait euangelium Corinthiis proponi, Deo præscio fore, ut invictus populus Deo congregetur, & gentibus Act. 13. Deo prædicente, juxta Esaiæ vaticinia fore, ut aperiantur ipsorum oculi, & Israelitis, Deo præsciente eos non audituros Ezech. 2. Ergo præscientia Dei hic intentionem comitetur, necesse est. At scio ipsos dicere Deum præscire inobedientiam reproborum, at eam non intendere juxta præscientiam: at vero rationem cedo, cur non secundum præscientiam intenderet? Hic hærebunt. At quando salvator dicit intendentem ædificaturam aut bellum virium suarum ignarum, temeritatis nomine apud omnes audire imprudentem, haud excusari si dixerit se intendisse, non secundum præscientiam eventus, sed ex benevolo effectu, at quomodo hic Deum excusabunt, qui ædificationem animarum reproborum in Christo intendit, non juxta eventus praescientiam? Sed tremenda sunt Dei judicia in homines spiritu soporis percussos, qui veritati Dei cedere recusant.
units.tr: 5. Perhaps he says that God does not always intend the end from foreknowledge, because he calls the elect according to the decree of predestination, by which he foreknows that they will obey, but does not call the reprobate in the same way. But what is the reason for such disparate callings? For it can happen that the elect and the reprobate are equally good and obedient in their present condition. Here there is no cause, unless one has recourse to the absolute decree of predestination in order to find the difference; but this is displeasing to Jacobus Arminius, like a snake or the Epidaurian serpent. 6. Scripture says that the gospel was to be preached to the Corinthians, with God foreseeing that an unconquered people would be gathered to God; and that to the Gentiles, Acts 13, God foretelling, according to the prophecies of Isaiah, that their eyes would be opened; and that to the Israelites, God foreknowing that they would not hear (Ezek. 2). Therefore the foreknowledge of God must of necessity accompany the intention here. But I know that they say God foreknows the disobedience of the reprobate, but does not intend it according to his foreknowledge. But I ask for the reason why he would not intend it according to his foreknowledge. Here they will stick fast. But when the Saviour says that a man who intends to build, or a king who intends war, does so without knowing his own strength, is heard by all as imprudent with the name of rashness; he is not excused if he said that he intended it not according to the foreknowledge of the outcome, but from a kindly effect. But how will they excuse God here, who intends the building up of the souls of the reprobate in Christ, not according to the foreknowledge of the outcome? But the judgments of God are terrible against men struck with the spirit of slumber, who refuse to yield to the truth of God.

units.la: 19. Alia est hic Arminii responsio, Deum hic non omni fine excidere. Nam satisfacit suae bonitati & amori erga vocatos. Et Corvinus ait Deum non praecise intendere obedientiam & salutem reproborum, sed vel gloriae justitiae illustrationem, vel salutem. Resp. Egregie Dei perfectionem propugnant, qui volunt eum esse non omnino imperfectum, & votorum impotem, sed tantum secundum quid.
units.tr: 19. Arminius's other answer here is that God does not fall away from every end. For he satisfies his own goodness and love towards the called. And Corvinus says that God does not precisely intend the obedience and salvation of the reprobate, but either the illustration of the glory of his justice or their salvation. Reply: They splendidly defend the perfection of God, who want him not to be wholly imperfect and powerless in his desires, but only imperfect in some respect.

units.la: 2. Dato & concesso, quod satisfactio amoris divini sit Dei finis, erit tantum finis generalis & communis, qui reprobos pariter & electos respicit. At quaestio est, quo fine speciali Deus vocet reprobos non parituros: itaque responsum est extra oleas.
units.tr: 2. Granted and conceded that the satisfying of divine love is God's end, it will be only a general and common end, which regards the reprobate and the elect alike. But the question is with what special end God calls the reprobate, who will not bring forth fruit; so the answer is beside the point.

units.la: 3. Quomodo Deus bonitati hic satisfaciat, haud in proclivi est lectori divinare: bonum enim ex mente dantis aestimandum putat Arminius, & ex fine propter quem datur: atqui hortationi nullum bonum intendit Deus, nisi salutem: hoc vero fine excidit: à ratione enim alienum est & bonitati Dei adversatur, quod Deus intendat salutem reproborum, per vocationem talem, qualem semper frustraneam fore praescit, & non intendat ipsam per talem vocationem, quae, salvis omnibus Dei attributis, ipsorum salutem indeclinabiliter producẗura esset: imo si Deus intendat & velit ipsorum salutem, sic non bonitati suæ, sed palpabili hypocrisi suæ satisfaceret. Qui enim intendat finem per me-dia, quæ scit esse fini imparia & inidonea; & non intendit per media, quæ scit fini ita fuisse accommodata ut ipsum indeclinabiliter producerent, ejus intentio est hypocritica. 4. Vult Deum hic satisfacere amori & bonitati suæ, nempe quia non potest esse bonus, nisi omnes vocet ad obedientiam & salutem. Ergo quatenus spiritus tenebrarum non vocat, est Deus malus, & creaturarum minime amans, quam absurdum? ʃ. At dicerent ipsam hortationem esse beneficium: atqui hoc largimur liberrime, age itaque, quando Deus præstrafdtis & contumacibus beneficium sæpius spretæ & sufquedeque habitæ vocationis indulget, eo fine ut gravius puniantur, (id enim docetur ab Arminianis) ex intentione Dei vocatio erit maximum malum & non bonum. Nam Ar-minius vult bonum æstimari ex mente dantis, & fine propter quem datur: atqui justissima Dei mens male affecta est in contumaces, uti docent, & ipsos vocat ut gravius puniantur, quod est iis maximum malum: jam fare Iacobe, quomodo Deus satisfaciat bonitati suæ & amori. 6. Hortatio tantum facit bonum oblatum possibile reprobis. Ideoq; Deus hortando reprobos, offert bonum potentiale, & juxta Dei præscientiam in graviores pœnas ceffurum, & infert malum actuale: scilicet hoc est satisfacere Deum luæ[?] bonitati & amori. 7. At quæro cui bonitati satisfacit Deus, bonitati in creaturas collatæ? An naturali bonitati Dei ad intra? Si prius, nec adhuc satisfactu tali bonitati: nam nihil boni reprobis confertur, quin imo miseriæ gravissimæ hoc bono implicantur. Si posterius, non satisfieri omnino potest bonitati Dei naturali ad intra, quippe cum nihil additur, nihil adimitur, cui nec feritur, nec metitur, etiamsi nullos mortales vocaret ad beatitudinem. 8. In voce (præcisè) Corvinus præcisum impostorem agit. Non enim per (præcisè) intelligit intense & vehementer: cur enim Dei desideria circa obedientiam, & salutem reproborum, sint minus remissa, quam ipsius desideria circa obedientiam & salutem electorum? In Dei præ如destinatione, nolunt causam quæri: at alibi esse non potest; si per (præcisè) intelligit absolute, tum Dei intentio circa obedientiam & salutem reproborum est conditionalis: at qua conditione intendit ut reprobi obediant? Ex hypothesi, quod velint, hoc est, ex hypothesi quod obediant. En quas dictitat nugas? At vero si Pharisæi rejecerunt Dei consilium conditionatum, idtam ponit Pharisæos non obedituros, quam obedituros, & sic non est spretum. Imo si Deus intendit damnare Pharisæos, si non obedierint, tam non obediendo, quam obediendo, spernunt Dei consilium: quo quid abfurdius? sic omnes electi obediendo fperi-nunt consilium Dei. o. At per vocem (præcisè) vult Deum modo pendulo intendere vel obedientiam, si obedierint, vel non obedientiam, si non obedierint, & sic vel gloriam justitiæ, vel misericordiæ intendit Deus. Sed quæro cur Deus utrumque finem indeterminatè proponat? Nempe quoniam videt se alterutrum determinatè (ut ita dicam) non assecuturum: at si hoc videt, conjicit & divinat, fore fortasse ut non obediat, ideoque ex scientiâ saltem conjecturali scit, se finem non assecuturum, ergo non intendit finem ex non præscientiâ 10. Si ignorat intentum finem, quod est blasphemum, quare sub disjunctione contrarios fines intendit? Hic capiantur necesse est: Deus enim sic præcisè intenderit unum finem, nisi de ipsius assecutione dubitaret, si vero non dubitat, non potest utrum libet, sub disjunctione sibi proponere. 11. Deum fluctuare inter duos fines contrarios est absurdum: nam ipsius voluntas est infinita & à nullâ creaturâ determinata. Aquinas. Si (inquit) præparatio ad gratiam, consideretur secundum quod est à Deo movente, tum habet necessitatem ad id, ad quod movetur, non quidem coactionis, sed infallibilitatis, quâ intentio Dei de deficere non potest. Suarez, sic, præparatio mediorum confusè modo & sub disjunctione, ut si unum medium non habuerit effectum, applicetur & aliud, non est consentanea divinæ perfectioni. Ita & Gregorius Valentia: quod Deus semel vult, semper & ab aeterno in aeternum vult. Et Petrus Fonseca: voluntas Dei in particulari cum omnibus necessariis circumstantiis accepta circa nullam rem in particulari est fusipensa & indeterminata.
units.tr: 3. How God satisfies his goodness here is not easy for the reader to divine. For Arminius thinks that good is to be judged from the mind of the giver and from the end for which it is given; but God intends no good in exhortation except salvation, and in this end he fails. For it is foreign to reason, and opposed to the goodness of God, that God should intend the salvation of the reprobate through such a calling as he foreknows will always be in vain, and should not intend it through such a calling as, all God's attributes being preserved, would unfailingly bring about their salvation. Indeed, if God intended and willed their salvation, he would then satisfy not his goodness but his own palpable hypocrisy. For whoever intends an end through means which he knows are unequal and unsuited to that end, and does not intend through means which he knows were so fitted to the end that they would unfailingly produce it, his intention is hypocritical. 4. Here they say God satisfies his love and goodness, namely because he cannot be good unless he calls all to obedience and salvation. Therefore, insofar as the spirit of darkness does not call, God is evil and not at all loving toward creatures. How absurd! 5. But they would say that the exhortation itself is a benefit. We grant this most freely. Come then: when God grants the benefit of a calling, often spurned and held cheap, to the hardened and the contumacious, in order that they may be punished more severely (for this is taught by the Arminians), then by God's intention the calling will be the greatest evil and not a good. For Arminius wants good to be judged from the mind of the giver and the end for which it is given; but the most just mind of God is ill disposed towards the contumacious, as they teach, and calls them so that they may be punished more severely, which is the greatest evil for them. Now, come, Jacobe, how does God satisfy his goodness and love? 6. The exhortation only makes a good offered possible to the reprobate. Therefore God, in exhorting the reprobate, offers a potential good, and according to God's foreknowledge it will issue in heavier punishments, and he inflicts an actual evil. Clearly this is how God satisfies his [?] goodness and love. 7.
