But I ask: to which goodness does God satisfy himself, the goodness bestowed upon creatures, or the natural goodness of God towards himself? If the former, he does not even yet satisfy such goodness, for no good is conferred on the reprobate; nay, they are entangled in the most grievous miseries by this good. If the latter, the natural goodness of God towards himself cannot be satisfied at all, since nothing is added or taken away, to which it neither bears nor measures, even if he called no mortals to blessedness. 8. In the word (precisely), Corvinus plays the precise impostor. For he does not understand by (precisely) intensely and vehemently; for why should God's desires concerning the obedience and salvation of the reprobate be less relaxed than his desires concerning the obedience and salvation of the elect? In God's predestination they do not want a cause to be sought, but elsewhere there can be none. If by (precisely) he understands absolutely, then God's intention concerning the obedience and salvation of the reprobate is conditional. But on what condition does he intend that the reprobate obey? On the hypothesis that they will, that is, on the hypothesis that they obey. Behold the trifles he prattles! But indeed, if the Pharisees rejected God's conditional counsel, it sets the Pharisees down as not going to obey as much as going to obey, and so it is not spurned. Nay, if God intends to damn the Pharisees if they did not obey, they spurn God's counsel as much by not obeying as by obeying. What could be more absurd? Thus all the elect, by obeying, spurn God's counsel. 9. But by the word (precisely) he wants God to intend, in a wavering way, either obedience if they obey, or non-obedience if they do not obey, and so God intends either the glory of justice or of mercy. But I ask, why does God propose both ends indeterminately? Surely because he sees that he will not attain either of them determinately (as I may say). But if he sees this, he conjectures and divines that perhaps they will not obey; therefore from a merely conjectural knowledge he knows that he will not attain the end, and therefore he does not intend the end from non-foreknowledge. 10. If he is ignorant of the end intended, which is blasphemous, why does he intend contrary ends under a disjunction? Here they must be caught: for God would thus precisely intend one end, unless he doubted its attainment; but if he does not doubt, he cannot propose to himself under a disjunction whichever he pleases. 11. For God to waver between two contrary ends is absurd: for his will is infinite and determined by no creature. Aquinas. "If" (he says) "the preparation for grace is considered as it is from God moving, then it has a necessity for that to which it is moved, not of compulsion but of infallibility, by which God's intention cannot fail." Suarez likewise: "a preparation of means in a confused way, and under a disjunction, so that if one means has not had its effect, another is applied, is not consonant with divine perfection." So too Gregory of Valentia: "what God wills once, he wills always and from eternity to eternity." And Peter Fonseca: "the will of God taken in particular with all necessary circumstances, concerning no particular thing, is suspended and indeterminate."

units.la: 10 Contendit vero Arminius Dei finem in vocatione reproborum nempe inexcusabilitatem non esse finem per se. At quare? Quia (inquit) hortatio non reddit inexcusabiles in fi spreta & rejecta, hoc autem accedit hortationi ex malitia vocatorum, neque illum finem intendit Deus, nisi & praescius quod frustranea futura sit admonitio, per malitiam vocatorum. Resp. 1. Assumo: Atqui obedientia accedit hortationi: est enim ipsius naturae extrinseca: salvatur enim natura hortationis, sive homines obediant, sive non. Nunquid igitur ex Arminio optime sequetur, etiam obedientiam vocatorum non esse Dei finem per se, sed per accidens? ut sic inobedientia erit finis per se, quod absurdum. 1. Arminius vult intentionem obediendi includi in conceptu quidditativo hortationis, quo nihil fallius. Sic enim Deus mandando Isaaci immolationem, immolationem intendisset, quod quam sit falsum, quis non videat? 2. Ipsa hortatio in se & sua natura tollit excusationem, & fundamentum ipsius (nempe non potui evangelio nunquam revelato obtemperare,) sive homo obedierit sive non, sicut non revelatio per se excusat non credentem: obedientia vero vel non obedientia vocati nihil vel addit, vel adimit essentiæ inexcusabilitatis. 4. Deus (inquit) præscius inanem fore admonitionem, intendit inexcusabilitatem. Ergo (inquam) hortatio Dei præ se fert Deum velle salutem reproborum, & tamen non vult eorum salutem, sed intendit eorum inexcusabilitatem. 5. Cur Deus quosdam secundum Præscientiam, quosdam non secundum præscientiam vocet? An causa est in absoluta voluntate Dei, an non à pari, obedituros vocet, nescius etiam futuræ obedientiæ? & sic vocatio secundum nullam præscientiam in Deo erit. 6. Quamvis inexcusabilitas & damnatio non sunt fines gemini respectu verbi, quod ex se suadet obedientiam & offert salutem, tamen Deo, cui nihil præter providentiam accidit, nullus eventus est per accidens, & qui hoc docent, non leviter peccant in providentiam Dei. 7. Arminius vult fundamentum inexcusabilitatis esse verbi propositionem & potentiam obediendi sufficientem: Ergo semper, & non quarta aut decima admonitione, sed prima, Deus reproborum inexcusabilitatem intendit, quod non feret Arminius. 8. Ut reprobi sint inexcusabiles est bonum: ergo à Deo intentum, qui est primum efficiens & ultimus finis omnis boni. At dicunt non esse bonum creaturæ: at quid ad hoc rem? Deus omne suæ gloriæ illustrandæ conducens intendit, nec mensurat bonum quod efficit aut intendit à convenientia vel disconvenientia cum creaturarum indole, sed quatenus ad ultimum finem conducitur vel non. Arminiani vero cum Antiquioribus Anabaptistis contendunt, Deum impetu naturae velle bonum creaturae, sicut corvi pullos, mater prolem suam diligit, quod salsissimum est. Nam Deus bonum creaturę libere vult: si enim naturaliter Deus vellet bonum creaturae, non posset permittere peccatum, certissimam viam ad creaturae interitum ineluctabilem, sicut nulla mater sciens & volens infantulum ad exitium ruere permitteret, siquidem salvo jure officii sui, inhibere posset: sed turpiter erratur quoties Deum humano pede homunciones audacter metiri praesumunt.
units.tr: 10 But Arminius contends that the purpose of God in calling the reprobate, namely their inexcusableness, is not an end in itself. Why not? "Because," he says, "an exhortation does not make men inexcusable if it is despised and rejected, and this happens to an exhortation through the malice of those who are called; and God does not intend that end unless he foresees, through the malice of those called, that the admonition will be in vain." Reply: (1) I grant the minor premise: "But obedience does belong to the exhortation, for it is extrinsic to its nature; the nature of the exhortation is preserved whether men obey or not." Does it then follow well from Arminius that obedience too is not God's end in itself but only an incidental one, so that disobedience would be the end in itself? That is absurd. (2) Arminius wants the intention to obey to be included in the quidditative concept of an exhortation, and nothing is more false. For on that view God, by commanding the sacrifice of Isaac, would have intended the sacrifice itself, and who does not see how false that is? (3) The exhortation in itself and by its very nature removes excuse, and the foundation of excuse (namely, "I could not obey a gospel never revealed to me") whether a man obeys or not; just as revelation by itself does not excuse the unbeliever. But the obedience or disobedience of the one called adds nothing to, and takes nothing from, the essence of inexcusableness. (4) God, he says, foreseeing that the admonition will be vain, intends inexcusableness. Therefore, I say, the exhortation of God shows outwardly that God wills the salvation of the reprobate, and yet he does not will their salvation, but intends their inexcusableness. (5) Why does God call some according to foreknowledge and others not according to foreknowledge? Is the cause in the absolute will of God, or does he call, without any similar reason, those who will obey, while ignorant also of future obedience? And so the calling will be according to no foreknowledge in God. (6) Although inexcusableness and damnation are not two ends alongside one another with respect to the Word, which of itself urges obedience and offers salvation, yet for God, to whom nothing happens apart from providence, no outcome is incidental, and those who teach this sin not lightly against the providence of God. (7) Arminius wants the foundation of inexcusableness to be the proposal of the Word together with a sufficient power to obey. Therefore God intends the inexcusableness of the reprobate always, and not only at the fourth or tenth admonition but at the first; which Arminius will not endure. (8) That the reprobate be inexcusable is a good; therefore it is intended by God, who is the first efficient cause and the last end of every good. But they say it is not a good for the creature. What does this matter? God intends everything that conduces to the illustration of his glory, and he does not measure the good that he effects or intends by its agreement or disagreement with the nature of creatures, but by whether or not it leads to the final end. The Arminians, however, with the older Anabaptists, contend that God by natural impulse wills the good of the creature, as the raven loves its young or the mother her offspring; and this is most false. For God wills the good of the creature freely. If God willed the good of the creature by nature, he could not permit sin, which is the most certain path to the creature's inescapable ruin; just as no mother, knowing and willing the death of her infant, would permit it to rush to destruction, since she could prevent it without any violation of her duty. But men err shamefully whenever they presume to measure God by the human foot, the puny creatures that they are.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: An Dei beneplacitum sit prima regula omnis justitiae moralis in Deo erga creaturas, ut & bonitatis & misericordiae.
units.tr: Whether God's good pleasure is the first rule of all moral justice in God towards creatures, as also of goodness and mercy.

units.la: Praesupponit quaestio justitiam Deo inesse essentialiter & antecedenter ad actum beneplaciti divini: quis enim diceret Deum libere decernere ut ipse sit justus, & infinite bonus, quasi esset libere justus, & libere bonus? & sic posset esse non justus & non-bonus. Sed quaestio est de justitia Dei erga creaturas: eadem disputatio potest in titul[?] de Dei misericordia, quae creaturas respicit. Volunt enim Arminiani misericordiam hanc relativam re-lativam lativam esse in Deo naturale desiderium, quod antecedenter ad creaturae meritum aut demeritum salutem omnium tum hominum tum angelorum cupit necessitate naturae, ita tamen ut fixa & peremptoria voluntate non magis hujus, quam illius, miseretur. At vero miseretur Deus quorum vult, & libere: non ergo impetu naturae. 2. Tale desiderium expers cognitionis Deo est prorsus indignum. 3. Inclinatio in Deo vel naturalis tendentiae in id quod certissime nunquam est futurum, est volitio aeterna Dei frustranea, quod cum infinitate Dei pugnat.
units.tr: The question presupposes that justice is in God essentially and antecedently to the act of the divine good pleasure. For who would say that God freely decrees that he himself be just and infinitely good, as if he were freely just and freely good, and so could be not just and not good? But the question concerns God's justice towards creatures. The same dispute can be raised about God's mercy, which also regards creatures. For the Arminians want this relative mercy to be in God a natural desire, which, antecedently to the merit or demerit of the creature, desires the salvation of all, both men and angels, by the necessity of nature, yet in such a way that with a fixed and peremptory will it has mercy on one no more than on another. But God has mercy on whom he wills, and freely; not therefore by an impulse of nature. 2. Such a desire, lacking knowledge, is utterly unworthy of God. 3. An inclination in God, or a natural tendency towards what will most certainly never be, is an idle eternal volition of God, which is incompatible with the infinity of God.

units.la: 4. Remonstrantes in apolo. negant Dei voluntatem determinari ab ullo agente externo, quaerimus quomodo ergo determinetur a miseria creaturae ad ipsis succurrendum, naturali impetu. Volunt alii misericordiam Deo quidem essentialem esse, ita tamen ut quoad actus secundos sumat moderationem & determinationem a sapienti Dei beneplacito, ideoque actum divinae erga creaturas misericordiae, causam remotam esse Dei misericordiam, propinquam vero beneplacitum Dei: causam itaque, cur Deus miseretur indefinite, esse Dei misericordiam; cur hujus potius, quam illius, miseretur esse Dei beneplacitum. Sed contra liceat mihi sic disceptare. 1. Misericordia Dei est vel remota causa naturalis, vel libera: si primum, necessitate naturae Deus indefinite miseretur aliquorum saltem: atqui hoc est falsum: potuit[?] enim omnes ad gloriam suæ justitiæ manifestandum rejecisse. Si secundum, idem sequitur, nempe Deum posse vel omnium vel multorum misereri: at dici non potest misericordiam esse formaliter causam liberam; adde quod si misericordia causa libera esset, non opus foret libero beneplacito, quo determinaretur. 2. Quod Deus agit ex misericordia naturali, id non libere, sed necessario agit: misericordia enim non est principium agendi in Deo, usquequaque liberum. Dico itaque cum doctissimo Gul Tuisso[?] in misericordiam Dei dupliciter considerari. 1. Ut est nativa & essentialis in Deo inclinatio ad suam bonitatem cum miseris communicandam. 2. Ut misericordia est creaturis manifestanda. Priore modo fateor me non posse videre (quæ mea forte est infantia) quomodo Deus possit misereri creaturæ libere, ita ut actus misericordiæ fluant à misericordia Dei, tanquam à principio vitali & formali. Si enim actus misericordiæ fluant à naturali Dei inclinatione propensà ad succurrendum miseris, non potest non omnium hominum & angelorum misereri. Quod enim fluit ab agente naturali, qua tali, id non ab eo fluit, fluxu libero, sed necessario. Sicut enim nulla est ratio, cur ignis hoc lignum aridum admotum, non vero illud combureret, quia agens naturale æqualiter agit in omnia subjecta æque approximata & disposita; ita nulla est ratio, cur Deus hujus Potius, quam illius misereatur. At vero longe alia est ratio misericordiæ, ut est creaturis manifestanda: hæc enim misericordia mihi videtur non nativa & essentialis illa quæ in Deo est, sed relativa & σχετικὴ[?], quæ inest Deo ex libera determinatione divini beneplaciti, & hanc misericordiam definio benevolum Dei affectum, qui Deo inest quatenus ex libero suo beneplacito creaturis miseris succurrit. Hic autem affectus benevolus præsupponit decretum & intentionem liberam miserendi: hinc fit, ut si Deus ex misericordia naturali misereretur, non posset hujus non misereri & illius miserari, nisi in suam naturam misericordiæ delinqueret. At procul dubio Deus non magis in misericordiam, quam in justitiam suam posset peccare: at per relativa hanc misericordiam, quæ præsupponit liberum Dei decretum respiciens hanc non illam personam, relinquitur Deo libertas miserendi. Sed hæc misericordia non est velleitas, seu naturalis voluntas succurrendi omnibus miseris, quantum potest, salva justitia & sapientia. Quoniam non potest Deus velle aut agere contra id, quod per justitiam & sapientiam licet: sequeretur enim tum esse in Deo potentiam solutam à justitia & peccandi potentiam: dicerent forte Dei omnipotentiam absolute considerari à theologis, ut antecedit actus divini beneplaciti, ipsi Deo liberè præscribentis volendi, agendique regulam, & in eo signo rationis potest Deus nulla facere facere per omnipotentiam, quæ non potest facere in signo rationis liberum decretum subsecuto, ut potuit Deus absolute liberalse Christum per plusquam duodecim legiones angelorum, ac non potuit post decretum hoc facere. Resp. Hæc potentia est tantum in Deo naturalis, non moralis, imo omnipotentia ne quidem naturaliter aliquid agit, sine Dei beneplacito: produceret enim effectum citra intentionem Dei sapientem, quod esset blasphemum; ideoque nulla est in Deo potentia agendi nisi ea, quam in actum (ut sic loquar) reducere potest advocato sapientissimo beneplacito, neque sequitur Deum non potuisse liberasse Christum a morte, sed non simpliciter, nisi ex hypothesi, quod hoc decrevisset: impossibilis enim simpliciter est novus complacentiæ actus citra præcedens æternum Dei decretum talem actum statuens fore. Hinc necessario semper limitabitur omnipotentia Dei beneplacito libero aliquo, quamvis non necesse est limitetur hoc vel illo actu beneplaciti. Hinc sequitur. 1. Æque late patere Dei potentiam, & Dei beneplacitum, neque esse Deo potentiam plura faciendi, quam beneplacito suo potest statuere, & omnipotentia simplex, & potentia sapienter volendi & agendi, æqualis plane sunt ambitus. 2. Hinc simpliciter respectu misericordiæ naturalis, potuit Deus eorum, qui reprobi jam sunt, misereri, & qui jam eleẽcti[?] sunt [?]ti sunt, non misereri, & æque sapiens suisset Dei misericordia [illegible, ~6 letters] in eo casu, quam nunc est. At vero respectu misericordiæ relativæ, subsecutæ jam liberam Dei determinationem, non poterat Deus aliorum misereri & non misereri, quam jam de facto miseretur, & non miseretur, adeo ut debita electis misericordia, fit debita nempe secundum regulam beneplaciti Dei præscribentis Deo hunc agendi modum, & reprobis non misericordia fit debita secundum ordinem æquabilitatis & constantiæ divinæ, quia non poterat sine inconstantiæ nota non facere, & non misereri, quando facere & misereri decrevit semel. Semper itaque Dei beneplacitum est ei regula volendi agendique, quemadmodum lex naturæ & verbum scriptum est angelis & hominibus volendi agendique regula. 3. Justitia etiam relativa est constans Dei voluntas remunerandi vitâ obedientes, damnandi inobedientes, & hæc volitio, est libera Dei constitutio, & (quod mirum videri poterit) justitia Dei scripturis revelata non est essentialis Dei voluntas tribuendi creaturæ, quod suum est, imo non inest Deo necessario, sed libere, non essentialiter, sed contingenter, (quod est verum de Dei etiam misericordia & bonitate relativa) Si enim Deus necessitate naturæ tribueret creaturæ quod suum est, tribueret omnibus æternum, quod commeriti sunt, exitium, omnes in peccatis relinqueret, omnes damnaret. Hoc enim est nostrum proprium; & quidem Deus non posset nobis hoc nolli tribuere, si hi actus fluerent formaliter iustitiae, sicut calefactio ab igne. Itaque quod Deus relinquat & induret peccatores, non sunt actus iustitiae Dei, quia sic actus non indurandi peccatores, & actus condonandi peccatoribus peccata, esset actus iniustitiae, & tamen sunt tales in Deo actus. Verum hoc discriminis est inter misericordiam & iustitiam, quod ii in quibus Deus iustitiam remunerantem, & vindicatricem declarat, sint determinati in scripturis per qualitatem cert̃m[?], nempe finaliter obedientes, & finaliter inobedientes; at vero vasa misericordiae saltem primae (quam ego credo esse efficacem vocationem, non electionem:) quamvis in Dei arcano decreto sunt signati homines & determinati nominatim & specialissimè, attamen n. la[?] est specialis determinatio in scripturis: nusquam enim scriptum est (hoc fac & efficaciter vocaberis) & Dei beneplacitum non revelatum designat homines primae misericordiae.
units.tr: 4. The Remonstrants in their Apology deny that the will of God is determined by any external agent. We ask, then, how it is determined by the misery of the creature to help it, by a natural impulse. Others want mercy to be indeed essential to God, yet in such a way that, as regards its secondary acts, it takes its moderation and determination from the wise good pleasure of God. So the remote cause of the act of divine mercy towards creatures is the mercy of God, but its proximate cause is the good pleasure of God. Thus the cause why God has mercy indefinitely is God's mercy, while the cause why he has mercy on this one rather than that one is God's good pleasure. But against this I may argue as follows. 1. The mercy of God is either a remote natural cause or a free one. If the first, then by the necessity of nature God has mercy indefinitely on at least some; but this is false, for he could have rejected all of them in order to manifest the glory of his justice. If the second, the same follows, namely that God can have mercy on all or on many. But it cannot be said that mercy is formally a free cause; and besides, if mercy were a free cause, there would be no need of a free good pleasure by which it is determined. 2. What God does from natural mercy, he does not do freely but necessarily, for mercy is not in God a principle of action that is wholly free. I say, therefore, with the most learned William Twisse, that the mercy of God is to be considered in two ways. 1. As it is the native and essential inclination in God to communicate his goodness to the wretched. 2. As mercy is to be made manifest to creatures. In the former way I confess I cannot see (perhaps this is my childishness) how God can have mercy on a creature freely, so that the acts of mercy flow from the mercy of God as from a vital and formal principle. For if the acts of mercy flow from God's natural inclination, disposed to help the wretched, he cannot but have mercy on all men and angels. What flows from a natural agent, as such, does not flow from it by a free flow but by necessity. For just as there is no reason why fire should burn this dry stick placed near it and not that one, since a natural agent acts equally on all subjects equally near and equally disposed, so there is no reason why God should have mercy on this one rather than that one. But the reason for mercy, as it is to be made manifest to creatures, is quite different. For this mercy seems to me not to be that native and essential mercy which is in God, but a relative mercy [σχετική], which inheres in God from the free determination of the divine good pleasure. I define this mercy as the benevolent affection of God, which inheres in God insofar as, by his free good pleasure, he helps creatures who are wretched. This benevolent affection, moreover, presupposes a free decree and intention to show mercy. Hence it follows that if God had mercy from natural mercy, he could not refrain from having mercy on this one and not on that one, unless he sinned against his own nature of mercy. But beyond doubt God could no more sin against his mercy than against his justice. Yet through this relative mercy, which presupposes a free decree of God regarding this person and not that one, freedom to show mercy is left to God. But this mercy is not a mere velleity, or a natural will to help all the wretched as far as possible, saving justice and wisdom. For God cannot will or do anything contrary to what is permitted by justice and wisdom; otherwise there would be in God a power released from justice and a power of sinning. Perhaps someone would say that theologians consider the omnipotence of God absolutely, as it precedes the act of the divine good pleasure, which freely prescribes to God the rule of willing and acting; and that in that order of reason God can do, by his omnipotence, whatever he cannot do in the order of reason after a free decree has followed. Thus God could absolutely have freed Christ by more than twelve legions of angels, yet could not do so after this decree. Reply: this power is only natural in God, not moral. Indeed, omnipotence does not even act naturally without the good pleasure of God. For it would produce an effect apart from the wise intention of God, which would be blasphemous. Therefore there is no power in God for acting except that which, with the most wise good pleasure called in, he can bring into act (so to speak). Nor does it follow that God could not have freed Christ from death; rather, it is not so simply, but only on the hypothesis that he had so decreed. For a new act of complacency, which settles that such an act will be, is simply impossible apart from a preceding eternal decree of God. Hence the omnipotence of God will always necessarily be limited by some free good pleasure, although it is not necessary that it be limited by this or that act of good pleasure. From this it follows: 1. God's power and God's good pleasure extend equally far; God has no power of doing more things than his good pleasure can settle, and simple omnipotence and the power of willing and acting wisely plainly have equal scope. 2. Hence, simply with respect to natural mercy, God could have had mercy on those who are now reprobate, and not had mercy on those who are now elect; and the mercy of God in that case would have been [illegible] just as wise as it now is. But with respect to relative mercy, which follows the free determination of God already made, God could not have had mercy on others, or refrained from having mercy, other than he now in fact has mercy and does not have mercy. So mercy is due to the elect, namely according to the rule of God's good pleasure, which prescribes to God this mode of acting; and mercy is not due to the reprobate according to the order of divine evenness and constancy, because God could not refrain from doing, and from having mercy, when he has once decreed to do and to have mercy, without the mark of inconstancy. So the good pleasure of God is always the rule for God's willing and acting, just as the law of nature and the written word are the rule of willing and acting for angels and men. 3. Relative justice too is the constant will of God to reward the obedient with life and to condemn the disobedient; and this volition is a free constitution of God. And (what may seem strange) the justice of God revealed in Scripture is not an essential will of God to give the creature what is its own. Indeed it does not inhere in God necessarily but freely, not essentially but contingently (which is true also of the mercy and relative goodness of God). For if God, by the necessity of nature, gave the creature what is its own, he would give everyone eternal destruction, which they have deserved; he would leave all in their sins, and condemn all. For this is what belongs to us; and God could not refuse us this, if these acts flowed formally from justice, as heat flows from fire. Therefore, that God leaves and hardens sinners are not acts of the justice of God; for an act of not hardening sinners, and an act of forgiving sins to sinners, would then be an act of injustice, and yet such acts are in God. However, this is the difference between mercy and justice: those in whom God declares his rewarding and avenging justice are determined in Scripture by a certain quality, namely as finally obedient and finally disobedient. But the vessels of mercy, at least of the first mercy (which I believe is effectual calling, not election), although men are marked out and determined in God's secret decree, by name and most specifically, nevertheless there is no special determination in Scripture. For nowhere is it written, "Do this and you will be effectually called." And a good pleasure of God not revealed designates the men of the first mercy.

units.la: 2. Ex absoluta Dei voluntate est, quod debeatur finali impoenitentiae mors secunda: comminationes enim Dei, quamvis fiant secundum ordinem iustitiae, ille tamen ordo iustitiae est ex absoluta Dei voluntate. Hinc patet demeritum peccati esse secundum ordinem iustitiae, & quoniam iustitia est ex beneplacito Dei, hinc patet damnatos graviores poenas mereri, quam actu incurrunt, non esse verum. Demeritum enim est proprie debitum ex ordine justitiæ, & mediate debitum ex ordine Dei beneplaciti: atqui nemo debet pœnas graviores incurrere, quam Deo visum est juxta sapiens ipsius beneplacitum infligere. At vero est & hoc verissimum, si Deus damnatis pœnas sextuplo graviores infligeret, id quidem justum fore: infligeret enim secundum sapiens beneplacitum, quod prima est regula justitiæ. Idcoque justum est omnes posteros Adami communicare cum reatu & primo Adami peccato, quia ita Deo visum est. Et si ex peccatore Adamo nascerentur omnes à peccato immunes, id æque justum fuisset: ita hæ ambæ veræ sunt (nos mortales longe graviores ærumnas & miserias mereri, quam patimur) & (nos mortales longe graviores ærumnas & miserias non mereri, quam patimur) Prius effatum verum est ex hypothesi Dei beneplaciti: non enim fuisset injustum si quidem Deus graviores ærumnas nobis peccatoribus inflixisset, si quidem ita visum fuisset Deo. Posterius est verum, quia non est æquum nec demeritum justum, ut graviores miserias patiamur, quam juxta actuale Dei beneplacitum, cui nunc de facto subjicimur, jam patimur. Non est itaque citra distinctionem verum, peccatores mereri graviora quam patiuntur, licet id genus loquendi vulgo obtineat, ex pia quadam in Dei voluntatem justissimam submissione.
units.tr: 2. It is from God's absolute will that the second death is owed to final impenitence. For God's threats, although they are made according to the order of justice, that order of justice itself arises from God's absolute will. Hence it is plain that the demerit of sin is according to the order of justice. And since justice rests on God's good pleasure, it is plain that the claim that the damned deserve heavier punishments than they actually incur is not true. Demerit is properly what is owed by the order of justice, and mediately what is owed by the order of God's good pleasure. But no one ought to incur heavier punishments than God has seen fit to inflict according to his wise good pleasure. Yet this too is most true: if God were to inflict on the damned punishments six times heavier, that would indeed be just, for he would inflict them according to his wise good pleasure, which is the first rule of justice. Therefore it is just that all posterity of Adam share in guilt and in the first sin of Adam, because so it has seemed good to God. And if all born of the sinful Adam were free from sin, that too would have been equally just. So both of these are true: (we mortals deserve far heavier miseries and sorrows than we suffer) and (we mortals do not deserve far heavier miseries and sorrows than we suffer). The former statement is true on the hypothesis of God's good pleasure, for it would not have been unjust if God had inflicted heavier sorrows on us sinners, had it so seemed good to him. The latter is true, because it is neither fair nor a just desert that we suffer heavier miseries than we now suffer under God's actual good pleasure, to which we are in fact subjected. It is therefore not true without distinction that sinners deserve greater things than they suffer, although that manner of speaking commonly prevails, out of a certain pious submission to God's most just will.

units.la: 3. At durum forte videtur, justitiam illam, quæ Deo essentialiter inest, nobis non revelari in scripturis, sed respondeo revelari. Nam Deum non esse Deum, si non sit justus, docet scriptura: at justitiam erga creaturas suas, de qua ubique scripturarum, Deo inesse non essentialiter, sed secundum ipsius liberum beneplacitum: at vero in justitia hac relativa aliquid est quod Deo inest essentialiter. Nam inobedientes finaliter damnari justum est, quia ita Deus libere decrevit, quando finaliter inobedientium potuit Deus citra jacturam & dispendium justitiæ absolute misereri, siquidem ita voluit. At vero constituto semel hoc, quod finaliter inobedientes sunt damnandi, Deus non potest non damnare finaliter inobedientes propter æquabilitatem, constantiam, & veracitatem suæ simplicissimæ naturæ. Æquabilitas enim constantissima & veracitas Dei postulant antecedenter ad Dei decretum, ut decreta exequatur & non rescindat, ut promissa constanter servet. Hæc autem Dei constantia non inest Deo juxta liberum beneplacitum, sed essentialiter, imo non esset Deus si non esset verax & constans. Hinc ista (num Jehova quaererunt [?] & non faceret?) (num judex mundi non recte & juste ageret?) Peccatum in sua formali ratione est quid divinæ voluntati approbanti plane contrarium, ideoque non potest peccatum Deo non displicere: esset enim non Deus si peccatum ei non displiceret: rectitudo enim & constantia est Deo essentialis, at vero punitio peccati non includitur formaliter in essentiâ peccati, sed est quid posterius naturâ peccato, jam in integrâ suâ essentiâ conflitutro, ideoque Deus nulla naturæ necessitate peccata punit, imo posset absolute non punire. Nam tantum juxta liberum beneplacitum punit., multis gratis condonat in Christo filio dilectionis suæ.
units.tr: 3. But it may seem harsh that that justice which is essentially in God is not revealed to us in Scripture. I answer that it is revealed. For Scripture teaches that God would not be God if he were not just. But the justice toward his creatures of which Scripture everywhere speaks is not in God essentially, but according to his free good pleasure; yet in this relative justice there is something which is essentially in God. For it is just that the finally disobedient be damned, because God freely decreed it, when God could, without loss or detriment to justice, have absolutely shown mercy to the finally disobedient, had he so willed. But once this has been established, that the finally disobedient are to be damned, God cannot but damn the finally disobedient, on account of the evenness, constancy and truthfulness of his most simple nature. For the most constant evenness and truthfulness of God require, antecedently to God's decree, that he carry out his decrees and not rescind them, and that he keep his promises constantly. Yet this constancy of God is not in God according to free good pleasure, but essentially; indeed he would not be God if he were not true and constant. Hence those words: (Hath he said, and shall he not do it?) (Will not the judge of the world act rightly and justly?). Sin in its formal nature is something plainly contrary to the approving divine will, and therefore sin cannot but displease God; for he would not be God if sin did not displease him. Uprightness and constancy are essential to God. But the punishment of sin is not formally included in the essence of sin; it is something posterior in nature to sin, which already constitutes its whole essence. Therefore God punishes sins by no necessity of nature; indeed he could absolutely not punish. For he punishes only according to his free good pleasure, and freely pardons many in Christ, his beloved Son.

units.la: 4. Aliud itaque & longe aliud est, Deum aliquid facere ex intentione revelandi & manifestandi suam justitiam, & aliquid facere ex justitia. Nam quod Deus facit ex intentione manifestandi justitiam, facit liberrime, quia reprobat ex intentione manifestandi justitiam, & quidem liberrime potest non reprobare: at quod facit ex ipsa justitia non potest non facere, nisi peccaret in justitiam, quia justitia præsupponit liberum Dei decretum. Atqui dicant illi qui reprobationem Esavi volunt esse actum justitiæ in Esavum, quod decretum liberum præsupponitur illi actui, nempe Deus decrevit reprobare Esavum priusquam reprobavit? Itane? Ergo priusquam Deus decernit, & sic in infinitum. Dei enim reprobatio est decretum. Dico itaque Deum ex justitia ut ex principio formali reprobare, Deum ex justitia multos in nativa corruptione derelinquere, ex justitia negare iis salvatorem, qui pro ipsis moriatur, ex justitia nolle efficaciter vocare, esse falsa. Prob. 1. Justitia est constans Dei voluntas creaturæ debitum tribuendi, idque juxta Dei voluntatem ad certam regulam coarctatam & determinatam. Atqui reprobatio non est debita Esavo: Deus enim contra debitum ageret, si eligeret Esavum, quod nemo sanus dicit. Deinde quaerenti regulam secundum quam Deus reprobaret Esavum, in peccato nativo derelinqueret, Christum & efficacem vocationem negaret, fingi non posse alia responsio, quae regulae sit instar, quam quia Esavus est peccator: atqui haec nulla est regula: sic enim omnes Deus reprobasset. 2.
units.tr: 4. It is therefore one thing, and quite another, for God to do something with the intention of revealing and manifesting his justice, and to do something from justice. For what God does with the intention of manifesting justice, he does most freely, because he reprobates with the intention of manifesting justice, and indeed he could most freely not reprobate. But what he does from justice itself he cannot but do, unless he sinned against justice, because justice presupposes God's free decree. Yet let those who wish the reprobation of Esau to be an act of justice toward Esau say: is a free decree presupposed to that act, namely that God decreed to reprobate Esau before he reprobated him? Really? Then God decrees before he decrees, and so on to infinity; for God's reprobation is a decree. I say, therefore, that it is false that God reprobates from justice as from a formal principle, that God from justice leaves many in their native corruption, that from justice he denies a Saviour who would die for them, and that from justice he is unwilling to call them effectually. Proof 1. Justice is the constant will of God to render to a creature what is owed, and this according to God's will, restricted and determined to a certain rule. But reprobation is not owed to Esau, for God would act against what is due if he rejected Esau, which no sane person says. Next, to one asking what rule would make God reprobate Esau, leave him in native sin, and deny him Christ and effectual calling, no other answer can be imagined that would serve as a rule than that Esau is a sinner. But this is no rule, for thus God would have reprobated all. 2.

units.la: Quod Deus ex justitia agit ut ex principio formali, id non potest non agere, nisi ageret contra justitiam, & sic injuste ageret: atqui ita reprobat, ita relinquit homines in peccato, ut posset citra omnem injustitiam, non relinquere, non reprobare &c. Dicunt hic Deo esse liberum, vel secundum misericordiam eligere, efficaciter vocare &c. vel reprobare, & Christum & efficacem vocationem negare.
units.tr: What God does from justice as from a formal principle, he cannot but do, unless he acted against justice and so acted unjustly. But so he reprobates, so he leaves men in sin, that he could, without any injustice, not leave them, not reprobate them, and so on. Here they say it is free for God, or according to mercy, to elect, to call effectually, and so on, or to reprobate, and to deny Christ and effectual calling.

units.la: Sed Resp. 1. hoc responso concedunt ex libero arbitrio non coarctato ad justitiam vel misericordiam Deum reprobare, & in peccatis relinquere, quod est concedere totum argumentum; & idem est, ac si dicant, Deum haec facere ex absoluto beneplacito. Error vero est in eo, quod non satis accurate distinguant inter liberam Dei voluntatem, & Dei voluntatem justam aut misericordem. Nam justitia aliquid superaddit voluntati Dei. 2.
units.tr: But I reply: 1. By this answer they concede that God, not restricted to justice or mercy in his free will, reprobates and leaves men in sins, which is to concede the whole argument. It is the same as if they said that God does these things from absolute good pleasure. The error lies in their failing to distinguish accurately enough between God's free will and God's just or merciful will, for justice adds something to the will of God. 2.

units.la: Deo non proprie est liberum agere secundum justitiam cum hominibus, est enim repugnans in adjecto. Nam liberum Deo est, quod potest facere vel non facere: justum vero quod non potest non facere, uti promissa[?] præstare & comminationes implere justum est, non Deo liberum, quin id non facere naturæ Dei adversatur.
units.tr: It is not properly free for God to act according to justice toward men, for it is a contradiction in terms. What is free for God is what he can do or not do. But what is just is what he cannot not do: to perform promises and fulfil threats is just, and not free for God, since not to do so would be contrary to the nature of God.

units.la: §. Hinc hæc consectaria. 1. Inanis est timor eorum, qui massam corruptam statuant prædestinationis objectum, ne scilicet periclitetur Dei justitia. At vero patefactio justitiæ est causa finalis reprobationis, ipsa tamen justitia non est principium aut causa, unde formaliter ortum habet reprobatio absque manifesto præjudicio absoluti Dei Domini, quale competit figulo in lutum Rom. 9. Figulo enim nulla est regula determinans ipsius voluntatem ad faciendum ex eadem massa vas honoris, & vas dedecorosum: neque Deo est aliqua regula justitiæ, qua alios reprobat, alios eligit. Cedo regulam & qui absolvant Iehovam crimine injustitiæ in electione angelorum plane gratuita, sine respectu ad ipsorum bona opera, & in reprobatione diabolorum nunquam videre potui, nec justitiam salvant, quia homo est Deo consideranti ut corruptus. At quæro an ut actu existens, an vero non? si ut actu existens, tum etiam peccatis actualibus gravatus: at sic & reprobatio & electio erunt ex provisione operum bonorum, quod Pelagianum est, si ut nondum existens, neque peccator. Nam actu existere & esse actu peccatorem, sicut simul & mente existere & mentali consideratione esse peccatorem, est non existere & non esse peccatorem simpliciter, scilicet notio mentalis salvat Dei justitiam: atqui Deus justitiam non exercet citra injustitiam, nisi homo non tantum mentali & objectiva consideratione, sed & actu & realiter peccator existat. 2. Sequitur solum Dei beneplacitum esse causam, cur Adami peccatum nostrum foret, & nostra Christo imponerentur.
units.tr: §. Hence these corollaries. 1. Vain is the fear of those who posit the corrupt mass as the object of predestination, lest God's justice be endangered. But the manifestation of justice is the final cause of reprobation, while justice itself is not the principle or cause from which reprobation formally arises, and so there is no manifest prejudice to the absolute dominion of the Lord, such as belongs to the potter over the clay, Rom. 9. For the potter has no rule determining his will to make from the same lump a vessel of honour and a dishonourable vessel, nor does God have any rule of justice by which he reprobates some and elects others. Let them show me the rule, those who absolve Jehovah of the crime of injustice in the wholly gratuitous election of angels, without regard to their good works, and in the reprobation of devils. I have never been able to see it, nor do they save justice, since man is regarded by God as corrupt. But I ask: is he regarded as actually existing, or not? If as actually existing, then also as burdened with actual sins; but thus both reprobation and election would be from the foresight of good works, which is Pelagian. If as not yet existing and not a sinner, then: to exist actually and to be actually a sinner, just as to exist in the mind and to be a sinner in mental consideration, is not simply to not exist and not be a sinner. That is, a mental notion saves God's justice. But God does not exercise justice without injustice, unless man exists as a sinner not merely in mental and objective consideration, but actually and really. 2. It follows only that God's good pleasure is the cause why Adam's sin would be ours, and why ours would be imputed to Christ.

units.la: 3. Sequitur illam comminationem (quo die comederis, morieris) ex intentione divina non fuisse purè legalem, neque ex ordine justitiae simpliciter prolatam, quia plurimi non sunt mortui pro peccato, sed pro ipsis Christus mortuus; ideoque foedus operum, quod formatum fuit secundum sapientissimam Dei voluntatem respectu electorum, ipsiusque imprimis Adami (qui gratia electionis illâ primâ transgressione non excidit) Dei gratiosam voluntatem euangelicam inclusisse, si Dei intentionem spectemus, & reproborum duntaxat respectu fuisse purè legalem, secundum justitiam rigidam, qua Deus peccatores tales punire constituerat. Si itaque illa comminatio in communi spectetur, prout indefinitè electos & reprobos concernebat; prolata erat ex puro Dei beneplacito, nondum ad certam & determinatam justitiae regulam coarctato. Nam ex absoluta Dei libertate Deus illam comminationem in quibusdam personis legaliter exequutus est, in aliis euangelicè in Christo ipsorum sponsore. Si itaque seponatur hypothesis decreti Dei, non laesa fuisset misericordia, si omnes in ipsorum personis proprius poenas aeternas illius transgressi nisi luisent, neque læsa justitia, si omnes in Christo eas poenas dedissent. 4. Inde est, quod fœdus operum essentialiter non flagitet obedientiam passivam personalem, ut multi opinantur, sed Deum ex absoluto suo beneplacito ita fœdus formasse, ut ipsius transgressi indifferenter, vel passione personali, vel fidei-justitia expiaretur, prout Deo fuisset libitum: non volo tamen hic obedientiam fidei-justitiam non esse passivam, sed legem qua talem essentialiter postulare passionem ipsius transgressoris, nego. Si enim illud fœdus necessario & ex ordine justitiæ flagitasset passionem personalem, totum euangelium, quod non personalem sed fidei justitiam passionem justitiæ Dei exhiberet, aperte justitiæ Dei adversaretur, quod absurdum est. Itaque Christus pro nobis obiit tam secundum fœdus operum, quam secundum fœdus gratiæ, quod passus fit, est justitiæ: misericordia enim Dei non exigit formaliter mortem a quoquam, nedum a Christo, sed justitia: quod vero pro nobis passus sit, est misericordiæ. Ita itaque hic accurate distinguenda sunt, (Christus passus est,) & (Christus pro nobis passus est.) Nulla itaque fronte Arminius dicit, præ destinationem nostram pugnare cum Dei justitia, quæ scilicet non patitur ut Deus velit alicui vitam, nisi prius Christus eam morte sua acquisierit: imo dicimus Deum ex absoluta voluntate voluisse electis vitam: & prædestinationem non esse justitiæ actum actu aut misericordiæ, sed absoluti Dei arbitrii libere volentis declaratione justitiæ & misericordiæ. Næ itaque grandis ille theologus egregiè philosophatur, qui diceret actum demonstrandi omnipotentiam divinam esse formaliter actum omnipotentiæ, & actum demonstrandi justitiam esse actum justitiæ. ç.
units.tr: 3. It follows that the threat ("on the day you eat of it, you shall die") was not, in God's intention, purely legal, nor was it uttered merely by the order of justice, since many are not dead for sin, because Christ died for them. Therefore the covenant of works, which was framed according to God's most wise will with respect to the elect, and especially to Adam himself (who did not fall from the grace of election by that first transgression), included God's gracious gospel will if we look at God's intention, and was purely legal only with respect to the reprobate, according to the rigid justice by which God had determined to punish such sinners. If therefore that threat is considered in general, as it concerned the elect and the reprobate indefinitely, it was issued from God's pure good pleasure, not yet confined to a certain and determinate rule of justice. For from God's absolute freedom, he executed that threat legally in some persons and evangelically in others, in Christ their surety. So if the hypothesis of God's decree is set aside, mercy would not have been impaired had all paid the eternal punishments of their transgression in their own persons, nor would justice have been impaired had all paid those punishments in Christ. 4. Hence the covenant of works does not essentially require personal passive obedience, as many think, but God by his absolute good pleasure so formed the covenant that its transgression might be expiated, indifferently, either by personal suffering or by the righteousness of faith, as it pleased God. I do not deny here that the obedience of faith is passive, but I deny that the law as such essentially demands the suffering of the transgressor himself. For if that covenant had necessarily and by the order of justice demanded personal suffering, the whole gospel, which presents to the justice of God the suffering of faith-righteousness rather than personal suffering, would openly oppose the justice of God, which is absurd. Thus Christ died for us both according to the covenant of works and according to the covenant of grace. That he suffered belongs to justice, for the mercy of God does not formally require death from anyone, much less from Christ, but justice does; that he suffered for us belongs to mercy. So here (Christ suffered) and (Christ suffered for us) must be carefully distinguished. Therefore Arminius nowhere says that our predestination fights against the justice of God, which, namely, does not permit God to will life for anyone unless Christ had first acquired it by his death. Rather we say that God willed life for the elect from his absolute will, and that predestination is not an act of justice or of mercy, but a declaration of the absolute will of God, freely willing, of justice and mercy. Truly that great theologian philosophizes excellently who would say that the act of demonstrating divine omnipotence is formally an act of omnipotence, and the act of demonstrating justice is an act of justice. ç.

units.la: Longe itaque illa differunt, (homo non est meritus, ut Deus mitteret salvatorem in mundum) & (homo meritus est ut non mitteret salvatorem) prius est verum, posterius salsum. Nam meritum est debitum justitiæ aut promissionis, aut pacti divini: atqui si justitiæ debitum fuisset, ut Deus non mitteret salvatorem, tum Deus impeditus plane esset à debito justitiæ, & justitiam plane violasset in missione salvatoris, quo quid absurdius? Neque ulla extat promissio aut pactum, quo Deus dixit aut statuerat mittere salvatorem se non voluisse. Hinc nemo non videt, quia Deus ex absoluta voluntate salvatorem mittit, eum ex amore aut misericordia naturali non mittere, & Dei voluntatem nunquam fuisse, neque justitia statutum fuisse ut lex violata non aliter quam personali supplicio peccatorum expiaretur, imo fœdus operum fuisse decretum tantum de plectendis peccatoribus, eo modo quo Deo est visum, vel pœna personali vel sponsoria.
units.tr: Those two propositions differ greatly: (man did not merit that God should send a saviour into the world) and (man merited that God should not send a saviour). The former is true, the latter false. For merit is a debt of justice, or of promise, or of divine covenant; but if it had been a debt of justice that God should not send a saviour, then God would have been plainly bound by a debt of justice, and would have plainly violated justice in sending the saviour, and what could be more absurd than that? Nor is there any promise or covenant by which God said or decreed that he was unwilling to send a saviour. Hence everyone sees that because God sends the saviour from absolute will, he does not send him from love or natural mercy; and that God's will was never, nor was it established by justice, that the violated law should be expiated only by the personal punishment of the sinner. Rather the covenant of works was a decree only concerning the punishment of sinners, in the manner that seemed good to God, either by personal punishment or by punishment in a surety.

units.la: 6. Recte itaque Durandus sic. Patet ergo (inquit) quod justitia in Deo tam communicativa quam distributiva, non est aliud quam condecentia divina in redditione praemiorum & poenarum, & in distributione proprietatum & principiorum agendi, prout convenit substantiae cujusque rei. Et jure quidem, non est enim proprie justitia commutativa in Deo, quoniam nulla est proportio inter Dei beneficia data, & nostra accepta officia. Nam, ut notat ibi Ditrandus, filius carnalem patrem nunquam compensare potest, a quo habet esse & nutriri, licet improprie compensat in quantum potest. Nec potest esse in Deo proprie justitia distributiva, qua unicuique tribuitur secundum dignitatem personarum: atqui omnis hic dignitas hominum est ex liberali Dei acceptantis gratiosa aestimatione: dignitas enim personae creatae ad Deum non est intrin-seca: Deus enim sic esset injustus, nisi ageret secundum personae intrinsecam dignitatem, & esset debitor suae creaturae, non tantum ex liberali pacto & decreto, sed etiam antecedenter ad Dei decretum, contra scripturas Rom. II. Quis ei largitus est, & ei retribuetur? Credo itaque saniores & profundiores Jesuitas ex ipsorum principiis non posse non negare omne meritum operum bonorum proprie dictum, sed utinam planius nobis tradidissent doctrinam de meritis. Eodem modo recte philosophatur Suarez de bonitate qua vult creaturas esse Deo convenientes & bonas, tanquam opera decentia ipsum & consentanea bonitati & sapientiae ejus, & certe per eandem rationem Deus erit creaturis bonus non essentialiter, quia sic necessitate naturae Deum esse, & bonitatem creaturis communicare necesse esset, & sic necessario mundum creavisset, quod absurdum est, neque dubium esset, quin si creaturæ habuissent longe diversam ab ea, quam habent convenientiam, cum Dei decentia, quin non minus essent bonæ, quam jam sunt: bonitas itaque Dei erga creaturas ex sapienti beneplacito dependet.
units.tr: 6. Rightly therefore Durandus says: "It is plain then (he says) that justice in God, both communicative and distributive, is nothing other than divine fittingness in the rendering of rewards and punishments, and in the distribution of properties and principles of acting, as befits the substance of each thing." And rightly so; for there is properly no commutative justice in God, since there is no proportion between the benefits God gives and the duties we owe. For, as Durandus notes there, a son can never repay his natural father, from whom he has his being and his nourishment, although he repays in an improper sense as far as he can. Nor can there properly be distributive justice in God, by which each is given according to the dignity of persons; for all such dignity of men arises from the free and gracious estimation of God who accepts them, since the dignity of a created person is not intrinsic to God. God would thus be unjust unless he acted according to the intrinsic dignity of the person, and he would be a debtor to his creature not only by a free pact and decree, but even antecedently to God's decree, contrary to Scripture (Rom. II.): "Who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him?" I believe, therefore, that the saner and more profound Jesuits, from their own principles, cannot but deny all merit of good works properly so called; but would that they had handed down the doctrine of merits to us more plainly. In the same way Suarez philosophizes rightly about the goodness by which God wills creatures to be fitting and good to him, as works befitting him and consonant with his goodness and wisdom. And certainly by the same reasoning God will not be good to creatures essentially, for then by the necessity of his nature God would have to be, and to communicate goodness to creatures, and so would have necessarily created the world, which is absurd. Nor would there be any doubt that if creatures had a fitness to God's decency far different from that which they now have, they would be no less good than they are now. Therefore God's goodness toward creatures depends on his wise good pleasure.

units.la: 7. Voluntas Dei non simpliciter est regula justitiæ, ut contradistinguitur à sapientia, sed quatenus à sapiente Dei intellectu determinatur, uti docent Aquinas & Henricus. 2. Voluntas Dei non est causa interna & essentialis rerum, nec est à voluntate Dei decernente, quod homo sit animal, quod obedientia sit legi divinæ conformitas. Nam necessario, non ex libero decreto essentia & essentiatum inter se cohærent: at vero homo non esset homo, quod absurdum, si non esset animal. 3. Res quælibet consideratur vel materialiter, denominativè, vel secundum esse possibile (hæc enim hic idem sunt) vel formaliter & secundum esse actuale. Priore modo Dei beneplacitum, cujus est rerum essentias & essentiarum gradus efficere & constituere, est causa cur talis res habeat talem essentiam & gradus entitatis ut 5. & 6. ut 7. non plures vel pauciores. Item cur immolatio Isaaci ut obedientia, cur homicidium, cur esus arboris scientiæ sit peccatum: & esus arboris vitæ non sit peccatum. Item cur res, quæ est futura homo, hoc est, cur homo habeat talem essentiam ex Dei dedecreto libero: at vero postquam res formaliter est, non habet talem essentiam ex Dei beneplacito, sed essentialiter. Postquam enim Deus voluit ut haec fit natura peccati, nempe quod fit id quod displicet voluntati Dei approbanti, tum si quaeratur, cur Deus nolit peccatum; Respondetur non quia vult, sed quia est essentialiter malum: sed si ulterius quaeratur, cur talis sit natura illius rei quae est peccatum, & illius rei quae est homo? recurrendum semper erit ad fontem altissimum, Dei aeternum beneplacitum, quaedam enim sunt bona & justa antecedenter ad Dei decretum, sed quomodo? Possibiliter nempe ut possint fieri bona & justa, siquidem Deus vellet: at vero nulla sunt bona actu & secundum debitum morale, ut debeant fieri, nisi quoniam Deus ea fieri voluit & decrevit. Ista itaque non sunt sine distinctione admittenda, nempe. 1. Deus non potest non velle bonum.
units.tr: 7. The will of God is not simply the rule of justice, as distinguished from wisdom, but insofar as it is determined by the wise intellect of God, as Aquinas and Henry teach. 2. The will of God is not the internal and essential cause of things, nor is it by God's decreeing will that man is an animal, or that obedience is conformity to the divine law. For essence and what has essence cohere necessarily with one another, not by a free decree; for man would not be man, which is absurd, if he were not an animal. 3. Any thing is considered either materially, denominatively, or according to possible being (for these are the same here), or formally and according to actual being. In the former way, God's good pleasure, whose office it is to make and constitute the essences of things and their degrees of being, is the cause why such a thing has such an essence and degree of entity, as 5 and 6, not 7, or more or fewer. Likewise why the sacrifice of Isaac is obedience, why homicide is murder, why eating of the tree of knowledge is sin and eating of the tree of life is not sin. Likewise why the thing that is to be a man is a man, that is, why man has such an essence from God's free decree. But once the thing actually exists formally, it does not have such an essence from God's good pleasure, but essentially. For once God willed that this should be the nature of sin, namely that it be what displeases the approving will of God, then if one asks why God does not will sin, the answer is not that he wills it, but that it is essentially evil. But if one asks further why the nature of that thing which is sin, and of that thing which is man, is such, one must always return to the highest source, God's eternal good pleasure. For some things are good and just antecedently to God's decree; but how? Possibly, namely that they could be made good and just if God so willed; but no things are good actually, and according to moral obligation, so that they ought to be made, except because God willed and decreed that they be made. These things therefore are not to be admitted without distinction, namely: 1. God cannot not will the good.

units.la: 2. Voluntas Dei id non potest non velle, quod sapientia ipsius[?] dictitat esse bonum. Duo enim sunt in divina volitione boni. 1. Res volita. 2. Modus volendi; respectu rei volitiae, falsum est, Deum non posse non velle bonum, & quidem quod ei ratio dictitat esse bonum: ratio enim dictitavit & sapientia infinita bonum esse mundi creationem, Christi in carnem missionem: at vero potuit Deus noluisse mundi creationem & salvatoris missione. At vero respectu modi volendi, & necessitate specificationis, quicquid vult Deus, necesse est sapienter velit, & sapientia dictaret[?] id esse volendum. Ratio præponderans (inquit Bradwardina) est quæ dictitat melius esse facere hoc quam illud, vel quod melius est, hoc facere, quam dimittere, & talis ratio non movet, nec concludit voluntati divinæ, nec eam determinat ad agendum: poterit enim Deus facere meliora, quam facit, & multa bona, quæ non facit.
units.tr: 2. The will of God cannot but will what his wisdom declares to be good. For there are two kinds of goodness in the divine volition: 1. the thing willed, and 2. the mode of willing. With respect to the thing willed, it is false that God cannot but will the good, and especially that which reason tells him is good. For reason, and infinite wisdom, declared the creation of the world and the sending of Christ in the flesh to be good; yet God could have been unwilling to create the world and to send the Saviour. But with respect to the mode of willing, and the necessity of its specification, whatever God wills he must will wisely, and his wisdom dictates that this is to be willed. The preponderating reason (says Bradwardine) is that which dictates that it is better to do this than that, or that what is better is to be done rather than left undone; and such a reason neither moves nor constrains the divine will, nor determines it to act: for God could do better things than he does, and many good things which he does not do.

units.la: Hoc videt acerrimi ingenii vir ille, nec sine ratione: ratio n. præponderans in hoc negotio est duplex, vel ratio præponderas[?] à rebus ipsis creatis, vel ratio præponderans respectu divinæ sapien-tiæ. Hæ duæ rationes præponderantes sæpe contrariantur: melior mundus & præstantiores creaturæ quam sunt, in se sunt præstantiores hoc mundo & rebus jam creatis: at vero Dei sapientiæ visum est melius esse, ut mundus minus præstans esset. Obedientia in se melior est inobedientia, si spectemus rationem præponderantem à rebus ipsis petitam: at vero ut inobedientia tam existat quam obedientia, melius visum est Deo secundum rationem præponderantem sapientiæ divinæ.
units.tr: That keen-witted man saw this, and not without reason. For the preponderating reason in this matter is twofold: either the preponderating reason taken from the created things themselves, or the preponderating reason with respect to the divine wisdom. These two preponderating reasons often conflict. A better world and more excellent creatures than those which exist would in themselves be more excellent than this world and the things already created; yet it seemed better to the wisdom of God that the world be less excellent. Obedience is in itself better than disobedience, if we consider the preponderating reason drawn from the things themselves; yet for disobedience to exist as well as obedience, it seemed better to God according to the preponderating reason of divine wisdom.

units.la: 8. Dicunt scholastici justitiam concedentiæ seu congruitatis antecedere actum divini beneplaciti, quoniam si Deus hoc volet, id non potest, non congruenter suæ justitiæ velle: at vero volunt justitiam debiti & obligationis subsequi Dei beneplacitum, sed libet sciscitari, quid sit hæc concedentia. Vel est attributum æternum, vel respectus rerum volitarum naturas respiciens: si priore modo, idem videtur quod sapientia Dei, aut saltem est communis modus & agendi virtus in Deo agendi convenienter suae infinitae naturae, & sic nihil verius Deum necessitate naturae non posse non convenienter suae sapientiae facere, neque sine gravi absurdo dici posset Deum liberè velle & decernere ut ipse condecens suae sapientiae in omnibus actibus suis sit, imo non potest non esse condecens in suis actibus: esset enim sic non Deus. At vero si condecentia haec respiciat non sapientem in Deo agendi modum, sed rerum extra Deum ordinem & dispositionem mediorum ad finem, tum haec condecentia non minus subsequitur Dei beneplacitum, quam condecentia justitiae. Nam à Dei voluntate est quod haec res sit medium, illa finis, & Deus, (inquit Durandus) volendo bonitatem suam, non necessario vult alia quae ordinantur ad ipsum tanquam finem. Et quod haec rerum ordinatio, non alia obtineat, est à sapientia Dei regulante & à voluntate Dei imperante: si enim contrarius ordo obtinuisset, is etiam sapientiae divinae congruus fuisset. Dici forte potest, necesse est, Deus media fini accommodata adhibeat, ac proinde externam rerum ordinationem necessitare divinam voluntatem ad eligendam hanc, non aliam ordinationem. Resp. 1. Non sequitur: illa accommodatio est tantum talis connexio, & [illegible, ~6 letters] ordinatio hujus rei ad illam: at vero est à Deo quod haec res sit finis, illa medium. Quid si Deus lapidem, non panem hominis alimentum instituisset? quid si res secundas non ærumnas & res adversas iter ad gloriam voluisset? Tam ille, quam qui nunc obtinet ordo, sapientiae divinae congruus fuisset. 2. Duo hic sunt distinguenda. 1. Extrema ordinatorum ad fe invicem. 2. Ordinatio, quamvis ipsa ordinatio in fe fit bona & sapiens, antecedenter ad Dei liberam electionem, attamen illa ordinatio non neceffitat Dei voluntatem, quia illam respuere & contrariam eligere poteft, & talis electio Dei libera effet fapientiffima. Non enim potest dari ordo ita adaequans divinam sapientiam, ut ipsam limitet ad hunc ordinem, ut docent Aquinas & Scotus. 3. Ordinationes omnes rerum possibiles convenientes sapientiae Dei antecedenter ad actum divini beneplaciti, quamvis sint convenientes in eo statu,non tamen actualis,sed possibilis est illa convenientia, qua res possunt fieri, five non-repugnantia, ut fiant convenienter, non vero ut actu fiant. Convenientia enim formalis & actualis est a libera Dei voluntate, quae ex multis poffibilibus modis operandi ab intellectu propofitis, hoc libere eligit non illud, ideoque hoc est bonum, quia a Deo eligitur,
units.tr: 8. The Schoolmen say that the justice of fitness or congruity precedes the act of the divine good pleasure, since if God will this, it cannot be that he wills it without being congruous with his justice; but they hold that the justice of debt and obligation follows God's good pleasure. But let us inquire what this fitness is. It is either an eternal attribute, or a relation regarding the natures of the things willed. If in the former way, it seems to be the same as the wisdom of God, or at least a common mode of acting and a power in God of acting in a manner suited to his infinite nature; and so nothing is truer than that God, by the necessity of his nature, cannot but act in a manner congruous with his wisdom. Nor could it be said without grave absurdity that God wills and decrees freely that he himself be fitting to his wisdom in all his acts; indeed he cannot but be fitting in his acts, for otherwise he would not be God. But if this fitness regards not the wise mode of acting in God, but the order and arrangement of things outside God, of means to an end, then this fitness follows God's good pleasure no less than the fitness of justice. For it is from the will of God that this thing is the means and that the end, and God (says Durandus) in willing his own goodness does not necessarily will other things which are ordered to him as end. And that this arrangement of things obtains rather than another comes from the wisdom of God ordering and the will of God commanding; for if a contrary order had obtained, that too would have been congruous with the divine wisdom. Perhaps someone may say: it is necessary that God employ means suited to the end, and therefore the external arrangement of things necessitates the divine will to choose this arrangement rather than another. Reply: 1. It does not follow. That suitability is only such a connection, and [illegible] the ordering of this thing to that; but it is from God that this thing is the end and that the means. What if God had appointed a stone, not bread, as the food of man? What if he had willed adversity and hardship, not prosperity, as the way to glory? That order would have been as congruous with divine wisdom as the one which now obtains. 2. Two things must be distinguished here: 1. the extremes of the things ordered to one another; 2. the ordering itself. Although the ordering itself is in itself good and wise, prior to God's free choice, nevertheless that ordering does not necessitate God's will, because he can reject it and choose a contrary one, and such a free choice of God would be most wise. For there cannot be an order so matching the divine wisdom that it limits wisdom to this order alone, as Aquinas and Scotus teach. 3. All the possible orderings of things which are congruous with the wisdom of God are congruous prior to the act of the divine good pleasure; yet this congruity is in a state not actual but possible, namely the congruity by which things can be made, that is non-repugnance, so that they may be made congruously, not that they actually be made. For formal and actual congruity comes from the free will of God, who from the many possible modes of operating proposed by the intellect freely chooses this one and not that; and therefore this is good because it is chosen by God.

units.la: 9. Omnem vero justitiam moralem ad creaturas relatam a Dei beneplacito regulari, probatur. 1. A libera Dei constitutione est, quod haec res fit justa obedientia, non illa, ut cur non manducatio fructus arboris scientiae boni & mali fit obedientia, non vero non-manducatio arboris vitae; cur immolatio Isaaci, spoliatio Aegyptiorum, aedificatio templi a Salomone non à Davide; quod homines juberentur confiteri Christum, vetarentur dæmones ipsum confiteri, cur ista omnia æqua & justa sunt, non aliunde est quam à Dei voluntate. 2. Si aliquid esset justum & bonum antecedenter ad Dei voluntatem, tum Deus ex obligatione & officio illud velle teneretur ut & faceret. Atqui Deus nullo officio aut obligationi morali subest, nisi suæ infinitæ sapientiæ, aut sibi, quæ obligatio est admodum [illegible, ~12 letters]. Non vero aliquid debet creaturæ, quia omne quod Deus debet creaturæ suæ, vel est ex promissione, vel comminatione libera. Atqui quod vel Deus promittit vel comminatur est ex libera voluntate: nihil ergo Deus debet velle aut facere ut justum antecedenter ad ipsius liberam constitutionem. 3. Si aliquid esset bonum & justum intrinsece ante Dei beneplacitum, necessario Dei beneplacitum regularetur ad id volendum: atqui Dei beneplacitum est prima regula, quæ à nullo priore regularetur. Prob. connexio, quia Deus non esset infinite justus & bonus, si contra justum & bonum velle aut facere posset. 4. Omnis justitia moralis vel lege naturæ, vel scripto, vel alio modo revelata, est à Dei sapiente voluntate libera; quia non ab eo necessitate naturæ; nam si impetu naturæ Deus * legem imponeret, tum non posset non eandem jubere, & vetare, quæ jubet & quæ vetat. Prob. conseq. quia non datur tertium. 5. Si aliquid esset justum & bonum antecedenter ad Dei beneplacitum, daretur bonum & justum, quod à summo bono & primo justo non fuisset, quod esset absurdum. Daretur enim effectus qui in causam primam resolvi non posset, nihil est hic quod dicant, nisi bonum & justum fluere à Deo, ut lumen à sole naturali impetu. Atqui quis diceret Deum necessitate naturæ interdixisse esu arboris vitæ? Iudæis legem præscripsisse? imo tum necessitate naturæ Deum creaturas intellectuales, quibus legem poneret, atque adeo mundum creasse, necesse fuit: et sic mundum ab æterno æterna emanatione à Deo fluxisse necesse esset. Nam nulla esset ratio cur mundus aliquando inciperet, sicut nulla est ratio cur Deus hodie potius quam mille abhinc annis sit infinite bonus, justus &c. Atqui clamat ratio, clamat experientia, testantur oracula sacra Deum mundum & omnia entia libere creasse propter gloriam suam. Apoc. 4. 11. Prov. 16. 4. Rom. 11. 36. Imo sic non potuit Deus creaturas alio modo, natura, specie, numero, pondere, mensura aut perfectione, creasse, quam nunc creata sunt, quod & scripturis adversatur: Rom. 9. 21. 22. 1. Cor. 15. 38. 6. Patres & Scholastici decent Deum non velle res, quia sint bonæ, sed eas bonas esse, quia à Deo sint volitæ. Adeo ut si vellet (inquit Gerson) eas vel non esse, vel aliter esse, id quoque jam bonum esset.
units.tr: 9. That all moral justice related to creatures is regulated by God's good pleasure, is proved thus. 1. It is by the free constitution of God that this is the just obedience and not that: why the eating of the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is obedience, and not the not-eating of the tree of life; why the sacrifice of Isaac, the spoiling of the Egyptians, the building of the temple by Solomon and not by David; that men were commanded to confess Christ and devils were forbidden to confess him: why all these things are equal and just, is due to nothing other than the will of God. 2. If anything were just and good prior to the will of God, then God would be bound by obligation and duty to will and do it. But God is subject to no duty or moral obligation, except to his infinite wisdom, or to himself; and that obligation is quite [illegible]. Nor does he owe anything to a creature, because everything that God owes to his creature is either from a free promise or a free threat. But what God promises or threatens is from his free will: therefore God owes nothing to will or do as just prior to his own free constitution. 3. If anything were intrinsically good and just before God's good pleasure, then God's good pleasure would necessarily be regulated to will that thing; but God's good pleasure is the first rule, which is regulated by no prior rule. The connection is proved, because God would not be infinitely just and good if he could will or do what is against the just and good. 4. Every moral justice, whether revealed by the law of nature, by writing, or in another way, is from the wise free will of God; for it is not from him by the necessity of nature. For if by the impulse of nature God imposed a law, then he could not but command the same things he commands and forbid the things he forbids. The consequent is proved because there is no third option. 5. If anything were just and good prior to God's good pleasure, there would be a good and a just thing which did not come from the supreme good and the first just, which would be absurd. For there would be an effect which could not be resolved into the first cause; and there is nothing they can say here except that the good and the just flow from God as light flows from the natural sun by natural impulse. But who would say that God by the necessity of nature forbade the eating of the tree of life? or prescribed the law to the Jews? Indeed, if God by necessity of nature had to create intellectual creatures to whom he would give law, and so to create the world, then the world would necessarily have flowed from God from eternity by eternal emanation. For there would be no reason why the world should begin at some time, just as there is no reason why God is infinitely good, just, and so on today rather than a thousand years ago. But reason cries out, experience cries out, and the sacred oracles testify that God freely created the world and all beings for his own glory. Rev. 4. 11. Prov. 16. 4. Rom. 11. 36. Indeed, in this way God could not have created the creatures in another way, by nature, kind, number, weight, measure, or perfection, than they now have been created; which also is contrary to the Scriptures: Rom. 9. 21, 22. 1 Cor. 15. 38. 6. The Fathers and the Schoolmen teach that God does not will things because they are good, but that they are good because they have been willed by God. So much so that if he had willed them either not to be, or to be otherwise, that too would already be good (says Gerson).

units.la: 10. Hinc patet illud (nihil est turpe respectu divinæ voluntatis) partim esse verum, partim falsum. Est verum, quia ex libera Dei constitutione est quod aliquid morale injustum sit: poterat enim hominibus nullam regulam præscripsisse, sicut fecit agentibus naturalibus, ita, ut si vel homines & angeli sequerentur rationis ductum, sive non, rei non forent peccati, quia nempe liberum relinquere poterat iis illum ductum sequi, vel non sequi, & quoniam lex est liberrimum Dei statutum, si nihil tale statuisset, turpe aut peccatum nullum fuisset: nam Deus legem non fecit naturæ impetu. Est etiam salsum quod nihil sit turpe respectu divinæ voluntatis, quoniam posito quod Deus bonum morale libere statuisset, & legem ab æterno posuerit, quicquid tali legi adversatur, Deo unice displicet, ut turpe & inhonestum, ideo ut Deus naturaliter adversetur peccato propter naturalem rectitudinem & constantiam naturæ divinæ, quia non potest non odisse, quod ipsius sapientiæ adversetur.
units.tr: 10. From this it is plain that the saying "nothing is base in relation to the divine will" is partly true and partly false. It is true, because it depends on God's free ordinance that something is morally unjust. For God could have prescribed no rule to men, as he did with natural agents, so that whether men and angels followed the guidance of reason or not, they would not be guilty of sin. He could freely leave them the choice to follow that guidance or not. And since the law is God's most free decree, if he had decreed nothing of the kind, there would be no baseness or sin at all, for God did not make the law by natural impulse. It is also false that nothing is base in relation to the divine will. Granted that God freely decreed the moral good and established the law from eternity, whatever opposes such a law is displeasing to God alone, as base and dishonourable. God is therefore naturally opposed to sin, because of the natural rectitude and constancy of the divine nature. He cannot but hate what is opposed to his own wisdom.

units.la: II. Quæ contra hoc afferunt adversarii, tam est in proclivi diluere, quam est imber quando cadit. Si loquamur (inquit Iacksonus) de bonitate actu existente in creatura, fieri non potest ut aliquid actu existat, sine precedente actu divinæ bonitatis: at vero objectiva est bonitas prior actu & exercitio voluntatis divinæ & quibusdam rebus consideratis, ut logicè possibilibus. Objectiva hæc bonitas adeo est annexa, ut si ipsius sit voluntas dare ipsis esse actuale, necesse est sint actu bonæ: potuit vitam & existentiam omnibus ante diluvium abstulisse, sed quod Noachum familiamque ipsius servaret homines, non vero creaturas irrationales, non est omnipotentiæ objectum. Respond. I. Recedit disputator à statu quaestionis, Deum non posse libero suo decreto efficere ut homo non sit animal rationale, nemo, opinor, negabit, neque hoc quaeritur. Supposito enim quod hæc res sit homo, necesse est sit animal, & quod hæc res sit peccatum, oportet sit malum. Deus enim non potest non velle, ut idem non sit idem. Sed ex Dei beneplacito est, quod hæc res materialiter & denominative sumpta (hoc est prout nondum habet esse, sed per Dei beneplacitum in signo rationis ante decretum Dei est esse acceptura) habeat tale & tale esse: Dei enim est rerum essentias & naturas effingere. 2. Non est hæc objectiva rei bonitas, non repugnantia ad esse: sic enim peccatum in suo esse objectivo antequam est, est bonum, quia in eo signo non repugnat peccatum esse. 3. Si Dei voluntas sit causa omnis boni actu existentis, tum erit etiam causa non existentiæ obedientiæ reproborum. Itaque quod non obediant reprobi, erit ex Dei voluntate, atqui Arminiani volunt peccatum neque secundum essentiam neque secundum existentiam à Dei voluntate esse.
