units.tr: 11. The objections our opponents raise against this are as easy to refute as it is to rain when it is raining. If we speak (says Jackson) of goodness actually existing in a creature, it cannot happen that anything actually exists without a preceding act of divine goodness. But goodness is objective, prior to the act and exercise of the divine will, and to certain things considered as logically possible. This objective goodness is so bound up with the will that if it is God's will to give them actual being, they must necessarily be actually good. He could have taken away life and existence from all men before the flood, but that he preserved Noah and his family, and not the irrational creatures, is not an object of omnipotence. Reply 1. The disputant departs from the state of the question. No one, I think, will deny that God cannot by his free decree make a man not a rational animal, and this is not the point at issue. For, supposing that this thing is a man, it must necessarily be an animal, and supposing that this thing is sin, it must be evil. God cannot fail to will that the same thing is not the same. But it is by God's good pleasure that this thing, taken materially and denominatively (that is, as not yet having being, but which by God's good pleasure is to receive such and such being in the conception of reason before God's decree), has such and such being. For it belongs to God to shape the essences and natures of things. 2. This is not the objective goodness of a thing, which is the absence of repugnance to being. For sin, in its objective being before it exists, is good, since in that conception it is not repugnant that sin should exist. 3. If the will of God is the cause of all good that actually exists, then it will also be the cause of the non-existence of the obedience of the reprobate. So it will be from God's will that the reprobate do not obey. But the Arminians want sin to be from God's will neither according to its essence nor according to its existence.

units.la: 12. Addit ibid. pa. 149. 150. Prout est natura volentis, ita sunt objecta voluntatis, similie gaudet similibus: id tantum velle (in Deo) quod ipsius naturæ consonum est tanto Deo essentiali alius, quam nobis, quanto simplicior est Dei natura quam nostra: unde prima regula omnis bonitatis extra ipsum est consonantia cum essentiali (Dei) puritate & justitia. Relp. 1. Blasphemum[?] est fingere inter creatorem & creaturam aliquam similitudinem: at quaero quam similitudinem cum Dei natura habeat creatio mundi, potius quam non creatio: atqui certum est Deum velle mundi creationem. Si ergo non voluisset ipsam, voluisset noncreationem mundi: atqui non-creatio est naturae divinae tam consona, quam creatio est, quia vero essentiale esse vult Iacksonus Deo id velle, quod ipsius naturae est consonum, sequitur Deum essentialiter velle mundi creationem, atque adeo omnia quae vult & facit. Ergo Deus esset non Deus, si non creasset mundum, si liberasset Christum per 12. legiones angelorum, si filios ex lapidibus Abrahamo excitaret, quam absurda theologia! Ipse enim Iacob.Arminius concedit Deum quicquid agit in objectum externum, id totum Deum facere libere. Iacksonus negabit Deum libere, sed omnia naturae necessitate velle & facere, & sic Deus non erit agens intellectuale. 2. Si prima regula omnis bonitatis extra Deum sit consonantia cum Dei essentiali puritate &c. Sequitur absurdissime ergo Deum vetantem sacrificia,vetare id quod convenit cum justitia ipsius essentiali,& Deum jubentem immolationem Isaaci & postea vetantem, vetare quod convenit cum ipsius justitia essentiali. 3. Hinc sequitur Deum velle & amare ipsius puritatem & justitiam liberè, quia negari haud potest Deum libere velle omnia extra se, quae vult, quippe ex illo habent convenientiam cum Dei essentiali puritate.
units.tr: 12. He adds in the same place, pp. 149–150: As is the nature of the one willing, so are the objects of the will; like delights in like. In God he wills only what is consonant with his nature, and this is the more essential to God than to us, as the nature of God is simpler than ours. Hence the first rule of all goodness outside himself is consonance with the essential purity and justice (of God). Reply 1. It is blasphemous to imagine any likeness between the Creator and the creature. But I ask what likeness the creation of the world has to the nature of God, rather than non-creation. Yet it is certain that God wills the creation of the world. If then he had not willed it, he would have willed the non-creation of the world. But non-creation is as consonant with the divine nature as creation is. Yet since Jackson says that God wills essentially that which is consonant with his nature, it follows that God essentially wills the creation of the world, and so everything that he wills and does. Then God would not be God if he had not created the world, if he had not delivered Christ by twelve legions of angels, if he had not raised up children to Abraham from stones. How absurd a theology! For Jacobus Arminius himself concedes that whatever God does towards an external object, he does freely. Jackson will deny that God wills and does things freely, and says that he wills and does all things by the necessity of nature, and so God will not be an intelligent agent. 2. If the first rule of all goodness outside God is consonance with the essential purity of God, etc., it follows most absurdly that God, forbidding sacrifices, forbids what agrees with his own essential justice, and that God commanding the sacrifice of Isaac and afterwards forbidding it, forbids what agrees with his essential justice. 3. Hence it follows that God wills and loves his own purity and justice freely, since it cannot be denied that God freely wills all the things outside himself that he wills, for they have their agreement with the essential purity of God from him.

units.la: Ob. 2. Diligit (inquit) ipse Deus veritatem & sinceritatem, quoniam ipse est verax & justus: non potest libidinem & intemperantiam approbare, aut condemnare castitatem in aliqua persona neque legitimare potest. violentiam. Libido promiscua, violentia non tantum mala sunt nobis, quibus vetantur, sed etiam in se, ita ut omnipotens non potuerit non vetare & condemnare ejusmodi, ut manifesto inimica facratiffimæ[?] suæ majestati. Refp. 1. Deum posse velle & jubere, id quod citra ipsius voluntatem mandantem esset vis & immanis barbaries, nemo sanus negavit: jussit Abrahamum immolare filium, Israelitas spoliare Ægyptios, Saulum Amalekitas, viros, uxores prægnantes, infantes gladio & internecioni devovere. 2. Recedit novator à statu quæstionis: posito hoc quod hæc res fit intemperantia, vis, libido impura, barbaries, non potest non inhibere, utpote voluntati approbanti contraria. Necesse fuit itaque Deum vim, posito hoc, quod sit vis, vetare: verum ea necessitas est hypothetica ex positione liberi Dei beneplaciti, qui potest creaturæ hoc jubere, vel vetare, vel non jubere, aut non vetare. 3. At vero si velit antecedenter ad Dei beneplacitum ista opponi hostiliter sacratissimæ Dei majestati, tantum non blasphemat: quid? essentialiter Dei naturæ repugnant, ejus arboris scientiæ boni & mali, non circumcidi Iudæos, quod Iudæi parcerent Cananitis, quos Deus funditus ab iis deleri voluit? Lex ergo de non manducando fructu vetito fluit a Deo necessitate naturæ, nihil absurdius.
units.tr: Obj. 2. God (says he) loves truth and sincerity, since he himself is true and just. He cannot approve lust and intemperance, nor condemn chastity in any person, nor can he legitimate violence. Promiscuous lust and violence are evil not only for us, by whom they are forbidden, but in themselves, so that the Almighty could not but forbid and condemn such things, as manifestly hostile to his most holy majesty. Reply 1. No sane person has denied that God can will and command what, were it not for his commanding will, would be violence and monstrous barbarity. He commanded Abraham to sacrifice his son, the Israelites to despoil the Egyptians, and Saul to devote to the sword and destruction the Amalekites, men, pregnant wives and infants. 2. The innovator departs from the state of the question. Supposing that this thing is intemperance, violence, impure lust, or barbarity, God cannot but forbid it, since it is contrary to his approving will. It was therefore necessary, supposing it to be violence, that God forbid violence. But that necessity is hypothetical, arising from the positing of God's free good pleasure, who can command this to a creature, or forbid it, or not command it, or not forbid it. 3. But if one wishes that those things be opposed to the most sacred majesty of God by a hostility antecedent to God's good pleasure, he is not far from blasphemy. What then? Are they essentially repugnant to God's nature? Was it essentially repugnant that he forbade the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, or that the Jews should not be circumcised, or that the Jews should spare the Canaanites, whom God wished to be utterly destroyed by them? The law about not eating the forbidden fruit therefore flows from God by the necessity of nature. Nothing could be more absurd.

units.la: Ob. 3. Deus (inquit) suam voluntatem infringere non potest aut vi torquere a stricta observatione illius regulæ justitiæ, quam nobis proponit imitandam. Resp. 1. ex hypothesi, quod hoc fit divinæ voluntatis statutum, non potest non suam voluntatem sequi: at vero absolute Deus nihil extra se vult aut facit, cujus contrarium non potest velle aut facere. 2. Nihil salsius Deum non posse non observare regulam justitiæ nobis propositam, nobis legem posuit, non sibi: quid? An ergo Deus natura sua sancta[?] tenetur legem & euangelium implere, nempe sese timere, colere, sabbathum fanctificare, credere in filium suum? Hanc enim justi-tiæ regulam nobis præscribit: at quæ lex obligat Deum ad permittendum peccatum, ad sacrificia & sacramenta instituenda, ad fidem potius, quam bona opera novi fœderis conditionem urgendum? scilicet a regula Mosaica sacrificandi obligatur Deus sacrificia imperare, atqui non exstat ulla talis regula, nisi recurremus ad Dei beneplacitum.
units.tr: Obj. 3. God (says he) cannot break his own will or be forced away from the strict observance of that rule of justice which he sets before us to imitate. Reply 1. On the hypothesis that this is a statute of the divine will, he cannot but follow his own will. But absolutely, God wills or does nothing outside himself the contrary of which he cannot will or do. 2. Nothing is more false than that God cannot but observe the rule of justice set before us. He has laid down the law for us, not for himself. What then? Is God by his holy nature bound to fulfil the law and the gospel, namely to fear himself, worship himself, sanctify the sabbath, believe in his Son? For this is the rule of justice he prescribes to us. But what law binds God to permit sin, to institute sacrifices and sacraments, to demand faith rather than good works as the condition of the new covenant? Surely God is bound by the Mosaic rule of sacrificing to command sacrifices, yet no such rule exists unless we have recourse to God's good pleasure.

units.la: Ob. 4. Hinc (inquit) patet exemplaria illa sanctitatis & perfectionis, quæ nos in Deo imitari par est, non sumenda a nudo ipsius mandato, aut revelatione voluntatis ipsius, sed ab objectis voluntatis revelatæ, aut a Dei æternis actionibus, quas nobis exhibuit tanquam a totidem expressis & testifitatissimis eatissimis argumentis, quod ipsius voluntas justa fit & sancta. Huic voluntati Dei nos conformes esse vult ut ipsius naturæ conformes evadamus, quippe jubet Deus nos esse sanctos & perfectos, quemadmodum ipse est. Resp. 1. Sanctitas quam Deus à nobis flagitat est conformitas cum nuda Dei libera voluntate revelata, non simpliciter cum Dei natura, quod patet. Nam quid aliud est lex Dei quam liberum Dei beneplacitum, quo voluit hoc, non illo modo à nobis coli, quando potuisset, si ita Dei sapienti beplacito visum fuisset alium longe modum cultus, imo contrarium cultum à nobis exigere? an ex necessitate divinæ naturæ est, quod evangelium non legem voluerit esse peccatoribus viam ad gloriam, quod fidem non opera legis voluit esse conditionem novi fœderis? Atqui omnes Arm. in Rom. 9. in eo ponunt absolutam Dei libertatem in justificandis vel operariis vel credentibus. An ex necessitate naturæ divinæ Deus aquâ in baptismo, panem & vinum in cœna dominica signa elementaria instituerit: quasi Deus in suam justitiam essentialem peccasset, si alia signa instituisset: & Deus injus-tus fuisset si gentibus circumcisionem, Judæis baptismum fœderis sigillum instituisset. 2. Vult exemplaria divinæ sanctitatis, quæ nos imitari par est, sumi ab objectis voluntatis revelatæ. Age itaque, Thoma, hoc est objectum voluntatis revelatæ, quod Chananæi sint delendi, quod Isaacus sit immolandus à patre, quod aqua sit signum in baptismo. Si exemplar divinæ sanctitatis est ab his, hoc erit verum antecedenter ad Dei voluntatem, quod Isaacus sit immolandus. Non ergo peccabant Iudæi qui tenent[?] s infantes immolarunt, sed in hoc imitati sunt sanctitatem Dei essentialem. Deinde hæc sunt sancta (delendi fuit[?] Chanmæi[?]) (Infantes baptizandi sunt aqua) vel quia Deus liberre hrc voluit, & sic exemplaria divinæ sanctitatis quæ nos imitari par est, sunt sumenda à Dei voluntate revelata, contra quod ille asserit; vel sunt in se sancta & justa essentialiter, & objectivè, ut ille ait, ideoque Deus est sanctus à sanctitate objectiva rerum creatarum, quo quid absurdius? 3. Si ab æternis Dei actibus, & praxi sumenda sit formalis ratio sanctitatis nobis mandatæ, age igitur; praxis erat Dei ut juberet patrem immolare filiū, ergo nobis licebit etiam immolare filios: praxis erat Dei ut peccatum permitteret. Ergo Eli sacerdos non peccavit permittendo filios suos peccare, sed in hoc fuit sanctus, sicut Deus est sanctus: Dei praxis est interimere reges, ergo licet nobis unctos Domini interficere, quam absurda theologia? 4. Naturæ divinæ nos conformes esse debere falsissimum est, & in creaturas ne quidem angelicas cadit: sunt enim homines & angeli Dei conformes, quia ipsius voluntati libere hoc mandanti, non quia naturæ ipsius sese conformant. 5. Et sanctitas illa Dei quam nos imitari par est, est sanctitas in agendo sancte & inculpate cum creaturis suis, & non inest Deo essenessentialiter, sed ex absoluto suo beneplacito, sicuti dixi de misericordia & iustitia Dei, quatenus ad creaturas referuntur. In hoc enim elucet Dei sanctitas, quod ferio amet & approbet, quæ creaturis rationalibus imperat, & si Deus tum angelis tum hominibus imperasset longe diversa, imo oppositia hisce quæ jam de facto imperat, non minus sanctus fuisset Iehovah, quam nunc est: jubet Christus simus misericordes & inimicorum propensi amatores, sicut est pater cœlestis. At vero pater cœlestis & æque misericors & æque perfectus fuisset, atque nunc est, si inimicis suis nec solis, nec pluviarum copiam fecisset, nec ullo modo ipsorum misertus fuisset, quippe miseretur, quorum vult.
units.tr: Objection 4. Hence (he says) it is clear that those patterns of holiness and perfection which we ought to imitate in God are to be taken not from the bare command or revelation of his will, but from the objects of the revealed will, or from God's eternal actions, which he has shown us as so many clear and most certain proofs that his will is just and holy. God wishes us to be conformed to this will of his, so that we may become conformed to his very nature, for God commands us to be holy and perfect, as he himself is. Answer 1. The holiness that God requires of us is conformity with the bare, freely revealed will of God, not simply with the nature of God, as is plain. For what else is the law of God but God's free good pleasure, by which he willed that he be worshipped in this way rather than that, when he could have demanded a far different mode of worship, or even the contrary, if it had seemed good to his wise pleasure? Is it by necessity of the divine nature that the gospel did not will the law to be the way for sinners to glory, and that he willed faith, not the works of the law, to be the condition of the new covenant? Yet all the Arminians on Romans 9 place in this the absolute freedom of God in justifying either workers or believers. Did God, by necessity of the divine nature, institute water in baptism and bread and wine in the Lord's Supper as elementary signs? As if God would have sinned against his essential justice had he instituted other signs, and as if God would have been unjust had he instituted circumcision for the Gentiles and baptism as the seal of the covenant for the Jews. 2. He wants the patterns of divine holiness, which we ought to imitate, to be taken from the objects of the revealed will. Come then, Thomas: is this an object of the revealed will, that the Canaanites are to be destroyed, that Isaac is to be sacrificed by his father, that water is the sign in baptism? If the pattern of divine holiness is taken from these, then it will be true, prior to the will of God, that Isaac is to be sacrificed. So the Jews who sacrificed tender infants were not sinning, but in this they imitated the essential holiness of God. Next, these things are holy (...) either because God willed them freely, and so the patterns of divine holiness which we ought to imitate are to be taken from the revealed will of God, which he denies; or they are holy in themselves and essentially and objectively, as he says, and so God is holy by the objective holiness of created things. What could be more absurd? 3. If the formal reason of the holiness commanded to us is to be taken from God's eternal acts and practice, then consider: it was God's practice to command a father to slay his son; therefore it will be lawful for us to slay our sons too. It was God's practice to permit sin; therefore Eli the priest did not sin in permitting his sons to sin, but in this he was holy, as God is holy. It is God's practice to slay kings; therefore it is lawful for us to kill the Lord's anointed. What an absurd theology! 4. That we ought to be conformed to the nature of God is most false, and does not apply even to angelic creatures. For men and angels are conformed to God because they obey his will in freely commanding this, not because they conform themselves to his nature. 5. And that holiness of God which we ought to imitate is holiness in acting holily and blamelessly toward his creatures; it is not in God essentially, but arises from his absolute good pleasure, as I have said of the mercy and justice of God, insofar as they are referred to creatures. For the holiness of God shines forth in this, that he loves and approves what he commands rational creatures. If God had commanded angels and men quite different things, indeed things opposite to those he now commands, Jehovah would have been no less holy than he now is. Christ bids us be merciful and inclined to love our enemies, as our heavenly Father is. But the heavenly Father would have been equally merciful and equally perfect as he now is, even if he had not given his enemies the abundance of sun and rain, and had in no way pitied them, since he has mercy on whom he wills.

units.la: 13. Aliam viam in quæstione enodanda ineundam censuit Ioan. Camero. Ait, nihil à Deo amari quia bonum sit, sed ideo bonum esse unumquodque, quia à Deo amatur. Refp. Camero. Ergo nec (inquit) seipsum amabit, quia bonus est, sed ideo bonus existimandus est quia seipsum amat, quod si hoc illis absurdum est, idem valere in Dei imagine necesse est. Si enim Deus naturali atqui immutabili propensione in amorem sui inclinat, consimili prorsus affectu imaginem sui complectetur.
units.tr: 13. John Cameron chose another way of unravelling the question. He says: nothing is loved by God because it is good, but each thing is good because it is loved by God. Answer to Cameron: Therefore (he says) neither will he love himself because he is good, but he must be judged good because he loves himself; and if this seems absurd to them, it must necessarily hold equally in the image of God. For if God is inclined to love himself by a natural and unchangeable propensity, he will embrace his image with a wholly similar affection.

units.la: Refp. Cameronus consequentia vana est, ergo Deus bonus quia sese amat. Est enim essentialiter, & non per participationem bonus: entia creata sunt bona per participationem divinæ bonitatis: atqui Deus libere bonitatem creaturis indulget, quia vult, ideoque eatenus sunt bonæ, quia Deus eas velit. 2. Nullo modo sequitur Deum naturali propensione imaginem sui amare, quippe quod patet filium foveat & vitæ ipsius consulat, quod mutuum reddatur, est imaginis Dei non exigua pars in homine, atqui potest Deus velle ut Abrahamum filium mactet, ut Israelitæ mutuum non reddant Ægyptiis. Ergo liberè, non naturæ impetu imaginem sui amat: nam nihil est imago Dei nisi sanctitas legalis in homine, atque sanctitas legalis est conformitas cum Dei voluntate liberâ, non cum naturali Dei desiderio: alioqui non potest Deus alia imperare, quæ quæ imperat, aut vetare, imo sic scriptura sacra non erit consilium liberum Dei, sed desiderium naturale Dei, quod non magis potest non esse in Deo, quâ Deus possit esse non Deus. Res (inquit) quædam sunt ἀδιάφορ[?]α quæ Dei imaginem non referunt nisi sub ratione entis, at non sub ratione boni moralis, hoc est qua Deus est ens, at non qua justus & sanctus est. Hæc potest imperare aut vetare prout libet. At vero (inquit tom. 4. p. §72.) neque Deus innocentem damnare, neque fontem absolvere, nec amorem sui prohibere, aut odium sui commendare, aut imperare potest. Pugnant hæc cum ipsius natura. Resp. 1. Futulis & vana prorsus distinctio. Omnes enim res creatæ & actiones humanæ nudè consideratæ sunt in se adiaphoræ & sunt bonæ moraliter, quatenus ipsas Deus velit & jubeat, malæ quatenus nolit & velit, ut sunt amare, colere, loqui, manducare, bibere, occidere hominem. Nam hæc omnia in physica confideratione, sunt neque bona neque mala, & amare Deum physice est adiaphoron, & moraliter bonum, quia à Deo jubetur. 2. Membra distinctionis nulla sunt: nam non est major ratio, quare res in fe sunt adiaphoræ, quia referunt Deum, qua ens, quam quia referunt Deum, qua justus & sanctus. Quæ enim referunt Dei justitiam & sanctitatem, non ideo sunt bonæ quia referunt Dei naturam, sed quia cum voluntate Dei justa & fancta attamen libera conveniunt. 3. Deus (inquit) innocentem damnare non potest, sed hæc non-potentia non habet ortum à Dei natura, sed à Dei voluntate. Nam innocentem suum filium damnavit, & nos fontes absolvit: atqui si Deus non statuisset ab æterno apud se, & potuisset liberrime fontes absolvere, potuit absolute fontes non absolvere. 4. Prohibere Dei amorem, non pugnat simpliciter cum Dei natura, sed cum voluntate libera: hoc enim ex eo dicit, quia amare Deum, Camero putat cum Dei natura convenire, ideoque non amare Deum credit Dei naturæ opponi: at quæro oppofitionem, an fit relativa, an contradictoria, an contraria, an privativa. Certe nihil Deo fuperessentiali substantiæ opponitur vel relativè, vel contrariè: Deus enim non est accidens, neque contradictorie, nisi eo modo, quo omnia entia creata opponuntur ei contradictorie. Necesse est ergo dicat n[?] non amare Deum, opposi Deo privativè; atqui sic n[?] non-amare Dei[?], tolletolleret privativè Deum, ejusque naturam, quo quid hlasphemius; Posita enim tum nonamatione Dei, tolleretur ipse Deus: atqui sicut τὸ amare Deum, convenit Deo extrinsecè, quatenus cum ipsius voluntate revelata convenit, nihil enim Deo accedit, quatenus impletur, quod vult, quo nihilo felicior est Deus. Itaque nihil ponitur divinae naturae adversum, ex hoc, quod homines Deum non ament, sed ponitur aliquid, quod Deus libere fieri non vult.
units.tr: Answer: Cameron's consequence is empty, namely that God is good because he loves himself. For God is good essentially, and not by participation; created beings are good by participation in the divine goodness. But God grants goodness to creatures freely, because he wills it, and so they are good in that respect because God wills them to be. 2. It by no means follows that God loves his image by natural propensity. For that God cherishes his Son and cares for his life, and that this love is returned, is no small part of the image of God in man; yet God can will that Abraham slay his son, and that the Israelites not return what they owed to the Egyptians. Therefore God loves his image freely, not by the impulse of nature. For the image of God is nothing but legal holiness in man, and legal holiness is conformity with the free will of God, not with God's natural desire. Otherwise God could not command other things than those he does command, or forbid what he forbids; indeed Holy Scripture would then be not the free counsel of God but God's natural desire, which can no more be absent from God than God can cease to be God. Certain things (he says) are adiaphora [ἀδιάφορα] which bear the image of God only under the aspect of being, not under the aspect of moral good; that is, in that God is a being, not in that he is just and holy. These he can command or forbid as he pleases. But indeed (he says, vol. 4, p. §72) God can neither condemn the innocent, nor absolve the wicked, nor forbid love of himself, nor commend hatred of himself, nor command it. These things are at odds with his nature. Answer: 1. This distinction is futile and utterly empty. For all created things and human actions, considered bare in themselves, are indifferent and become morally good insofar as God wills and commands them, and evil insofar as he is unwilling and forbids them, as to love, worship, speak, eat, drink, or kill a man. For all these, considered physically, are neither good nor evil; to love God is physically indifferent and morally good, because it is commanded by God. 2. The members of the distinction are no distinction at all. For there is no greater reason why things are indifferent in themselves because they refer to God as being than because they refer to God as just and holy. For things that refer to God's justice and holiness are not good because they refer to God's nature, but because they agree with the will of God, which is just and holy yet free. 3. God (he says) cannot condemn the innocent, but this inability does not arise from the nature of God but from his will. For he condemned his innocent Son, and absolved us sinners; and if God had not decided from eternity within himself, and could most freely have absolved sinners, he could absolutely have not absolved sinners. 4. To forbid the love of God does not simply clash with the nature of God, but with his free will. For Cameron says this because he thinks loving God agrees with the nature of God, and so he believes that not loving God is opposed to the nature of God. But I ask what kind of opposition this is: is it relative, contradictory, contrary, or privative? Certainly nothing is opposed to the supra-essential substance of God either relatively or contrarily: God is not an accident, nor opposed contradictorily, except in the way all created beings are opposed to him contradictorily. It is necessary, then, that he say not loving God is opposed to God privatively; but thus not loving God would privatively take away God and his nature, what could be more blasphemous? For if not loving God were posited, God himself would be taken away. But just as loving God [τὸ ἀγαπᾶν] belongs to God extrinsically, insofar as it agrees with his revealed will (for nothing is added to God when what he wills is fulfilled, and God is no happier for it), so nothing is posited adverse to the divine nature from the fact that men do not love God. Rather, something is posited that God does not wish to happen freely.

units.la: 14. Ejusdem genii sunt, quae tertio loco objecit Arminius. Multa sunt (inquit) quae Deus vult, quia justa sunt; justum est, ut solus Deus à creatura pro vero agnoscatur, hoc Deus vult, quia justum est, & non est justum, quia Deus velit &c. Resp. Totum sano sensu conceditur; semper enim à statu quaestionis recedit; postquam enim Deus hoc semel verbo expresserit, & menti humanae in creatione certa naturae lege indiderit (aequum est ut Deus pro vero Deo à creatura rationali agnoscatur) tum Deus istud non potest non velle sine nota inconstantiae. Vult itaque Deus quae justa sunt, nempe quoniam priore actu beneplaciti sui eadem justa esse statuerat. Postquam vero Deus libere aliquid fieri statuerit, id non cadit sub aliam constitutionem Dei liberam, ut possit, ab eo liberè fieri, vel non. Jam enim necessitate hypothetica Deus non potest id velle: at vero res in esse objectivo, & materialiter sumptæ, hoc est in signo rationis, quo esse ipsorum per liberum Dei decretum est sanciendum & nondum sancitum, possunt vel cadere sub Dei liberam constitutionem, ut justa, vel ut non justa per decretum negativum, ideoque si τῷ[?] colere Deum natura creaturæ rationalis & quidditate includatur (quod nolo jam disputare) recederetur plane à statu quæstionis. Nam non quæritur an æquum sit ab æterno quod homo coleret Deum, & an Deus ipsum velit, quoniam est æquum, sed si τῷ[?] colere Deum separari posset quoad æquitatem obligationis naturalis à natura creaturæ rationalis, tum dico fieri posse, si Deo ita visum fuisset, ut æquum non sit ut creatura rationalis coleret creatorem. Nam si Deus statuisset ut creatura rationalis non coleret creatorem, id non minus æquum & justum fuisset, quam jam æquum est ipsius contrarium. Nam involvitur hic quæstio: est enim à Dei libertate quod creatura rationalis sit, est ab eādem, quod cultus Dei sit, quamvis ut Deus sit, non sit à Dei libertate: At non est dubium, quin Deus creaturam rationalem potuisset effinxisse, vel non effinxisse.
units.tr: 14. Of the same kind is the objection he raised in third place: Arminius. Many things (he says) God wills because they are just; it is just that God alone be acknowledged by the creature as the true God; God wills this because it is just, and it is not just because God wills it, etc. Answer: The whole of this is granted in a sound sense, for he always departs from the state of the question. Once God has expressed this in a word, and has implanted in the human mind at creation, by a certain law of nature, that it is fitting for God to be acknowledged by the rational creature as the true God, then God cannot but will this without a mark of inconstancy. God therefore wills what is just, namely because by a prior act of his good pleasure he had determined that these things should be just. But once God has freely decided that something is to be done, that does not fall under another free constitution of God by which it might be done by him freely or not. For by hypothetical necessity God cannot now will otherwise. Yet things, taken in objective being and materially, that is in the sign of reason, by which their being is to be sanctioned, or not yet sanctioned, by the free decree of God, can fall under God's free constitution either as just, or as not just, through a negative decree. Therefore, if the "to" of "to worship God" [τῷ] is included in the nature and quiddity of the rational creature (which I do not now wish to dispute), we would plainly depart from the state of the question. For the question is not whether it is fitting from eternity that man should worship God, and whether God wills it because it is fitting. Rather, if the "to" of "to worship God" could be separated, as regards the fittingness of natural obligation, from the nature of the rational creature, then I say it could be done, if it had so seemed good to God, that it is not fitting for the rational creature to worship its creator. For if God had decreed that the rational creature should not worship its creator, that would be no less fitting and just than its contrary is now fitting. A question is involved here: the rational creature exists from God's liberty, and the worship of God likewise exists from the same liberty, although that he is God does not arise from God's liberty. But there is no doubt that God could have fashioned the rational creature, or not fashioned it.

units.la: 15. Affinis hisce est quæstio, an teneamur nos in objecto conformare nostram voluntatem divinæ voluntati, & quatenus: ad quod respondetur ratione objecti materialis non teneri nos. Nam Dei intentio & voluntas erat ut Abrahamus non immolaret Isaacum: at vero in Abrahamo ipsum immolare jussò, fuit contraria plane voluntas & intentio ut immolaret ipsum, & ea Abrahami voluntas justissima fuit. Unde patet Dei voluntatem approbante nullo modo includerere Dei intentionem ut objecto voluntatis approbantis actuexistat. VultDeus ut pater senio gravis moriatur, non peccat filius volendo, ut senex superviveret, ut observat August. Enchir.c.10. At vero tenemur conformate voluntate nostram Dei voluntati approbanti quatenus nobis revelatur. Si loquamur de objecto formali, dicunt Durand. & Valent. nos debere velle omne bonum in relatione ad Dei gloriam, quod commode intelligi debet. Nam omnes homines ipsam habitudinem rerum, etiam peccati, ad gloriam velle tenentur. Nam quamvis non liceat nobis vel velle peccatum ut Dei gloria illustretur, attamen debemus velle hoc, quod peccatum actu dirigatur ad Dei gloriam, Est enim haec voluntas Dei revelata & aequa & sancta, ideoque possumus nos velle id a Deo fieri, cujus objectum vel materiam ipsi nec facere nec velle possumus absque horrendo reatu. Nec dici potest, debere nos velle voluntate nostra permissiva peccatum quatenus divinae gloriae illustrandae conducit, id quod Deus citra officii sui violationem velle jure optimo potest, & vult: & hujus discriminis sola causa est, quoniam Deus legi se non subjecit, sed liberae suae constitutioni, nos vero legi subjicimur. Hinc patet Deum non praecise suam voluntatem aligasse[?] certae regulae, cui nos alligavit: vult filii a patre occisionem esse homicidium, ita tamen ut ipse mandare posset ut pater filium occidat; res alienas invitis Dominis eripere ita voluit esse peccatum, ut ipse tamen posset Israelitis imperare, ut res pretiosas Ægyptiorum ipsis subtrahat. Sed de hoc, in disputatione de providentia Dei.
units.tr: 15. Akin to these is the question whether we are bound to conform our will in the object to the divine will, and in what respect. To this it is answered that, with regard to the material object, we are not bound. For God's intention and will was that Abraham should not sacrifice Isaac; yet when Abraham was commanded to sacrifice him, the will and intention was plainly contrary, that he should sacrifice him, and that Abraham's will was most just. Whence it is evident that God's approving will in no way includes God's intention that the object of the approving will should actually exist. God wills that a father, weighed down by old age, should die; the son does not sin in willing that the old man should survive, as Augustine, Enchiridion c.10. observes. But we are indeed bound to conform our will to God's approving will insofar as it is revealed to us. If we speak of the formal object, Durandus and Valentia say that we ought to will every good in relation to the glory of God, which ought to be understood in a sensible way. For all men are bound to will even the very relation of things, even of sin, to God's glory. For although we may not will sin so that God's glory may be illustrated, nevertheless we ought to will this: that sin is actually directed to God's glory. For this will of God is revealed, and is both fair and holy; and therefore we can will that God bring about that which we ourselves may neither do nor will, its object or matter, without horrible guilt. Nor can it be said that we ought, by our permissive will, to will sin insofar as it conduces to illustrating the divine glory, which God can will with the best right, and does will, without violation of his office. The sole cause of this difference is that God has not subjected himself to a law, but to his own free constitution, whereas we are subject to law. Hence it is evident that God has not bound his own will precisely to a certain rule, to which he has bound us. He wills that a father's killing of a son be murder, yet so that he himself could command a father to kill a son; he willed that taking things belonging to others from unwilling owners be sin, yet he himself could command the Israelites to take the precious things of the Egyptians from them. But of this, in the disputation on the providence of God.

units.la: CAP. IV. De Dei voluntate antecedente & Consequente.
units.tr: CAP. IV. On the Antecedent and Consequent Will of God.

units.la: I. Quid docuerit de voluntate Dei sub hisce notionibus Chrysostomus, quid etiam Damascenus, ex ipsorum scriptis liquet; nec diffiteor Arminianos ipsorum vestigiis insistere. At vero Scotus ait Deum id velle antecedenter quod non in se & immediate, sed quod vult in antecedente causa, ex qua (inquit Durandus) effectus sequitur, quamvis non necessario; ut Deus antecedenter vult omnes salvari, quatenus dedit omnibus naturam salutis capacem, & media sufficientia non negavit, & Deus id vult consequenter quod non in causa sua, sed in se vult, ut credentes salvari. Estius, Bannes, Cumel. volunt talem Deo voluntatem non inesse. Et credo scripturam nusquam Deo voluntatem, hoc sensu, tribuere: sic enim Deus tam omnium peccata & exitium æternum velle dicendus esset: nam omnibus dedit naturam obedientiæ & inobedientiæ, salutis & exitii capacem, imo sic Deus diabolorum obedientiam & salutem, & bonorum angelorum inobedientiam & exitium velle dicendus esset: natura enim angelica salutis & exitii capax est. 2. Deus volendo causam non propterea vult omnes effectus ab illa causa Producibiles. Nam vult causam esse propter tales & alios effectus producendos: expressè dicit se voluisse extare Pharaonem ut in ipso gloria potentiæ & iræ suæ declaretur: at si ullo voluntatis actu voluit ut salvaretur Pharaoh, quæritur quo fine? ut patefiat gloria misericordiæ. At vero contrarium finem intendit, neque confusè omnes fines intendere potest. Beza noster vult voluntatem antecedentem esse εὐδοκίαν & rei per se gratæ complacentiam, & sic est Dei voluntas approbans à decernente contradistincta, quod sano sensu concedi potest. Am. Polanus & Hier. Zanchius recte docent esse improprie dictam voluntatem. Did. Alvarez sensu non improbando ait voluntate antecedente Deum velle aliquid boni absolute & voluntate consequente, & in individuo secundum omnes circumstantias adjunctas, Deum idem nolle; ut antecedenter vult salutem reproborum, est enim res in se & absolute amabilis: at consequenter non vult, quia secundum omnes circumstantias, & universi ordinem, non est bona: nam salus reproborum privaret mundum gloriosâ providentiâ justitiæ divinæ declarativâ.
units.tr: I. What Chrysostom taught about the will of God under these notions, and what Damascene taught too, is clear from their own writings. Nor do I deny that the Arminians follow in their footsteps. But Scotus says that God wills something antecedently when He does not will it in itself and immediately, but wills it in an antecedent cause, from which (says Durandus) the effect follows, though not necessarily. Thus God antecedently wills all to be saved, insofar as He has given all a nature capable of salvation and has not denied them sufficient means. God wills consequently what He wills not in its cause but in itself, namely that believers be saved. Estius, Bannes and Cumel hold that there is no such will in God. And I believe that Scripture nowhere attributes to God a will in this sense. For in that case God would have to be said to will the sins and the eternal destruction of all, since He has given all a nature capable of obedience and disobedience, of salvation and destruction. Indeed, God would have to be said to will the obedience and salvation of the devils, and the disobedience and destruction of the good angels, since the angelic nature is capable of both salvation and destruction. 2. By willing a cause, God does not thereby will all the effects that can be produced from that cause. For He wills the cause to exist for the sake of producing such and other effects. He expressly says that He willed Pharaoh to stand so that in him the glory of His power and wrath might be declared. But if by any act of will He willed that Pharaoh be saved, the question is: for what end? That the glory of mercy might be made manifest? Yet He intends the contrary end, and He cannot intend all ends confusedly. Our Beza holds that the antecedent will is εὐδοκία [eudokia, good pleasure] and the complacency in a thing pleasing in itself, and so it is a will of God approving, distinguished from the decreeing will; this can be conceded in a sound sense. Amandus Polanus and Hieronymus Zanchius rightly teach that it is improperly called a will. Didacus Alvarez, in a sense that is not to be disapproved, says that by the antecedent will God wills something good absolutely, and by the consequent will, and in the individual according to all the attendant circumstances, God wills the same thing not to be. Thus He antecedently wills the salvation of the reprobate, for the thing is lovable in itself and absolutely; but consequently He does not will it, because according to all the circumstances and the order of the universe it is not good. For the salvation of the reprobate would deprive the world of the glorious providence declaring the justice of God.

units.la: 2. Iesuitæ recentiores præsertim, Gab. Vasquez & Francisc. Suarez. & Arminiani docent voluntatem antecedentem esse naturalem in Deo affectum, quâ naturæ impetu vult bonum & salutem creaturarum intelligentium quatenus sunt creaturæ, & nihil adhuc merito aut demerito egerunt: at quatenus obedientes sunt vel inobedientes, consequenter vult quosdam damnari. Hinc ex amore antecedente omnes vocat, gratia communi afficit; omnibus Christum dedit in mortem, verbum evangelii omnibus offerre paratus est, nisi ipsi sibi ponant obicem; hinc consequenter quosdam prout peccatis sunt commeriti, vocationem specialiorem negat, indurat, euangelium non indulget secundum sapientiam & justitiam suam. Ita Arminius, Corvinus, Greuinchovius; sed quibusdam placet voluntatem antecedentem vocare conditionatam, & verbo optativi modi explicandam, id quod Vafquezii palato minime sapit, qui vult eam esse voluntatem simplicis affectus, & complacentiæ absolutæ; conditionatam vero dici, non quia fertur in objectum suum conditionatè, sed quia ex illa quæ præsens est, alia (voluntas) oriretur, si conditio in objecto poneretur. Ioanni Cameroninosiro placet amor quidem antecedens, & voluntas conditionata, qua pro omnibus Deus pater Christum tradidit in mortem, omnes vocat, omnium salutem vult, qui quantum ab antecedente hac voluntate differat, ex ejus scriptis colligere haud est in proclivi.
units.tr: 2. The more recent Jesuits, especially Gabriel Vasquez and Francisco Suarez, and the Arminians teach that the antecedent will is a natural affection in God, by which, from the impulse of nature, He wills the good and salvation of intelligent creatures insofar as they are creatures, and have not yet acted with merit or demerit. But insofar as they are obedient or disobedient, He consequently wills that some be damned. Hence, by the antecedent love, He calls all, favours all with common grace, has given Christ to all unto death, and is ready to offer the word of the gospel to all, unless they themselves place an obstacle in the way. Hence, consequently, according to what they have deserved by their sins, He denies a more special calling to some, hardens them, and does not grant them the gospel according to His wisdom and justice. So teach Arminius, Corvinus and Grevinchovius. But some are pleased to call the antecedent will conditional, and to explain it by the optative mood. This is by no means to the taste of Vasquez, who holds that it is a will of simple affection and absolute complacency, and that it is called conditional not because it is directed conditionally to its object, but because another will would arise from it, if a condition were placed in the object. Our John Cameron approves of an antecedent love and a conditional will, by which God the Father delivered Christ to death for all, calls all, and wills the salvation of all. How far this differs from that antecedent will one can hardly gather from his writings.

units.la: 3. Hæc tamen voluntas antecedens multis nominibus divina majestate indigna est. 1. Si sit in Deo voluntas salvandi omnes & singulos, quæ nunquam expleatur, erit in Deo potentia finita & infirmitas, quia sua desideria explere non posset. Resp. Arminius, non sequi: Dei enim potentia non est instrumentum affectus sui desiderij, seu velleitatis divinæ, sed volitionis libera ultimum divinæ sapientiæ judicium secutæ, quanquam Deus eousque utatur potentia ad obtinendum id quod defiderat, qua deceat, Resp.
units.tr: 3. Yet this antecedent will is unworthy of the divine majesty in many respects. 1. If there is in God a will to save all and each, which is never fulfilled, there will be in God finite power and weakness, since He would not be able to fulfil His desires. Answer: Arminius says that this does not follow. "For the power of God is not the instrument of His affection or desire, or divine velleity, but of the free volition that follows the last judgment of divine wisdom, although God uses His power to the extent that is fitting to obtain what He desires." Answer.

units.la: 1. Contradictio hic est plana. Potentia Dei non est instrumentum affectus naturalis, quanquam Deus utitur potentia sua ad desiderium suum implendum qua deceat. Ergo non est instrumentum, & est instrumentum. 2. Fabulatur de ultimo divinæ sapientiæ judicio, quo innuit esse in Deo primum judicium sapientiæ divinæ prævium, ideoqne judicium sensitivum & temerarium, quod corrigitur ab ultimo judicio. Est hic Deus Anthropomorphi-ticus. 3. Dicit in Deo esse affectum naturalem, quem Deus per nullam potentiam implet. At quare hoc? Est hic affectus brutinus, mere naturalis, qualis est lapidis deorsum vergentis appetitus, qui a cognitione primæ causæ dirigitur. Itane? Quis Deo superior ipsum dirigit? Est enim affectus expers cognitionis: nondum enim accessit ultimum judicium sapientiæ: ergo hic affectus appetitui sensitivo in brutis dignitate longe cedit. Nam brutorum appetitus sensitivus cognitione non vacat: amabit ergo Deus ignorans, quid amet. 4. Quid Deus contra decentiam suam ageret, si actu salveret omnes, quos cupit salvari naturaliter? Agitne contra decentiam suam in procuranda electorum salute? Nihil minus. At cur decentiæ divinæ adversaretur ut reprobos salvaret? Novit enim notione congrua abipso Arminio concessa, quanquam reclamantibus ipsius discipulis, omnium voluntates ex æquo indeclinabiliter, idque illibata libertate, movere & permovere. Sed ego pandam pudendum hoc mysterium, adversatur Dei potentiae ut alios convertat, quam qui convertuntur.
units.tr: 1. The contradiction here is plain. The power of God is not the instrument of a natural affection, although God uses His power to fulfil His desire as far as is fitting. Therefore it is not an instrument, and it is an instrument. 2. He invents a "last judgment of divine wisdom," by which he hints that in God there is a first judgment of divine wisdom that precedes, and therefore a sensitive and rash judgment, which is corrected by the last judgment. Here is an anthropomorphic God. 3. He says that there is in God a natural affection, which God fulfils by no power. But why so? This affection is brutish, purely natural, like the appetite of a stone falling downward, which is directed by the knowledge of the first cause. Really? Who superior to God directs it? For the affection is without knowledge: the last judgment of wisdom has not yet come in. Therefore this affection falls far short, in dignity, of the sensitive appetite in brute beasts. For the sensitive appetite of brutes is not without knowledge. So God would love while ignorant of what He loves. 4. What would God be doing contrary to His fittingness if He actually saved all whom He naturally desires to be saved? Would He be acting contrary to His fittingness in procuring the salvation of the elect? Not at all. But why would it be contrary to divine fittingness to save the reprobate? For He knows, by a concept that is suitable and conceded by Arminius himself, though his own disciples object, that He moves and moves again the wills of all equally and unchangeably, and that without impairing freedom. But I will reveal this shameful mystery: it is contrary to the power of God to convert others than those who are converted.

units.la: Nam antecedenter ad Dei decretum, & ad scientiam mediam, damnandi libere restituerunt Dei vocationi, & salvandi obtemperarunt, & Deus salvare non potest per ullam potentiam eos qui ante omnes actus decreti divini vocationem rejecerunt. 5. Quæro quid intelligat per Dei decentiam? Estne haec decentia talis modus agendi à Deo libere institutus? Credo hoc negari non posse.
units.tr: For before the decree of God and before middle knowledge, the damned freely resisted God's calling and did not obey the call to salvation. And God cannot save by any power those who, before all acts of the divine decree, rejected the calling. 5. I ask what they mean by God's fittingness. Is this fittingness a manner of acting freely instituted by God? I believe this cannot be denied.

units.la: At quæro, quare hunc modum agendi decentem esse voluit respectu electorum, indecentem vero respectu reproborum. Nam libere hos modos vocandi instituit: hic haerebunt, nisi ad absolutam Dei libertatem confugerunt, quo statuit absolute, hos vocare, modo decentiae suae conveniente, illos modo decentiae suae plane adversanti; at hoc non concedent Iesuitis Arminiani. 6. At illud est, quod dicunt decentiam hanc esse modum connaturalem justitiae divinae, & alienum esse à Dei justitia ut Deus reluctantes, eo modo vocet quo non reluctantes vocantur. At tum Deus necessitate justitiae non potest procurare ut damnandi, quos Deus salvari vult, obediant & non peccent resistendo vocanti, quod ipsi Arminio displicebit dicenti Deum præter illa
units.tr: But I ask why He willed this manner of acting to be fitting with respect to the elect, but unfitting with respect to the reprobate. For He freely instituted these modes of calling. Here they will be stuck, unless they take refuge in the absolute freedom of God, by which He decided absolutely to call these, in a mode agreeing with His fittingness, and those in a mode plainly opposed to His fittingness. But the Arminians will not concede this to the Jesuits. 6. But they say this: that this fittingness is the mode natural to the divine justice, and that it is foreign to God's justice that He should call the resisting in the same way in which the non-resisting are called. But then, by the necessity of justice, God cannot bring it about that those whom God wills to be saved, the damned, obey and do not sin by resisting the one calling. This will displease Arminius himself, who says that God, besides those [...]

units.la: [?] Note text in the margin beside the lines above is only partly legible; see notes. sufficientia impedimenta etiam efficacia habere in sapientiæ suæ thesauro, quibus productis certo & mfallibiliter[?] peccatum impediretur. Sed audi, Iacobe, illa impedimenta vel adversantur Dei decentiæ & justitiæ, vel non. Si primum, dici non potest esse in promptuario divinæ sapientiæ impedimenta, quibus productis impediretur peccatum, puta resistentia facta ab omnibus non conversis divinæ vocationi: Sapientia enim Dei non potest aliquid Deo dictitare quod decentiæ & justitiæ adversatur: num quæso Dei sapientia præscriberet Deo aliquid indecens & injustum? Absint blasphemiæ. Si vero illa impedimenta non adversantur Dei decentiæ & justitiæ, Deus potest non obstante decentia sua & justitia, implere sua desideria circa conversionem & salutem omnium, qui nec convertuntur nec salvantur: non enim impedit justitia: ergo nec ipsorum peccatum. Ergo impedit sola Dei absoluta libertas, quod fidei Arminianæ adversatur. Nec ulla sanà ratione dici potest absolutam Dei voluntatem non nixam vel ulli in peccatoribus rationi, vel decentiæ, vel sapientiæ, vel justitiæ divinæ, impedire quo minus Deus impleat sua desideria naturalia: imo sic Dei voluntas absoluta peccaret in voluntatem hanc antecedentem; quo quid absurdius? 7. Dicant quare Deus non utatur potentia sua ad complendum affectum suum naturalem, non minus quam ad complendam voluntatem consequentem. Est enim utrobique par ratio, nisi dixerint non constare Deo ratiorationem affectuum naturalium, sicut constat ei ratio voluntatis consequentis: sed hoc tantum non est blasphemum. Quid enim Deus desideraret quod rationi aut decentiae suae repugnaret? Nam pro culdubio, si Deus omnes converteret & salvaret, respectu Dei id decens fuisset & justum: alioqui dedisset creaturae liberum arbitrium, quod non posset omnes effectus possibiles producere, absque laesione divinae decentiae & justitiae, quod est absurdum. 8. Optime notat Guliel Tuissius, quamvis Deus non corrigat naturam, ut sic desideria naturalia impleret per omnipotentiam, non sequitur alio modo corrigi non posse, nempe per gratiam ex praescientia efficacem, id quod subdole dissimulat Arminius. At quaero ex Arminio cur Deus quosdam vocet secundum decretum praedestinationis, cum certa scientia fore ut obediant, & impleatur sic naturale Dei desiderium; alios vero secundum decretum providentiae communioris, ex praescientia, qua scit eos nunquam obedituros, ut sic nunquam expleretur voluntas antecedens, id n. Arminius ait convenire & Augustini doctrinae & fors etiam scripturae. Atqui fors etiam scripturae ex Arminio pari ratione conveniat necesse est, ut Deus ex sola absoluta libertate utatur erga pares, vocationibus tam disparibus. Nulla enim est ratio a justitia, a decentia Dei, a praevisa fide & contumacia hominum, cur circa homines duo decreta tam disparia ab ae-terno posuerit apud se. Si dicunt ex justitia Dei esse ut obsequentiores vocentur motione congrua, redibit quæstio in infinitum. At facti sunt obsequentes per motum congruum: & si inobsequentes ita fuissent vocati, fuissent procul omni dubio obsequentissimi.
units.tr: [?] Note text in the margin beside the lines above is only partly legible; see notes. have sufficient impediments, also efficacious ones, in the treasury of His wisdom, by bringing forth which sin would be certainly and infallibly[?] prevented. But listen, James, those impediments either oppose God's fittingness and justice, or they do not. If the first, it cannot be said that there are in the storehouse of divine wisdom impediments by bringing forth which sin would be prevented, such as the resistance offered by all the unconverted to the divine calling. For the wisdom of God cannot prescribe to God anything that opposes fittingness and justice. Would the wisdom of God, I ask, prescribe to God anything unfitting and unjust? Far be such blasphemy. But if those impediments do not oppose God's fittingness and justice, God can, notwithstanding His fittingness and justice, fulfil His desires concerning the conversion and salvation of all, including those who are neither converted nor saved. For justice does not hinder; therefore neither does it hinder their sin. Therefore only the absolute freedom of God hinders, which is contrary to Arminian belief. Nor can it be said by any sound reason that the absolute will of God, not resting on any reason in sinners, or on the fittingness, wisdom or justice of God, hinders God from fulfilling His natural desires. Indeed, in this way the absolute will of God would sin against that antecedent will. What could be more absurd? 7. Let them say why God does not use His power to fulfil His natural affection, no less than to fulfil the consequent will. For the reason is equal in both cases, unless they say that God does not know the reason of natural affections as He knows the reason of the consequent will. But that is not blasphemous, only so. For what could God desire that was repugnant to His reason or fittingness? For undoubtedly, if God converted and saved all, that would have been fitting and just with respect to God. Otherwise He would have given the creature a free will which could not produce all possible effects without injury to divine fittingness and justice, which is absurd. 8. Gulielmus Tuissius rightly notes that although God does not correct nature so as to fulfil natural desires by omnipotence in this way, it does not follow that they cannot be corrected in another way, namely by grace that is efficacious through foreknowledge. This Arminius craftily dissembles. But I ask Arminius why God calls some according to the decree of predestination, since with certain knowledge they will obey, and so God's natural desire is fulfilled; but others according to the decree of a more general providence, by foreknowledge, by which He knows they will never obey, so that the antecedent will is never fulfilled. For Arminius says that this agrees with the doctrine of Augustine and perhaps also with Scripture. Yet, by Arminius's own reasoning, it must be that perhaps Scripture also agrees, so that God, from absolute freedom alone, deals with equals by callings so unequal. For there is no reason, from justice or fittingness of God, from foreseen faith or stubbornness of men, why He should have posited from eternity two such unlike decrees in Himself concerning men. If they say that it is from the justice of God that the more obedient are called by a fitting motion, the question will return to infinity. But they became obedient through the fitting motion; and if the disobedient had been called in the same way, they would without doubt have become most obedient.

units.la: 4. Verum mihi cæteris Arminianis hac saltem re explicatius Jacksonus mentem ipsorum declarasse videtur. Ait enim æternæ æquitatis regulas non pati ut Deus ulterius porrigat manus ad homines salvandos, quam actu porrigit: Resp.
units.tr: 4. Indeed, of all the Arminians, Jackson seems to me to have declared their mind more clearly on this one point. For he says that the rules of eternal equity do not allow God to stretch out his hands further to save men than he actually stretches them out. Answer:

units.la: 1. Quæro an ulla regula sit Deo præscripta, qua quosdam convertat, quosdam non, præter liberam Dei voluntatem, qua miseretur quorum vult: scriptura aliam non assignat. 2. An non quivis videat promtuarium sapientiæ Dei vacuatum, & evacuatum, quo infinitos modos apud se reconditos habet, docente Arminio, quibus productis, peccatum neglectæ vocationis impediretur; & non posse Deum sine nota injustitiæ alios convertere quam qui actu convertuntur, quasi vero definieret Deus esse justus, si gratiam conversionis efficacem omnibus gratificaretur. 3. Sequitur Deum necessitate naturali justitiæ convertere; quos convertit, & non convertere quos non convertit. Imo ab æterno Deus avertere non potuit, quin perirent omnes, qui pereunt, nisi vellet esse injustus, & sic Deus fatali necessitate salvatos salvat, damnatos perdit, & fato tot, non plures, non pauciores. Mihi crede Jupiter Homerianus, primus motor Aristotelicus Stoicorum Deus arctioribus vinculis constrin-gi non
units.tr: 1. I ask whether any rule is prescribed to God by which he converts some and not others, apart from his free will, by which he has mercy on whom he wills. Scripture assigns no other. 2. Does anyone not see that the storehouse of God's wisdom is emptied and exhausted, in which, according to Arminius, he holds infinite ways hidden away, which, if they were brought forth, would prevent the sin of neglected calling? And that God cannot convert others than those who are actually converted without a mark of injustice, as if God would cease to be just if he granted efficacious grace of conversion to everyone. 3. It follows that God, by natural necessity of justice, converts those whom he converts and does not convert those whom he does not convert. Indeed, from eternity God could not have turned away from this, unless all who perish were to perish, unless he wished to be unjust; and so God by fatal necessity saves the saved, damns the damned, and by fate as many as he does, no more and no fewer. Believe me, Homeric Jupiter, Aristotelian prime mover, god of the Stoics, cannot be bound by tighter chains

units.la: si[?] non potest. 4. At vero ipse novator sui oblitus pag. 179. c. 15. Apostolus (inquit) subindicat argumentum fuisse immensæ Dei misericordiæ, quod Deus permitteret Pharaonem diutius superesse, postquam jam evaserat vas iræ æternæ pœnæ in gehenna, destinatum. Ergo concedit Deum ulterius porrexisse manus ad salvandum Pharaonem: quam passa est æternæ æquitatis regula, Nam post septimam plagam erat vas iræ. Ergo secundum justitiæ regulam potuit Deus tum ipsum intermisse: atqui pœnam distulit, & ulterius manus porrexit: nam vocationes plures post septimam plagam indulsit. Ergo id contra omnem justitiam Deus fecit & regulas æternæ æquitatis violavit. O theologiam prodigiosam!
units.tr: cannot. 4. But the innovator himself, forgetting himself, says on p. 179, chapter 15: The Apostle (he says) indicates that it was an argument of God's immense mercy that God allowed Pharaoh to survive longer, after he had already escaped the vessel of wrath destined for the punishment of eternal fire in hell. Therefore he concedes that God further stretched out his hands to save Pharaoh, which the rule of eternal equity would not have allowed, for after the seventh plague he was a vessel of wrath. Therefore, according to the rule of justice, God could then have stopped him; yet he deferred the punishment and further stretched out his hands, for he granted several calls after the seventh plague. Therefore God did this against all justice and violated the rules of eternal equity. O prodigious theology!

units.la: 5. Neque video qui se expediant Remonstrantes, qui dicunt supremum & nulli juratum Dominum ac legislatorem non ponere sibi-ipsi legem, sed semper jus sibi suum integrum reservare extra ordinem agendi (prout libet. Sed quæro an Deus jus habeat faciendi contra justitiam & decentiam suam in quibusdam, in aliis vero non. Certe tum reservavit sibi Deus jus peccandi, & injuste agendi, unde sequitur necessario justitiam & decentiam Dei nullo modo esse regulam, quam Deus sequitur in voluntatis antecedentis impletione, sed Deum hic regulari à sola sua libertate absoluta, quam quoniam non exsequitur, invictè stat Deum infirmum esse, qui desideria expleta dare non possit.
units.tr: 5. Nor do I see how the Remonstrants extricate themselves, who say that the supreme Lord and Lawgiver, sworn to no one, does not set a law for himself, but always keeps his own right whole to act outside the order (as he pleases). But I ask whether God has the right to act against his justice and decency in some cases but not in others. Certainly then God has reserved to himself the right to sin and to act unjustly; from which it follows necessarily that the justice and decency of God are in no way the rule which God follows in fulfilling his antecedent will, but that God is here governed by his own absolute liberty alone. Since he does not carry this out, it stands unconquered that God is weak, being unable to grant the desires that are fulfilled.

units.la: 6. 2. Arg. Nostrum. Ex hac distinctione perit Dei libertas miserendi quorum vult, ergo'est Deo indigna. Prob. antecéd. Deus non liberè, sed necessitate naturæ vult bonum antecedenter suæ creaturæ, ut ait Arminiu. 1-mo (inquit Corvinus) Deus tali actu non potest non velle bonum, & hæc voluntas ex Grovinchov. antecedit Dei libertatem & decretum. Ergo in antecedente Dei voluntate nulla est libertas, sed neque in consequente voluntate ulla est libertas, quoniam voluntas consequens, regulatur necessario à naturali Dei justitia, qua non potest nonvelle illius conversionem qui convertitur, & nolle illius conuersionem qui non convertitur.
units.tr: 6. 2. Our argument. From this distinction the liberty of God to have mercy on whom he wills perishes; therefore it is unworthy of God. The antecedent is proved: God wills the good of his creature antecedently not freely but by the necessity of nature, as Arminius says in the first place (Corvinus says), God cannot not will good by such an act; and this will, according to Grevinchovius, precedes God's liberty and decree. Therefore there is no liberty in the antecedent will of God; but neither is there any liberty in the consequent will, since the consequent will is necessarily regulated by God's natural justice, by which he cannot but will the conversion of him who is converted and not will the conversion of him who is not converted.

units.la: 7. 3. Arg. Nullum naturalem affectum miferendi agnoscit scriptura. Nam si Deus impetu naturæ dedit filium mundo, tum necesse fuit, conderetur genus humanum & conditum in peccatum laberetur. Atqui sic necessitate naturæ Deus mundum creavit, & hominem labi permisit, quia, quæ Deus naturaliter vult, ea non potest non procurare ut fierent. Nam eodem naturæ impetu, pater filios amat, & generat filios, quos amet. Si Deus impetu naturæ miseretur generis humani, eodem impetu necesse est objectum misericordiæ suæ procuret, 2. Oporteret etiam ut lapsis angelis (quandoquidem sunt creaturæ rationales, at naturalis desiderii Dei objecta necessaria) remedium pararet. At dicent obstare justitiam Dei quó minus paretur lapsis angelis qui liberrime & nullo suadente aut tentante peccarunt, remedium. Sed respondeo primo, nata est hæc iustitia ex libero Dei decreto, vel inest Deo naturaliter. Si primum, non esset injustum', siquidem Deus voluisset, si ipsis remedium parasset. Si secundum, tum necesse est dicant, non esse in Dei sapientiæ infinita promptuario modos possibiles salvandi omnes creaturas rationales, quod Arminio adversatur, ne quid dicam gravius. Nam probatum dedimus iustitiam Dei erga creaturas Deo contingenter, non naturaliter inesse. 2. Turpe & indignum est Deo quòd multorum conversionem & salutem velit respectu amoris communis, cuorum[?] non potest misereri respectu iustitiæ; quasi vero posset aliquem amare iniuste, aut iustitiam vel exhibere contra aliquem naturalem ipsius amorum, vel amare aliquem naturaliter contra iustitiam, quum Dei liberras sit & iustitiæ & amoris erga creaturas regula. 3. Imo hinc sequitur tam converti homines secundum rigorem iustitiæ divinæ, quam secundum divitem misericordiam, & tam homines debitores esse iustitiæ divinæ, adeoque suo reti sacrificare debere, quam diviti Dei misericordiæ, cui in solidum scriptura nostri conversionem, nullo modo iustitiæ debere acerrimè contendit. Ephes. 2. 4, 5, 6 Iac. 1. 18. Tit. 3. 5. 6. 2. Tim. 1. 9. Rom. 9. 15.
units.tr: 7. 3. Argument. Scripture acknowledges no natural affection of mercy. For if God gave his Son to the world from the impulse of nature, then it was necessary that the human race be created and, having been created, would fall into sin. But God created the world by necessity of nature and permitted man to fall, because what God wills naturally, he cannot but bring about that it be done. For by the same impulse of nature a father loves his sons and begets sons whom he may love. If God has mercy on the human race by an impulse of nature, he must by the same impulse procure the object of his mercy. 2. He would also have to prepare a remedy for the fallen angels (since they are rational creatures, and the objects of God's natural desire are necessary). But they will say that the justice of God stands in the way of a remedy being prepared for the fallen angels, who sinned most freely and without anyone persuading or tempting them. But I answer: first, this justice either arises from a free decree of God, or it is inherent in God naturally. If the first, it would not be unjust, since God would have been willing, had he prepared a remedy for them. If the second, then they must necessarily say that there are no possible ways of saving all rational creatures in the infinite storehouse of God's wisdom, which is opposed to Arminius, not to say something more grave. For we have shown that the justice of God towards creatures is contingent to God, not inherent naturally. 2. It is shameful and unworthy of God that he should will the conversion and salvation of many out of common love, yet cannot have mercy on them with respect to justice; as if he could love anyone unjustly, or exhibit justice against someone contrary to his natural love, or love anyone naturally against justice, whereas the liberty of God is the rule both of his justice and of his love towards creatures. 3. Indeed, from this it follows that men are converted as much according to the rigour of divine justice as according to rich mercy, and that men are as much debtors to divine justice, and so ought to sacrifice to its net, as to the rich mercy of God, to which Scripture most sharply contends that our conversion is owed wholly and in no way to justice. Eph. 2. 4, 5, 6; Jas. 1. 18; Tit. 3. 5, 6; 2 Tim. 1. 9; Rom. 9. 15.

units.la: 3. Naturalia in Deo sunt æterna, sicut ipsa Dei natura est æterna, unde sequitur in æternum Deum velle damnatos homines & reprobos angelos salvari. Nam nihil naturale Deo accedit aut recedit tanquam extraneum essentiae ipsius, & sic Deo est naturale remedia invenire, quibus omnes damnatos ex æternis cruciatibus redimat, & hic revivisset error Originis afferentis cruciatus damnatorum non esse æternos. Prævidit hoc argumentum Arminius & ei dupliciter occurrit. Nam. 1. dicit Deum voluisse (attende, non dicit Deum, jam velle) antecedente voluntate salutem dæmonum; Sed quare voluit ipsorum salutem, & jam non vult? Nam naturale Dei desiderium est æternum: quid enim naturæ divinæ decéderet? Et adhuc & in æternum Deus naturaliter diligit creaturas suas qua tales, atqui dæmones nondum desierunt esse Dei creaturæ; sed utinam pervideret ecclesia Dei fœdum atheismum sectæ Arminianæ, nempe cum Vorstio mutatum jam olim esse Deum & exoletum, atque evanuisse naturale Dei desiderium erga salutem Dæmonum. 2. Dicunt Arminiani Dei sapientiam & justitiam determinationem aut quandam modificationem imponere Dei assectibus naturalibus. Age vero videamus, ecquid rei sit hæc determinatio: Dei sapientia & justitia vel determinant Dei desideria naturalia ut tandem non sint, quando olim erant, vel ut sint modificata & determinata. Quæro, an Dei sapientia efficiat ut non sit in Deo jam naturale desiderium salvandi damnatos angelos & homines; at quæro rationem, quare non jam desideret ipsorum salutem. Ratio vel est in Deo, vel in ipsis damnatis. In Deo quæ potest esse ratio, cur olim desiderarit salutem damnatorum, nunc vero non desideret? an quia absolute nunc non vult desiderare, olim voluit? atqui libertas Dei quia est causa libera, nullo modo potest esse causa desiderii naturalis & necessarii, neque ulla potest esse in Deo ratio quare mutentur & intereant Dei volitiones: sic enim Deus a principio interno esset mutabilis, atque adeo corruptibilis. Neque potest esse ratio in ipsis damnatis, quia manente objecto formali desiderii, manet ipsum desiderium, atqui in ipsis damnatis manet esse ipsorum, neque per hoc quod damnantur, desinunt esse Dei creaturæ. Ergo necesse est adhuc Deus velit damnatos salvari, quatenus sunt Dei creaturæ: Dei ergo sapientia non refcindit in Deo aliquid naturale. Si vero Dei sapientia tantum determinat Dei desiderium ut sit decens & justum, tum in Deo erunt proprie dictæ passiones antevertentes actum sapientiæ divinæ ex se injustæ & indecentes, donec in ordinem redigantur per rectæ rationis imperium. Quod enim est capax moderationis, id ex se natum aptum est deviare; quare sic Deus erit Iovi poetarum passionibus obnoxio haud impar. Præterea; quando dicit Deus, (volo congregari Hyerosolymitanos,) vel id juste & sapienter vult, vel non juste. Si priùs, non antecedentis voluntatis actu, sed antecedentis & voluntatis restrictæ & determinatæ actu vult illos congregari: at vero sic vult ipsos voluntatis consequentis & non antecedentis actu congregari. Nam voluntatis restrictae & determinatae per sapientiam & justitiam, actus, non est actus naturalis desiderii Dei, quod terminatur in solum esse creaturae intellectualis. Nam voluntas per justitiam restricta praesupponit creaturae actus obedientiae & inobedientiae, quos nullo modo praesupponit voluntas antecedens. Si vero vult Hierosolymitanos congregari non juste sed naturali tantum inclinatione, non videmus hic ullam determinationem factam a Dei sapientia & justitia: sed actum mere naturalem non modificatum. Atqui quaero, quando modificatur, si non quando Deus actu vult illos obedire & salvari; sed huc inclinent, necesse est, Arminiani, ut dicant Deum in exercito nunquam actu, sed voluntate antecedente, sed propensione seu inclinatione tantum velle aliquid antecedenter, id quod diserte dicit Corvinus, Tum certe (inquit) quatenus Deus desiderat hominum salutem, eatenus id desiderium impletur quia eam desiderat, nisi quatenus id justitia permittit. Atqui hoc est voluntate consequente a justitia determinata salutem reproborum velle & hoc est nolle reprobos salvari: reclamat enim justitia, quo minus salventur. Itaque ex Arminio & Corvino Deus non actu antecedentis voluntatis vult reprobos salvari.
units.tr: 3. Natural things in God are eternal, just as the very nature of God is eternal; whence it follows that God wills the damned men and reprobate angels to be saved for ever. For nothing natural accrues to or recedes from God as something foreign to his essence; and so it is natural to God to find remedies by which he might redeem all the damned from eternal torments, and here would revive the error of Origen, who asserted that the torments of the damned are not eternal. Arminius foresaw this argument and meets it in two ways. For, 1. he says that God willed (note, he does not say God wills, now) the salvation of the demons by his antecedent will. But why did he will their salvation, and now does not will it? For God's natural desire is eternal: for what would be lost from the divine nature? And still and for ever God naturally loves his creatures as such, yet the demons have not ceased to be God's creatures; but would that the Church of God might see the foul atheism of the Arminian sect, namely that God has long since changed and grown old along with Vorstius, and that his natural desire for the salvation of the demons has vanished away. 2. The Arminians say that the wisdom and justice of God impose a determination or some modification upon the natural affections of God. Come now, let us see what this determination amounts to: either the wisdom and justice of God determine God's natural desires so that at last they are not, when once they were, or so that they are modified and determined. I ask whether the wisdom of God brings it about that there is no longer in God a natural desire for saving the damned angels and men; but I ask the reason why he does not now desire their salvation. The reason is either in God or in the damned themselves. What reason can there be in God why he once desired the salvation of the damned but now does not desire it? Is it because he now absolutely does not will to desire, but once willed to? Yet the liberty of God, since it is a free cause, can in no way be the cause of a natural and necessary desire; nor can there be any reason in God why God's volitions should change and perish: for thus God would be mutable from an inner principle, and so corruptible. Nor can the reason be in the damned themselves, since, the formal object of the desire remaining, the desire itself remains; yet in the damned their being remains, and by being damned they do not cease to be God's creatures. Therefore God must still will the damned to be saved, insofar as they are God's creatures; so the wisdom of God does not cut away anything natural in God. But if the wisdom of God only determines God's desire so that it is fitting and just, then in God there will be properly so-called passions preceding the act of divine wisdom, which in themselves are unjust and unbecoming, until they are brought into order by the command of right reason. For what is capable of moderation is by nature apt to deviate; so God will be no less subject to passions than Jupiter of the poets. Moreover, when God says, I will that the Jerusalemites be gathered, he either wills this justly and wisely, or not justly. If the former, he wills them to be gathered not by an act of antecedent will, but by an act of restricted and determined will, that is, of the will determined by wisdom and justice; yet thus he wills them to be gathered by an act of consequent will and not of antecedent will. For an act of will restricted and determined by wisdom and justice is not an act of God's natural desire, which terminates only in the being of an intellectual creature. For a will restricted by justice presupposes the creature's acts of obedience and disobedience, which the antecedent will in no way presupposes. But if he wills the Jerusalemites to be gathered not justly but by natural inclination only, we do not see here any determination made by God's wisdom and justice, but a purely natural act, unmodified. Yet I ask: when is it modified, if not when God actually wills them to obey and be saved? But the Arminians, who lean this way, must say that God in the exercise of his will never wills anything actually, but only antecedently by will, by propensity or inclination only, which Corvinus says expressly: Then certainly (he says) insofar as God desires the salvation of men, to that extent that desire is fulfilled, because he desires it, except insofar as justice permits. Yet this is to will the salvation of the reprobate by a consequent will determined by justice, and this is to will the reprobate not to be saved: for justice protests against their being saved. Therefore, according to Arminius and Corvinus, God does not by an act of antecedent will will the reprobate to be saved. 8. To have desires in God that are without justice and wisdom is blasphemous.

units.la: 8. Esse in Deo desideria justitiae sapientiae expertia blasphemum est. Imo satis est (inquit Corvinus ) quod sint benevola. Sed an non damnantur in creaturis intelligentibus cæcus & brutus amor eorum, quæ ignorant sintne affecuturæ, an non uti Coridon ardebat Alexin (ut ait Maro) nec quid speraret habebat. Eodem modo Deus ardebit amore salutis omnium hominum & diabolorum nesciens, sitne id obtenturus. Imo (inquit Corvinus) non necesse est, ut Deus quando aliquid intendit ac vult, consideret sitne id obtenturus nec ne, sed sufficit ut consideret quod cum ex bonitate, tum ex amore erga iustitiam ipsum defiderare, deceat. Sed 1. naturalia Dei desideria antevertunt decreta libera & actus sapientiæ divinæ, uti cum Arminianis docet Grevinchovius: hoc vero resorbet Corvinus & vult Deum velle & intendere salutem creaturæ ex amore erga iustitiam, & ex sua decentia uti fabulatur Corvinus. Ergo Dei decentiæ & sapientiæ actus, quibus considerat, æquum esse & iustum ut talia desideret, priores erunt voluntate antecedente at naturalia libero in Deo priora esse creditur, id quod ipsi docent. Ecce hic erit aperta contradictio. 2. Nullus appetitus brutinus est expers cognitionis sensitivæ in suo genere perfectissimæ: non ergo datur in Deo affectus expers cognitionis infinitæ, quæ penetret non tantum in decentiam & sapientiam desiderii sive affectus, sed etiam in desiderii impletionem. In hoc enim amor creaturæ intelligentis est imperfectus, quod non præsupponit scientiam perfectam, qua scitur, sitne illi amori satisfaciendum, nec ne. 3.
