units.tr: 8. To posit in God desires that are without the judgement of justice and wisdom is blasphemous. "Indeed," says Corvinus, "it is enough that they are benevolent." But are not the blind and brutish love of creatures who have understanding condemned, when they love things they do not know will be attained? Are they not like Coridon, who burned for Alexis, as Virgil says, and had no hope of what he wanted? In the same way God will burn with love for the salvation of all men and devils, not knowing whether he will obtain it. "Indeed," says Corvinus, "it is not necessary that God, when he intends and wills something, consider whether he will obtain it or not. It is enough that he consider that it is fitting for him to desire it, both from his goodness and from his love of justice." But, first, the natural desires of God precede his free decrees and the acts of his divine wisdom, as Grevinchovius teaches with the Arminians. Corvinus, however, absorbs this and wills that God wills and intends the salvation of a creature out of love of justice and from his own fittingness, as Corvinus fabricates. Therefore the acts of God's fittingness and wisdom, by which he considers it right and just that he should desire such things, will be prior in the antecedent will; and natural things are believed to be prior to the free in God, which they themselves teach. Here there will be a plain contradiction. Second, no appetite is brutish that lacks sensitive knowledge, which is most perfect in its kind. Therefore there is no affection in God lacking infinite knowledge, which penetrates not only the fittingness and wisdom of the desire or affection, but also its fulfilment. For the love of an intelligent creature is imperfect in this respect, that it does not presuppose perfect knowledge by which it is known whether that love should be satisfied or not. Third,

units.la: Omnia naturalia desideria æqua & sancta præsupponunt media sufficientia & apta ad fines intentos asequendos, ut inductione constat, in appetitu movendi, generandi, nutriendi, & rationabiliter volendi. Ergo voluntas antecedens præsupponit gratiam ex præscientia efficacem ad salvandos omnes homines & angelos: ergo omnes homines & angeli salventur, necesse est.
units.tr: All natural desires presuppose fair and holy means, sufficient and apt for attaining the ends intended, as induction shows in the appetite for moving, begetting, nourishing, and rationally willing. Therefore the antecedent will presupposes grace, foreknown as effective for saving all men and angels. Therefore all men and angels necessarily will be saved.

units.la: 9. 4. Argum: Voluntas hæc antecedens est indeterminata, incerta, suspensa, & mutatur in absolutam & peremptoriam voluntatem salvandi, si impleatur conditio, vel damnandi, si non impleatur. Ergo non est in Deo. Corvinus ait unam esse & eandem voluntatem, quæ prius cum sit conditionata, posita conditione, transit in absolutam. Resp. 1. Posita conditione transit (inquit) voluntas antecedens conditionata in absolutam: atqui, ponitur conditio in tempore: homines enim in tempore obediunt. Ergo in tempore voluntas antecedens mutatur in voluntatem absolutam, & ab æterno suspensa erat voluntas salvandi Petri, donec Petrus in tempore finaliter crederet, quam absurdum. Si vero dixerit Deum ab æterno præscivisse conditionem ponendam, tum voluntas antecedens ab æterno transfiit in absolutam. Quomodo ergo docent Arminiani Deum antecedente voluntate velle in tempore omnes obedire & salvari? 2. Docent Arminiani Deum velle omnes obedire: at quomodo, aut quæ conditio hic ponenda est, ut voluntas conditionata transfeat in absolutam ? nempe si obedierint, aut si velint credere. Ecce theologiam ? Vult homines obedire velle, siquidem velint obedire. 3. Voluntas naturalis in voluntatem liberam transfire non potest, quoniam docent Arminiani & Iesuitæ liberum & naturale opponi contradictorie. Si vero vult voluntatem antecedentem ita transfire, ut ipsa non maneat voluntas antecedens, ecce tum evanuit voluntas antecedens, & definit esse. Atqui hoc est Deum mutabilem ponere. Sed neque (inquit Arminius) potest incertitudo tribui illius voluntati, qui infinitâ suâ sapientiâ omnia habet præsentia, & omnia etiam maxime contingentia certo præscit futura. Resp. 1. At oportet voluntas antecedens incerta sit & suspensa, quia Deus ea voluntate intendit & obedientiam & salutem omnium & singulorum, non sciens sintne omnes obedituri & salvandi. 2. At vero si non utatur infinita sua scientia, sed cæco impetu naturæ, desiderat ex nulla præscientia, sit ne id, quod desiderat futurum nec ne, eodem plane modo Dei voluntas hic erit suspensa, quo hominum voluntates suspensæ dicuntur, quippe nescientes sintne id assecuturi, quod volunt. 3. Corvin. citans Verst. mutabilitate hic manifesto astruit respectu decretorum hypotheticorum, ideo dici potest per partes seorsim accepta ea mutari, quia conditio respectu hominis vel præstatur, vel non præstatur, atque ita vel existit, vel non existit, & cum extitit aliquandiu etiam sæpe existere definit, & rursus postquam aliquandiu definit, existere incipit. Ita ipse Vorstius. Eventum (inquit) duntaxat aliquem particularem à causa secundâ contingente pendentem aliquando mutari dico, cujus deinde respectu decretum Dei per partes seorsim acceptum aliquatenus mutabile dici possit. Habemus hic reos confitentes; quoniam centies in uno anno, homo credit, homo non credit, ideoque exi-stit & non existit conditio; ideo mutatur Dei voluntas per partes, & aliquatenus. Deus ergo eritDeus aliquatenus,& immutabilis aliquatenus,& non Deus & mutabilis aliquatenus,hoc est,secundum quid non æternus,secundum quid non Deus. 2. Si decretū Dei per partes & seorsim sumptum sit mutabile,quare decretum integrum non minus sit mutabile,nullam rationem reddunt Armin. & certe si Deus sit ad horā mutabilis, & non Deus, cur non in æternum mutabilis& non Deus, ratio nulla excogitari potest. 3. Operæ prætium est observatu quomodo Corvinus loco citato accerrime propugnet hanc in Deo mutabilitatem, & rationem, quæ ad scholæ Arminianæ palatum imprimis facit, reddat, nég[?]er tamen conclusionem, nempe Dei voluntatem ullo modo esse mutabilem, & hoc est præmissis largiter suffragari, conclusioni vero contraniti. 4. Suarez, quem ubique Arminiani sequuntur concedit manere voluntatem antecedentem in Deo etiam erga damnatos: qua Deus velit ipsos salvari, & tum quidem, quando est in Deo efficax voluntas inferendi pœnam. Ita etiam Remonstrantes in apolog. Ita etiam Corvinus contr. Molinæ, c.5.
units.tr: 9. Fourth, an argument: this antecedent will is indeterminate, uncertain, suspended, and is changed into an absolute and peremptory will to save, if the condition is fulfilled, or to damn, if it is not fulfilled. Therefore it is not in God. Corvinus says that it is one and the same will, which, since it is at first conditional, when the condition is posited, passes into an absolute will. Reply: First, "once the condition is posited," he says, "the conditional antecedent will passes into the absolute." But the condition is posited in time, for men obey in time. Therefore in time the antecedent will is changed into an absolute will, and the will to save Peter was suspended from eternity until Peter finally believed in time. How absurd! But if he says that God foreknew from eternity the condition to be posited, then the antecedent will has passed into the absolute from eternity. How then do the Arminians teach that God, by his antecedent will, wills that all in time obey and are saved? Second, the Arminians teach that God wills all to obey. But how, or what condition must here be posited, so that the conditional will passes into the absolute? Namely, if they obey, or if they are willing to believe. Behold the theology! He wills men to obey, if indeed they are willing to obey. Third, a natural will cannot pass into a free will, since the Arminians and Jesuits teach that the free and the natural are contradictorily opposed. But if he wills the antecedent will to pass over in such a way that it does not remain the antecedent will, then behold, the antecedent will has vanished and ceased to be. But this is to posit God as mutable. "But," says Arminius, "uncertainty cannot be ascribed to that will which, by its infinite wisdom, has all things present and foreknows with certainty all things, even the most contingent, as future." Reply: First, the antecedent will must be uncertain and suspended, because by that will God intends the obedience and salvation of all and each, not knowing whether all will obey and be saved. Second, but if he does not use his infinite knowledge, but a blind impulse of nature, and desires without any foreknowledge whether what he desires will be future or not, then in exactly the same way the will of God here will be suspended, just as the wills of men are said to be suspended, since they do not know whether they will attain what they will. Third, Corvinus, citing Vorstius on mutability, here clearly asserts it with respect to hypothetical decrees. Therefore it can be said that those things, taken separately in parts, are changed, because the condition is either fulfilled or not fulfilled by man, and so either exists or does not exist; and when it has existed for a while it often ceases to exist, and again, after it has ceased for a while, it begins to exist. So Vorstius himself. "I say," he says, "that some particular event, depending on a contingent second cause, is sometimes changed, and with respect to it the decree of God, taken separately in parts, can be said to be to some extent mutable." Here we have guilty men confessing. For a hundred times in one year a man believes, a man does not believe, and so the condition exists and does not exist. Therefore God's will is changed in parts, and to some extent. God will therefore be God to some extent, and immutable to some extent, and not God and mutable to some extent; that is, according to something not eternal, according to something not God. Second, if the decree of God, taken in parts and separately, is mutable, the Arminians give no reason why the whole decree is not equally mutable. And certainly, if God is mutable for an hour and not God, no reason can be devised why he should not be mutable forever and not God. Third, it is worth observing how Corvinus, in the place cited, most vehemently defends this mutability in God, and gives the reason which especially pleases the palate of the Arminian school, yet denies the conclusion, namely that God's will is in any way mutable. This is to lend ample support to the premises while resisting the conclusion. Fourth, Suarez, whom the Arminians everywhere follow, concedes that the antecedent will remains in God even toward the damned, by which God wills them to be saved, and indeed at the time when there is in God an effective will to inflict punishment. So also the Remonstrants in their Apology. So also Corvinus against Molina, chapter 5.

units.la: Et hic Corvinus & Vorstius volunt ex conditione posita, vel non posita oriri vel desinere in Deo decreta, ideoque mutari decreta: at vero remota conditione, nulla tum erit ratio, cur removeretur, aut desineret decretum. Nam quando homo non credit, per ipsorum doctrinam potest Deus decernere, ut salvaretur homo, siquidem crederet: ergo & manebit decretum, remota conditione decreti, & non manebit, quae sunt contradicentia.
units.tr: And here Corvinus and Vorstius want decrees to arise or cease in God from the condition being posited or not posited, and therefore decrees to be changed. But when the condition is removed, there will then be no reason why the decree should be removed or cease. For when a man does not believe, by their doctrine God can decree that the man be saved, if indeed he were to believe. Therefore the decree will remain, with the condition of the decree removed, and will not remain; which are contradictory.

units.la: 10. Argum. ç. Voluntas antecedens pugnat cum Dei felicitate: Absolute enim beatus non est, qui ad desideriorum impletionem pervenire non potest. Respondet Suarez, Deum hic nihilo infeliciorem, quoniam non vi externa à fine depellitur, sed ex infinita sua justitia vult damnationem inobedientium, & nihil Deum desiderare tanquam alicujus rei indigum supra dixit Corvinus. Sed Resp. 1. Posita scientia media, quam ordine naturae antecedit futuritio inobedientiae & damnationis reproborum, vi maxime externa & fatali necessitate antegrediente & Dei scientiam & decretum liberum, Deus non potest magis implere suam naturalem voluntatem, de salute damnatorum, quam efficere potest, ut quod jam est, non fit, quod simpliciter Deo est impossibile & omnipotentiae divinae ἀσύστατον[?].
units.tr: 10. Argument 5. The antecedent will is inconsistent with the happiness of God. For he is not absolutely blessed who cannot attain the fulfilment of his desires. Suarez replies that God is here no less happy, since he is not driven from his end by external force, but out of his infinite justice wills the damnation of the disobedient; and Corvinus said above that God desires nothing as one needing something. But the reply is: First, given the middle knowledge, which in the order of nature precedes the future disobedience and damnation of the reprobate, and given the most external force and fatal necessity going before both God's knowledge and his free decree, God cannot more fulfil his natural will concerning the salvation of the damned than he can bring it about that what already is does not happen. This is simply impossible for God and inconsistent [ἀσύστατον] with divine omnipotence.

units.la: 2. Voluntates contumaces reproborum, quae sunt agentia externa, determinant in genere causae moralis voluntatem Dei ad homines damnandos: ergo Deus externa vi à fine depellitur.
units.tr: 2. Stubborn wills of the reprobate, which are external agents, determine the will of God to damn men in the genus of moral cause. Therefore God is driven from his end by external force.

units.la: 3. Nihil Dei beatitudini decederet, si non sciret omnia, quae actu sunt, quod factum fuisset, si nihil creasset, uti libere potuit non creasse, & tamen absolute perfectus non esset Deus, si enim iam actu existentia ignoraret: ullas vero esse in Deo facultates & potentias (ut sic loquar) quae in sua obiecta indeclinabiliter non ferantur, argueret felicitatem mancam. 4. Omnia Deum facere quae vult, nota est ipsum a non diis discriminans Psal. 115. 4, 5. Eatenus itaque erit non Deus, quatenus vult, quod facere non potest. 5. Delirat plane Iesuita, dum ait Deum propter suam iustitiam non posse salvare omnes, quos vult. Quid? an ex iustitia, an potius ex absoluta voluntate quibusdam vocationem congruam indulget, quibusdam negat? Non ex iustitia id provenire dicet, nisi fuisset oblitus, sed ex absoluta voluntate salvandi quosdam prae aliis, neque iustitiam suam laederet, si omnes congrue vocaret. Dices: quidam propter contumaciam & contemptum vocationis communioris commeriti sunt ut ipsis negaretur, ex iustitia, vocatio congrua, sed hoc est ludificare lectorem. Nam illa contumacia vel est ex vocatione congrua, vel non congrua: si ex vocatione congrua, tum non erant contumaces, sed Dei motioni obsequentes: si ex vocatione non-congrua, redibit rursus quaestio, cur Deus negarit primam motionem congruam, quam secuta est prima contumacia; an ex iustitia, an ex absoluta voluntate? Non ex iustitia: nulla enim est iustitia, homini nondum contumaci negare vocationem, qua posita, nulla foret in ipso contumacia: si ex absoluta voluntate, vicimus. Denique nec Arminiani cum suis Iesuitis admitterent repugnare Dei iustitiæ quod omnes liberi arbitrii genio & ingenio convenienter moveret & permoveret ad obedientiam finaliter. Hoc enim esse in promptuario sapientiæ divinæ (quæ nullo modo potest iustitiæ adversari) fatetur ipse Arminius, ut supra audivimus.
units.tr: 3. Nothing would be taken from God's blessedness if he did not know all the things that actually exist, namely what would have happened had he created nothing, since he could freely have refrained from creating. Yet God would not be absolutely perfect if he were ignorant of things already actually existing. To say that there are in God faculties and powers (so to speak) that are not indeclinably directed to their objects would argue an incomplete happiness. 4. That God does whatever he wills is a known truth, which distinguishes him from the non-gods, Psalm 115:4, 5. So God will not be God insofar as he wills what he cannot do. 5. The Jesuit plainly raves when he says that God cannot, on account of his justice, save all whom he wills. What? Does he grant effectual calling to some from justice, and deny it to others, or does he do so rather from absolute will? He will say it arises from justice, unless he has forgotten himself; but it arises from an absolute will to save some before others, and God would not violate his justice if he called all congruously. You will say that some, on account of obstinacy and contempt of the more common calling, deserved that congruous calling be denied them, justly. But this is to mock the reader. For that obstinacy either arises from a congruous calling or not. If from a congruous calling, then they were not obstinate but obedient to God's motion. If from a non-congruous calling, the question returns: why did God deny the first congruous motion, which the first obstinacy followed? Was it from justice or from absolute will? Not from justice, for there is no justice in denying a calling to a man who is not yet obstinate; given that calling, there would be no obstinacy in him. If from absolute will, we have won. Finally, the Arminians with their Jesuits would not admit that it is contrary to God's justice that he should move and persuade all, in a manner suited to the disposition and wit of free will, finally to obedience. For Arminius himself confesses that this lies in the storehouse of divine wisdom (which can in no way be opposed to justice), as we heard above.

units.la: II.[?] Argum. 6. Pugnat etiam cum infinita Dei sapientia, ut id intendat, quod se nunquam assecuturum præscit, & in homine talis intentio stulta est, & vana. Corvinus putat sufficere hic in Deo cognitionem, qua novit creaturam, cujus salutem & obedientiam desiderat, à se utriusque capacem esse conditam. Sed I. hinc infero Deum jam intendere salutem diabolorum & damnatorum jam infernis adjudicatorum, & pari ratione etiam exitium & inobedientiam electorum angelorum & hominum, qui jam corpore soluti æterno gaudio fruuntur. Novit enim & Diabolos & beatos obedientiæ & inobedientiæ, salutis & exitii capaces à se conditos esse. Si dixerint, Deum id non posse jam sapienter intendere, quoniam novit damnatos homines & Dæmones, & beatos angelos & homines non posse jam ullo modo esse objecta talium intentionum rationabilia, at quare non possunt? rogo, quia scit damnatos jam extra metas obedientiæ constitutos esse. At quid tum postea? Sunt tamen capaces obedientiæ, quandoquidem sunt creaturæ intelligentes. Deinde concedit itaque intentionem antecedentem Dei esse secundum scientiam perfectiorem, quam qua scitur, creaturam conditam esse capacem obedientiæ & salutis. Si vero per scientiam, qua scit creaturam capacem conditam esse obedientiæ & salutis, intelligit scientiam qua novit eos nondum ad metam pervenisse, sed pervenire posse, tum objectum amoris antecedentis non est creatura qua talis, uti illi docent, sed creatura talis, nempe quia ad metam nondum pervenerit obedientiæ aut inobedientiæ. 2. Deus pari jure intendit creationem plurium mundorum & angelorum & hominum, quippe novit se esse causam potentem & sufficientem ad producendum plures mundos: & tum quæritur quid impediret quo minus Deus satisfaceret tali intentioni, & plures mundos, angelos, & homines faceret? Non enim resistunt hic creaturæ Dei voluntati: at vero ipsum Deum resistere est longe absurdum: nunquid Deus Deo resisteret? 3. Ipse Arminius contendit Augustini doctrinam esse, addit, fors etiam scripturæ, Deum decreto providentiæ negare gratiam efficacem, adeoque vitam reprobis, & eorum obedientiam intendere tali scientia, qua novit ipsos nunquam persuadendos fore ut obediant, & electos vocare decreto prædestinationis, & scientiâ, quâ certò novit ipsos obtemperaturos, ac proinde fors etiam scripturæ conveniet, vel ipso Arminio judice, voluntatem hanc antecedentem, quam nulla præscientia niti volunt merum somnium Chymericum esse. 4. Neque rationabilis est Dei cognitio, qua scit creaturam posse obedire ad fundandam sapientem Dei intentionem, quando scit se eo modo moturum esse eorum voluntatem, quibus antecedenter vult & intendit salutem, quo nunquam actu obedituri sunt, quasi vero apud se Deus diceret: Ego naturaliter desidero seriò & ex animo obedientiam & salutem omnium: scio tamen me plerosque ita vocaturum, & eo modo moturum quo nunquam obedituri & salvadi sunt. Item qui potest Deus decernere justitiam vindicatricem quam patefacere nullo modo Deus potest, si impleretur voluntas antecedens?
units.tr: II.[?] Argum. 6. It is also contrary to the infinite wisdom of God to intend that which he foreknows he will never attain; and in a man such an intention is foolish and vain. Corvinus thinks it is enough here that God has the knowledge by which he knows the creature, whose salvation and obedience he desires, to have been made capable of both. But, first, I infer from this that God already intends the salvation of the devils and of the damned who are already adjudged to hell, and by the same reasoning also the ruin and disobedience of the elect angels and men, who, already loosed from the body, enjoy eternal joy. For he knows that both devils and the blessed have been made by him capable of obedience and disobedience, of salvation and ruin. If they say that God cannot now wisely intend this, since he knows that damned men and demons, and blessed angels and men, cannot now in any way be reasonable objects of such intentions, I ask: but why can they not? Because, he knows, the damned are already placed beyond the limits of obedience. But what follows from that? They are nonetheless capable of obedience, since they are intelligent creatures. Next, then, they concede that God's antecedent intention is according to a more perfect knowledge than that by which it is known that the creature has been made capable of obedience and salvation. But if by the knowledge by which he knows the creature to have been made capable of obedience and salvation they mean the knowledge by which he knows that they have not yet reached the goal but can reach it, then the object of antecedent love is not the creature as such, as they teach, but the creature as such, namely because it has not yet reached the goal of obedience or disobedience. 2. God with equal right intends the creation of many worlds, angels and men, since he knows that he is a powerful and sufficient cause for producing many worlds. Then the question arises: what would hinder God from satisfying such an intention and making more worlds, angels and men? For creatures do not here resist God's will; but to say that God himself resists himself is far absurd. Would God resist God? 3. Arminius himself contends that it is the doctrine of Augustine, and adds, perhaps also of Scripture, that by the decree of providence God denies efficacious grace, and so intends life to the reprobate and their obedience by such knowledge as knows that they will never be persuaded to obey; and that he calls the elect by the decree of predestination, and by knowledge by which he certainly knows that they will obey. Accordingly, perhaps even Scripture agrees, or, by Arminius's own judgment, this antecedent will, which they want to rest on no foreknowledge, is a mere chimerical dream. 4. Nor is the knowledge of God reasonable by which he knows that the creature can obey, in order to found a wise intention of God, when he knows that he will move the will of those whom he antecedently wills and intends to save in such a way that they will never actually obey and will never be saved. As if God were to say to himself: I naturally desire, seriously and from the heart, the obedience and salvation of all; yet I know that I will call most in such a way, and move them in such a way, that they will never obey and never be saved. Likewise, how can God decree vindictive justice, which God can in no way make manifest, if the antecedent will were fulfilled?

units.la: 12. Argum. 7. Alienum est etiam à justitia Dei; ut Deus velit omnes salvari, priusquam ipsos consideret obedientes. Talis enim amor antecedens, quo amplectitur nondum credentes, non fundatur in meritis Christi, neque amat ipsos in Christo. Ergo secundum dogmata Arminiana erit amor injustus. Hoc enim argumento conantur labefactare decretum nostrum electionis absolutum, quo Deus dicitur iis velle vitam æternam nondum partam Christi meritis, & priusquam ipsos consideret ut credentes. Scio hic ipsos negare non esse parem rationem affectus naturalis & decreti. Volunt enim voluntatem antecedentem antecedere Dei justitiam, & ex se formaliter non esse justam nec injustam, sed benevolam & naturalem. Sed Resp. 1. Ipsos sic statuere in Deo naturam omnis scientiæ, sapientiæ, & justitiæ expertem, eodem modo quo philosophi ponunt in homine naturam sensitivam rationali priorem, quo nihil est indignius Deo.
units.tr: 12. Argument 7. It is also foreign to the justice of God that he should will all to be saved before he considers them as obedient. For such antecedent love, by which he embraces those not yet believing, is not founded on the merits of Christ, nor does he love them in Christ. Therefore, according to the Arminian dogmas, it will be unjust love. For by this argument they try to overthrow our absolute decree of election, by which God is said to will eternal life for those to whom it is not yet obtained by the merits of Christ, and before he considers them as believers. I know that here they deny that natural affection and decree are of equal standing. For they want antecedent will to precede God's justice, and in itself to be formally neither just nor unjust, but benevolent and natural. But I reply: 1. They thus set up in God a nature devoid of all knowledge, wisdom and justice, in the same way as the philosophers place in man a sensitive nature prior to the rational; and nothing is more unworthy of God.

units.la: 2. Volunt ex pura Dei voluntate & natura ipsius promanare voluntatem antecedentem, sed accipimus non probata. Ex pura Dei bonitate Deus vult bonum creaturæ; quatenus Deus est bonus, ipsius affectus necessario fertur in bonum: hæc enim ipsorum mens est. Jam assumo ego: atqui creaturam peccatricem æternas pœnas luere, vel est malum: vel bonum. Si malum, justitia erit malum, opus divinæ justitiæ erit malum & injustum, Deus qua justus, injustus, malus & mali perpetrator, audite Arminiani, quo rapiat vos insania? Si bonum, tum antecedens Dei voluntas necessario in illud feratur oportet: atqui ita Deus naturali affectu vult omnes homines utpote peccatores in æternum perire, non minus quam salvari. Eant itaque Arminiani cum suis consequentiis, Deus vult omnes salvari: Ergo orandum pro omnibus: sic ego convenienter ipsorum placitis, textui apostolico contrarium urgeo, Deus antecedente voluntate vult omnes & singulos peccatores in æternum perdi: est enim hoc bonum justitiæ: ergo pro nemine orandum. Utinam hunc nodum mihi eximerent: si dixerint bonum tantum creaturæ esse voluntatis antecedentis objectum, bonum vero justitiae non est creaturae bonum, id quod mihi videtur affirmare Corvinus: Imo vero (inquit) quando posita conditione Deus aliquid vult absolute manet de opposito ejus, quod ita est volitum voluntate consequente (si objectum est bonum) in Deo velleitas, quae antecedens voluntas dicitur. Tum dico falsum esse, bonum justitiae non appeti naturaliter a Deo: Deus enim necessario suam justitiam amat, ideoque quando Deus vult & decernit, ut credentes salvantur, manet velleitas antecedens, qua Deus ipsos perdi velit: puta si inobedientes fuissent. Quid? an negabit Corvinus objectum hoc bonum esse & justum, ut inobedientes perdantur? theologi nomen vix meretur, qui talia neget. An nihil est bonum nisi quod creaturae est bonum? Cur dicat itaque (si objectum est bonum) non capio nisi velit Deum antecedenter velle aliquid mali, quod est dictu horrendum. 3. Ipse Grevinchov. ponit in Deo affectum naturalem perdendi idololatras, naturalem & decreto Dei libero priorem, quo necessario sequetur voluntatem antecedentem ferri naturaliter in bonam justitiae, adeoque in interitum creaturae peccatricis. Imo Corvinus contra Molinae vult sapientiam ita moderari Dei affectus, ut officium creaturae a Deo magis, quam ejus bonum ametur ac fortius desideretur. At vero quoniam officium creaturae est bonum naturale in se, non minus quam salus creaturae, Deus antecedente voluntate officium creaturae necessario velit, oportet & pari ratione poenam. creaturae inobedientis: est enim in se bonum naturale.
units.tr: 2. They want antecedent will to flow from the pure will and nature of God, but we accept this without proof. From the pure goodness of God, God wills the good of the creature; insofar as God is good, his affection is necessarily borne toward the good: for this is their own mind. Now I assume: but a sinful creature to suffer eternal punishments is either evil or good. If evil, then justice will be evil, the work of divine justice will be evil and unjust, and God, as just, will be unjust, evil and the perpetrator of evil. Hear, Arminians, to what madness is carrying you! If good, then the antecedent will of God must necessarily be borne toward it: but thus God, by natural affection, wills that all men, as sinners, perish forever, no less than that they be saved. Let the Arminians go on with their consequences: God wills all to be saved; therefore prayer must be made for all. So I, consistently with their own opinions, press against the apostolic text: God by antecedent will wills all and each sinner to be lost forever; for this is a good of justice; therefore prayer must be made for no one. Would that they would free me from this knot! If they say that only the good of the creature is the object of antecedent will, and the good of justice is not a good of the creature, which seems to me what Corvinus asserts: Indeed (he says) when, the condition being posited, God wills something absolutely, there remains the opposite of what is thus willed by consequent will (if the object is good), in God a velleity, which is called antecedent will. Then I say it is false that the good of justice is not naturally desired by God: for God necessarily loves his own justice, and therefore when God wills and decrees that believers be saved, there remains a velleity, antecedent, by which God would wish them to perish: suppose they had been disobedient. What? Will Corvinus deny that this object, that the disobedient should perish, is good and just? A theologian scarcely deserves the name who would deny such things. Is nothing good except what is good for the creature? Why then does he say (if the object is good)? I do not understand, unless he means that God antecedently wills something evil, which is horrible to say. 3. Grevinchovius himself posits in God a natural affection to destroy idolaters, natural and prior to the free decree of God, from which it necessarily follows that the antecedent will is naturally borne toward the good of justice, and so toward the destruction of the sinful creature. Indeed Corvinus, against Molina, wills that wisdom so moderate the affections of God that the duty of the creature is loved and more strongly desired by God than its good. But since the duty of the creature is a natural good in itself, no less than the salvation of the creature, God by antecedent will must necessarily will the duty of the creature, and by the same reasoning the punishment of the disobedient creature: for it is in itself a natural good.

units.la: 13. Notari tamen hic velim, Arminianos eo inclinare, ut doceant punire peccatorem esse à Dei natura alienum, & opus plane extraneum, quam blasphemiam manifesto astruit Thomas Jacksonus. Naturæ Dei (inquit) adversatur punire figmentum manus suæ. Ita Corvinus: à Deo invite aut cum ægritudine quæ passio fit, quicquam fieri non fingimus, tantum dicimus præter ejus inclinationem naturalem fieri, ut perdat eum quem ex desiderio suo naturali salvum vellet, & postea Deum ex intrinseca sua bonitate benefacere, quod autem puniat (hoc est justitiæ vindicatricis exercitium) ex nobis esse. Hoc est Deum pertinaci hominum malitia compulsum punire. Resp. 1. Si Deus operatur omnia secundum consilium voluntatis suæ, ut docet Paulus, Ephes. 1. 11. Nihil agit contra naturam suam, imo manifesta est contradictio, Deum non agere quicquam invite, & punire tamen compulsum pertinaci hominum malitia: sic enim invite, & non invite, naturaliter & violenter idem ageret. 2. Dicit Deum nihil agere cum ægritudine quæ passio fit, quo innuere videtur, Deum perdere peccatores cum tali ægritudine, quæ non fit passio, hoc est, ponere passiones non humanas, sed divinas in Deo: at quænam fit illa passio, scire percupio; nempe est Deum aliquid velle & facere consequenter, quæ impetu naturæ non vult, atqui hæc ipsissima passio est humana, sed determinata per rationem. 3. Ait Deum benefacere ex intrinseca sua bonitate: at assumo, punire peccatores est ab intrinseca Dei bonitate & naturali justitia, & punire est non tantum bene, sed & optime facere in se, licet non creaturae. Hoc si neget, necesse est dicat, opus justitiae vindicatricis esse malum, & Dei bonitati contrarium, adeoque iniquum.
units.tr: 13. Yet I would have it noted here that the Arminians incline to teach that punishing the sinner is alien to God's nature and a work altogether foreign to him. Thomas Jackson openly asserts this blasphemy: "It is contrary to the nature of God (he says) to punish the work of his own hands." So Corvinus: "We do not imagine that anything is done by God unwillingly or with grief, which is a passion; we only say that it is done beyond his natural inclination, so that he destroys the one whom he would wish saved out of his natural desire. And we say that God, from his intrinsic goodness, does good, but that he punishes (that is, the exercise of avenging justice) comes from us. That is, God is compelled to punish by the stubborn malice of men." Reply: (1) If God works all things according to the counsel of his will, as Paul teaches (Eph. 1.11), then he does nothing against his own nature. It is a plain contradiction to say that God does nothing unwillingly, and yet punishes when compelled by the stubborn malice of men; for in that case he would be acting both willingly and unwillingly, both naturally and by force. (2) He says God does nothing with grief, which is a passion. By this he seems to hint that God destroys sinners with a grief that is not a passion, that is, he posits in God passions that are not human but divine. But I long to know what that passion is. Surely it is for God to will and do something in a consequent way, which he does not will by the impulse of nature. Yet this very thing is a human passion, only determined by reason. (3) He says that God does good from his intrinsic goodness. But I assume that punishing sinners comes from God's intrinsic goodness and natural justice, and that to punish is not only to do good but to do what is best in itself, even if it is not good for the creature. If he denies this, he must say that the work of avenging justice is evil and contrary to the goodness of God, and therefore unjust.

units.la: 4. Quod vero ait esse ex nobis, quod Deus puniat, non ex intrinseca Dei bonitate, innuit justitiam Deo inesse accidentaliter, ideo Deus erit justus per accidens, ac proinde erit per se injustus. Nam si ita ex nobis sit, quod puniat, ut non sit actus justitiae & voluntatis Dei optimae, quod puniat contra voluntatem & invitus Deus puniat, necesse, dicet forte Deum punire contingenter, esse justum essentialiter, sed id ego non gravate concedo, at tum ex antithesi Corviniana, Deus benefacit creaturae contingenter, hoc est, erit creaturae bonus, & amans ipsius salutis contingenter, in se vero & essentialiter bonus, hoc vero non concedit Corvinus.
units.tr: 4. As for his saying that it is from us that God punishes, and not from God's intrinsic goodness, he implies that justice is in God accidentally. Then God would be just per accidens, and therefore would be unjust per se. For if it is from us that he punishes, in such a way that it is not an act of justice and of God's best will, and if God punishes against his will and unwillingly, then perhaps he will say that God punishes contingently but is essentially just. That I concede without difficulty. But then, by the Corvinian antithesis, God does good to the creature contingently: that is, he will be good to the creature and loving of its salvation only contingently, while in himself and essentially he is good. Corvinus does not concede this.

units.la: 4. Quaero rationem quare Deus ex intrinseca bonitate benefaciat creaturae. Respondent Arminiani & Jacksonus loco citato, quia Deus est naturaliter bonus, ideo non potest non bene-velle naturali voluntate creaturae suae. Tum ergo infero, ideo Deus punit creaturas peccatrices, quoniam est naturaliter & essentialiter justus, per parem omnino consequentiam. Ideoque non potest Deus naturali voluntate non velle malum creaturae peccatrici, ideoque tam Deus ab intrinseca bonitate punit, quam benefacit. Hoc non possunt negare Arminiani, nisi velint Deum non esse tam essentialiter iustum, quam bonum, quod est absurdum: nulla enim attributa essentialia insunt Deo per magis, aut minus, imo neque creaturæ. Homo enim tam essentialiter est animal, quam est rationalis, quamvis Deus non essentialiter benefaciat ulli creaturæ: sic enim necessitate naturæ, creaturam, *cui benefaceret, condidisse oportuit: quod dogma non est Christianum, sed potius Aristotelicum. Ideoque necesse est, Deus antecedente voluntate velit omnes homines peccatores perire, ideoque non potuit Christum redemptionem humani generis in mundum mittere. Arminiani enim docent omnes homines esse peccatores antecedenter ad missionem, imo ad decretum mittendi Christum. Rationem jam quæro ex Arminianis, cur Deus ex naturali voluntate salvandi homines, qua creaturas, mitteret salvatorem, euangelium indulgeret, vocaret omnes, promissis & poenis propositis &c. & non pari ratione ex naturali Dei voluntate perdendi omnes homines qua peccatores, negaret omnibus Christum redemptorem, euangelium, & vocationem, tum communem, tum specialem, & gratiam sufficientem, omniaque salutis media. Sed ego vereor ne negent voluntatem naturalem perdendi peccatores, quam Grevinchovius ipsorum doctrinæ convenienter admodum & occuoculate satis astruit. Imo id Corvinus astruat necesse est: Ita enim loquitur: Deus amat hominem, & ex illo amore propensus est ad ei benefaciendum; amat etiam justitiam, & magis quidem quam hominem, ideoque non vult ei benefacere, nisi justitiam operetur, si eam homo non operatur, statuit eum punire. Hæc verba obiter examinabo. Nisi Deus amat hominem naturaliter, & naturaliter propendet ad ei benefaciendum, tum an non naturaliter Deus odio habet, & naturaliter propendet ad perdendum hominem inobedientem: nam Deus magis amat justitiam, quam hominem: certe optima est consequentia. 2. Si Deus necessitate naturæ amat hominem, non magis amat justitiam quam hominem, sed æque, hoc est, naturaliter amat utrumque. Nam attributa in Deo necessaria & essentialia non admittunt gradus intentionis & remissionis. 3. Si Deus magis amat justitiam quam hominem, tum amat justitiam. Nam ex comparativo gradu satis norunt logici positivum sequi. Hinc arguo: Deus vel amat juftitiam vindicatricem ( de tali enim loquitur ) naturaliter, vel contingenter. Si naturaliter, odio habet, ideoque ad reprobandum omnes peccatores naturaliter propendet, quod est, institutum. Si contingenter amat justitiam, potest non amare, quod est absurdum. 4. Quod ait Deum non velle benefacere creaturæ, nisi operetur justitiam, est salsissimum. Nam Deus benefacit creaturæ antequam operetur justitiam, siquidem primam vocationem, & primam gratiam sufficientem indulgere creaturæ, quæ nihil adhuc operata est, nedum justitiam operata est, benefacere creaturæ est, & talem in Deo beneficientiam erga creaturam, quæ nondum operata fuerit justitiam, nec negare audent Arminiani.
units.tr: 4. I ask the reason why God does good to the creature from his intrinsic goodness. The Arminians and Jackson, in the place cited, answer that because God is naturally good, he cannot but will good to his creature by his natural will. Then I infer: therefore God punishes sinful creatures because he is naturally and essentially just, by a wholly parallel consequence. So God cannot by his natural will not will evil to a sinful creature, and therefore God punishes from his intrinsic goodness just as he does good. The Arminians cannot deny this, unless they want to say that God is not as essentially just as he is good. That is absurd, for no essential attributes belong to God by more or less, nor to a creature either. A man is as essentially an animal as he is rational. Yet God does not do good to any creature essentially. For by the necessity of nature he would have had to create the creature to which he did good. That dogma is not Christian but rather Aristotelian. Therefore it is necessary that, by his antecedent will, God wills all men who are sinners to perish, and therefore he could not send Christ into the world to redeem the human race. For the Arminians teach that all men are sinners antecedently to the sending of Christ, indeed antecedently to the decree to send Christ. Now I ask the Arminians for a reason why God, from his natural will to save men as creatures, would send a Saviour, grant the gospel, call all men, propose promises and penalties, and so on; and why, by a parallel reason of God's natural will to destroy all men as sinners, he would not deny to all men Christ the Redeemer, the gospel, and calling, both common and special, and sufficient grace, and all the means of salvation. But I fear they will deny a natural will to destroy sinners, which Grevinchovius, quite in agreement with their doctrine and rather clearly, asserts. Indeed Corvinus must assert it, for he speaks thus: "God loves man, and from that love he is inclined to do him good; he also loves justice, and indeed more than man; therefore he does not wish to do him good unless he works justice. If man does not work justice, he decrees to punish him." I will examine these words in passing. (1) If God naturally loves man and is naturally inclined to do him good, then does he not also naturally hate and naturally incline to destroy the disobedient man? For God loves justice more than man; the consequence is certainly sound. (2) If God loves man by the necessity of his nature, he does not love justice more than man, but equally: that is, he loves both naturally. For necessary and essential attributes in God do not admit degrees of intensity or remission. (3) If God loves justice more than man, then he loves justice. For logicians well know that the positive follows from the comparative degree. Hence I argue: God loves avenging justice (for of such justice he speaks) either naturally or contingently. If naturally, then he hates it, and therefore is naturally inclined to reprobate all sinners, which is what has been set up. If he loves justice contingently, he can not love it, which is absurd. (4) His saying that God does not wish to do good to the creature unless it works justice is most false. For God does good to the creature before it works justice, since he grants to the creature the first calling and the first sufficient grace, while it has not yet worked anything, much less justice. To do good to the creature is this, and the Arminians do not dare to deny such a beneficence in God toward the creature, which has not yet worked justice.

units.la: 14. Argum. 8. Multis etiam nominibus pugnat voluntas antecedens cum Dei perfectione. Nam 1. Sequitur affectus inordinatos & passiones Deo inesse. Nam voluntas antecedens est votum Dei naturale, omnino frustraneum, haud aliter quam æger febricitans contra medici sapientis præceptum expetit vinum, quod valetudinem offenderet, & medicus ei invito & sitienti & appetenti vinum negat, ita Deus naturaliter vult omnes Diabolos & Homines salvari, & scit sapienter decretum à se esse, ut patefieret gloria justitiæ vindicatricis in perditione angelorum reproborum & hominum. Hoc autem decretum necessario irritum erit, si Deus antecedenti voto naturali satisfaceret in actuali salvatione omnium, & si decretum hoc sit ratum & firmum, necesse est voluntati antecedenti in plerisque nunquam satis fit factum. Erunt itaque in Deo volitiones duæ, quæ, citra sapientiæ divinæ jacturam impleri non possunt. Voti frustrationem Deo tribui concedit Corvinus, sed quomodo? Audi dictatoris sententias. Θεοπνευστῶς[?] (inquit) hoc est ita ut nullam in Deo imperfectionem ac defectum arguant. Sed estne hoc, Domine Dictator, petere principium? Hoc ipso quod vota sint inefficacia ponetur maxime in Deo imperfectio. Neque (inquit Corvinus) est ex defectu potentiæ quod Deus desideriis suis frustretur, sed ex modo & termino quem istius potentiæ exercitio posuit sapientia. Sed 1. Hic Dei sapientiæ vitio dat, quod Deus votis frustretur: qualis hæc sapientia, quæ talem statuit potentiæ determinationem, ut Deus votis frustretur? sapientia itaque vota ista corrigat tanquam insulsa, & talia quibus sapienter non potest satisfieri, necesse est. Putabam Arminianis magis allubescere frustrationem votorum Dei ab hominis stultitia, quam à Dei sapientia fieri? sed jure merito, quæritur an ea sit sapientia, quæ ita res administret, ut Dei naturalia desideria sint frustranea, nisi eo rerum ventum sit, ut sapientia Dei aliter disponere non possit, quin Dei desideria inania fiant, ideoque sapientia Dei non poterat media ita disponere, quibus indeclinabiliter salvarentur omnes homines & angeli, quam prodigiosum dogma? Addit etiam, ideoque fit (quoniam Deus nihil desiderat ex indigentia) ut in ordinato desideriorum, secundum eandem mensuram exercitio, ipse Deus acquiescat. Sed quid hoc sit vix capi potest, mensuram desideriorum Dei ponit sapientia, ut non ulterius Deus desideret, quam patitur sapientia infinita, sed acquiescat: sed & hoc salsissimum est. Sapientia enim ita mensurat desideria, (ut illi dictitant) ut non velit Deus salutem creaturæ nisi quatenus crea-tura operatur justitiam, ut loquutum supra habuimus Corvinum: atqui non acquiescit Deus in tali mensuratione. Nam postquam Deus peremptorie decreverit damnare Iudam infidelem, non acquiescit Deus, sed adhuc etiam manet in Deo velleitas salvandi Iudam, puta si infidelis non esset. Itaque nullam hic video in Deo acquiescentiam, nullam velleitatis naturalis terminationem; sed in aeternum voluntatem Dei naturalem salvandi omnes & singulos mortales exuberantem, & extra terminos justitiae & sapientiae cancellos exspaciantem & errantem, nemo vel mediocriter nasutus non videt. 2. Sequitur Deum naturali amore velle multa posse ibilia, quae ut actu fierent, reclamat sapientia & libera Dei voluntas, hoc est velle multa contra rationis & sapientiae dictamen. Haec est passio vere humana & inordinata, & ut Deo tribuatur Θεωρητικῶς est ἀναγκαστ- ικόν[?]. 3. Impossibile est sine nota imperfectionis maxima, tribuere aliquem effectum voluntati antecedenti, donec conditio sub qua Deus aliquid vult antecedenter impleatur vel infringatur. Quid hic Corvinus? ait dari effectum voluntatis antecedentis etiam ante absolutum decretum; atcedo effectum; nempe. Quod Deus (inquit) sub conditione omnes homines voluerit servare. Itane? Deus itaque non sola inclinatione & actu primo, sed actu secundo vult omnes salvari: hic actus vel est determinatus a justitia & sapientia Dei: quo ad modum & objectum, uti clamant Arminiani, vel non. Si primum, justitia & sapientia non determinant sint[?], ut Deus vellet omnes sub conditione servari, sed tantum ut Deus vellet credentes servari, non credentes non servari: nam voluntas conditionata salvandi omnes non eget determinatione: quæro enim, ad quid determinatur & restringitur hæc voluntas, ad voluntatem absolutam? At tum non est volitio conditionata, ut ait Corvinus: si vero manet conditionata non restringitur: si vero non determinatur, falso dicunt sapientiam & justitiam & sapientiam voluntatem antecedentem determinare. Nam volitio actualis salvandi omnes, si crederent, est volitio Dei in latitudine maximâ, non vero restricta & determinata.
units.tr: 14. Argument 8. The antecedent will also clashes with God's perfection in many respects. For (1) it follows that inordinate affections and passions are in God. For the antecedent will is a natural wish of God, altogether vain, no differently from a feverish patient who against the command of a wise physician craves wine, which would harm his health. The physician, against his will, though he is thirsty and craving the wine, refuses it to him. So God naturally wills all devils and men to be saved, and yet knows wisely that his decree is that the glory of avenging justice should be made manifest in the perdition of the reprobate angels and men. But this decree will necessarily be void if God satisfied the natural antecedent wish by the actual salvation of all. And if this decree is firm and stable, then the antecedent will is in most cases never satisfied. There will therefore be two volitions in God which cannot be fulfilled without loss of divine wisdom. Corvinus concedes that the frustration of a wish is attributed to God, but how? Hear the Dictator's opinions: "Theopneustōs" [Θεοπνευστῶς] (he says), "that is, so that they indicate no imperfection or defect in God." But is this, Lord Dictator, not begging the question? By the very fact that the wishes are ineffective, the greatest imperfection will be posited in God. "Nor (says Corvinus) is it from a defect of power that God is frustrated in his desires, but from the mode and limit which wisdom has set for the exercise of that power." But (1) here he charges God's wisdom with the fault that God is frustrated in his wishes. What kind of wisdom is this, which has set such a determination of power that God is frustrated in his wishes? Wisdom therefore must correct those wishes as foolish, and such as cannot be satisfied wisely. I had thought the Arminians would rather like the frustration of God's wishes to come from man's folly than from God's wisdom. But it is rightly asked whether that is wisdom which so administers things that God's natural desires are vain, unless matters have come to the point where the wisdom of God cannot arrange otherwise, without God's desires becoming empty. And so God's wisdom could not arrange the means by which all men and angels would be saved without fail. What a monstrous dogma! He adds too: "And so it comes about (since God desires nothing from need) that in the ordered arrangement of his desires, according to the same measure of exercise, God himself acquiesces." But what this means can scarcely be grasped. Wisdom sets the measure of God's desires, so that God does not desire further than infinite wisdom allows, but acquiesces. This too is most false. For wisdom measures the desires (as they keep saying) so that God wills the creature's salvation only in so far as the creature works justice, as we have said Corvinus put it above. But God does not acquiesce in such a measure. For after God has peremptorily decreed to condemn the unbelieving Judas, God does not acquiesce; the velleity to save Judas still remains in God, as if he were not an unbeliever. So I see here no acquiescence in God, no termination of his natural velleity. Rather, the natural will of God to save all and each mortal overflows eternally, and wanders beyond the limits of justice and wisdom. No one with even moderate discernment fails to see this. (2) It follows that God by natural love wills many impossible things, which, if they were to be done in fact, are opposed by wisdom and the free will of God. That is, he wills many things against the dictate of reason and wisdom. This is a truly human and disordered passion, and if it is ascribed to God theōrētikōs [Θεωρητικῶς] it is anankastikon [ἀναγκαστικόν]. (3) It is impossible, without the greatest mark of imperfection, to attribute some effect to the antecedent will before the condition under which God antecedently wills something is either fulfilled or broken. What does Corvinus say here? He says there is an effect of the antecedent will even before the absolute decree. I grant the effect, namely: "That God, under the condition, has willed to save all men." Really? So God wills all to be saved not only by inclination and first act, but by a second act. This act is either determined by the justice and wisdom of God, as to manner and object, as the Arminians loudly maintain, or it is not. If the first, then justice and wisdom do not determine that God should will all to be saved under a condition, but only that God should will believers to be saved and unbelievers not to be saved. For a conditional will to save all does not need determination. For I ask, to what is this will determined and restricted: to an absolute will? But then it is not a conditional volition, as Corvinus says. If it remains conditional, it is not restricted. If it is not determined, then they falsely say that wisdom and justice determine the antecedent will. For the actual volition to save all, if they believed, is a volition of God in its widest latitude, not restricted or determined at all.

units.la: 15. Argum. 9, Si talis antecedens voluntas, qua bonum vult creaturæ naturaliter, Deo convenit, tum per eandem rationem Deus antecedente voluntate voluit esse creaturas, & ab æterno mundi creationem impetu naturæ voluit: at tum cur Deus infinita sæcula ante mundi creationem, naturali isti volitioni non satisfecit? Quid hic Deo restitit? non mundus, non homines, non materiæ defectus. Dicent Dei absoluta voluntas restitit voluntati naturali, at quam absurdum. Deus libere mundam creavit, ut contra Aristotelem, Proclum & alios disputant Christiani: ergo potuit in æternum non creasse, & talis voluntas in æternum irrita fuit, & pari ratione in æternum Deus vult m[?] esse infinitorum hominum & angelorum, & quid impedit quo minus potius satisfaceret voluntati naturali, qua vult fidem & salutem electorum, quam qua vult infinita alia? imo quia attributa in Deo necessaria & æterna nunquam incipiunt, nunquam desinunt, ab æterno Deus naturaliter voluit omnes homines salvari, & naturaliter quidem, ac proinde naturæ necessitate mundum creavit, & non potuit eum non creasse.
units.tr: 15. Argument 9. If such an antecedent will, by which God naturally wills good to a creature, belongs to God, then by the same reasoning God by antecedent will willed the existence of creatures, and from eternity willed the creation of the world by natural impulse. But then why did God, for infinite ages before the creation of the world, not satisfy that natural volition? What resisted God here? Not the world, not men, not any defect of matter. They will say that God's absolute will resisted the natural will, but how absurd that is. Christians argue, against Aristotle, Proclus and others, that God created the world freely. Therefore he could have refrained from creating it for eternity, and such a will would have been void for eternity. By the same reasoning, God would for eternity will that infinitely many men and angels not exist. And what prevents God from satisfying, rather than his natural will by which he wills the faith and salvation of the elect, his natural will by which he wills infinitely many other things? Indeed, because the necessary and eternal attributes in God never begin and never cease, God from eternity naturally willed all men to be saved, and naturally indeed, and therefore by natural necessity he created the world, and could not have failed to create it.

units.la: 16. Neque hili sunt Arminiana pro hac distinctione argumenta. Nam 1. sic arguunt: Deus est infinite bonus: ergo non potest non naturaliter creaturæ bonum velle. Resp. 1. Non sequitur. Nam ex bonitate mundum creavit, bonitate libere communicanda, non necessitate, alioqui sequitur Deum naturaliter mundum condidisse. 2. Deus est infinite justus: ergo etiam naturaliter vult perditionem omnium peccatorum, quod non admitterent. 3. Deus est infinite bonus in se, non sequitur: ergo est infinite bonus erga creaturas suas. Nam si omne bonum iis vellet, adeoque communicaret, & sic non posset non servare omnes & singulos mortales, quod experientiæ reclamamat. 4. Ex bonitate Dei, Deus omnia facit propter seipsum, non propter bonum creaturæ, ideoque tam primaria intentione ex bonitate, qua Deus omnia propter seipsum facit, Deus vult exitium creaturæ, quam salutem. Nam exitium æque medium est illustrandi gloriam justitiæ, quam salus est medium illustrandi gloriam misericordiæ, quia Deus est æq; infinite, & æq; primario justus & sapiens, atque bonus & misericors; Arminiani itaque gratis confingunt primariam & antecedentem voluntatem Dei, qua fertur in bonum & salutem creaturæ, & secundario & consequenter in exitium creaturæ, nisi probarent, misericordiam & bonitatem essentialius Deo competere, quam justitiam; quod excogitatu est impossibile.
units.tr: 16. Nor are the Arminian arguments for this distinction worthless. For first they argue thus: God is infinitely good, therefore he cannot but will good to the creature by nature. Answer 1: It does not follow. For he created the world out of goodness, a goodness that communicates itself freely, not by necessity; otherwise it would follow that God founded the world by nature. 2. God is infinitely just; therefore he also naturally wills the destruction of all sinners, which they would not admit. 3. God is infinitely good in himself; it does not follow that he is infinitely good towards his creatures. For if he willed all good to them, and so communicated it, he could not but save every single mortal, which experience contradicts. 4. From the goodness of God, God makes all things for his own sake, not for the good of the creature. Therefore, with the same primary intention arising from that goodness by which God makes all things for himself, God wills the destruction of the creature just as much as its salvation. For destruction is as much a means of displaying the glory of justice as salvation is a means of displaying the glory of mercy, since God is equally infinite, and equally primarily just and wise, as he is good and merciful. The Arminians therefore gratuitously invent a primary and antecedent will of God, by which he is borne toward the good and salvation of the creature, and a secondary and consequent will toward the creature's destruction. They would have to prove that mercy and goodness belong to God more essentially than justice, which is unthinkable.

units.la: Ob. 2. Deus non volenter punit. Thren. c. 3. Ergo voluntate antecedente vult hominis obedientiam. Resp. 1. Non libenter punire dicitur, quoniam causa punitionis & interitus tota quanta est, quæ nomine meritoriæ venit, ex nobis est, nempe peccatum, & non ex Deo: alioqui si rigidè illa verba urgaentur, num quæso Deus punit invitus, aut ex animi ægritudine? 2. Dicant illi nobis, an quoniam Deus ridet interitum reproborum & contumaciam Prov. 1. An non sequitur Deum antecedente voluntate velle peccatorum interitum? Scio Deum non ridere: istud Deo ἀνθρωποπαθῶς[?] tribuitur, non proprie; id quod ego lubens concedo, sed an non etiam φιλανθρωπῶς[?], & eodem sensu, quo dicitur optare nostram salutem, exspectare ut vinea fructus faceret, ideoque tam in proclivi mihi erit probare Deum primario & antecedenter velle interitum peccatorum, quam omnium salutem, si dixerint Deum velle consequenter interitum peccatorum, non antecedenter. Sed resp. si consideremus Deum, uti ex se & intrinsece justus & in justitiam propensus exitium peccatoris est æque primarium objectum divinæ volitioni natu-rali, qua suam justitiam naturaliter amat, quam salus creaturæ est objectum volitioni, ex naturali erga creaturas amore fluenti, objectum.
units.tr: Objection 2. God does not punish willingly. Lam. 3. Therefore by antecedent will he wills man's obedience. Answer 1: He is said not to punish willingly because the whole cause of punishment and ruin, which is called meritorious, lies in us, namely sin, and not in God. Otherwise, if those words are pressed strictly, does God punish unwillingly, I ask, or from grief of mind? 2. Let them tell us: because God laughs at the destruction of the reprobate and their obstinacy (Prov. 1), does it not follow that God by antecedent will wills the destruction of sinners? I know God does not laugh; that is attributed to God in human terms, not properly. I gladly concede this, but is it not also attributed philanthropically [φιλανθρωπῶς], and in the same sense in which he is said to desire our salvation, or to wait for the vineyard to bear fruit? Therefore it will be just as easy for me to prove that God primarily and antecedently wills the destruction of sinners as that he wills the salvation of all, if they say that God wills the destruction of sinners consequently and not antecedently. But I answer: if we consider God as just of himself and intrinsically, and inclined to justice, the destruction of the sinner is as primary an object of the divine natural volition, by which he naturally loves his own justice, as the salvation of the creature is an object of the volition that flows from natural love towards creatures.

units.la: Ob. 3. Deus antecedente voluntate voluitset stabilire regnum Sauli, siquidem obediisset. 1.Sam. 13. 13. At consequente voluntate, noluit stabilire, sed evertere. Resp. Deus igitur naturæ imperu Saulo obedienti voluit regnum; at cur non Samuelis etiam obedienti? Est hic idem formale objectum voluntatis antecedentis, at tum sequitur Deum velle omnes homines esse reges antecedente voluntate, & obedierint. Hoccine est gravem agere theologum? 2. Textus ne syllabam habet de Dei voluntate aut decreto, sed tantum de externo actu stabiliendi: qui est actus externus & temporarius: at Dei volitiones & decreta sunt actus immanentes & æterni: quia itaque Propheta illic non loquitur de Dei voluntate, qui hinc antecedentem voluntatem cuderent[?], mirum est. 3. Supra vero probavimus, non esse in Deo voluntatem conditionatam propriè dictam, licet proponantur præmia & pœnæ nobis conditionatè: ista enim toto cœlo differunt. Vita æterna est conditionata, sed voluntatem Dei dandi viram[?] æternam conditionata non norunt oracula sacra. Nam erat in Deo voluntas, qua hæc concatenarentur, stabilitio regni Sauli & obedientia Sauli, sicut miraculorum & conversio Tyriorum concatenantur, ut supra memini; obedientiam Sauli secuta fuisset regni stabilitio hoc sensu, at Deus & decrevisset & per Patriarch. Iacobum longe ante prædixerat Gen. 49. 10. regiâ potestatem penes tribum Iudæ fore, & ex eo Silob hoc est Christum, oriundum? Quid? An illa promissio falsa fuisset, si Saulus obediisset? Qualia somnia sunt hæc? Dicet Corvinus loc. cit. si stabilisset Deus regnum Sauli ex 'conditione quod obediisset, tum voluisset stabilire; Nam si (inquit) id fecisset Deus, conditione posita, voluit sane id facere ante conditionem præstitam, eâ lege si præstaretur. Duo enim includit conditionalis voluntas. 1. Formaliter & expresse affectum simplicis complacentiæ. 2. Eminenter & implicite, efficacem & absolutam voluntatem, quæ quidem actu non est, esset tamen, si conditio præstaretur, prout vero in absolutam vertitur, per præstationem conditionis, conditionata dicitur. Resp.
units.tr: Objection 3. God by antecedent will willed to establish the kingdom of Saul, provided he obeyed. 1 Sam. 13. 13. But by consequent will he did not will to establish it, but to overthrow it. Answer: Then God by the impulse of nature willed the kingdom for Saul, obeying; but why not also for Samuel, obeying? It is the same formal object of the antecedent will, and so it follows that God wills by antecedent will that all men be kings, if they obey. Is this how a serious theologian argues? 2. The text does not have a syllable about the will or decree of God, but only about the external act of establishing, which is an external and temporary act. But the volitions and decrees of God are immanent and eternal acts. Therefore, since the prophet is not speaking there of God's will, it is strange that they should forge an antecedent will from it. 3. But above we have proved that there is no conditional will in God properly so called, although rewards and punishments are set before us conditionally; for these differ entirely. Eternal life is conditional, but the sacred oracles do not know of a conditional will of God in giving eternal life. For there was in God a will by which these things were linked together: the establishing of Saul's kingdom and Saul's obedience, just as miracles and the conversion of the Tyrians are linked together, as I mentioned above. The establishing of the kingdom would have followed Saul's obedience in this sense. But God had both decreed, and long before had foretold through the patriarch Jacob (Gen. 49. 10) that royal power would rest with the tribe of Judah, and from it Shiloh, that is Christ, would come. What then? Would that promise have been false if Saul had obeyed? What dreams are these? Corvinus, in the passage cited, will say: if God had established Saul's kingdom on condition that he obeyed, then he would have willed to establish it. "For if (he says) God had done this, with the condition set, he certainly willed to do it before the condition was fulfilled, under the law that it would be fulfilled. For a conditional will includes two things. 1. Formally and expressly, an affection of simple complacency. 2. Eminently and implicitly, an efficacious and absolute will, which indeed is not actual, but would be if the condition were fulfilled; when it is turned into an absolute will through the fulfilment of the condition, it is called conditional." Answer:

units.la: 1. Nulla est consequentia. Si stabilisset Deus regnum Sauli ex hypothesi obedientiæ, hoc Corvinus pro suo more fraudulenter supponit, non probat, utinam attulisset argumentum. Hoc enim tantum sequitur, Ergo voluisset & decrevisset stabilire, si stabilisset, quod est verissimum & à nobis minime negatum; sed quia Deus mittit salvatorem, si homines sint peccatores, non sequitur ullo modo: ergo decrevit mittere salvatorem, ex hypothesi quod homines sunt peccatores. Nam æternum Dei decretum nullo modo pendet ex temporali conditione ab hominibus præstanda:
units.tr: 1. There is no consequence. If God had established Saul's kingdom on the supposition of obedience, Corvinus, after his usual fashion, supposes this fraudulently; he does not prove it. Would that he had brought an argument! For what follows is only this: therefore he would have willed and decreed to establish it, if he had established it. That is most true and by us not denied at all. But because God sends a Saviour if men are sinners, it does not follow in any way that he decreed to send a Saviour on the supposition that men are sinners. For the eternal decree of God does not in any way depend on a temporal condition to be fulfilled by men.

units.la: sic enim non esset æternum. 2. Si Deus stabilisset regnum Sauli, decrevisset stabilire, si decrevisset stabilire, decrevisset etiam in Saulo per gratiam efficacem obedientiam operari, prout in Davide id præstitit. Ex conditione itaque præstita secutus fuisset actus temporarius & externus Dei, nullo vero modo ex eadem secutus fuisset actus æternus & immanens.
units.tr: For then it would not be eternal. 2. If God had established Saul's kingdom, he would have decreed to establish it; and if he had decreed to establish it, he would also have decreed to work obedience in Saul through efficacious grace, as he did in David. So from the fulfilment of the condition there would have followed a temporary and external act of God, but in no way from the same condition would there have followed an eternal and immanent act.

units.la: Quid? An penes creaturam esset, quod sint in Deo actus æterni, & æternæ volitiones? tum penes creaturam esset, ut sit Dei voluntas, ac proinde ut sit ipse Deus: Dei enim volitiones idem sunt cum ipso Deo. 3. Ait voluntatem conditionatam complecti assectum simplicis complacentiæ, hoc est, volitionem absolutam. An ergo Deus absolute amat, & vult Iudæ vitam æternam, & etiam conditionate vult Iudæ vitam æternam? At hæc sunt contradicentia. Si enim Deus salutem Iudæ simpliciter affectaret, tum id etiam efficeret, ideoque adhuc petit principium. 4. Ait voluntatem conditionatam eminenter continere absolutam Dei voluntatem, quæ actu non esset tamen, si conditio præstaretur, atqui præscit ab æterno conditionem nunquam impletum iri. Quomodo igitur voluntas conditionata vel eminenter, vel formaliter continet talem voluntatem efficacem, quam Deus & præscit & decernit nunquam fore? Somnium hoc est. 5. An non conditio præstanda, id tale est, ex quo pendet absoluta voluntas Dei? Hoc negant Armimani : nolunt enim primam causam à secunda suspendi. 6. Prout in absolutam vertitur (inquit) conditionata dicitur. At vero verte vocem (vertitur) in vocem (mutatur) & tum æterna Dei voluntas conditionalis mutatur in absolutam. Itane mutabilis est Dei voluntas? At quomodo vertitur naturale Dei desiderium in absolutum decretum, tum eadè Dei voluntas erit & naturalis & libera, hoc est, libera & non libera. Si jam Deus desiit velle salutem electorum credentium voluntate antecedente, & absolutè jam vult ipsos salvari, quia credunt, tum datur finis æterni Dei desiderii. At vero quoniam desiderat electorum salutem, quia bonus est erga creaturas, ' si jam evanuit illud desiderium, utpote mutatum in absolutam voluntatem, definit esse bonus erga credentes. 7. Hæc absoluta voluntas præstitâ conditione, vel sequitur necessario, vel contingenter. Si necessario, non tum decretum Dei efficax de salvandis credentibus est liberum, sed necessario, & naturæ necessitate sequitur tum ex hominis actu electio. At Arminius ipse concedit electionem esse decretum liberum. Si vero contingenter seu libere sequitur decretum, tum Deus decrevit decernere, voluit velle absolutè salutem credentium: quam absurdum est, quod decernat prius decernere, quam decernat? at hoc est ponere progressum in infinitum.
units.tr: What then? Would it lie with the creature whether there are eternal acts and eternal volitions in God? Then it would lie with the creature whether there is a will of God, and consequently whether there is God himself, for the volitions of God are the same as God himself. 3. He says that the conditional will embraces an affection of simple complacency, that is, an absolute volition. Does God then absolutely love and will eternal life for Judas, and also conditionally will eternal life for Judas? But these are contradictories. For if God simply desired Judas's salvation, he would also bring it about, and so they are still begging the question. 4. He says that the conditional will eminently contains the absolute will of God, which would not be actual if the condition were fulfilled. But God foreknew from eternity that the condition would never be fulfilled. How then does a conditional will, either eminently or formally, contain such an efficacious will, which God both foreknows and decrees will never be? This is a dream. 5. Is the condition to be fulfilled not such that the absolute will of God depends on it? The Arminians deny this, for they will not have the first cause suspended from a secondary one. 6. "When it is turned into an absolute will (he says), it is called conditional." But change the word "turned" into the word "changed," and then the eternal conditional will of God is changed into an absolute one. Is the will of God then changeable? But how does the natural desire of God turn into an absolute decree? Then the same will of God will be both natural and free, that is, both free and not free. If God has now ceased to will the salvation of believing elect by antecedent will, and now absolutely wills them to be saved because they believe, then the eternal desire of God has an end. But since he desires the salvation of the elect because he is good towards creatures, if that desire has now vanished, as changed into an absolute will, he ceases to be good towards believers. 7. This absolute will, once the condition is fulfilled, either follows necessarily or contingently. If necessarily, then God's efficacious decree concerning the saving of believers is not free but necessary, and by natural necessity the election then follows from the human act. But Arminius himself concedes that election is a free decree. If, however, the decree follows contingently or freely, then God decreed to decree, and willed absolutely to will the salvation of believers. How absurd it is that he should decree first to decree before he decrees! But this is to posit an infinite progression.

units.la: Ob. 4. Deus voluit antecedente voluntate Hierosolymitanos congregari, ac ipsorum domum everti voluntate consequente, postquam prophetas lapidassent & occidissent. Resp. 1. (Quoties volui ?) non notat actum volendi in Deo, qui immanens & aeternus est, continuari aut per temporum intervalla interrumpi, ut notat adverbium, quoties. Quod enim Deus vult ab aeterno, in aeternum vult. Significatur itaque illic mera invitatio ministerialis, qua Deus ipsorum ad se congregationem approbavit, ut officium debiti. 2. Si voluntate naturali Deus voluit Hierosolymitanos per assiduum prophetarum ministerium congregari, quatenus sunt creaturae Dei ad ipsius imaginem conditae, pari ratione debuit Deus omnes mortales etiam gentes alienas a foedere congregare. Sunt enim Dei creaturae ad ipsius imaginem conditae: at non fecit sic omni nationi Psal. 147. At dicit Corvinus Deum adhibita libertate, & advocata sapientia etiam antecedenter his subministrare media salutis copiosiora, illis minus copiosa, sed sufficientia. Sed tum respondeo non voluntati naturali tum Hierosolymitanos restitisse, sed libertati & sapientiae divinae; at Dei sapientia & libertas non postulant, ut Deus bene velit creaturae, nisi quatenus justitiam operetur, ut supra dixit Corvinus. 3. Voluntas, qua voluit Christus ipsos congregari, erat libera: poterat enim non congregari ipsos voluisse: at voluntas antecedens est naturalis, non libera. 4. Si ex mero naturali affectu & desiderio voluit ipsos congregari, tum antecedenter ad justitiam, sapientiam, praescientiam & liberum decretum id vult. Haec enim ipsis est voluntas antecedens: at vero sic voluntas antecedens prophetis revelata non revelasset Iudaeis Dei sapientiam, iustitiam, praescientiam, sed tantum meram naturalem Dei propensionem, quae haec omnia antecedat, quo quid absurdius? Caetera fumo leviora facile dilui possunt.
units.tr: Ob. 4. God willed by his antecedent will that the Jerusalemites be gathered together, and by his consequent will that their house be overthrown, after they had stoned and killed the prophets. Reply 1. The phrase "how often would I have" (quoties) does not indicate an act of willing in God, which is immanent and eternal, and which is not continued or interrupted through intervals of time, as the adverb quoties implies. For what God wills from eternity, he wills for eternity. What is signified there is therefore only a ministerial invitation, by which God approved their gathering to himself as a matter of duty. 2. If God by his natural will willed the Jerusalemites to be gathered through the constant ministry of the prophets, insofar as they are creatures made in his image, then by the same reasoning God ought to have gathered all mortals, even the foreign nations, into the covenant. For they too are God's creatures made in his image; yet he has not dealt thus with every nation (Psal. 147). But Corvinus says that God, by his freedom and by calling in his wisdom, even antecedently supplies to these people more abundant means of salvation, and to those less abundant, but sufficient. My reply is that the Jerusalemites resisted not the natural will but the freedom and wisdom of God; yet the wisdom and freedom of God do not require that God wish well to his creatures except insofar as he works righteousness, as Corvinus himself said above. 3. The will by which Christ willed them to be gathered was free, for he could have not willed them to be gathered; but the antecedent will is natural, not free. 4. If he willed them to be gathered from mere natural affection and desire, then he wills this antecedently to his righteousness, wisdom, foreknowledge and free decree. For this is the antecedent will as far as they are concerned. But if the antecedent will was thus revealed through the prophets, it would not have revealed to the Jews the wisdom, righteousness and foreknowledge of God, but only a bare natural inclination of God that comes before all these things. What could be more absurd? The rest, which are lighter than smoke, can easily be dissolved.

units.la: EXERCITATIO III. De actibus Dei temporariis in li- bertatem humanam.
units.tr: EXERCITATIO III. Of God's temporal acts upon human liberty.

units.la: QVÆST. I. An liberum arbitrium determinetur à Deo tum in actibus naturæ, tum gratiæ.
units.tr: QUAEST. I. Whether the free will is determined by God both in the acts of nature and in the acts of grace.

units.la: I. QVæstioni grauissimæ de efficacia gratiæ lucem non mediocrem fœneratur quæstio de voluntatis determinatione. Vt à voce exordiar, determinare est terminos ponere, quo indeterminatio & indifferentia removeatur. [ὁρίζειν?] graece id notat: [סמ?], vt & [גְּבוּל?] est agrorum limites statuere, & delineare Iof. 15. 9. 21. Deut. 19. 14.
units.tr: I. The question of the determination of the will sheds no small light on the most weighty question concerning the efficacy of grace. To begin with the word: to determine is to set limits, so that indeterminacy and indifference are removed. The Greek [ὁρίζειν?] expresses this, and so does the Hebrew [סמ?], as also [גְּבוּל] means to fix the boundaries of fields and mark them out (Josh. 15. 9, 21; Deut. 19. 14).

units.la: 2. Quoniam tres præcipuæ causæ in actibus liberis concurrunt, nempe voluntas, ratio naturalis, in sacris actibus, Dei verbum. &
units.tr: 2. Since three principal causes concur in free acts: the will, natural reason, and, in sacred acts, the Word of God; and

units.la: 3. Deus primum movens; in spiritualibus vero gratia Spiritus Sancti, ideo statuo tres determinationes. Prima est obiectiva materialis sive moralis, quando ratio vel à natura, vel à sacrorum oraculorum luce deprompta intellectus mediatione voluntati propolita ipsam moveat. Hic ratio sive verbum Dei est voluntatis obiectum non materiale, sed formale, qua movens & afficiens ipsam: ideo determinatio moralis ethica vel obiectiva dicitur.
units.tr: 3. God as the first mover, and, in spiritual matters, the grace of the Holy Spirit. Therefore I lay down three determinations. The first is objective, material or moral: when reason, drawn either from nature or from the light of the sacred oracles, is proposed to the will through the mediation of the intellect and moves it. Here reason or the Word of God is the object of the will, not a material but a formal object, by which it moves and affects the will. Therefore this determination is called moral, ethical or objective.

units.la: 2.
