Quia Deus est motor omnis causae secundae, idque vel physico impulsu ad volendum, eligendum, repudiandum, prout fit in actibus naturae, vel hyperphysico impulsu, ut est in actibus gratiae, haec determinatio est realis (non quia obiectiva est mera imaginaria: est enim in suo genere realis, minimeque conficta) effectiva (sive etiam aequivoca. 3. Ipsa voluntas mota & praedeterminata à Deo, à ratione à Dei verbo & gratia Spiritus Sancti se formaliter & vitaliter determinat, & haec est formalis & univoca determinatio, & nihil aliud est, quam ipsa volitio. De hac postrema determinatione non est praesens inter nos & Iesuitas & Arminianos controversia, nec à Deo, nec à ratione formaliter, sed ab ipsa voluntate est volitio & nolitio.
units.tr: 2. Since God is the mover of every secondary cause, and this either by a physical impulse to will, choose or reject, as happens in the acts of nature, or by a hyperphysical impulse, as is the case in the acts of grace, this determination is real (not because it is objective, a mere imagining, for it is real in its own kind and by no means fictitious), effective (or also equivocal). 3. The will itself, moved and predetermined by God, by reason, by the Word of God and by the grace of the Holy Spirit, determines itself formally and vitally. This is the formal and univocal determination, and it is nothing other than the volition itself. Concerning this last determination there is no controversy between us and the Jesuits and Arminians: volition and nolition come not from God, nor from reason formally, but from the will itself.

units.la: 3. De prima determinatione intellectus nimirum, qui voluntatem determinat, nolo litem anxie movere cuiquam, quoniam exploratum satis habeo nostram sententiam orthodoxam sartam tectam fore, si sic vel secus sententiamus. Dicam tamen quid potissimum hic quaequæratur, & quid mihi potius arrideat. ra[?] Non quæritur, an judicium intellectus specificet actus libertatis: a voluntate est, non ab intellectus judicio, quod actus voluntatis talis fit in specie, puta volitio non volitio, electio non repudiatio. 2. Nec an mens moveat aut luminis pondere inclinet voluntatem: hoc utrinque conceditur. 3. Judicium aliud est ultimum secundum quid, aliud simpliciter: prius est ultimum conditionaliter, ut conscientia dictitat fugiendum esse adulterium, conditionaliter, si velimus Deo placere, non absolute, quoniam fieri potest, ut carni indulgere magis arrideat, ideoque voluntas hic resistere potest. Aliud est simpliciter ultimum & absolute, quod mens absolute hic & nunc faciendum judicat simpliciter: hoc ultimo formaliter stante sub motione Dei videtur, quod necessario determinet voluntatem: dico stante ultimo sub motione Dei, qui per lumen infallibile, amotis omnibus tenebris suadeat & persuadeat. At vero stante ultimo in se & formaliter, videtur quod possit voluntas intellectui avocare a cogitando de illo objecto ita ultimate proposito, ad alia quæ quamvis minus efficaciter movent & suadeant voluntatem, quam illud ultimum: attamen quia voluntas potest duo hic præstare. 1. avocare mentem a consideratione illius ultimi objecti ad aliud contemplandum, & 2. avocare mentem ab actuali collatione hujus posterioris boni terreni, cum illo cœlesti, quod in se efficacius movebat voluntatem, ideo non necessario determinat libertatem. 2. Si necefsario & in se ultimum judicium determinet voluntatem, gratia esset mera suasio, nec necessaria foret interna gratia ad sanandam voluntatem, sufficeret amotio tenebrarum, & ut edoceretur mens, quod latebat, quæ gratia est Pelagiana. Et sic reprobi mens per habitum fidei acquisitum & evidentiam clarissimam objecti edoceretur, quod mihi videtur possibile, in hoc casu, quod nempe mens cerneret in actu obedientiæ, i. facilitatem. 2. suavitatem, 3. utilitatem, & voluntas uti posset, non avocaret mentem ad indagandum in illo actu, vel rationem difficultatis, vel alterius rei, sub qua malum appareret, & non avocaret ad terrena cogitanda, ab illa actuali contemplatione, in hoc casu fine ulla voluntatis sanatione posset credere, & actum supernaturalem præstare, nec opus esset ablatione cordis saxei & infusione cordis carnei.
units.tr: 3. Concerning the first determination, namely that of the intellect which determines the will, I am unwilling to stir up anxious strife with anyone, since I hold it sufficiently well established that our orthodox doctrine will remain intact whether we judge one way or the other. Yet I will say what is chiefly sought here, and what pleases me more. The question is not whether the judgement of the intellect specifies the acts of liberty: they are specified by the will, not by the judgement of the intellect, so that an act of the will is of a certain kind, for instance volition or non-volition, choice or rejection. 2. Nor is the question whether the mind moves the will or inclines it by the weight of its light: this is conceded on both sides. 3. One judgement is ultimate in a certain respect, another simply. The former is ultimate conditionally, as conscience declares that adultery must be avoided, conditionally, if we wish to please God, not absolutely, since it may happen that indulging the flesh appeals more, and so the will can resist here. The other is simply and absolutely ultimate, which the mind judges absolutely to be done here and now. While this ultimate judgement stands formally under the motion of God, who by an infallible light, with all darkness removed, persuades and convinces, it seems that it must necessarily determine the will. I say, while the ultimate judgement stands under the motion of God, who persuades and convinces through an infallible light, with all darkness removed. But when the ultimate judgement stands in itself and formally, it seems that the will can call the intellect away from thinking about that object so proposed as ultimate, to other things which, though they move and persuade the will less effectively than that ultimate object, nevertheless, because the will can do two things here: 1. call the mind away from considering that ultimate object to contemplate something else, and 2. call the mind away from the actual comparison of this later earthly good with that heavenly one, which in itself moved the will more effectively, therefore it does not necessarily determine liberty. 2. If the ultimate judgement, necessarily and in itself, determined the will, grace would be mere persuasion, and internal grace would not be needed to heal the will; it would suffice to remove the darkness, and for the mind to be taught what lay hidden. Such grace is Pelagian. And so the mind of the reprobate, through the acquired habit of faith and the clearest evidence of the object, would be taught, which seems possible in this case: namely that the mind would perceive in the act of obedience 1. its ease, 2. its sweetness, 3. its usefulness, and the will could use this, and it would not call the mind away to inquire in that act either into the reason for its difficulty or into anything else under which the evil would appear, nor call it away to think of earthly things from that actual contemplation. In this case, without any healing of the will, it could believe and perform a supernatural act, and there would be no need for the taking away of the heart of stone and the infusion of a heart of flesh.

units.la: 4. Loca scripturæ contrarium non probant: at dici poterit. Psal. 9. 10. Qui nomen tuum cognoscunt, fidunt in te. Si cognitio illa non determinaret voluntatem, fieri posset ut cognoscentes nomen Dei non siderent in Iehova. Item Iohan. 4. verf. 1. Si scires donum illud Dei, & quis sit is, qui dicit tibi, da mihi bibere, tu ab illo aquam vivam peteres. Si illa cognitio nondeterminaret voluntatem ad petendum aquam vivam a Christo, tum poterat mulier scire donum illud Dei, & non petiisse ab eo aquam vivam, & falsum dixisset Christus. Resp. In ejusmodi propositionibus semper subintelligitur physica Dei motio: alioqui si ad literam praemerentur, sequeretur nudam cognitionem objecti sufficere ad actum credendi absque infusione novae potentiae, quod nemo diceret. Similiter illud, si Tyrij vidissent signa, resipuissent: non sequitur visionem miraculorum indeclinabiliter determinare voluntatem ad resipiscentiam. Consequens enim est aperte falsum, ideoque semper ad resipiscentiam requiritur tacita conditio,non expressa, sed subintellecta, ex praevia motione efficacis gratiae: alioqui poterant Tyrij vidisse signa & quidem plura quam viderunt Capernaum & Bethsaida, nunquam tamen resipuisse. Sed non statui hic funem contentionis trahere, utraque opinio sua probabilitate non caret.
units.tr: 4. The passages of Scripture do not prove the contrary, but it may be said: Psal. 9. 10. They that know thy name trust in thee. If that knowledge did not determine the will, it could happen that those who know the name of God would not trust in Jehovah. Likewise John 4. 10. If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink, thou wouldest have asked of him living water. If that knowledge did not determine the will to ask Christ for living water, then the woman could have known the gift of God and not have asked him for living water, and Christ would have spoken falsely. Reply: in propositions of this kind a physical motion of God is always understood. Otherwise, if they were taken strictly to the letter, it would follow that bare knowledge of the object suffices for the act of believing, without the infusion of a new power, which no one would say. Similarly, if the Tyrians had seen the signs, they would have repented: it does not follow that the sight of miracles determines the will to repentance inescapably. The consequence is plainly false, and therefore a tacit condition is always required for repentance, not expressed but understood, arising from a prior motion of efficacious grace. Otherwise the Tyrians could have seen signs, and indeed more than Capernaum and Bethsaida saw, and yet never have repented. But I do not intend here to drag the rope of contention further; each opinion has its own probability.

units.la: 5. De determinatione itaque secundae classis, nempe aequivoca, tota instituitur disputatio tum in actibus naturae, tum gratiae, & de utrisque brevitatis studio simul disceptabo.
units.tr: 5. Therefore the whole dispute concerns the determination of the second class, namely the equivocal, both in the acts of nature and in the acts of grace. I shall discuss both together, with a view to brevity.

units.la: Adversarii varias hic determinationes nobis dant, illiberali tamen munificentia. 1. Fonseca ait Deum movere voluntatem efficientia motiva per modum affectus, suadendo (quod nec negavit Pelagius) non efficientia Physica, quae sit determinativa absoluti consensus. 2. Distinct. ib. vult actionem Dei in voluntatem esse motivam, per modum naturae, quatenus author naturae tribuit ei vim sele determinandi, non vero indeclinabiliter determinativam. Ita etiam Molina. 3. dist. Sola (inquit ibid. Fonseca) voluntas sese determinat non solitudine (ut ita dicam) concurrentis, sed folitudine determinantis. Ita Arminius, ita Grevinchovius. Deus movet (inquiunt) arbitrium ut se determinet, & officit cum arbitrio determinationem. §. Distinct. est Suarezij, Vasquezij, Lessij, & aliorum Iesuitarum, nempe Deum movere voluntatem actu approbativo in bonis, permissivo in malis, & repudiativo in actibus qui nunquam fiunt. Sed quid hoc est aliud quam Deum non omnino movere voluntatem? actus enim permissivus Iesuitis est actus negatio, quo voluntas a Deo omnino suae indifferentiae relinquitur. Ideoque nihil agit Deus in voluntatem: actus approbativus praesupponit voluntatis actum jam factum. Iraque ne quidem sit actus liber per Dei approbationem, nedum determinatur, sed jam factus approbatur: nullus hic est actus praefinitivus. 6. Distinct. Bellarminus, Fonseca, Suarez, & Vasquez determinationem congruam & incongruam cudunt, quae distinctio quanti sit, postea declarabitur. 7. Distinct. Arminiani dicunt Deum movere voluntatem secundum modum naturae, vel ut est affectus naturalis, quia Deus in affectus desiderium boni inspirat, non vero secundum modum libertatis: sed hic Dei actio nullo modo terminatur in liberam voluntatem, sed in affectus intellectuales: affectus etiam intensissime propendentes in amorem Dei negant Arminiani voluntatem ad amorem Dei determinare. Sed an satis sani sunt hi viri? qui docent fieri posse ut affectibus ex toto corde, & omnibus viribus impensè diligamus Deum, & tamen libera voluntas non tantum aversa ab amore Dei, sed & odio flagrare posset, tum Dei, tum proximi, quod est homines odio habere Deum, & non odio habere Deum.
units.tr: Our opponents offer us various determinations here, but with a niggardly generosity. 1. Fonseca says that God moves the will by efficient motive causality, by way of affection and persuasion (which even Pelagius did not deny), not by efficient physical causality, which would determine absolute consent. 2. In the same distinction he holds that God's action upon the will is motive, after the manner of nature, insofar as the author of nature gives it the power to determine itself, but not determinative in an unavoidable way. So also Molina. 3. In the same distinction Fonseca says: the will determines itself, not by the solitude (as I may say) of a concurring cause, but by the solitude of a determining one. So Arminius, so Grevinchovius. They say that God moves the will so that it may determine itself, and he works together with the will in the determination. §. The distinction belongs to Suarez, Vasquez, Lessius and other Jesuits, namely that God moves the will with an approving act in good things, a permissive act in evil things, and a repudiating act in acts that never occur. But what is this other than to say that God does not move the will at all? For a permissive act, to the Jesuits, is a negative act, by which the will is wholly left to its own indifference by God. Therefore God does nothing upon the will; an approving act presupposes an act of the will already performed. Thus the act is not even free through God's approval, much less determined; it is already done and then approved. There is no predetermining act here at all. 6. Bellarmine, Fonseca, Suarez and Vasquez coin the distinction between congruous and incongruous determination, and how important this distinction is will be shown later. 7. The Arminians say that God moves the will according to the manner of nature, or as it is a natural affection, because God inspires in the affections a desire for the good, but not according to the manner of liberty. But this action of God does not terminate in the free will in any way; it terminates in intellectual affections. The Arminians also deny that affections which lean most intensely toward the love of God determine the will to the love of God. But are these men sane enough? They teach that it is possible to love God with the whole heart, and with all our powers, zealously, in our affections, and yet that the free will could blaze not only with aversion from the love of God, but with hatred both of God and of neighbour: that is, to hate men and not to hate God.

units.la: Nam quid sunt quæso affectus intellectuales, gaudium, amor, spes, &c: forte dicerent esse propensiones intellectuales, in voluntate.
units.tr: For what, I ask, are intellectual affections such as joy, love, hope, and so on? Perhaps they would say they are intellectual propensions in the will.

units.la: Esto, neque hoc differeor, sed an non tum actus gaudii & amoris intellectualis, sint actus voluntatis, negari non potest: tum voluntas, actum gaudii, & amoris in Deum elicere potest, & simul Deum nec velle, nec eligere, sed omnino repudiare potest, hoc est, voluntatem Deum velle, & non velle.
units.tr: Granted, nor do I differ from them on this point. But it cannot be denied that acts of joy and intellectual love are acts of the will. Then the will can elicit an act of joy and love toward God, and at the same time not will God, not choose him, but utterly reject him. That is, the will can both will God and not will him.

units.la: 6. Ad enodationem quæstionis, notandum gratiam posse determinare voluntatem dupliciter: 1. secundum specificationem, ita ut si voluntas agat secundum inhærens gratiæ principium, necessario, actio erit gratiosa. De hac determinatione non quæritur: respectu enim exercitii necessitas hæc est conditionalis, quia fieri potest, ut voluntas non agat secundum inhærens gratiæ principium, ut patet in lapsibus sanctorum. 2. Quæstio est de actuali determinatione voluntatis quoad exercitium, & dicimus habitualem gratiam non determinare voluntatem in exercitio, quoniam ipsa est potentia, quæ actuatione indiget.
units.tr: 6. To clear up the question, we must note that grace can determine the will in two ways. (1) According to its specification, so that if the will acts according to the indwelling principle of grace, the action will necessarily be gracious. This determination is not what is in question. With respect to the exercise, this necessity is only conditional, since the will may fail to act according to the indwelling principle of grace, as appears in the falls of the saints. (2) The question concerns the actual determination of the will as to its exercise. We say that habitual grace does not determine the will in its exercise, since it is a power which needs to be actuated.

units.la: 7. At vero nos asserimus, Deum in omnibus actibus tum naturæ tum gratiæ voluntatem determinare per impulsum vere realem ad modum causæ physicæ. Quoniam vero communis est cantilena Arminianorum scripturis à nobis allegatis respondentium, non exprimi modum, quo Deus moveat voluntatem, quando præcipua quæstio est (inquiunt) non an Deus moveat voluntatem, sed an moveat & determinet voluntatem per impulsum physicum, id quod illi nusquam scripturarum probari posse contendunt. Sed ausim dicere ipsos pondere argumentorum victos pervertere statum quæstionis: nam non est ille quæstionis casus, sed nos de voce physicæ prædeterminationis non movemus litem. Quæstio enim est, an non ita moveat voluntatem Deus, ut sub illa motione non possit mota non permoveri? vel an non actio Dei in voluntatem ita ipsam flectat, ut non possit non libere se flectere illuc quo Deus ipsam inclinat? nos vero e scripturis probamus necessitationem voluntatis à Dei motione quo indeclinabiliter permoveatur. Quæstio itaque præcipue est de indeclinabilitate actus liberi, quam, si quidem illi nobis tribuerent, physicæ prædeterminationi valedicere parati sumus: quamvis revera Deus ad modum causæ physicæ voluntatem determinet.
units.tr: 7. We assert that God, in all acts both of nature and of grace, determines the will by a truly real impulse, in the manner of a physical cause. The Arminians have a common refrain in answer to the Scriptures we have cited: the mode by which God moves the will is not expressed. The chief question, they say, is not whether God moves the will, but whether he moves and determines the will by physical impulse, which they contend can nowhere be proved from Scripture. But I would dare to say that, being defeated by the weight of the arguments, they pervert the state of the question. This is not the case of the question, and we are not contending over the term "physical predetermination." The question is whether God does not so move the will that, under that motion, the moved cannot but be moved; or whether God's action does not so bend the will that it cannot but freely turn toward where God inclines it. We prove from Scripture that the will is necessitated by God's motion, so that it is moved indeclinably. The question, then, is chiefly about the indeclinability of the free act. If they would grant us this, we are ready to bid farewell to physical predetermination, although in reality God determines the will in the manner of a physical cause.

units.la: 8. Ago itaque. 1. Scripturis. 2. Rationibus. 3. Testimoniis.
units.tr: 8. I proceed therefore: (1) from Scripture; (2) from reasons; (3) from testimonies.

units.la: 1. Gen.33[?]. Deus cor & voluntatem Esavi ab odio in gratiam,idque Iacobi precibus commutat. Quid si (inquit Corvinus) mutatum est cor Esavi per aspectum fratris & fraterna soboles & mite alloquium?
units.tr: 1. Gen. 33 [?]. God changes the heart and will of Esau from hatred to favour, and this at the prayers of Jacob. "What if," says Corvinus, "the heart of Esau was changed by the sight of his brother, by fraternal affection and a gentle address?"

units.la: R. At non disputabimus de modo: textus probat ita mutatum fuisse cor Esavi, ut non potuerit non fratrem Iacobum sereno & gratioso vultu, & miti & leni alloquio dignari. Nam si suasione morali, tum ita mutavit Deus cor Esavi, ut potuerit non mutari. At vero Iacobus Genes. 32. 11. fide oravit, ut Deus ipsum sibi faceret propitium, non modo extraordinario: qua enim fide Iacobus oraret Deum, ut miraculum faceret? Ergo Iacobus oravit fretus Dei omnipotentia & sapientia, ut ita faceret propitium, ut non posset iracundus & invidus permanere. 2. Esto: Deus suasione mutavit cor Esavi: ergo non reali impulsu: non sequitur. Imo contrarium sequitur. Non enim datur actio causae secundae, sine actione causae primae. Ita Iacobus Genes. 45. 14. Deus fortis det vobis invenire gratiam in oculis viri, nempe Iosephi, quem patriarcha Aegyptium irreligiosum esse credidit. Quaero an non senex fide innixus omnipotenti Dei providentiae, qua omnium hominum voluntates flectit, Deum orat? Id nemini dubium esse confido. Nam nisi Deum posse opitulari, firmiter credamus, frustra oramus: ergo oravit ut Deus vel indeclinabiliter vel declinabiliter voluntatem Iosephi ab odio in gratiam commutaret. Si ut indeclinabiliter commutaret, habeo institutum, fidem nempe patriarcharum & prophetarum esse Deum determinare indeclinabiliter voluntates humanas. Si oravit ut Deus declinabiliter commutaret ipsius voluntatem, oravit Deum ad hunc modum: Deus fortis det vobis ut rector ille Æ-gyptiacus, se erga vos exhibeat vel propitium, vel inexorabilem, difficilem & votis vestris infestissimum. Num quaeso aliquid boni magis quam mali filiis suis tum precaretur? Quin imo Esther & ancillae ipsius omnesque Iudaei non tam Deum, quam voluntatis Ahasueriana indifferentiam orassent, ut Estheri precibus rex ille vitam Iudaeorum concederet, si non obstante motione Dei, qua regum corda inflectit, poterat saxeus & inexorabilis consistere. Itaque hic Arminiani vel hominis arbitrium, vel providentiam actuum regum indeclinabiliter determinatricem in folio collocabunt.
units.tr: A. We will not dispute about the mode. The text proves that the heart of Esau was so changed that he could not but deign to regard his brother Jacob with a serene and gracious countenance and a mild and gentle address. For if it was by moral persuasion, then God so changed Esau's heart that it could also have remained unchanged. But Jacob, in Gen. 32:11, prayed in faith that God would make Esau propitious to him, and not merely by an extraordinary means. For with what faith would Jacob pray that God work a miracle? Therefore Jacob prayed, relying on God's omnipotence and wisdom, that he would make Esau so propitious that he could not remain angry and envious. 2. Granted that God changed Esau's heart by persuasion. Therefore it was not by real impulse? That does not follow; rather the contrary follows. For there is no action of a secondary cause without the action of the primary cause. So Jacob, in Gen. 45:14, says: "May God Almighty grant you to find grace in the eyes of the man," namely Joseph, whom the patriarch believed to be an irreligious Egyptian. I ask whether the old man, relying on faith in the omnipotent providence of God, by which he bends the wills of all men, did not pray to God. I am confident that no one doubts this. For unless we firmly believe that God can help, we pray in vain. Therefore he prayed that God would change Joseph's will from hatred to favour, either indeclinably or declinably. If he prayed that God would change it indeclinably, I have my point, namely that the faith of the patriarchs and prophets is that God indeclinably determines human wills. If he prayed that God would change his will declinably, he prayed thus: "May God Almighty grant that this Egyptian ruler show himself toward you either propitious or inexorable, difficult and most hostile to your prayers." Would he, I ask, pray anything good rather than evil for his sons at that time? Indeed, Esther and her maidservant and all the Jews would have prayed not so much to God as for the indifference of Ahasuerus's will, so that by Esther's prayers that king would grant the Jews their lives, if, notwithstanding God's motion by which he bends the hearts of kings, he could remain stony and inexorable. Thus here the Arminians will set either man's free choice, or a providence which indeclinably determines the acts of kings, in the seat of judgment.

units.la: 1. Sam. 10. v. 26. Insecuti sunt Saulum viri, quorum cor Iehovah tetigerat. Esra. 7. v. 7. Benedictus Dominus Deus patrum nostrorum, qui rem talem regis cordi indidit, ut domum Iehovae Hierosolymis decoraret. 2. Chron. 30. 12. Etiam manus Dei erat supra Iehudae viros, ut qui darent iis cor ad faciendum mandatum regis secundum verbum Iehovae. 2 Chron. 29. v. 18. Ita orat Salomon, o Iehovah Domine Deus Abrahami, Isaaci, & Iacobi, serva hoc semper in imaginationibus cogitationum cordis huius populi, & eorum corda tibi praepara. 1. Reg. 8. 57. Sit Iehovah Deus noster nobiscum, quemadmodum fuit cum majoribus nostris, ne derelinquat nos, neque deferat nos. §8. Inclinando animum nostrum ad se, ut ambulemus in omnibus viis ejus &c. Occurrunt sic Remonstrantes in apologia ad faciendum inclinare animum, significare potest finem non effectum divinae beneficentiae. Resp. 1. Potest illud interpretibus significare quod non significet, sed quid significet quaeritur? 2. Si significet finem quem Deus indeclinabiliter assequitur, habemus intentum: si declinabiliter, tum orat Salomon, ut Deus ita inclinet animum: & ita ad obedientiam flectat, ut possint abjecta numinis reverentia ab obedientia prorsus deficere, quod est nulla fide, sed dubia & conjecturali scientia fideles orare debere.
units.tr: 1 Sam. 10:26. "Men went with Saul, whose hearts Jehovah had touched." Ezra 7:27. "Blessed be the Lord God of our fathers, who has put such a thing into the king's heart, to beautify the house of Jehovah at Jerusalem." 2 Chr. 30:12. "The hand of God was also upon the men of Judah, to give them one heart to do the commandment of the king according to the word of Jehovah." 2 Chr. 29:18 (as printed). "Thus Solomon prays: O Jehovah, Lord God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, keep this forever in the imaginations of the thoughts of the heart of this people, and prepare their hearts for thee." 1 Kgs 8:57. "May Jehovah our God be with us, as he was with our fathers; may he not leave us nor forsake us." §8. "Inclining our heart to himself, that we may walk in all his ways, etc." The Remonstrants, in their Apology, have recourse to the claim that "to incline the heart" can signify the end, not the effect, of divine beneficence. Reply: (1) It may be that the interpreters can take it so, but that does not show what it signifies; the question is what it does signify. (2) If it signifies an end which God attains indeclinably, we have our point. If it signifies one attained declinably, then Solomon prays that God so incline the heart, and so bend it to obedience, that men could, having cast off reverence for the Deity, fall away entirely from obedience. This is something the faithful ought to pray for not with faith, but with doubtful and conjectural knowledge.

units.la: 2. Resp. Modus iste determinandi voluntatem, non obscure redarguitur a Salomone verf. praeced. Si peccaverint tibi, & iratus fueris contra eos &c. Nam eo significatur fieri posse, ut populus aversus sit a Deo &c. Sed Resp. Quis neget populum posse peccare ex defectu gratiosae determinationis? sed probare debebant illi doctores, populum, ita a Deo inclinatum peccare posse, siquidem thesi nostrae se opponere voluissent, hoc vero se onere levant solo silentio. At vero istos qui peccaverunt a Deo fuisse inclinatos gratiosa flexione ad ambulandum in viis Iehovae, & tamen peccasse non dicit Salomon, ideoque confirmat determinationem hanc, non redarguit.
units.tr: 2. Reply: this manner of determining the will is plainly refuted by Solomon in the preceding verse: "If they sin against thee, and thou art angry with them," etc. For by this it is signified that it may happen that the people turns away from God, etc. But I reply: who denies that the people can sin through a lack of gracious determination? Those teachers ought to prove that a people so inclined by God can sin, if they wished to oppose our thesis. But they relieve themselves of this burden by silence alone. Solomon does not say that those who sinned had been inclined by God with a gracious bending to walk in the ways of Jehovah, and yet sinned. Therefore he confirms this determination; he does not refute it.

units.la: 3. Resp. Si vero addatur v. 39. apparebit (inquiunt) Salomonem indicare fieri posse, ut illa ipsa refive occasione, qua movetur hic ad resipiscendum, sive qua hujus cor inclinatur ad timendum Deum, alius non moveatur, atque ita Deus moveatur ad dandum unicuique secundum vias suas. Refp. Quis spiritum soporis hic non videat? Dicunt nobis, (ipsa illa re live occasione qua moveatur cor hujus ad timendum Deum, alius non moveatur.) At quis hoc neget? Sed an res an occafio determinent voluntatem hominis ad Deum timendum; an potius gratiosa Dei flexio? Viden' lector Pelagianos hosce judiciis Dei, pesti, uredini, rubigini, locustis, terram & fruges exedentibus tribuere, quod homines moveantur per haec ad Deum timendum, quod Spiritus Sanctus disertis verbis tribuit v. 57, 58. gratiosae Dei praesentiae, non derelictioni divinae, efficaci & gratiosae flexioni voluntatis: en locustae & fames Arminiana est gratia, digna quidem hostibus gratiae gratia: at dicant ex conscientiis, an quaestio fit utrum determinetur voluntas ab occasionibus loci, temporis, rerum fecundarum aut adversarum?
units.tr: 3. Reply: but if one adds verse 39, "it will appear" (they say) "that Solomon indicates it can happen that by that very thing or occasion by which this man is moved to repent, or by which his heart is inclined to fear God, another is not moved; and thus God is moved to give to each according to his ways." Reply: who here does not see a spirit of drowsiness? They tell us that by the very thing or occasion by which the heart of this man is moved to fear God, another is not moved. But who denies this? The question is whether the thing or occasion determines man's will to fear God, or rather God's gracious bending of it. Do you see, reader, how these Pelagians attribute to the judgments of God, pestilence, mildew, rust, and locusts eating up the land and its fruits, the fact that men are moved by these to fear God? The Holy Spirit in express words attributes this, in verses 57 and 58, to the gracious presence of God, not to divine desertion, and to the efficacious and gracious bending of the will. Behold, the Arminian locusts and famine are grace, indeed a grace worthy of enemies of grace! But let them say from their consciences whether the question is whether the will is determined by occasions of place, time, and prosperous or adverse things.

units.la: 2. Antithesis illis probanda est ex pluribus eadem Dei flexione motos quosdam ad resipiscendum moveri, quosdam non. Hoc astutè praetereunt, & ad externas occasiones, quibus bonos recte uti, pravos vero abuti conflat, illi velut ad anchoram confugiunt.
units.tr: 2. The antithesis must be proved against them from many passages showing that some people are moved to repentance by the same bending of God while others are not. They craftily pass this over, and when pressed they cling to external occasions as to an anchor, since it is plain that good men use these well and bad men abuse them.

units.la: 4. Sic respondent. Sensus verborum per fe clarus est: Deus benefaciat populo huic, sicut benefecit patribus nostris ut ab istis beneficiis causam habeat cur Deo suo individuo adhaerere, & praecepta ac statu-[illegible, ~6 letters] ta ejus perpetuo ob oculos habere, & custodire ultro ac libenter velit: beneficiis enim adjunguntur animi, & corda inclinantur ad spontaneum obsequium.
units.tr: 4. They answer thus: The sense of the words is clear in itself: may God do good to this people, as he did good to our fathers, so that from these benefits they have a reason to cling to their God undividedly, and to keep his precepts and statutes ever before their eyes [illegible], and he is willing to guard them readily and gladly: for minds are joined to benefits, and hearts are inclined to willing obedience.

units.la: Resp. Sensum verborum per fe clarum qui hunc vocet, næ quidem ille lynceus est. Nam 1. Salomonem orare, ut benefaciat populo certum est, sed an beneficiis? At quibus? Externis tantum & temporariis? pace, copia frugum, hostium debellatione? fi hoc velint turpiter errant: fit Iehovah Deus noster nobiscum, quemadmodum fuit cum patribus, quorum nempe Deus fuit, & cordium circumcisor: at fi talis præfentia Dei fit in terrenarum rerum possessione, sic Deus Moabitis, & Ammonitis adfuit: nihilne ulterius igitur orat Salomon? Certe hic sensus per fe clarus, porcis, quam fœderato Dei populo, est dignior. 2. Si beneficia etiam spiritualia notant, quæro num cordis circumcisionem, & obedientiæ & refipiscentiæ effectionem intelligant: non audent hoc dicere. Nam sic ratione sumpta à regenerationis beneficio, Deus regenerationem efficeret, quod plane est absurdum. 3. Si itaque omnia alia beneficia temporalia & spiritualia, hisce solis exceptis, notari velint, audio beneficia suasoriè moventia, hoc est externam gratiam moraliter excitantem, quod tradidit Pelagius, ita Augustino referente, qua Deus operatur in nobis velle quod bonum & sanctum est, dum nos terrenis cupiditatibus deditos mutorum more animalium tantummodo præsentia cælesti[?].
units.tr: Reply: whoever calls this sense clear in itself must be a lynx indeed. For first, that Solomon prays that God would do good to the people is certain, but by what benefits? Only external and temporal ones? Peace, plenty of crops, the defeat of enemies? If they mean this, they are shamefully wrong. Let Jehovah our God be with us, as he was with the fathers, whose God indeed he was, and the circumciser of their hearts. But if such a presence of God consists in the possession of earthly things, then God was present with the Moabites and Ammonites too. Does Solomon then pray for nothing further? Surely this sense, clear in itself, is more fitting for pigs than for the covenant people of God. Second, if they mean that the benefits include spiritual ones, I ask whether they understand them to include the circumcision of the heart, and the effecting of obedience and repentance. They do not dare say so. For then, on the reasoning drawn from the benefit of regeneration, God would be effecting regeneration, which is plainly absurd. Third, if they wish all other benefits, temporal and spiritual, to be noted, with these alone excepted, I hear of benefits that move by persuasion, that is, external grace that morally stirs. This is what Pelagius taught, as Augustine reports, by which God works in us to will what is good and holy, while we, given over to earthly desires like dumb animals, are moved only by a heavenly presence [?].

units.la: Note: marginal notes at this place read "Augustin. lib. de grat. Christi cont. Pelag. & cælest. c. 14[?]" (right margin); a second, short marginal note "Pelag. & cælest. c. 1[?]" stands beside the line with "dum nos terrenis". diligentes, futurae gloriae magnitudine, & præmiorum pollicitatione suscitat[?], dum revelatione sapientiae in desiderium Dei stupentem suscitat voluntatem, dum nobis (quod tamen alibi negare non metuit) sua det omne quod bonum est. Vides Lector Remonstr. multo generalius & jejunius ipso Pelagio loqui de gratia Dei interna cor inclinante ad obedientiam. Hi enim tantum beneficiis Deum movere contendunt, at qualia beneficia non docent: at Pelagius æternæ gloriæ beneficii expresse meminit. 4. Sensus ita per se clarus hic est. Salomon ait, adsit nobis Iehovah, ut cor ad obedientiam flectat & inclinet. Remonstrantes sic, ita adsit Iehovah beneficiis ut possimus mandata Dei vel præstare, vel non præstare, & sic Salomon tam orat inobedientiam, quam obedientiam. Hic nihil in contrarium dici potest, sed tantum Deum per beneficia illa intendere obedientiam, non inobedientiam: at vero intentio Dei est actus merè immanens & internus, nihil agens ad extra ut actu inclinetur cor ad obedientiam, sed tantum Dei desiderium notatur, quod non deest Cajino, Saulo, Pharaoni, quos Deus non dedit beare beneficiis temporalibus & spiritualibus, & quorum obedientiam desideravit.
units.tr: Note: the marginal notes at this point read "Augustin. lib. de grat. Christi cont. Pelag. & cælest. c. 14[?]" (right margin); a second, shorter marginal note "Pelag. & cælest. c. 1[?]" stands beside the line containing "dum nos terrenis". [God moves those who are] loving, by the greatness of future glory and the promise of rewards, while by the revelation of wisdom he rouses a wondering will toward the desire of God, while he gives us (which he nonetheless does not fear to deny elsewhere) all that is good. You see, reader, that the Remonstrants speak far more generally and meagrely than Pelagius himself about God's internal grace inclining the heart to obedience. For they only contend that God moves us by benefits, but do not say what benefits these are, whereas Pelagius expressly mentions the benefit of eternal glory. 4. The sense, clear in itself, is therefore this: Solomon says, let Jehovah be with us, so that he may bend and incline our heart to obedience. The Remonstrants say, let Jehovah be present with benefits, so that we may either perform or not perform God's commands; and thus Solomon prays for disobedience as much as for obedience. Nothing can be said against this, except that God by those benefits intends obedience and not disobedience. But God's intention is a purely immanent and internal act, doing nothing outwardly so that the heart is actually inclined to obedience. It only denotes God's desire, which was not lacking for Cain, Saul and Pharaoh, whom God did not give to be blessed with temporal and spiritual benefits, and whose obedience he desired.

units.la: 5. Textus longe aliud vult, quam innuunt Remonstrantes. Sit Iehovah Deus noster fœdere novo nobis junctus, quo dat cor novum, ut doceamur à Deo, & à Patre ad Christum trahamur, ut habetur, Ier. 31. 33. 34. Ezech. 36. 26. Ioh. 6. 44. 45. 2. Additur sicut fuit cum patribus, nempe Abrahamo, Isaaco & Iacobo, at quaero quomodo illis adfuerit? Per gratiam externe suadentem [?] duntaxat? Appello conscientiam ipsorum, an non divinæ præsentiæ cum Patriarchis & fœderato populo fuerit, quod ipsorum corda circumciderit, quod fide & religionis [?] donarit? An hoc nullius præsentiæ divinæ erit Remonstrantibus? 3.
units.tr: 5. The text means something quite different from what the Remonstrants suggest. Let Jehovah our God be joined to us in a new covenant, by which he gives a new heart, so that we are taught by God and drawn by the Father to Christ, as is found in Jer. 31. 33, 34; Ezek. 36. 26; John 6. 44, 45. 2. It is added, "as he was with the fathers," namely Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. But I ask, how was he present with them? By grace merely externally persuading? I appeal to their own consciences: was there no presence of God with the patriarchs and the covenant people, which circumcised their hearts and gave them faith and religion? Or will this be no presence of God at all for the Remonstrants? 3.

units.la: Additur modus quo adfuerit illis, & quo Salomon populo præsenti adesse precatur, ne derelinquat nos, neque deserat nos, quod illustratur (ad faciendum inclinare animum, ut ambulemus in præceptis ejus) quæro quid sit hæc non-desertio? certe Arminianis erit sola subftractio gratiæ moraliter suadentis [?] & beneficiorum, non talis desertio, qua posita, necesse est ut non ambulent in viis Ichovæ: atqui constat hanc esse maximam desertionem. 4.
units.tr: Then there is the manner in which he was present to them, and in which Solomon prays that God be present with us, that he not leave us or forsake us, which is illustrated by "to make our heart incline, so that we walk in his precepts." I ask, what is this not-forsaking? Surely for the Arminians it will be only the withdrawal of grace that morally persuades, and of benefits, and not a forsaking of such a kind that, if it occurs, they necessarily do not walk in the ways of Jehovah. Yet it is established that this is the greatest forsaking. 4.

units.la: Ut ambulemus] exponitur à Remonstrantibus per hoc ut velimus indivulse [?] adhærere, & præcepta ejus custodire, & quidem libenter velimus. Jam quæro à vobis, doctores, quid est libenter velle? Estne libere velle, & quid libere velle vobis est aliud quam ita velle ut possitis nolle? Ergo Ichovah adlit, ut inclinet animum ut ambulemus, idem erit atque hoc, Ichovah adsit ut inclinet animum ut non ambulemus: consideret jam lector sensum per se clarum, quando sensus hic clarus textui aperte contradicet.
units.tr: "That we may walk" is explained by the Remonstrants as "that we may be willing to cling undividedly to him and keep his precepts, and indeed be willing gladly." Now I ask you, teachers, what is it to will gladly? Is it to will freely? And what does it mean for you to will freely, other than to will in such a way that you are able to be unwilling? Therefore, if Jehovah is present so as to incline the heart that we may walk, this will be the same as: Jehovah is present so as to incline the heart that we may not walk. Let the reader consider the sense that is clear in itself, when this clear sense plainly contradicts the text. [That we may walk] is explained as: that we may be willing to cling undividedly, and keep his precepts, and indeed be willing gladly.

units.la: 9. Pergo ad reliquos textus Psal. 119. 36. flecte animum meum ad statuta tua, hoc flectere est determinare. Remonstr. ib. resp. Si David ea oratione petit auxilium determinans, tum petit David, ne Deus determinaret voluntatem ejus ad malum puta ad avaritiam: ita enim David, inclina cor meum ad testimonia tua, & non ad avaritiam, ideoque Deus erit author peccati eo modo quo est boni. R. 1. Retorqueo resp. sic. Erit Remonstrantibus sensus, moraliter excita animam, & suade ad testimonia servanda, & ne suadeas ad avaritiam. Ergo Deus eo modo erit author peccati quo est boni, siquidem suadentem Deum illi velint esse efficientem.
units.tr: 9. I pass on to the other texts. Ps. 119. 36: "Incline my heart to your statutes." This "incline" means to determine. The Remonstrants reply there: "If David by that prayer seeks a determining help, then David asks that God not determine his will to evil, for instance to avarice: for thus David would be saying, incline my heart to your testimonies and not to avarice; and so God will be the author of sin in the same way as he is of good." Answer 1. I retort the reply thus. For the Remonstrants the sense will be: morally stir the soul and persuade it to keep the testimonies, and do not persuade it to avarice. Therefore God will be the author of sin in the same way as he is of good, since they want God, as persuading, to be the efficient cause.

units.la: 2. Nihil respondent nisi per incommodum & quidem quod non sequitur, ideoque non solvunt argumentum.
units.tr: 2. They answer nothing except by an inconvenience, and indeed one that does not follow, and so they do not resolve the argument.

units.la: 3. Sic firmo argum. David vel fide orat, vel non: hoc posterius à nemine Christiano dici debet. Si fide, quæro objectum fidei in orationibus sanctorum, nempe id indicatur à Christo Ioan. 14. v. 13. 14, nempe omnipotentiam & benevolentiam Dei patris in Christo, qua dicit se daturum, quod petimus in nomine Christi. Ergo David credidit Deum flexurum esse cor ipsius ad Dei testimonia & non ad avaritiam. At si Deus moraliter ita flectit voluntatem, ut possit non flecti, debebat David tam credere Deum non flexurum cor ad statuta Dei quam flexurum, quoniam voluntas sub illa suasione semper est indifferens. Imo sic David orat, ô Iehovah ita flecte cor meum ad testimonia tua servanda, ut possim tam non servare ea, quam servare. Scio ipsos responsuros, Deum flectere voluntatem Davidis ad statuta Dei, ex hypothesi quod ipsa voluntas se flexerit, hoc est, Deus efficiet velle, siquidem effecerit velle: at tum David tam confidit in hac oratione, in suo libero arbitrio, quam in Dei gratia, imo magis in arbitrio suo, quoniam non a gratia, sed ab arbitrio pendet actualis flexio ut sit, vel non sit, quippe posita motione Dei efficacissima, tam potest sequi non-actualis flexio, quam actualis flexio. 4. Nullo modo sequitur Deum determinare voluntatem ad peccatum, quia ad actum determinet, non magis quam sequitur, Deus coefficit collaterali influxu actum peccati. Ex Arminianus, ergo est coefficiens causa peccati: nam tam firma est haec, quam illa sequela, neque sequitur Deum esse authorem peccati, quia determinat ad actum propter eandem rationem, sed quoniam ex Arminianis Deus generali influxu concurrit ad omnes actus liberos, ita ut ex Deo non sit, quod actus potius sit bonus quam malus, optime sequitur eodem modo Deum esse authorem peccati, quo est boni, ex Arminianis placitis.
units.tr: 3. Thus I confirm the argument. David either prays in faith or not; the latter must be said by no Christian. If in faith, I ask what the object of faith in the prayers of the saints is. This is indicated by Christ, John 14. 13, 14: namely the omnipotence and benevolence of God the Father in Christ, by which he says he will give what we ask in his name. Therefore David believed that God would bend his heart to God's testimonies and not to avarice. But if God so morally bends the will that it can not be bent, David ought to have believed that God would not bend his heart to God's statutes as much as that he would, since the will under such persuasion is always indifferent. Indeed, this is how David prays: O Jehovah, so bend my heart to keep your testimonies that I may be able to keep them as much as not keep them. <bl>I know they will reply</bl> that God bends David's will to God's statutes on the hypothesis that the will itself has bent itself: that is, God will effect willing, if he has effected willing. But then David trusts in this prayer as much in his own free choice as in God's grace, indeed more in his own choice, since the actual bending depends not on grace but on choice, so that it either is or is not. For, given God's most efficacious motion, the non-actual bending can follow as readily as the actual bending. 4. It in no way follows that God determines the will to sin because he determines it to the act, any more than it follows that God concurs with the act of sin by a collateral influx. Therefore, by the Arminians' reasoning, he is a co-efficient cause of sin. For that inference is as firm as the other. Nor does it follow that God is the author of sin because he determines to the act for the same reason. Rather, since on Arminian tenets God concurs with all free acts by a general influx, so that it is not from God that the act is good rather than bad, it follows very well that God is the author of sin in the same way as he is of good, on Arminian principles.

units.la: 10. Item sanctificetur nomen tuum, adveniat regnum tuum, fiat voluntas tua &c. Resp. Remonstr. ibi sol. 145. Absurdum esse Christum iussisse fidelibus orare Patre, ut non modo nostram, sed & omnium omnino hominum determinet voluntatem, ad sanctificandum nomen ejus quando Christus sciverit Dei, de reprobanda maxima parte humani generis, confilium : sciunt enim fideles Deum hoc nolle, ac proinde se nunquam exauditum iri. Resp.
units.tr: 10. Likewise, hallowed be thy name, thy kingdom come, thy will be done, etc. Answer: The Remonstrants, in the same place, solution 145, say it is absurd for Christ to have commanded the faithful to pray to the Father that he would determine not only our will but the wills of all men without exception, to sanctify his name, since Christ knew God's counsel concerning the reprobation of the greatest part of mankind. For the faithful know that God does not want this, and therefore they will never be heard. Answer:

units.la: 1. Nos orare ut Deus omnium & singulorum voluntates determinet ad sanctificandum Dei nomen citra Dei decreti, electionis, & reprobationis absoluti dominii salvationem, à nostris non docetur, tantum oramus, ut Deus omnium & singulorum voluntates determinet, quatenus ipse velit, relinquendo ei potestatem talem in creaturas qualem habet figulus in lutum, quam Remonstrantes Deo au[?]su sacrilego adimere non verecundantur, non contremiscunt. 2. Nulla est haec consequentia, Christus scivit consilium reprobationis, ergo non potuit jubere fidelibus orare, ut Deus omnium voluntates determinet. Licet enim nobis orare ea quae pugnant cum Dei decreto, pius filius potest orare salutem patris, quem Deus ab aeterno reprobavit : voluntates enim nostrae Dei voluntati revelatae conformari, non arcanae tenentur usquequaque adaptari si-mo[?] quilibet fidelis jure potest orare, ne Deus ipsum tentari aut peccare permittat, à primo conversionis suae momento ad extremum vitae punctum, & interim certo scit hoc pugnare cum Dei decreto, quo statuit absolute permittere lapsus & peccata regenitorum. Imo Petrus & discipuli abnegantes & derelinquentes Christum in passione tenebantur credere praedictionem Dei, adeoque decretum quo statuit permittere, ut oves dispergerentur & scandalizarentur in Christo, ut ipse praedixerat. Matth. 26. 31. ex Zachariæ vaticinio cap. 31. verf. 7. & tamen tenebantur absolute velle & orare Deum, ut ipsorum voluntates non permitteret in tam grande & scandalosum peccatum incidere. Idem certum est de Juda proditore, de Iudæis crucifigentibus Dominum, hoc dato quod ipsis revelatum foret, ipsos tam horrendi in salvatorem peccati, authores fore. Ergo potest quis jure & absque peccato id absolute velle, quod certo scit[?] ȩ¦Diametro cum Dei absoluto decreto pugnare. Neque insulsa sed pia & licita esset oratio: certa etiam fide in eo casu credere possent se exauditum iri, quatenus Dei gloriæ & ipsorum humiliationi atque adeo salutis suæ promotioni conduceret. Nunquam hic evadent ullis sophisticationum technis: si negent decretum à Deo fuisse peccatum illud Petri, quod tum lucri erit ipsorum causæ? & prædicta & decreta erat permissio Dei decreto effectivo.
units.tr: 1. Our people do not teach that we pray that God would determine the wills of all and each to sanctify God's name, apart from the salvation that rests on the absolute dominion of God's decree of election and reprobation. We pray only that God would determine the wills of all and each as far as he himself wills, leaving to him such power over creatures as the potter has over the clay. The Remonstrants do not blush or tremble to take this power from God by a sacrilegious presumption. 2. This is no valid consequence: Christus knew the counsel of reprobation, therefore he could not command the faithful to pray that God would determine the wills of all. For it is lawful for us to pray for things that are contrary to God's decree. A godly son may pray for the salvation of a father whom God has reprobated from eternity. Our wills are bound to be conformed to God's revealed will, not to his hidden will, and they are not bound to be fitted to it in every respect. Any believer may rightly pray, from the first moment of his conversion to the last breath of his life, that God would not permit him to be tempted or to sin, and yet he knows for certain that this is opposed to God's decree by which he has absolutely decided to permit the falls and sins of the regenerate. Indeed, Peter and the disciples, who denied and forsook Christus in his passion, were bound to believe God's prediction, and so the decree by which he decided to permit the sheep to be scattered and to be scandalized in Christ, as he had foretold (Matth. 26. 31, from the prophecy of Zachariæ, cap. 31, verf. 7). Nevertheless they were bound absolutely to will and to pray to God that he would not permit their wills to fall into so great and scandalous a sin. The same is certain of Judas the traitor, and of the Iudæis who crucified the Lord, even granting that it had been revealed to them that they would be the authors of so horrible a sin against the Saviour. Therefore a man may rightly and without sin will absolutely that which he knows for certain to be diametrically opposed to God's absolute decree. Such a prayer would be neither silly but pious and lawful; and in that case they could with certain faith believe that they would be heard, insofar as it would serve God's glory, their own humiliation, and so the promotion of their salvation. These men will never escape by any tricks of sophistry. If they deny that the sin of Peter was decreed by God, what gain will that be for their cause? That foreknown sin was permitted by God, and that permission was part of his effective decree.

units.la: Permissio enim peccati non est peccatum, sed res sancta & licita, & à Deo propriè volita, vel Arminio judice, & tamen tenebatur Petrus nolle illam permissionem, & orare ne Deus ipsum permitteret, & sic dabitur in Petro voluntas pia & sancta contraria Dei decreto effectivo. Videant itaque qui sese expediant sophistæ. 3. Scivit Christus scientia media nunquam credituros reprobos antecedenter & ad scientiam mediam, & Dei decretum. Futuritio enim omnium actuum liberorum præcedit & scientiam mediam, & decretum Dei, ex statutis Arminianis & Jesuiticis : ergo non potuit Christus jubere fidelibus ut reproborum in ecclesia visibili, vel suas voluntates moraliter Deus inclinaret ad sanctificandum Dei nomen, & faciendum Dei voluntatem. Quomodo enim oraret quis, ut Deus illud faceret, quod ante omnem Dei voluntatis actum & scientiam futuritionem habuit? An non Arminiani preces vere infulfas sanctis ex Christi mandato tribuant, ipsorum appello conscientiam. 4. Oratio haec qua petimus, ut homines Dei in terris voluntatem faciant prompte & alacriter, sicut angeli in caelis, ut habet catachef. Palatina domi. 49. q. 124. invictissime probat voluntates hominum ad obedientiam indeclinabiliter flecti. Si enim petimus ut Deus morali suasione det, ut faciamus Dei voluntatem, tum non magis petimus, ut Deus det nobis prompte obedire, quam non obedire omnino. At quis putaret Deum angelorum voluntates ita flecti ad obedientiam, ut possint non obsequi Deo? 10. Pfal. 86. 11. Aduna animum meum ad timendum nomen tuum. Adunare animum Deo in suo conceptu includit actualem cordis ad Deum adhaesionem, nisi dicerent illud (aduna cor meum tibi,) esse etiam, ne adunes cor meum tibi, hoc est aduna vel ne aduna, quae monstrosa essent commenta. Pf. 5. 8. Deduc me Iehova in tua justitia. Pf. 25. 4. 5. Deduc me in veritate tua & doce me. Pfal. 119. 18. Aperi oculos meos. 27. Fac ut intelligam viam praeceptorum tuorum, 29, Amove viam mendacio-rum tum à me, & legem tuam gratiosè largire mihi v. 35. Fac incedam in itinere praeceptorum tuorum. 37. Averte oculos meos ne vanitatem respiciam- v. 133. Pedes meos instítue in sermone tuo, Utinam Remonstrantes sincere dicerent, ecquid David his petitionibus petat? Num potentiam obediendi tantum? At reclamant textus tot luculenti. Petitur enim actualis oculorum apertio, actualis deductio in via, incessio in itinere mandatorum Dei. Si vero petat actualem obedientiam, eam Deus praestare non potest indeclinabiliter nisi per determinationem physicam. Remonstrantes dicunt: Auxilium itaque quod petitur non est potentia bene agendi libera, imo ne quidem actus ipse fidei. sed omne id quod ad animandum, stimulandum & roborandum voluntatem ejus, qui jam credit, facere potest, ut causas habeat gravissimas, cur in actu fidei, quo jam imbuta est, perseverare velit, contra omnia blandimenta & delimenta mundi ac carnis. R. I. Nolunt peti potentiam bene agendi, sed quicquid animat, stimulat & roborat voluntatem: at quid hoc est, vel stimulat & roborat potentiam, vel actum juvet? At vero haec sunt argumenta suasoria, quibus voluntas habet causas gravissimas cur velit perseverare, hoc nihil aliud est, quam quibus potest perseverare, ideoque contradictio hic est plana, non petitur potentia bene agendi libera, sed bene agendi potentia petitur. Si petitur aliquid, quo roboratur voluntas, quid illud est? moralis suasio non roborat voluntatem Phyfice per additionem virium internarum ex horum doctrina. Sic enim adderetur obnixe orantibus nova & auctior potentia Physice & realiter voluntatem efficiens & corroborans, ideoque adhuc peteretur potentia bene agendi, at vero voluntatis roboratio per argumenta suasoria est figmentum. Tum enim qui compedibus ferreis vinctum fortissimis & suasissimis argumentis alloqueretur, vinctum corroboraret, & vires e vinculis Iefe[?] expediendi adderet, quo quid absurdius? 3. Potentiam bene agendi liberam negant peti à sanctis, si potentiam naturae velint, uti innuere videntur per additionem vocis (libera) Ludunt. Ea enim potentia est indita à creatore: sed si intelligant potentiam gratiae, quis sanctus negaret sanctos perere à Deo vires & potentiam obediendi Deo? Id Paulus orat & precatur Ephes. 3, 18. ut fortiter corroborentur per Spiritum Sanctum in interiore homine, ut valeant assequi cum omnibus sanctis, quaenam sit illa latitudo &c. Hic ne potentiam & vires spirituales assequendi magnitudinem charitatis Dei in Christo Deum orat? An potius velint Ephesios per vires naturae hoc assequi? Vel hoc vel illud dicant necesse est. 1. Pet. 5. 10 Heb. 13. 20. 21. 2. Cor. 12. 9. Gratia mea sufficit tibi. Quis neget gratiam illam esse potentiam ferendi onus illud? Quaero an Sancti Spir.tum sanctum precibus postulent & gratiam & gratiae incrementum? At vero gratiam potentiam obediendi & adhaerendi Deo in tentationibus includere, si quis neget, ne theologi nomen meretur.
units.tr: For the permission of sin is not sin, but a holy and lawful thing, and one that God, according to Arminius, wills properly. Yet Peter was bound to be unwilling of that permission and to pray that God would not permit it. So in Peter there will be a pious and holy will contrary to God's effective decree. Let the sophists, then, see how they will extricate themselves. 3. Christus knew by middle knowledge that the reprobate would never believe, both antecedently to middle knowledge and to God's decree. For, according to the doctrines of the Arminians and the Jesuits, the futurition of all free acts precedes both middle knowledge and God's decree. Therefore Christus could not command the faithful to pray that God would morally incline the wills of the reprobate in the visible Church to sanctify God's name and to do God's will. For how would anyone pray that God would do what he had, before every act of God's will and knowledge, as something future? Do not the Arminians themselves attribute truly foolish prayers to the saints on Christ's command? I appeal to their own conscience. 4. This prayer, by which we ask that men on earth do God's will promptly and eagerly, as the angels do in heaven, as the Palatine Catechism, Lord's Day 49, Question 124, has it, most invincibly proves that the wills of men are inflexibly bent to obedience. For if we ask that God, by moral persuasion, would bring it about that we do God's will, then we ask no more that God give us to obey promptly than that he give us not to obey at all. But who would think that God so bends the wills of the angels to obedience that they can fail to obey God? 10. Pfal. 86. 11. Unite my heart to fear thy name. To unite the heart to God, as the phrase is understood, includes an actual adhesion of the heart to God. Unless they say that this means (unite my heart to thee) is also (do not unite my heart to thee), that is, unite or do not unite, which would be monstrous fabrications. Ps. 5. 8. Lead me, Jehovah, in thy righteousness. Ps. 25. 4, 5. Lead me in thy truth and teach me. Pfal. 119. 18. Open my eyes. 27. Make me understand the way of thy precepts. 29. Remove from me the way of lies, and graciously grant me thy law. v. 35. Make me walk in the path of thy precepts. 37. Turn away my eyes lest I look upon vanity. v. 133. Direct my steps in thy word. I wish the Remonstrants would say sincerely what David seeks by these petitions. Is it only the power to obey? But so many clear texts cry out against this. For what is asked is the actual opening of the eyes, the actual leading in the way, the actual walking in the path of God's commandments. But if he asks for actual obedience, God cannot grant that inflexibly except by physical determination. The Remonstrants say: The help therefore that is asked for is not the free power of doing good, nor even the act of faith itself, but everything that can animate, stimulate and strengthen the will of one who already believes, so that he has the most weighty reasons why he should wish to persevere in the act of faith, with which he is already imbued, against all the allurements and enticements of the world and the flesh. Answer: First, they do not want the power of doing good to be asked for, but whatever animates, stimulates and strengthens the will. But what is this, unless it strengthens the power itself, or helps the act? Yet these are persuasive arguments by which the will has the weightiest reasons for wishing to persevere, and this is nothing other than arguments by which it can persevere. So the contradiction here is plain: it is not the free power of doing good that is asked for, but the power of doing good. If something is asked by which the will is strengthened, what is it? Moral persuasion does not strengthen the will physically, by the addition of internal powers, according to their doctrine. For in that case there would be added to those who pray earnestly a new and greater power that physically and really makes and strengthens the will. Therefore the power of doing good would still be asked for. But the strengthening of the will by persuasive arguments is a fiction. For then someone who addressed a man bound in iron fetters with the strongest and most persuasive arguments would strengthen the bound man, and would add strength to free himself from the chains. What could be more absurd? 3. They deny that the free power of doing good is asked for by the saints, if they mean the power of nature, as they seem to hint by adding the word (free). They trifle. For that power is implanted by the Creator. But if they mean the power of grace, what saint would deny that the saints ask from God the strength and power to obey God? Paul prays for this, Eph. 3. 18, that they be mightily strengthened through the Holy Spirit in the inner man, that they may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, etc. Here does he not pray to God for spiritual powers and strength to comprehend the greatness of God's love in Christ? Or do they rather want the Ephesians to comprehend this by the powers of nature? They must say either this or that. 1 Pet. 5. 10. Heb. 13. 20, 21. 2 Cor. 12. 9. My grace is sufficient for you. Who would deny that this grace is the power to bear that burden? I ask whether the saints, by their prayers, seek from the Holy Spirit both grace and the increase of grace. But if anyone denies that grace includes the power to obey and to cleave to God in temptations, he does not deserve the name of theologian.

units.la: 4. Actum fidei a Deo peti a sanctis negant, at quid igitur petunt discipuli, quando dicunt: Domine adauge fidem.
units.tr: 4. They deny that the saints ask God for the act of faith. But what, then, do the disciples ask when they say: Lord, increase our faith?

units.la: 5. Cur negant actum fidei potius non peti, quam amoris, spei, refipiscentiae? quia nempe fides est conditio electionis illis, & esse conditionem a Deo flagitatam, & a Deo effectam per gratiam indeclinabiliter afystata[?] esse volunt. At vero Deus omnes actus obedientiae liberos, & non tantum fidei a nobis flagitat lege, & evangelio, & tamen ipse operatur in nobis velle & perficere in omnibus actibus obedientiae, & imprimis fidei.
units.tr: 5. Why do they deny that the act of faith is asked for, rather than the act of love, hope, or repentance? Clearly because faith is for them the condition of election, and they want this condition to be asked of God and effected by God through grace, fixed and unchangeable. But God requires all acts of obedience freely from us, by law and gospel, and not only the act of faith. Yet he himself works in us both to will and to perform in all acts of obedience, and above all in faith.

units.la: 6. Non possint explicatius scripturis contradicere, quam negare sanctos a Deo petere actum obedientiae, fac ut intelligam viam mandatorum tuorum, vel est, fac ut intelligam, vel sic, ut possim, intelligere; fac ut incedam in itinere mandatorum tuorum, vel est fac ut actu obediam, vel fac ut obedire possim. At negant potentiam obediendi peti: ergo petitur actus: at vero immanis est haec licentia sic exponere. Da moralia argumenta quibus possum moveri ad incedendum in itinere mandatorum tuorum, vel non moveri. Quis credetet vel sanctos orare, ut non obedirent, vel Deum jubere ut sancti id orent? At vero si sancti petunt id quod moraliter stimulet voluntatem ad obediendum, petunt, vel ut obediant, vel ut non obediant. Nam scimus illis quicquid stimulet voluntatem ad obediendum, petunt vel ut obediant vel non obediant. Nam scimus illis quicquid stimulet voluntatem ad obediendum relinquere voluntatem tam non-actui, quã actui. At dicunt dari illa auxilia ex Dei intentione ut obediant: quod vero non obediant ex ipsorum nequitia esse: sed quid hoc ad institutum? Imo negant Deum per illa auxilia intendere absolute & praecise nostram obedientiam, sed conditionate vel obedientiam, vel sin minus, ut voluntate conseq. nos puniat. At scire percupio quid hisce petatur: Amove viam mendaciorum, aperi oculos &c. & huiusmodi quibus petimus à Deo ut ipsas mentis tenebras & cordis malitiam & duritiem qua fit ut possimus non obedire Deo, amoveat. Hic enim oratur ut ipsa Dei actio terminetur realiter & physice, in ipsam nequitiam & perversitatem. An Deus nequitiam amovet ex hypoth., quod nos non ponamus obicem? atqui maxima est nequitia obicem ponere Deo amoventi nequitiam. Ergo petimus ut Deus actu efficiat ne ponamus obicem: & non ponere obicem actu est actu Deo obedire: alioqui non petimus apertionem oculorum & amotionem viae mendaciorum.
units.tr: 6. They could not contradict Scripture more explicitly than by denying that the saints ask God for an act of obedience. "Make me understand the way of your commandments" means either "make me understand" or "so that I may be able to understand"; "make me walk in the way of your commandments" means either "make me actually obey" or "make me able to obey." But they deny that the power to obey is asked, so the act is asked. It is an outrageous liberty to explain it thus: "Give me moral arguments by which I may be moved to walk in the way of your commandments, or not be moved." Who would believe that the saints pray not to obey, or that God commands the saints to pray for this? But if the saints ask for what morally stirs the will to obey, they ask either that they obey or that they do not obey. For we know that whatever stirs the will to obey leaves the will as free to not act as to act. They reply that those aids are given by God's intention that they obey, and that if they do not obey, this comes from their own wickedness. But what has this to do with the matter? Indeed they deny that God by those aids absolutely and precisely intends our obedience, and say instead that he intends it conditionally: either obedience, or, if not, that he may punish us as a consequence of our will. But I very much want to know what is asked in such prayers as: Take away from me the way of lies, open my eyes, and the like, by which we ask God to remove from us the very darkness of mind, the malice and hardness of heart, by which it comes about that we can disobey God. For here we pray that God's action itself terminate, really and physically, upon that very wickedness and perversity. Does God remove the wickedness hypothetically, provided we place no obstacle? But it is the greatest wickedness to place an obstacle against God removing wickedness. Therefore we ask that God actually bring it about that we place no obstacle; and not placing an obstacle is actually obeying God. Otherwise we would not be asking for the opening of our eyes or the removal of the way of lies.

units.la: 11. Et in omnibus omnino actibus tum naturae tum gratiae voluntatem determinari ait Salomon, Prov. 24. 1. Cor regis in manu Iehovæ, sicut rivi aquarum, quocunque vult; illud inflectit. Vox נָטָה [?] est dirigere, inclinare, flectere, & significat actum divinae omnipotentiae Exod. 15. 12. Zach. 1. 12. Psal. 116. 2. & omnipotentiae conjungitur voluntas, ideoque Augustinus ita explicat: Deus cor regis occultissi-ma & efficacissima potestate convertit ab indignatione ad lenitatem, hoc est, de voluntate laedendi ad facultatem favendi. Si Deus cor regis, qui inter mortales liberrimus videtur, inflectit quocunque vult; multo magis omnium hominum.
units.tr: 11. Solomon also says that the will is determined in all acts whatsoever, both of nature and of grace: Prov. 24. 1. The king's heart is in the hand of Jehovah, like streams of water; he turns it wherever he wills. The word [נָטָה] means to direct, incline, or bend, and it signifies an act of divine omnipotence (Exod. 15. 12; Zech. 1. 12; Ps. 116. 2). Will is joined to omnipotence, and so Augustine explains it thus: God converts the king's heart from anger to gentleness by a most hidden and most effective power, that is, from the will to harm to the ability to show favour. If God inclines the heart of a king, who among mortals seems most free, wherever he wills, then much more does he incline the hearts of all men.

units.la: Hic locus unicus, si nulli alii forent, mihi videtur invictissime non tantum probare nostram assertionem, sed esse ipsissima thesis nostra.
units.tr: This passage alone, if there were no other, seems to me most invincibly to prove not only our assertion but to be our very thesis itself.

units.la: Multa hic replicant adversarii. Nam 1. Corvi-nus. Non negamus (inquit) regum corda ita esse in manu Dei, ut quo vult ea possit inflectere, etiam necessitanda (necessitari enim posse corda ultro concedimus) fatemur vero etiam saepe a Deo corda ad quae vult inclinari, sed cum Deus aliquo inclinat corda, id aut ita fieri ut ea determinet ordinarie saltem, aut quod ita fiat necessario esse statuendum nego. Potest ea inclinare, cum per obiecta externa, tum per interna auxilium, ut integram tamen servet libertatis rationem.
units.tr: The opponents raise many objections to this. First, Corvinus: We do not deny (he says) that the hearts of kings are so in the hand of God that he can incline them wherever he wills, even to the point of necessitating them (for we readily concede that hearts can be necessitated). But we also admit that God often inclines hearts to what he wills; yet I deny that when God inclines hearts to something, this is done so that he determines them, at least ordinarily, or that it must be held to be done necessarily. He can incline them both through external objects and through internal help, while still keeping the whole nature of freedom intact.

units.la: R.1. Deū extraordinarie posse necessitare corda regum concedit, sed an locus hic de tali necessitatione loquatur, non dicit, quod est declinare ictum argumenti, non respondere. Locus enim est de ordinaria providentia, qua Deus aquas per suos alveos dirigit, & eodem modo prout vult, inflectit voluntatem regis.
units.tr: Reply 1. He concedes that God can extraordinarily necessitate the hearts of kings. But whether this passage speaks of such necessitation he does not say. That is to evade the force of the argument, not to answer it. For the passage concerns ordinary providence, by which God directs the waters through their channels, and in the same way turns the will of the king as he wills.

units.la: 2. Deum necessitare posse corda regum ait: at locus hic ait eum necessitare & flectere, quocunque vult: at (inquit) per obiecta externa: esto quocunque modo inflectit, nobis sufficit, si ita circumagat voluntates, quocunque vult, at si suasorie[?], non quocunque vult, sed voluntatem actui vel non-actui relinquit.
units.tr: 2. He says that God can necessitate the hearts of kings, but this passage says that he necessitates and turns them wherever he wills. "But," he says, "through external objects." Granted, however he turns them, it is enough for us if he so turns the wills wherever he wills. But if he does so persuasively, and not wherever he wills, then he leaves the will free either to act or not to act.

units.la: 3. Si in manibus Iehovæ est cor regis, quoniam actui suasionis moralis per objecta externa subjicitur, tum cor regis est in manibus Diaboli, & sic Diabolo sua erit providentia, & in manibus Aristotelis, qui probaret mundum esse æternum, imo in manibus cujuslibet hæretici, ut ejus suasu falsa & heterodoxa crederet.
units.tr: 3. If the heart of the king is in the hand of Jehovah only because it is subjected to the act of moral persuasion through external objects, then the king's heart is also in the hand of the Devil, and providence would be his. It would also be in the hand of Aristotle, who would prove the world eternal; indeed it would be in the hand of any heretic, so that by his persuasion one might believe falsehoods and heterodox doctrines.

units.la: 2. Respondet Grevinchovius, sensum non esse quod Deus præDeterminante influxu moveat libertatem, sed quod (hominem) jam volentem dirigat consequenter in finem & objectum, quod vult; sive homo eundem finem & objectum velit, sive nolit, imo & in finem quandoque prorsus ci contrarium, quem homo vult. Resp. 1. Si Deus non applicat prævia motione voluntatem ad nolle, potius quam ad velle, sed collaterali jam influxu comitatur voluntatem jam volentem, tum voluntas non est in Dei manibus, ut inflectat ipsum, quocunque vult. Si potest absolute voluntas velle vel a vel b vel c & intendat Deus ipsam moraliter inflectere ad volendum c, non vero a & b, quippe prohibuit has voluntiones lege sua, fieri tum potest, ut voluntas vellet a aut b, & non c, (indifferenter enim & libere potest velle vel a, vel b, vel c,) tum Deus non posset inflectere voluntatem quocunque vult, quia non ad volitionem c. Et sic voluntas regis est in manibus ipsius regis, non Dei hoc modo, quippe rex inflectit suam voluntatem, quocunque vult. 2. Quando duo trahunt navim viribus collateralibus, unus vult versus ortum, alter versus occasum navim volvere, non potest de utroque simul volvente dici, quod uterque inflectat navim, quocunque vult. Jam Arminiani & Jesuitæ dicunt regem flectere suam voluntatem quocunque vult, & Arminiani & Jesuitæ concedunt etiam Deum inflectere voluntatem, quocunque vult. Ergo hominis voluntas semper conspirabit in idem objectum, in quod à Deo moraliter flectitur. Atqui semper à Deo moraliter flectitur ad bonum nunquam ad malum: homo igitur nunquam peccabit. 3. Hoc vult Grevinchovius quod vult Bellarminus, non agi hic de actibus voluntatis internis, sed de imperatis, ideoque ex Merceri, Toffani & Calvini expositionibus, hoc tantum velle sapientem, Deum sæpe impedire, quo minus reges, quæ volunt & intendunt, exequantur, nec penes fuisse malam Iudæorum voluntatem, crucifixionem salvatoris, in hunc optimum finem dirigere, generis humani redemptionem, id enim Deum ad tam excellentem finem direxisse. Sed quamvis Mercerus & Toffanus, cum Calvino locum hunc applicent externis eventibus rerum, qui speciali Dei providentiæ subjiciuntur, locum tamen de actibus voluntatis elicitis interpretantur: quin ipse textus clarissime loquitur de internis volitionibus cordis humani, quo ab ira & odio in gratiam & favorem, à nolle & velle, à Deo pro libitu suo circumagitur, non secus ac rivi aquarum per suos alveos, hac vel illa via ab agricola ad sata vel hortos irrigandum deductos, defluunt. Deus enim bonum eventum ex malis voluntatis actibus elicit, sed tum nullo modo agit in voluntatem, aut ipsam, quocunque vult, inflectit, sed tantum externos eventus, praeter hunc anae voluntatis intentum dirigit, voluntate sese, quocunque vult, inflectente, & hoc etiam effet manus pro corde ponere, & a textus genuino sensu plane alienum. 4. Negari etiam haud potest, Iudæos Domini crucifixionis causas liberas & contingentes fuisse, ideoque ex Arminiana secta, absolute potuisse non crucifixisse: quo casu ne quidem penes Deum esset redemptionem humani generis elicuisse. Nam ex non ente quis eventus extraheretur? Imo sic ne quidem per tale medium redimeretur genus humanum, ideoque ne quidem externi eventus penes Deum eruut. Qui enim penes Deum ex venditione Iosephi & missione in Ægyptum esset cibationem ecclesiae fame contabescentis extrahere, si venditio, & in Ægyptum missio non effet in determinatione Dei, sed in arbitrio plane indifferenti causarum liberarum nempe fratrum Iosephi & Ismaelitarum? Sic enim penes homines erit Deum omnibus eventibus bonis, quos intendit per media contingentia excutere.
units.tr: 2. Grevinchovius replies that the meaning is not that God, by a predetermining influx, moves freedom, but that he directs the man, who already wills, consequently to the end and object which he wills, whether the man wills that same end and object or not, and sometimes even to an end quite contrary to what the man wills. Reply: First, if God does not apply a prior motion to move the will to refuse rather than to will, but only accompanies the will already willing with a concurrent influx, then the will is not in God's hands so that he can turn it wherever he wills. If the will can absolutely will a or b or c, and God intends to move it morally to will c, but not a or b, since he has forbidden those acts by his law, then it can happen that the will wills a or b, and not c (for it can will a, or b, or c indifferently and freely). Then God could not turn the will wherever he wills, since he cannot turn it to the volition c. In this way the king's will would be in the hands of the king himself, not of God, since the king turns his own will wherever he wills. Second, when two men draw a ship by concurrent forces, one wills the ship to turn toward the east and the other toward the west, it cannot be said of either one turning it that he turns the ship wherever he wills. Yet Arminians and Jesuits say that the king turns his own will wherever he wills, and Arminians and Jesuits also concede that God turns the will wherever he wills. Therefore the human will will always agree with the object toward which God morally moves it. But God always morally moves it toward good, never toward evil. Therefore man will never sin. Third, Grevinchovius wants what Bellarmine wants: that this passage is not about the internal acts of the will but about commanded acts. Thus, following the expositions of Mercerus, Tossanus and Calvin, it says only that the wise God often prevents kings from carrying out what they will and intend, and that the evil will of the Jews, in the crucifixion of the Saviour, was not in their power to direct to this best end, the redemption of mankind, since God had directed it to so excellent an end.
