But although Mercerus and Tossanus, with Calvin, apply this passage to external events, which are subject to God's special providence, they nevertheless interpret the passage as concerning the elicited acts of the will. Indeed the text itself speaks most clearly of the internal volitions of the human heart, by which God turns it at his pleasure from anger and hatred to favour and goodwill, from unwilling to willing, just as streams of water flow through their channels, by which the farmer leads them this way or that to irrigate the crops or gardens. For God brings good outcomes out of evil acts of the will, but in no way does he then act upon the will or turn it wherever he wills. He only directs the external events beyond the intention of the will, while the will turns itself wherever it wills. To put the hand for the heart would be to do this too, and it is entirely alien to the genuine sense of the text. Fourth, it cannot be denied that the Jews' causes of the Lord's crucifixion were free and contingent, and therefore, on the Arminian view, they could absolutely have not crucified him. In that case it would not even have been in God's power to bring about the redemption of mankind. For how could an event be drawn out of what does not exist? Indeed in that case mankind could not even be redeemed by such a means, and so not even external events would lie in God's power. For how could God, by the sale of Joseph and his sending into Egypt, have drawn out the feeding of a Church wasting away with famine, if the sale and the sending into Egypt were not in God's determination, but in the entirely indifferent choice of free causes, namely Joseph's brothers and the Ishmaelites? In that way it would be in men's power to frustrate, through contingent means, all the good outcomes that God intends.

units.la: 5. Si nulla hic erit Dei determinatio voluntatis, tum sic flueret textus. Voluntas Iehovæ in manibus regis: quocunque vult Rex inflectit voluntatem, tum suam, tum Iehovæ. Probatur: Iudæi libere crucifigunt Dominum gloriæ: ergo non obstante qualibet Dei motione possunt crucifigere, vel non crucifigere. Si crucifigant, inclinant Dei voluntatem ad concursum illum generalem & collateralem, ne daretur actio causae secundae, citra influentiam causae primae, quod est omnino impossibile. Si non crucifigunt, sed pia moti numinis reverentia abstineant, trahunt tum Dei actionem ad illud pium nolle, & sic ex utraque actione vel nolendi vel volendi trahent Dei decretum ad aliquem eventum bonum eliciendum, ne hic vacaret providentia & sapientia Dei. Dicit ibid. Bellarmin. & cum eo Arminiani, Deum hic non pendere a nutu voluntatis creatae, sed a libero suo decreto, quo se obligavit semper cum causa secunda concurrere. Sed Resp. Dependentia Dei a suo decreto non tollit ipsius dependentiam a nutu causae contingentis, penes quam est absolute agere, vel non agere, quicquid decretum & voluntas Dei in contrarium statuerit, ideoque invitissimo Deo fiunt volitiones & nolitiones, tum humanae tum angelicae, omnesque actus contingentes. 3. Resp. Gregorius Valentinus, cor regis auxilio specialissimo corroboratum a Deo flecti, quocunque vult. Sed occurro. 1. Si intelligit auxilium specialis gratiae, textui contradicit, qui est de communi Dei providentia in regum, & synecdochice, in omnium hominum voluntates. 2. Tale auxilium solis in gratia confirmatis tribuitur a Iesuitis. 4. Respond. Suarez, Deum inflectere cor moraliter inspirationibus. At vero Suarez, Valent, Vasqu. motionem conguam Dei in voluntates humanas astruunt: sed & hoc figmentum cum bono Deo postea refutabitur. Motio enim congrua (ut observat Fonseca) in suo conceptu includit consensum congrue moti, & tum dicunt nobis quorum voluntates Deus movet, quo vult, eorum voluntates movet, quo vult. 2. Notum est nolle & velle in motione congrua præcedere in suâ futuritione scientiam mediam, ideoque nolle & velle indifferenter est in libero arbitrio, & non in manibus Iehovæ.
units.tr: 5. If there is no determination of the divine will here, the text would have to read thus: The will of Jehovah is in the hand of the king: wherever he wills, the king turns the will, both his own and that of Jehovah. This is proved as follows: the Jews freely crucify the Lord of glory; therefore, notwithstanding any motion of God, they could crucify or not crucify. If they crucify, they incline the will of God toward that general and collateral concurrence, otherwise there would be an action of a secondary cause without the influence of the primary cause, which is wholly impossible. If they do not crucify, but refrain out of a pious reverence for the divine majesty, they draw God's action toward that pious unwillingness, and so from either action, of unwilling or willing, they draw God's decree to bring about some good outcome, lest providence and the wisdom of God be idle here. The same passage is cited by Bellarmine and with him the Arminians, who say that God does not depend here on the nod of the created will, but on his own free decree, by which he bound himself always to concur with the secondary cause. But I reply: God's dependence on his own decree does not remove his dependence on the nod of the contingent cause, in whose power it lies absolutely to act or not to act, whatever God's decree and will have determined to the contrary; and therefore the volitions and nolitions, both human and angelic, and all contingent acts, occur with God most unwilling. 3. The reply of Gregory of Valencia is that the heart of the king, strengthened by a most special help, is turned by God wherever he wills. But I object. (1) If he means the help of special grace, he contradicts the text, which speaks of God's common providence over the hearts of kings and, by synecdoche, over the wills of all men. (2) The Jesuits attribute such help only to those confirmed in grace. 4. The reply of Suárez is that God inclines the heart morally by inspirations. But Suárez, Valentia and Vásquez assert a congruous motion of God upon human wills; but this fiction too will later be refuted together with the goodness of God. For a congruous motion (as Fonseca observes) includes in its very concept the consent of the one congruously moved; and then they tell us that whose wills God moves, as he wills, he moves their wills as he wills. (2) It is well known that, in congruous motion, the will to will and not will is preceded, in its futurition, by middle knowledge; and therefore willing and not willing are indifferently in free choice, and not in the hand of Jehovah.

units.la: 2. Daniel. 5. 3. Deum, in cujus manu est anima tua & penes quem est totum iter tuum, non glorificasti: viæ & itinera illius Tyranni Babylonici erant omnino actus liberi, ita ut non penes illum esset contra hanc gentem potius, quam contra illam, Israelitas potius, quam Ammonitas bellum gerere, vel non gerere, sed penes Deum. Deus etiam Prov. 3. 1,2,3,4. mandata ipsius observantibus gratiam apud homines promittit:at vero si homines sese ab odio ad favorem a favore ad odium ergo observantem mandata determinent & inflectant, etiam posita motione Dei efficacissima, penes homines erit, ut Deus in promissis sit verax. At dicunt promissiones ejusmodi conditionales esse ex hypothesi, quod homines velint. At vero nulla est hæc justitia, nulla Dei veracitas[?], quod Danieli, Ieremiæ, Sadrecho, Mefacho & Abednagoni obnixe Domini mandata cum summo vitæ, rei, patriæ, famæ, & pacis dispendio & extremo discrimine observantibus Deus gratiam conciliet ex promisso speciali apud Chaldæos, ex hypothesi, si forte Chaldæi ipsos gratia prosequi velint. At forte nolunt non odio ipsos prosequi, an culpa Chaldæorum mercede fraudabantur Deum colentes, præsertim cum nec sanguine, nec ullo necessitudinis vinculo Chaldæis sint conjuncti? An hic Deus justus & verax erit siquidem Chaldæi voluerint, & Deus servis suis nullo suo merito promissa non præstabit?
units.tr: 2. Dan. 5. The God in whose hand is your life and to whom belong all your ways, you have not glorified. The ways and courses of that Babylonian tyrant were entirely free acts, so that it was not in God's power whether he waged war against this nation rather than that, or against the Israelites rather than the Ammonites, or whether he waged war at all; the power lay in the tyrant himself. God also, in Prov. 3:1–4, promises favour with men to those who keep his commandments. But if men determine and turn themselves from hatred to favour, and from favour to hatred, and so do not observe his commandments, then, even with God's most efficacious motion posited, it would lie in men's power whether God is true in his promises. But they say that such conditional promises hold on the hypothesis that men will it. Yet this is no justice, and no truthfulness in God, that he should, on the hypothesis that the Chaldeans might perhaps wish to favour them, grant favour through a special promise among the Chaldeans to Daniel, Jeremiah, Sadrach, Meshach and Abednego, who steadfastly observed the Lord's commandments at the greatest cost of life, property, country, reputation and peace, and in extreme peril. Or perhaps the Chaldeans were unwilling to favour them, not from hatred; was it through the fault of the Chaldeans that those who worshipped God were cheated of their reward, especially since they were not joined to the Chaldeans by blood or by any bond of kinship? Will God be just and true here, if the Chaldeans were willing, and yet he will not fulfil his promises to his servants, which they had in no way merited?

units.la: Prov. 16. v. 7. Quando hominis via Deo placent, ei pacem apud inimicos conciliat. Jerem. 15. v. 11. An non pro te intervenerint tempore mali & tempore angustiæ apud inimicum? Esai. 14. v. 27. Nam Iehova exercituum inivit consilium, & quis irritum faciat? & manum ejus extentam quis avertet? At si Deus non indeclinabiliter determinet voluntatem, tum Medi, Persæ, Macedones, Parthi, aliique qui libere vastarunt Babylonios, poterant non vastasse, & sic non ratum foret Dei decretum de ipsorum vastatione. Imo (inquiunt Arminiani) manus tua extenta erat gladius Medorum & Persarum, quem illi in alias gentes & non in Babylonios strinxisse poterant. Arminiani respondent Deum decrevisse illam vastationem ex prævisione animorum Medorum & Persarum malevolorum erga Babylonios, & ex hac prævisione, decretum non potuit esse irritum.
units.tr: Prov. 16:7. When a man's ways please the Lord, he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him. Jer. 15:11. Did they not intercede for you in the time of evil and in the time of affliction before the enemy? Isa. 14:27. For Jehovah of hosts has purposed, and who shall annul it? And his outstretched hand, who shall turn it back? But if God does not determine the will irrevocably, then the Medes, Persians, Macedonians, Parthians and others who freely laid waste the Babylonians could have refrained from doing so, and thus God's decree concerning their devastation of them would not have been fixed. Indeed (the Arminians say) your outstretched hand was the sword of the Medes and Persians, which they could have drawn against other nations and not against the Babylonians. The Arminians reply that God decreed that devastation from his foreknowledge of the malevolent minds of the Medes and Persians towards the Babylonians, and from this foreknowledge the decree could not be void.

units.la: R. At vero animus ille malevolus an decretus a Deo, an non? Et si decretus, an absolute, an conditionate? Si conditionate, qua conditione? Silebunt hic Arminiani. 2. Sam. 15.31. Converte quaso Iehovah (inquit David) consilium Achitophelis in stultitiam. At sciebat Absalomum & ipsius consilium libere amplecti vel respuere potuisse: quorsum ergo orat Deum, si penes Absalomum absolute fuit sequi vel non sequi illud consilium? Certe sine fide orasset, quod patet esse falsum. Iob. 12. v. 17. Facit (Deus) ut consulti deveniant in amentiam, & iudices stultos reddit, v. 20. Amovet sermonem eloquentibus & iudicium senum recipit. v. 24. Amovet animum primoribus populi terræ. Eccles. 9. 1. Iusti & sapientes & facta eorum in manu Dei. Ier. 10. v. 23. Novi Iehova non esse penes hominem viam ejus, neque esse viri dirigere gressus suos. Prov. 16. 9. Animus hominis excogitat viam suam, sed Iehova statuit gressus ejus. Prov. 20. v. 24. Multitudo cogitationum in homine, sed responsum linguæ a Iehova. Iac c. 4. 15. Pro eo quod dicere debuistis, si Dominus voluerit & vivamus, faciemus hoc aut illud. Quid magis liberum quam proficisci in civitatem & mercari? & tamen non est liberi arbitrii, sed Dei voluntatis hoc. An non Arminianis in promptu erit dicere? imo mercator proficiscitur in urbem, si ipse vult; Deus concurrit influxu collaterali: si vero mercatori non arrideat iter, Deus non concurrit. 2. Cor. 8. verf. 16. Sed gratia Deo, qui Tito indiderat eandem solicitudinem pro vobis. Infinita sunt alia in scripturis, quæ nunc allegare superfedeo.
units.tr: Reply: But was that malevolent mind decreed by God or not? And if decreed, was it absolutely or conditionally? If conditionally, on what condition? Here the Arminians will fall silent. 2 Sam. 15:31. O Jehovah, I pray, turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness, says David. But he knew that Absalom could freely embrace or reject that counsel; why then did he pray God to do so, if it lay absolutely in Absalom's power to follow that counsel or not? Surely he would have prayed in vain, which is plainly false. Job 12:17. He makes counsellors go away stripped, and makes judges foolish. v. 20. He removes speech from those who are eloquent and takes away the discernment of the elders. v. 24. He takes away the heart of the chiefs of the people of the earth. Eccl. 9:1. The righteous and the wise and their works are in the hand of God. Jer. 10:23. I know, O Jehovah, that the way of man is not in his own power, nor is it for a man to direct his steps. Prov. 16:9. A man's heart devises his way, but Jehovah establishes his steps. Prov. 20:24. The thoughts of man are many, but the answer of the tongue is from Jehovah. James 4:15. Instead of saying, If the Lord wills, we shall live and do this or that. What is freer than to set out for a city and trade? And yet this is not of free choice, but of the will of God. Will not the Arminians readily say: the merchant sets out for the city if he himself wills it; God concurs by a collateral influence; but if the journey does not please the merchant, God does not concur? 2 Cor. 8:16. But thanks be to God, who put the same earnest care for you into the heart of Titus. There are countless other passages in Scripture which I now forbear to cite.

units.la: -Rationes & testimonia, quoniam etiam probant efficaciam divinæ gratiæ non à libero arbitrio, sed ab actuali Dei determinatione pendere, ideo capiti de efficacia gratiæ subjiciam.
units.tr: -Since the reasons and testimonies which also prove that the efficacy of divine grace depends not on free choice but on God's actual determination, I shall append them to the chapter on the efficacy of grace.

units.la: EXER. 3. CAP. II.
units.tr: EXERCITATION 3, CHAPTER II.

units.la: De efficaciâ divinæ gratiæ.
units.tr: On the efficacy of divine grace.

units.la: I. QUando quæritur an à gratia, an vero à libero arbitrio pendeat efficacia gratiæ, status quæstionis diligenter figendus est. Nam varios admittit sensus. 1. Sensus esse potest, an à libero arbitrio gratia habeat suam intrinsecam virtutem operandi ad modum gratiæ & agentis supernaturalis? Omnino negative jam respondendum est. Nam à libero arbitrio gratia nec habet essendi, nec operandi modum naturalem & congenitum. Hinc Grevinchovius: Voluntas (inquit) nullam vim confert gratiæ, sed potius gratia vim & propensionem voluntati ad consensum. Ita Suarez & addit orationem. Unde (inquit) nec proprie dicitur, gratiam pendere à libero arbitrio in sua efficacitate, quia dicit causalitatem vel subordinationem inferioris à superiore. Quæro tamen obiter, quam propensionem tribuat gratia libero arbitrio? Nam vel determinativam consensus tribuit, quod non admittent, vel indifferentem. At propensionem indifferentem habuit voluntas naturaliter à se. Si propensionem indifferentem supernaturalem, tum à gratia erit quod voluntas sit indifferens ad credendum, vel non credendum, & sic gratia disponit voluntatem ad τὸ non credere, & ad τὸ peccare. O theologi ubi animus, ubi sal[?][?]? At forte propensionem tribuit inclinativam duntaxat. At dent ruditati meae veniam: nescio quomodo gratia inclinet voluntatem ad actum vitalem & intrinsecum, cujusmodi est electio, repudiatio, & suspensio, non auferendo indifferentiam: siquidem quis sanus neget, inclinationem propensionis indifferentis ad agendum, esse oblationem quandam graduum saltem indifferentiae, & sic inclinatio illa quae a gratia est minuat libertatem Arminiani, necesse est. Sin voluntatem omnino indifferentem relinquat, quomodo inclinet, quaero: nam inclinare est pondus dispositionis ad τὸ velle potius, quam ad τὸ nolle addere. 2. Sensus est utrum actualis gratiae efficientia secundum specificationem sit a libero arbitrio? nec hoc dici potest. Nam actualis actio vitalis, & intrinseca, quae est liberi arbitrii, & gratiae, quae non est vitalis, sed omnino externa & non-vitalis, omnino sunt actus heterogenei & impermixti. 3. Prius sensus quaestionis est utrum, a gratia, an a libero arbitrio fit, quod hic & nunc elicitur assensus divinae actioni in conversionis negotio, potius quam dissensus, ita ut penes gratiam sit, quod existat in natura talis actus, quoad exercitium. Arminiani volunt a libero arbitrio, non ab actuali Dei motione esse, quod assentiamur potius, quam ut dissentiamus. Nos a gratiae natura, & ab actuali Spiritus Sancti motione id pendere asserimus, & à decreto electionis, quo fit, ut credant, quotquot ordinati sunt ad vitam æternam, quoniam ordinati sunt Act. 13. Itaque non simpliciter quæritur, an à gratiâ fit actualis gratiæ efficientia, sed cur gratia efficax fit actu secundo ad productionem conversionis in Petro potius quam in Iuda: id nos in solidum à gratia esse profitemur, illi negant, & libertati humanæ adscribunt. Huic iis theologica.
units.tr: I. When it is asked whether the efficacy of grace depends on grace or on free will, the state of the question must be carefully fixed, for it admits of several senses. (1) It may be asked whether grace has from free will its intrinsic power of acting, in the manner of grace and of a supernatural agent. To this we must answer at once in the negative, for grace has from free will neither its mode of being nor its natural and innate mode of acting. Hence Grevinchovius: The will (he says) contributes no power to grace, but rather grace gives power and propensity to the will for consent. Suárez says the same and adds this: Hence (he says) it is not strictly said that grace depends on free will in its efficacy, since that implies a causal subordination of the inferior to the superior. Yet I ask in passing what propensity grace gives to free will. For either it gives a determining propensity to consent, which they will not admit, or an indifferent one. But the will had of itself by nature an indifferent propensity. If it is a supernatural indifferent propensity, then it will be from grace that the will is indifferent to believing or not believing, and so grace disposes the will to not believing and to sinning. O theologians, where is your wit, where is your sense? But perhaps they give only an inclining propensity. Let them pardon my dullness: I do not know how grace inclines the will to a vital and intrinsic act, such as choosing, rejecting, or suspending, without removing indifference. For who in his senses would deny that an inclination of indifferent propensity toward acting is a certain offering of at least degrees of indifference? So that inclination which comes from grace must necessarily diminish the freedom of the Arminians. But if grace leaves the will wholly indifferent, I ask, how does it incline? For to incline is to add the weight of a disposition toward willing rather than not willing. (2) It may be asked whether the actual efficacy of grace, in its specific character, comes from free will. This cannot be said either. For an actual act that is vital and intrinsic, which belongs to free will, and grace, which is not vital but wholly external and non-vital, are wholly heterogeneous and unmixed acts. (3) The former sense of the question is whether it comes from grace or from free will that here and now an assent to the divine action in the business of conversion is elicited rather than a dissent, so that it lies with grace that such an act exists in nature, as far as its exercise goes. The Arminians want it to come from free will and not from the actual motion of God that we assent rather than dissent. We assert that this depends on the nature of grace, on the actual motion of the Holy Spirit, and on the decree of election, by which all who are ordained to eternal life believe, since they are ordained to it (Acts 13). So the question is not simply whether the actual efficacy of grace comes from grace, but why grace is efficacious in act, producing conversion in Peter rather than in Judas. We profess that this is wholly from grace; they deny it and ascribe it to human liberty. This is the theological question between them and us.

units.la: 2. Iesuitæ volunt videri inter se dissentiri, & tamen satis sunt concordes. Nam Fonseca & Bellarminus dicunt, si efficacia gratiæ, non à Dei congrua motione sed à liberi arbitrii cooperatione pendere dicatur, tum contra scripturas homo seipsum discernet, quæ fuit Pelagij & Maffilienfium sententia. Nemo congruæ vocationis propugnator vehementior est Suarezio qui tamen ita loquitur. Si efficacia gratiæ nihil aliud sit, quam actio seu efficientia gratiæ, aut denominatio inde sumpta, etiam concedi potest efficaciam gratiæ pendere à libero arbitrio. Ergo judicio Bellarmini & Fonseca, Suarez aperte pelagianizat. Ita Valentia: Si (inquit) itaque quæratur, cur ex duobus, qui parem omnino gratiam vocantem habent, hic convertitur, ille non convertitur, respondendum est, quia cum hic esset liber, ut à Deo efficaciter vocante converteretur, eamque ipsam gratiam ab eodem adjutus per conversionem suam tanquam per aliquid prius in alio genere (scilicet causæ materialis) acceptaret, ita plane conversus est, & eam gratiam acceptavit, scilicet ab eadem adjutus, alter autem &[?] cum ad id faciendum liber e-rat, id non fecit. Ita Becan.: Si ergo quaeratur prima radix, quare haec gratia sit efficax, illa inefficax, recurrendum erit ad liberam cooperationem voluntatis, non autem ad praescientiam Dei, qua praevidet hanc & illam gratiam congruam fore. Ita etiam Leonard. Leffius. Ita Lod. Molina: Locus (inquit) relinquendus libero arbitrio in conversione, a quo pendet quod peccator convertatur vel non convertatur, & ob id conversio laudi ipsimet peccatori tribuitur, imo etiam in meritum vitae aeternae ipsi cedit, si semel in gratia reponatur. Quare conversio non in solum influxum gratiae praevenientis referenda est, sed etiam in liberum arbitrium & in externa auxilia, & circumstantias. Eodem modo Arminiani, sed pro suo more, astutius Remonstr. Synodistae Dordrac. Si quaeratur (inquiunt) quae causa, cur hic convertatur, ille non, respondemus quoniam Deus hunc non opponentem novam contumaciam non convertit; ille non convertitur, quia novam contumaciam, opponit. Quaeres, cur hic opponat novam contumaciam, alter non? Respondemus hic opponit, quia opponere vult; ille non opponit, quia a gratia movetur ne opponere velit. Quaeres an non ille, qui non opponit novam contumaciam, & per consequens, convertitur, majorem habet gratiam, quam qui opponit & per consequens, non convertitur. Respondemus antecedentem & praevenientem gratiam aequalem esse posse, sed cooperantem habet prior, non posterior. Bone Deus quam callide! 1. Non opponentem contumaciam volunt moveri a gratia ne opponere velit: sed alter movebatur etiam, &c & tamen opposuit: Ergo ille qui convertitur non opponit contumaciam, quia movetur à gratia, sed quia vult. Atqui non opponere contumaciam est libere convertere se: ergo convertitur quia vult. Candidius multo Grevinchovius: Totius autem hujus complexi (quare scilicet in Paulo, & in Petro, totius quam in Iuda gratia fit efficax?) causa communis alia dari non potest, quam libertas voluntatis. Iacob. Arminium deferunt Arminiani: ipse enim gratiam congruam, quam illi respuunt, arripit. Hoc tantum verbulo annoto, gratiam efficacem non dici illam, quae necessario accipitur, sed quae certo accipitur, & à nullo, cui applicatur, rejicitur. Ipse vero Suarez licet congruam gratiam admittat, tamen ita resolvit. Huic vero cooperanti gratiae adjungendam dicimus cooperationem liberam nostrae voluntatis, in cujus potestate est impedire effectum gratiae (hoc est ut sit inefficax, praestat voluntas) & illum efficere, (hoc est ut sit efficax, facit) si voluntas resistat gratiae, digna est poena: si vero illi cooperatur, digna est laude & gloria. Hic Iesuitae omnes, judicio Fonsecae & Bellarmini aperte sunt in haeresi Pelagiana, & cum illis etiam Arminiani, qui nolunt ita videri, imo magis immerguntur, quam Iesuitae, qui gratiam congruam ab Arminianis rejectam, saltem commenti sunt, ut invidiam haeresis pelagianae declinarent, licet revera non declinent. Arminiani vero nullo velo se tegi volunt, rem profitentur, nomen pernegant Pelagianorum.
units.tr: 2. The Jesuits wish to appear to disagree among themselves, and yet they are quite in agreement. For Fonseca and Bellarmine say that if the efficacy of grace is said to depend not on a fitting divine motion but on the cooperation of free will, then against the Scriptures man would discern himself, which was the opinion of Pelagius and the Massilians. No defender of congruous vocation is more vehement than Suárez, who nevertheless speaks thus: If the efficacy of grace is nothing other than the action or efficiency of grace, or a denomination taken from that, it may also be conceded that the efficacy of grace depends on free will. Therefore, by the judgment of Bellarmine and Fonseca, Suárez plainly Pelagianizes. So Valentia: If (he says) therefore it is asked why of two men who have altogether the same calling grace, one is converted and the other is not, it must be answered that, since the one was free to be converted by God calling efficaciously, and, being helped by the same God, through his conversion as through something prior in another genus (namely of material cause) received that same grace, he was plainly converted and accepted that grace, namely, being helped by the same; but the other, although he was free to do so, did not do it. So Becanus: If therefore the first root is asked, why this grace is efficacious and that one inefficacious, we must recur to the free cooperation of the will, and not to the foreknowledge of God, by which he foresees that this or that grace will be congruous. So too Leonard Lessius. So Lodewijk Molina: The place (he says) must be left to free will in conversion, on which it depends whether the sinner is converted or not; and for that reason conversion is ascribed as praise to the sinner himself, and indeed it even accrues to him as merit of eternal life, if once he is established in grace. Therefore conversion is to be referred not only to the influence of preventing grace, but also to free will and to external aids and circumstances. The Arminians, the Remonstrant Synodists of Dort, do the same, but more craftily in their own way: If it is asked (they say) what is the cause why this one is converted and that one is not, we answer: because God does not convert the one who does not oppose new obstinacy; the other is not converted because he opposes new obstinacy. You will ask, why does this one oppose new obstinacy and the other not? We answer: this one opposes because he wishes to oppose; the other does not oppose because he is moved by grace not to wish to oppose. You will ask whether the one who does not oppose new obstinacy, and consequently is converted, does not have more grace than the one who opposes and consequently is not converted. We answer that antecedent and preventing grace can be equal, but the prior has cooperating grace, not the latter. Good God, how crafty! (1) They want the one who does not oppose obstinacy to be moved by grace not to wish to oppose; but the other was also moved, etc., and yet he opposed. Therefore he who is converted does not oppose obstinacy because he is moved by grace, but because he wills. But not to oppose obstinacy is to convert oneself freely; therefore he is converted because he wills. Grevinchovius is far more candid: Now for the whole of this complex (why, namely, grace is efficacious in Paul and in Peter and not in Judas) no other common cause can be given except the freedom of the will. The Arminians cite Arminius against themselves, for he himself embraces the congruous grace which they reject. I note only this little word, that efficacious grace is not that which is necessarily received, but that which is certainly received and is rejected by no one to whom it is applied. Suárez himself, although he admits congruous grace, nevertheless resolves the matter thus: To this cooperating grace we add the free cooperation of our will, in whose power it is to hinder the effect of grace (that is, to make it inefficacious, the will supplies that) and to bring it about (that is, to make it efficacious, the will does that); if the will resists grace, it deserves punishment; if it cooperates with it, it deserves praise and glory. Here all the Jesuits, by the judgment of Fonseca and Bellarmine, are plainly in the Pelagian heresy, and with them also the Arminians, who do not wish to appear so, and indeed sink deeper than the Jesuits. The Jesuits, who have at least invented congruous grace, which the Arminians rejected, did so to avoid the odium of the Pelagian heresy, although in fact they do not avoid it. The Arminians, however, wish to be covered by no veil; they profess the thing itself and flatly deny the name of Pelagians.

units.la: 3. Iesuitæ & Arminiani hic maxime innituntur gratiæ sufficientis & efficacis distinctioni. Volunt enim omnibus dari gratiam sufficientem, quâ possunt, siquidem vellent, converti, non vero efficacem, quâ convertuntur. At quæres quare non detur efficax gratia omnibus? Respondent Arminiani, sufficientem & efficacem non natura, non specie, imo sæpe nec gradu distingui. Nam qui ponunt obicem gratiæ sufficienti per liberum arbitrium, impediunt quo minus gratia sufficiens efficax fiat, ideoque ex Dei justitiâ dari efficacem non ponentibus obicem, ex justitia negari ponentibus; Deum vero paratum & propensum esse omnibus dare gratiam efficacem, siquidem liberum arbitrium Deo dandum propenso, haud deesset. Nos vero gratiam sufficientem, uti non omnino negamus: ita etiam ab efficaci specie, & natura distingui volumus, & efficacem negari & dari, quibus datur & negatur non ex justitia Dei formaliter, sed ex absoluto Dei beneplacito. Itaque gratiam sufficientem sex modis agnosco. 1. Sufficientem ad π[?] posse in Adamo: poterat enim per se: at vero talem ad π[?] posse in conversione hominis negamus, nisi eademmet gratia, quæ & efficax est, intelligatur. 2. Sufficientem in genere mediorum externorum, sive legis naturæ, sive euangelii revelati, quibus filius Dei vult. 3. Sufficientem ad æternam Dei intentionem de manifestanda gloria justitiæ, addo etiam efficacem. Deus enim talem reprobis indulget gratiam, ex qua repudiatâ manifestò refulget gloria divinæ justitiæ in ipsorum perditione. 4. Sufficientem ad ἀναπληρωτικόν[?]. 5. Sufficientem in electis regenitis ad posse nôn ad velle: opus itaque est ut actuationem superaddat Deus gratiæ habituali. 6. Sufficientem in non electis ad externam disciplinam, quantum humanæ societati confervandæ par est, & æquum Deo ita statuenti ex admiranda sua libertate. 2. Quin imo vox sufficientiæ ex scripturæ phraseologia ab efficaci non distinguitur. 2. Cor. 12. 9. Ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου, polli-ceri Deum illic Paulo gratiam sufficientem, quâ tamen posita poterat Paulus tentationi obedire, adeoque deficere, ridiculum est. Nam sic tam non exauditæ, quam exauditæ essent preces Pauli, quod nemo sanus diceret. Matt. 25. 9. Prudentes vero virgines fatuis dixerunt, non ita ne nobis & vobis, ἐκ δεξιᾶς[?] non sufficiat, nempe actu, adveniente sponso quo tempore necessaria fuit tanta gratia efficax, quanta glorificatis convenit: ea vero non est tantum sufficiens, ut ab efficaci contradistinguitur. Illa enim certe non satis fuisset sponso recipiendo. Joh. 6. 7. Dixit Philippus: ducentorum denariorum panes non sufficerent iis, ut singuli paululum quiddam accipiant. Philippus ignarus futuri miraculi intellexit procul dubio tantum panis actu non sufficere tot alendis. Joh. 14. 8. Philippus dixit ei. Domine, ostende mihi patrem ἀρκεῖ ἡμῖν, ita sonat vox ἱκανός[?] 2. Cor. 3. 5. 4. Videamus an hæc distinctio ferat limam examinimis Scholastici. Dico itaque à ratione omnino alienum esse, ut medicina novem graduum applicata debite vulneri octo graduum, id vulnus non curet. Si enim non curet, plures gradus humorum fortiorum vulneri inerant, quam medicinæ, ideoque medicina non erat sufficiens, sed vulneri impar & minus sufficiens, & eodem plane modo res habet in operatione gratiæ sufficientis. Jam causa alia est in potentia, ut medicina non applicata potest curare morbum; alia in actu, quæ nempe actu causatur: ideoque vana est consequentia à causa in potentia, ad effectum in actu, ut omnes norunt.
units.tr: 3. The Jesuits and Arminians chiefly rest their case here on the distinction between sufficient and efficacious grace. They hold that sufficient grace is given to all, by which they are able to be converted if they were willing, but not efficacious grace, by which they are actually converted. But you will ask, why is efficacious grace not given to all? The Arminians answer that sufficient and efficacious grace are not distinguished in nature, in kind, or even often in degree. For those who place an obstacle to sufficient grace in free choice prevent it from becoming efficacious. Therefore, by God's justice, efficacious grace is given to those who do not place the obstacle, and is denied by justice to those who do. God is ready and inclined to give efficacious grace to all, provided that free choice is granted to God and is disposed towards him, and this would not be lacking. We, however, do not altogether deny sufficient grace, but we want it to be distinguished from efficacious grace in kind and in nature. Efficacious grace is denied and given to those to whom it is given and denied not formally by God's justice, but by God's absolute good pleasure. Accordingly, I recognise sufficient grace in six ways. (1) Sufficient for the power [πῶς?] to be able in Adam: for he was able of himself. But we deny that such sufficiency for the power to be able exists in the conversion of man, unless it is understood as the very same grace that is also efficacious. (2) Sufficient in the general class of external means, whether of the law of nature or of the revealed gospel, by which the Son of God wills to act. (3) Sufficient for God's eternal intention to manifest the glory of his justice; I add, also efficacious. For God grants to the reprobate such grace that, when it is rejected, the glory of divine justice shines forth clearly in their destruction. (4) Sufficient for [anaplērōtikon?]. (5) Sufficient in the regenerate elect for being able, but not for willing; therefore God must add actuation to habitual grace. (6) Sufficient in the non-elect for external discipline, as much as is fitting for preserving human society, and as is fair for God to decree in this way by his admirable freedom. (2) Indeed, the word "sufficiency" in the phraseology of Scripture is not distinguished from efficacious grace. 2 Cor. 12. 9. ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου [my grace is sufficient for you]. That God there promises Paul sufficient grace, by which, if it were granted, Paul could nevertheless have yielded to temptation and so failed, is ridiculous. For in that case Paul's prayers would be as much not heard as heard, which no sane person would say. Matt. 25. 9. But the wise virgins answered the foolish, saying, not so, lest there be not enough for us and for you [ἐκ δεξιᾶς? non sufficiat], namely in act, when the bridegroom arrives, at which time such efficacious grace was necessary as befits the glorified. That grace is not merely sufficient in the sense in which it is distinguished from efficacious grace. For that sufficiency would certainly not have been enough to receive the bridegroom. John 6. 7. Philip said: two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for them, so that each might receive even a little. Philip, unaware of the miracle to come, understood without doubt that so little bread was not, in act, sufficient to feed so many. John 14. 8. Philip said to him: Lord, show us the Father; it is enough for us [ἀρκεῖ ἡμῖν]. So sounds the word [hikanos?]. 2 Cor. 3. 5. (4) Let us see whether this distinction can bear the file of the Scholastics' examination. I say, then, that it is entirely alien to reason that if a medicine of nine degrees is duly applied to a wound of eight degrees, it does not cure that wound. For if it does not cure, the wound contains more degrees of stronger humours than the medicine does; therefore the medicine was not sufficient, but unequal to the wound and less sufficient. And the matter stands in exactly the same way in the operation of sufficient grace. Now one cause is in potency, as an unapplied medicine can cure a disease; another is in act, which is actually causing: therefore the inference from a cause in potency to an effect in act is vain, as everyone knows.

units.la: Tria jam hic suppono, 1.ut sit causa. 2.ut sic sufficiens sit gratia sufficiens ut octo, corruptio ut septem. 3. sit causa actu, non in potentia. Jam præsentibus omnibus debitis requisitis gratia naturam morbidam sanat, alioqui gratia erat minus sufficiens. At clamant Arminiani: quia voluntas est causa libera & moraliter agens, male comparatur cum causa physica, cujusmodi est medicina: quia esto, quod gratia sit sufficiens, ut octo, & corruptio ut septem; ea tamen est libertatis natura, ut applicationem gratiæ impedire possit, quia voluntas libera ita agit, ut possit non agere, ideoque fieri potest ut resistat corruptio ut septem, gratiæ ut 8. Resp. 1. Non male à me institui ejusmodi collationem qualem instituunt oracula sacra, secundum virtuales gradus augendi in gratia & in corruptione. Applicatio etiam ētiam gratiæ est à Dei gratia, non à libero arbitrio. Si ergo corrupta voluntas impedierit applicationem gratiæ, gratia sic impedita non erat sufficiens contra hypothesin: & corruptio ei prædominans, & impediens gratiæ applicationem erat gratia fortior. Rom. 7. 5. Cum enim essemus in carne, affectus peccatorum per legem vigebant in membris nostris ad fructum ferendum mortis. 1. Ioh. 2. 14. Scribo vobis adolescentes, quia fortes estis, & verbum Dei habitat in vobis, & improbum illum vicistis. 1. Ioh. 4. 4. Vos autem ex Deo estis filii, & vicistis eos, quoniam major est is qui in vobis est, quam qui in mundo, Ephef. 3. 16. Ut det vobis secundum divitias gloriæ suæ, ut fortiter corroboremini per spiritum suum in interiori homine. 17. Ut inhabitet Christus per fidem in cordibus vestris. 18. Ut in charitate radicati & fundati valeatis assequi cum omnibus sanctis, quæ sit illa latitudo & c. 1. Cor. 10. 13. Fidelis autem Deus qui non sinet vos tentari, supra id quod poteritis, sed una cum tentatione præstabit exitum, ut possitis eam sufferre. Si tentatio itaque ad peccandum sit viribus impar gratiæ qua resistitur, & si gratia sit major, necesse est corruptionem vincat. Alioqui Ioannes non adscriberet fortitudini & robori, quod fideles dæmonem qui per nostræ corruptionis vires certet nobiscum, devincant. 2. Quæro enim, qui fit ut peccatum vincamus, an non per gratiam Dei? Et tum quæro, in quo sita sit prævalentia virium gratiæ supra vires corruptionis. Respondent Arminiani in hoc, quod gratia eliciat conconsensum ad bonum: At vero hæc est tantum actualis exuberantia, quæ tam potest non esse, siquidem liberum arbitrium vellet, quam esse. At vero robur gratiæ prævalentis situm est in hoc quòd rebellionem, contumaciam, & duritiem auferat, juxta illud, 3. Quod dicant eam esse naturam libertatis, quod possit impedire gratiæ effectum, occurro sic: quæstio est, an non corruptio sit maxima pars cordis lapidei, quod possit opponere contumaciam, & quod opponat? Certè cæcus sit oportet, qui hoc negat: quid enim est opponere posse contumaciam, & actu opponere, nisi voluntatis perversitas, & durities? ergo si gratia hoc tollat, uti ait scriptura, tum ubi non tollitur, gratia non est sufficiens. Ea enim est causa sufficiens, quæ virtutem habet exuberantem ad effectum producendum, si secundum omnes virtutis gradus actu applicetur: at talis est illa actio Spiritus Sancti, quâ removetur cor lapideum. Nam gratia removet nullos gradus duritiei, vel aliquos tantum, vel omnes. Si nullos, non igitur removet cor lapideum, contra quod asserit scriptura. Quando revertetur cor ad Dominum, auferetur velum. Nunc autem Deum precor, ne quid mali faciatis. Si gratia removet aliquos gradus duritiei, per eandem rationem removebit omnes. Nam eadem est ratio, cur enim tres gradus removeret & non leseptem? dicent, quoniam semper potest voluntas nolle, etiam posita gratia sufficientissimâ. Resp. 1. Tum etiam in remorione[?] trium graduum duritei[?], potest voluntas nolle. Ergo gratia nullos omnino gradus removebit, contra scripturas adhuc. 2. Esto, remaneat potentia purae naturae, gratia potentiae adhaerentem contumaciam & duritiem removeat oportet: ea enim est cordis (ut sic loquar) lapidofitas. Quo casu si illa potentia purae naturae exercebit actum purum naturalem nolendi, tum fieri poteft, ut homo resistat Deo vocanti, & non peccet, quod absurdum est. 3. Posse ponere obicem Deo vocanti, vel est corruptio: & sic actus ponendi obicem, per eandem rationem erit peccatum, vel non est corruptio posse Deo reluctari vocanti: sed tum quaero an lapideum cor nihil sit nisi actualis resistentia, & non curvitas potentiae. Si sit tantum actualis resistentia, tum Deus auferendo cor lapideum aufert τὸ actu resistere, quod Arminiani negabunt. Si dixerint Deum auferre τὸ actu resistere ex hypothesi, cedo hypothesin, nempe quod actu non restiterint: si vel malleo cerebra contuderint, hypothesin non dabunt. 4. Nihil vitiositatis inesse potentiae voluntatis, aut nihil vitiositatis habitualis nobis post lapsum inesse, nemo nisi Pelagius diceret. At si aliquid infit, an non removetur, quando removetur cor lapideum? 5. Si natura libertatis talis sit ut possit impedire ne gratia sufficiens secundum omnes gradus applicetur, tum gratia non est sufficiens causa in actu. Causa n. non applicata, non est causa in actu, sed tantum in potentia, & sic non est formaliter causa. Absurdissimè itaque appellatur causa sufficiens, si Deo auserenti cor lapideum resistit voluntas nostra: ergo cor lapideum resistet Deo auferenti cor lapideum, non ergo aufertur tale cor, sed remanet contra Ezech. 36. Itaque ex Arminianorum sententia male dicitur reprobos resistere gratiæ sufficienti non applicatæ, imo sic non essent rei spretæ vocationis internæ. 6. At dicent esse reos quoniam ipsi impediunt applicationem gratiæ sufficientis; sed semper recurret in ipsos hoc saxum, impedire applicationem gratiæ sufficientis esse cordis lapidei non exiguam partem. At promittit Deus se electis suis cor lapideum ablaturum, id quod non præstat, quoniam impedit voluntas libera, quominus applicetur gratia sufficiens. 7. Quæritur an non impeditio applicationis gratiæ sufficientis sit peccatum. Si sit, est evitabile per aliam gratiam sufficientem, quæ vel operatur declinabiliter, quoniam libertas etiam impedit applicationem illius gratiæ, vel indeclinabiliter. Si prius, impeditio illa est peccatum evitabile per aliam gratiam sufficientem, & dabitur progressus in infinitum: en vertiginosos spiritus; si posterius, habemus institutum.
units.tr: Three things I now assume here. (1) That there is a cause. (2) That, as eight is sufficient grace, so seven is corruption. (3) That the cause is in act, not in potency. Now, with all due requisites present, grace heals the morbid nature; otherwise grace was less sufficient. But the Arminians cry out: because the will is a free and morally acting cause, it is badly compared with a physical cause such as medicine. For granted that grace is sufficient as eight, and corruption as seven, yet such is the nature of freedom that it can hinder the application of grace, because the free will so acts that it can not act; and so it may happen that corruption as seven resists grace as eight. Answer. (1) I have not wrongly instituted such a comparison as the holy oracles institute, according to the virtual degrees of increase in grace and in corruption. The application of grace too is from God's grace, not from free choice. If therefore a corrupt will hinders the application of grace, grace so hindered was not sufficient, contrary to the hypothesis; and the corruption which prevailed over it and hindered the application of grace was the stronger grace. Rom. 7. 5. For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions, which were through the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death. 1 John 2. 14. I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God dwells in you, and you have overcome the evil one. 1 John 4. 4. But you are of God, little children, and have overcome them, because greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world. Eph. 3. 16. That he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner man; 17. that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith; 18. that you, being rooted and grounded in love, may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, etc. 1 Cor. 10. 13. But God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear, but with the temptation will also provide the way out, that you may be able to endure it. If therefore temptation to sin is too strong for the grace by which it is resisted, and if grace is greater, it must be that corruption is conquered. Otherwise John would not ascribe to the strength and vigour of the faithful that they overcome the demon, who contends with us by the powers of our corruption. (2) For I ask: how does it come about that we overcome sin, if not by the grace of God? And then I ask in what the prevailing of the powers of grace over the powers of corruption consists. The Arminians answer that it consists in grace drawing forth consent to the good. But this is only an actual abundance, which can as well not be as be, provided that free choice were willing. Yet the strength of prevailing grace consists in this, that it takes away rebellion, obstinacy, and hardness, according to that saying (Ezekiel 36:26). (3) As for their claim that it is the nature of freedom that it can hinder the effect of grace, I answer thus: the question is whether corruption is not the greater part of the stony heart, which can oppose obstinacy and does oppose it. Surely one must be blind who denies this. For what is it to be able to oppose obstinacy, and to actually oppose it, except the perversity and hardness of the will? Therefore, if grace removes this, as Scripture says, then where it is not removed, grace is not sufficient. For that is a sufficient cause which has an abundant power to produce its effect, if it is actually applied according to all degrees of its power. But such is that action of the Holy Spirit by which the stony heart is removed. For grace removes no degrees of hardness, or only some, or all. If none, then it does not remove the stony heart, against what Scripture asserts: When the heart turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away (2 Cor. 3:16). Now I pray God that you do no evil (2 Cor. 13:7). If grace removes some degrees of hardness, by the same reasoning it will remove all. For the reason is the same: why would it remove three degrees and not seven? They will say: because the will can always be unwilling, even when the most sufficient grace is given. Answer. (1) Then, even in the removal of three degrees of hardness, the will can be unwilling. Therefore grace will remove no degrees at all, still contrary to Scripture. (2) Granted that the power of pure nature remains, grace must remove the obstinacy and hardness that adhere to that power; for this is the stony-ness (so to speak) of the heart. In that case, if that power of pure nature exercises its pure natural act of unwilling, it may happen that a man resists God calling him and does not sin, which is absurd. (3) To place an obstacle to God calling is either corruption, and so the act of placing the obstacle will by the same reasoning be sin; or it is not corruption to be able to resist God calling. But then I ask whether the stony heart is nothing but actual resistance, and not a crookedness of the power. If it is only actual resistance, then God, by taking away the stony heart, takes away the actual resisting, which the Arminians will deny. If they say that God takes away the actual resisting by hypothesis, I demand the hypothesis, namely that they have not actually resisted; if they have crushed their brains with a hammer, they will not give the hypothesis. (4) That there is no viciousness in the power of the will, or that no habitual viciousness remains in us after the fall, no one but Pelagius would say. But if something of it remains, is it not removed when the stony heart is removed? (5) If the nature of freedom is such that it can prevent sufficient grace from being applied according to all its degrees, then grace is not a sufficient cause in act. For a cause not applied is not a cause in act, but only in potency, and so it is not formally a cause. Therefore it is most absurdly called a sufficient cause if our will resists God taking away the stony heart. Then the stony heart will resist God taking away the stony heart; therefore such a heart is not taken away, but remains, contrary to Ezek. 36. Thus, on the Arminian view, it is wrongly said that the reprobate resist sufficient grace not applied; indeed, in that case they would not be guilty of spurning the internal calling. (6) But they will say that they are guilty because they themselves hinder the application of sufficient grace. But this rock will always return against them: to hinder the application of sufficient grace is not a small part of the stony heart. Yet God promises to his elect that he will take away the stony heart, which he does not do, since free will hinders sufficient grace from being applied. (7) The question is whether the hindrance of the application of sufficient grace is not sin. If it is, it is avoidable through another sufficient grace, which works either avoidably, since freedom also hinders the application of that grace, or unavoidably. If the former, that hindrance is a sin avoidable through another sufficient grace, and there will be an infinite progress: behold dizzying spirits! If the latter, we have what we set out to establish.

units.la: 5. Quicquid argumentorum ab adversariis adsertur, est absurda petitio principii. Nunquam quam enim dabunt causam sufficientem, quæ ab efficaci contradistinguatur sensu Arminiano.
units.tr: 5. Whatever arguments the adversaries advance is an absurd petitio principii. For they never give a sufficient cause that is distinguished from an efficacious one in the Arminian sense.

units.la: Dicunt medicinam esse sufficientem causam sanandi morbi, sed non efficacem, quoniam æger ex contumace intemperie bibere recusat: sontem aquæ frigidæ esse sufficientem extinguendæ siti, esse non efficacem, quia sitiens bibere recusat: Deum esse causam pluribus mundis creandis sufficientem, non vero efficacem, quoniam decrevit non creare plures: orator sufficienter suadet pacem inter Thebanos & Athenienses, at non efficaciter persuadentur: rationes tamen Demosthenis sunt in se validissimæ.
units.tr: They say medicine is a sufficient cause of curing disease, but not an efficacious one, since a sick man who is stubbornly intemperate refuses to drink it. They say a spring of cold water is sufficient to quench thirst, but not efficacious, because the thirsty man refuses to drink. They say God is a sufficient cause of creating several worlds, but not an efficacious one, since he has decided not to create more. They say an orator sufficiently persuades peace between the Thebans and the Athenians, yet they are not efficaciously persuaded. Nevertheless, the arguments of Demosthenes are in themselves most powerful.

units.la: Resp. 1. Qui medicinam morbi sanandi caufam statuunt, næ illis opus est hellebori medicina. Quis tum non curaretur, qui morbo laborat, si causa in potentia esset causa? at puto medicinam sumptam & applicatam esse causam sufficientem morbi sanandi, & tum si non sanet, erat medicina insufficiens; nec aqua est sufficiens causa extinguendæ siti, nisi intelligatur causa potens, sumpta & hausta aqua est sufficiens causa. Qui Deum simpliciter volunt mundi creatorem, hallucinantur: sic enim, quoniam Deus ab æterno fuit, mundus ab æterno fuisset. At vero Deus ut agens liberum est sufficiens causa mundi creati:alioqui ipse Deus est causa potens mundi: hoc nisi dicatur, necesse est Dei libera voluntas nullam sufficientiam causativam habeat ad actualem creationem mundi. Denique nulla oratio est per se sufficiens causa effectus liberi, quoniam necesse est ad actualem causationem interveniat libera determinatio voluntatis, omnes hæ causæ sunt causæ potentes, non sufficientes, quoniam ad sufficientiam requiritur vis causativa ulterior ad productionem effectus. 2. Ad totius rei enodationem, notandum in eo maxime hallucinari adversarios, quod non animadvertant causam sufficientem bifariam dici: 1. physice. 2+ moraliter: physicè, talis homo, qui metaphysicæ peritus est, sufficiens est causa erudiendæ juventutis in ea facultate; at moraliter non statim est sufficiens, quia ut supponimus, non vult ipsos erudire. Sic medicus est sanandis morbis multorum egenorum causa sufficiens physica: at vero in genere causæ moralis, non est sufficiens, quia curare non potest absque mercede, neque vult. At vero ars medendi solitariè sumpta non agit, sed ars adhibita per liberum arbitrium medici. Deus est causa sufficiens sufficientia physica duobus aut tribus mundis creandis, sed in genere causæ moralis non est sufficiens: sanctissimum e-nim suum arbitrium non determinavit, nisi ad unum mundum creandum. Sic itaque argumentantur Arminiani cum Iesuitis: gratia est sufficiens convertendis reprobis: ergo ipsis vitio verti debet, quod non convertantur. Quamvis consequens sit verissimum, attamen consequentia est vana & nulla. Si enim gratia sit sufficiens physicè tantum, uti revera est, sic mihi licebit arguere: hic medicus causa est sufficiens huic egeno febricitanti curando: ergo vitio verti debet febricitanti egeno, quod non curetur: consequentia nihil ineptius. Non enim potest operam & artem medici pecuniis redimere prae egestate. Ita hic gratia illa Arminiana sufficiens hoc ipso moraliter non est sufficiens, quod vel non applicetur, & sic est causa in potentia tantum, vel hoc dato, quod applicaretur, si non fit uno saltem gradu, nempe ut octo, actuosior & validior, voluntate rebelli ut septem, causa sufficiens non est, & si fit hoc gradu actuosior & a Deo debite applicata, procul dubio est etiam causa efficax. Non igitur datur sufficiens gratia simpliciter, quae non sit efficax. Nam sufficiens illa gratia, vel potest duritiem omnem expellere, & sic erit efficax: non enim resistit Deo vocanti cor nisi durum contumax & rebelle; vel non potest omnem duritiem expellere. Quilibet videre potest Arminianos nihil causativae sufficientiae tribuere gratiae suae sufficienti qua voluntatem applicet ad opus. Id enim illi purae naturae libertatis tribuunt, & sic usus gratiae illis est a pura natura libertatis, non a Dei gratia. Ea enim, ex eorum mente, potest esse sufficiens, etsi voluntas nunquam applicetur ad opus. Atqui omnibus sane philosophantibus hactenus vulgo creditum semper, causam quae effectum producere non potest, causam insufficientem esse. Sed dicunt esse insufficientem non ex defectu virtutis in ipsa gratia, sed eo quod semper agat gratia ut non auferat nolle vel velle Deo vocanti consentire. Sed occurro : defectus hic maximus est virtutis gratiæ, quod non possit peccaminosum τὸ[?] nolle consentire, auferre, atque adeo rebellionem expugnare, præsertim cum victoria nostra, & de peccato, mundo, & diabolo triumphus expresse tribuatur divinæ gratiæ robori in scripturis. 1.Pet.1. 5. Phil. c. 4. v. 13. 1. Ioh. 4. 4. Ephes. 3. 16. Juxta enim Arminianos, si posita sufficienti gratia ejusque actione, manet in me τὸ[?] nolle consentire Deo vocanti, procul dubio non vinco Diabolum & peccatum, ut ait Ioannes, quoniam spiritus sanctus per gratiam inhabitans in me est fortior Diabolo & peccato, quippe posito robore spiritus gratiosi, fieri potest ut vincat Diabolus qui est in mundo, & non spiritus qui est in nobis. Si enim non fit ex virtute & robore gratiæ, quod non fit in me non τὸ[?] nolle consentire Deo vocanti, potius quam in Iuda, tum erit a pura natura liberi arbitrii, ideoque victoria naturæ, non gratiæ debebitur : dent adversarii tertium, & causa volens excidam.
units.tr: Answer, first: those who hold that medicine is the cause of curing disease need a dose of hellebore themselves. For who would not be cured of his illness if the cause were only a cause in potential? But I hold that medicine taken and applied is a sufficient cause of curing disease, and if it does not cure, then the medicine was insufficient. Nor is water a sufficient cause of quenching thirst unless it is understood as a potent cause; water taken and drunk is a sufficient cause. Those who simply call God the creator of the world are mistaken. For in that case, since God has existed from eternity, the world would have existed from eternity. But God, as a free agent, is the sufficient cause of the created world; otherwise God himself is only a potent cause of the world. Unless this is said, it follows that the free will of God has no causative sufficiency for the actual creation of the world. Finally, no speech is in itself a sufficient cause of a free effect, since a free determination of the will must necessarily intervene for actual causation. All these are potent causes, not sufficient ones, since sufficiency requires a further causative power for the production of the effect. Second, for the full unfolding of the matter, note that the adversaries go most astray in this: they do not observe that a sufficient cause is spoken of in two ways: (1) physically, and (2) morally. Physically, a man who is skilled in metaphysics is a sufficient cause of teaching young people that discipline; but morally he is not at once sufficient, since, as we suppose, he is not willing to teach them. So a physician is a physically sufficient cause of curing the diseases of many poor people; but in the sense of a moral cause he is not sufficient, since he cannot cure without a fee, and does not wish to. Yet the art of healing taken alone does not act; the art acts when applied through the free choice of the physician. God is a sufficient cause, by physical sufficiency, of creating two or three worlds, but in the sense of a moral cause he is not sufficient, for his most holy will has determined only the creation of one world. So the Arminians argue, along with the Jesuits: grace is sufficient for converting the reprobate; therefore it must be imputed to them as a fault that they are not converted. Although the consequent is most true, the consequence is empty and null. For if grace is sufficient only physically, as it truly is, then I may argue thus: this physician is a sufficient cause of curing this poor feverish man; therefore it must be imputed to the feverish poor man that he is not cured. Nothing could be more absurd than this consequence. For on account of his poverty he cannot buy the work and skill of the physician with money. So here that Arminian sufficient grace, by this very fact, is not morally sufficient: either it is not applied, and so it is a cause only in potential; or, granting that it is applied, if it is not stronger and more active by one degree, namely eight rather than seven while the will remains rebellious at seven, it is not a sufficient cause. And if it is more active by that degree and duly applied by God, then undoubtedly it is also an efficacious cause. Therefore there is no grace that is simply sufficient and yet not efficacious. For that sufficient grace either can expel all hardness, and so will be efficacious (for it resists God calling the heart only when the heart is hard, stubborn and rebellious), or it cannot expel all hardness. Anyone can see that the Arminians ascribe no causative sufficiency to their sufficient grace by which it applies the will to the act. For they ascribe that to the freedom of pure nature, and so for them the use of grace comes from pure nature's freedom, not from God's grace. For in their view grace can be sufficient even if the will is never applied to the act. Yet all philosophers have hitherto commonly believed that a cause which cannot produce its effect is an insufficient cause. But they say that grace is insufficient not from any defect of power in grace itself, but because grace always acts in such a way that it does not take away the unwillingness, or the willingness, to consent to God calling. But I object: this is the greatest defect in the power of grace, that it cannot take away the sinful [τὸ] not-willing to consent, and so cannot overcome rebellion; especially since our victory and our triumph over sin, the world and the devil are expressly attributed in the Scriptures to the strength of divine grace: 1 Pet. 1.5; Phil. 4.13; 1 John 4.4; Eph. 3.16. For according to the Arminians, if sufficient grace is posited and its action, and the [τὸ] not-willing to consent to God calling remains in me, then undoubtedly I do not conquer the devil and sin, as John says, since the Holy Spirit dwelling in me through grace is stronger than the devil and sin. Indeed, given the strength of the gracious Spirit, it could happen that the devil, who is in the world, conquers, and not the Spirit, who is in us. For if it is not from the power and strength of grace that what is not in me, the not-willing to consent to God calling, does not arise in me rather than in Judas, then it will be from the pure nature of free will, and the victory will be owed to nature, not to grace. Let the adversaries give a third option, or I shall be cut off as a willing cause.

units.la: 6. Ut jam gratiæ efficacia & actualis prædeterminatio magis appareat, notari velim. Quando nos docemus gratiam prædeterminantem ex vi sua intrinseca inclinare voluntatem ad τὸ[?] consentire potius quam ad dissentire, id tripliciter intelligitur. 1. Quod gratia efficax impediat impetum & motum obliquitatis & irrectitudinis vitiosæ, quæ libertati extrinsecè adhæreat, & hunc sensum lubens admitto. Nisi enim Deus actualem duritiem in actibus gratiæ præpediat & præoccupet, non video quomodo Deus auferat cor lapideum. Ezech. 36. 17.
units.tr: 6. So that the efficacy of grace and its actual predetermination may appear more clearly, I wish to note the following. When we teach that predetermining grace, by its intrinsic power, inclines the will to consent rather than to dissent, this may be understood in three ways. (1) That efficacious grace checks the impulse and motion of crooked and vicious perversity, which clings to liberty from outside; and I gladly admit this sense. For unless God restrains and forestalls actual hardness in the acts of grace, I do not see how God takes away the heart of stone. Ezech. 36. 17.

units.la: 2. Sensus hic est, quod gratia prædeterminans vi sua intrinseca penetret quasi ad profunditatem vitalis inclinationis & impetuositatis electivæ, atque ita primam ὁρμὴν[?] & impetum naturæ in libertate cohibeat, & voluntatem inclinantem ad angulum, (ut sic loquar) borealem talis volitionis, & Dei prædeterminatio torqueat ad angulum australem: hunc sensum salsissime nobis affingunt adversarii, 3. Quod Dei gratia prædeterminans non vi ita penetrans, sed insidens impetuositati naturæ, ita indeclinabiliter flectat voluntatem, ut modo admirando gratia fortiter & voluntas vitaliter & electivè conspirent in idem objectum numero, eodem tempore, loco, & intensione, & voluntas sub illa Dei motione non in aliud tenderet objectum, quam in illud idem in quod liberè se inclinasset, hoc dato quod per impossibile, nulla fuisset in Deo prædeterminatio, ita tamen ut gratia primo & principaliter id objectum non aliud prædeterminet, & voluntas subordinatè & dependenter, ex vi interna, vitali, & imperiali, & electivâ libertatis in illud idem objectum tenderet. Hic etiam est verus sensus.
units.tr: (2) The sense here is that predetermining grace, by its intrinsic power, penetrates, as it were, to the depth of vital inclination and elective impetuosity, and so restrains the first impulse and impetus of nature within liberty, and turns the will, which inclines towards the northern angle of such a volition (if I may so speak), by God's predetermination to the southern angle. Our adversaries very wittily fasten this sense upon us. (3) That God's predetermining grace does not penetrate in this way by power, but sits upon the impetuosity of nature, and so bends the will with such inevitability that, in a marvellous manner, grace and will conspire vitally and electively in the same object, in number, at the same time, place and intensity; and the will under that motion of God would tend to no other object than the very one to which it would have freely inclined, supposing (per impossibile) that there had been no predetermination in God. Yet grace predetermines that object first and principally, and the will, subordinately and dependently, by its internal, vital, commanding and elective power of freedom, tends to that same object. This too is the true sense.

units.la: 7. Ita enim distinguimus efficacem à prædeterminatione, quod tota gratiæ efficacia sita sit in prædeterminatione hac. Nos vero non ab eventu aut à libera cooperatione voluntatis gragratiam efficacem esse volumus, sed tum à natura gratiæ prædeterminantis, tum etiam à Dei vocantis intentione. Hisce scripturis probamus Deut. 29. 4. Vidistis signa, virtutes, & tentationes &c. Cur ergo non sunt conversi? Certe si Moses Arminianæ fidei fuisset, satis habuit, brevi respondisse, quoniam vos præfracti Iudæi noluistis obedire: atqui non ab iis, sed ab ipso Deo rationem altissimi mysterii reddit. Sed (inquit) Deus non dedit vobis cor ad intelligendum. Resp. Corv. Deus non potuit à vobis impetrare, ut daret cor ad intelligendum; præfracti enim fuistis. Resp. 1. Quid coactius? Imo impetravit ut daret, & quantum potuit, illæsa iustitia, ad actualem dationem fecit, ut alii Arminiani docent. 2. Quam distorta responsio? Deus non dedit vobis, id est, vos non recepistis: hoccine est exponere, an potius ponere, Dare pro accipere, relatum pro correlato? non est pater[?], id est, non est filius.
units.tr: 7. For we distinguish efficacious grace from predetermination in this way: the whole efficacy of grace lies in this predetermination. We, however, do not want efficacious grace to be defined by the outcome or by the free cooperation of the will, but both by the nature of predetermining grace and by the intention of God who calls. We prove this from these Scriptures. Deut. 29. 4: "You have seen the signs, the powers, and the temptations, etc. Why then were they not converted?" Certainly if Moses had held the Arminian faith, he would have been content to answer briefly that you stubborn Jews were unwilling to obey. But he does not give the reason for this deepest mystery from them; he gives it from God himself. But (he says) God has not given you a heart to understand. Answer (Corvinus): God could not obtain from you that he should give a heart to understand, for you were stubborn. Answer 1: What could be more forced? Indeed he obtained that he should give, and, as far as he could without harm to his justice, he made the actual giving, as other Arminians teach. 2: How distorted is this answer? "God did not give to you" means "you did not receive." Is this to expound the text, or rather to impose on it, taking "to give" for "to receive" and "relative" for "correlative"? It is not "father," that is, it is not "son."

units.la: 2. Remonstrantes Resp. Dedit, quia ea omnia fecit, quæ ad cor intelligens in ipsis efficiendum longe erant aptissima, nisi velimus Deum de seipso conqueri. Resp 1. At dicite quæ sint longe aptissima ad efficiendum cor intelligens: Signa, & miracula, & verbum? at sic dedit Pharaoni cor novum. 2. Nec hæc sunt longe aptissima, quia tantum externe & suasorie excitant, non addunt novas vires læsæ & debili libertati, imo gratia interna longe aptius est, sed vultis altum silentium esse de tanta gratia, 3. Non sequitur Deum de seipso conqueri, sed de Iu-dæis, dæi[?], qui mediis externis abusi sunt, nisi veritis Deum ex iustitia obligari ad dandum cor intelligens. At qua lege? Vos hoc docete.
units.tr: 2. The Remonstrants answer: He gave it, because he did all those things that were far most apt for producing an understanding heart in them, unless we want God to complain about himself. Answer 1: But tell us what is far most apt for producing an understanding heart. Signs and miracles and the word? Yet thus he gave Pharaoh a new heart. 2. Nor are these far most apt, since they only stir up from outside and by persuasion; they do not add new powers to a wounded and weak liberty. Indeed inner grace is far more apt, but you wish there to be a deep silence about so great a grace. 3. It does not follow that God complains about himself, but about the Jews, who abused the external means, unless you maintain that God is bound by justice to give an understanding heart. But by what law? You teach us this.

units.la: 8. Esai. 44. 3. Effundam aquam super sitientem, & fluenta super aridam, effundam Spiritum meum super semen tuum, & benedictionem meam super prognatos tuos; & efflorescent veluti gramen, & veluti salices inter progressus aquarum. Ratio cur efflorescant in operibus sanctitatis, uti exponitur in sequentibus? est effusio Spiritus Sancti super ipsos, ideoque gratia determinans ejusque efficacia probatur. Resp. Remonstr. Conflat quod eo loco agitur de benedictionibus temporariis. Resp. Constat eos executire[?]: (effundam spiritum meum) aliud clamat. Unus dicet. Ego sum Iehovæ, alius vocabit se non Iacobi, id est, adjunget se verae ecclesiæ: ergo de gratia spirituali agitur. 2. Resp. Remonstr. Alloquitur Israelem rectum, ergo non agitur de gratia ad conversionem necessaria. Resp. non sequens promissio facta est semini Iacobi, quid? an semen nondum natum rectum est? an accidens prius subjecto? par est ratio gratiæ conversionis, & gratiæ conversionem subsequentis. Utraque enim determinat indeclinabiliter voluntatem populi Dei ad vegetationem instar plantarum irriguarum in bonis operibus, & ad subscribendum manu Iehovæ, & ad evangelio credendum, ut est v. 5. secus promittit Deus, quod penes se præstare non est. 3. Resp. Remonstr. Non promittitur gratia determinans, quia gratia hæc promittitur Israeli recto, quia tum eâ carebat Israel & indigebat eâ. At gratia determinans ista, jam tum locum habebat in Israele recto. Israel enim rectus non erat sine ea gratia. Resp. 1. Fumo leviora omnia: non tantum Israeli recto, sed & feminini nondum nato, nedum recto fit promissio.
units.tr: 8. Isaiah 44. 3: I will pour water upon the thirsty, and streams upon the dry ground; I will pour out my Spirit upon your seed, and my blessing upon your offspring; and they shall spring up as grass, and as willows among the running waters. The reason why they flourish in works of holiness, as is explained in what follows, is the outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon them; therefore determining grace and its efficacy is proved. Answer of the Remonstrant: It is clear that this passage speaks of temporal blessings. Answer: It is agreed that they... (I will pour out my Spirit) cries out otherwise. "One will say, I am of Jehovah; another will call himself by the name of Jacob," that is, will join himself to the true church. Therefore spiritual grace is being spoken of. 2. Answer of the Remonstrant: He addresses Israel as upright, therefore the passage is not about grace necessary for conversion. Answer: The following promise is made to the seed of Jacob. What then? Is a seed not yet born upright? Is an accident prior to its subject? The reasoning is the same for the grace of conversion and for the grace that follows conversion. For each determines the will of the people of God, without turning aside, to flourish like well-watered plants in good works, and to subscribe with the hand of Jehovah, and to believe the gospel, as is said in v. 5. Otherwise God promises what is not in his power to perform. 3. Answer of the Remonstrant: Determining grace is not promised, because this grace is promised to Israel when upright, since then Israel lacked it and needed it. But this determining grace already had a place in upright Israel, for Israel when upright was not without that grace. Answer 1: All these objections are lighter than smoke. The promise is made not only to upright Israel but also to the seed not yet born, let alone to the upright.

units.la: 2. Gratia determinans parcior non deerat tum Israeli: ergo auctior sub Messia non promittitur quæ voluntatem determinet. non sequitur: veteri populo non defuit fides in Christum. Heb. 11. An sequitur nusquam in prophetis auctiorem & copiosiorem promitti? Tollatur igitur totum vetus testamentum. 4. Nec juvat, si dicas vocationem gentium hic promitti, gentes non sunt semen Israelis: deinde quæ ratio effet istius præcedentis hortationis? Ne timeto serve mi Iacob: nam aliquando ego vocabo gentes etiam ad fidem, puta post ostingentos[?] annos aut 100. annos. Quid? Timebat Israel ne hoc fieret &c. Resp.
units.tr: 2. A lesser determining grace was not lacking to Israel at that time; therefore a greater grace that would determine the will under the Messiah is not promised. It does not follow. Faith in Christ was not lacking to the old people (Heb. 11). Does it follow that a greater and more abundant grace is promised nowhere in the prophets? Then let the whole Old Testament be removed. 4. Nor does it help if you say that the calling of the Gentiles is promised here; the Gentiles are not the seed of Israel. Further, what would be the point of that preceding exhortation, "Do not fear, my servant Jacob," for at some time I will call the Gentiles also to faith, say after eight hundred or a hundred years? What? Did Israel fear that this would happen, etc.? Answer.

units.la: Pudetne nugarum tantos magistratos? Gentes sunt spirituale semen Israelis. Rom. 2. 29. Sed is est Iudæus qui in occulto est &c. Rom. 9. v. 8. Non qui filii carnis, ii filii Dei, sed qui sunt filii promissionis censentur in semine. Quin & Philippenses qui spiritu colunt Deum sunt circumcisio. Phil. 3. v. 3. Obliti estis scripturarum? 2. Hortationis apposita admodum est ratio, & solamen non mediocre Iudæis tantum non ab hostibus pene devoratis. Nam cap. 43. 28. Dederat Deus Iacobum execrationi, & Israelem opprobriis: ita poterant plane animos despondere, &c. & ecclesiam Dei pene deficere, pro ea, quâ erant fidei infirmitate, putare: solatur Deus fideles, eo quod ipsorum semen ramos extensurum per progressus aquarum, gentium vocatione esset. Ita Isai. 54. 1, 2, 3. &c. Gal. 4. 27. Esai. 2. v. 1, 2, 3. dixerim vix legisse scripturas qui assereret non esse vocationem gentium, judæis solatio. 5. Resp. Remon. lib. Promissio ad totum populum dirigitur: at gratia ista peculiaris non ad totum populum pertinet: denique si ad paucos tantum quosdam, ex gentibus nominatum à Deo ab æterno electos promissio pertinere dicatur, quænam erat solatio hæc qua Israelem Deus vult erigere contra metum &c. R. 1.
units.tr: Are you not ashamed of such trifles, you great magistrates? The Gentiles are the spiritual seed of Israel. Rom. 2. 29: But he is a Jew who is one inwardly, etc. Rom. 9. 8: Not those who are children of the flesh are the children of God, but those who are children of the promise are counted as the seed. Indeed the Philippians, who worship God in the Spirit, are the circumcision. Phil. 3. 3. Have you forgotten the Scriptures? 2. The reason given for the exhortation is very apt, and a no small comfort to the Jews, who were all but devoured by their enemies. For in chap. 43. 28 God had given Jacob to execration and Israel to reproaches. Thus they could clearly lose heart, and, given the weakness of their faith, think that the church of God was all but failing. God comforts the faithful by saying that their seed would spread its branches along the course of the waters, through the calling of the Gentiles. So Isa. 54. 1, 2, 3, etc.; Gal. 4. 27; Isa. 2. 1, 2, 3. I would say I have hardly read the Scriptures if I were to assert that the calling of the Gentiles is no comfort to the Jews. 5. Answer of the Remonstrant (lib.): The promise is directed to the whole people; but this peculiar grace does not pertain to the whole people. Finally, if the promise is said to pertain only to some few from the Gentiles, named by God and elected from eternity, what comfort was this by which God wishes to raise Israel against fear, etc.? Answer 1.

units.la: Communi hac cantilenâ nihil frigidius: an ex Dei intentione & decreto promissiones evangelicæ ad reprobos spectent, vos dicite, id nos negamus.
units.tr: Nothing is colder than this common tune. Whether the evangelical promises, by God's intention and decree, look to the reprobate, you must tell us. We deny it.

units.la: 2. Solamen non mediocre est electis promissio gratiæ determinantis: reprobis nihil in scripturis solatio esse dicimus: quid illis cum pace, cum solatio, cum spiritus sancti gaudio?
units.tr: 2. The promise of determining grace is no small comfort to the elect. We say that there is nothing in Scripture that is a comfort to the reprobate. What have they to do with peace, with comfort, with the joy of the Holy Spirit?

units.la: 3. Dicite ex conscientiis ecquid solatii sit ullis filiis Adami, ex promissione illius gratiæ, adversus omnes hujus vitæ, mundi, peccati, Diaboli, ærumnarum omnium, mortis, & infernalis terroris, insultus & tentationes, quâ posita fieri potest ut omnes in æternum exitium ruant, & illis omnes tentationes cedant in extremum malum, liquidem ipsi, uti liberè possent, voluntatem flectant ad assentiendum tentationi. Certe hic in libero arbitrio sive in nova Dea contingentiâ aut fortunâ, non in Deo, gratiâ, providentiâ solatia quærant necesse est: vos solamen Christianorum hoc esse vultis? ut ait Arminius. Non posse nos de Petra deturbari, nisi volentes stationem deseramus, quasi præcipue timendum foret, ne vi cogamur à fide deficere, velle cedere, tentationibus compulsi, quod est timere ne cœlum ruat, aut ne Deus non sit Deus. Nam velle coacte est velle & non velle, hoc est timendum ne deficiamus, si defecerimus. Imo par dæmonum & hominum consolatio, custodia par à Deo, ne peccent si modo nolint peccare ita dæmones, ita qui jam delapsi sunt in peccatu in Spiritum S., consolatione Arminiana non destituuntur: addo e. damnatis ad inferos assatim solationis esse hoc modo.
