Vereminine quæsò doctores, ne damnati velint aliquid coacti, nempe ne desperent, nisi velint desperare?
units.tr: 3. Tell us from your own consciences whether any sons of Adam have any comfort from the promise of that grace against all the assaults and temptations of this life, of the world, of sin, of the Devil, against all miseries, death and infernal terror. Given that grace is placed thus, it can happen that all fall into eternal ruin, and all temptations turn to their extreme evil, since those who could freely bend their will to assent to temptation do so. Certainly here they must seek comfort in free will, or in a new goddess of contingency or fortune, not in God, grace, or providence. Do you want this to be the comfort of Christians? As Arminius says: we cannot be torn from the Rock unless we willingly leave our station. As if the chief thing to be feared were lest we be forced by violence to fall from faith, to wish to yield, compelled by temptations. That is to fear lest the sky fall, or lest God cease to be God. For to wish under compulsion is both to wish and not to wish. This is what must be feared: that we fall away, if we have fallen away. Indeed the consolation of demons and of men is equal, and the custody from God is equal, lest they sin, provided only they are unwilling to sin. So demons, and those who have already fallen into sin against the Holy Spirit, are not deprived of the Arminian consolation. I add that for the damned in hell there is plenty of consolation in this way. Pray tell us, learned teachers, do you fear that the damned might wish something under compulsion, namely that they might despair, unless they wish to despair?

units.la: 9. Deut. 30. v. 9. Circumcidet Iehova cor tuum, & cor seminis tni[?] ad diligendum Dominum Deum tuum, ex toto corde tuo. Quid sit circumcidere, si non præputium cordis, & callum obdurationis, quo Deo resistimus, amputare, cupimus, ut doceant Arminiani. Resp. 1. Promittitur circumcisio ex hypothesi quod ad Deum fuerint conversi v. 1. & 10. & audierint vocem Iehovæ. R. 1. At circumcisio ipsa est conversio; ergo promittitur conversio ex hypothesi quod conversi fuerunt, hoc est circumcidam, si circumcidero. Nam Col. 2. ii. circumcisio est amotio corporis peccati.
units.tr: 9. Deut. 30. v. 9. The LORD your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your seed, to love the LORD your God with all your heart. What does circumcision mean, if not cutting away the foreskin of the heart and the callus of hardness by which we resist God? That is what the Arminians want us to believe. Answer 1. Circumcision is promised on the condition that they have turned to God (vv. 1 and 10) and have heard the voice of the LORD. Answer 1. But circumcision itself is conversion. Therefore conversion is promised on the condition that they have been converted; that is, "I will circumcise, if I shall have circumcised." For Col. 2. 11: circumcision is the putting off of the body of sin.

units.la: 2. Dicit v. 2. Si auscultaveris voci Iehovæ, tu & & liberi tui, in omnibus quæ præcipio tibi, ex toto corde tuo, & ex tota anima tua. Quid hic ad persectam circumcisionem desideratur? Certe nihil; Ergo erant circumcisi, antequam effent circumcisi. 3. Si conversio illa antecedanea sit actus liber, quod negari non potest, tum posito uno actu libero determinatur voluntas ad alium actum liberum indeclinabiliter. Alioqui fieri potest, ut homo impleret conditionem perficiendo illam conversionem antecedaneam, & Deus non circumcidat cor uti promittit, quod veracitati Dei plane repugnat. Ergo agnoscant gratiam determinantem, necesse est. 2. Resp. Arminiani per cor, affectus, non voluntatem designari. Resp. Per cor intelligitur id quo homines obediunt voci Iehovæ in omnibus v. 2. per quod diligunt Deum supra omnia, ut vivant in æternum, quæ legis est impletio. Nam si volunt Arminiani homines præstare perfectam obedientiam mente & affectibus voci Iehovæ, ut vivant v. 6. ut Iehovah iis benefacere tanquam dilecto populo gaudeat, ut est v. 9. & quidem exclusa voluntate, tum homines coacti obediunt voci Iehovæ, & ad vitam æternam vi perrahuntur, nonne satius fuisset hoc tacuisse?
units.tr: 2. He says in v. 2: If you shall hearken to the voice of the LORD, you and your children, in all things which I command you, with all your heart and with all your soul. What is lacking here for perfect circumcision? Surely nothing. Therefore they were circumcised before they were circumcised. 3. If that antecedent conversion is a free act, which cannot be denied, then once one free act has been posited, the will is determined without fail to another free act. Otherwise it may happen that a man fulfils the condition by performing that antecedent conversion, and God does not circumcise the heart as he promises, which plainly contradicts the truthfulness of God. Therefore they must of necessity acknowledge determining grace. 2. Answer: the Arminians say that the heart designates the affections, not the will. Answer: by the heart is understood that by which men obey the voice of the LORD in all things (v. 2), by which they love God above all, so that they live forever, which is the fulfilling of the law. For if the Arminians want men to render perfect obedience with mind and affections to the voice of the LORD, so that they live (v. 6), so that the LORD rejoices to do them good as to a beloved people (v. 9), and indeed with the will excluded, then men are compelled to obey the voice of the LORD and are dragged by force to eternal life. Would it not have been better to keep silent about this?

units.la: 10. Ezech. 36. 23. Cor novum etiam dabo vobis, & spiritum novum ponam in medio vestri. Duo hic dubia Arminiana diluit. Prius est hoc, imo Domine, paratus es voluntate antecedente dare cor carneum, modo nos tibi danti non opponamus cor lapideum» Resp. Imo non penes vos erit opponere, & danti resistere. Ego enim auferam à vobis cor lapideum, ut non velitis mihi danti reluctari: quid clarius? 2. Dub. Armini. Postquam, Domine, nobis cor novum indideris, quo bene velle possumus, fieri potest, ut actu non obediamus, quippe non determinata est libertas ad actus bonos, ita diluit v. 27. Spiritum meum ponam in medio vestri, & faciam ut ambuletis in praeceptis meis.
units.tr: 10. Ezech. 36. 23. A new heart also will I give you, and I will put a new spirit in the midst of you. Here he dissolves two Arminian doubts. The first is this: "Yes, Lord, you are ready, by your antecedent will, to give a fleshly heart, provided we do not oppose to your giving a stony heart." Answer: indeed it will not be up to you to oppose and resist the giver. For I will take away from you the stony heart, so that you do not wish to struggle against me in giving. What could be clearer? 2. The Arminian doubt: "After you, Lord, have implanted in us a new heart, by which we are able to will well, it may still happen that we do not obey in act, since liberty is not determined to good acts." He dissolves this in v. 27: I will put my Spirit in the midst of you, and will make you walk in my precepts.

units.la: Resp. Remonstrantes, & Corvinus. Deus non indeclinabiliter movet voluntatem & absolute, populus enim Novum Testamentum in quo impleta est promissio, incircumcisi cervice & corde manserunt Act. 7. Diem salutis non acceperunt &c. Sed tantum hoc facit iis, quorum cor post res abhorrendas non ambulat.
units.tr: Answer: the Remonstrants and Corvinus say that God does not move the will indeclinably and absolutely. For the people of the New Testament, in whom the promise was fulfilled, remained uncircumcised in neck and heart (Acts 7). They did not receive the day of salvation, and so on. But this only does to those whose heart does not walk after abominable things.

units.la: Resp. 1. Glossa textui repugnat, quoniam Deus aufert illud ipsum cor lapideum, quod post res abominandas ambulat: & dicant illi, quid discriminis sit inter cor lapideum & cor incircumcisum, & cor non acceptans diem salutis. Certe haec idem sunt: Deus autem & abstulit cor lapideum & non abstulit. Nec idem est populus incircumcisus Act. 7. & hic Ezech. 36. petunt insulse principium. Nam probare debebant in eodem populo, hoc est, in iisdem numero hominibus, in quibus Deus promittit se effecturum cor novum, manifeste cor lapideum & incircumcisum, hoc dictatorie ponunt, non probant. 2. Cor circumcisum & non ambulans post abominationes est respromissa. Ergo non est conditio antecedanea promissionis implendæ. Idem enim non est & conditio rei promissæ, & res promissa: res promissa est futurum. Deus enim non jam promittit mundi creationem, & Noachi in arca liberationem. Antecedanea vero conditio prius habet esse & impleta est, quam Deus rem promissam actu existere efficiat. 3. Facta est hæc promissio iis qui sanguinem fuderunt in sua terra v. 18. & Dei nomen inter gentes profanarunt. v. 20. & v. 32. ait. Non propter vos ista facio, ait Iehovah Deus, notum sit vobis, erubescite & confundamini domus Israelis propter vias vestras non bonas. Imo (inquiunt Arminiani) non est quod vitam anteactam erubescant. Nam prius res abominandas abjecerunt, quam Deus cor novum in ipsis crearit. Hæc res profecto est laudi, non putlori. Itaque Arminiani sic; propter vos, & vias vestras bonas, ut pote qui res abominandas abjecistis, ista facio, hoc est, cor novum indo, lapideum aufero; quorum vero cor post res abominandas ambulat, in iis non pono cor novum: quid spiritui sancto contradicentius? 4. Pollicetur Deus eos purgatum iri ab omnibus pollutionibus: Ergo vel resistere Deo danti novum cor, nulla est pollutio, vel ab illa duritie purgantur. 5. Quod Arminiani vocant cordis novi antecedaneam conditionem, id Deus effectum novi cordis vocat. v. 31. Tunc (nempe postquam indiderim vobis cor novum) recordabimini viarum malarum & vosmet fastidietis, id est, res vestras detestandas abjicietis.
units.tr: Answer 1. The gloss contradicts the text, since God takes away that very stony heart which walks after abominable things. And let them say what difference there is between a stony heart and an uncircumcised heart, and a heart that does not receive the day of salvation. Certainly these are the same; yet God both took away the stony heart and did not take it away? Nor is the uncircumcised people of Acts 7 the same as the people here in Ezek. 36. They beg the question foolishly. For they ought to prove that in the same people, that is, among the same number of men in whom God promises to effect a new heart, there is manifestly a stony and uncircumcised heart. This they lay down dictatorially; they do not prove it. 2. A circumcised heart, and one not walking after abominations, is promised in return. Therefore it is not an antecedent condition of the promise to be fulfilled. For the condition of the thing promised is not the same as the thing promised, and the thing promised is future. God does not now promise the creation of the world, or Noah's deliverance in the ark. An antecedent condition, however, must exist first, and it is fulfilled before God brings about the promised thing actually existing. 3. This promise was made to those who shed blood in their land (v. 18) and profaned the name of God among the nations (v. 20). And v. 32 says: I do not do this for your sake, says the Lord GOD; let it be known to you; be ashamed and confounded, house of Israel, for your ways which are not good. Indeed (the Arminians say) there is no reason for them to blush at their former life. For they cast off abominable things before God created a new heart in them. This is surely a matter for praise, not for shame. Therefore the Arminians put it thus: "For your sake, and for your good ways, since you, as those who cast off abominable things, I do this: I give a new heart and take away the stony one. But those whose heart walks after abominable things, in them I do not place a new heart." What could be more contrary to the Holy Spirit? 4. God promises that they will be cleansed from all pollutions. Therefore either there is no pollution in resisting God as he gives a new heart, or they are cleansed from that hardness. 5. What the Arminians call the antecedent condition of a new heart, God calls the effect of a new heart. v. 31: Then (namely, after I have given you a new heart) you will remember your evil ways, and you will loathe yourselves; that is, you will cast off your detestable things.

units.la: 2. Refp. Remonft. Promissio hæc fit toti populo:at promissio gratiæ determinantis tantum paucis absolute electis fit,non toti populo quoniam Ier.31.&Heb.8.fit domui Israelis & Iehudæ. Nam per utramq; domū notantur ii in quibus cor & spiritus vetus erat:in quibus cor non carneum,sed lapideū erat:per quos si notentur electi,tum nulli in populo tum erant,qui cor novū & carneum habebat, quo tempore hæc promissio fiebat: præter electos autem non fuerunt in populo, nisi reprobi: at nec reprobi habuerunt cor carneum, nec electi, quia alioqui id dari iis opus non fuisset: ergo nulli. R.
units.tr: 2. Answer of the Remonstrants: this promise is made to the whole people, but the promise of determining grace is made only to a few absolutely elect, not to the whole people, since Jer. 31 and Heb. 8 say it is made to the house of Israel and Judah. For by both houses are meant those in whom the heart and spirit were old: in whom the heart was not fleshly but stony. If by these the elect are meant, then at the time this promise was made there were none in the people who had a new and fleshly heart. Apart from the elect, however, there were none in the people except the reprobate; but neither did the reprobate have a fleshly heart, nor did the elect, because otherwise it would have been unnecessary to give it to them. Therefore none. Answer.

units.la: 1. Merae conjecturae, & falsa omnia. Hæc promissio non fit toti populo ex intentione Dei, sed proponitur ecclesiae visibili, & ex intentione Dei fit & præstatur in solis electis: & domum veri Israelis & Iehudæ corde circumcisorum solos electos notare quis dubitaverit? Rom. 11. 26.27. Totus Israel servabitur: fit enim Ier.31.33. promissio iis in quibus Deus legem cordi insculpturus erat, & quorum peccata Deus.est remissurus, ita ut peccatorum eorum non fit amplius recordaturus & cap.36. Ezech. de ecclesia electorum planissime loquitur. 2. Deinde si fit toti populo ex intentione Dei, omnes & singuli aqua pura aspergetur,remissionem peccatorum consequentur, leipsos sufti[?]dio habebunt propter peccata, & v.29. ab omnibus immunditiis liberabuntur, ac propinde à ponendo Deo vocanti obicem, quæ non est mediocris immunditia: quod abjurdum. 3. Fieri promissionem iis in quibus cor vetus erat & lapideum simpliciter, ita ut non omnino regeniti essent falsum est. Cor novum enim cor novum habentibus sæpius promittitur, & præsenti isti populo ex parte fiebat. Christus enim ait habenti dari sic, Luc. 11. 9. Deus dat Spiritū S. potentibus; quæro, an quis possit petere Spiritum S. sine fide, ac proinde sine Spiritu S.? Non potest: ergo si Deus Spiritum S. habenti Spiritum S. dat, promittere potest novum cor habenti novum cor. 2. Refp. Remonstr. Cum promissio hæc effectum foretitura dicatur post multos dies, adeoque non nisi temporibus Messiæ, uti scriptor ad Heb. non obscure indicat, tum nemo convertetur usque ad ista tempora. Refp. Puerilius nihil.
units.tr: 1. Mere conjectures, and all false. This promise is not made to the whole people by God's intention; it is addressed to the visible church, and by God's intention it is made and performed only in the elect. And who would doubt that the house of true Israel and Judah, those circumcised in heart, means only the elect? Rom. 11. 26, 27: All Israel shall be saved. For the promise in Jer. 31. 33 is made to those in whom God was going to inscribe his law on the heart, and whose sins God is going to forgive, so that he will no longer remember them; and Ezek. 36 speaks most plainly of the church of the elect. 2. Next, if the promise is made to the whole people by God's intention, then all and each would be sprinkled with pure water, would obtain remission of sins, would loathe themselves on account of their sins, and (v. 29) would be freed from all uncleanness. Therefore they would not put an obstacle in the way of God calling them, which is no small uncleanness. This is absurd. 3. That the promise was made simply to those in whom the heart was old and stony, so that they were not wholly regenerate, is false. For a new heart is often promised to those who already have a new heart, and it was partly fulfilled in that present people. For Christ says to one who has, it will be given: God gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask (Luke 11. 9). I ask whether anyone can ask for the Holy Spirit without faith, and therefore without the Holy Spirit? He cannot. Therefore if God gives the Holy Spirit to one who has the Holy Spirit, he can promise a new heart to one who has a new heart. 2. Answer of the Remonstrants: since this promise is said to be going to take effect after many days, and so not until the times of the Messiah, as the writer to the Hebrews not obscurely indicates, then no one will be converted until those times. Answer: nothing could be more puerile.

units.la: Non negant Remonstrantes cor novum effici suasorie & refiftibiliter, & hoc eo loci promitti: ergo ex Arminiana sententia sequitur neminem conversum fuisse usque ad tempora Messiæ. Nam temporibus Messiæ, suasorio modo datur novum: hoc dubium ipsos itaque premet.
units.tr: The Remonstrants do not deny that the new heart is effected persuasively and resistibly, and that this is what is promised in the passage here; therefore, on the Arminian view it follows that no one was converted until the time of the Messiah. For in the time of the Messiah the new heart is given in a persuasive manner; this dilemma will therefore press them.

units.la: 2. Quamvis plenarium effectum fortitura fit hæc promissio temporibus Messiæ ut est Heb. 8. non sequitur Deum quotidie in ecclesia judaica eam promissionem non implevisse, sed parcius pro mensura gratiæ, cujus plenitudo ad Messiæ tempora refervanda fuit Esai. 40. 4. Luc. 3. 6. Ioel. 2. 28. Act. 2. 16. 17. At quis adeo rudis est, qui assereret non fuisse Spiritum Sanctum & cor novum in Sanctis, ante adventum Christi, quoniam largior effufio fpiritus promittitur fub Meffia? 3. Remonft. Addunt ex noftra oppofitione fequi id promitti temporibus Meffiæ, quod femper antea factum fuerat: gratia enim Phyfice determinans femper Phyfice determinat. Refp. Retorqueo: fequitur promitti gratiam fuaforie & declinabiliter operantem cor novum, ideoque promitti temporibus Meffiæ id fore, quod femper ab initio mundi fiebat. Gratia enim declinabiliter operans femper declinabiliter operatur. 2. Sequitur bene promitti largiorem & copiofiorem gratiam determinantem utpote ad plures extenfam, ad juvenes, fenes, virgines, fervos &c. Ioel. 2. 28. Non ergo promittitur id quod femper fiebat ab initio mundi? 4. Refp. Remonft. fol. 165. apol. Tum neceffe eft ut dicas omnes eos qui tum vivebant, & inter tempora ifta morituri erant, non tantum fuiffe reprobos, fed fciviffe etiam, aut fcire faltem, ex hujus promiffionis fenfu, potuiffe fe æternum omnes & fingulos reprobatos fuiffe, atque à privilegio iftius gratiæ, decreto peremtorio, feclufos. Refp. 1. Nullo modo fequitur: inter eos enim qui tum vivebant multi habuerunt cor novum, & fpiritum novum, licet plenaria promiffio Chrifto refervanda foret. Supponunt enim falfum, Deum nullis ante adventum Chrifti cor novum dediffe, quod falfiffimum eft. 2. Ex dogmate Arminiano de fcientia media fequitur non plures nec pauciores potuiffe cor novum libere recipere, quam qui actu recipiunt. Hoc dato quod Deus intensissime id voluisset, ideo positis peremptoriis volitionibus humanis, quarum futurit o antecedit Dei tum scientiam, tum decretum, sequitur Deum peremptorie exclusum esse ab omni possibilitate salvandi Iudam, aut ullos alios, qui damnantur, aut perdendi Petrum aut alios ullos, qui salvantur, nisi velit iustitiae & veracitati suae renunciare. Quienim enim potest Iudam salvare, aut velle peremptorie ut salvetur, quando futuritio omnium flagitiosorum actuum Iudae prior sit Dei tum scientia, tum decreto, quod vere horrendum est.
units.tr: 2. Although this promise is to be fulfilled fully in the time of the Messiah, as Heb. 8 shows, it does not follow that God did not fulfil that promise day by day in the Jewish Church, but rather more sparingly, according to the measure of grace, whose fullness was to be kept for the time of the Messiah: Isa. 40. 4; Luke 3. 6; Joel 2. 28; Acts 2. 16, 17. But who is so crude as to assert that the Holy Spirit and a new heart were not present in the saints before the coming of Christ, because a more abundant outpouring of the Spirit is promised under the Messiah? 3. The Remonstrants add that from our opposition it follows that what was always done before is promised for the time of the Messiah, for grace that determines physically always determines physically. Answer: I retort: it follows that a grace that works persuasively and resistibly is promised to produce the new heart, and so it is promised that in the time of the Messiah there will be what was always being done from the beginning of the world. For grace that works resistibly always works resistibly. 2. It follows well enough that a larger and fuller determining grace is promised, extended as it is to more people, to young men, old men, virgins, servants, etc. (Joel 2. 28). Therefore it is not promised that which always happened from the beginning of the world? 4. Answer to the Remonstrants, in their Apology, p. 165. Then you must say that all those who were living at that time, and who were to die between those times, were not only reprobate, but also knew, or at least could know from the sense of this promise, that they had been eternally reprobated, all and each, and excluded by a peremptory decree from the privilege of this grace. Answer 1. It does not follow in any way: for among those who were living at that time many had a new heart and a new spirit, although the full promise was to be kept for Christ. For they assume a falsehood, that God gave a new heart to none before the coming of Christ, which is most false. 2. From the Arminian doctrine of middle knowledge it follows that no more and no fewer could freely receive a new heart than those who actually receive it. Granting that God had most intensely willed it, still, with human peremptory volitions posited, whose futurition precedes both God's knowledge and his decree, it follows that God is peremptorily shut out from every possibility of saving Judas, or any others who are damned, or of destroying Peter or any others who are saved, unless he is willing to renounce his justice and truthfulness. For how can he save Judas, or will peremptorily that he be saved, when the futurition of all Judas's wicked acts is prior both to God's knowledge and to his decree? This is truly horrible.

units.la: 5. Resp. Remonstr. & Corvinus. Intelligendam dicunt promissionem de tali operationis modo, qui singularem, & admirabilem vim habituras erat ad corda populi totius, licet alioqui valde a divinorum praeceptorum observatione alienata, amore Dei & legum divinarum de novo accendendum & inflammandum, adeoque in officio & fide semper retinendum, sic tamen ut res, quanquam non verisimiliter, adhuc aliter cadere posset, id est, ut vel non inflammaretur amore ipso vel inflammatus semel iterum refrigesceret, & ad ingenium rediret. Haec illi. Corvinus ait promissionem hanc respicere congeriem beneficiorum Dei quae non possunt non permovere eos ad obedientiam, nisi omnem Dei timorem exuissent & particulam [illegible, ~1 letter] non semper notare eventum & effectum, sed saepe finem & intentioonem Ezech. 24. 13. Mundavite, & nón[?]es mundata. Ier, 15. 9. Curavimus Babylonem, & non est curata: ita falsi doctores dicuntur facere confidere mendacio. Ier. 29. 31. & Cananæi [?] avocaturi filios Israelitarum post se Deut.7. 4. Resp. 1. Dant nobis singularem modum, quo Deus corda ad obediendum inflammat, licet contrarium cadere possit, quamquam non verisimiliter: quid illud [non verisimiliter] sit, quis scit? Nempe non probaliter, scilicet, quia Deus movet voluntatem, ignarus futuri actus liberi, probabili tamen aut verisimili conjectura opinatur Deus, ni fallat augurium, fore ut persuadeantur: nempe hic Arminiani volunt Deum struere syllogismos tropicos, quasi rudis esset tyro in logica. Ah blasphemiae orco relegandae. 2. Sic tamen ut res aliter cadere posset, id est, ut non inflammaretur isto amore: sic totam vim singularem & admirabilem enervant, dum vis illa nihil praestat, sed cor non inflammatum relinquit, ideoque posita illa promissione Deus tam non dat cor novum, quam dat. Imo Arminianis figmentis stantibus, tam est haec comminatio gravissima, quam promissio gratiosa, tam a justitia quam a misericordia profecta. Si enim Deus tali admirabili vi utitur in affectione cordis novi: ex qua tam sequitur cor lapideum, & prava & contumax Deo regeneranti reluctatio facta, quam cor novum & spiritus novus, tum Deus æque minatur iis cor lapideum, quam promittit cor novum, & tum ridiculæ & vere hypocriticæ sunt hæ promissiones, & tum illud v. 32. non propter vos ista facio, nempe propter vos & vias malas, cor lapideum vobis aufero, huc certè redeat sensus necesse est, ideoque non indurabuntur propter peccata, sed propter nomen Dei gloriosum. Hoc non audent afferere Remonstrantes. At vero multa beneficia gratiosa hic promissa, ut quod Deus sanctificari se velit. v. 23. quod pax conscientiæ & vera tranquillitas v. 28. promittatur, & dolor secundum Deum v. 31. remissio peccatorum v. 28. & 33. preces ipsorum exaudiendæ v. 37. & gentes agnituræ sint, Deum esse ipsorum Deum v. 36. & quod id certo fore prædicat v. 36. Quia (inquit) ego Iehovah loquutus sum & id præstabo. Omnia (inquam) hæc certissime notant, non verisimiliter & probabiliter sed certissime fore, ut ipsis indatur novum cor & novus spiritus, & si certissime, tum indeclinabiliter. Omnis enim scientiæ divinæ certitudo supponit objectum necessari-um. 3. Ex Arminiana sententia quam ridiculæ & histrionicæ essent hæ consolationes, dulcissimæ? nempe ita vobiscum acturus sum, ut fieri possit ut non sanctificetur, sed profanetur nomen meum, ut non purgemini ab immunditiis, ut maneat in vobis cor lapideum, ut non fit in vobis cor novum, ut ambuletis non in meis præceptis, sed in viis vestris malis, ut non tangamini dolore & fastidio male anteactæ vitæ, ut gentibus fitis prædæ, ut terra desolationi fit. Qualis hæc, & quam jejuna consolatio? Quis inter Deum consolantem, & judicia tonantem, inter ipsum gratiosè & euangelicè promittentem, & dira comminationum legalium fulmina vibrantem discernere poterit? 4. Quod dicunt [sic tamen, ut res aliter cadere posset,] satis infinuunt Deum dare tantum potentiam faciendi sibi cor novum & potentiam ambulandi in præceptis Dei. At quid contradicentius textui [faciam ambuletis &c.?] nempe hoc est actum, per potentiam, & ambulare per ejus contradictorium, non ambulare exponere, quod est invertere Sacras Scripturas. Atqui quæro, an non liceat populo Dei orare cor novum hic promissum? Non negabunt, opinor. Et tum sequitur fideles orare potentiam obediendi, quod supra ipsos negasse audivimus.
units.tr: 5. Answer to the Remonstrants and Corvinus. They say the promise is to be understood of such a mode of operation as would have a singular and admirable force to kindle and inflame anew the hearts of the whole people with love of God and of the divine laws, even though otherwise they were far estranged from the observance of the divine precepts, and so keep them always in duty and faith; yet in such a way that the matter could, though not probably, still turn out otherwise, that is, that they might either not be inflamed with that love, or, once inflamed, might grow cold again and return to their former nature. So far they. Corvinus says that this promise regards the heap of God's benefits, which cannot fail to move them to obedience, unless they had cast off all fear of God and [illegible, about one letter] not always note the event and effect, but often the end and intention: Ezek. 24. 13, "I have cleansed you," and you were not cleansed; Jer. 51. 9, "We would have healed Babylon, but she is not healed"; so false teachers are said to make the people trust in a lie, Jer. 29. 31; and the Canaanites are going to draw the sons of Israel away after them, Deut. 7. 4. Answer 1. They give us a singular mode by which God inflames hearts to obedience, although the contrary could happen, though not probably: what that [not probably] means, who knows? Namely, not probably, because God moves the will, ignorant of the future free act, yet God, by a probable or likely conjecture, supposes, unless the augury deceives, that they will be persuaded: here, namely, the Arminians want God to construct tropical syllogisms, as if he were a raw beginner in logic. Ah, blasphemy to be banished to hell! 2. Yet so that the matter could turn out otherwise, that is, that they might not be inflamed with that love: so they weaken the whole singular and admirable force, since that force accomplishes nothing but leaves the heart uninflamed; and so, with that promise posited, God no more gives a new heart than he does not give it. Indeed, with the Arminian fictions standing, this threat is as grievous as the promise is gracious, as much from justice as from mercy. For if God uses such an admirable force in the affection of the new heart, from which there follows a stony heart and a perverse and stubborn resistance to God regenerating, just as much as a new heart and a new spirit, then God threatens them with a stony heart just as he promises a new heart, and then these promises are ridiculous and truly hypocritical; and then the verse 32, "I do not do these things for your sake," namely, "for your sake and your evil ways I take away the stony heart from you," must necessarily come back to this sense, that they will not be hardened because of their sins, but for the glorious name of God. This the Remonstrants do not dare to assert. But indeed many gracious benefits are promised here: that God wishes to be sanctified (v. 23); that peace of conscience and true tranquillity (v. 28), and sorrow according to God (v. 31), are promised; remission of sins (vv. 28, 33); their prayers are to be heard (v. 37); and the nations will acknowledge that God is their God (v. 36); and he declares that this will certainly come to pass (v. 36): "For I, Jehovah, have spoken, and I will do it." All these (I say) most certainly signify that it will not probably and likely, but most certainly come to pass, that a new heart and a new spirit will be given to them; and if most certainly, then indeclinably. For the certainty of divine knowledge presupposes a necessary object. 3. On the Arminian view how ridiculous and theatrical would these most sweet consolations be? Namely: "I will so deal with you that it may happen that my name is not sanctified but profaned; that you are not cleansed from your uncleannesses; that the stony heart remains in you; that a new heart is not in you; that you walk not in my precepts but in your own evil ways; that you are not touched by sorrow and disgust at your ill-spent life; that you become a prey to the nations; that the land becomes a desolation." What kind of consolation is this, and how empty? Who will be able to distinguish between God comforting and God thundering judgments, between him promising graciously and in the gospel, and brandishing the dire thunderbolts of legal threats? 4. What they say, [yet so that the matter could turn out otherwise,] sufficiently hints that God gives only the power of making for themselves a new heart and the power of walking in the precepts of God. But what could be more contradictory to the text [I will cause you to walk, etc.]? Namely, this is to act, through power, and to explain walking as its contradictory, not walking, which is to subvert the Holy Scriptures. And yet I ask, is it not lawful for the people of God to pray for the new heart promised here? They will not deny it, I think. And then it follows that the faithful pray for the power of obeying, which we have heard them deny above.

units.la: 5. Corvinus hoc per congeriem beneficiorum effici, & Remonstrantes, vi singulari & admirabili fieri docent. At hic nihil de infusione supernaturalis potentiæ, nihil de gratia interna: totares per beneficia, morali suasione moventia transfigitur. At vero tum quando populum ex Ægypto deduxit, quo beneficio quid præstantius? Quando ad ipsos liberandos, spoliis hostium ditandos, naturam toties miraculis permultis commutavit, mare rubrum divisit, luce & igne cælitus lucente deduxit, hostes submersit, ipsis novum cor dederat, & legem cordi inscripserat, quod aperte negat Deus. Ier. 31. v. 31. 32. An non sic Moabitis, Ammonitis & Chaldæis novum cor dedit?
units.tr: 5. Corvinus teaches that this is effected through a heap of benefits, and the Remonstrants teach that it is done by a singular and admirable power. But here there is nothing about the infusion of a supernatural power, nothing about internal grace: rather, the people are driven along by benefits that move them through moral persuasion. Yet when God led the people out of Egypt, what benefit could be greater? When, to free them and enrich them with the spoils of their enemies, he so often changed nature by very many miracles, divided the Red Sea, led them by a light shining from heaven and by fire, and drowned their enemies, had he given them a new heart and written the law on their hearts? This God plainly denies. Ier. 31. v. 31. 32. Did he not in this way give a new heart to the Moabites, Ammonites and Chaldeans?

units.la: 6. Dicit Corvinus hæc beneficia ipsos permovere potuisse, nisi omnem Dei timorem exuissent. At eos quibus inest cor saxeum, uti est in irregenitis, omnem Dei timorem exuisse, quis dubitat? At quid est exuere omnem Dei timorem? nempe ego credo nihil aliud esse, quam ita saxeos esse homines, ut nolint permoveri ad obedientiam, nolint ambulare in Dei præceptis. Huc ergo redit Corvini sophisticatio, ipsos potuisse non exuisse omnem Dei timorem, & potuisse permoveri ad obediendum, si non exuissent omnem Dei timorem, & non permoti non fuissent ad obediendum, & potuisse ipsos cor lapideum abjecisse, nisi retinuissent, & Deum ipsis cor novum dedisse, si non negaverit: quæ vertigo est hæc malesani cerebri? 7. Particulam 5[?] non notare eventum, sed finem, quo Deus potest excidere, est Deum veracem esse in promissis; siquidem homines velint: quo quid absurdius? Nec sufficit si dixerint promissiones has esse conditionales, nempe Deus promittit dare cor novum, siquidem velint recipere: at vero an corde lapideo cor novum recipiunt? Monstrofum hoc esset dictu: si corde novo recipiunt cor novum, tum habent cor novum, antequam habeant (loquor de hominibus in primo conversionis momento) quod absurdum est; vel pura natura cor novum recipiunt, qui Pelagianismus est: dent illi quartum. At quæro conditionem postulatam à nobis, nempe si velimus, hoc est, Deus efficit in nobis novum velle, si efficiat in nobis novum velle. 8. Loca scripturæ citata sunt plane heteroclita, quasi vero non efficacius Deus efficeret cor novū in electis, quam comminationibus & externis beneficiis curata fuit Babylon, aut pari efficacia, qua Cananæi & Diabolus advocat homines àDeo: valde sapit hoc gratiam pelagianam.
units.tr: 6. Corvinus says these benefits could have moved them, unless they had cast off all fear of God. But who doubts that those who have a stony heart, as the unregenerate have, have cast off all fear of God? What, however, is it to cast off all fear of God? I believe it is nothing other than to be so stony that men will not be moved to obedience and will not walk in God's precepts. So Corvinus' sophistry comes down to this: they could have been moved to obey, had they not cast off all fear of God, and they were not moved to obey; they could have cast away the stony heart, had they not kept it; and God, if he does not deny that he gave them a new heart. What a vertigo this is, from a deranged brain! 7. That the particle (here "if") does not denote the outcome but the end, by which God could fail to be true to his promises, provided men are willing: what could be more absurd? Nor is it enough for them to say that these promises are conditional, namely that God promises to give a new heart, provided they are willing to receive it. But do they receive a new heart with a stony heart? This would be monstrous to say. If with a new heart they receive a new heart, then they have a new heart before they have it (I speak of men at the first moment of conversion), which is absurd; or they receive a new heart by pure nature, which is Pelagianism. Let them add a fourth alternative. But I ask for the condition demanded by us: that if we are willing, that is, God works in us a new willing, if he works in us a new willing. 8. The passages of Scripture cited are plainly irregular, as if God could not work a new heart in the elect more effectively than Babylon was healed by threats and external benefits, or with the same efficacy by which the Canaanites and the Devil summon men away from God. This smacks strongly of Pelagian grace.

units.la: 9. Quæro an unquam Dei populo dubium tale in mentem venire potuit: Deum daturum cor novum ipsis, siquidem non reluctarentur, sed si ipsi velint habere: quasi vero timuissent, ne reluctantibus & invitis novum cor dedisset, imo sic Diabolus, quos multa patientia tolerat, & omnibus nationibus cor novum dat.
units.tr: 9. I ask whether any such doubt could ever have come into the mind of God's people: that God would give them a new heart, provided they did not resist, but only if they themselves were willing to have it; as if they feared that he would give a new heart to those resisting and unwilling. Indeed, that is how the Devil behaves, whom he tolerates with much patience, and to whom he gives a new heart among all nations.

units.la: 11. Addunt Remonstr. in apol. Hæc promissio eodem cap. 11. 17 Dabo vobis cor carneum, allegatur tanquam ratio, qua futurum dicitur, ut amoverent omnia detestabilia, & tamen subjicitur, & quorum cor ambulat post abominationes suas, viam eorum in caput eorū dabo. At ridiculæ comminationes sunt, si efficacia talis promissa statuatur, quæ voluntatem eorum ad amovendum abominationes determinatura erat. R. 1. Manifesta est distinctio inter electos v. 17. & reprobos de quibus v. 21. & illa promissio est non tantum ratio, sed & causa efficax quare amoveant detestabilia. Comminationes optime consistunt cum tali efficacia, ut & præcepta, quoniam ii, quibus deest talis efficacia, liberrime defectui talis efficaciæ subscribunt, vel potius absentiam ipsius amant, ideoque jure puniuntur, & optime manet locus præceptis, quoniam electi liberrimè tali efficaciæ subscribunt: nec pugnat aliquem non posse non obedire, & tamen ei præcipi ut obediatur, quod in Christo clarum est, qui non potuit non ponere animam pro ovibus suis, & tamen hoc mandatum ponendi animam à Patre accepisse testatur, Iob 10. 17.18. & in Paulo qui mandato obedivit ut Act. 26.19. collat. cum Act. 9. 11. & 20 & tamen Iesuitæ & Arminiani volunt eum non potuisse non obedire, propter motionem extraordinariam, quâ eum actum fuisse docent.
units.tr: 11. The Remonstrants add in their Apology: this promise, I will give you a fleshly heart, in the same chapter 11, verse 17, is alleged as a reason why it is said they would put away all detestable things. And yet it is added: "And as for those whose heart walks after their abominations, I will bring their way upon their own head." But these threats are ridiculous if such a promise is held to be efficacious, one which would determine their will to put away abominations. Answer 1. The distinction between the elect (v. 17) and the reprobate, of whom v. 21 speaks, is plain; and that promise is not merely a reason but an effective cause why they put away detestable things. Threats agree very well with such efficacy, just as precepts do: for those who lack such efficacy most freely consent to its lack, or rather love its absence, and so are rightly punished; and there remains good room for precepts, since the elect most freely consent to such efficacy. Nor is it contradictory that someone cannot but obey and yet is commanded to obey. This is clear in Christ, who could not but lay down his life for his sheep, and yet testifies that he received this command from the Father to lay it down, Iob 10. 17, 18; and in Paul, who obeyed the command, Act. 26. 19, compared with Act. 9. 11 and 20. Yet the Iesuitæ and Arminiani want him to have been unable not to obey, on account of an extraordinary motion by which, they teach, he was actuated.

units.la: 12. Ier. 24. 7. Indam cor iis ad me cognoscendum, & revertentur ad me toto corde suo. Ier. 32. 40. Disponam cum iis fœdus sempiternum, non recedam ab eis, ut benefaciam iis. At Arminiani clamant, penes nos esse (utpote cum indeclinabiliter non flectatur à Deo libera voluntas) à Deo recedere. Mihi videtur Spiritus Sanctus, hisce explicatissimè contradixisse, quando ib. addit ad affruendam fœderis, ex utraque parte contrahente, sempiternitatem. Et indam timorem meum in cordibus eorum, ut à me non recedant. Ita Ier. 31. 33. 37. 39 Iesai. 54. 10. Iesai. 50. 20. 21. Imo & fœdus Dei juramento stabilitum Heb 6 13 luculentissimè demonstrant fieri non posse, quin violetur hoc novum fœdus, si non Deus ad obediendum & libere perseverandum in gratia ita moveat & flectat voluntates hominem, ut non possint eo non permoveri, & illuc suaviter trahi & duci quo Deus velit & intendat.
units.tr: 12. Ier. 24. 7. I will give them a heart to know me, and they shall return to me with their whole heart. Ier. 32. 40. I will make with them an everlasting covenant; I will not turn away from them, that I may do them good. But the Arminians cry out that it is in our power (since free will is never bent indeclinably by God) to turn away from God. It seems to me the Holy Spirit has most explicitly contradicted this, when in the same place he adds, to secure the everlastingness of the covenant on both contracting sides: And I will put my fear in their hearts, that they may not depart from me. Ita Ier. 31. 33. 37. 39, Iesai. 54. 10, Iesai. 50. 20. 21. Indeed, the covenant made firm by God's oath, Heb 6. 13, most clearly shows that this new covenant cannot fail to be broken unless God so moves and bends the wills of men to obey and to persevere freely in grace, that they cannot but be moved by it, and are gently drawn and led wherever God wills and intends.

units.la: Putant fe expediisse nodum hunc Herculeum, quando dicunt fœdus novum esse æternum, quoniam Deus juravit fe promissa præftiturum, siquidem nos non deerimus cooperando, hoc est, fi nos velimus obedire. At vero sic fœdus operum erat æternum: Deus enim fanćte dicit, qui faciet hæc vivet in illis, & præstantibus legem non minus vitam reddit operibus promissam, quam implentibus fœdus novum: sic & fœdus operum cum angelis qui lapsi sunt, eo sensu effet æternum. Imo sic illud Cajino dictum à Iehovah Genef. 4. Nonne fi benefeceris, eris acceptus? effet fœdus æternum, quod tamen statim violavit Cajin homicidio & miserâ conscientiæ desperatione, & merces non manducationi fructuum arbotis vetitæ promiffa, effet æternum fœdus: quo quid abfurdius dici potest? At Ieremias statuit discrimen effentiale inter fœdus cum patribus à discessu ex Ægypto ictum, nempe quatenus erat legale, & fœdus hoc novum, quod illud ruptum effet à patribus, ideoque æternum non erat; hoc vero æternum erit, ideoque à fœderatis non magis posset rumpi, quam fœdus Dei naturale, cum nocte & die, quam latitudo cœli, utterræ profunditas indagari posset. Ier. 31. v. 34. 35, 36, 37.
units.tr: They think they have untied this Herculean knot when they say the new covenant is eternal, since God has sworn that he will perform the promises, provided we do not fail to cooperate, that is, provided we are willing to obey. But in that case the covenant of works was eternal too. For God rightly says: He who does these things shall live in them, and to those who keep the law he gives life, promised to works no less than to those who fulfil the new covenant. In the same sense the covenant of works with the angels who fell would be eternal. Indeed, by that reasoning the saying of Jehovah to Cajino, Iehovah Genef. 4., Nonne fi benefeceris, eris acceptus? (Is it not so, if you do well, you will be accepted?), would be an eternal covenant, which yet Cain at once violated by homicide and by a wretched despair of conscience. And the reward promised not for eating the fruit of the forbidden tree would be an eternal covenant. What could be said more absurd? But Ieremias establishes an essential difference between the covenant struck with the fathers at the departure from Egypt, namely insofar as it was legal, and this new covenant. That covenant was broken by the fathers and therefore was not eternal; but this one will be eternal, and therefore cannot be broken by those in covenant any more than God's natural covenant with day and night can be broken, or the breadth of heaven or the depth of the earth searched out. Ier. 31. v. 34, 35, 36, 37.

units.la: 2. Aliud effugium innuit Arminius. Inter alia (inquit) ille status (Adami sub fœdere operum) non habuit promissionem remissionis peccatorum, fi contingeret Adamum vel semel peccare: fidelium vero (status) ista promissione fit beatior: peccatorum illoillorum non recordabor amplius. Unde accidit ut fides Dei non reddatur irrita, etiamsi fœderati ipsius peccent. Rom. 3. Est enim fœdus gratiæ, fidei &c.[?]
units.tr: 2. Arminius suggests another escape. Among other things (he says): that state (of Adam under the covenant of works) did not have the promise of remission of sins, if it happened that Adam sinned even once; but the state of believers is made happier by this promise: I will remember their sins no more. Hence it happens that God's faithfulness is not made void, even if his covenanted people sin. Rom. 3. Est enim fœdus gratiæ, fidei &c.[?]

units.la: Pone tamen quascunque voles differentias, necesse semper fatearis perseverantiam (ac proinde omnem obedientiam: est enim par ratio & eadem) voluntariam, liberam & mutabilem in utroque statu ad salutem.R.1. At non tantum Deus Ier. 31. vult fœdus novum ornari beatitudine remissionis promissæ, sed & indeclinabilitatis in statu illo beato, sicut consistunt, immota & fixa lege, nox & dies, solis, lunæ, & astrorum revolutiones constantissimæ, imo sicut montes in suis sedibus stabilissime consistentes Esai. 54. 10. uti textus dicit, & Arminio aperte contradicit. 2.
units.tr: Grant whatever differences you like, you must always admit that perseverance (and therefore all obedience, for the reasoning is the same and equal) is voluntary, free and mutable in both states as regards salvation. Answer 1. But God in Ier. 31. wills that the new covenant be adorned not only with the blessedness of promised remission, but also with indeclinability in that blessed state, just as night and day, and the most constant revolutions of the sun, moon and stars, stand by a fixed and immovable law; indeed, as mountains stand most firmly in their seats, Esai. 54. 10., as the text says, and this openly contradicts Arminio. 2.

units.la: Concedit Arminius peccatis fidelium non irritam reddi Dei fidem, at ambiguè & falsò; quid? An peccato Adami Deus fide & veritate excidit? Quid tibi vis Iacobe? debebas dixisse peccatis fidelium non irritum esse fœdus Dei? ita enim vult Apostolus. Rom. 3. Hoc non audes dicere: tum enim cum omnibus apostatis & finali impœnitentia diem suum claudentibus, ratum staret fœdus novum, præsertim si fide excidissent, uti tu doces. Vis igitur per peccata quæ Dei fidem irritam non faciunt, omnia peccata notari præter impœnitentiam. At quare exciperes impœnitentiam? Impœnitentiæ enim promittitur remissio, & data fuit Paulo, Zachæo, Mariæ Magdalenæ, Latroni resipiscenti in cruce. Nam Ezech. 36, 33. ubi eadem est promisso[?]; testibus Remonstrantibus illa apologia, promittitur in illo fœderę purgatio ab omnibus iniquitatibus. Ergo vel impoenitentia non est iniquitas, quod est dictu iniquum, vel certe promittitur remissio impoenitentiæ. Ergo necesse est Deus tandem aliquando gravissimum apostatam fœderatum resipiscentia indeclinabiliter donet, vel non manebit fides Dei rata; etiam peccantibus fœderatis. At cur peccatorum & non impoenitentiæ venia promittatur, non concipio. 3. Quomodo rata manet fides Dei, si fœderati gratia excidere & perire possunt, non minus quam pereunt, qui fœdus operum violárunt? quia nempe Deus præstat fidem credentibus & resipiscentibus. At sic manet rata Dei fides in fœdere operum, Deus etiam fidem præstat operantibus. 4. Si in utroque fœdere semper est par & naturalis illa indifferentia peccandi vel non peccandi, tum fœdus operum erit tam stabile, atque montes, atque Dei fœdus naturale cum die & nocte, quod elogium æternitatis Scripturæ adimit primo fœderi aperte. Ier. 31. 32. Non secundum fœdus quod pepigi cum patribus eorum, eo die quo ipsos manu prehendi, & ex terra Ægypti eduxi, quod fœdus meum violárunt. Atqui violari potest novum fœdus, si sit talis indifferentia peccandi vel non peccandi in voluntate. At vero fortius astruitur stabilitas & perpetuitas hujus fœderis. Ier. 32. 40. Faciam cum iis fœdus sempiternum, non recedam ab iis ut ipsis benefaciam: & indam timorem meum in cordibus ipsorum, quo minus à me reci-[?] recedant. §. Huc inclinat Arminius, quod fœdus legale hoc nomine sit æternum, quod postquam semel violatum est, cessat esse via ordinaria perveniendi ad salutem, & vero etsi homines peccent in fœdus novum, non cessat esse via ordinaria ad salutem, quoniam semper resipiscentibus vitam promittit: at vero nec sic satisfacit. Non cessat fœdus legale simpliciter, sed secundum quid, esse via perveniendi ad salutem, nempe propter carnis impotentiam. Rom. 8. Quo sensu fœdus novum præfractis non magis est via ad salutem quam fœdus operum; imo adhuc fœdus operum dicit (fac hoc & vives Rom. 10.): at si non promittatur in fœdere novo gratia determinans, nullo modo est fœdus stabile, uti dicit scriptura, sed tam instabile, atque fœdus operum, quando aperte contradicit scripturæ.
units.tr: Arminius concedes that the faith of God is not made void by the sins of believers, but he does so ambiguously and falsely. What then? Has God lost faith and truth through the sin of Adam? What do you mean, Jacob? You ought to have said that the covenant of God is not made void by the sins of believers, for that is what the Apostle wills, Rom. 3. You do not dare to say this. For then, since all apostates who end their days in final impenitence would remain, the new covenant would stand firm, especially if they had fallen from faith, as you teach. Do you want, then, that by the sins which do not make void the faith of God, all sins are meant except impenitence? But why would you except impenitence? For remission is promised to impenitence, and it was granted to Paul, to Zacchaeus, to Mary Magdalene, and to the thief who repented on the cross. For Ezek. 36.33, where the same promise is made, as that Remonstrant apology bears witness, cleansing from all iniquities is promised in that covenant. Therefore either impenitence is not iniquity, which is absurd to say, or certainly the remission of impenitence is promised. It is necessary, then, that God at some time grant repentance irrevocably even to the most grievous apostate in the covenant, or the faith of God will not remain firm, even with covenant members who sin. But why the pardon of sins, and not of impenitence, is promised, I do not understand. 3. How does the faith of God remain firm if covenant members can fall from grace and perish, no less than those perish who violated the covenant of works? Because, of course, God gives faith to those who believe and repent. But in that case the faith of God remains firm in the covenant of works also, since God gives faith to those who work. 4. If in both covenants there is always that equal and natural indifference to sinning or not sinning, then the covenant of works will be as stable as the mountains, and as God's natural covenant with day and night. This is an attribute of eternity which Scripture plainly denies to the first covenant: Jer. 31.32: Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers, on the day I took them by the hand and led them out of the land of Egypt, which covenant they broke. Yet the new covenant can be broken if there is such an indifference in the will to sinning or not sinning. But the stability and perpetuity of this covenant are asserted more strongly: Jer. 32.40: I will make with them an everlasting covenant, I will not turn away from them to do them good; and I will put my fear in their hearts, so that they do not depart from me. § Arminius inclines to this view, that the legal covenant is called eternal for this reason: once it has been violated, it ceases to be the ordinary way of attaining salvation; but even if men sin against the new covenant, it does not cease to be the ordinary way to salvation, since it always promises life to those who repent. But he does not satisfy even so. The legal covenant does not simply cease to be a way of attaining salvation, but only in a certain respect, namely because of the weakness of the flesh (Rom. 8). In this sense the new covenant is no more a way to salvation for the obstinate than the covenant of works is; indeed the covenant of works still says (do this and you will live, Rom. 10). But if in the new covenant no determining grace is promised, it is in no way a stable covenant, as Scripture says, but as unstable as the covenant of works, since it plainly contradicts Scripture.

units.la: 13. Matth. 11.25. Gratias ago tibi Pater (inquit Christus,) Domine cœli & terræ, quoniam hæc abscondideris à sapientibus, & parvulis detexeris. 26. Ita est ō Pater, quoniam ita est beneplacitum coram te. Hinc arguo sic: causa efficax cur illuminentur parvuli, & non sapientes est Dei εὐδοκία, cujus nomine Christus solus Dei gratias agit, tanquam ei a quo pendet τῷ actu illuminari, potius quam non illuminari. Alioqui, si ex libera hominis cooperatione pendeat, quod hic illuminetur, & alter pari gratiâ præveniente instructus, non illuminetur; homini non Deo, agendæ essent gratiæ. Arminiani dicunt ex humititate hujus esse, quod illuminetur, ex fastuosâ sapientiæ affectatione esse, quod hic non illuminetur, & decretum Dei esse illam ἐνδοξίαν[?]. R.1. Certum est Cassianum & Faustum hanc interpretationem à Pelagio haustam tradidisse. Arminiani vero vocem meriti declinant, rem ipsam vero tradunt. Imo illi sicut & Pontificii, ad meriti quidditatem gratiam Dei requiri docuerunt, ut observarunt Prosper & Fulgentius. 2. Sit hoc igitur decretum & ἐνδοξίαν[?] Dei; Decerno ut omnes convertantur, fiquidem parvuli sint. Et hujus contrarium erit (decerno ut nulli convertantur fi sapientes sint) non extat tale decretum in tota scriptura. Sic enim omnes humiles converterentur & nulli sapientes: at hoc posterius falsum. 1. Cor. 1. Nonnulli nobiles, non multos sapientes Deus elegit. Ergo quidam, licet non multi, sapientes convertuntur, & sic Deus ipse hoc decretum rescinderet, quod absurdum. 3. Si per parvulos, hic intelligit habitu humiles, sic non potest non rescindi decretum hoc, quoniam habitualis humilitas non indeclinabiliter determinat voluntatem ad conversionem, & sic multi humiles non convertuntur. Si vero per τῷ[?] parvulum esse, intelligitur τῷ[?] actu assentiri Deo revelanti, hoc certe non est aliud, quam τῷ[?] actu converti. Aqui actu converti non potest esse conditio prærequisita in convertendo, & sic hoc dato, quod τὸ[?] esse parvulum determinaret Dei voluntatem ad hunc convertendum, non illum, Deus necessitate justitiæ & veracitatis suæ hunc indeclinabiliter converteret, non illum, & sic efficacia gratiæ reducenda foret in Dei voluntatem determinantem, non in liberum arbitrium humanum. 4. Hæc ἐυδοκία[?] discriminat non tantum fastuosos ab humilibus, sed & totum genus humanum in duas classes dividit v 27. Neque cognoscit quis Patrem, præter filium, ᾧ ἂν βούληται ὁ υἱὸς ἀποκαλύψη[?]. Discriminatio itaque hæc directe refertur, non in voluntates sapientum & parvulorum, sed in Dei voluntatem revelantem patrem, cui vult. 5. Nullo colore Christus gratias agit Patri propter nudum decretum, sed eo quod suis discipulis & parvulis, non principibus hujus mundi dignitate & sapientia præclaris Christum revelaret. 6. Grevinchovius negat hic agi de revelatione fidei( nisi ( inquit ) forte fidem pro objecto fidei acceperis. Atqui doctrina fidei non tantum parvulis, sed & sapientibus revelata fuit. Alioqui quomodo fieri potuit ut sapientes hanc doctrinam odio & fastidio haberent? non revelata quis odio haberet? Si vero per τὸ[?] revelare hic notent actu fecundo illuminare, loquaturtu[?] necesse est hic Salvatorde[?] fidei ingeneratione, & sic humilitas habitualis erit causa efficaciæ hujus revelationis, quod absurdum est. 7. Si sapientes & parvuli sunt objectnm[?] formale hujus decreti, tum ii quibus revelatur hoc mysterium semper erunt indigniores & deteriores hisce, quibus non revelatur. Hoc autem Arminius gravate concedet, qui fatetur Deum paribus præstare imparem, imparibus vero parem gratiam, imo vero & pejoribus majorem adhibere gratiam, ac proinde minus bonis revelat mysterium hoc, & melioribus & humilioribus non revelat: hoc itaque decretum rescinderetur adhuc.
units.tr: 13. Matt. 11.25: I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to infants. 26. Yes, Father, for so it has pleased you. From this I argue as follows. The efficient cause why infants are enlightened and the wise are not is the good pleasure of God (εὐδοκία), for which alone Christ gives thanks to God, as to the one on whom it depends that he is enlightened rather than not. Otherwise, if it depended on the free cooperation of the man, that this one should be enlightened and the other, equally instructed by prevenient grace, should not be, thanks would have to be given to the man, not to God. The Arminians say that it is from the humility of the one that he is enlightened, and from the proud affectation of wisdom in the other that he is not, and that this good pleasure (ἐνδοξία) of God is a decree. 1. It is certain that Cassian and Faustus handed down this interpretation, drawn from Pelagius. The Arminians indeed avoid the word merit but hand down the thing itself. Indeed they, like the Papists, taught that the grace of God is required for the very quiddity of merit, as Prosper and Fulgentius observed. 2. Let this then be the decree and good pleasure of God: I decree that all be converted, provided they are infants. The contrary of this will be (I decree that none be converted, if they are wise). There is no such decree in all of Scripture. For thus all the humble would be converted and none of the wise, but the latter is false: 1 Cor. 1: Not many wise, not many noble, did God choose. Therefore some wise men, though not many, are converted, and so God himself would rescind this decree, which is absurd. 3. If by infants he means those humble in disposition, then this decree cannot but be rescinded, since habitual humility does not irrevocably determine the will to conversion, and so many humble men are not converted. But if by being infants is meant actually assenting to God revealing, this is certainly nothing other than actually being converted. But actually being converted cannot be a prerequisite condition in converting, and so, granting that being an infant determined God's will to convert this one rather than that one, God would of necessity of his justice and truthfulness convert this one irrevocably and not that one; and so the efficacy of grace would have to be referred to the determining will of God, not to human free will. 4. This good pleasure (εὐδοκία) distinguishes not only the proud from the humble, but divides the whole human race into two classes: v. 27: Nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him. So this distinction refers directly not to the wills of the wise and of infants, but to the will of God revealing the Father to whom he wills. 5. Christ gives thanks to the Father in no way for a bare decree, but because he revealed Christ to his disciples and infants, not to the princes of this world who are distinguished by dignity and wisdom. 6. Grevinchovius denies that revelation of faith is treated here (unless, he says, you take faith for the object of faith). But the doctrine of faith was revealed not only to infants but also to the wise. Otherwise how could it come about that the wise held this doctrine in hatred and disdain? Who would hate what has not been revealed? If, however, by revealing here they mean actually enlightening in the second sense, then the Saviour must necessarily be speaking of the generation of faith, and so habitual humility will be the cause of the efficacy of this revelation, which is absurd. 7. If the wise and infants are the formal object of this decree, then those to whom this mystery is revealed will always be worthier and better than those to whom it is not revealed. But Arminius will concede this with reluctance; for he confesses that God gives equal grace to the equal and unequal grace to the unequal, indeed even greater grace to the worse; and consequently he reveals this mystery less to the better and does not reveal it to the more excellent and humble. Thus this decree would still be rescinded.

units.la: 14. Quoscunque mihi dedit Pater, ii veniunt ad me Ioh. 6, 37. Item, omnes qui audiverunt, & didicerunt à Patre veniunt ad me. Iam norunt omnes logici propositiones [illegible, ~10 letters] esse necefsarias: hinc necessario dati à Patre, & necessari ò docti à Patre veniunt ad Christum, hoc est, credunt: atqui necessitatio nulla provenit ex libero arbitrio; ergo ex Deo ejusque gratia. Necessitas enim cum fit modus entis, ab iis causis oritur, àquibus ipsum ens: nullæ vero hic sunt causæ, nisi gratia, verbum, & creata libertas: non dicent necessitatem ab hisce duobus ultimis fluere: ergo à Deo gratiose movente fluat, necesse est. Si dati & docti à Patre, ita veniant ad Christum, uti ex indifferente humanæ libertatis determinatione possint non venire, tum posset hæc contradicens esse vera (quidam dati, & docti à Patre, non veniunt ad Christum:) &sic Christus(absint blasphemiæ) falsum dixisset. Subtilius est hic effugium Corvini, per [audire] (inquit) & [discere] notatur certa dispositio in nobis effecta per gratiam, qua fiat ut faciamus. id quod jubetur, hoc est, ut veniamus ad Christum. Resp. 1. Si notetur gratia qua fiat ut faciamus quod jubetur, indeclinabiliter habeo ininstitutum, gratiam nempe indeclinabiliter movere voluntatem: si declinabiliter, adhuc infero hoc esse verum: | Quidam qui audiverunt & didicerunt a Patre non veniunt ad Christum. | Sed latere voluit Sophista & vult hic notari certam dispositionem per gratiam effectam, qua fiat ut faciamus, quod jubetur. Sed an per hanc gratiam fiat, ut faciamus necessario, an contingenter, declinabiliter an indeclinabiliter, lectori, quem ludificari satagit, relinquit conjiciendum, ne causam malam proderet.
units.tr: 14. Whoever the Father has given me, they come to me (John 6.37). Likewise, everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me. Now all logicians know that propositions of this kind are necessary. Hence those necessarily given by the Father and necessarily taught by the Father come to Christ, that is, they believe. But no necessity arises from free will; therefore it arises from God and his grace. For necessity, since it is a mode of being, arises from the causes from which the being itself arises. But there are no causes here except grace, the word, and created liberty. They will not say that necessity flows from the last two; therefore it must flow from God graciously moving. If those given and taught by the Father come to Christ in such a way that, through the indifferent determination of human liberty, they could fail to come, then this contradictory could be true: some who are given and taught by the Father do not come to Christ. And so Christ (far be blasphemy) would have spoken falsely. The subtler escape of Corvinus is this: by hearing and learning (he says) is noted a certain disposition effected in us through grace, by which it comes about that we do what is commanded, that is, that we come to Christ. Reply: 1. If the grace is noted by which it comes about that we do what is commanded, I have this firmly established: grace indeclinably moves the will. If declinably, I still infer that this is true: some who have heard and learned from the Father do not come to Christ. But the sophist wished to hide this, and here wishes it to be noted, that a certain disposition is effected through grace, by which it comes about that we do what is commanded. But whether through this grace it comes about that we act necessarily or contingently, declinably or indeclinably, he leaves for the reader, whom he strives to mock, to conjecture, lest he betray his bad cause.

units.la: 2. Corvinus subti-lius quam solidè, per eos, qui audiverunt & didicerunt a Patre, intelligi vult eos qui ita audiverunt & didicerunt ut actu veniant ad Christum, & sic dixisset Salvator: omnes qui actu veniunt ad Christum, ii actu veniunt ad Christum: quæ insulsa quæstio inter Christum & Capernaitas nunquam agebatur, sed quæstio erat, cur quidam veniant ad Christum, quidam non? quasi vero mortales ulli Christo moverent quæstionem, an qui ita moventur a Patre ut actu veniant ad Christum, ii actu veniant ad Christum? An causa cur frigus aëris intensum ut actu causatur glaciem, actu causatur glaciem? An Corvinus actu errans cum Arminio sit causa cur erroribus Arminianis pertinaciter patrocinetur, quid stultius dici potuit?
units.tr: 2. Corvinus, more subtly than soundly, wants "those who have heard and learned from the Father" to mean those who have so heard and learned that they actually come to Christ. On this reading the Saviour would have said: all who actually come to Christ, they actually come to Christ. This empty question was never debated between Christum and the Capernaites. The question was why some come to Christum and others do not. As if any mortal ever put to Christ the question whether those who are so moved by the Father that they actually come to Christ actually come to Christ! Or is it as if the intense cold of the air actually causes ice only because it actually causes ice? Or is Corvinus, erring in fact along with Arminio, the reason why he stubbornly defends Arminian errors? What could be said that is more foolish?

units.la: 3. Hæc est Salvatoris consequentia: omnes docti erunt a Deo, ut scriptum est Jer. 31.34. Esai. 54. 13. Ergo venient ad me. Atqui ex Arminio & Corvino Christus sophistam (dominus meliora) egisset. Omnes qui ita docti erant à Patre, ii veniant ad me, ergo venient ad me: hoc ita habe. Omnes venient ad me: ergo omnes venient ad me. At si antecedens Christi stet sensu Arminiano, omnes erunt docti à Deo, nempe manente libertate indifferente, quâ fieri potest, ut vel veniant, ad Christum vel non veniant, conseq. Christi nihil salsius. Imo mihi tum licebit cū illis sic rhetoricari: omnes erunt docti àDeo: ergo non venient adChristū.
units.tr: 3. This is the Saviour's inference: "They shall all be taught of God, as it is written" (Jer. 31.34. Isa. 54.13.). Therefore they will come to me. But by the reasoning of Arminio and Corvino, Christ would have argued like a sophist (may the Lord do better): all who were so taught by the Father come to me; therefore they will come to me. That is how it stands: all will come to me, therefore all will come to me. But if Christ's antecedent is taken in the Arminian sense, that all will be taught by God, namely with indifferent liberty remaining, by which it can happen that they either come to Christ or do not come, then Christ's consequence is nothing more absurd. Indeed, I shall then be free to argue with them thus: all will be taught by God; therefore they will not come to Christ.

units.la: 15. Arminius vero naufragi more sic: Spiritus Sanctus (inquit) ita agit in liberum arbitrium, prout aptum & congruum novit, ut certò & infalliabiliter moveatur. Idem de tractu patris intelligi velim. Ita Fonseca, Suarez, Valentia. Sed Resp. Fonseca ib. fig. 9. ait vocationem congruam suo conceptu quiddam tativo includere obedientiam vocati. Et Suarez, ib. f. 9. aiti discere, idem esse quod credere, atqui venire ad Christum & credere prosus i- demfunt Itaque adhuc in omnes veniunt ad Christum & credent, qui veniunt & credunt. Suarez vero ait Deum respectu moralis infallibilitatis praevidentem omnes capacitatis libera angulos, infallibiliter determinare libertatem: at negat determinari à Deo, respectu infallibilitatis Metaphysicae, ita ut repugnet deficere, quia semper manet potentia Physica resistendi. Resp. 1. At quid tum postea? ea potentia vel est sopita, & sic ex tua philosophandi via tollitur libertas, & impeditur usus & exercitium, quod non est dicendum: vel non est sopita, & sic determinatio antecedens stat cum libertate quod in nostra doctrina, tu redarguis. 2. Ex Iesuitæ principiis inclinatio æqualiter indifferens ad nolle & velle, non est objectum infallibilis scientiæ, nec potest sciri determinatus actus ab illa inclinatione fluens, nisi in decreto Dei determinante; quod nunquam admittet Suarez. Scientia enim infallibilis in se prærequirit objectum scibile, quod sit necessarium vel in se, vel in alio determinante. Nam certitudinem mentis absque omni entis certitudine & necessitate, omnes metaphysici docent esse impossibilem, ideoque contra negantes principia non est disputandum. 3. Si metaphysicæ potentia libertatis deficere potest, nihil absurdi ponetur, si[?] actu deficeret, ut alibi Suarez & Vafquez contra decreta absoluta philosophantur, ac proinde moralis illa fvafio fallibiliter, non infallibiliter, determinet voluntatem, necesse est. Si vero vult, uti certe Iesuitæ mens est, moralem hanc determinationem includere præscientiam liberæ cooperationis arbitrii humani, puerilliter ludit, non disputat: quasi vero Deus dicendus esset moraliter determinare libertatem humanam, quoniam præscit ipsam esse determinaturam libere. Quis Deo determinationem tribueret, aut rationi à Deo moraliter adhibitæ, quando tota causalitas determinativa, quanta est, nec à Deo, nec quanta à ratione (quippe uterque libertatem indifferentiæ metaphysicæ relinquit) sed ab ipsa libertate humanâ, proficiscatur? dignus certe disputator, qui ex Academiâ Coymbricensi & è schola peripateticā[?], mihi crede, exfibiletur. Rotundè tamen Bellarminus efficaciam conversionis ex Joan. 6. 44. 45. tribuit excellentiae doctoris, non studio & industriae discipuli, sed non convenienter suae doctrinae: si hoc verum sit, Bellarmini vocatio congrua & theologia exterminabitur.
units.tr: 15. Arminius, like a shipwrecked man, says this: "The Holy Spirit (he says) so works upon free will, as he knows to be fitting and suitable, that it is moved certainly and infallibly. I would have the same understood of the drawing of the Father." So Fonseca, Suarez, Valentia. But the reply: Fonseca, ib. fig. 9, says that a congruous calling by its very concept somehow includes the obedience of the one called. And Suarez, ib. f. 9, says that to learn is the same as to believe, and that to come to Christ and to believe are altogether the same thing. So, on this view, all who come and believe will come to Christ and believe. Suarez however says that God, foreseeing with respect to moral infallibility all the free corners of capacity, infallibly determines liberty; but he denies that it is determined by God with respect to metaphysical infallibility, so that it would be impossible for it to fail, since the physical power of resisting always remains. Reply: (1) But what follows? That power is either lulled to sleep, and then by your way of philosophizing liberty is taken away and its use and exercise hindered, which must not be said; or it is not lulled, and then antecedent determination stands together with liberty, which is what you rebuke in our doctrine. (2) On Iesuitæ principles, an inclination equally indifferent to unwilling and willing is not the object of infallible knowledge, and a determinate act flowing from that inclination cannot be known unless in God's determining decree; which Suarez will never admit. For infallible knowledge in itself presupposes a knowable object that is necessary either in itself or in another that determines it. For all metaphysicians teach that certainty of mind without all certainty and necessity of being is impossible; therefore one must not dispute with those who deny principles. (3) If the metaphysical power of liberty can fail, nothing absurd is posited if it actually did fail, as Suarez and Vafquez elsewhere philosophize against absolute decrees; and so that moral persuasion must determine the will fallibly, not infallibly. But if he wishes to include in this moral determination the foreknowledge of the free cooperation of the human will, which surely is the Iesuitæ mind, he plays like a child and does not dispute: as if God were to be said to determine human liberty morally, because he foreknows that it will be determined freely. Who would ascribe determination to God, or to reason as morally applied by God, when all the determining causality, however great it is, proceeds neither from God nor from reason (for each leaves metaphysical liberty of indifference) but from human liberty itself? Certainly a worthy disputant, who has come from the Coymbricensi Academy and from the peripatetic school, believe me, should be hissed off the stage. Bellarmine, however, bluntly ascribes the efficacy of conversion (from John 6.44, 45) to the excellence of the teacher, not to the zeal and industry of the disciple; but this is not consistent with his own doctrine. If this is true, Bellarmine's congruous calling and his theology will be banished.

units.la: 16. 1. Corint. 4. 7. Quis te separavit? aut quid habes, quod non recepisti? Si autem recepisti, quid gloriaris, quasi non receperis? Si vero ex duobus gratia praeveniente ut 7. instructis, hic credit & efficit gratiam actu secundo & eventu efficacem, ille vero non credit, refistit, tum homo fe separavit, & gloriari potest hic, prae illo, in suo actu libero, nec est necesse, ut hic gratias Deo suae conversionis potius tribuat, quam non conversus. Contra Paulus suae conversionis laudes tribuit. 1. Tim. 1, 17. Regi aeterno immortali, & invisibili. Apoc. 5. 9. Glorificati deferunt laudes Agno, quoniam (inquiunt) tu mactatus eras, & redemisti nos Deo in sanguine tuo ex omni tribu & lingua, & populo, & gente. Jam si aliae gentes & populi pari gratia praeveniente donatae noluerunt credere, hi vero eadem tantum gratia liberè crediderunt, & separarunt se ab aliis, libero arbitrio faciente gratiam redemptionis & vocationis efficacem eventu & actu secundo, tum suae salutis gratias sibi, quam Christo potius debent. Nam norunt omnes logici, effectus productos in hoc objecto, & non in illo, non tribuendos esse causae communiter agenti, tam in hoc quam in illo objecto. Suppono solem omnes flores in horto æqualiter luce & calore suo imbuere, hic flos vegetat aliis arefcentibus, num recte dicerem floris vegetanti? o tu reliquis beatior, plus debes soli, quam reliqui. Sic enim subinnuerem, solem reliquos flores luce & calore non illustrare, hunc vero tantum beare, quod patet esse salsum.
units.tr: 16. (1 Cor. 4.7) "Who maketh thee to differ? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? Now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?" But if of two men, both equipped with prevenient grace in the same way, one believes and makes grace effective in the second act and in result, while the other does not believe and resists, then the man has separated himself, and the one can glory over the other in his own free act; nor is it necessary that he ascribe the thanks for his conversion to God rather than the one who was not converted. Paul, on the contrary, ascribes the praise of his own conversion to God. (1 Tim. 1.17) "To the King eternal, immortal, invisible." (Rev. 5.9) "The glorified ones bring praises to the Lamb, for (they say) thou wast slain and didst redeem us to God in thy blood, out of every tribe and tongue, and people and nation." Now if other nations and peoples, endowed with the same prevenient grace, were unwilling to believe, but these alone believed freely by that same grace, and separated themselves from the others, with free will making the grace of redemption and calling effective in result and in the second act, then they owe the thanks for their salvation to themselves rather than to Christ. For all logicians know that effects produced in this object and not in that one are not to be attributed to a cause that acts in common, equally in this object and in that. I suppose the sun imbues all the flowers in a garden equally with its light and heat; if one flower thrives while the others wither, would I rightly say that the flower thrives because of the sun? Oh, you are happier than the rest; you owe more to the sun than they do. For thus I would hint that the sun does not illuminate the other flowers with its light and heat, but blesses this one alone, which is plainly false.

units.la: R. I. Suarez ait: non expedit de suis gloriari. Valentia, gloriari (inquit) potest (conversus) non in Domino solo, sed tum in Domino, tum deinde in se. Fonseca ait, posse homines in se gloriari, sed tutius esse (ut dicunt Chrysostomus & Ambrosius) non gloriari ob periculum superbiæ & inanis gloriæ. Arminiani collat. hag. p. 333. Negant omnem gloriationem esse malam. Corvinus contr. Tilen. c. 5. p. 136. hominem tam se feparare dici posse, quam ait scriptura, hominem se sanctificare, purgare, vivificare, salvare. Rcsp 1. An homines in Domino gloriari possint, insanit qui in quæstionem aut ad partes vocet, ut ait scriptura, 1.Cor. 1. 30. & 31. Sed quæritur an liceat gloriari in eo quod recepimus, quasi non recepissemus. Ex adversariorum vero doctrina conversus, gratia præveniente, ut o&o [?], instructus, sicut & instruitur non conversus, potest gloriari in actu libero suæ conversionis activæ, quam a Deo non magis habet, quam nonconversus. 2. Quod in nobis & Domino velint gloriari, superbia est intolerabilis, nos cum Deo gloriam dividere contra scripturas.
units.tr: R. I. Suarez says: "it is not expedient to boast of one's own." Valentia says: "the converted man may glory (he says) not in the Lord alone, but both in the Lord and then in himself." Fonseca says that men can glory in themselves, but that it is safer (as Chrysostom and Ambrose say) not to glory, because of the danger of pride and vainglory. The Arminians, Hague Colloquy, p. 333, deny that all boasting is evil. Corvinus, against Tilenus, ch. 5, p. 136, says that a man can be said to separate himself as Scripture says that a man sanctifies, cleanses, quickens and saves himself. Reply: (1) Whether men can glory in the Lord is a question only a madman would raise or bring into dispute, as Scripture says (1 Cor. 1.30, 31). But the question is whether it is lawful to glory in what we have received, as if we had not received it. Yet by the doctrine of our opponents, the converted man, equipped with prevenient grace (just as the unconverted man is equipped too), can glory in the free act of his own active conversion, which he has no more from God than the unconverted man does.
