(2) That they wish to glory in us and in the Lord is an intolerable pride, which divides the glory between us and God, contrary to the Scriptures.

units.la: Psal.115. 1. Non nobis, non nobis, sed tibi, Iehova, gloria. 3. Quod non tutum esse velint in nobis gloriari, fateantur necesse est, se viam ad gloriam æternam minus tutam, nos vero tutiorem incedere: fruantur per nos ea periculosa via. 4. Scriptura ait homines se sanctificare, purgare, liberare, ut Dei instrumenta & agentia libera gratiæ prædeterminanti subordinata, sed hominem esse causam separantem se à numero reproborum pariter secum externe vocatorum, nusquam dicit Scriptura.
units.tr: Psal. 115. 1. Not unto us, not unto us, but unto thy name, O Jehovah, is the glory. 3. If they must admit that they do not think it safe to glory in us, they must also confess that they walk a less safe road to eternal glory, while we walk a safer one. Let them enjoy that perilous way through us. 4. Scripture says that men sanctify, cleanse and free themselves, as instruments and free agents subordinate to prevenient predetermining grace. But Scripture nowhere says that man is the cause that separates him from the number of the reprobate, who were equally called outwardly along with him.

units.la: 1. Refp. Suarez & cum eo servilis ille declamator Grevinchovius, sic Greci. Quis enim te discernit? id est, quis te dijudicat, aut unde te majore laude aut honore dignum censes, cum fallax sit humanum judicium? Refp. At sic Apostoli ratio contra vanam gloriationem, nec caput, nec caudam habet. Sive n. homo, sive Deus judex sit donorum, quibus aliis alii antecellunt, si homo à se habeat dona, in se potest gloriari, quod Apostolus illic reprehendit. Ideoque 3. addit Suarez ib admittendo receptam expositionem, apostolum nempe loqui de causa discretionis & differentiæ inter sanctum & non sanctum. Id autem fit duobus modis. Uno modo ut referatur in Deum solum: alio modo, ut referatur in Deum, ut in principalem authorem, non tamen solum. Priore modo id est secundum ordinem intentionis seu prædestinationis divinæ, non tamen secundum executionem. Quod enim ita Deus inter duos discre-
units.tr: 1. Reply. Suarez, and with him that servile declaimer Grevinchovius, quote the Greek: "For who makes you to differ?" [Τίς γάρ σε διακρίνει;] That is, who judges you, or why do you think yourself worthy of greater praise or honour, since human judgement is deceptive? Reply. But this argument of the Apostle against vain boasting has neither head nor tail. For whether man or God is the judge of the gifts by which some excel others, if man has the gifts from himself, he can glory in himself, which is exactly what the Apostle rebukes there. Therefore 3. Suarez adds, admitting the received exposition, that the Apostle speaks of the cause of distinction and difference between the holy and the unholy. This happens in two ways. In one way it is referred to God alone; in another, it is referred to God as the principal author, though not alone. In the first way, that is according to the order of intention or divine predestination, though not according to execution. For that God so distinguished between two that he chose this one and not that one, and prepared a fitting calling for this one and not for that one, was of the divine will alone. But that this one in fact obtains glory and is sanctified, and not that one, is not of the divine will alone, but also of the human will and cooperation, as the Council of Trent said. So far Suarez. Reply. 1. The sense of the Apostle will therefore be: who distinguished you in eternal election? What could be more forced? Does the Apostle have a syllable about predestination? Did it come into the mind of the over-proud Corinthians that they had predestined themselves from eternity? Are you not ashamed, Jesuit, to have written such inventions? 2. The Apostle is dealing with gifts and graces formally received by man from God; he does not touch that question about the cause why God predestines and effectually calls. Why say more? The question concerns acts and gifts in man; the Jesuit dreams that the question concerns the acts of God. 3. If free will together with God distinguished this one from that one with respect to the execution of the decree, why does the Apostle say, "Why do you glory?" Indeed, one may glory formally in free will distinguishing Peter from Judas.

units.la: 4. f. 9. discreverit, ut hunc elegerit, & non illum, & huic praeparaverit congruam vocationem,& non illi, solius divinæ voluntatis fuit. Quod vero in re iste assequatur gloriam, & sanctificetur, & non ille, non est solius voluntatis divinæ, sed etiam & voluntatis & cooperationis humanæ, ut dixit Concil. Trident. Hæcille. Refp. 1. Sensusigitur Apostoli erit: qu s te[?] discrevit in electione æterna? Quid coactius? An syllabam habet Apostolus de praedestinatione? An Corinthiis praetumidis in mentem venit se ab æterno sese praedestinasse? Erubuistine Iesuita, talia scripturiisse commenta? 2. Apostolus agit de donis & charismatis à Deo in homine formaliter receptis, non tangit quæstionem illam, de causa cur Deus praedestinet & efficaciter vocet. Quid multis? Quæstio est de actibus & donis in homine: Iesuita somniat quæri de actibus Dei. 3. Si liberum arbitrium una cum Deo discrevit hunc ab illo respectu executionis decreti, quare dicit Apostolus, quare gloriaris? Imo licet in libero arbitrio formaliter Petrum à Iuda discernente gloriari.
units.tr: 4. f. 9. Let it be granted that God distinguished between two in such a way that he chose this one and not that one, and prepared a fitting calling for this one and not for that one, was of the divine will alone. But that this one in fact obtains glory and is sanctified, and not that one, is not of the divine will alone, but also of the human will and cooperation, as the Council of Trent said. Thus far he. Reply. 1. The sense of the Apostle will therefore be: who distinguished you in eternal election? What could be more forced? Does the Apostle have a syllable about predestination? Did it come into the mind of the over-proud Corinthians that they had predestined themselves from eternity? Are you not ashamed, Jesuit, to have written such inventions? 2. The Apostle is dealing with gifts and graces formally received by man from God; he does not touch that question about the cause why God predestines and effectually calls. Why say more? The question concerns acts and gifts in man; the Jesuit dreams that the question concerns the acts of God. 3. If free will together with God distinguished this one from that one with respect to the execution of the decree, why does the Apostle say, "Why do you glory?" Indeed, one may glory formally in free will distinguishing Peter from Judas.

units.la: 4, Addit Iesuita: si illa, [quis te discernit?] dicta essent, quia Deus per physicam praedeterminationem hunc movet ad actum supernaturalem & non alium, eadem ratione in quocunq; bono actu morali æq; dicendum esseset solum Deum discernere operante à non operante: item & in malis actibus, idem effet dicendu. R. 1. Nihil hoc est absurdi, imo & necesfarium est hunc velle, quoniam Deus ipsum ad volendum determinat, hunc non velle, etiam in actibus naturæ peccato substratis, quia Deus ipsum non determinat. Nam Deus flectit cor Regis, quocunq; vult; gressus hominis, responsum linguæ, occisio viatoris a securi casu, ut videtur, delapsa, egressus fortuni[?] sunt a Deo absolute ista determinante. 2. At vero alio longe modo in actibus supernatuarlibus separat operantem a non operante, quoniam hisce actibus Deus & habitum supernaturalem & specialem influxum gratiæ determinantis contribuit: in actibus vero naturæ aut in malis actibus tantum communem prædeterminationem potentiis in creatione inditis tribuit, ideoque nullo modo est par separatio in his, & in illis. Nam ex speciali gratia & beneplacito quo prædestinamnr ad gloriam, Deus in actibus supernaturalibus nos separat ab aliis: at in actibus naturæ ex communi providentia fit separatio, ideoque Jesuita falso supponit nos statuere eandem prædeterminationem Physicam in actibus supernaturalibus & in naturalibus, quod non docemus. 3. Hoc absurdum vere gravabit Jesuitam, qui motionem congruam & non congruam in omnibus actibus liberis statuit,præsertim quoniam Dei influxum physicum parem in omnibus, hoc est, collateralem & indifferentem & generalem statuit.
units.tr: 4. The Jesuit adds: if those words, [who makes you to differ?], were said because God by physical predetermination moves this one to a supernatural act and not that one, then by the same reasoning it would have to be said equally in every morally good act that God alone distinguishes the one who acts from the one who does not act; and the same would have to be said of evil acts. Reply. 1. There is nothing absurd in this. Indeed it is necessary that God determines this one to will and that one not to will, even in natural acts that underlie sin, because God does not determine the other. For God turns the heart of the king wherever he wills; the steps of a man, the answer of the tongue, the killing of a traveller by an axe that falls by chance, as it seems, and the outcome of lots, all come from God absolutely determining them. 2. But in supernatural acts he separates the one who acts from the one who does not act in a far different manner, since in these acts God contributes both a supernatural habit and a special influx of determining grace. In natural acts, or in evil acts, he gives only a common predetermination to the powers implanted in creation. Therefore there is in no way an equal separation in these and in those. For by the special grace and good pleasure by which we are predestined to glory, God separates us from others in supernatural acts; but in natural acts the separation comes from common providence. So the Jesuit falsely supposes that we posit the same physical predetermination in supernatural acts and in natural ones, which we do not teach. 3. This absurdity will truly burden the Jesuit, who posits a congruous and non-congruous motion in all free acts, especially since he posits God's physical influx as equal in all, that is, collateral, indifferent and general.

units.la: 4. Refp. Corvinus, Grevinchov. Marc. Antonius de Dominis Archiepiscop. Spalatensis dicunt non agi hic de fide, aut de conversione ( verba sunt Corvini)sed de talibus donis, ob quæ doctores inter se gloriabantur, puta linguarum, eloquentiæ, sapientiæ, quæ simpliciter pendebant à pura Dei donatione, & quod aliquis vel careat istis donis, vel ea parcius habeat, ad id nullum momentum adfert libertas voluntatis, cum contra in discretione fidelis ab infideli, ista libertas momentum' afferat. R. 1. Augustin. Chrysost. Cyprian. Concil. Aranfi[?]. can. 6. 3. Concili. Melivita[?] temporibus Honorii & Arcadii in Africa habitum, ita exposuerunt. 2.
units.tr: 4. Reply. Corvinus, Grevinchovius, Marc Antonius de Dominis, Archbishop of Spalato, say that here it is not about faith or conversion (the words are Corvinus's), but about such gifts as teachers boasted of among themselves, for example of tongues, eloquence and wisdom, which depended simply on the pure gift of God; and that whether someone lacks these gifts or has them more sparingly contributes nothing to them, the freedom of the will, whereas in the distinction of the faithful from the unfaithful that freedom does contribute. Reply. 1. Augustine, Chrysostom, Cyprian, the Council of Orange, can. 6. 3. The Council of Milevis in the times of Honorius and Arcadius in Africa held and expounded it thus. 2.

units.la: Non stamus hominum authoritate, verum quidem est κατ' ἀρχὴν[?] non agi ib. de conversione hominis, neque nos eo sensu textum urgemus, sed Apostolus ex majore universali, [Quis te discernit? quid gloriaris?] infert conclusionem, non gloriandum in donis divinitus collatis, & universaliter verum vult, neminem se difcernere, ne in donis gratiæ collatis. Hinc nos inferimus, multo minus gloriandum in nobis, de dono longè omnium excellentissimo & electorum proprio, nempe salutari ad Deum conversione in qua major laus, & gloria longè eminentior Deo debetur, quam in collatione donorum, quæ Deus reprobis etiam gratificari nonnunquam solet.
units.tr: It is true that we do not stand on human authority. It is true that, at the outset, the passage is not about the conversion of man, and we do not press the text in that sense. But the Apostle, from the general major premise, [Who makes you to differ? Why do you glory?], draws the conclusion that one must not glory in gifts bestowed by God, and he means it as a universal truth: that no one distinguishes himself, not even in the gifts of grace conferred. From this we infer that there is much less reason to glory in ourselves about the gift by far the most excellent of all, and proper to the elect, namely salutary conversion to God. In that conversion greater praise and a far more eminent glory is due to God than in the bestowal of gifts, which God is accustomed sometimes to bestow even on the reprobate.

units.la: 3. Ad hoc nullum momentum afferre libertatem humanam, quod careat, vel parcius habeat hæc dona, salsissimum est. Quod enim Apollos eloquentia & scripturarum peritia polleret, libertas ipsius in scripturarum lectione vale-bat, bat. Alioqui frustra Paulus Timotheum hortaretur ad lectionem scripturarum. 1.Tim 4. 13. & v. 14. non vult illum negligere donum, quod ei per prophetiam conferebatur. 4.De illis donis vel tantum loqui Apostolum, vel de nullis aliis, nihil salsius, imo de omnibus donis apostolicis, quibus alii aliis antecellebant, & Corinthiis admirationi vanae essent, ita ut alii Paulum, alii Cephan, alii Apollinem magistrum fidei suspicerent, loquitur uti patet ex cap. 1. v. 13. 14. & cap. 2. v. 1, 2, 3. & cap. 3. v. 20. 21. 22. 23. & cap. 4. 1, 2, 3, 4. Et Apostolus omnem materiam gloriandi in libero donorum apostolicorum exercitio plane adimit, quando requirit ut ipsos habeant loco dispensatorum Dei, & fidelitatem requirit, in qua usum libertatis esse nemo non videt, & Apostolos a multarum afflictionum nempe infamiae, famis, sitis, nuditatis perpessione v. 10. 11, 12. falsis apostolis anteponit. In his autem perpessionibus relucebat libertas gratia divina ipsos a falsis doctoribus separante instructa. 5. Falsum etiam est ex Arminiana schola humanam libertatem nihil conferre ad hoc, ut quis parcius ista dona habeat. Quis enim neget Apostolis segnescentibus Deum sapientiam, eloquentiam, donum prophetiarum vel diminuturum, vel prorsus ablaturum, sicut servo defidi & ignavo aufert talentum, & Deum dona ista gnaviter laborantibus augere, siquidem Paulus per Dei gratiam diligentius reliquis omnibus laboravit 1,Cor. 15.10.
units.tr: 3. That human freedom contributes nothing to this, that someone lacks these gifts or has them more sparingly, is most false. For since Apollos excelled in eloquence and skill in the Scriptures, his freedom was at work in reading the Scriptures. Otherwise Paul would exhort Timothy to the reading of Scripture in vain (1 Tim. 4. 13), and at v. 14 he does not want him to neglect the gift that was given him through prophecy. 4. That the Apostle speaks either only of those gifts or of no others is nothing more false. Indeed he speaks of all apostolic gifts, in which some excelled others, and which were an object of vain admiration to the Corinthians, so that some revered Paul, some Cephas, and some Apollos as teacher of the faith. This is clear from ch. 1 v. 13-14, ch. 2 v. 1-3, ch. 3 v. 20-23, and ch. 4 v. 1-4. And the Apostle wholly removes every matter for boasting in the free exercise of apostolic gifts, when he requires that they hold them in the place of God's stewards, and requires faithfulness, in which no one fails to see the use of freedom. He sets the Apostles before false apostles by their endurance of many afflictions, namely infamy, famine, thirst and nakedness (v. 10-12). In these sufferings there shone forth the freedom of divine grace, which separated them from false teachers and equipped them. 5. It is also false that human freedom, on the Arminian view, contributes nothing to whether someone has these gifts more sparingly. For who would deny that God either diminishes or wholly takes away wisdom, eloquence and the gift of prophecy from Apostles who grow slack, just as he takes the talent from the faithless and idle servant? And that God increases these gifts for those who labour diligently, since Paul, by the grace of God, laboured more diligently than all the rest (1 Cor. 15. 10).

units.la: §. Refponfio honestior longe reliqvis est M. Antonii de Dominis Archiepiscopo Spalatensis: in ordinariis hominibus (inquit) nihil est absurdi, quod salvati nihil plus debeant Deo, damnati. R. Hoc reliqui coguntur admittere: hoc vero qui scripserit, equus an theologus dici mereatur, divinare mihi haud est in proclivi. Et tum, qui jam cruciatibus infernalibus sunt adjudicati agno, qui ipsos ex omnibus nationibus redemerit, gratias agere possunt, non minus quam qui ante thronum Dei stant. Hem theologiam damnatorum & nouum canticum[?]
units.tr: §. The more honest answer, far better than all the rest, is that of Marcus Antonius de Dominis, Archbishop of Spalato: "In ordinary men (he says) there is nothing absurd in the saved owing no more to God than the damned do." Reply: The rest are compelled to admit this; but whether the man who wrote it deserves to be called a horse or a theologian is not easy for me to guess. And then, those who have already been condemned to infernal torments can give thanks to the Lamb who redeemed them out of every nation, no less than those who stand before the throne of God. Behold the theology of the damned and a new song [?]

units.la: 6. Refp. Est Corvini. exastam (inquit) rationem causarum disparis istius eventus (conversionis, & non-conversionis) nobis esse incognitam fateor: in solo libero arbitrio eandem diversitatem quaerendam non esse similiter agnosco. R.I. Agnosce igitur errorem Arminianum, exactam rationem electionis & reprobationis, non esse fidem hujus & infidelitatem illius. Atqui Arminio tuo hæc prædestinatio est fundamentum christianismi (heu fragile fundamentum vel Corvino judice!) materies euangelii est, imo ipsum euangelium est. Atqui fluctuans & dubium est hoc Corvino Arminianorum, meo judicio, facile doctissimo, euangelium. Atqui semper rationem ante hac ex parte Dei, à justitia Dei convertente volentem, non convertente obicem ponentem, & ex parte nostri ab humano arbitrio accersendam confultissimum duxerunt Arminiani: nunc vero
units.tr: 6. Reply. He says: "I admit that the exact reason for the causes of this unequal outcome (of conversion and non-conversion) is unknown to us. I likewise acknowledge that the same diversity is not to be sought in free will alone." Reply: Acknowledge, then, the Arminian error: that the exact reason of election and reprobation is not the faith of the one and the unbelief of the other. Yet this predestination is, for your Arminius, the foundation of Christianity (alas, a fragile foundation, at least in the judgement of Corvinus!). It is the subject matter of the gospel, indeed it is the gospel itself. Yet this gospel is, in the judgement of Corvinus, the most learned of the Arminians (in my opinion, he is easily the most learned), wavering and doubtful. Yet the Arminians have always thought it most prudent to seek the reason on God's side, from the justice of God, who wills to convert, and who places an obstacle to the non-converting, and on our side, from human free will. But now

units.la: hæc ratio non est exacta: quam anceps & pendula fides Arminianorum est? 2. Ratio cur ex duobus pari gratia præveniente instructis hic convertatur, ille non, non est in solo libero arbitrio: ergo vel id in libero arbitrio & in Deo simul, vel in solo Deo. Si in Deo, tum quoniam non conversio activa Iudæ est peccatum, quærenda erit ratio & causa peccati aliquo modo in Deo, hoc non ferent Arminiani, & si ratio ullo modo sit alibi quam in solo libero arbitrio, num in fortuna? num in fato? num in constellatione? Absurda, bone Deus, omnia. Si in Deo, vel in justitia. At hoc dici non potest: sic enim causa ex parte hominis esset in solo libero arbitrio, quod negat Corvinus. Non in Dei misericordia, aut in bonitate. Quæ enim bonitas, quæ misericordia, aut bonitas, quæ misericordia, quod Iudas non convertatur? Si in Dei libertate, cur causam disparis istius eventus incognitam esse velis? At fare quæso, an non cognita fatis hæc causa? Miseror quorum volo misereri. Convictus est, & non audet se convictum fateri, sed erubescit.
units.tr: this reason is not exact: how wavering and unstable is the faith of the Arminians! 2. The reason why, of two men equipped with the same preventing grace, one is converted and the other not, does not lie in free will alone. Therefore it lies either in free will and in God together, or in God alone. If in God, then, since the active non-conversion of Judas is sin, the reason and cause of sin must be sought in some way in God. The Arminians will not bear this. And if the reason is in any way elsewhere than in free will alone, is it in fortune? In fate? In the constellation? Absurd, good God, all of these! If in God, is it in his justice? But this cannot be said, for then the cause on the human side would be in free will alone, which Corvinus denies. Is it in God's mercy, or his goodness? For what goodness, what mercy, is there in the fact that Judas is not converted? If it is in God's liberty, why do you wish the cause of this unequal outcome to be unknown? But tell me, I beg you, is this cause not known to the fates? "I have mercy on whom I will have mercy." He is convicted, and does not dare to confess himself convicted, but blushes.

units.la: 7. Refp. Duo hic Grevinchovius dicit 1. Nihil hic esse, in quo arbitrium gloriari possit. Duo enim sunt in arbitrio: 1. Quod effectivè suum actum producat, 2. Quod se ad actus determinet, & utrumque est a Deo. 3. Dicit vocationem esse conversionis fontem & fidei nostræ, & hanc esse a solo Deo: actualem vero applicationem remissionis peccatorum ad Petrum potius quam ad Iu-dam esse conversionis consummationem. Resp. Quod voluntas effective actum producat, quod se ad actum determinet, vult esse à Deo; atquomodo? à Deo ut creatore; mi bone vir. Atqui hoc dixit Pelagius, qui naturam & gratiam confundebat at sic τὸ[?] velle erit à Deo, sicut τὸ[?] currere in equo, & moveri ad centrum in lapide. Hæccine tua gratia? Si vis à Deo esse, quod voluntas se ad opus determinet, conscientia tua hoc dictitat esse falsum. Quid est determinare? nonne est removere indifferentiam ad nolle & velle? atqui vis Deum semper relinquere voluntatem suæ indifferentiæ: alioqui everteret libertatem, si tolleret indifferentiam. At vis hoc, Deum efficere ut ipsa voluntas tollat indifferentiam? atqui dico voluntatem tollere indifferentiam ad nolle vel velle, esse voluntatem velle & non nolle, vel nolle & non velle. Sed si Deus non efficit velle, nisi hoc modo, quoniam efficit ut voluntas possit nolle vel velle, sic Deus diceretur tollere indifferentiam, quoniam non tollit, sed voluntatem indifferentiæ relinquit. 2. Conversio ut est actus supernaturalis in nobis, (quo sensu jam de eâ disputamus) ex Arminianus est effectus divinæ vocationis, & causa conversionis comparativæ, Petri potius quam Iudæ, est merum arbitrium Petri, non Dei vocatio, non gratia præveniens, non cooperans. 3. Idem docuit Pelagius, principium conversionis esse à sola gratia Dei, quoniam lex & divina eloquia sunt à solo Deo. Augusti. de gestis Pelag. l. 1. c 11.
units.tr: 7. Reply. Here Grevinchovius says two things: 1. There is nothing here in which the will can glory. For there are two things in the will: (a) that it effectively produces its act, and (b) that it determines itself to the act; and both are from God. 3. He says that the calling is the source of conversion and of our faith, and that this comes from God alone; but that the actual application of the forgiveness of sins to Peter rather than to Judas is the completion of conversion. Reply: That the will effectively produces the act, and that it determines itself to the act, he wants to be from God. But how? From God as creator; my good man. Yet this is what Pelagius said, who confused nature and grace. So then the "to will" [τὸ θέλειν] will be from God in the way that the "to run" [τὸ τρέχειν] is in a horse, and the moving to the centre is in a stone. Is this your grace? If you want it to be from God that the will determines itself to the act, your conscience keeps saying that this is false. What is it to determine? Is it not to remove indifference to unwilling and willing? Yet you want God always to leave the will in its indifference; otherwise he would destroy liberty, if he removed indifference. But do you want God to bring it about that the will itself removes indifference? I say that for the will to remove indifference to unwilling or willing is for the will to will and not to unwill, or to unwill and not to will. But if God does not bring about willing except in this way, since he brings it about that the will can unwill or will, God would be said to remove indifference, since he does not remove it but leaves the will in indifference. 2. Conversion, as it is a supernatural act in us (and it is in this sense that we are now disputing about it), is, according to the Arminians, the effect of divine calling; and the cause of comparative conversion, of Peter rather than Judas, is the mere free choice of Peter, not the calling of God, not preventing grace, not co-operating grace. 3. Pelagius taught the same thing: that the beginning of conversion is from the grace of God alone, since the law and the divine oracles are from God alone. Augustine, On the Deeds of Pelagius, book 1, ch. 11.

units.la: Objicitur in tertio capitulo scripsisse Cœlestium gratiam Dei & adjutorium non dari ad singulos actus, sed in libero arbitrio esse, vel in lege ac doctrina.Grevinchov. in vocatione per legem & euangelium ponit gratiam. Augusti. l. de grat. Christi contra Pelag. & Coelest. c. 7. Adjuvat enim nos (inquit Pelag.) Deus per doctrinam & revelationem suam, dum cordis nostri oculos aperit, dum nobis, ne præsentibus occupemur, futura demonstrat, dum Diaboli pandit insidias, dum nos multiformi & ineffabili dono gratiæ cœlestis illuminat. Et ibid. c. 41. Ipsum vero auxilium, quo possibilitatem naturalem perhibet, adjuvari in lege constituit, atque doctrina, quam nobis fatetur Spiritu sancto revelari, propter quod adorandum esse concedit.
units.tr: It is objected that in the third chapter he wrote that the grace and help of God is not given for each individual act, but is in free will, or in the law and teaching. Grevinchovius places grace in the calling through law and gospel. Augustine, On the Grace of Christ against Pelagius and Coelestius, ch. 7. "For God helps us" (says Pelagius) "through his teaching and revelation, while he opens the eyes of our heart, while he shows us the future so that we are not occupied with the present, while he lays bare the snares of the devil, while he enlightens us with the manifold and ineffable gift of heavenly grace." And in the same work, ch. 41: "As for the help itself, by which he says natural possibility is aided, he holds that it is helped by the law and by the teaching, which he confesses is revealed to us by the Holy Spirit, on account of which he concedes that it is to be worshipped."

units.la: 17. Antequam vero ad alia loca vindicanda progrediar, hic ostendam Arminianos, non minus quam Pelagianos, divinæ gratiæ inimicos habere & posse, & debere. Docent enim, actum fidei, & liberæ ad Deum conversionis esse actum liberum contingentem, refistibilem, à suasoria verbi actione productum.
units.tr: 17. Before I proceed to vindicate other passages, I will show here that the Arminians, no less than the Pelagians, both have and must have enemies of divine grace. For they teach that the act of faith and of free conversion to God is a free act, contingent, resistible, produced by the persuasive action of the word.

units.la: Ita loquitur Grevinchovius: Forma (inquit) fidei est assensus, & assensus est a libera voluntate.
units.tr: Thus Grevinchovius speaks: "The form of faith (he says) is assent, and assent is from a free will."

units.la: Ita Corvinus: Nam sicut (inquit) voluntas sua natura est libera, ita fides est actus obedientialis, de cujus natura etiam est esse liberum. Ideoque actus fidei & conversionis consideratur vel ut supernaturalis, vel ut liber. Priore modo, nempe ut est supernaturalis, non est actus liber obedientialis à Deo mandatus, laude vel præmio dignus. Nam illis, quod non est liberum, non est obedientia, non est laude vel vituperio dignum, non cadit sub præceptum. Ideoque actus fidei, ut est liber, hoc est, ut est à puro arbitrio, ut à principio activo libero, est laude dignus, & tale quid, cui debeatur corona gloriæ, merces, & bravium. Et id quod Deum moveat ad eligendum hunc, non illum, Petrum, non Iudam, quid crassius à Pelagio, à Cœlestio, ab hæreticis gratiæ Dei inimicissimis docetur? Nam actus conversionis qua supernaturalis, nullo modo est à libero arbitrio, ac proinde nullo modo obedientia, neque supernaturalitas actus ullo modo est ab influxu arbitrii creati, sed à Dei gratiæ influxu, & est qualitas posterior & superaddita actui, qua libero seu contingenti, & à Deo mandato. Itaque à libero arbitrio est, quod fit assensus & conversio, potius quam dissensus & non conversio, & à gratia quod assensus fit supranaturalis & gratiosus. Id quod Grevinchovius ita probat, id lex Dei immediatè jubet & vetat, quod est in potestate hominis facere, vel non facere. Sed bonitas & malitia actus non sunt in potestate hominis, nisi ratione actus. Vult itaque actum proprie sub præceptum cadere affirmativum vel negativum, non proprie gratiositatem aut malitiam actus nisi secundario, ideoque actus qua actus liber est in nostra potestate, non actus qua supernaturalis.Hinc sequitur omnem & totam conversionis nostræ laude deberi in solidum puro puto arbitrio humano, nullo vero modo Deo, quia aliquid in homine est laude dignum, quatenus est liberum.Atqui sic conversio, quia est essentialiter actus liber, & obedientialis, erit sic laude dignus, & aliquid est non laude dignum, quatenus est non liberum, ideoque conversio qua supernaturalis (quandoquidem sic non est actus liber, sed à principio non libero nempe Dei gratia agente, determinato,non indifferente) non est laude digna in nobis,ideoque hic homo in se, non in Deo gloriabitur.
units.tr: Thus Corvinus: "For just as the will by its nature is free, so faith is an obedient act, of whose nature it is also to be free." Therefore the act of faith and of conversion is considered either as supernatural or as free. In the former way, namely as it is supernatural, it is not a free obedient act commanded by God, worthy of praise or reward. For what is not free is not obedience, is not worthy of praise or blame, does not fall under a command. Therefore the act of faith, as it is free, that is, as it proceeds from pure free choice, as from a free active principle, is worthy of praise, and something to which the crown of glory, a reward, and a prize are owed. And that which moves God to choose this man rather than that one, Peter rather than Judas, is taught by Pelagius, by Coelestius, and by the heretics most hostile to the grace of God in a cruder form than this. For the act of conversion, as supernatural, is in no way from free choice, and therefore in no way obedience; nor is the supernaturalness of the act in any way from the influence of created will, but from the influence of God's grace; and it is a quality posterior to and superadded to the act, by which the act is free or contingent, and commanded by God. Thus it is from free choice that assent and conversion, rather than dissent and non-conversion, come about; and it is from grace that the assent becomes supernatural and gracious. Grevinchovius proves this thus: the law of God immediately commands and forbids what is in man's power to do or not to do. But the goodness and malice of an act are not in man's power, except by reason of the act. He wants, therefore, that the act itself properly falls under the affirmative or negative command, and that the graciousness or malice of the act is only secondarily; so that the act, as an act, is free and in our power, not the act as supernatural. Hence it follows that all the praise of our conversion is owed wholly to pure human free choice, and in no way to God, because something in man is worthy of praise insofar as it is free. But so conversion, because it is essentially a free and obedient act, will be worthy of praise in this way; and something is not worthy of praise insofar as it is not free. Therefore conversion as supernatural (since in this way it is not a free act, but determined by a non-free principle, namely by God's grace acting, not indifferent) is not worthy of praise in us; and therefore this man will glory not in himself, but in God.

units.la: 18, Hinc videat lector, quam falso asserat Corvinus, liberum arbitrium non simpliciter sed gratia adjutum credere & sese convertere, quoniam nec gratia præveniens, nec concomitans, aliquid contribuunt in actum conversionis, qua liberum, qua obedientialem, quâ laude dignum, quâ à Deo mandatum. Nam influxus gratiæ (uti illi docent) non terminatur in voluntatem, qua est principium activum. Sic enim Deus id mandaret, quod ipse efficeret, quod Arminiani plane deridet in confess. Si dicant moralem, & suasorium gratiæ influxum terminari in voluntatem, quam stupentem excitat; agnosco & phrasin & stilum Pelagianum, quasi vero is mihi ære alieno obruto debita persolveret, quoniam suadet, ut ipse persolvam; is vinculis ferreis me constrictum expediret, & absolveret qui ut memet expedirem, suaderet. Suadere esse adjuvare, vires addendo, quis sanus vel in fomniis fingeret? At vero influxus gratiæ prævenientis terminatur non in voluntatem, sed in conversionem, & non in eam simpliciter, sed in ipsius supernaturalitatem, id quod dicit Grevinchovius. Ratio operandi (libera) est arbitrii: ratio autem sic operandi est opus pietatis. At vero nec gratia concomitans aliquid contribuit in actum liberum. Nam illud esse causativum, vel est effectivum, vel materiale, vel formale vel finale: alioqui non est causa. At vero si esse contribuat omnino, necesse est esse gratiæ, non esse liberum tribuat, quoniam gratia est causa agens ad modum naturæ, & causa non vitalis, ideoque non confert esse liberum formaliter. Nam formaliter esse liberum à causa libera, electiva, & vitali fluit. Si gratia concomitans effectivè tribuat esse liberum, necesse est effectivè determiner[?]. Nam esse liberum effectivè tribuere, est efficere effectivè π[?] velle, & sic removere indifferentiam ad π[?] velle & nolle. Atqui docent illi effectivè gratia determinare voluntatem, esse libertatem evertere; at vero dicent gratia efficientia partiali & collaterali voluntatem determinare, non totali & prævia. Sit ita efficientia hæc collateralis gratiæ: vel est prior voluntatis efficientia collaterali, vel simul, vel posterior. Si prior, tum gratia motione præviâ determinabit voluntatem, quod illi negabunt. Si simul, nulla erit ratio cur voluntas velit, nisi gratia simul influxum contribuat, & si gratia non contribuat influxum, non-operatio non imputabitur voluntati humanae. Ita enim illi arguunt contra nostram physicam praedeterminationem, & si simul gratia contribuat influxum suum, necessitabitur voluntas ad suum simultaneum influxum accommodandum, alioqui daretur actio causae primae sine actione fecundae, quod absurdum est. Si vero influxus gratiae concomitantis sit posterior influxu voluntatis, tum voluntas determinabit gratiam cooperantem, & gratia cooperans non determinabit voluntatem. Determinans enim in suo actu determinandi, non potest esse posteriori determinato, sed prior.
units.tr: 18. From this the reader may see how falsely Corvinus asserts that free will, not merely assisted by grace, believes and converts itself, since neither preventing nor concomitant grace contributes anything to the act of conversion that is free, obedient, worthy of praise, and commanded by God. For the influx of grace, as they teach, does not terminate in the will, which is the active principle. In that case God would command what he himself brings about, which the Arminians plainly mock in the Confession. If they say that the moral and persuasive influx of grace terminates in the will, which it stirs from its torpor, I recognise the phrasing and style of the Pelagians, as if someone whose debts had overwhelmed him were paid by a creditor who urged him to pay them himself, or as if someone bound in iron chains were freed and released by one who advised him how to free himself. Who, even in a dream, would imagine that to persuade is to help by adding strength? Indeed the influx of preventing grace terminates not in the will but in conversion, and not in conversion simply but in its supernaturalness, as Grevinchovius says: "The reason for acting (freely) belongs to the will; but the reason for acting in this way is the work of piety." Nor does concomitant grace contribute anything to the free act. For its causal being is either effective, material, formal, or final; otherwise it is not a cause. But if it contributes being altogether, it must be the being of grace, not the being of freedom, since grace is an agent cause acting in the manner of nature, and is a non-vital cause, and so does not formally confer free being. For free being formally flows from a free, elective and vital cause. If concomitant grace effectively confers free being, it must effectively determine the will. For to confer free being effectively is to bring about effectively a willing, and so to remove indifference to willing or not willing. Yet they teach that grace effectively determines the will, which would destroy freedom; but they will say that grace determines the will by a partial and collateral efficiency, not a total and prior one. Let this collateral efficiency of grace be so: it is either prior to the efficiency of the will, or simultaneous with it, or posterior. If prior, then grace will determine the will by a preceding motion, which they will deny. If simultaneous, there will be no reason why the will should will, unless grace at the same time contributes its influx; and if grace does not contribute its influx, the non-operation will not be imputed to the human will. For so they argue against our physical predetermination; and if grace at the same time contributes its influx, the will will be necessitated to accommodate itself to grace's simultaneous influx, otherwise there would be an action of the first cause without an action of the second cause, which is absurd. But if the influx of concomitant grace is posterior to the influx of the will, then the will will determine the cooperating grace, and the cooperating grace will not determine the will. For what determines in its act of determining cannot be posterior to what is determined, but must be prior.

units.la: 19. At scio quid hic Corvinus respondeat: vult gratiam & liberum arbitrium esse causas partiales operis boni, non partialitate essectus, quasi una pars effectus sit à gratia, altera à libero arbitrio, sed partialitate causae, ita ut totus effectus simul sit à gratia & libero arbitrio. Ita ille exponit Grevinchovium, sed potius depravat. Nam Grevinchovius intelligit partialitatem effectus: ait enim rationem operandi esse arbitrii, & sic operandi, pietatis: quid clarius? 2. Secundum Arminianam fidem non possunt commisceri libertas & gratia partialitate causae, quoniam libertas est causa libera, indifferens, eleCtiva, at gratia causa determinata ad unum effectum producendum. Et haec causae illis distinguuntur ut contingens & necessarium, quae Arminio infinita oppositione & contradictorie distant, & quaquoniam dividunt rotam entis amplitudinem, non possunt hæ inter se junctæ unum effectum contingentem producere, cujusmodi est conversio, quoniam tum effectus erit partim necessarius, partim contingens, quod novæ metaphysicæ Magni Arminii grave ἀλόγημα[?] erit. Utinam mihi hic sese expedi-
units.tr: 19. But I know what Corvinus here will reply: he wants grace and free will to be partial causes of the good work, not by a partiality of effect, as if one part of the effect were from grace and the other from free will, but by a partiality of cause, so that the whole effect is at once from grace and from free will. This is how he explains Grevinchovius, but he rather distorts him. For Grevinchovius understands partiality of effect: he says that the reason for acting belongs to the will, and the reason for acting in this way to piety. What could be clearer? 2. According to the Arminian faith, freedom and grace cannot be combined by partiality of cause, since freedom is a free, indifferent, elective cause, whereas grace is a cause determined to produce one effect. These causes are distinguished by them as contingent and necessary, which are separated by Arminius in infinite and contradictory opposition; and since they divide the whole range of being, these cannot, being joined together, produce one contingent effect, such as conversion, since the effect would then be partly necessary and partly contingent, which would be a grave absurdity [ἀλόγημα] in the new metaphysics of the great Arminius. Would that here I might extricate myself...

units.la: 20. Neque est à gratia Dei, quod sit in ho-rent[?] mine conversio, potius quam non-conversio.
units.tr: 20. Conversion in a man is not from the grace of God rather than non-conversion.

units.la: Nam ut actus voluntatis (inquit Armin.) hanc potius habeat essentiam, quam illam, seu potius sit actus hic, quam alius ut potius actus vetitus, quam non vetitus (hoc est potius sit conversio, quam non-conversio, vel contra) potius contra hoc, quam contra illud præceptum, pendet à libertate voluntatis quoad speciem actus, ideoque quod hic convertatur, ille non, est à voluntate pura, qua conversus se à non converso discernit. Non tamen verecundatur Corvinus totam actuositatem in spiritualibus gratiæ tribuere: quo quid contradicentius Arminio? Neque etiam usus gratiæ dici potest esse à gratia. Ita enim Gervinchov. auxilium efficax ordine causalitatis non antecedit efficientiam voluntatis, eoque nec prius in voluntatem agit, quam influit in actum seu actionem voluntatis, sed una cum voluntate (gratia præveniente jam excitata) efficit actum. Hinc probo usum gratiæ non esse principaliter à gratia, sed principaliter à libero arbitrio, contra quod ait Corvinus: usus gratiæ est actualis gratiæ ad actum applicatio: atqui non gratia, sed liberum arbitrium gratiam actu applicat ad actum. Ergo usus gratiæ est principaliter à libero arbitrio, non à gratia. Major est clara ex definitione usus gratiæ. Prob. min. Nec gratia præveniens, nec cooperans applicat gratiam ad opus. Ergo solum liberum arbitrium id præstat. Prob. antecedens: gratia præveniens, quia est potentia quædam, indiget alia gratia actuante se. Ergo ea non potest gratiam ad opus applicare. Nulla enim potentia qua talis sese actuat: sic enim seipsa præstantior esset, nam omne actuans, actuabili est præstantius. Nec gratia cooperans gratiam ad opus applicat, quoniam si gratia cooperans non applicat voluntatem ad actum gratiosum, nec ordine causalitatis antecedit efficientiam voluntatis, non potest gratiam applicare ad opus. Sed prius est verum. Ergo & posterius. Honestior hac in parte est Tylenus reliquis Arminianis, qui fatentur rotundè voluntatem uti gratia, ideoque gratiam confert gladio, quem miles ignavus rubigine consumi, & in vagina hebescere finit; strenuus vero miles utitur ad pugnam. Ita Molina Iesuita: A propria (inquit) industria, conatuve majore vel minore liberi arbitrii provenit, quod quisque plus aut minus lucretur ex talentis sibi datis. Atqui Corvinum & Arminianos à doctrina Iesuitarum (si vocationem congruam excipies) nec volam, nec vestigium recedere hac in parte nemini non liquet. Imo utrique cum Fausto & Cassiano eandem viam tenent, nent. Ita Faustus : Ego arbitror quod libertas arbitrii sibi sola sufficere absque praesidio gratiae non posset. Ita & Cassianus, ut ait Prosper : Cum enim gentes, quae legem non habent, naturaliter ea quae legis sunt, faciant, manet in homine liberum semper arbitrium, quo gatiam[?] Dei possit, vel negligere vel amare, inquit Cassianus, & lib. 13. c.
units.tr: For (says Arminius) that the act of the will should have this essence rather than that, or rather that it should be this act rather than another, as a forbidden act rather than a non-forbidden one (that is, that it should be conversion rather than non-conversion, or the reverse), or rather against this command than against that one, depends on the freedom of the will as regards the species of the act; and therefore that one man is converted and another not is due to the pure will, by which the converted man distinguishes himself from the unconverted. Yet Corvinus is not ashamed to attribute the whole activity in spiritual matters to grace: what could be more contrary to Arminius? Nor can the use of grace be said to be from grace. For Grevinchovius says that "efficacious help," in the order of causality, does not precede the efficiency of the will, and so does not act upon the will before it flows into the act or action of the will, but together with the will (grace already stirred up by preventing grace) it produces the act. Hence I prove that the use of grace is not principally from grace but principally from free will, against what Corvinus says: the use of grace is the actual application of grace to the act; but it is not grace but free will that actually applies grace to the act. Therefore the use of grace is principally from free will, not from grace. The major is clear from the definition of the use of grace. I prove the minor: neither preventing nor cooperating grace applies grace to the work. Therefore only free will accomplishes this. I prove the antecedent: preventing grace, since it is a kind of power, needs another grace to actuate it. Therefore it cannot apply grace to the work. For no power as such actuates itself; otherwise it would be superior to itself, since whatever actuates is superior to what is actuable. Nor does cooperating grace apply grace to the work, since if cooperating grace does not apply the will to a gracious act, and does not precede the efficiency of the will in the order of causality, it cannot apply grace to the work. But the former is true. Therefore so is the latter. Tilenus is more honest in this respect than the other Arminians, who openly confess that the will uses grace, and so compares grace to a sword, which a lazy soldier lets rust away and grow dull in its sheath, while a vigorous soldier uses it for battle. So too the Jesuit Molina: it arises (he says) "from one's own industry and greater or lesser effort of free will, that each man gains more or less from the talents given to him." Yet that Corvinus and the Arminians have not departed in this respect, not a hair's breadth or a footprint, from the doctrine of the Jesuits (unless you except congruous vocation), is plain to everyone. Indeed both sides keep the same path as Faustus and Cassian. Thus Faustus: I hold that the freedom of the will could not suffice of itself without the protection of grace. So too Cassian, as Prosper reports: since the Gentiles, who have no law, naturally do what the law requires, there remains in man always a free will by which he can either neglect or love the grace of God, says Cassian, in book 13, chapter

units.la: 13. Nonnunquam (inquit) gratia Dei ab homine quosdam conatus bonae voluntatis vel exigit, vel exspectat, ne penitus dormienti aut inerti otio dissoluto, sua dona conferre videatur. Eodemplane modo loquitur Jesuita Suarez stylo Cassiani: Constat (inquit) post vocationem exspectare Deum ut homo aperiat & consentiat. Et eodem stylo utitur Arminius: Sed si (inquit) in exspectatione non tantum illam cognitionem, verum & summum desiderium consideremus, quo, cui exspectatio tribuitur, fructuum productionem postulat, ipso respectu Deo proprissime exspectatio tribuetur.
units.tr: 13. Sometimes (he says) God either requires or awaits certain efforts of a good will from man, lest he seem to bestow his gifts on one wholly asleep or dissolved in inert idleness. The Jesuit Suárez speaks in exactly the same way, in the style of Cassian: it is agreed (he says) that after vocation God waits for man to open himself and consent. Arminius uses the same style: But if (he says) in this waiting we consider not only that knowledge but also the highest desire, by which the one for whom waiting is attributed demands the production of fruits, then waiting will be most properly attributed to God in that very respect.

units.la: 21. Imo in tota hac disputatione de effi-cacia gratiae nihil aliud jam quaeritur, quam olim quaesitum est inter Augustinum & Pelagianos. Ita Prosper con. collat. Magna quaestio, utrum quia initium bonae voluntatis praebuerimus, misereatur nostri Deus, an quia Deus misertur, consequamur bonae voluntatis initium. Ita Prosper, ita Hilarius contendebant cum Massiliensibus & Augustin. Inter nos agitur, utrum praecedat haec gratia, an subsequatur hominis voluntatem, hoc est, ut planius id eloquar, utrum ideo nobis detur, quia volumus, an per ipsum Deus hoc efficiat, ut velimus. In omni itaque opere [?]ancto prior est voluntas Dei, posterior liberi arbitrii, id est, operatur Deus, cooperatur homo. Quod si dicis ut dicere consuevisti: quia ego prior volui, Deus voluit, jam meritum facis, ut gratia ex operibus jam non fit gratia, sed merces. Et Augustinus: Si convertuntur homines, quia Deus per gratiam efficit in iis posse & velle, nonne homines boni sunt (inquit Iulianus) fatali necessitate? Nonne hoc idem est, quod ait Corvinus? Deus non jungit influxum suum, nisi ubi causa secunda est in ipso momento & instanti influxionis, adeoque non influit nisi creatura volente influere. Hoc est Cassiani meritum: Deus nos convertit & miseretur, si nos volumus. Ita Grevinchovius: Auxilium efficax ordine causalitatis efficientiam voluntatis non antecedit &c.
units.tr: 21. Indeed, in this whole dispute about the efficacy of grace, nothing else is now being asked than what was asked long ago between Augustine and the Pelagians. So Prosper, in his Contra Collatorem: "The great question is whether God shows mercy to us because we have provided the beginning of a good will, or whether we obtain the beginning of a good will because God shows mercy." So Prosper and Hilary contended with the Massilians and Augustine. Between us the question is whether this grace goes before the human will or follows it. To put it more plainly: is it given to us because we will, or does God by it bring about that we will? In every holy work, then, the will of God is prior and the will of free choice is posterior; that is, God works and man co-operates. But if you say, as you are accustomed to say, "Because I willed first, God willed," you already make merit, and grace ceases to be grace from works and becomes a wage. And Augustine: "If men are converted because God by grace produces in them the power and the will, are not men good (says Julian) by fatal necessity?" Is this not the same thing that Corvinus says? "God does not join his influence except where the secondary cause is present, at the very moment and instant of the influence, and so he does not influence unless the creature is willing to be influenced." This is the merit of Cassian: God converts us and shows mercy if we are willing. So too Grevincovius: "Efficacious help, in the order of causality, does not precede the efficiency of the will," etc.

units.la: 22. Pergo ad alia, Phil. 1. 19. Vobis datum est pro Christo non solum in ipsum credere, sed etiam pro ipso pati. Phil. c. 2. v. 13. Deus enim efficit in vobis, velle & perficere pro suo beneplacito. Hinc qui dat credere, & efficit ipsum τὸ velle, is per gratiam praedeterminat voluntatem ad credendum, patiendum, volendum, perficiendum, & efficacia gratiae in Deum volentem & determinantem reducetur, & non in liberum arbitrium.
units.tr: 22. I pass on to other passages. Phil. 1. 19: "To you it has been given for Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him." Phil. 2. 13: "For it is God who works in you both to will and to perform, for his good pleasure." Hence he who gives to believe, and brings about the very to will [τὸ θέλειν], by grace predetermines the will to believe, to suffer, to will, and to perform; and the efficacy of grace is to be referred to a God who wills and determines, and not to free choice.

units.la: Resp. 1. Corvin. Deum dare ut credamus, quia dat credendi potentiam, & quoniam auxilio supernaturali concurrit ad actum credendi. Et Remonstrantes: Deum & morali & physico influxu concurrere: & Collat. Hag. Quamvis tollatur actualis resistentia, manet potentia resistendi; & sic volunt Deum efum efficere in nobis τῷ velle. Refpond. 1. Quamvis det potentiam volendi, & concursu collaterali & indifferente concurrat ad actum, non magis hoc pacto dat credere & efficit velle, quam dat non credere & efficit non velle.
units.tr: Answer 1. Corvinus says that God gives us to believe because he gives the power of believing and concurs with the supernatural help to the act of believing. And the Remonstrants: that God concurs by both a moral and a physical influence. And the Collatio Hagiensis: "Although actual resistance is removed, the power of resisting remains." And so they want God to bring about in us the to will [τῷ θέλειν]. Answer 1: Although he gives the power of willing, and concurs with the act by a collateral and indifferent concurrence, he no more gives us to believe and brings about our willing in this way than he gives us not to believe and brings about our not willing.

units.la: 2. Hoc pacto dat, ex hypothesi, quod nos velimus, hoc est postquam nos effecerimus in nobis velle, ipse efficit velle. An is est causa τῷ εἶναι[?], qui postquam res habet esse, dat esse? mysterium mirum.
units.tr: 2. In this way he gives, on the hypothesis that we will; that is, after we have brought about in ourselves the willing, he himself brings about the willing. Is he the cause of being [τοῦ εἶναι] who gives being after a thing already has being? A wonderful mystery.

units.la: 3. Si Deus removeat τῷ actu resistere, finita est disputatio. Potentiam nolendi manere in iis, inquibus Deus efficit velle, ultro concedunt, at minus candide. Nam volunt tolli actu resistere convenienter naturae libertatis, hoc est, ut maneat indifferentia, & sic non magis tollitur actu resistere, quam actu non resistere.
units.tr: 3. If God removes the act of resisting, the dispute is over. They readily concede that the power of not willing remains in those in whom God brings about the willing, but they do so less candidly. For they want the act of resisting to be removed in a way consistent with the nature of liberty; that is, so that indifference remains. And so the act of resisting is no more removed than the act of not resisting.

units.la: 4. Si efficit velle & perficere, quoniam efficit potentiam volendi, & actu efficit, si nos velimus, efficit cum Deus in nobis velle & perficere, non pro suo beneplacito, sed pro hominis beneplacito, quod docuit Cajetanus & Massiliensis.
units.tr: 4. If he brings about the willing and the performing because he brings about the power of willing, and actually brings it about that we will, then God does not bring about in us the willing and the performing for his good pleasure, but for man's good pleasure. This is what Cajetan and the Massilian taught.

units.la: 2. Refp. Suarez ait. [Deum operari ut velimus,] nihil aliud esse, quam operari in nobis aliquid, quo disponamur vel inclinemur ad volendum, & eo animo & intentione ut velimus. Refp. Illa dispositione vel fit, ut indeclinabiliter velimus, & habemus institutum sic; vel declinabiliter, & sic non magis efficit τὸ velle, quam τὸ non velle. Nam intentio Dei cum fit actus pure immanens, non ponit in nobis velle, vel non velle actu transiente. Si vero velit Deum, congrua motione efficere in nobis velle, quia nempe praescit quod ex hac non ex illa motione, tali modo administrata, sequatur velle, scilicet postquam nos voluimus, & ille praescit scientia media nos volituros, tum efficit velle. Fabula Jesuitis certe dignissima.
units.tr: 2. Answer. Suarez says: [that God works that we may will] is nothing other than working in us something by which we are disposed or inclined to will, with that mind and intention that we should will. Answer: that disposition either makes us will indeclinably, and we have it fixed in this way, or it makes us will declinably, and then he no more brings about the to will than the to not will. For the intention of God, since it is a purely immanent act, does not put in us the willing or the not willing as a transient act. But if God wills to bring about in us the willing by a suitable motion, because he foresees that the willing will follow from this motion and not from that, when it is administered in such a way, namely after we have willed, and he foresees by middle knowledge that we will will, then he brings about the willing. This is certainly a fable most worthy of the Jesuits.

units.la: 3. Remonft. Refp. 1. Non agitur hic (inquiunt) de ea efficacia qua Deus in nobis operatur fidem in mente & voluntate, sed de efficacia, qua Deus utitur in nobis, qui jam credimus. Dicitur enim ὁ ἐνεργῶν: non autem ὁ ἐνεργήσας[?]. Refp. 1. At quae est illa efficacia, qua utitur in credentibus? An non velle, perficere, credere, perseverare, operari salutem cum tremore? qui sunt actus liberi ejusdem plane naturae cum primo actu libero conversionis nostrae. Utrobique enim manet libertas naturae, ac proinde utrobique Deus efficit velle. 2. Non agit de ea efficacia qua Deus operatur fidem. Misera est conjectura ex voce, ἐνεργῶν, quasi nulli essent, qui convertendi forent inter Philippenses. Audax omnium. 2. R. ib. Non dicit: Deus efficit ut bene & recte velitis, sed ut velitis, supponit jam esse bonam voluntatem, quia jam fideles erant: sed dicit Deum, ne illa bona voluntas langueat, & quasi jaceat, excitare, accendere, inflammare illam a parte sua, ut eam, quantum in se est, in perpetuo vigore retineat. Refp. 1. Deus efficit velle indeclinabiliter: ergo & bene & recte velle. Est n. par utrobique ratio. 2. Quia jam fideles erant, supponere volunt in Philippenfibus bonam voluntatem. Atqui volunt illi hortationem ad omnes & singulos dirigi. At an omnes & singuli erant fideles? At inter ipsos fuisse canes & malos operarios liquet & quorum venter effet Deus v.19. Ideoque somnia hic venditant. 2. Si Deus voluntatem, ne langueat, accendat, an non hoc est bene velle efficere & continuare? at negant Deum bene velle, efficere. 3. Deum, quantum in se est, voluntatem inflammare dicunt suasionibus procul dubio, quibus posse velle inflammatur. At plus dicitur à Paulo, Deum ipsum velle & perficere, efficere: ipsorum glossa textu est longe jejunior. 3. Refp. Non exprimi volunt modum quo Deus efficit velle. Qui enim suadet, dicitur velle efficere, & Apostoli eos, quibus evangelium annunciant, gignere, regenerare, aperire oculos eorum, convertere &c. & Diabolus ἐνεργεῖ in filiis contumaciæ Eph. 2. 2. & evangelium ἐνεργῇ[?] 1. Thess. 2. 3. R. 1. Quando Deus dicitur efficere velle pro suo beneplacito, satis exprimitur modus. Si enim efficit, ita ut sequatur non velle tum Deus pro suo beneplacito, efficit male velle. At nunquam sic loquitur scriptura. 2. Apostoli, ut Dei instrumenta, indeclinabiliter regenerant, & sic etiam evangelium, imo sic Diabolus ut instrumentum divinæ justitiæ in filiis contumaciæ; Deus enim non punit contumaces declinabiliter. 3. Solenne est Arminiasis[?], non fortiorem aut validiorem actionem Deum, per specialem gratiam operanti, tribuere, quam hominibus suadentibus, aut Diabolo tentanti. Sic audacter produnt quam minus honorificè sentiant, de Dei gratiæ operatione.
units.tr: 3. The Remonstrants answer, first: "The question here is not about that efficacy by which God works faith in the mind and will, but about the efficacy which God uses in us who already believe. For it is said ὁ ἐνεργῶν [who works], not ὁ ἐνεργήσας [who has worked]." Answer 1: But what is that efficacy by which he works in believers? Is it not to will, to perform, to believe, to persevere, to work out salvation with fear and trembling? These are free acts of exactly the same nature as the first free act of our conversion. For in both cases the liberty of nature remains, and therefore in both God brings about the willing. 2. He is not speaking of that efficacy by which God works faith. It is a wretched conjecture from the word ἐνεργῶν, as if there were no one among the Philippians who needed to be converted. Bold of all of them! 2. Answer 2, from the same place: "He does not say: God brings it about that you will well and rightly, but that you will. He presupposes that there is already a good will, because they were already believers. But he says that God, so that this good will may not grow faint and as it were lie idle, stirs up, kindles, and inflames it on his part, so that as far as in him lies he may keep it in perpetual vigour." Answer 1: God brings about the willing indeclinably, therefore also the willing well and rightly. For the reasoning is equal in both cases. 2. Since they were already believers, they want us to presuppose a good will in the Philippians. Yet they want that exhortation to be addressed to all and each. But were all and each of them believers? It is plain that there were dogs and evil workers among them, and whose belly is their god, v. 19. Therefore they peddle dreams here. 2. If God kindles the will so that it does not grow faint, is this not to bring about and continue the good willing? Yet they deny that God brings about the good willing. 3. They say that God, as far as in him lies, inflames the will doubtless by persuasions, by which the power of willing is inflamed. But Paul says more, that God himself wills and performs, and brings about; their gloss is far thinner than the text. 3. Answer: They do not want to express the manner in which God brings about the willing. For one who persuades is said to bring about the willing, and the Apostles are said to beget, regenerate, open the eyes of those to whom they preach the gospel, convert them, etc.; and the Devil works [ἐνεργεῖ] in the sons of disobedience, Eph. 2. 2; and the gospel works [ἐνεργῇ], 1 Thess. 2. 13. Answer 1: When God is said to bring about the willing for his good pleasure, the manner is sufficiently expressed. For if he brings it about so that not-willing follows, then God for his good pleasure brings about ill-willing. But Scripture never speaks in this way. 2. The Apostles, as God's instruments, regenerate indeclinably, and so too the gospel; indeed the Devil too does so, as an instrument of divine justice against the sons of disobedience, for God does not punish the disobedient declinably. 3. It is the custom of the Arminians to attribute to God, when he works by special grace, no stronger or more powerful action than that of men persuading or of the Devil tempting. Thus they boldly betray how little honourably they think of the working of God's grace.

units.la: 4. Resp. Quid ineptius Operamini salutem vestram cum tremore, & statim rationem hanc subjicere? Quia Deus in vobis, ut operemini salutem vestram cum timore ac tremore, efficit, ea efficacia qua fieri non potest, quin operemini salutem vestram cum timore ac tremore. R. Ineptum hoc videtur lance humanæ prudentiæ ponderanti Dei sapientiam.Nam quia fides nostra languet, ne in tentationibus Deus nos deferat, opus est, confirmetur fides in cursu obedientiæ spe, & promissione divinæ virtutis & omnipotentiæ, qua suos invicte fulcit, & corroborat, ne deficiant: & quoniam nos sumus hic agentia ethica, non mediocri solatio est, quod Deus invicta potentia, id in nobis efficiat, quod ex fidei infirmitate, ne minus fiat, subinde metuimus.
units.tr: 4. Answer. Is it not absurd to say, "Work out your salvation with fear and trembling," and then to add this reason: "Because God works in you, so that you work out your salvation with fear and trembling, by an efficacy such that it cannot but happen that you work out your salvation with fear and trembling"? R. To one who weighs God's wisdom on the scales of human prudence, this may seem absurd. For since our faith grows weak, and we fear that God may forsake us in temptations, it is necessary that our faith be strengthened in the course of obedience by hope and by the promise of divine power and omnipotence, by which He invincibly upholds and strengthens His own, so that they do not fail. And since we are here acting creatures, it is no small comfort that God, by invincible power, brings about in us what we from the weakness of faith fear may come about only in part.

units.la: Sic Esai. c. 38. 21 Idem & par plane est mandatum, Ezechiæ applicetur palatha ficuum ulceri, & tamen promiserat Deus, se ea efficacia curaturum regis morbum, qua non poterat non ad quindecim annos vitam ulterius prorogare. Christus non poterat non ponere animam pro ovibus suis, & tamen mandatum ponendi animam a Patre recepit, Ioh. 10. 10. Omnipotentia invicta promiserat Deus se expulsurum Chananæos, & ita quidem ut non potuerint non expelli. Deut. 3. 16,27,28. Et tamen Deus hortatur Ioshuam, ut sit forti & bono animo Iosh. 1. 5, 6. ut ad pugnam se accingat. Deus omnipotentia sua efficit, ut terra fruges producat, & tamen jubet agricolam, aret, fodiat, metat. Gen.49. Iacob vaticinatur de divisione sanctæ terræ in tribus, & quam partem Deus unicuique daturum fe decreverat, ipse prædicit, & tamen Deus per Mosem præceperat ut forte divideretur Iofh. 14.2. Vaticinium illud eventum fortitutum erat indeclinabiliter, & tamen fortilegium respectu causæ fecundæ plane contingens erat. Sic Iob. 14. 5. Dies vitæ cujuflibet, & limites menfium ita fixi & determinati sunt, ut ipsos tranfgredi non possit, & tamen preces, & medicina pro longævitate tali determinationi optime fubordinantur. Petunt itaque principium, nempe medium contingens non posse Dei actioni & intentioni irreliftibili fubordinari, quod est salsissimum. 2. Ipsos operari falutem cum timore necefle fuit, quoniam nisi hoc facerent, frustra considerent & sperarent fore, ut Deus in ipsis velle & perficere effecturus effet. Non enim Deus velle & perficere in nobis efficit, ut in truncis & stipitibus mere passive nos habentibus, sed efficit Deus efficaciter velle & perficere in nobis volentibus, & per Dei gratiam efficacem perficientibus. At vero ridicula effet hortatio, fi nos nihil ageremus, ut supponunt sophistæ. Deus enim sic vel nobis dormientibus & sopitis velle & perficere efficeret indeclinabiliter, quod absurdum: & sic stipites hortaretur, cum ipse totum faceret irreliftibiliter. At Deum hortari ut nos, quod nostri est officii, faceremus. mus libere, quando ipse nos liberimè a-gentes efficaciter determinet, non tantum non est absurdum, sed ita necessarium, ut Deo alioquin laus & gloria operum supernaturalium minime constaret. §. Resp. Deum in ipsis per praedeterminantem gratiam efficere istam ipsam solicitudinem & curam operandi salutem, ad quam eos hortabatur, est absurdum. R. Ipsos per liberum arbitrium efficere solicitudinem illam citra gratiam determinantem, ignominiosum est Dei gratiae. Nam sic exigi curam & solicitudinem per talem gratiam falsum est, & ad hoc millies à nostris responsum. Quaero enim an Deus decreverit ut sancti essemus, & an absolutè, an conditionatè? Si conditionatè, quando conditionem dederint Ar-miniani, cupio scire: hactenus nunquam de-derunt: si absolutè, tum solicitudo non pu-gnat cum invicto decreto, & per eandem ra-tionem nec cum gratiae efficacia irrefistibili[?]. 6. Resp.Hortatio est ad omnes Philippenses: atqui non omnes ea efficacia sunt donati. Multi enim multa per contentionem & inanem gloriam agebant c. 2. 18. Resp. 1. Contradicunt sibi: hic volunt multos contentionis & inanis gloriae studiosos esse: supra dixerunt, omnes esse fideles, & Apostolum supponere bonam voluntatem in iis omnibus, in quibus Deus efficit velle & operari. Atqui hic Deum in omnibus citra exceptionem volunt efficere, velle, & perficere. 2. Hortatio latius patet illo (Deus efficit in vobis velle & per-ficeficere) Nam in eadem epistola & in eadem prophetia, sermonem accommodari ad populum, interdum respectu fidelium, interdum respectu infidelium, norunt omnes in Dei verbo esse vulgatissimum. 3. Ut nobis opponerent, debebant probasse ipsos illos numero homines in iidem actibus, in quibus Deus velle & perficere, quantum est a parte sua effecit, multa tamen fecisse per contentionem & inanem gloriam: sed hoc non probant. At vero Deum efficere in Philippensibus velle & perficere respectu credentium & electorum, & non efficere velle, & perficere in aliis, qui inani gloriae dediti essent, quis neget? aut quid hoc ad thefeos[?] oppugnationem? Alia loca alibi forte, cum bono Deo, vindicaturus, hic sisto.
units.tr: So in Isa. 38.21: the same and quite plainly the same command, "Let a poultice of figs be applied to the boil," and yet God had promised that He would cure the king's sickness by an efficacy such that He could not but extend his life by fifteen years. Christ could not but lay down His life for His sheep, and yet He received the command from the Father to lay it down (John 10.10). Almighty and invincible, God had promised that He would drive out the Canaanites, and indeed in such a way that they could not but be driven out (Deut. 3.16, 27, 28). And yet God exhorts Joshua to be strong and of good courage (Josh. 1.5, 6) and to gird himself for battle. By His omnipotence God causes the earth to bring forth its fruits, and yet He bids the farmer plough, dig and reap. In Gen. 49 Jacob prophesies about the division of the holy land among the tribes, and God Himself foretold which part He had decreed to give to each; and yet God had commanded through Moses that it be divided by lot (Josh. 14.2). That prophecy was inevitably fulfilled, and yet the casting of lots, with respect to the secondary cause, was entirely contingent. Likewise Job 14.5: "The days of each man's life, and the limits of his months, are so fixed and determined that he cannot pass beyond them"; and yet prayers and medicine for longevity are most properly subordinated to such a determination. They therefore beg the question, namely that a contingent means cannot be subordinated to the irresistible action and intention of God, which is most false. 2. It was necessary that they work out their salvation with fear, since unless they did so they would vainly consider and hope that God would effect in them that He would will and perform. For God does not will and perform in us as in logs and stumps that have us merely passive, but He efficaciously wills and performs in us, while we are willing, and by His efficacious grace we perform. But it would be a ridiculous exhortation if we did nothing, as the sophists suppose. For God would then, even while we slept and were drowsy, will and perform indeed, by necessity, which is absurd: and so He would be exhorting stumps, since He Himself would be doing everything irresistibly. But that God exhorts us, as is our duty, to do it, is not only not absurd, but so necessary that otherwise the praise and glory of supernatural works could not belong to God at all, since He, acting most freely, determines us efficaciously. §. Answer. That God, through predetermining grace, should bring about in them that very solicitude and care to work out their salvation, to which He exhorts them, is absurd. R. That they should bring about that solicitude by free will apart from determining grace is dishonourable to the grace of God. For to claim that care and solicitude are exacted through such grace is false, and our people have answered this a thousand times. For I ask whether God has decreed that we should be holy, and whether absolutely or conditionally. If conditionally, I want to know what condition the Arminians have given: hitherto they have never given one. If absolutely, then solicitude does not clash with an invincible decree, and for the same reason not with an irresistible efficacy of grace. 6. Answer. The exhortation is addressed to all the Philippians; but not all were endowed with that efficacy. For many did many things through strife and vainglory (Phil. 2.18). Answer 1: They contradict themselves. Here they want many to be devoted to strife and vainglory; above they said that all are believers, and that the Apostle presupposes good will in all those in whom God brings about the willing and the working. Yet here they want God to bring about willing and performing in all without exception. 2. The exhortation extends more widely than that statement ("God works in you to will and to perform"). For everyone knows that in the same epistle, and in the same prophecy, the discourse is adapted to the people, sometimes with respect to believers, sometimes with respect to unbelievers; this is most common in God's Word. 3. To oppose us they ought to have proved that those same persons, in the very acts in which God, as far as lies on His part, brings about willing and performing, nevertheless did many things through strife and vainglory. But they do not prove this. That God in the Philippians brings about willing and performing with respect to believers and the elect, and does not bring about willing and performing in others who were given over to vainglory, who would deny this? Or what has this to do with the overthrow of the thesis? Other passages I will perhaps, with God's good leave, take up elsewhere to vindicate; here I stop.

units.la: 23. Iam rationibus hic evinco efficaciam & praedeterminationem gratiae divinae. 1. Si non Deus efficaciter praedeterminet voluntatem, frustraneae & fallae possint omnes promissiones esse, à Deo Patre filioque factae, quod nempe sit visurus semen Esai. 53. 10 quod populus ab aquilone, & occidente, ab insulis. Esai. 49. v. 1. 12, ad ipsum accessuri sint, quod hereditario iure gentes & fines terrae, adeoque nos penitus toto divisos orbe Britannos, possessurus sit. Ps. 2. 8. quod dominium ipsius futurum sit a mari ad mare, a fluvio usque ad fines terrae, quod deserti incolae ipsi sin. inservituri. Ps. 72. 8, 9, 10. quod ad eum accursurus sit populus voluntarius. Ps. 100. 3. quod ipsius diebus salvandus sit[?]-Iudah, & Israel Ier. 23. 5, 6. quod unum pastorem Davidem gregi suo præfecturus sit, qui ipsos pasceret. Ezech. 34. 23. Quid? an omnes hæ promissiones falsæ erunt, nisi homines sese determinarunt ad præstandum liberum Deo cultum? an Dei fœ-dus cum filio (quod Arminio est inviolabile & juramento Dei sancitum) irritum erit? Et Deus non verax, nisi hominis arbitrium efficacem reddiderit Dei promissionem? At sic Christus, quod ipsius esset in fœdere, nempe animam pro captivis ponere potuerit. Deus vero populum & semen non daret: & sic Christus mercede falli potuit. Quid hic Arminiani? Deum promittere populum voluntatium filio, non absolutè, sed ex præscientiâ, quod præsciverit fore, ut populus liberè filio inserviturus esset: scilicet si credere dignum, postquam populus inservierit Christo, Deus ipsos inservituros promisit. Næ illi lemas in oculis suis habent, qui sibi talibus figmentis blandiuntur. At vero Christo propmittitur hoc laborum suorum præmium, quod populus ei voluntarius obsequatur, quod semen illi ministraturum sit.
units.tr: 23. Now by arguments I here prove the efficacy and predetermination of divine grace. 1. If God does not efficaciously predetermine the will, all the promises made by God the Father and the Son may be vain and false: namely that He will see the seed (Isa. 53.10); that the people from the north and the west, from the isles (Isa. 49.1, 12), will come to Him; that by hereditary right He will possess the nations and the ends of the earth, and so us Britons, wholly divided from the whole world (Ps. 2.8); that His dominion will be from sea to sea, from the river to the ends of the earth, that the inhabitants of the desert will serve Him (Ps. 72.8, 9, 10); that a willing people will run to Him (Ps. 100.3); that in His days Judah shall be saved and Israel (Jer. 23.5, 6); that He will set one shepherd, David, over His flock, who will feed them (Ezek. 34.23). What? Will all these promises be false, unless men have determined themselves to render free worship to God? Or will God's covenant with the Son (which even Arminius holds inviolable and sanctioned by God's oath) be void? And would God not be truthful, unless man's will made God's promise effective? But so Christ, whose part in the covenant it was, could have laid down His soul for the captives; and God would not have given Him the people and the seed; and so Christ could have been disappointed in His reward. What do the Arminians say to this? That God promised the Son a willing people not absolutely, but on the basis of foreknowledge, because He foreknew that the people would freely serve the Son; namely, if it is right to believe it, after the people had served Christ, God promised that they would serve Him. Nay, they have beams in their own eyes, who flatter themselves with such fictions. But to Christ is promised this reward of His labours, that a willing people will obey Him, and that He will have a seed to serve Him.

units.la: 24. 2. Rat. Si efficacia gratiæ, quoad eventum à libero arbitrio penderet, tum salus erit volentis & currentis, non Dei miserentis, neque Deus sic miserebitur, quorum vult. Re-spond. Tilenus. Misereor (inquit) quorum, nempe miseriam angoscentium, misereor, & quos volo induro, nempe qui indurationem commerentur, ex contemptu communioris gratiæ. Ita & Corvinus. Resp. 1. Ita plane Faustus: miserebor cui volucro, id est quem justum esse cognovero, cui jus promptam fidem videro, quem praeceptis meis obedire perspexero, quem meam facere voluntatem probavero. 2. Nullo modo constabit hic Deo sua miserendi libertas. Nam si hic suum arbitrium ad credendum determinarit, tum necessitabitur Deus ex ordine justitiae & veracitatis suae, hujus potius, quam alterius miserari.
units.tr: 24. 2. Reason. If the efficacy of grace, as to its outcome, depended on free will, then salvation would belong to the one who wills and runs, not to God who shows mercy, and God would not have mercy on whom He wills. Tilenus answers: "I have mercy on whom I will," that is, I have mercy on those who are distressed in their misery, and "whom I will I harden," that is, those who merit hardening through contempt of the more general grace. So also Corvinus. Answer 1: Quite so, says Faustus: "I will have mercy on whom I will," that is, whom I shall have known to be just, whom I shall have seen to have ready faith, whom I shall have perceived to obey my precepts, whom I shall have proved to make my will his own. 2. In no way will God's liberty of showing mercy be established here. For if He has determined the will to believe, then God will be necessitated, by the order of His justice and truthfulness, to show mercy on this one rather than on another.

units.la: 25. 3. Si Deus decernit gratiam in hisce efficacem facere, in illis non item, tum ex Dei, non hominum libertate pendet Dei gratiæ efficacia. Sed prius est verum ex scripturis. Ephes. 2. 10. Ipsius conditura sumus, creati ad bona opera, quæ præparavit Deus, ut in iis ambularemus. Resp. Arminiani Deum non peremptorie decernere, ut vel Petrus vel Judas præcise crederet, sed tantum conditionate ex prærequisita conditione, quod Petrus vellet. Resp. 1.
