Redibit in infinitum quæstio, si prærequisita conditio fit decreta a Deo, & an absolute an conditionate: 2. Fatuum est hoc decretum, quo Deus decrevit, ut Petrus vellet credere, siquidem vellet credere. Iam hic velle credere, non minus est actus supernaturalis, quam ipsum credere. 3. Insulsius longe est decretum, quo Deus decrevit, ut Petrus crederet, vel non, siquidem vellet, quando antecedenter ad tale decretum scientia media Deus præscivit Petrum crediturum finaliter, Iudam finaliter non crediturum.
units.tr: 25. 3. If God decrees to make grace efficacious in these persons but not in those, then the efficacy of God's grace depends on God's freedom, not on men's. But the first is true, from Scripture: Ephes. 2. 10. For we are his workmanship, created unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them. The Arminians reply that God does not decree peremptorily that Peter or Judas should believe, but only conditionally, on the condition, foreseen, that Peter should be willing. Answer. (1) The question will regress to infinity, whether the prerequisite condition is decreed by God, and whether absolutely or conditionally. (2) That decree is foolish by which God decreed that Peter should be willing to believe, if indeed he should be willing to believe. For here, to be willing to believe is no less a supernatural act than believing itself. (3) Far more insipid is the decree by which God decreed that Peter should believe, or not, if he should be willing, when, prior to such a decree, God by middle knowledge foreknew that Peter would finally believe and Judas would finally not believe.

units.la: 26. 4. Tollitur usus precum & gratiarum actionis pro conversione. Quid stultius (inquit Augustin.) quam Deum orare ut facias, quod in potestate habeas? Quorsum ego Apostolus agat Deo gratias propter fidem & charitatem Thessaconicensium? 2. Thess. c. 1. v. 3. Quid ? non debet Petrus magis, quam Iudas suae conversionis gloriam, & gratias Deo deferre?
units.tr: 26. 4. The use of prayer and of thanksgiving for conversion is taken away. "What is more foolish," says Augustine, "than to pray God to do what you have in your power?" Why did the Apostle give thanks to God for the faith and love of the Thessalonians? 2 Thess. ch. 1, v. 3. What? Ought not Peter to ascribe the glory of his conversion, and give thanks to God for it, more than Judas?

units.la: 27. 5. Tollitur plane providentia Dei. Nam nullum hic refulget Dei dominium, quo Iacobum, aut Petrum, potius quam Esavum, & Iudam converteret. Si enim pendet efficacia eventus ex hoc, quod Petrus velit, & noneventus, quod Iudas non velit, non potest vel per Dei providentiam & Dominium fieri, ut Iudas convertatur & salvetur, & Petrus non convertatur & damnetur. Mihi hic vel Iesuita Suarez consentit. Nam juxta (inquit) illam (sententiam) veluti ex accidente contingit respectu divinae voluntatis, quod in uno gratia sufficiens fiat efficax, & non in alio solum, quia alter non vult cooperari, & alius vult. Quod licet non possit dici casu fieri respectu Dei, quia fit ex praescientia, & ex generali voluntate, qua vult creaturam sinere motus suos agere, tamen respectu divinae voluntatis non potuerit ea differentia illi peculiariter attribui, etiam quoad actualem efficaciam, quam habet gratia in eo qui convertitur. Arrigite aures Arminiani: magnus ille Doctor Suarez, cui vos doctrinam vestram inprimis debetis, sententiam vestam de efficacia gratiae in Dei providentiam ignominiosam censoriã[?] virgulà notat. Imo quoniam efficacia hæc ab eventu, quæ ab arbitrio humano pendet, futuritionem habuit antecedenter ad Dei scientiam mediam & decretum, dico Deum ne per omnipotentiam suam posse plures convertere, quam qui actu convertuntur, aut plures non convertere, quam qui actu non convertuntur. Hinc, 6. pugnat hæc efficacia cum Dei omnipotentia. 7. Cum Dei absoluta libertate. 8. Cum Dei sapientia simul & libertate. Non enim potest Deus alio ordine, modo, aut serius, ocius homines convertere quam convertuntur. Nam antecedenter ad Dei scientiam mediam & decretum ipsorum conversio, eo, quo fit, modo, ordine, loco, anno, die, hora, momento, futuritionem æternam habuit, & sic Deus fato longe fatalissimo ipsius voluntatem antegrediente constringitur. O misera ecclesiæ fata! O tempora!
units.tr: 27. 5. Plainly, the providence of God is taken away. For no lordship of God shines forth here, by which he should convert James or Peter rather than Esau and Judas. For if the efficacy of the outcome depends on Peter's willing and not on Judas's not willing, it cannot come about, by God's providence and dominion, that Judas is converted and saved while Peter is not converted and is damned. Here even the Jesuit Suárez agrees with me: For according to that opinion (he says), it happens as if by accident, with respect to the divine will, that in one case sufficient grace becomes efficacious and in another it does not, because the one does not want to cooperate and the other does. Although this cannot be said to happen by chance with respect to God, since it comes about from foreknowledge and from the general will by which he wills to let creatures act their motions, nevertheless, with respect to the divine will, that difference could not be attributed to it peculiarly, even as regards the actual efficacy that grace has in the one who is converted. Prick up your ears, Arminians: that great Doctor Suárez, to whom you owe your doctrine above all, marks your opinion of the efficacy of grace with the censor's rod, as dishonouring the providence of God. Indeed, since this efficacy, which depends on the human will, had its futurition prior to God's middle knowledge and decree, I say that God cannot by his omnipotence convert more people than those who actually are converted, or fail to convert more than those who actually are not converted. Hence (6) this efficacy fights against the omnipotence of God; (7) against the absolute freedom of God; (8) against the wisdom and freedom of God together. For God cannot convert men in another order, mode, or time, sooner or later, than they are converted. For prior to God's middle knowledge and decree, their conversion had eternal futurition in the manner, order, place, year, day, hour and moment in which it happens, and so God, by a far more fatal fate, is constrained, his own will going before. O the wretched fates of the Church! O the times!

units.la: 28 9. Perit tota fidei ratio, adeoque usus ministerii. Nemo enim in Deum confidat propter accretionem fidei, patientiæ, charitatis, si Deus non efficaciter voluntatem determinet ad hosce actus. Si enim ipsa voluntas efficaciter diligit, credit, & Deo se patienter submittit, homo in se potius, quam in Deo, imo nullo modo in Deo fidere potest, siquidem positis omnibus actionibus gratiæ validissimis, tam potest non credere, sperare, diligere, quam credere, sperare vel diligere. At dicunt hominem confidere in Deo debere, quod nempe Deus præstet, quod ipsius est; & ad omnes hos actus, paratum esse propensumque Deum, præstandos, nisi ipse sibi homo deerit. Nugæ vanissimæ: quid hoc est, nisi homo deerit? At an non credendum, Deum efficere per gratiam, ne homo sibi ipsi desit? egregia fides & spes; Deus efficiet ut homo in fidei, spei, & charitatis actibus perseveret, siquidem ipse perseverârit. At ipsaest fidei & spei vacillatio, ne ego mihi deero: quomodo tum in Deo siderem & in ipsius potentissima gratia, ne mihi desim? An fidendum Deum adjuvare me, ne mihi desim, si non ipse mihi deero? Heu vana solatia, vana & ludicra spes! At hoc est mysterium, non esse fidendum mihi in Deo & ejus gratia, quâ ad finem perseverem in data gratia. At contrarium habetur 1. Cor. 1. 8. Philip. 1. v. 6. Iud. v. 24.
units.tr: 28. 9. The whole ground of faith perishes, and with it the use of the ministry. For no one would trust in God for an increase of faith, patience and love, if God does not efficaciously determine the will to these acts. For if the will itself efficaciously loves, believes, and patiently submits itself to God, man trusts in himself rather than in God; indeed he cannot trust in God in any way, since, with all the most powerful actions of grace posited, he can as well not believe, hope and love as believe, hope or love. But they say that a man ought to trust in God that God will perform what is his; and that God is ready and inclined to perform all these acts, unless man himself fails himself. Most vain trifles! What is this but "unless man fails"? But is it not to be believed that God will by grace bring it about that man does not fail himself? An excellent faith and hope! God will bring it about that man perseveres in the acts of faith, hope and love, provided he himself persevere. But this is the very wavering of faith and hope: "lest I fail myself." How then could I rest in God and in his most powerful grace, lest I fail myself? Or ought I to trust that God will help me, lest I fail myself, if he himself will not fail me? Alas, vain comforts, vain and idle hope! But this is the mystery: that I must not trust in myself in God and his grace, by which I persevere to the end in the grace given. Yet the contrary is taught: 1 Cor. 1. 8; Philip. 1. v. 6; Jude v. 24.

units.la: 29. 10. Evertit omnem solidam consolationem & patientiam sanctorum in illis malis, quæ ipsis à causis liberis eveniunt, si à libero arbitrio sit efficacia determinationis causæ liberæ. Frustra enim me Deo submitterem ob odia, contumelias, & injurias, quæ liberè inferunt mihi homines, si Deus ipsorum voluntates influxu indifferente & collaterali moveat, ita ut tam[?] possint homines ea mala non facere, quam facere; & Dei motio nihil momenti afferet ad actualem efficaciam in his malis.
units.tr: 29. 10. It overturns all solid consolation and the patience of the saints in those evils which come upon them from free causes, if the efficacy of the determination of a free cause is from free will. For in vain would I submit myself to God for the hatreds, insults and injuries which men freely inflict on me, if God moved their wills by an indifferent and collateral influence, so that men could as well not do those evils as do them; and God's motion would contribute nothing to the actual efficacy in these evils.

units.la: 30. II. Pugnat cum Dei gratiæ naturâ & perfectione, ut ipsius influxus & efficientia actualis pendeat à libero hominis arbitrio, ut fit, vel non fit. Sic enim Deus miseretur, & salvat secundum opera, quæ nos facimus, & hominum merita, non vero nos convertimur secundum divitem misericordiam, & Dei gratuitam φιλανθρωπίαν, aut quia Deus gratiose miseretur, sed quoniam nos volumus.
units.tr: 30. 11. It is inconsistent with the nature and perfection of God's grace that its influence and actual efficiency should depend on the free will of man, whether it happens or does not. For thus God would show mercy and save according to the works which we do and the merits of men; but we are not converted according to his rich mercy and God's gratuitous love of mankind [φιλανθρωπίαν], nor because God mercifully has mercy, but because we are willing.

units.la: 31. 12. Pugnat cum vera humilitate. Quis enim in Deum non superbiret, pariter & in homines, qui credat se ita credere, & semet convertere, ut non Deo, sed sibi, sed suo arbitrio imputandum, quod actu convertatur, & separetur à filiis hujus saeculi & mancipiis Diaboli?
units.tr: 31. 12. It is inconsistent with true humility. For who would not be proud toward God, and likewise toward men, if he believed that he so believes and converts himself, that it is to be imputed not to God but to himself, to his own will, that he is actually converted and separated from the children of this age and the slaves of the Devil?

units.la: 32. 13. Si omnis effectus dependet à Deo in fieri, quoniam est ens, per eandem rationem omnis causa dependet à Deo in facere, quoniam τὸ facere in causa est æque ens à primo ente dependens, atque τὸ fieri in effectu. Atqui voluntatem sese active determinare est ens, non minus quam ipsa volitio. Respondent Molina, Fonseca, Grevinclovius[?]. Tilen. Determinationem voluntaris esse ipsam volitionem & formalem voluntatis actum, ideoque proprie Deo non magis tribui posse, quam τὸ velle. Respondetur. primo τὸ velle quo ad fieri tribuitur Deo, tanquam causæ efficienti (insanit enim, qui Deum causam
units.tr: 32. 13. If every effect depends on God in becoming [τὸ fieri], because it is being, by the same reasoning every cause depends on God in acting, because the acting [τὸ facere] in the cause is equally being, depending on the first being, as the becoming [τὸ fieri] in the effect. But to determine oneself actively is being, no less than volition itself. Molina, Fonseca and Grevinclovius reply. Tilenus: the determination of the will is volition itself and the formal act of the will, and therefore cannot be attributed to God any more properly than the willing [τὸ velle]. Answer: first, the willing [τὸ velle], as regards becoming, is attributed to God as efficient cause (for he is mad who would hold that God is the formal, or even vitally efficient, cause of the volition

units.la: { } volitionis formalem aut vitaliter etiam efficientem velit.) Ergo τὸ[?] velle quoad facere tribuitur Deo. Si enim (ut notat folidiffime Guilielmus Tuiffus) effi-cientia passiva immediate dependet à Deo, cur non etiam efficientia activa. Nam facere est æque ens in categoria actionis, atque fieri in categoria passionis. 2 Determinatio æquivoca, externa & effectiva Dei, non est idem actus cum volit one vitali, quod sic probo. Determinatio Dei externa, & volitio differunt ut causa & effectus. Nam Deus determinatione externa efficit in nobis τὸ[?] velle: atqui volitionem efficere τὸ[?] velle, est absurdum. 2. Hi actus differunt terminis formalibus. Nam terminus formalis determinationis externæ, quam nos Deo tribuimus est voluntas in primo sui influxus actu constituta: at vero terminus formalis in quem fertur determinatio formalis, sive volitio est bonum eligibile, quod voluntas eligit. 3. Deus inflectit cor. ho-minis, quocunque vult hac determinatione, ut absolutus dominus actuum liberorum: at ipsa voluntas non se ut absoluta domina inflectit quocunque vult. Sic enim divinæ providentiæ non subjiceretur. E.4. Determinationi opponitur indifferentia: at electioni non opponitur formaliter indifferentia, sed nolitio, seu repudiatio.
units.tr: volition, the formal or even vital efficient cause). Therefore the willing [τὸ velle], as regards acting, is attributed to God. For if (as William Twisse most solidly observes) passive efficiency depends immediately on God, why not also active efficiency? For acting is equally being in the category of action, as becoming is in the category of passion. (2) The equivocal, external and effective determination of God is not the same act as vital volition, which I prove thus. God's external determination and volition differ as cause and effect. For by external determination God produces in us the willing [τὸ velle]; but for volition to produce the willing is absurd. (3) These acts differ in their formal terms. For the formal term of the external determination which we attribute to God is the will, constituted in the first act of its influence; but the formal term toward which the formal determination, or volition, tends is the eligible good which the will chooses. (4) God bends the heart of man wherever he wills, by this determination, as absolute lord of free acts; but the will itself does not bend itself wherever it wills, as absolute mistress. For in that case it would not be subject to divine providence. Therefore: indifference is opposed to determination; but indifference is not formally opposed to choice, but non-willing, or rejection.

units.la: 14. Sic Alvarez[?], & alii Dominicani. Omnis causa principalis determinat instrumenta sibi fubordinata ad suos actus: atqui omnes creaturæ, adeoque voluntas humana, instrumenta Dei sunt. E. à Deo ad suos actus determinantur. Minor est scripturæ. Efai. 10. Assur (inquit Deus) baculus furoris mei & securis in Dei manu. Ib. dicitur, Scio Gul. Tussjum acute admodum censere hoc argumentum Alvarianum. Ait enim non posse hoc concludi ex peculiari notione instrumenti, licet causis omnibus secundis accommo-dabili, quia instrumenta rati nalia[?] movent se ipsa, idque tanquam causæ principales: non sic instrumenta passiva. At vero puto non necesse esse, ut Alvarez & alii rationem ducant ex communi natura instrumenti, sed potius ex ratione talis instrumenti. Servus enim heri instrumentum est, sed non necesse est herus determinet singulos actus servi forte operantis in villa rustica 20 milliaribus ab hero. At vero sic argumentum concludit optime: Omnis causa subordinata ita Deo, ut quodlibet instrumentum passivum agenti libero, uti securis fabro lignario, baculus moventi baculum, determinatur à Deo in sua actione: atqui omnes creaturæ sic subordinantur Deo, ex Efai. 10. Ergo omnes creaturæ sunt à Deo ad actus suos determinatæ. Ratio majoris est, quoniam instrumenta passiva vitæ & sensus expertia, motionem non habent causalem ullo modo, quoad τὸ[?] facere ab agente libero independentem. Quid? an securis à fabro non flexa, & non mota scinderet? Ratio vero minoris est, quia omnes creaturæ magis Deo in operando propter perfectionem prudentiæ divinæ subordinantur, quam quælibet creatura alii creaturæ: alioqui Deus non posset absolute dominari omni actui creaturæ, quod absurdum est.
units.tr: 14. So Alvarez[?] and the other Dominicans. Every principal cause determines the instruments subordinate to it to their acts. But all creatures, and therefore the human will, are instruments of God. Therefore they are determined by God to their acts. The minor premise is from Scripture: Isaiah 10. Assyria (says God) is the rod of my fury and the axe in the hand of God. Ibid. is cited: I know that William Twisse judges this Alvarian argument very shrewdly. For he says it cannot be concluded from the peculiar notion of an instrument, although that notion is applicable to all secondary causes, because rational instruments move themselves, and do so as principal causes; passive instruments do not. But I think it is not necessary for Alvarez and the others to draw their reasoning from the common nature of an instrument, but rather from the nature of this particular kind of instrument. A servant is indeed his master's instrument, but it is not necessary that the master determine each act of a servant who may be working on a farm twenty miles from him. Rather, the argument concludes very well in this form: every cause subordinate to God in such a way that any passive instrument, such as an axe to a woodcutter or a staff moved by a staff-bearer, is determined by God in its action, when it serves a free agent, is so determined; but all creatures are so subordinated to God, as Isaiah 10 shows. Therefore all creatures are determined by God to their acts. The reason for the major premise is that passive instruments, which lack life and sense, have no causal motion of their own, independent of the free agent, in respect of their doing. Indeed, would an axe not moved and not bent by the woodcutter cut wood? The reason for the minor premise is that all creatures are subordinated to God in acting, because of the perfection of the divine wisdom, more than any creature is subordinated to another creature. Otherwise God could not rule absolutely over every act of a creature, which is absurd.

units.la: 15. Non potest necessitari prima causa, cum sit agens liberum ad suum concursum causæ secundæ contribuendum: Sic enim quilibet flagitiosus Deum ad actum peccandi necessitaret, & creatura determinaret influxum creatoris ad omnes actus causæ secundæ. Atqui causæ secundæ si primo movent, & se ad actus suos determinant, vel necessario Deus concurreret ad omnes actus causæ secundæ, ita ut possim ego efficere Deum, qui omnia secundum consilium suæ voluntatis agit. Ephes. 1. 11. facere omnia, quæ ego, volo ad nutum meæ voluntatis, vel daretur actio causæ secundæ absque actione causæ primæ.
units.tr: 15. The first cause cannot be necessitated, since it is a free agent in contributing its concurrence to the second cause. For in that way every wicked man would necessitate God to the act of sinning, and the creature would determine the Creator's influence to every act of the second cause. But if the second causes move first and determine their own acts, then either God would necessarily concur in every act of the second cause, so that I could make God, who works all things according to the counsel of his will, do Ephesians 1:11 whatever I wish at the nod of my will; or there would be an action of a second cause without the action of the first cause.

units.la: 16. Tandem Patres & Scholastici determinationem voluntatis humanæ & gratiæ efficaciam Deo, non libertati tribuunt. August, Certum est nos velle cum volumus, sed ille facit, ut velimus, præbendo vires efficacissimas qui dixit, faciam ut ambuletis &c. Et idem: Tantum spiritu sancto accenditur voluntas eorum (qui convertuntur) ut ideo possint, quia sic volunt, & ita velint, quia Deus operatur ut velint. Et idem Orandus est Deus ut velit, nam si ille velit, necesse est esse. Et idem: Cum enim alius sic, alius sic moveatur ad fidem, eademque res sæpe alio modo dicta moveat, alio modo dicta non moveat, aliumque moveat, alium non moveat, quis dicat defuisse Deo modum vocandi, quo etiam Esau ad eam fidem mentem applicaret, voluntatemque conjungeret, in quo Iacob justificatus est? Et idem: Quid est, [ Omnis qui audivit à Patre & didicit, venit ad me ] nisi nullus est, qui audiat, & discat à Patre, & non veniat ad me? Si enim omnis, qui audivit & didicit, venit ad me, profecto omnis qui non venit, non audivit à Patre, nec didicit. Nam si audivisset & didicisset, veniret. Et inferius: Hæc gratia quæ occulte humanis cordibus divina largitate tribuitur, à nullo duro corde respuitur: ideo quippe tribuitur ut cordis durities pri-mitus auferatur. Et ibid. Cæteris vero juste non dat, quamvis si ipsos docere voluisset, procul dubio venirent & ipsi. Non enim fallit aut fallitur qui ait: omnis qui audivit, & didicit à Patre venit ad me. Ab-fit ergo ut quisquam non veniat, qui à Patre audivit & didicit. Idem: Quamvis dicamus Dei donum esse obedientiam, tamen homines exhortamur ad eam sed illis qui veritatis exhortationem obedienter audiunt, ipsum donum Dei datum est hoc obedienter obedire: illis autem, qui non sic obediunt, non est datum. Et ibid. Nam si omnis qui didicit, venit, profecto qui non venit, non didicit, hoc dicendi modo, quo per spiritus gratiam, ita docet Deus, ut quodquisque didicerit non tantum cognoscendo videat, sed etiam volendo appetat, agendoque perficiat. Et idem: Vocatio illa alta atque secreta, sic agit sensum ut ac-commodet assensum Videat qui volet Augustin. de prædestinat. c. 16. & lib de cor. & grat. c. 11, & de bono perseverant. c. 6, Concil. Aranf. Hoc salubriter profitemur quod, in omni bono opere nos non incipimus, sed Deus operatur in nobis velle. Nec loquuntur de actione Dei morali, ut patet ex textu, nec hæretici quos impugnabant, de hoc litem movebant. Synod. Diespolyta. c, 2. Victoria nostra non ex libero arbitrio, sed ex Dei gratia. Concil. Senonens. an. Dom. 1528. Deus prius natura influit in opus, quam liberum arbitrium. Bernard. de lib. arbitr. Deus author meriti voluntatem applicat operi; & opus voluntati. Hieronym. Certe (inquit) fulgor ille & majestas divinitatis occulta, quæ etiam in humana facie relucebat, ex primo se videntes trahere poterat aspeētu. Si enim in Magnete lapide & Succinis hæc esse vis dicitur, ut annulos & stipulam & festucas sibi copulet, quanto magis Dominus omnium creaturarum ad se trahere poterat, quos volebat? Hic fatetur Suarez gratiam excitantem prædeterminantem moraliter voluntatem: & quamvis Chrysostomus minus versatus fit in doctrina Pelagiana, tamen certum est eum agnovisse moralem prædeterminationem. Aquinas, Deus (inquit) non solum movet res ad operandum, quasi applicando formas & virtutes ad operandum, sicut etiam artifex applicat securim ad scindendum, sed etiam dat formas creaturis agentibus. Et ib. art. 4. Proprium est Dei voluntatem movere sufficienter, & efficaciter, imo interius efficaciter inclinando. Scotum, Bellarminum, Bonaventuram, Toletum, Picerium pro hac sententia citat Guil. Tuiff. loco citat. Bannes ait, eos qui contrarium sentiunt, declinare in hæresin Pelagianam. Eftius multis argumentis contendit efficaciam gratiæ à natura gratiæ, non à libero arbitrio pendere. Did. Alvarez ait esse doctrinam scripturæ, Augustini, Thomæ, & omnium Scholasticorum.
units.tr: 16. Finally, the Fathers and the Schoolmen attribute the determination of the human will and the efficacy of grace to God, not to freedom. Augustine: It is certain that we will when we will, but he makes us will, by giving most efficacious powers, he who said, I will make you walk, etc. And again: The will of those who are converted is so kindled by the Holy Spirit that they can therefore do so because they so will, and they so will because God works that they should will. And again: God must be prayed to that he should will, for if he wills, it must be. And again: Since one person is moved to faith in one way and another in another way, and the same thing, spoken in one manner, moves some and, spoken in another manner, does not move others, and moves one but not another, who would say that God lacked a way of calling by which he might apply the mind and join the will even to Esau for that faith, in which Jacob was justified? And again: What is this, [Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me], except that there is no one who hears and learns from the Father and does not come to me? For if everyone who has heard and learned comes to me, certainly everyone who does not come has not heard from the Father nor learned. For if he had heard and learned, he would come. And further on: This grace, which is secretly bestowed on human hearts by divine generosity, is rejected by no hard heart; it is indeed bestowed so that the hardness of the heart may first be taken away. And in the same place: To the rest, however, he does not justly give it, although if he had wished to teach them, without doubt they too would come. For he who says, everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me, neither deceives nor is deceived. Far be it, therefore, that anyone who has heard and learned from the Father should not come. Likewise: Although we say that obedience is the gift of God, yet we exhort men to it; but to those who obediently hear the exhortation to the truth, the very gift of God is given, to obey obediently; but to those who do not so obey, it is not given. And in the same place: For if everyone who has learned comes, certainly he who does not come has not learned; in this way of speaking, by the grace of the Spirit, God so teaches that whoever has learned sees not only by knowing, but also by willing desires, and by acting, performs. And again: That high and secret calling so works on the mind that it brings about assent. Let him who wishes see Augustine, On Predestination, ch. 16, and On the Gift of Perseverance, ch. 11, and On the Good of Perseverance, ch. 6. The Council of Orange: We profess this for our salvation, that in every good work we do not begin, but God works in us to will. Nor do they speak of God's moral action, as is clear from the text, nor did the heretics they opposed dispute this point. The Synod of Diespolis, ch. 2: Our victory is not from free will but from the grace of God. The Council of Sens, in the year of our Lord 1528: God naturally influences the work before free will does. Bernard, On Free Will: God, the author of merit, applies the will to the work, and the work to the will. Jerome: Certainly (he says) that splendour and the hidden majesty of divinity, which shone even in the human face, could draw those who saw it from the first glance. For if it is said that this power is in the magnet stone and in amber, so that it joins to itself rings and straw and chaff, how much more could the Lord of all creatures draw to himself whom he wished? Here Suarez confesses that exciting grace morally predetermines the will. And although Chrysostom was less versed in Pelagian doctrine, it is nevertheless certain that he acknowledged moral predetermination. Aquinas: God (he says) not only moves things to act, as by applying forms and powers to acting, as the craftsman applies the axe to cutting, but he also gives forms to acting creatures. And in the same place, art. 4: It is proper to God to move the will sufficiently and efficaciously, indeed to incline it inwardly and efficaciously. William Twisse, in the place cited, cites Scotus, Bellarmine, Bonaventure, Toledo and Piccherio for this opinion. Bañez says that those who think otherwise decline into Pelagian heresy. Estius contends by many arguments that the efficacy of grace depends on the nature of grace, not on free will. Didacus Alvarez says it is the doctrine of Scripture, of Augustine, of Thomas, and of all the Schoolmen.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: Jesuitarum & Arminianorum argumentis, contra gratia efficaciam prædeterminatricem occurritur.
units.tr: The arguments of the Jesuits and Arminians against the predetermining efficacy of grace are answered.

units.la: CAusa cur hic converratur non ille, an sit Dei libertas absoluta, an vero justitia, quâ hunc peccatorem deserat, illum volentem converti, non deserat, sed convertat, quæstio palmaris hic nobis est cum Arminianis. Ita loquitur Arminius: Quærat enim quis (inquit) cur Deus illum deserat, illum assumat? Respondetur, quia vult. Cur autem velit, causa extra illum non est, at cur velle posset. Illa autem causa est peccatum, non efficiens actualem desertionem, sed promerens, & dignum faciens peccatorem desertione certò deserendum, si Deus ipsum pro merito punire vellet, quod velle ipsius libero arbitratui permittitur. Et alibi sic: Obduratio & excæcatio denunciatur iis, qui Deo vocanti parere recusarunt. Hinc non-conversionis hujus potius, quam illius causa meritoria statuitur peccatum ex parte hominis, ex parte vero Dei statuitur non Dei absoluta libertas, sed justitia, ideoque exnostrâ sententiâ si efsicacacia gratiæ ab ipsa gratia non à libero arbitrio proveniat, Deus erit causa non-conversionis (uti declamitat Arminius) sicut homo ruinæ ædium causa est, quibus nutitantibus, & in casum inclinantibus, fulcra non supponit, aut suppofira removet.
units.tr: The reason why God converts one man and not another, whether it is God's absolute freedom or rather a justice by which he forsakes this sinner while not forsaking, but converting, the one who is willing to be converted, is the chief question we have here with the Arminians. Thus Arminius speaks: "For someone may ask," (he says) "why God forsakes this man and takes up that one?" The answer is, because he wills it. But why he wills it, there is no cause outside him; there is only a cause why he could will it. That cause, however, is sin, not as the efficient cause of the actual desertion, but as deserving it and making the sinner one who is certainly to be forsaken, if God should wish to punish him according to his desert, which wish is left to his free choice. And elsewhere he puts it thus: Hardening and blindness are announced to those who refuse to obey God when he calls. Hence sin on man's side is set up as the meritorious cause of this non-conversion rather than of that one, while on God's side what is set up is not God's absolute freedom but his justice. Therefore, on our view, if the efficacy of grace does not come from grace itself but from free will, God will be the cause of non-conversion (as Arminius declaims), just as a man is the cause of the collapse of a building: he does not put supports under walls that are tottering and leaning towards falling, or he removes the props that were there.

units.la: 2.Sed observari velim simile objectum suisse Pelagio: hinc jam objiciuntur Pelagio alia Cœlestii capitula capitulia. Si enim per gratiam omnia facimus quando vincimur à peccato, non nos vincimur, sed Dei gratia quæ noluit nos adjuvare omnimodo & non potuit. Et iterum ait: Si gratia Dei est, quando vincimus peccata, ergo ipse est in culpa, quando à peccato vincimur, quia omnino custodire nos non potuit, aut noluit. R. 1. Ait Arminius causam, cur Deus velle potest peccatorem deserere, qui converti non vult, esse peccatum. At vero peccatum vel est causa, cur Deus velle potest deserere peccatorem, potentia absoluta vel potentia justitiæ restricta. Primum non dicet Arminius, nemo enim dicet peccatum esse causam, cur Deus absolute aliquid velle potest. Nam absolutæ Dei volitionis non est ulla extra Deum causa, & dato, quod non esset peccatum, absolute Deus velle potest, quicquid absolute vult. Nec dici potest peccatum esse causam, cur Deus velit voluntate justitiæ restricta aliquem deserere, quia sic Deus omnes peccatores desereret, Nemo enim convertitur à peccato, qui non fuerat peccator, & sic Deus in justitiam suam delinqueret, si non omnes desereret. At vide, erudite lector, impofturam Arminii lepidam. Vult peccatum esse causam cur Deus posset deferere peccatorem, causam nempe meritoriam, non actu efficientem desertionem, sed ipsam promerentem, & certo promerentem certoque efficientem, fi Deus eum pro merito punire vellet. At fi peccator meretur ex ordine juf-titiæ desertionem, quæritur cur Deus eum pro merito punire nolit, vel quia non est peccator, quod hypothefin destruit, vel quia absolute nollet. Si quia absolute non vult deferere peccatorem, tum non ex justitia-vult[?] Deus punire, sed ex absoluta voluntate, quod Arminius vociferabitur (sat scio,) esse ἀθεολόγον[?]. At forte dicet Deum nolle, pro merito, punire peccatorem hunc desertione, quia pro eo punivit Christum. Respondeo: dic eum etiam nolle punire illum desertione, quia pro eo non punivit Christum, & sic Christus pro eo, qui punitur desertiones non est, mortuus, nec punitus, & Christus ex Arminio pro omnibus & singulis est mortuus. At dicet Deum nolle punire hunc pro merito, quia est in Christo ut fidelis, velle punire illum desertione, quia non est in Christo ut fidelis. Refp. Tum Deum non posse absoluta voluntate nunc non credentem punire desertione, imo non erit justus nisi puniat non-credentem, nec erit justus, fi vellet credentem in Christum punire desertione. 2. Vult peccatum non efficere actualem desertionem, sed commereri. Esto, sed vel indeclinabiliter sequitur actualis deftio, peccatum, & sic pessime addit & insulse, [ Si Deus peccatorem pro merito punire vellet. ] Quid si punire nollet Deus pro merito? Ergo erit peccator & non desertus,ideoque conversus[?] at cum peccare in negotio conversionis sit ponere obicem Deo convertenti, sequetur eum converti, qui ponit obicem Deo convertenti, ideoque hominem reluctantem converti, vel declinabiliter, sequitur actualis desertio peccatum, & sic fieri potest ut quis peccet, & relistat Deo convertenti, & tamen non defertur, ideoq; convertatur, quod est absurdum & Arminæ justitiæ repugnans[?]. 3. Quod dicit Arminius obdurationem & excæcationem denunciari iis, qui Deo vocanti parere recusant, patet ex Arminii, eo loci, ad Perkinsium, reponsione, per obdurationem intelligi actum justitiæ divinæ, quo non convertitur peccator, & sic lepidè Arminius vult denunciari non conversionem ut poenam iis, qui non convertuntur. At vero Arminio non-conversio non potest esse & poena & peccatum. Hinc sequitur, ut solidissime observavit doctissimus vir Gul.Tuiffus, quoniam Deo vocanti parere est credere & relipiscere, Deum denunciare se non daturum fidem & relipiscentam iis, qui non credunt & relipiscunt, quam insulsa comminatio? si vos non credidertis, ego vobis-interminor me non daturum vobis, ut credatis.
units.tr: 2. But I would have it noticed that a similar objection was made to Pelagius: other chapters of Caelestius are objected to Pelagius in the same way. For if we do everything through grace when we are overcome by sin, it is not we who are overcome, but the grace of God, which was unwilling to help us in every way and could not. And again he says: If it is the grace of God when we overcome sins, then he himself is at fault when we are overcome by sin, because he could not, or would not, keep us completely. Answer 1. Arminius says that the cause why God can will to forsake a sinner who does not wish to be converted is sin. But sin is either the cause why God can will to forsake a sinner by his absolute power, or by his restricted power of justice. He will not say the first, for no one would say that sin is the cause why God can will anything absolutely. For there is no cause outside God of God's absolute willing, and even if there were no sin, God could absolutely will whatever he absolutely wills. Nor can it be said that sin is the cause why God wills, by his restricted will of justice, to forsake anyone, because in that case God would forsake all sinners: no one is converted from sin who was not a sinner, and so God would act against his own justice if he did not forsake everyone. But see, learned reader, the charming trickery of Arminius. He wants sin to be the cause why God could forsake the sinner, namely a meritorious cause, not actually effecting the desertion, but deserving it, and deserving it with certainty and effecting it with certainty, if God wished to punish him according to his merit. But if the sinner by the order of justice deserves desertion, the question is why God is unwilling to punish him according to his merit: either because he is not a sinner, which destroys the hypothesis, or because God absolutely does not wish it. If it is because God does not absolutely wish to forsake the sinner, then God does not wish to punish from justice but from absolute will, which Arminius will certainly cry out to be atheological [ἀθεολόγον]. But perhaps he will say that God is unwilling to punish this sinner with desertion according to his merit, because God punished Christ for him. I reply: then say also that God is unwilling to punish him with desertion because he did not punish Christ for him, and so Christ did not die for the one who is punished with desertion, nor was he punished for him; yet according to Arminius Christ died for all and each. But he will say that God is unwilling to punish this man according to his merit, because he is in Christ as a believer, and wishes to punish that man with desertion because he is not in Christ as a believer. Answer: then God could not, by his absolute will, punish with desertion the one who does not now believe; indeed he would not be just unless he punished the unbeliever, and he would not be just if he wished to punish with desertion the one who believes in Christ. 2. He holds that sin does not bring about the actual desertion but merely deserves it. Granted; but either the actual desertion follows inevitably from sin, and so he has added, very badly and foolishly, [if God wished to punish the sinner according to his merit]. What if God were unwilling to punish according to merit? Then the sinner will not be forsaken, and therefore will be converted; but since to sin in the matter of conversion is to place an obstacle before God converting, it will follow that the one who places an obstacle before God converting is converted, and so a man who resists is converted. Or, if the actual desertion follows inevitably from sin, it can happen that someone sins and resists God converting, and yet is not forsaken, and so is converted; which is absurd and repugnant to the justice of Arminius. 3. What Arminius says, that hardening and blindness are announced to those who refuse to obey God when he calls, is shown from Arminius's answer to Perkins in the passage in question, where he explains hardening as an act of divine justice by which the sinner is not converted. Thus Arminius charmingly wants non-conversion to be announced as a punishment for those who are not converted. But for Arminius non-conversion cannot be both punishment and sin. Hence it follows, as the most learned man William Twisse has very solidly observed, that since to obey God when he calls is to believe and repent, God announces that he will not give faith and repentance to those who do not believe and repent: how foolish a threat! "If you have not believed, I threaten you that I will not give you to believe."

units.la: 3. Distingui hic velim hæc quatuor. 1.Quod sit, hic naturalis in homine infidelitas & contumacia. 2. Non-curatio nativæ contumaciæ. 3. Voluntaria dilectio nativæ infidelitatis, unde fit ut actu quis resistat Deo vocanti. 4. Fides quæ est actus supernaturalis. Naturalis infidelitas est à nobis, & originalem contumaciam docent plerique esse causam meritoriam nonconversionis, quod quia magnæ tum famæ, tum pariter eruditionis viris dicitur, damnare simpliciter non audeo. At vero si sit causa meritoria non-conversionis, omnes homines merentur non-conversionem, & sic Deus quosdam non convertendo ageret contra demeritum. At vero demeritum proprie est malum, quod Deus ex justitiæ ordine non tantum potest (ut pote qui absolute omnia potest, quæ contradictionem non involvunt) sed & debet infligere. Unde hic cogentur dicere, Deum convertendo multos, agere contra id quod debet agere: quod absurdum est, ideoque hic videtur esse sensus eorum, quod τ[?] mereri hic fit homines dignos esse non-conversione, ex hypothesi divini beneplaciti, unde sensus est Deum jure posse nullos convertere, siquidem ita ei visum fuisset, ideoque nullo modo est ex merito, quod quidam convertantur quidam non. Deus itaque hic non agit, qua justus (sic enim nullos converteret) sed qua agens ex absoluto beneplacito. At vero Arminius Antiperkinf. vult Deum non citra injustitiam posse negare alicui motionem efficacem vel generalem vel specialem, si fit gratiæ morigerus. Sic enim argumentor: Arminius vel loquitur de gratia efficaci, vel de gratia sufficiente. Sit igitur aliquis solicitus ad servandam gratiam datam. Deus enim tum non potest sine injustitiâ ei negare gratiam efficacem, & sic necessario solicitus erit in illo actu, & per eandem rationem non potest ei negare aliam motionem efficacem, & sic necessario adhuc erit solicitus, & sic vel nunquam negare potest Deus motionem efficacem, adeoque semel solicitus nunquam peccabit, quod absurdum. Vel si neget Deus solicito gratiam efficacem, erit injustus, & in promissis praestandis fallax, quippe non dat omni solicito motionem efficacem.
units.tr: 3. I would have these four things distinguished here. 1. That natural unbelief and obstinacy exist in man here. 2. Neglect of the native obstinacy. 3. Voluntary love of the native unbelief, from which it comes about that someone actually resists God calling. 4. Faith, which is a supernatural act. Natural unbelief is from us, and most men who are of great repute and equally great learning teach that original obstinacy is the meritorious cause of non-conversion; since this is said by men of such great standing and learning, I do not dare to condemn it outright. But if it is the meritorious cause of non-conversion, then all men deserve non-conversion, and so by not converting some God would act against desert. But desert is properly evil, which God by the order of justice can not only (since he can do absolutely all things that do not involve contradiction) but must inflict. Hence here they will be forced to say that God, in converting many, acts against what he ought to do; which is absurd. So the meaning of those who say this seems to be that men are made worthy of non-conversion by the hypothesis of the divine good pleasure, so that the sense is that God could rightly convert no one, if it had so seemed good to him; and therefore it is in no way from desert that some are converted and some are not. God therefore does not act here as just (for so he would convert no one), but as acting from absolute good pleasure. But Arminius in Antiperkins holds that God cannot, without injustice, deny to anyone an efficacious motion, whether general or special, if he is obedient to grace. For I argue thus: Arminius speaks either of efficacious grace or of sufficient grace. Let there be someone who is diligent in keeping the grace given. For then God cannot, without injustice, deny him efficacious grace, and so he will necessarily be diligent in that act; and by the same reasoning God cannot deny him another efficacious motion, and so he will necessarily still be diligent; and so either God can never deny an efficacious motion, and thus the one who has once been diligent will never sin, which is absurd; or if God denies efficacious grace to the diligent man, he will be unjust and false in fulfilling his promises, for he does not give an efficacious motion to every diligent man.

units.la: Si vero loquatur de gratia sufficiente, dico tum Deum solicito iniquè & injustè negare motionem efficacem, concedendo tantùm sufficientem, quam praescit effectu carituram, adeoque periclitatur justitia. Nam ratio postulat necessario, ut si Deus motionem suam hic ex ordine justitiae contribuat, plus indulgeatur solicito, quam inerti & ignavo. Atqui certum est Deum interdum ignavo tribuere motionem efficacem, quippe alioqui ex ignavia nunquam resipisceret, imo nihil plus ulli studioso & solicito hic indulgebit, quam praefractis & obduratis. Nam obduratis & omnibus ignavis Deus non potest ex justitia negare motionem sufficientem, sive invigilent, sive non. Alioqui actus peccaminosus iis jure imputari non posset, fatentibus Iesuitis & Arminianis. Si motioni efficaci dixerint resisti posse, contradicunt sibi ipsis. Nam motionis efficacis conceptu quidditativo includitur actuale obsequium illius, qui efficaciter movetur: alioqui motio illa esset insufficiens, non efficax. 2. Non video, quo jure ex Iesuitarum & Arminianorum placitis, Deus potuerit Adamo primum peccatum admittenti tribuisse motionem sufficientem & inefficacem: negasse vero motionem efficacem: Si enim Deus negaverit motionem efficacem ex justitiâ & ex demerito. Adami, eam negavit propter peccatum praecedens. At sic urgebunt eos duo absurda ineluctabilia, nempe. 1. Dari peccatum prius primo. 2. Importune semper recursare idem dubium de illo praecedente peccato priore. Ac proinde cogentur nobiscum dicere Deum non ex justitiae debito, sed secundum ἐνδικίως[?] in nobis efficere velle, & quia sic est ei complacitum Phil. 1. 13. Matth. 11. 26. 3. Si dixerint ex justitiae debito Deum deseruisse Adamum se prius deserentem, hoc videamus. Nam volunt Deum praesto esse & motionem suam in promptu obtulisse Adamo, si Adamus voluisset. At quid est hoc, si Adamus voluisset? Deus tum efficit velle in Adamo efficaciter, siquidem ipse vellet: quam absurdum? Deinde non potest Deus desertione punire primum actum peccaminosum, donec prius actu exiterit ille actus peccaminosus. Nam ex justitiae ordine prius est peccatum, quā poena. Sed si in primo pecato non concurrebat Dei motio efficax, sed tantum Deus paratus erat exhibere motionem efficacem, noluit vero actu exhibere, quia homo noluit illam motionem recipere, sequitur simul natura esse pœnam cum ipso actu peccaminoso, adeoque pœnam non esse posteriorem culpâ, prout postulat æquitas & ordo iustitiæ: imo sequitur simul Adamum peccare, & puniri a Deo. At ordo iustitiæ postulat, ut pœna sequatur tum peccatum, tum sententiæ dictionem. Dicent forte prius natura extitisse non-influxum liberum Adami, negatione motionis divinæ, ideoque peccatum Adami deferentis Deum prius est divina desertione. Sed respondeo, non-influxum liberum Adami, in eo momento, in quo primum extitit non-motio Dei, non esse peccatum in esse completo. Si enim actus peccaminosus Adami prius natura est Dei non-influxu, tum influxus Dei nullo modo est actus boni causa. Quis enim adeo est obtuso ingenio, qui diceret causam esse naturam posteriorem effectu? 4. Certum est Adamum ad tempus Deo obedivisse, & actus obedientiæ præstitisse. Quo jure igitur Deus illos actus non potuit efficaci motione in posterioribus actibus remunerari, juxta illud quod urget Arminius tanquam Dei æquitati consonum? an ex iustitia debuit Deus post quosdam pios obedientiæ actus tribuisse Adamo motionem sufficientem tantum? quem minime efficacem fore præscivit. Hic cogentur dicere Deum ex absoluta libertate, & non ex iustitia negasse motionem ex præscientia sua efficacem propter nullum Adami meritum. Idem dicendum de lapsu angelorum, & ad nostrum institutum, eodem modo philosophandum est de non-conversione hominis, qui probus, pius, & humilis fuit semper usque ad actum non-conversionis. Quo enim jure Deus humili & probo neget motionem efficacem propter non actívam conversionem liberam, quæ nondum est in actu completo? Deus enim non punit peccatum nondum plene existens, & quare actus plos humilitatis & præviæ probitatis non remuneratur motione efficaci secundum præscientiam? §. Sed non video adhuc causam meritoriam non-conversionis Iudæ, potius quam Petri, nec quomódo contumax positio obicis in Iuda sit talis causa. Nam positio contumax impedimenti est non conversio actíva Iudæ contumax, & sic causa meritoria non-conversionis Iudæ erit non conversio. Quid? An idem erit sui ipsius causa? Alva-rez hic dicit: quia homo non vult uti gratia excitante vel sufficiente, ideo non convertitur. Ideoque non conversionem privativam seu peccaminosam rejicit in voluntatem hominis, qui non vult uti gratia excitante. Atqui uti gratia excitante est Deo excitanti moraliter hominem ad conversionem parere, adeoque credere & sese converteré, ideoque causa cur homo non convertatur, est quia non se convertit: quam absurdum? At vero carentiam conversionis ne-
units.tr: But if he speaks of sufficient grace, I say that God then unjustly and wrongfully denies effective motion to the diligent man, granting only a sufficient motion, which he foresees will not produce its effect, and so justice is put in peril. For reason necessarily requires that if God here bestows his motion in accordance with the order of justice, more indulgence be shown to the diligent man than to the sluggish and idle. But it is certain that God sometimes grants effective motion to the idle, since otherwise they would never repent of their idleness. Indeed, he will show no more favour here to any zealous and diligent man than to the stubborn and hardened. For God cannot, out of justice, deny sufficient motion to the hardened and all the idle, whether they are watchful or not. Otherwise a sinful act could not justly be imputed to them, as the Jesuits and Arminians concede. If they say that effective motion can be resisted, they contradict themselves. For the actual compliance of the one who is effectively moved is included in the quidditative concept of effective motion; otherwise that motion would be insufficient, not effective. 2. I do not see by what right, on the principles of the Jesuits and Arminians, God could have granted sufficient but ineffective motion to Adam when he admitted the first sin, and yet denied him effective motion. For if God denied effective motion out of justice and on account of Adam's demerit, then he denied it on account of a preceding sin. But so they will be pressed by two inescapable absurdities: (1) that there is a sin prior to the first; (2) that the same doubt about that prior sin must be raised again and again without end. And so they will be forced to say with us that God wills to work in us not from a debt of justice but according to his good pleasure [εὐδοκία], and because it has so pleased him, Phil. 1. 13. Matth. 11. 26. 3. If they say that God, from a debt of justice, forsook Adam, who was himself first forsaking God, let us examine this. For they want God to be at hand and to have offered his motion to Adam readily, if Adam had willed. But what does this mean, "if Adam had willed"? Then God brings about Adam's willing effectively, supposing that he himself willed it: how absurd! Moreover, God cannot punish the first sinful act by desertion until that sinful act has actually come into being. For in the order of justice sin comes before punishment. But if God's effective motion did not concur in the first sin, but God was merely ready to exhibit effective motion and did not actually exhibit it because man was unwilling to receive that motion, it follows that punishment is naturally simultaneous with the sinful act itself. Thus punishment would not be posterior to guilt, as equity and the order of justice require; indeed, it would follow that Adam sins and is punished by God at the same moment. But the order of justice requires that punishment follow both the sin and the pronouncing of sentence. They will perhaps say that Adam's free non-influx, by the negation of divine motion, existed first in nature, so that Adam's sin in forsaking God is prior to divine desertion. But I answer that Adam's free non-influx, at the moment in which God's non-motion first arose, is not sin in complete being. For if Adam's sinful act is naturally prior to God's non-influx, then God's influx is in no way the cause of a good act. For who is so dull of wit as to say that a cause is naturally posterior to its effect? 4. It is certain that Adam for a time obeyed God and performed acts of obedience. By what right, then, could God not reward those acts with effective motion in later acts, according to that principle which Arminius urges as consonant with God's equity? Ought God, out of justice, after some pious acts of obedience, to have granted Adam only sufficient motion, which he foresaw would not be effective? Here they will be forced to say that God denied effective motion, which by his foreknowledge he knew would be ineffective, from absolute freedom and not from justice, on account of no merit of Adam's. The same is to be said of the fall of the angels; and, to our purpose, we must reason in the same way about the non-conversion of a man who was upright, pious and humble up to the very act of non-conversion. For by what right does God deny effective motion to the humble and upright on account of a free conversion not yet actively performed, which is not yet in complete act? For God does not punish a sin that does not yet fully exist; so why is the act of humility and prior uprightness not rewarded with effective motion according to foreknowledge? §. But I still do not see the meritorious cause of Judas's non-conversion rather than Peter's, nor how a contumacious obstacle in Judas is such a cause. For the contumacious obstacle is Judas's non-conversion of his active will, and so the meritorious cause of Judas's non-conversion will be non-conversion. What? Will it be the cause of itself? Alvarez here says: "Because a man does not want to use exciting or sufficient grace, therefore he is not converted." So he throws the privative or sinful non-conversion back onto the will of the man who does not want to use exciting grace. But to use exciting grace is for a man to yield to God morally exciting him towards conversion, and so to believe and convert himself; therefore the cause why a man is not converted is that he does not convert himself: how absurd! Yet he throws the negative lack of conversion back onto God, who does not convert and who denies effective grace. But for this Alvarez is most justly and most heavily beaten by Gul. Tuisso.

units.la: {y} Hh 3 gativam rejicit in Deum non convertentem, & negantem gratiam efficacem : Sed hoc nomine Alvarez jure meritissimo largissime vapulat à Gul. Tuisso. §. Conscientias Arminianorum hic fluctuare, quando ad justitiam Dei confugiunt, patet quoniam supra audivimus Corvinum fatentem causam disparis istius eventus cur hic convertatur, & ille eadem gratiâ praeveniente instructus non convertatur, sibi incognitam esse, & in solo libero arbitrio non esse positam. Sed & ipse Arminius aliam viam incedere, sed plane fluctuante & obstrepente conscientia faragit [?]. At vero (inquit) haec interna Spiritus Sancti suasio duplex est, una sufficiens, altera efficax. Illa qua potest velle & credere & converti, cui adhibetur; ista qua vult credit & convertitur, cui accomodatur. Illa adhibetur decreto providentiae, cum certa praescientia fore, ut rejiciatur a libero arbitrio hominis. Ista ex decreto praedestinationis, administratu cum certa praescientia fore, ut re ipsa velit, credat & convertatur, cui accommodatur & adhibetur, propterea quod ita accommodatur, prout Deus novit congruum esse persuadendo & convertendo, illi, cui adhibetur. Decreto, reprobationis ib. negat proprie negari gratiam sufficientem, sed eo decreto ait negari efficacem, & haec ait esse ex mente Augustini, forte etiam ex scripturae sensu. At ne vel apice vel literula ex Augustino, vel ex scriptura id comprobare nititur Arminius, & se & lectorem in latebris & conjecturis maluit relinquere. At non ita hæsitanter[?] asserit in collat. cum D. Iunio sed dictatorie potius. Hic itaque non simpliciter vult Arminius, sed fors etiam ex sensu scripturæ ex libero arbitrio esse, quod hic convertatur, non ille, pro vario modo accommodandi gratiam Dei, de quo alibi, ideoque Arminius vult forte decretum absolutum prædestinationis & vocationem congruam, non secundum regulam justitiæ, sed secundum absolutam Dei voluntatem, non minus scripturæ consentaneum esse, quam Arminianam sententiam. 6. Vocatione Arminiana ex Dei voluntate justitiæ restricta stante, non potest Deus non convertere Petrum volentem converti, & non potest ex ordine justitiæ convertere Iudam nolentem converti, præsertim quū rebellio Iudæ finalis Christi merito expiata non fit, ideoque & Deoinvito posset fieri utrumque. Nec hic miseretur quorum vult, non magis quam Deus est justus, quia vult. Nam necessitate naturæ est justus, & necessitate naturæ volentes converti, convertet.
units.tr: §. That the consciences of the Arminians waver here, when they flee to the justice of God, is clear, since above we heard Corvinus confessing that the cause of this unequal outcome, why this man is converted and that one, though equipped with the same preventing grace, is unknown to him and not placed in free will alone. But Arminius himself takes a different path, yet his conscience, plainly wavering and murmuring, drives him on. "But indeed," he says, "this internal persuasion of the Holy Spirit is twofold: one sufficient, the other effective. The former is that by which one can will and believe and be converted, to which it is applied; the latter is that by which he wills, believes and is converted, to which it is accommodated. The former is applied by a decree of providence, with the certain foreknowledge that it will be rejected by the free will of man. The latter is administered by the decree of predestination, with the certain foreknowledge that he will in fact will, believe and be converted, to whom it is accommodated and applied, because it is so accommodated as God knows to be fitting for persuading and converting him to whom it is applied." By the decree of reprobation, in the same place, he denies that sufficient grace is properly denied, but says that effective grace is denied by that decree, and he says this is the mind of Augustine, and perhaps also the sense of Scripture. But Arminius does not strive to prove this even by a jot or tittle from Augustine or from Scripture, and he preferred to leave both himself and the reader in hiding-places and conjectures. Yet in the collation with Junius he does not assert it so hesitantly, but rather dictatorially. Here, therefore, Arminius does not simply will, but perhaps, also from the sense of Scripture, it is from free will that this man is converted and not that one, according to the varied manner of accommodating God's grace, of which elsewhere; and so Arminius perhaps wants the absolute decree of predestination and the congruous vocation, not according to the rule of justice but according to the absolute will of God, to be no less consonant with Scripture than the Arminian opinion. 6. On the Arminian vocation, with the will of God restricted to justice, God cannot fail to convert Peter, who wills to be converted; and he cannot, from the order of justice, convert Judas, who is unwilling to be converted, especially since Judas's final rebellion is not expiated by the merit of Christ, and therefore either could happen even though God was unwilling. Nor here does he have mercy on whom he wills, any more than God is just because he wills. For by the necessity of his nature he is just, and by the necessity of nature he will convert those who are willing to be converted.

units.la: 4. Iam ad secundum venio. Est ea noncuratio nativæ contumaciæ: hæc non-curatio est à solo Deo. Solus enim Deus curat ideoque ex lege affirmationis & negationis, Dei non-curatio erit causa adæquata & totalis nativæ contumaciæ non-curatæ, non simpliciter nativæ contumaciæ, sed contumaciæ non-curatæ, sicut medicus non curans omnes morbos sanabiles, & quos ex artis peritia sanare potest, non est morborum causa: potest tamen dici causa morborum non-curatorum physica, non vero moralis, quoniam medicus ex debito & conductus ad curandum, si tum non curet, est causa morbi non sanati, non tantum physica, quia non curavit ipsos, sed etiam ethica & moralis, quoniam non curavit, & tamen ex officio curare debuit. Itaque Deus hic consideratur tribus modis. 1. physice. 2. ethice, ut agens ex solo suo beneplacito. 3. ethice, ut agens ex justitiae debito ad agendum obligatus. Primo modo Deus est physica causa non curatae nativae contumaciae, quoniam potest in omnibus ipsam curare, & tamen non curat. Ideoque est causa eo modo, quo sol per sui absentiam di-citur causa noctis, quoniam per sui in nostro hemisphaerio praesentiam, est causa diei. In Arminii simili, de ruina aedium ex non appositis fulcris sophisticatur, a positione causae physicae, ad positionem effecti non physici, sed moralis, quae nulla arte confunduntur. Nam Dei negatio gratiae praedeterminantis, quae physica est causa non-conversionis privativae & culpabilis, nullo modo causative terminatur in culpabilem non-conversionem, sed tantum in negativam non-conversionem, ut causa physica in effectum physicum, & voluntas corrupta quae causa est ethica, terminatur in non-conversionem culpabilem, ut causa moralis in effectum moralem, nullo vero modo terminatur in negativam non-conversionem, qui est effectus physicus, non moralis: uti causa cur tali chartæ nihil inscribatur, resp. est à penna non-denigrante : absentia denigrationis, & absentia non-denigrationis artificiosæ est à scribente artem suam negante. Ideoque ex hac Dei causatione sequitur nuda non conversio physica & negativa, non proprie conversio privativa & culpabilis. Nam ex causa præcise physica non sequitur ullo modo culpa. Culpa enim est defectus moralis, ideoque ortum habere non potest, nisi ex causa morali & deficiente: ideoque ex non appositione fulcri physice sequitur ruina ædium physica ut habet similitudo Arm.Si dominus teneatur ædes servo suo suppositis fulcris sustentare, casus ædium moraliter imputatur domino non apponenti fulcra, quæ ex pacto aut data fide apponere debuit, & hoc posteriore sensu simile Arminianū urget, & tamen nihil concludit.
units.tr: 4. I now come to the second point. There is a non-care of native obstinacy, and this non-care comes from God alone. For God alone cares for it, and so by the law of affirmation and negation, God's non-care will be the adequate and total cause of the native obstinacy that is left uncared for, not of native obstinacy simply, but of obstinacy left uncared for. Thus a physician who does not treat all curable diseases, including those he could cure by his skill, is not the cause of the diseases. Yet he can be called the physical, though not the moral, cause of the untreated diseases. For a physician bound by duty and hired to treat them, if he then does not treat them, is the cause of the unhealed disease, not only physically, because he did not treat it, but also ethically and morally, because he did not treat it when he ought to have done so by his office. So God is considered here in three ways: (1) physically; (2) ethically, as acting from his own good pleasure alone; (3) ethically, as acting under obligation from the debt of justice. In the first way, God is the physical cause of the untreated native obstinacy, since he could cure it in all, and yet does not. He is therefore a cause in the way the sun is said to be the cause of night by its absence, just as by its presence in our hemisphere it is the cause of day. In Arminius's simile about the collapse of a house for want of props, he slides from the position of a physical cause to that of a non-physical but moral effect, and these are confused by no art. For God's withholding of predetermining grace, which is the physical cause of the privative and culpable non-conversion, in no way terminates causally in culpable non-conversion, but only in a negative non-conversion, as a physical cause terminates in a physical effect. And the corrupt will, which is the ethical cause, terminates in culpable non-conversion, as a moral cause terminates in a moral effect. It in no way terminates in a negative non-conversion, which is a physical effect, not a moral one. Compare: the reason why nothing is written on such paper is the non-blackening pen; the absence of blackening and the absence of skilful blackening come from the writer who withholds his art. So from this causation by God there follows a bare, physical and negative non-conversion, not properly a privative and culpable conversion. For from a purely physical cause no fault follows in any way. Fault is a moral defect, and so it cannot arise except from a moral and deficient cause. Therefore from the physical non-application of a prop there follows the physical collapse of the house, as the simile has it. If a master were bound to support his servant's house with props, the fall of the house would be morally imputed to the master who did not apply the props he ought to have applied by agreement or pledged faith. The Arminian presses the simile in this latter sense, and yet it concludes nothing.

units.la: Deus enim ex debito neminem convertit, sed ex beneplacito suo.' Secundo modo, si consideretur Deus, ut agens ex beneplacito suo, cujusmodi agens tantum hic est Deus, nullo modo imputatur moraliter non-conversio Deo. Non enim pacto, statuto aut ullo officio Deus se astrinxit ad homines convertendos. Nam non extat statutum aut pactum illud Dei ex promissione ulla [hoc fac, & ego te efficaciter vocabo:] [qui hoc fecerit, conversionis mercedem facti in laboris compensationem repertabit.] Iam quoniam hoc in tota scriptura, aut ex ullo Dei attributo Arminiani, & Iesuitæ ad hunc usque diem nunquam demonstrarunt, neque possunt id ostendere, Deus neminem tenetur etiam ex hypothesi volentem converti, convertere: neque vel Adam ante lapsum, vel Angeli qui lapsi sunt, aut ullus homo habet in sua potestate Dei motionem præviam, neque ulli imputatur moraliter, carentia Dei motionis efficacis. Neque ulla lex mihi imperet, ut ipsam vel habeam, vel non habeam. Sic enim actus Dei creaturis juberentur, quo quid, bone Deus, infulsius? Nobis ne imperatur, ut Deum agere vel non agere astringamus? Ideoque longe differunt nobis imperari actus ex Dei motione causaliter resultantes, ex motione (inquam) Dei efficaci, & ipsam efficacem motionem nobis imperari. Nam illud æquum est, hoc iniquum. Quin imo Deus operatur in nobis velle & perficere Phil. 2. 13. ὑπὲρ τῆς εὐδοκίας: non igitur ex debito: quoniam ita est Dei placitum Math. 11. 26. Non ergo quoniam est debitum. Ideoque tertio modo Deus nullo modo hic potest considerari, ut agens ex debito justitiæ aut æquitatis naturalis.
units.tr: For God converts no one from debt, but from his own good pleasure. In the second way, if God is considered as acting from his own good pleasure, which is the only kind of agent God is here, non-conversion is in no way morally imputed to God. For God has bound himself by no covenant, statute or office to convert men. There is no such statute or covenant of God, arising from any promise, [do this, and I will call you effectually] or [whoever does this shall find the reward of conversion as a recompense for his labour]. Since the Arminians and Jesuits have never shown this from the whole of Scripture or from any attribute of God to this day, and cannot show it, God is bound, even on the hypothesis that a man is willing to be converted, to convert no one. Neither Adam before the fall, nor the angels who fell, nor any man has it in his power to have God's prior motion, and no one is morally blamed for lacking God's efficacious motion. And no law commands me either to have it or not to have it. For in that case God's acts would be commanded of creatures. What, good God, could be more absurd? Are we commanded to bind God to act or not to act? So it is very different to command us to perform acts that result causally from the motion of God, that is, from God's efficacious motion, and to command us the efficacious motion itself. For the first is fair, the second unjust. Indeed God works in us both to will and to perform [Phil. 2. 13] for his good pleasure [ὑπὲρ τῆς εὐδοκίας]. Therefore not from debt, since it is so by God's pleasure [Matt. 11. 26]. Therefore not because it is owed. So in the third way God cannot be considered here at all as acting from the debt of justice or natural equity.

units.la: §. Ad tertium accedo: ea est voluntaria non-curatæ contumaciæ dilectio & volitio, & est peccatum & consequens non-curatæ contumaciæ. Et ex ea est non-conversio culpabilis, ideoque ex libera & absoluta Dei non-curatione nativæ contumaciæ & ex liberrima Dei non-conversione, sequitur nonconversio culpabilis & resistentia facta Deo vocanti, non ut effectus ex causa, sed ut consequens ex antecedente. Duas dico hic esse causas, cur resistentia & non-conversio culpabilis non rejici debeat in Deum, ut in causam moralem. 1. Quoniam non est ulla causa moraliter rea, eo quod non agat, nisi debito, lege, aut pacto, teneatur agere. Deus autem non tenetur hic agere: & non obligatur non agere, sed miseretur quorum vult, indurat, quos vult. 2. Quoniam in-ter Dei non-conversionem & resistentiam intervenit voluntaria dilectio nativæ contumaciæ, & libera voluntatis corruptæ volitio, qua quis, qui obligatur Deo vocanti parere, ideoque credere & resipiscere, non vult credere & resipiscere, ideoque Grevinchov. ma-le argumentatur. Denegatio (inquit) auxilii prædeterminantis est causa adæquata carentiæ boni usus gratiæ, & resistentiæ. At denegatio auxilii prædeterminantis est à solo Deo. Ergo carentia boni usus gratiæ adeoque tota resistentia, & non-conversio hominis est à solo Deo. Nam resp. 1. Quod denegatio auxilii prædeterminantis non est causa carentiæ boni usus gratiæ & resistentiæ, imo non est causa omnino. Quomodo ergo est causa adæquata? hoc probet ille, prorsus audiemus altum silentium, ubi probationes postulamus. Concedi musresistentiam sequi ex denegatione auxilii prædeterminantis, ut consequens ex antecedente; ut effectus ex causa negamus. Hoc si probasset, causam nostram lædisset. Nam intervenit inter negationem auxilii prædeterminantis & resistentiam libera volitio voluntatis depravatæ, unde causaliter fit resistentia. At vero quoniam resistentia fit ex causa ad agendum moraliter obligata, & Deus negans auxilium prædeterminans, non est causa moraliter obligata, nullum (esse) effectivum aut causativum omnino Deus contribuet resistentiæ. Negamus itaque non usum gratiæ culpabilem, non conversionem privatam & culpabilem ex Deo esse causative.
units.tr: §. I come to the third point. The wilful love and willing of the non-cared-for obstinacy is itself sin, and it follows from the non-care of obstinacy. From it comes culpable non-conversion. So from God's free and absolute non-care of native obstinacy, and from his most free non-conversion, there follows culpable non-conversion and resistance offered to God calling, not as an effect from a cause, but as a consequent from an antecedent. I say there are two causes here why the resistance and culpable non-conversion ought not to be cast upon God as a moral cause. (1) Because no cause is morally guilty if it does not act, unless it is bound to act by debt, law or pact. But God is not bound to act here, nor is he obliged not to act; rather he has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills. (2) Because between God's non-conversion and the resistance there intervenes the voluntary love of native obstinacy and the free willing of the corrupt will. By this a man who is bound to obey God calling, and so to believe and repent, does not will to believe and repent. Therefore Grevinchovius argues badly. (He says:) "The denial of predetermining help is the adequate cause of the lack of good use of grace, and of resistance. But the denial of predetermining help is from God alone. Therefore the lack of good use of grace, and so the whole resistance and non-conversion of man, is from God alone." I reply: first, that the denial of predetermining help is not the cause of the lack of good use of grace and of resistance; indeed it is not a cause at all. How then is it an adequate cause? Let him prove this; when we ask for proofs, we hear a profound silence. We grant that resistance follows from the denial of predetermining help as a consequent from an antecedent; we deny that it follows as an effect from a cause. If he had proved this, he would have damaged our cause. For between the denial of predetermining help and the resistance there intervenes the free willing of the corrupt will, from which resistance comes causally. But since resistance comes from a cause that is morally bound to act, and God who withholds predetermining help is not a morally bound cause, God contributes no effective or causative element at all to the resistance. Therefore we deny that the culpable non-use of grace and the private and culpable non-conversion are causatively from God.

units.la: 6. Sed in eo hærent, quod dicamus nos, voluntatem non posse, aliud neque aliter velle, quam prout prædeterminanti Dei motioni subest, ideoque quoniam illa prædeterminatio non est in nostra potestate, non-conversio imputatur Deo, non nobis, qui aliud & aliter haud possumus, quam id, ad quod a gratia determinante impellimur facere. R. [Voluntate determinationi gratiæ substratam non posse aliud velle, quam vult] æquipollet huic, | voluntatem actu eligentem hoc non illud, non posse aliud eligere, quam eligit. | Nam Dei determinatio, & humana determinatio admiranda consociatione in idem objectum, numero, mensura, & intensione conspirant, hoc tantum discrimine,quod Dei determinatio sit externa, æquivoca, non vitalis, principalis: humana vero interna, univoca, vitalis, & subordinata. Nam si carentia divinæ prædeterminationis voluntati non conversi aliud volenti, aut quoad æternam futuritionem volituræ, & inclinaturæ obstaret, & vi aliorsum impellerct ipsam, argumentum aliquid probaret. Sed Dei prædeterminatio ad illud flectit voluntatem conversi, ad quod,quoad æternam futuritionem, ipsa vitaliter, electivè, & subordinatè se flectit. Et quamvis non conversi in sua potestate non habeant Dei prædeterminationem, attamen jure rei sunt, & culpandi, quoniam eorum prava voluntas in id tendit liberrimè, in quod Dei non prædeterminatio gratiosa, juxta decretum reprobationis, tendit: ideoque hoc ipso sunt damnationi obnoxii,quod ipsorum voluntas subscribit consequenter, interpretativè, & in ipso effectu, nempe liberâ non-conversione culpabili, non-prædeterminationi gratiosæ, seu sigillum suum apponunt, Dei auxilii determinantis negationi liberæ.Quoniam vero & conversio Judæ, & non-conversio Judæ æternam futuritionem habere non possunt (hoc enim impossibile simpliciter) nullo modo Dei prædeterminatio superveniens inclinationi Judæ, ipsamque salva libertate determinans, ad id, quod toto libertatis suæ vitioso impetu, de facto eligit, officit vel Judæ reatui, vel libertati. Quando superior causa est physica & à lege soluta, & inferior moralis, & legi subdita, esto quod superior physice influit in inferiorem, tamen si inferior est libera, rea esse potest inferior, & non superior.
units.tr: 6. But they cling to this: we say that the will, being subject to predetermining motion of God, cannot will otherwise or differently than that motion moves it. Therefore, since that predetermination is not in our power, non-conversion is imputed to God and not to us, who cannot will or choose otherwise than what grace determining us impels us to do. I reply: that the will, subject to the determination of grace, cannot will otherwise than it wills, is equivalent to this: that the will, actually choosing this and not that, cannot choose otherwise than it chooses. For God's determination and man's determination concur, in a wonderful union, on the same object, in number, measure and intensity. The only difference is this: God's determination is external, equivocal, not vital, principal; man's is internal, univocal, vital and subordinate. For if the lack of divine predetermination stood in the way of the will of the unconverted, who wills otherwise, or of what is going to will and be inclined, as regards its eternal futurition, and forced it to the contrary by some force, then the argument would prove something. But God's predetermination bends the will of the converted to that to which, as regards eternal futurition, it itself bends vitally, electively and subordinately. And although the unconverted do not have God's predetermination in their power, yet they are guilty and deserve blame, because their wicked will tends most freely to that to which God's non-gracious predetermination, according to the decree of reprobation, does not tend. Therefore they are liable to damnation for this very reason: their will subscribes consequently, interpretatively, and in the effect itself, namely in free culpable non-conversion, and thus they set their seal to the free denial of the predetermining help of God. But since neither the conversion of Judas nor the non-conversion of Judas can have eternal futurition (for this is simply impossible), the predetermination of God, which comes upon Judas's inclination and determines it, while preserving its liberty, to what he chooses de facto with the whole vicious impetus of his freedom, in no way lessens either Judas's guilt or his liberty. When the superior cause is physical and free from law, and the inferior is moral and subject to law, even though the superior influences the inferior physically, nevertheless, if the inferior is free, it can be guilty, and the superior cannot.

units.la: Sic aliquis absolutus Monarcha, supra legem aliquam humanam positivam: consentiat rex, ut subditus eam legem violet. & suppono, quod idem subditus, fit ex se & sua sponte, eam legem violaturus, hoc dato, quod Monarcha, qui est supra talem legem, non consentiret, hic rex non est reus, & subditus est violatae legis reus. Ratio est, quia reatus venit ab obligatione illius, qui cum sit agens rationale legi subditur. At reatus non est formaliter ab ulla influentia physica: alioqui gladius, venenum & alia quae physicam causandi influentiam contribuunt homicidio, reatui subessent, quod est ridiculum.
units.tr: Thus an absolute monarch, above some positive human law, may consent that a subject violate that law. I suppose the subject, of his own accord and by his own will, is going to violate it. Granted that the monarch, who stands above such a law, would not consent, the king is not guilty, and the subject is guilty of violating the law. The reason is that guilt arises from the obligation of the one who, as a rational agent, is subject to the law. But guilt does not arise formally from any physical influence.
