Otherwise the sword, poison and other things that contribute physical causal influence to a homicide would be liable to guilt, which is absurd.

units.la: 7. Quartum est ipsa fides & actus supernatu-ralis, qui ut fit, & ut fit supernaturalis, non aliunde est quam ab actuali efficientia seu efficacia divinae gratiae, ideoque, ut notavit Alvarez, solus Deus est causa conversionis. Solus enim Deus efficaciter vocat: at non est solus causa actus conversionis liberi. Hic enim humanae libertati non est deneganda sua activitas subordinata, electiva & vitalis.
units.tr: 7. Fourthly, there is faith itself and the supernatural act. Both that it comes about and that it is supernatural come from nothing else than the actual efficiency or efficacy of divine grace. Therefore, as Alvarez observed, God alone is the cause of conversion. For God alone calls effectually, but he is not alone the cause of the act of free conversion. Here human freedom must not be denied its subordinate, elective and vital activity.

units.la: 8. Sed non se satis explicant Arminiani in modo, quo Deus tenetur concursum suum omnibus vocatis praebere. Mihi enim ex eorum scriptis nunquam constare potuit, utrum haec Dei obligatio fundetur in Dei æquitate naturali, an vero in libera Dei promissione. Vel enim Deus adjuvat nos bene utentes gratia communi efficace gratia, ex libera constitutione, & positiva promissione, vel æquitate naturali. Si ex libera constitutione, potest tum non tribuere gatiam efficacem, & tamen culpam nobis imputare, & sic metet Deus, ubi non jecerit sementum, quod Arminiani naturali Dei æquitati repugnare volunt. Si vero necessitate æquitatis naturalis; tum post primum actum gratiosum, necessario concurret ad sequentem, & propter illum, ex justitiæ debito ad sequentem, & sic in infinitum, & post primum actum gratiosum, sequeretur neminem deinceps peccare, cui reclamant quotidiani sanctorum lapsus, & oracula sacra; & sequeretur per eandem rationem, post primum actum inobedientiæ, Deum ex debito justitiæ negare debere gratiam efficacem, & ad tertium & quartum: & sic qui semel peccavit, non potest non semper ex ordine justitiæ peccare, quod etiam in multis impiis ad sanctorum vitæ frugem convertentibus se, patet esse salsissimum. Sed dicunt ex hypothesi, quod voluntas prius natura suam influentiam præstet, Deum promisisse se præstiturum suum etiam efficacem influxum. At vero tum non libera constitutione, aut liberali promissione, præstat Deus suum influxum, sed æquitate naturali, imo hoc in flagitiosissimis apostatis, non potest non præstare: secus daretur actio causæ secundæ, absque influentia causæ primæ. At vero quid prodest sancto multos actus obedientiæ elicuisse, si omnes illi actus compensentur, motione non efficaci, sed tantum eâ motione, quâ posset, si vellet, in posterum habere in sua potestate motionem Dei efficacem ? Memini enim Arminium dixisse : vide mihi (inquit) an non isto Christi dicto [habenti dabitur] promissio ista continetur, qua Deus spondet se gratia supernaturali illuminaturum, qui lumine naturali recte utetur, aut saltem utetur, quantum poterit, minus male. Ex hoc textu Arminii, sequitur Deum ex promisso obligari eis, qui probi & humiliores fuerunt, indulgere gratiam conversionis efficacem: nam habenti dabitur. Et ex Arminio habenti multos bonos actus naturæ, dabitur actus conversionis. Atqui sic per hanc promissionem saltem post conversionem, nunquam peccaret. Deus enim verax habenti actum gratiosum præstaret motionem efficacem ad alium actum gratiosum, & post illum ad alium. Scio tamen Arminianos responsuros, habenti ex Dei promisso, dari siquidem accipere velit, & suum influxum libere contribuere voluit, R. At sic etiam non habenti dabitur. Christus vero ait, non habenti auferri, quod habuit. Nam habenti nullos actus bonos, dabitur motio Dei efficax, siquidem ipse influxum suum libere contribuere volet, imo si Diabolus, si profligatissimi apostatæ libere voluerint, nunquid creator & prima causa influxum suum efficacem denegare poterit? Credo non posse ; imo si posset, daretur actus secundæ causæ, sine actione primæ. Ita jam, Arminiani [habenti dabitur] vobis est, non habenti dabitur, & non habenti auferetur, vobis est,. non habenti dabitur , non auferetur. At non impetrabamus tamen ab Arminianis hic ut in converfione Deo absolutam suam libertatem relinquamus: & tamen Dei libertatem in missione salvatoris ad redimendum genus humanum non negant: cum lapsis angelis tale remedium absolute negarit. Heb. 2. 16. & Deum potuisse omnes & singulos ita vocare , ut illibatâ libertate converterentur , non negabunt.
units.tr: 8. But the Arminians do not sufficiently explain the manner in which God is bound to offer his concurrence to all who are called. From their writings I have never been able to discover whether this obligation of God is grounded in God's natural equity or in his free promise. For God either helps us when we use common grace well, by a free constitution and a positive promise, or by natural equity. If by a free constitution, then he can refuse efficacious grace and yet impute the fault to us, and so God reaps where he has not sown, which the Arminians want to be contrary to natural divine equity. But if by the necessity of natural equity, then after the first gracious act he would necessarily concur to the next, and on account of that one, by a debt of justice, to the following, and so on to infinity. And after the first gracious act it would follow that no one would sin afterwards, which the daily lapses of the saints and the sacred oracles contradict. By the same reasoning it would follow that after the first act of disobedience God ought by a debt of justice to refuse efficacious grace, and likewise after the second and third and fourth. So he who has once sinned could not but sin always by the order of justice, which is also clearly most false in the case of many impious men who turn to the godly life of the saints. But they say that, on the hypothesis that the will first exerts its own influence by nature, God has promised that he will also exert his efficacious influx. But then God exerts his influx not by a free constitution or a gracious promise, but by natural equity, and indeed in the most shameful apostates he cannot but exert it; otherwise there would be an action of a secondary cause without the influence of the first cause. But what does it profit a saint to have elicited many acts of obedience, if all those acts are compensated by a motion that is not efficacious, but only by that motion by which he could, if he wished, have in future the efficacious motion of God in his own power? For I remember Arminius saying: See for me (he says) whether that promise is not contained in that saying of Christ, [to him that hath shall be given], by which God pledges that he will illuminate with supernatural grace whoever uses the natural light rightly, or at least uses it as far as he can, less badly. From this text of Arminius it follows that God is bound by promise to grant efficacious grace of conversion to those who have been upright and more humble: for to him that hath, it shall be given. And according to Arminius, to him who has many good acts of nature, the act of conversion shall be given. Yet by this promise, at least after conversion, he would never sin. For God, being truthful, would give to him who has a gracious act an efficacious motion to another gracious act, and after that to another. I know, however, that the Arminians will reply that to him who has, it is given by God's promise, provided he is willing to receive, and has willingly contributed his influx. I answer: but then also to him who has not, it shall be given. Yet Christ says that from him who has not, what he had is taken away. For to him who has no good acts, the efficacious motion of God will be given, provided he himself is willing to contribute his influx freely. Indeed, if the Devil and the most abandoned apostates willed it freely, could the Creator and first cause deny them his efficacious influx? I believe not. And even if he could, there would be an act of the secondary cause without the action of the first. So now, Arminians, [to him that hath shall be given] is for you, and to him that hath not shall be given, and from him that hath not shall be taken away, is for you; to him that hath not shall be given, shall not be taken away. Yet we do not ask the Arminians here to leave God his absolute freedom in conversion, and yet they do not deny God's freedom in sending the Saviour to redeem the human race, since he absolutely denied such a remedy to the fallen angels (Heb. 2. 16.). Nor will they deny that God could have called all and each in such a way that they would be converted with their freedom unimpaired.

units.la: 9. Ob.2. Si sub hac determinatione manet libertas, aut manet in ordine ad receptionem determinationis extrinsecæ, aut in ordine ad suum proprium influxum. Non primum: quia, ut ait Grevinchovius, voluntas patitur recipiendo determinationem Dei, & passio qua passio non est actus liber, uti ait Corvinus. Nec fecundum dici potest: penna enim non libera dicitur in fcriptione, quoniam ducitur à libero agente, nec voluntas noftra erit libera, fi ita torqueatur à Deo principaliter agente, ut non ita velit, eligat, repudiet, ut posset nolle, non eligere, non repudiare. Ita Marcus Antonius de Dominis. R[?]
units.tr: 9. Objection 2. If freedom remains under this determination, it remains either in order to receiving an extrinsic determination, or in order to its own proper influx. Not the first, because, as Grevinchovius says, the will suffers in receiving God's determination, and suffering, as such, is not a free act, as Corvinus says. Nor can the second be said. For a pen is not called free in writing, since it is driven by a free agent; nor will our will be free if it is so turned by God, the principal agent, that it does not will, choose or reject as it could have not willed, not chosen, not rejected. So Marcus Antonius de Dominis. I answer:

units.la: 1. Non docent nostri libertatem formaliter cofiftere in receptione divinæ determinationis. Non enim lege ulla injungitur,ut eam determinationem Dei vel habeamus vel non habeamus.
units.tr: 1. Our people do not teach that freedom formally consists in receiving the divine determination. For no law enjoins that we have or do not have that determination of God.

units.la: 2. Postquam voluntas jam recepit Dei determinationem non proprie est in potentia ad agendum, quia jam actu libere agit. Hoc enim puerili argumento, non magis Dei determinatio evertit libertatem, quam ipsius libertatis actuale exercitium evertit libertatem, & tamen libertas in ordine ad suum influxum actu libere agit. 3. Non dicitur voluntas nostra libera per participationem, quoniam est instrumentum Dei liberi agentis. Penna enim nulla ingenita electione & judicio scribit. Deus vero ita utitur voluntate, ut ipsa voluntas sese electivè, vitaliter, & ex practico rationis judicio agat. Nec aliud nobis hic objiciunt, quam olim Pelagiani Augustino & Prospero. Dei opus defendimus, nec ex illius potentia vel in malum vel in bonum aliquem invitum cogi, non reluctanti studium. Pelagiani se Dei opus, Arminiani se naturam libertatis defendere contendunt.
units.tr: 2. Once the will has already received God's determination, it is not properly in potency to act, because now it acts freely in act. For by this puerile argument, God's determination no more overthrows freedom than the actual exercise of freedom itself overthrows freedom; and yet freedom, in order to its own influx, acts freely in act. 3. Our will is not said to be free by participation, since it is the instrument of God who acts freely. For a pen writes without any innate choice or judgment. But God so uses the will that the will itself acts electively, vitally, and from the practical judgment of reason. Nor do they object to us here anything other than what the Pelagians once objected to Augustine and Prosper. We defend God's work, and that no one is forced by his power, against his will, to evil or to good, the zeal of one who is not reluctant. The Pelagians contend that they defend God's work, and the Arminians that they defend the nature of freedom.

units.la: Ob. 3. Causae naturales habent potentiam non operandi in sensu diviso. Sic enim cessare possunt a motu, si Deus a motione cesset, imo paries albus in sensu diviso potest esse niger, quia simul cum albedine retinet potentiam ad nigredinem. Non itaque sufficit potestas in sensu diviso ad potestatem activam arbitrii, ipso ista potestas in sensu diviso, quid est aliud quam potestas carendi gratia, si non detur, vel carendi consensu, ad quem gratia movet, si gratia data auferatur? hoc modo lapis sursum projectus potest in sensu diviso carere impulsu quo movetur. Grevinchov.
units.tr: Objection 3. Natural causes have the power not to act in the divided sense. Thus they can cease from motion if God ceases to move them. Indeed a white wall can in the divided sense be black, because together with its whiteness it retains the potency to blackness. Therefore power in the divided sense is not sufficient for the active power of the will. For what is this power in the divided sense other than the power of lacking grace, if it is not given, or of lacking the consent to which grace moves, if the grace given is taken away? In this way a stone thrown upward can, in the divided sense, lack the impulse by which it is moved. Grevinchov.

units.la: -R. Post Suarezium doctorem suum, delirat Grevinchovius. Nam i.[?] nuda & simplex cessatio ab actu nolendi & volendi, non statuitur a nobis actiactiva potentia libertatis in divisio sensu, sed cessatio ex judicio mentis, & electiva vi libertatis, quam potentiam, si lapidi aut parieti inesse velit, fungus & lapis sit, oportet. 2, Tum etiam absurdè dicitur potestas libertatis in sensu diviso esse carentia gratiæ. Non enim est penes nos vel habere vel carere gratia efficace. Distinctionem illam sensus compositi & divisi, prout causis naturalibus suo modo aptari potest, male nobis impingunt. Nam dicimus nos, non posse simul componi Dei determinationem gratiosam ad talem actum, & actualem diffensum libertatis, & tamen manere sub illa determinatione vim electivam repudiandi, qualis vis ad nigredinem, non manet in pariete albo.
units.tr: After Suarez, his teacher, Grevinchovius is raving. For we do not posit a bare and simple cessation from the act of not willing and willing, nor an active power of liberty in the divided sense; we posit a cessation that comes from the judgment of the mind and from the elective force of liberty. If one wishes this power to be present in a stone or a wall, the stone or wall would have to be a mushroom or a stone. (2) Moreover, it is absurdly said that the power of liberty in the divided sense is the lack of grace. For it is not up to us to have or to lack efficacious grace. They wrongly press upon us that distinction between the composite and divided sense, as it may be applied in its own way to natural causes. For we say that God's gracious determination to such an act and the actual dissent of liberty cannot be combined at the same time, and yet the elective power to reject remains under that determination, just as the power to be black does not remain in a white wall.

units.la: Quid ?,Quoniam potestas passiva in sensu composito & diviso dari potest, an propterea potentia activa & electiva in voluntate dari non potest? Imo contrarium plane sequitur. Quod dicit Suarez antecedentem hanc necessitatem non minus fortiter astringere libertatem, quam si esset causa mere naturalis, hallucinari in re gravi non verecundatur: nam nullo modo sequitur. Nam quamvis Deus inevitabiliter necessitet eventum & effectum libertatis, non super-imponit libertati necessitatem inevitabilem, quoniam infinitæ Dei perfectionis & omnipotentiæ est, quod necessitare posset libertatem, & non evertere, non aliter quam libertas in exercitio se necessitat, & non evertit. Nam quando ipsa libertas vitaliter suam indifferentiam removet, eodem modo praedeterminans gratia illam eandem indifferentiam externe & non vitaliter removet, quoniam Deus non ad alium angulum flectit libertatem principaliter, quam ad illum, ad quem se flectit libertas subordinatè. Quo pacto, si illi dicant Deum necessitare libertatem, ego dicam tum libertatem sese necessitare pari modo. Haec vero necessitatio non tollit libertatem, ac proinde neque illa. At dicent primo, principaliter, & ab aeterno Deum actum liberum determinare, ideoque libertatem humanam non posse alium actum elicere. R. Deus primo, principaliter & ab aeterno actum liberum determinat, sed non ad alium, sed ad eundem numero actum, ad quem voluntas determinavit in tempore sese. Quia Dei determinatio aeterna respectum habet ad actum illum ut futurum, & libere ponendum, quamvis non ut jam positum, cujusmodi respectum & habitudinem dicit decretum conditionatum ad actum liberum, non ut ponendum sed ut positum, & quidem positum antecedenter ad Dei decretum, quod plane Dei providentiam evertit.
units.tr: What then? Because a passive power can exist in the composite and divided sense, does it follow that an active and elective power cannot exist in the will? On the contrary, the opposite plainly follows. That Suarez says this antecedent necessity binds liberty no less strongly than if it were a merely natural cause is a mistake he is not ashamed to make in a serious matter, for it in no way follows. For although God inevitably necessitates the event and effect of liberty, He does not impose on liberty an inevitable necessity, since it belongs to the infinite perfection and omnipotence of God that He can necessitate liberty without destroying it, just as liberty in its exercise necessitates itself and does not destroy itself. For when liberty itself removes its own indifference vitally, grace, predetermining in the same way, removes that same indifference externally and not vitally, since God does not bend liberty principally to any other angle than that to which liberty itself bends subordinately. So if they say that God necessitates liberty, I shall say that liberty likewise necessitates itself. Yet this necessitation does not take away liberty, and therefore neither does that one. But they will say first that God determines the free act principally and from eternity, and therefore human liberty cannot elicit another act. Answer: God does determine the free act principally and from eternity, but not to another act; He determines it to the same numerical act to which the will has determined itself in time. For God's eternal determination regards that act as future and to be freely posited, though not as already posited; this is the sort of respect and relation that a conditional decree to a free act expresses, not as to be posited but as already posited, and indeed as posited antecedently to God's decree, which utterly overthrows God's providence.

units.la: Ob. 4. Si Dei determinatio praecedit volitionem humanam, jam est velle, priusquam homo velit, nec necesse est ut voluntas velit, tantum patiendo ab omnipotente recipiat velle. Ita Lessius. Resp. Est homonymia in voce (jam) & in voce determinationis. Iam propprie notat ordinem naturæ: & determinatio vel est externa & effectiva, quæ est solius Dei in hoc negotio; vel interna & formalis, quæ est voluntatis creatæ. Sicitaque distinguo. Si voluntas humana [jam] id est, prius ordine naturæ, determinetur, nempe externè & effectivè à Deo, non necesse est, ut voluntas velit, quia jam est velle: illud nego. Si velint priustempore Deum velle efficere in nobis, quam velimus, quærant sibi larvas, cum quibus dimicandum sit: nos tale quid non cogitamus. At vero Deus prius natura voluntatem determinat, & quidem solus in genere causæ efficientis externæ & solitudine prædeterminantis. At ipsa voluntas posterius naturâ, & simul tempore se determinat in genere causæ formalis, & sola quidem solitudine causæ formalis & vitaliter eligentis: Ideoque tria hic sunt distinguenda. 1. Vitalis & electiva propensio voluntatis, quæ est & naturalis & à voluntate, vel supernaturalis & divinitus infusa: hic voluntas est in statu potentialitatis tantum. 2. Et actuario illius potentiæ: hæc est effective à Deo. Et 3. actualis volitio, hæc formaliter sine ullo temporis intervallo est à voluntate, sed jam actuata & determinata externè & effectivè à Deo. Ideoque nullo modo sequitur, non necesse esse ut voluntas velit: tantum sequitur, quod efficientia τ[?] velle sit natura prius τ[?] velle, quod est necessarium: non absurdum, uti prius natura est efficientia causæ, quam effectus est.
units.tr: Objection 4. If God's determination precedes human volition, then there is already willing before the man wills, and it is not necessary that the will wills, but by suffering alone it receives the willing from the Almighty. So Lessius. Answer: there is an ambiguity both in the word jam (already) and in the word determination. Iam properly denotes order of nature; and determination is either external and effective, which belongs to God alone in this matter, or internal and formal, which belongs to the created will. Therefore I distinguish. If the human will is [already], that is, determined prior in order of nature, namely externally and effectively by God, it is not necessary that the will wills because there is already willing: that I deny. If they want God to bring it about in us in time before we will, let them seek out bogeys to fight with; we do not think any such thing. But God determines the will prior in nature, and indeed He alone does so in the kind of external efficient cause and by a predetermining solitary action. The will itself, posterior in nature, and at the same time in time, determines itself in the kind of formal cause, and indeed by the sole solitary action of a formal cause and vitally choosing. Hence three things must be distinguished here. 1. The vital and elective propensity of the will, which is either natural and from the will, or supernatural and divinely infused; here the will is only in a state of potentiality. 2. The actuation of that power; this is effected by God. And 3. the actual volition; this is formally from the will without any interval of time, but already actuated and determined externally and effectively by God. Therefore it in no way follows that it is not necessary that the will wills; it only follows that the efficiency of God's willing is prior in nature to the willing, which is necessary; not absurd, just as the efficiency of a cause is prior in nature to its effect.

units.la: Ob.ς[?]. Si Deus determinet actus liberos, determinat etiam potentias. Nam potentiæ sunt causæ actuum. At si potentiæ determinetur, nullo modo manet potentia volendi & nolendi. Ita Rem. R. Potentias voluntatis particulares numero actibus futuris commensurari, & ad laudem gloriosæ providentiæ determinari assero, ab eo qui numerat capillos capitis & pluviarum guttulas: at manet potentia voluntatis universalis indeterminata. 2. Non satis accurate dicunt doctores hi, potentiam esse causam actuum. Causa est præstantior essectu, potentia actu ignobilior posita causa, ponitur effectus, posita vero potentia non ponitur actus. Accurate itaque loquendo causa actu liberi est potentia determinata, non simpliciter potentia.
units.tr: Objection 6? If God determines free acts, He also determines the powers, for the powers are causes of the acts. But if the power is determined, the power of willing and not willing does not remain in any way. Thus Remonstrants. Answer: I assert that the particular powers of the will are measured by the number of future acts and determined to the praise of glorious providence, by one who counts the hairs of the head and the drops of rain; but the universal power of the will remains undetermined. 2. These teachers do not speak accurately enough in saying that the power is the cause of the acts. A cause is more excellent than its effect; a power, being less noble than the act, is posited, and when it is posited the effect is posited, but when the power is posited the act is not necessarily posited. Speaking accurately, then, the cause of a free act is a determined power, not simply a power.

units.la: Ob. 6. Si ponatur talis efficacia determinans, tolletur studium & pia bene operandi solicitudo. Exspectabimus enim semper efficaciam talem. R. Non potest non esse solicitus aliquis, quamdiu talem efficaciam in conversione non sentiat, ideoque contrarium potius sequetur.
units.tr: Objection 6. If such a determining efficacy is posited, study and pious care in doing good will be removed, for we shall always wait for such efficacy. Answer: someone cannot but be anxious as long as he does not feel such efficacy in conversion; therefore rather the contrary would follow.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAP. IV.

units.la: Suarezij, Fonseca, Bellarmini, & aliorum de congrua vocatione nova fabula adpare- tes vocatur.
units.tr: The new fable of the congruous calling, as it is put forward by Suarez, Fonseca, Bellarmine and others.

units.la: EFficaciam gratiæ Iesuitæ, nova monstra Ecclesiæ in vocationis congruitatem refolunt. Eam in tribus posuit Alvarez hujus congruitatis impugnator 1 in suasione. 2. in tali contemperatione suasionis, tali personae, sic dispositae, tali loco & tempore. 3 in scientia media qua praescit, quo inclinatura fit voluntas in tali tempore & occasionibus locata. Sub judice lis est, an efficacia gratiae in ipsam congruitatem suasionis referenda fit, ut putant quidam Iesuitae. Cautius tamen Suarez, qui docet congruitatem non sufficere ad efficaciam gratiae argumento satis valido. Nam hæc (inquit) vocatio est medium accommodatum intentioni Dei efficaci: implicat autem contradictionem, voluntatem Dei efficacem non impleri. Ergo non potest illa vocatio esse proportionatum medium, nisi sit ita infallibilis, ut prorsus repugnet, & contradictionem implicet non consequi effectum suum. Sed tota illa congruitas ex se solum inducit moralem quandam certitudinem, cui absolute non repugnat ut vocationi congruae sic liberum arbitrium resistat. Sapit, mihi crede, Iesuita congruitatem rejiciens & ad scientiam mediam confugiens, eam viam incedunt, Bellarminus, Fonseca, Valentia, Suarez. Quid (quaeres lector) Arminiani. Fluctuat ipse magnus doctor Armin. Num ait fors ex sensu scripturae teneri posse. Remonstr. in collat. Hag. Nihil esset absurdi (inquiunt) si Dei operatio dicatur efficax, quia illa pro infinita Dei scientia, circiter illud tempus, ejusmodi hominibus, tali statu, administratur. At tum viri fratres, nihil absurdi est tenere Calvini decretum absolutum. Corvinus enim hoc nomine rejicit vocationem congruam, quod necesse est assertoribus ejus tenere decretum absolutum. At exclamant Arminiani hoc esse factum, sed tanta est haereticorum à fide aberrantium fluctuatio, ut hanc vocationem directè rejecetint Remonstrantes in confessione sua.
units.tr: The Jesuits, new monsters of the Church, reduce the efficacy of grace to the congruity of the calling. Alvarez, the opponent of this congruity, placed it in three things: (1) in the persuasion; (2) in the fitting adjustment of that persuasion to such a person, so disposed, at such a place and time; (3) in the middle knowledge by which God foreknows towards what the will will be inclined at such a time and in such circumstances. It is a disputed question whether the efficacy of grace is to be referred to the congruity of the persuasion itself, as some Jesuits think. Suarez, however, is more cautious, since he teaches that congruity is not sufficient for the efficacy of grace, and he argues from a strong enough reason: For this calling (he says) is a means suited to God's efficacious intention; but it implies a contradiction that God's efficacious will should not be fulfilled. Therefore that calling cannot be a proportionate means unless it is so infallible that it is utterly impossible, and implies a contradiction, for it not to attain its effect. But all that congruity of itself produces only a certain moral certainty, to which it is not absolutely repugnant that free will should resist a congruous calling in this way. Believe me, the Jesuit who rejects congruity and takes refuge in middle knowledge smells of the same thing; Bellarmine, Fonseca, Valentia and Suarez walk this road. What of the Arminians (you will ask, reader)? Their great teacher Arminius wavers himself. He says perhaps it can be held from the sense of Scripture (Remonstrants, in the Collatio Hagiensis). "There would be nothing absurd," they say, "if God's operation were called efficacious, because it is administered, according to God's infinite knowledge, at that time, to such men, in such a state." But then, brethren, there is nothing absurd in holding Calvin's absolute decree. For Corvinus rejects the congruous calling on this very ground, that its advocates must hold an absolute decree. But the Arminians cry out that this has been done; yet such is the wavering of heretics who have strayed from the faith, that the Remonstrants in their Confession directly rejected this calling.

units.la: 2. Fieri itaque posse docent, ut si spectetur substantia vocationis, par sit gratia & eadem in converso, & non-converso. Imo (inquit Fonseca ibid.) major forte in non-converso. Eo tamen solo (inquit) quod talis vocatio applicatur ei qui conversus est, quo praescitur obediturus, ei autem qui conversus non est in ea occasione, qua praescitur repugnaturus (tametsi alia vocari posset, qua obediturus praesciretur) illius vocatio est efficax, huius autem non efficax. Si quaeramus unde est, quod quidam congrue, quidam vocentur incongrue? respondent: electi vocantur congrue secundum praedestinationis decretum absolutum, quo administratur gratia efficax; reprobi incongrue, secundum decretum communis providentiae, quo confertur iis gratia tantum sufficiens quidem, quia Deus vult omnes salvari, & non deficit in necessariis (alioqui homines non essent inexcusabiles) sed tamen non efficax. Nam praescit Deus sufficientem nunquam fore efficacem, & tamen reprobis eam Deus dat secundum decretum communis providentiae. Haec illi.
units.tr: 2. They teach, therefore, that it can happen that, if one looks at the substance of the calling, the grace is equal and the same in the converted and the unconverted, indeed (says Fonseca, ibid.) perhaps greater in the unconverted one. Yet this alone (he says) makes the difference: that such a calling is applied to the one who is converted, whom God foreknows will obey, whereas in the case of the one who is not converted, in the occasion in which he is foreknown to resist, his calling is efficacious for the one but not for the other, though he could have been called by another means by which he would have been foreknown to obey. If we ask whence it is that some are called congruously and some incongruously, they answer: the elect are called congruously according to the absolute decree of predestination, by which efficacious grace is administered; the reprobate are called incongruously according to the decree of common providence, by which they are given a grace that is indeed sufficient, because God wills all to be saved and does not fail in what is necessary (otherwise men would not be inexcusable), but still not efficacious. For God foreknows that the sufficient grace will never be efficacious, and yet God gives it to the reprobate according to the decree of common providence. So they say.

units.la: Sic vero primo impugno. Haec gratia efficax & congrua vel est necessaria ad singulos actus supernaturales, adeoque ad conversionem, vel
units.tr: But I attack this first in the following way. This efficacious and congruous grace is either necessary for each supernatural act, and so for conversion, or

units.la: ‡ Not transcribed as a note mark; the margin symbol beside the last paragraph is a reference sign. vel non. Si primum, non congrue vocati carent sufficiente gratia, quod non fert theologia Iefuitica. Nam congruitas ad conversionem neceffaria iis deest. At Fonfeca Dei providentiae adversari vult, quod aliquis adjumentis ad salutem necessariis careat. Si non est necessaria, tum non congrue vocati non minus possunt converti, qua congrue vocati. Si vero sit congruitas necessaria, quia non est in hominis potestate, quod Deus vel congrue vel non congrue vocet, non imputabitur non-conversio culpabilis ei, qui non convertitur; quoniam ex carentia congruitatis, quae est in sola Dei, non hominis potestate, refultat: quod optime sequi ait Suarez differens contra determinationem physicam. R. Suarez nihil deesse non-congrue vocato ex parte hominis, aliquid tamen ei deesse ex parte Dei. Deest enim (inquit) praescientia effectus in uno & non in alio: tamen haec ipsa differentia non est ex solo Deo, sed etiam ex libero arbitrio. Nam in potestate hominis, de quo Deus praescivit non consensurum voanti, est, facere ut Deus praesciverit ipsum consensurum vocationi. Nam in potestate ejus revera est consentire, atque ita est in potestate ejus habere vocationem efficacem. R. 1. Damnatur Iesuita verbis Fonfecae: Pelagius enim (inquit) nimium tribuens nostri[?] arbitrii voluntati efficaciam divinae vocationis voluntatis libero consensui attribuebat. Bellarmin. Haec opinio (inquit) aliena est a sententia divinarum scripturarum. Sed an credit Suarez lectorem esse Medufœo cerebro qui nihil intelligat. Si est enim in potestate non conversi facere, ut Deus praesciverit ipsum consensurum vocationi, tum actualis conversio adeoque efficacia gratiae praecedit Dei praescientiam. Quod enim facit Deum praescire hoc non illud, illud prius est Dei praescientia. At quorsum se torquet in reductione efficaciae gratiae ad Dei praescientiam, qua praescit quid infallibiliter moveat libertatem, quando fateatur efficaciam gratiae esse priorem Dei praescientia? an quod est prius reduci potest in id quod est posterius, ut in causam? Quid? Non rides Iesuita? Et quid aliud Pelagius? Ex hoc responso congrua vocatio, saltem quando adhibetur, est in potestate congruè vocati. Frustra ergo commenti sunt congruitatem hanc ad declinandum errorem Pelagij. 2. Quia est in omnium potestate audire concionatores, legere & meditari Dei verbum, quo omnes vocantur, omnes possunt congruè vocari ac proinde frustra commenti sunt duo decreta, alterum providentiae communis, alterum praedestinationis, secundum quae vocantur reprobi incongruè, & electi congruè. Si enim possunt omnes congrue vocari, expungi potest decretum providentiae, & per eandem rationem, omnes possunt incongruè vocari, ideoque inane est & alterum. 3. Supra dixit Iesuita non reducendam efficaciam gratiae in ipsam incongruitatem, hic negat reduci posse in Dei praescientiam quid superest? Non in gratiam ipsam restat solum liberum arbitrium.
units.tr: vel non. If the first, then those not congruously called lack sufficient grace, which Jesuit theology does not bear. For congruity for conversion is lacking to them, which is necessary. Yet Fonseca wants to oppose the providence of God by saying that someone lacks the aids necessary for salvation. If it is not necessary, then those not congruously called can be converted no less than those congruously called. But if the congruity is necessary, then, because it is not in man's power whether God calls him congruously or not congruously, the non-conversion of the one who is not converted will not be imputed to him as culpable; for it results from the lack of congruity, which lies in God's power alone and not in man's; which Suarez, disputing against physical determination, says rightly follows. Reply: Suarez says that nothing is lacking on the part of man to the one not congruously called, yet something is lacking on the part of God. For (he says) foreknowledge of the effect is lacking in the one and not in the other. Yet this very difference does not come from God alone, but also from free will. For it is in man's power, concerning whom God foreknew he would not consent to the calling, to bring it about that God foreknows he will consent to the calling. For it is truly in his power to consent, and so it is in his power to have an efficacious calling. Reply 1: The Jesuit is condemned by Fonseca's own words: For Pelagius (he says), attributing too much to the will of our free choice, attributed the efficacy of the divine calling to the free consent of the will. Bellarmine: This opinion (he says) is alien to the sense of the divine Scriptures. But does Suarez think his reader is a Medusa-headed brain that understands nothing? For if it is in the power of the unconverted man to bring it about that God foreknew he would consent to the calling, then actual conversion, and so the efficacy of grace, precedes God's foreknowledge. For what makes God foreknow this rather than that is prior to God's foreknowledge. But why does he twist himself in referring the efficacy of grace to God's foreknowledge, by which he foreknows what infallibly moves the freedom, when he admits that the efficacy of grace is prior to God's foreknowledge? Or can what is prior be reduced to what is posterior, as to a cause? What? Do you not laugh, Jesuit? And what else is this but Pelagius? From this answer it follows that the congruous calling, at least when it is applied, is in the power of the one congruously called. Therefore they have invented this congruity in vain to avoid the error of Pelagius. 2. Because it is in everyone's power to hear preachers, to read and meditate on the Word of God, by which all are called, all can be called congruously, and consequently the two decrees, one of common providence and the other of predestination, by which the reprobate are called incongruously and the elect congruously, were invented in vain. For if all can be called congruously, the decree of providence can be struck out; and by the same reasoning all can be called incongruously, and so the other also is empty. 3. Above, the Jesuit said that the efficacy of grace is not to be reduced to the incongruity itself; here he denies that it can be reduced to God's foreknowledge. What is left? Nothing remains but free will, not grace itself.

units.la: 3. 2. Arg. Vocatio non congrua qua Deus vocat multos, ea occasione, qua scit non obedituros, pugnat cum voluntate Dei antecedente, qua omnes & singulos vult salvari, & hoc pugnat cum omnibus Dei votis, deideriis, supplicationibus, obtestationibus, optationibus quibus Iesuitæ volunt Deum serio testari, quam vere desideret ipsos reprobos salvari. Imo sic id desideraret naturaliter, & tamen eo modo vocaret, quo praescit ipsos in longe graviorem poenam & tormentum incursuros, quam si omnino Deus non voca-ret, essent in Deo voluntates veræ contradictoriæ, & Deus malo dolo & hypocrisi non careret. Multa hic Suarez respondet. 1. Quod (inquit) ad voluntatem permittentem spectat, nihil absurdi est in eo, quod Deus certo sciens & prævidens fore, ut servatæ tali providentiæ modo, tot homines damnentur, illud permittere voluerit, sed habet solam illam admirationem de qua Paulus. O altitudo &c. Quod vero spectat ad voluntatem ordinantem, Deus non eligit hunc modum providentiæ, neque observavit ea tempora in quibus homines repugnaturos vocat, ut eos non salvet cum efficacia. Id enim & indignum est bonitate Dei, & ab illa voluntate alienum, qua vult omnes homines salvos fieri. Resp. 1. Non esse absurdum quod Deus repugnaturos vocet, nos cum Iesuita dicimus, sed hoc dato, quod omnes & singulos salvari velit ut docet Iesuita, est absurdissimum.
units.tr: 3. 2. Argument: A non-congruous calling, by which God calls many on an occasion in which he knows they will not obey, is at odds with God's antecedent will, by which he wills all and each to be saved; and this is at odds with all the desires, longings, entreaties, pleadings and wishes by which the Jesuits want to testify to God in earnest how truly he desires the reprobate themselves to be saved. Indeed, he would desire this naturally, and yet would call them in such a way that he foreknows they will incur a far heavier punishment and torment than if God did not call them at all; there would be in God truly contradictory wills, and God would not be free of wicked deceit and hypocrisy. Suarez answers many things here. 1. As far as the permissive will is concerned (he says), there is nothing absurd in God, who knows and foresees with certainty that, given the working of such a providence, so many men will be damned, being willing to permit this; but he has only that wonder of which Paul speaks: O the depth, etc. As for the ordaining will, God does not choose this mode of providence, nor does he observe those times in which he calls men who will resist, so that he does not save them with efficacy. For this is both unworthy of God's goodness and alien to that will by which he wills all men to be saved. Reply 1: We with the Jesuit say that it is not absurd that God calls those who will resist; but granting this, that God wills all and each to be saved, as the Jesuit teaches, is most absurd.

units.la: Quis enim pater terrenus naturali amore, impetu impensissimo diligens filium, ipsum sciens & volens permitteret ruere in cruciatus nunquam finiendos, ideoque, quamvis dicendum ò altitudo, nunquid dicendum ò monstrosum? ò voluntas permittens Deo indigna? & naturali Dei amore effusissimo, quo reprobos salvari obnixè cupit, aliena qui ipsos secundum voluntatem permittentem sineret ruere in exitium æternum, & eo modo vocet, quum aliter vocare possit, salvis omnibus Dei attributis, quo ipsorum damnatio, quam ille naturali amore non vult, longe gravior fit. 2. Non pudet Iesuitam palam agnoscere, voluntatem permittentem esse indignam Dei bonitate, & alienam à voluntate, qua vult naturaliter omnes salvari. Hic contrariæ plane in Deo sint voluntates, oportet, quin imo nunquam videre potui, quomodo Iesuitæ & Arminiani contrarietatem inter Dei voluntatem antecedentem, & voluntatem qua maximam humani generis partem permittat peccare, & in æternum perire, diluere possint. 3. Voluntas Dei permittens habet locum tantum in peccatis: atqui incongrue non nullos vocare non est peccatum, sed actus tum justitiæ, tum bonitatis. At vero absurdum est Deum actus justitiæ & bonitatis permissive, non voluntate effectiva facere: nec unquam scriptura bonos actus Dei voluntati permittenti tribuit, nec recta ratio id patitur. Secundum (inquit) voluntatem ordinantem Deus non eligit hunc modum providentiæ. At si hæc voluntas ordinans est absoluta, & à creaturis non dependens, tum absolute voluit Deus interitum reproborum, & antecedenter ad eorum merita. Jam Jesuita tu salva Dei voluntatem naturalem salvandi omnes, si potes, si absoluta non fuit, sed à creaturis dependens, idque naturali Dei iustitia, fato pereunt & salvantur omnes.
units.tr: For what earthly father, loving his son with natural affection and the utmost ardour, would knowingly and willingly allow him to rush into torments that never end? So, although we must say "O depth!", must we not also say "O monstrous!"? O will that permits what is unworthy of God! And with God's most abundant natural love, by which he earnestly desires the reprobate to be saved, would he who lets them, according to the permissive will, rush to eternal destruction, and calls them in that way when he could call them otherwise, with all God's attributes preserved? By this, their damnation, which he does not will by natural love, becomes far more grievous. 2. The Jesuit is not ashamed to acknowledge openly that the permissive will is unworthy of God's goodness and alien to the will by which he naturally wills all men to be saved. Here the wills in God must be plainly contrary, and indeed I have never been able to see how the Jesuits and the Arminians can explain away the contrariety between God's antecedent will and the will by which he permits the greater part of mankind to sin and perish for ever. 3. The permissive will of God has place only in sins. But to call some in an unfitting way is not a sin, but an act of both justice and goodness. Yet it is absurd that God should do acts of justice and goodness only permissively and not by an effective will. Scripture never assigns good acts to the permissive will of God, and right reason does not allow it. "According to the ordaining will," he says, "God does not choose this mode of providence." But if this ordaining will is absolute and does not depend on creatures, then God willed absolutely the destruction of the reprobate, and antecedently to their merits. Now, Jesuit, preserve God's natural will to save all, if you can. If it was not absolute but depended on creatures, and this by God's natural justice, then by fate all perish and all are saved.

units.la: 2. In omni sententia necessario fatendum multos repugnaturos vocanti. R. In Arminiana sententia fatendum, in Jesuitica fatendum, at quid tum? Incommodum non tollit argumentum. At vero in nostra, qui statuimus Deum libere & ex absoluto decreto, omnes creaturæ actus antecedente, hisce vitam æternam ad gloriam misericordiæ, illis mortem æternam ad gloriam iustitiæ illustrandam, vocare repugnaturos non est absurdum, imo dignissimum est Dei libertate, qui miseretur quorum vult, & de suo potest facere, prout est ei libitum, ut multos repugnaturos vocet. At vero, ut omnibus & singulis Deus velit vitam æternam, & interim talem providentiæ modum ordinet, quo præscit ipsos mortem æternam infallibiliter incursuros, ponit in Deo contrarias voluntates.
units.tr: 2. In every opinion it must necessarily be granted that many will resist the one calling. Reply: in the Arminian opinion it must be granted, and in the Jesuit opinion it must be granted; but what follows? An inconvenience does not overturn an argument. But in our opinion, which holds that God freely and by an absolute decree, prior to any act of the creature, calls some to eternal life for the illustration of his mercy and others to eternal death for the illustration of his justice, it is no absurdity that God should call some who will resist. Indeed it is most worthy of God's freedom, who has mercy on whom he wills and may do with his own as it pleases him, to call many who will resist. But that God should will eternal life for all and each, and yet ordain such a mode of providence, by which he foresees that they will infallibly incur eternal death, this posits contrary wills in God.

units.la: 3. R.* Suarez: igitur in toto hoc providentiæ genere, Deus per se primo intendit hominum salutem, quam cum infinitis modis, quos in thesauro sapientiæ suæ habet reconditos, procurare potuisset, ex omnibus illis, hunc eligit suâ voluntate & arbitrio & fortasse eadem scientiâ, qua prævidit, servato hoc providentiæ modo, tot homines fore damnandos, praevidit idem accedere debuisse vel creando alios homines, vel aliter iis providendo, nisi omnibus & singulis specialissima dona gratiae conferret, quod nec tenebatur Deus facere, nec fortasse expediebat, ut divina gratia simul & justitia magis offenderetur. Resp. Deum in toto hoc ordine primo & per se intendere hominum salutem, falsum est ex Jesuitica doctrina. Tum enim primo & per se intenderet hominum obedientiam, quod falsum est. Nam omnium hominum & obedientia libera, & inobedientia futuritionem habuit antecedenter ad Dei intentionem, decretum & scientiam conditionatam, ut docet Jesuita. At Deum intendere ut id fit, quod est antecedenter ad ipfius intentionem, est vere absurdum. Si Deus hominum salutem primo & per se, & modis quidem infinitae sapientiae infinitis possibilibus, cur hoc non fecit? vis igitur sapientiae Dei congruum esse, ut nulli sint reprobi? prosecto tum, esse reprobos, & tot perire, quot pereunt Dei sapientiae adversatur, & insipiens erit decretum reprobandi & damnandi homines. O blasphemiae! imo vis libero hominum pereuntium arbitrio, Deum coactum & depulsum ab omnibus modis salvandi omnes & singulos, quos impetu naturae vult salvari, uti mater infantes diligit, contra primarium intentum & sapientiae infinitae dictamen, adigi fato; ad plures & non pauciores salvandos, quam qui salvantur, ideoque liberum-arbitrium hominis Deum fine primitus intento excutit, & ab omnibus illis modis, in sapientiæ thesauro, infinitis salvandi omnes & singulos homines depellit. O providentiam infinitam sopitam! Dices, Deum sua voluntate & arbitrio hunc providentiæ modum elegisse. Quæro, an arbitrio ab omni conditione in hominibus soluto. Si sic, tum Deus absolute convertet, & non convertet omnes, & vocatio congrua est inutile figmentum. Si arbitrio dependenti ab indifferenti libertate humana, tum necessitate non voluntate hunc modum eligit. 2. [ Deum omnium salutem primo & per se, intendere ] hoc sub se habet reconditum, damnationem reproborum,non primo & per se a Deo intendi sed & præter ipsius intentionem, ideoque fortuito evenire. 3. Deum infinitis modis potuisse procurare salutem omnium & singulorum quam primo & per se intendit, & tamen eum modum sapientiæ sequi, ex quo Deus illa intentione optima excideret, & ex quo, maxima humani generis pars intenta salute excidens, rueret in tormenta ineluctabilia nunquam finienda, cum contrarium Deus naturali desiderio voluisset, non arguit sapientiam, sed subdolum Jesuitæ ingenium. 4. Vult Deum eadem scientia præscivisse tot homines damnandos, quot nunc damnantur, si alium providentiæ ordinem statuisset. At omnem Dei sapientiam hoc modo & providentiam prosternit, quia nempe semper libertas humana soluta ab omni prædeterminante Dei providentia, poterat eadem peccata facere, quae nunc facit, quo casu iidem homines, qui nunc damnantur, damnandi fuissent, quia nempe antecedenter ad Dei decretum & scientiam peccant, & sic iidem homines poterant etiam finaliter peccare, sicuti nunc faciunt, & sic possunt iidem damnari, qui nunc damnantur. Nam antecedenter ad Dei scientiam & voluntatem, ideoque antecedenter ad omnem Dei providentiam peccarunt. Ludit igitur Jesuita, quando meminit modorum infinitorum in divinae sapientiae thesauro reconditorum quibus posset omnium salutem procurare. Nam si homines sint agentes liberi, praemio & poena digni, non patet alius sapientissimo Deo modus providentiae, quam hic unicus & solus (ecce lector numerum infinitum tibi redigam ad non numerum, nempe unitatem misellam) quod nempe omnes homines, qui nunc peccant finaliter, antecedenter ad providentiam Dei poterant, uti nunc faciunt, finaliter peccare & damnari. Nam si alium modum Deus elegisset, procul dubio aliud dominium in actus liberos habere necesse fuit, quam ut omnes futuritionem haberent antecedenter ad Dei providentiam, & sic everteretur libertas ex fide Jesuitica. Alioqui poterant iidem & non plures, vel pauciores damnari, quam nunc damnantur. ʒ. [?] Ait non forte expediisse ad ostensionem gratiae & justitiae ut omnibus conferret dona gratiae specialissima, quia sic omnes salvati essent, & latuisset iustitia vindicatrix. An non Jesuita innuit Deum negasse reprobis gratiam efficacem, qua salvarentur, quia nimirum antea statuisset absolute iustitiam vindicatricem offendere in vasis irae, quae nostra est sententia? certe vini, mulierum, regum, maxima vis, sed omnia vincit veritas, & Jesuitam hic vicit. Nam quaerenti, cur Deus intendens omnium & singulorum salutem, non det omnibus[?] & singulis gratiam efficacem, respondet Jesuita, quia fortasse, ut docet ‘Calvinus, antea intenderit Deus absolute iustitiam vindicatricem offendere in multis, quibus non tenebatur (inquit) specialissima dona gratiae conferre. Certe gratias tibi debuisset Calvinus profusissimas, Jesuita, si vel vocula illam [fortasse] obliterasses, ideoque fortasse tu erras, non Calvinus. Et Jesuita opinatur, Calvinum esse probabiliter hic Orthodoxum.
units.tr: 3. Reply. Suarez: therefore in this whole kind of providence, God primarily and of himself intends the salvation of men. Among the infinite ways which he has hidden in the treasury of his wisdom, he could have procured it. From all those he chooses this one by his will and judgment, and perhaps by the same knowledge by which he foresaw that, with this mode of providence preserved, so many men would be damned. He foresaw that the same would have had to happen either by creating other men, or by providing for them otherwise, unless he conferred on all and each the most special gifts of grace, which God was neither bound to do nor perhaps expedient, so that divine grace and justice might not be offended all the more. Reply: that God in this whole order primarily and of himself intends the salvation of men is false, according to Jesuit doctrine. For then he would primarily and of himself intend the obedience of men, which is false. For both the obedience and the disobedience of all men had their futurition antecedently to God's intention, decree and conditional foreknowledge, as the Jesuit teaches. But that God should intend what comes to be, which is antecedent to his own intention, is truly absurd. If God primarily and of himself intends the salvation of men, and by infinite possible ways of infinite wisdom, why has he not done so? Do you then mean that it is fitting to the wisdom of God that there should be no reprobate? Surely, then, that there are reprobate, and that so many perish, is contrary to the wisdom of God, and the decree to reprobate and damn men will be foolish. O blasphemy! Indeed, by the force of the free will of the perishing men, God would be compelled and driven away from all the ways of saving all and each, whom by the impulse of nature he wills to be saved, as a mother loves her infants, against the primary aim and the dictate of infinite wisdom, and be driven by fate to save more men rather than fewer than those who are saved. Thus human free will shakes God from his primarily intended end, and drives him away from all those infinite ways, hidden in the treasury of wisdom, of saving all and each man. O infinite providence put to sleep! You will say that God by his will and judgment chose this mode of providence. I ask whether by a judgment loosed from every condition in men. If so, then God absolutely converts and does not convert all, and a fitting calling is a useless fiction. If by a judgment dependent on the indifferent freedom of man, then he chooses this mode by necessity, not by will. 2. [That God primarily and of himself intends the salvation of all] has hidden under it the damnation of the reprobate, which is not primarily and of himself intended by God, but is beside his intention, and so happens by chance. 3. That God could have procured the salvation of all and each in infinite ways, which he primarily and of himself intends, and yet follow that mode of wisdom by which God would fall from that best intention, and by which the greatest part of mankind, falling from the intended salvation, would rush into inescapable torments never to end, when God by natural desire would have willed the contrary, does not show wisdom but the Jesuit's crafty mind. 4. He wills that God by the same knowledge foreknew that so many men would be damned as are now damned, if he had established another order of providence. But in this way he overthrows all the wisdom and providence of God. For human freedom, loosed from every predetermining providence of God, could have committed the same sins it now commits. In that case the same men who are now damned would have been damned, because they sin antecedently to God's decree and knowledge; and so the same men could also have sinned finally, just as they now do, and so the same men who are now damned could be damned. For they sinned antecedently to God's knowledge and will, and therefore antecedently to all God's providence. The Jesuit therefore plays when he speaks of the infinite modes hidden in the treasury of divine wisdom by which he could procure the salvation of all. For if men are free agents, worthy of reward and punishment, there is no other mode of providence open to most wise God than this one and only one (behold, reader, I will reduce for you the infinite number to a non-number, namely the wretched unity): that all men who now sin finally could, antecedently to God's providence, sin and be damned finally, as they now do. For if God had chosen another mode, he would undoubtedly have had to have another dominion over free acts than that all should have futurition antecedently to God's providence, and so freedom would be overthrown on Jesuit faith. Otherwise the same men could be damned, and not more or fewer, than are now damned. 3. [?] He says it perhaps was not expedient, for the showing forth of grace and justice, that God should confer the most special gifts of grace on all, because then all would be saved and justice which avenges would have lain hidden. Does not the Jesuit hint that God denied to the reprobate efficacious grace, by which they would be saved, because he had determined beforehand absolutely to offend avenging justice in the vessels of wrath? That is our opinion. Surely wine, women and kings have great power, but truth overcomes all things, and here the Jesuit has been overcome. For when one asks why God, intending the salvation of all and each, does not give efficacious grace to all and each, the Jesuit answers that perhaps, as Calvin teaches, God had previously intended absolutely to offend avenging justice in many, to whom, he says, he was not bound to confer the most special gifts of grace. Surely Calvin would have owed you most abundant thanks, Jesuit, if you had blotted out that little word "perhaps"; so perhaps it is you who are wrong, not Calvin. And the Jesuit thinks that Calvin is here probably orthodox.

units.la: 4. 2.[?] Argum. Ex libero consensu vel dissensu facto vocationi; congruae & incongruae antecedente Dei praescientiam conditionatam, sequitur: non posse Deum convertere ullo modo, quem finaliter dissensurum vocanti praescit, & non posse non convertere, quem praescit cessurum, & etiam ad finem pariturum congruae vocationi. At hoc repugnat omnipotentiae Dei & dominio in actus creaturae liberos. Ergo illud ex quo hoc sequitur non est admittendum. Prob. connexio majoris? quoniam objectum praescientiae conditionatae est contingens quod potest vel esse, vel non esse. Ergo possunt reprobi, siquidem libere obediunt finaliter non obedire, ut & electi etiam possunt finaliter non obedire. Ergo Deus non potest per omnipotentiam illos convertere, nec potest hoc non convertere. Suarez: potest (inquit) homo esse ita dispositus, ut nulla ordinaria vocatione convertendus sit. Unde non est inconveniens, quod potuerit Deus, illa conditionata scientia, de aliquo praevidere non esse convertendum omnibus ordinariis auxiliis gratiae. Tamen quia praeter haec auxilia, potest Deus infinitis modis adjuvare hominem & vocare, ideo simpliciter fieri non potest, quin praecognoscat Deus plures gratias seu auxilia, quibus de facto cognosceret hominem convertendum fore, si vellet illa praestare data illa hypothesi (de homine probo semper resituro Dei vocationi) sequitur Deum non posse talem voluntatem efficaciter & libere convertere, quia praesupponitur, cognovisse resituram semper, si liber usus ei concedatur: posset tamen illam convertere, quo vellet, impediendo libertatis usum, & in hoc divina potentia satis ostenditur: tamen illa hypothesi, ut dixit, simpliciter impossibilis est. Resp. O conscientiam Jesuiticam! Si homo antecedenter ad scientiam conditionatam est pariturus Deo vocanti, & alter nunquam pariturus est necessitate antecedente Dei decretum, Deus non potest efficere, ut futurum non fit futurum. Hoc fatum satalissimum, Deo Jesu tæ[?] & Arminiani nunquam amovebunt, ullis effugiorum machinis. Si enim Deus aliter disponere potest actus hos voluncatis, decreto libero hoc faceret. Atqui omnes actus pravi reproborum, omnes actus obedientiales electorum, Iesuitis, Dei liberum decretum & scientiam mediam antecedunt. At Deum libere efficere, ut id, quod est futurum antecedenter ad ipsius libertatem, non fit futurum, implicat contradictione sempiternam.
units.tr: 4. 2.[?] Argument. From the free consent or dissent given to the calling, congruent or incongruent, which precedes God's conditional foreknowledge, it follows that God cannot convert in any way the one whom he foreknows will finally dissent from the calling, and cannot fail to convert the one whom he foresees will yield, and even bring to the end by the congruent calling. But this conflicts with the omnipotence of God and his dominion over the free acts of creatures. Therefore that from which this follows is not to be admitted. Proof of the connection of the major premise: the object of conditional foreknowledge is the contingent, which can either be or not be. Therefore the reprobate can, since they freely obey by finally not obeying, just as the elect can also finally not obey. Therefore God cannot by his omnipotence convert those, nor can he fail to convert them. Suarez: a man can be so disposed that he is to be converted by no ordinary calling. Whence it is not inconsistent that God, by that conditional knowledge, could foresee of someone that he is not to be converted by all the ordinary aids of grace. Yet because, beyond these aids, God can help and call a man in infinite ways, it simply cannot be that God does not foreknow several graces or aids by which he would know in fact the man would be converted, if he willed to bestow them. Given that hypothesis (of a man who will always yield to God's calling), it follows that God cannot efficaciously and freely convert such a will, since it is presupposed that he knew it would always yield, if free use were granted to it. He could, however, convert it wherever he wished, by impeding the use of its freedom, and in this the divine power is sufficiently shown. Yet that hypothesis, as he said, is simply impossible. Reply: O Jesuitical conscience! If a man is going to yield to God's calling antecedently to conditional knowledge, and another never will yield, by an antecedent necessity of God's decree, then God cannot bring it about that the future does not become future. This most fatal fate the Jesuits and the Arminians will never remove by any contrivances of escape. For if God could dispose those acts of the will otherwise, he would do so by a free decree. But all the sinful acts of the reprobate and all the obedient acts of the elect, according to the Jesuits, precede God's free decree and his middle knowledge. Yet that God should freely bring it about that what is future, antecedently to his own freedom, does not become future, implies a perpetual contradiction.

units.la: 2. Si Deus extraordinarias vocationes cognoscit, quibus reprobi de facto converterentur, vel libere convertendi essent, vel necessario. Si libere, recurret argumentum idem pari robore. Si necessario, extra oleas disputatur. Conversio etenim laudabilis & obedientia Iesuitis erit non obedientialis & non necessaria. 3. Reducit totam Dei omnipotentiam ad impeditionem usus libertatis. Non ergo Dei dominium & omnipotentia facere possunt, ut plures libere convertantur, quam qui actu convertantur nec plures, non, converterentur & damnarentur, qua qui actu convertuntur. At si Dei dominium ad actus necessarios extenditur, pari etiam ratione ad actus liberos. Sed audi, Iupiter, Iesuitæ nostrũ Iehovam tecum catenis fati adamantinis alligarunt. 4 Hanc hypothesin esse impossibilem statuit Iesuita, quando dicit: Impossibile est ut sola voluntate resistat, sed infallibile erit, ut aliquo modo tentationis cadat. Satis innuit ad unum ictum tentationis, cor ad duos stare posse, & per eandem rationem, quia nulla tentatio determinat voluntatem, sed eam indifferentiae suae relinquit (alioqui ex Iesuitis, si necessitate peccatur, non peccatur omnino [?]). ideo fieri potest, ut non cedat ulli omnino tentationi. Sed quomodo probas? Id (inquis ibid.) à fortiore patet: quia Deus sinat hominem tentari à dæmone omnibus modis quibus ille novit & potest ipsum tentare, impossibile est ut sola libertate et[?] resistat. Sed infallibile erit, ut aliquo modo tentationis cadat. Sed multo potentior est divina gratia, & plures modos novit Deus inclinandi & trahendi voluntatem, ut bonus consentiat. Ergo non est contingens ut ex tot gratiæ auxiliis & vocationibus non præcognoscatur aliqua; cui homo consensurus sit.
units.tr: 2. If God knows extraordinary callings by which the reprobate would in fact be converted, they would have to be converted either freely or necessarily. If freely, the same argument recurs with equal force. If necessarily, the dispute is beside the point. For on the Jesuits' view, the laudable conversion and obedience will be non-obedient and not necessary. 3. He reduces the whole omnipotence of God to impeding the use of liberty. Therefore neither the dominion nor the omnipotence of God can bring it about that more are freely converted than those who are actually converted, nor that more would be converted and damned than those who actually are converted. But if God's dominion extends to necessary acts, then by the same reasoning it extends to free acts. But hear, Jupiter: the Jesuits have bound our Jehovah along with you in the adamantine chains of fate. 4. The Jesuit declares this hypothesis to be impossible when he says: It is impossible that he resist by will alone, but it will be infallible that he fall in some way of temptation. He sufficiently implies that one heart can stand against one stroke of temptation, and against two; and by the same reasoning, because no temptation determines the will but leaves it to its indifference (otherwise, by the Jesuits' account, if sin is committed by necessity, it is not sin at all), it can happen that it yields to no temptation whatever. But how do you prove it? This (you say, ibid.) is plain a fortiori: because God allows a man to be tempted by the devil in every way by which the devil knows and is able to tempt him, it is impossible that he resist by freedom alone. But it will be infallible that he fall in some way of temptation. But divine grace is far more powerful, and God knows more modes of inclining and drawing the will so that it consents willingly. Therefore it is not contingent that, out of so many aids of grace and callings, there is not some one foreknown to which the man will consent.

units.la: Resp. 1. Ait impossibile esse, ut homo sola libertate omnibus modis possibilibus à Satana impetitus resistat, imo si sola libertate ulli tentationi posset non cedere, frustra oratur, ne nos inducas in tentationem. 2. Si impossibile est ut sola libertate omnibus resistat, tum non peccat non resistendo. Jesuitis enim nihil est peccati in impossibilibus. 3. Si talis homo sufficiente gratia instruatur, tam potest omnibus resistere, quam omnibus succumbere. Alioqui gratia non est sufficiens, & homini sufficiente gratia instructo non est contingens peccare vel non peccare. Dic: necessarium igitur, non audes. Tum enim ego inferam, nec illic peccari, nec non peccari, si Jesuitica non corruerent dogmata. 4. Quia multo potentior est Dei gratia tentatione diabolica, non concludit Jesuita negatum, nisi gratia indeclinabiliter flectat voluntatem, & sic non manet libertas, ideoque contingit semper moveri vel non moveri ad obediendum hominem per illam gratiam potentiorem. 5. Et quid; si Deus noverit plures modos trahendi voluntatem ad consensum? sint ter millies milleni modi. Si semper iuasorie[?] & resistibiliter, dari potest homo qui ad exitum vitæ Deo vocanti resisteret, & tum quæro an Deus posset talem, salva libertate Iesuitica, convertere, imo hoc esset impossibile 6: Turpiter sibi Iesuita contradicit. Ille enim supra dedit hypothesin possibilem fig.8. p.148. Nam (inquit) tota illa congruitas (adeoque tractio moralis voluntatis per quoslibet modos) ex se solum inducit quandam moralem certitudinem cui absolute non repugnat, ut vocationi sic congruæ liberum arbitrium resistat. 7. Tandem ait: Ergo non est contingere ut ex tot gratiæ auxiliis & vocationibus (nempe moraliter & resistibiliter moventibus libertatem: hoc nisi dixeris, nihil dicis) non præcognoscatur aliqua cui homo consensurus sit. Audesne, Iesuita, dicere: Ergo est necessarium ut Deus cognoscat aliquam vocationem resistibiliter agentem cui homo resistere non potest? at tum profecto erit vocatio & resistibilis & irresistibilis, quod involvit contradictionem, ut non dicam Deum male dici contingenter cognoscere futurum. Si enim est futurum, Deus id non potest non cognoscere. At vero quia est futurum contingenter, ideoque fieri potest, ut nunquam fit scientia illius, potuit Deo non inesse, ideoque non inest necessario.
units.tr: Reply. 1. He says it is impossible for a man, by freedom alone, to resist when assailed by Satan in all possible ways. Indeed, if by freedom alone he could resist any temptation, we pray in vain, "lead us not into temptation." 2. If it is impossible that by freedom alone he resist all, then he does not sin by not resisting. For for the Jesuits there is no sin in impossibilities. 3. If such a man is furnished with sufficient grace, he can resist all as much as he can succumb to all. Otherwise grace is not sufficient, and for a man furnished with sufficient grace it is not contingent whether he sins or does not sin. Say: "therefore necessary," if you dare not. For then I will infer that there is neither sin nor non-sin there, if the Jesuit doctrines did not fall. 4. Because God's grace is far more powerful than diabolical temptation, the Jesuit does not conclude what is denied, unless grace bends the will indeclinably; and so liberty does not remain, and it is therefore contingent whether man is moved or not moved to obey by that more powerful grace. 5. And what if God knows more modes of drawing the will to consent? Let there be three thousand times a thousand modes. If they always act persuasively and resistibly, there can be a man who would resist God's calling at the end of his life. Then I ask whether God could convert such a man, with Jesuitical liberty preserved; indeed, this would be impossible. 6. The Jesuit contradicts himself shamefully. For above he gave a possible hypothesis, fig. 8, p. 148: For (he says) that whole congruity (and so the moral drawing of the will by whatever modes) of itself induces a certain moral certainty, to which it is not absolutely repugnant that free will resist so congruent a calling. 7. Finally he says: "Therefore it is not contingent that, out of so many aids of grace and callings (namely those morally and resistibly moving liberty; unless you say this, you say nothing), there is not some one foreknown to which the man will consent." Dare you say, Jesuit, "Therefore it is necessary that God know some calling acting resistibly to which the man cannot resist"? But then surely the calling will be both resistible and irresistible, which involves a contradiction, not to mention that God is wrongly said to know the future contingently. For if it is future, God cannot fail to know it. But since it is future contingently, and so can happen that it never comes to be, its knowledge could be absent from God, and therefore it is not in him necessarily.

units.la: 5. Argum. 4. Causa alia efficax dari hic non potest, quam voluntas humana. Suppono enim ex adversariorum doctrina eandem gratiam prævenientem gradu & mensura parem, in non-congrue vocato, & congrue vocato, uti concedunt Fonseca & Suarez[?]. Causa cur gratia fit efficax non in illo, sed in hoc, non est vocatio congrua. Nam præscientia Dei efficaciam gratiæ præsupponit, uti omnis scientia suum objectum, ideoque non facit: ergo ea nō est causa. 2. Tempus & locus nō sunt causæ. Suntenim adjuncta externa omni causalitate destituta, nisi dixerint tempus à natura esse præscriptum humanæ conversioni ad Deum, licut mense lunii rosæ florent: quod risui erit lectori. Nec quidquam conferre potest causalitatis, locus: Matthæus in civitatis porta. Petrus in mari, Zachæus luper ficu convertitur: quid momenti ista afferant ad liberum assensum, cogitatu non est possibile. 3. Voluntatis dispositio naturalis non potest esse causa. Si enim fit supernaturalis, voluntatem tamen suæ indifferentiæ relinquit. Non enim evertit libertatem, nec vero naturalis dispositio influere potest effectivè ex se in essectum supernaturalem. Nec 4. nuda applicatio & approximatio agentis ad passum est causa: ea enim est modus causandi, & conditio, non causa. Nam approximatio ad ignem non est illud, quod calefacit, sed conditio tantum calefaciendi: solus ignis calefacit. Si enim nuda approximatio vel applicatio talis aliquid virtutis causativæ superadderet gratiæ prævenienti, tum non esset par gratia in noncongrue vocato, cui deesset talis applicatio, atqui in congrue vocato, contra hypothesin. Vocatio ergo qua congrua, quoniam est omni vi causativa destituta, non potest esse causa. Relinquatur ergo ƒ. loco quod solum liberum arbitrium est causa. Nam Deus præscit hominem prius natura vocationi pariturum, quam congrue vocet, quia nemo dicit hominem parere vocanti, quia Deus præscit, sed contra. Quid hic Suarez qui ingenium versare & torquere didicit ad omnes formas, ut Prothea dixeris, non theologum? In executione (inquit) nunquam exercetur illa efficacia sine cooperatione liberi arbitrii, quamvis non reducatur in illud simpliciter, sed in gratiam vocantem & adjuvantem. In intentione autem seu præparatione talis vocationis, & auxilii, quod non solum fit sufficiens, sed infallibiliter fit futurum efficax, reductio fit in solam divinam voluntatem. Candidius Vasquez. Non est (inquit) in nostra potestate, ut detur vocatio congrua, bene tamen ut fit efficax. Et Fonseca reducit in decretum absolutum. R. Suarez putat se non patrocinari Pelagio. Si dixerit efficaciam gratiæ reducendam non in solum liberum arbitrium & tamen in liberum arbitrium. 2. In gratiam vocantem reducendam esse vult: at falso. In id enim ultimatè & causaliter reducitur efficacia gratiæ, à
units.tr: 5. Argument 4. No other efficacious cause can be given here than the human will. For I assume, from the doctrine of our opponents, that the same prevenient grace, equal in degree and measure, is present in the one not congruently called and in the one congruently called, as Fonseca and Suarez concede. The cause why grace becomes efficacious in this one and not in that one is not the congruent calling. For God's foreknowledge presupposes the efficacy of grace, as all knowledge presupposes its object, and therefore does not make it; therefore foreknowledge is not the cause. 2. Time and place are not causes. For they are external circumstances destitute of all causality, unless they say that time is prescribed by nature for human conversion to God, just as roses bloom in June, which will make the reader laugh. Nor can place contribute any causality: Matthew at the city gate, Peter at the sea, Zacchaeus converted beneath the fig tree. What weight these things bring to free assent cannot be conceived. 3. A natural disposition of the will cannot be the cause. For if it is supernatural, it still leaves the will its indifference; for it does not overthrow liberty, and a natural disposition cannot flow effectively of itself into a supernatural effect. Nor 4. is bare application and approach of the agent to the patient a cause, for that is a mode of causing and a condition, not a cause. For approach to fire is not what warms, but only the condition of warming; fire alone warms. For if bare approach or application added such causative power to prevenient grace, then the grace in the one not congruently called, who lacks such application, would not be equal to that in the congruently called, contrary to the hypothesis. Therefore the congruent calling, since it is destitute of all causative force, cannot be the cause. It remains, therefore, that free will alone is the cause. For God foreknows that man will by nature yield to the calling before he calls him congruently; no one says that man yields to the caller because God foreknows, but rather the reverse. What does Suarez here, who has learned to twist and torture his wit into every form, like Proteus you might say, make of himself? Not a theologian. In execution (he says) that efficacy is never exercised without the cooperation of free will, although it is not reduced to that simply, but to the grace that calls and helps. But in the intention or preparation of such a calling and aid, which not only becomes sufficient but is infallibly going to be efficacious, the reduction is made to the divine will alone. More candidly, Vasquez: It is not in our power that a congruent calling be given, but it is in our power that it be made efficacious. And Fonseca reduces it to the absolute decree. Suarez thinks he does not favour Pelagius, if he says the efficacy of grace is to be referred not to free will alone, and yet to free will. 2. He wants it referred to the grace that calls, but falsely. For the efficacy of grace is ultimately and causally referred to that on which conversion depends, that it rather happens than does not, and rather happens in this man than in another. But it is not from the calling, nor from the helping grace, that it is rather… from

units.la: Ib. sol. 3. — P. 151. — Vasquez. tom. 1. p. 549. quo pendet conversio, ut potius fit, quam non fit, & potius fit in illo, quam in alio. Atqui non à vocatione, non ab adjuvante gratia est, quod potius fit conversio, quam non, & potius convertatur Petrus, quam Iudas. Nam par vocatio quoad substantiam, ideoque quoad vim causativam est vocatio, & gratia adjuvans conversi, & non conversi, imo ex Iesuitis est à voluntate Petri potius quam Iudæ, quod convertatur, imo à causa communi & conversio, & non conversio nullo modo potest esse efficacia gratiæ, hoc est, actualis efficientia gratiæ. 3. Dei voluntas & intentio non est id, in quod reducitur efficacia gratiæ. Nam intentio hæc vel est conditionata, vel absoluta: in neutram, fecundum placita Iesuitica, reduci potest efficacia gratiæ. Si conditionata fit intentio & voluntas, tum Deus ab æterno voluit gratiam efficacem fore in Petro non in Iuda, ex hypothesi. Cedo jam ex animo candido, hypothefin, nempe quod Petrus eflet pariturus gratiæ vocanti: alia fingi non potest conditio. Age itaque sic Deus statuit: Ego ex fenestrā scientiæ mediæ præscio fore ut gratia fit efficax, in Petro non in Iuda, ideoque ego volo & intendo ut efficax fit in Petro potius quam in Iuda. Quisquam ne sobrius diceret efficaciam, quæ esse habet antecedenter ad Dei voluntatem, esse à Dei voluntate, ut essectum à causa? expergiscere tandem aut edormi, Iesuita, crapulam istam Pelagianam. Si voluntas est absoluta, tum Deus decreto absoluto determinavit omnes liberas conversiones omnium electorum, & per eandem rationem omnes etiam liberas non-conversiones reproborum. Ferrum prius quam hoc decoxerit Itomachus[?] Jesuiticus aut. Arminianus. O jam tollitur (inquiunt) libertas, evertitur omnis religio, introducitur fatum, Stoicismus, Manechismus, & quid non? Suis hic opitulari cupit Grevinchov. ita etiam & nobile ingenium Petri Fonsecae. Omnia volunt reduci ad decretum absolutum, ut in causam altissimam. Ita enim illi, si Petrus in hisce & non in aliis occasionibus & rerum ordine collocabitur, & tali modo dispositus vocabitur, tum obsequetur divinae vocationi. Sed ego decerno (inquit Deus) absolute collocare Petrum in tali rerum ordine, & ipsum tali modo dispositum vocare. Ergo absoluta mea voluntas prima est causa, cur Petrus meae obsequatur vocationi. Sed Resp.
units.tr: Ib. sol. 3. — P. 151. — Vasquez. tom. 1. p. 549. On what does the conversion depend, so that it happens rather than does not happen, and happens in this man rather than in that? It is not from the call, nor from the assisting grace, that conversion rather than non-conversion takes place, or that Peter rather than Judas is converted. For the call is equal in substance, and therefore equal in causative force, to both the converted and the unconverted, and the assisting grace is the same for both.
