Indeed, according to the Jesuits, it is from the will of Peter rather than of Judas that he is converted. So conversion and non-conversion can in no way come from the common cause, and this cannot be the efficacy of grace, that is, the actual efficiency of grace. 3. The will and intention of God is not that to which the efficacy of grace is reduced. For this intention is either conditional or absolute, and by Jesuit principles the efficacy of grace can be reduced to neither. If the intention and will are conditional, then God from eternity willed that grace would be efficacious in Peter and not in Judas, on the hypothesis. Now let me concede, with an honest mind, the hypothesis, namely that Peter would yield to the grace calling him; no other condition can be imagined. Let God then decide thus: I foresee, from the window of middle knowledge, that grace will be efficacious in Peter and not in Judas, and therefore I will and intend that it be efficacious in Peter rather than in Judas. Would any sober person say that efficacy, which has its being antecedently to the will of God, has its being from the will of God as an effect from its cause? Wake up at last, or sleep off that Pelagian drunkenness, Jesuit. If the will is absolute, then by an absolute decree God determined all the free conversions of all the elect, and by the same reasoning all the free non-conversions of the reprobate. Before he has digested this, let the Jesuit or the Arminian [?] take heed. "Oh," they cry, "liberty is removed, all religion is overthrown, fate is introduced, Stoicism, Manichaeism, and what not!" Grevinchov wants to help his own side here, and so does the noble wit of Peter Fonseca. They want everything reduced to an absolute decree, as to the highest cause. For they say: if Peter is placed in these circumstances and this order of things, and is so disposed, and called in this way, then he will obey the divine call. But I decree (says God) absolutely to place Peter in such an order of things, and to call him, so disposed. Therefore my absolute will is the first cause why Peter obeys my call. But I reply.

units.la: 2. Non est hic primus & altissimus ille syllogismus in quem reducetur tota vocationis efficacia, 1. Major non est necessaria, imo stante indifferentia Jesuitica & Arminiana in voluntate Petri, non magis vera quam falsa, & falsa, quam vera est major propositio connexa. Nam in quocunque rerum ordine collocetur Petrus, nunquid ille ordo ipsius voluntatem ad assentiendem Dei vocationi determinabit? Num quaeso tantum convivium, mens hilaris, timor aliquis gehennae aut ejusmodi circumstantiae Petrum ad parendum Dei vocationi determinent? Certe tum in tantum convivium, non in Dei voluntatem reducetur efficacia gratiae, & quoniam Petri voluntas libere movetur à lauto convivio, aut à mente paulo post pocula,facetiore, haec libera motio antecedat,necesse est, & Dei scientiam mediam & decretum. Quomodo igitur reducetur indecretū? En ubi iam decretū absolutum evanuit, tenuesque recessit in auras? 2. Nec assumtio illius syllogismi est tam vera, quam falsa, stante indifferentia à voluntatis Petri. Deus enim non absolute collocat Petrum in tali rerum ordine: Petrus libere bibit, convivam agit, adit sacram concionem tali hora, & loco, quo convertitur, libere dormivit, ideoque melius per hoc disponitur: imo libere audit concionatorem proponentem Dei nomine vocationem congruam, quippe potest non audire, libere animum advertit ad sensum, literam, scopum, aequitatem vocationis, & momenta rationum. Potest enim voluntas libera, & affectus tanquam Rhetores Diaboli avocare intellectum ad res terrenas & varias, eo tempore & loco, ponderandas, ideoque nisi dixerint actus liberos absolute à Deo decerni, quod illis est fatalissimum factum, assumptionis veritas non pendet ullo modo ex Dei decreto, imo assumptio est vera, vel falsa antecedenter ad Dei voluntatem, & scientiam mediam. Hinc sequitur conclusio plane contraria: voluntas Petri, non Dei absolutum decretum est causa, cur Petrus congrue vocatus vocationi Dei respondeat. 3. Fatetur Gwinchov. Deum praescivisse Petrum collocatum in talibus circumstantiis pariturum Dei vocationi: ita & Fonseca, ita Suarez, ita Bellarminus. At quis non jam videat humanam absolutam voluntatem Dei voluntate hic priorem esse? Nam scientia media non antecedit actus liberos voluntatis tum divinae, tum humanae. 4 Sic fluit eorum syllogismus [Si Petrus in talibus circumstantiis vocatus fuerit, parebit vocationi: atqui Deus absolute decrevit collocare Petrum in talibus circumstantiis: ergo Petrus parebit] conclusio non est absoluta, uti debet esse, si actus credendi in Petro ultimate resolvatur in absolutum Dei decretum. Nam conclusio sequitur deteriorem partem, atqui major est veritatis contingentis, non necessariae: ergo talis erit conclusio, uti est haec. Si Petrus currit, necesse est moveatur. Atqui Petrus currit. Ergo necesse est moveatur. Conclusio non potest esse veritatis necessariae, quia non necesse est Petrum currat: imo contingenter currit. 5. Ego vero ipsis formabo syllogismum priorem illo syllogismo, quem illi formarunt, imo cujus veritas erit causa cur ipsorum syllogismus consistat, uti hic est: Si Petrus collocabitur in talibus circumstantiis, liberum erit ei credere, vel noncredere. Atqui Petri voluntas est collocare, vel non-collocare se in talibus circumstantiis. Ergo Petri voluntas erit credere, vel noncredere. Hic syllogismus Dei decretum absolutum antecedit. Est enim scientiæ conditionatæ objectum, ideoq; decretum ipsorum absolutum resolvitur in voluntatem creatam.
units.tr: 2. This is not the first and highest syllogism to which the whole efficacy of the call is reduced. 1. The major premise is not necessary; indeed, while the Jesuit and Arminian indifference in the will of Peter stands, it is no more true than false, and it is as false as the connected major proposition is true. For in whatever order of things Peter is placed, will that order determine his will to assent to God's call? Pray, will such a great banquet, a cheerful mind, some fear of hell, or circumstances of this kind determine Peter to obey God's call? Certainly, in that case the efficacy of grace would be reduced to the banquet and not to the will of God. And since the will of Peter is moved freely by a lavish banquet, or by a mind rather jolly after the cups, this free motion must necessarily precede both God's middle knowledge and his decree. How then is it reduced to an absolute decree? Here is where the absolute decree has vanished and withdrawn into thin air! 2. Nor is the assumption of that syllogism as true as its falsity, while the indifference of the will of Peter stands. For God does not absolutely place Peter in such an order of things. Peter drinks freely, plays the guest, attends the sacred sermon at such an hour and place, where he is converted; he slept freely, and so is disposed the better by this; indeed he freely listens to the preacher proposing, in God's name, the congruous call, since he can choose not to listen, and he freely attends to the sense, the letter, the aim, the fairness of the call, and the force of its arguments. For a free will, and the affections like the devil's rhetoricians, can draw the intellect away to various earthly things, at the time and place for weighing the call. So unless they say that free acts are absolutely decreed by God, which is the most fatal thing for them, the truth of the assumption does not depend in any way on God's decree. Indeed the assumption is true or false antecedently to the will of God and to middle knowledge. Hence follows the plainly contrary conclusion: the will of Peter, not the absolute decree of God, is the cause why Peter, rightly called, answers God's call. 3. Grevinchov admits that God foreknew Peter placed in such circumstances that he would obey God's call. So too Fonseca, so Suarez, so Bellarmine. But who does not now see that here the human absolute will is prior to the will of God? For middle knowledge does not precede the free acts of the will, either divine or human. 4. Thus runs their syllogism: [If Peter is called in such circumstances, he will obey the call; but God has absolutely decreed to place Peter in such circumstances; therefore Peter will obey]. The conclusion is not absolute, as it ought to be if the act of believing in Peter is ultimately resolved into God's absolute decree. For the conclusion follows the weaker part; but the major is of contingent truth, not of necessary truth. Therefore the conclusion will be of this form: If Peter runs, it is necessary that he moves. But Peter runs. Therefore it is necessary that he moves. The conclusion cannot be of necessary truth, because it is not necessary that Peter runs; indeed he runs contingently. 5. I, for my part, will form for them a syllogism prior to that syllogism which they have formed, indeed one whose truth will be the cause why their syllogism holds, in this form: If Peter is placed in such circumstances, it will be free for him to believe or not to believe. But the will of Peter is to place himself, or not to place himself, in such circumstances. Therefore the will of Peter will be to believe or not to believe. This syllogism precedes God's absolute decree. For it is the object of conditional knowledge, and therefore their absolute decree is resolved into the created will.

units.la: Argum. §.[?] Si non congrue vocatis datur gratia sufficiens, quâ possint converti, siquidem velint, ergo non obstante omni incongruitate vocationis, fieri potest, ut convertantur. Nam incongruitas non infallibiliter, nec indeclinabiliter voluntatem flectit, sed suæ indifferentiæ relinquit. Hoc autem est absurdum 1. quoniam Fonseca vult actuale obsequiū congrue vocati includi in conceptu quidditativo congruæ vocationis, & actualem inobedientiam in essentia etiam congruæ vocationis: 2. etiam hic gratiæ efficacia reducetur in liberum arbitrium: & 3. sequetur non necessario requiri congruitatem, ad hoc ut quis convertatur, quoniam non congrue vocati etiam converterentur. Nec satisfacient, si dixerint incongruam vocationem supponere voluntatem vocationi repugnaturam esse. Tum dico voluntatem repugnaturam esse prius natura, quam incongruitas habeatlesse[?]: quod absurdum. Nam effectus non est prior vel causa, vel modo sive ratione agendi in causa, ideoque repugnantia voluntatis non potest præsupponi & congruitate. At forte dicent gratiam sufficientem in se posse obedientiam producere respectu voluntatis humanæ in specie, non vero de facto producere respectu voluntatis talis in individuo, nimirum, Iudæ sic sub talibus circumstantiis collocati, & dispositi. Sic diluo Gratia sufficiens ad convertendam voluntatem in specie, est etiam sufficiens ad convertendam hanc voluntatem in individuo. Alioqui si fortior fit corruptio in Iudæ, quam ut à gratia sufficiente possit auferri, tum gratia non est sufficiens huic voluntati, nempe Iudæ, convertendæ, & sic non peccat Iudas, eo quod converti non vult. 2. Ait Fonseca vocationem congruam de facto removere rebellionem. At vel aufert, qua vocatio, vel qua congrua. Si qua gratia, adhuc cum sit eadem vocatio quoad substantiam, fatente Fonseca, adhibita congruè vocato, & non-congruè vocato; tum adhuc converti potest non congruè vocatus, non minus quam congrue vocatus, quod absurdum. Si vero vocatio auferat rebellionem, qua congrua, tum congruitati nudæ & applicationi tali præcisè consideratæ inerit causativa vis edomandi rebellionem. At qui id habere vim causandi quod non est ens, sed modus entis, mihi erit causa postulandi, ut qui me docuit metaphysicam, reddat minam Diogenes. Certe Bellarminus nasutus, satis, ut ictum hujus argumenti declinaret, ait: ad gratiam non solum pertinet motio sive excitatio interna sed etiam circumstantia loci, temporis, personæ. R. Certe non potuit magnus Iesuita obmutescere: maluit dicere gratiam esse Petro, quod sit piscator, quod in navi audiat Christum concionantem. Tibi igitur mare, & navis & hora forte dici tertia, gratiæ sunt. Gratia certe digna schola Iesuitica, inimicissima præ aliis pontificiis Dei gratiæ. At sint gratiæ non congrue vocato, non desunt tot circumstantiæ quot congrue vocato. Audite evasionem Fonsecæ: Si vocatio quidem congrua vocatis fuerit, hoc est, effectum in iis sortitura, ad prævenientem quoque gratiam, quemadmodum & ipsa vocationis substantia pertinebit. Magna enim gratia fit ei, qui in ea occasione vocatur, in qua præscitur obediturus. Sin autem congrua non fuerit, ut quæ non sortitura fit effectum, ipsa quidem vocationis substantia ad prævenientem gratiam spectabit, non tamen hujus modi applicatio, sed ad communem providentiam referenda erit, qua Deus non omnibus æqualia tribuit, satisque habet, si ea euique conferat, quæ, nisi ille sibi deesse velit, ipsi sufficiant ad salutem.
units.tr: Argument. If grace sufficient for converting is not given to those not congruously called, by which they could be converted if they wished, then, notwithstanding any incongruity of the call, it can happen that they are converted. For incongruity does not bend the will infallibly or irrevocably, but leaves it to its own indifference. But this is absurd: 1. because Fonseca wants the actual obedience of the congruously called to be included in the quidditative concept of a congruous call, and actual disobedience to be included even in the essence of a congruous call; 2. grace's efficacy here too will be reduced to free choice; and 3. it will follow that congruity is not necessarily required for anyone to be converted, since those not congruously called would also be converted. Nor will they satisfy themselves if they say that an incongruous call presupposes a will that will resist the call. For then I say that the will's resistance is prior in nature to the incongruity that it has, which is absurd. For an effect is not prior either as cause, or in the mode or manner of acting in the cause, and therefore the resistance of the will cannot be presupposed by the congruity. But perhaps they will say that sufficient grace can in itself produce obedience with respect to the human will in general, but does not in fact produce it with respect to such a will in the individual, namely Judas, so placed and disposed in such circumstances. I answer thus: sufficient grace to convert the will in general is also sufficient to convert this will in the individual. Otherwise, if corruption in Judas is stronger than can be removed by sufficient grace, then grace is not sufficient to convert this will, namely Judas's, and so Judas does not sin in that he does not wish to be converted. 2. Fonseca says that a congruous call in fact removes rebellion. But either it removes it as a call, or as a congruous call. If as a grace, then, since it is the same call in substance, as Fonseca admits, applied to the congruously called and to the not congruously called, the not congruously called could still be converted no less than the congruously called, which is absurd. But if the call removes rebellion as a congruous call, then the bare congruity, and such an application considered precisely as such, has the causative power of subduing rebellion. But that which has the power of causing is not a being, but a mode of being; so it is for me a cause to demand that Diogenes return the mina to him who taught me metaphysics. Certainly Bellarmine, being shrewd enough to dodge the blow of this argument, says: Grace pertains not only to internal motion or excitation but also to the circumstance of place, time, and person. I reply: certainly the great Jesuit could not keep silent; he preferred to say that grace is to Peter because he is a fisherman, because he hears Christ preaching in a boat. So for you the sea, the boat, and perhaps the third hour are graces. Truly a grace worthy of a Jesuit school, most hostile of all the Papists to the grace of God. But even if there are graces for the not congruously called, they lack as many circumstances as for the congruously called. Hear Fonseca's evasion: If the call is indeed congruous for those called, that is, destined to produce its effect in them, then it will pertain to preventing grace, just as the very substance of the call does. For great grace is given to him who is called on that occasion in which he is foreknown to obey. But if it is not congruous, as one that is not destined to produce its effect, then indeed the very substance of the call will pertain to preventing grace, but not such an application, which must be referred to common providence, by which God does not give equal things to all, and it is enough for him to confer on each what, unless he himself wishes to be lacking to himself, will be sufficient for him for salvation.

units.la: R. 1. Non erit par gratia prævenientis in congrue vocato & incongrue vocato, imo nec possibile est, si ipsa congrua vocatio est pars gratiæ prævenientis. 2. Tali modo & tempore applicatio vocationis, non potest esse gratia, nisi naturam sanet. Hic enim est Valentiæ & scholasticis magnis, formalis effectus gratiæ, sed talis applicatio non sanat naturam, neque ullam habet causalitatem formaliter. Est enim non causa, nec ens, sed modus & conditio causæ sive entis. Delirat in principiis itaque notissima Iesuita.
units.tr: Reply 1. The prevenient grace will not be equal in the congruously called and the incongruously called. Indeed it is not even possible, if congruous calling is itself part of prevenient grace. 2. An application of the calling in such a manner and at such a time cannot be grace unless it heals nature. For according to Valencia and the great scholastics, this is the formal effect of grace, but such an application does not heal nature and has no formal causality at all. It is neither a cause nor a being, but a mode and condition of a cause or being. The Jesuit therefore raves against the most well-known principles.

units.la: 3. Si tali modo, vocari fit gratia, est gratuita & non debita. Atqui antecedenter ad Dei scientiam mediam, ideoque ad decretum verum fuit Deum vocaturum tali modo & tempore pariurum, ideoque si fatum Deum constringens est gratia, an potius fatale debitum, ipsi judicent. 4. Unde est hæc vocationum disparitas, quod Deus secundum decretum prædestinationis vocet quosdam congrue, & secundum decretum communis providentiæ, quosdam vocet incongrue? an à decreto absoluto? Atqui supra probavi, non dari in Deo tale decretum erga homines absque insigni, libertatis humanæ, læsione, adeoque tolletur omnis obedientia, proculcabitur religio ex Iesuitis, ideoque à meritis hominum disparitas harum vocationum & decretorum erit. Ergo merita & actus liberi obedientiæ & inobedientiæ, decretum primum absolutum antecedent. Ergo decretum hoc non est altissima causa efficaciæ gratiæ, contra quod docent Iesuitæ.
units.tr: 3. If calling is grace in this way, it is gratuitous and not owed. But before God's middle knowledge, and therefore before the true decree, it was true that God would call in such a manner and at such a time that they would obey. So let them judge whether fate binding God is grace, or rather a fatal debt. 4. Whence comes this disparity of callings, that God calls some congruously according to the decree of predestination, and others incongruously according to the decree of common providence? Or does it come from an absolute decree? But above I proved that there is no such decree in God towards men without a notable injury to human liberty. Thus all obedience would be taken away and religion trampled underfoot, by the Jesuits' own account. Therefore the disparity of these callings and decrees will arise from the merits of men. So merits and free acts of obedience and disobedience precede the first absolute decree. Therefore this decree is not the highest cause of the efficacy of grace, contrary to what the Jesuits teach.

units.la: Argum. 6. Si gratia vocationis infallibiliter conversionem operetur, quia tali tempore & modo homines vocantur, insulse & falso Deus urgeret conversionem: Argumento ducto à temporis opportunitate. Atqui hoc facit sæpius in scripturis. Ps. 95. 7. Hodie si audietis vocem, ne obduretis corda Esai. 55. [?] 6. Quærite Dominum, dum inveniri potest. 2. Cor. 6 2. Ecce nunc est tempus acceptum, ecce nunc dies salutis. Ioel. 2. 12. Nunc itaque, dicit Iehova, revertimini ad me, ex toto corde. Immo hoc falsum esset: in multis enim hoc esset verum: non est hodiernus dies salutis, non est hoc præsens tempus revertendi acceptum, non fumus dispositi hodie, crastinus dies & sequens annus, nempe quum fit tempus, quo congrue vocandi fumus, est tempus acceptum. Imo Deus sciret non esse praefens tempus eorum conversioni accommodatiffimum, ideoque sciret Deus fe falsum loqui, quod est blasphemum. Quasi vero sic Deus diceret: scio nondum esse tempus opportunum & acceptum, quo plerique vestrum convertendi eltis, hortor tamen ut hoc tempore, quod maxime opportunum est, ad me revertamini ex toto corde. Nec posset Deus dicere, quid potui amplius facere vineæ? Nam etiam in genere mediorum externorum, Deum sibi deesse quererentur. Nam medicus qui in debito modo & tempore applicet sciens & prudens emplastrum ivulneri[?], & eo modo quo scit non curatum iri? Num quis diceret eum naturali desiderio voluisse, ut curetur, aut eum posse dicere, quid amplius potui facere ægro meo.
units.tr: Argument 6. If the grace of calling infallibly works conversion because men are called at such a time and in such a manner, then God would urge conversion foolishly and falsely. This is an argument drawn from the opportuneness of time. But Scripture does this often: Ps. 95. 7. Today if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts. Isa. 55. 6. Seek the Lord while he may be found. 2 Cor. 6. 2. Behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation. Joel 2. 12. Now therefore, says Jehovah, turn to me with all your heart. Indeed this would be false, for in many cases it would be true that today is not the day of salvation, this is not the present accepted time for turning, we are not disposed today, but tomorrow and the following year. Yet when the time comes at which we are congruously called, that is the accepted time. Indeed God would know that this is not the present time most suited to their conversion, and so God would know that he speaks falsely, which is blasphemous. As if God were to say: I know it is not yet the opportune and accepted time in which most of you are to be converted; nevertheless I urge you to turn to me with all your heart at this time, which is most opportune. Nor could God say, "What more could I have done for my vineyard?" For even in the general sphere of external means, men would complain that God had failed them. Would a physician who, knowing and prudently, applies a plaster to a wound at the proper manner and time, do so in a way he knows will not cure it? Would anyone say that he wished by natural desire for it to be cured, or that he could say, "What more could I have done for my sick patient?"

units.la: Argum. 7. Causa, cur homines à Deo non convertuntur, est quia non sunt ex ovibus Christi, quia non trahuntur à patre, quia Deus iis non dedit cor ad intelligendum, quia non audiverunt, & didicerunt à patre, quia non circumcidit Iehovah cor eorum, non qua tali modo & tempore, non trahit ipsos Deus.
units.tr: Argument 7. The reason why men are not converted by God is that they are not of Christ's sheep, that they are not drawn by the Father, that God has not given them a heart to understand, that they have not heard and learned from the Father, that Jehovah has not circumcised their heart. It is not because God does not draw them in such a manner and at such a time.

units.la: Argum. 8. Gratia congrua vel producit effectum necessario, vel contingenter. Si primum conversi non possunt non converti, ideoque non convertuntur libere. Si contingenter, tum possunt non converti, quod illis est falsum: eadem ratio de non-congrua conversione urgebit. At dicunt congruitatem includere praescientiam mediam, qua Deus praescit actum libere futurum infallibiliter, licet non necessario. Resp. Praescientia media praescitur a Deo actus liber possibilis & nunquam suturus, infallibiliter etiam non minus, quam actus liber futurus, ideoque repugnabit ullos actus liberos plures posse esse, quam sunt, & illos non posse non esse, qui non sunt, ideoque quoniam sunt futuri antecedenter ad congruitatem istam, & hoc dato, quod Deus incongrue vocaret ipsos, non possunt non converti, nisi Dei scientia media falleretur, quod absurdum est, & dato quod non conversos congruissime Deus vocaret, non fuissent converti. At dicent conversione congrua essentialiter includi conversionem. Resp. Jam nemo non videt ipsos petere principium, quin imo effectum liberum in causa contingenter operante essentialiter includi, est absurdorum absurdissimum.
units.tr: Argument 8. Congruous grace either produces its effect necessarily or contingently. If the first, the converted cannot but be converted, and so they are not converted freely. If contingently, then they can fail to be converted, which is false for them; the same reasoning will press against incongruous conversion. But they say that congruity includes middle knowledge, by which God foreknows an act that will be free, infallibly though not necessarily. Reply: middle knowledge is God's foreknowledge of a free act that is possible and will never be, infallibly no less than a free act that will be. Therefore it would be contradictory for more free acts to be possible than there are, and for those that are not to be unable not to be. Since they are future before that congruity, and given that God would call them incongruously, they could not fail to be converted unless God's middle knowledge were deceived, which is absurd. And given that God would call the unconverted most congruously, they would not have been converted. But they will say that congruous conversion essentially includes conversion. Reply: now everyone sees that they beg the question. Indeed, that a free effect is essentially included in a contingently operating cause is the most absurd of absurdities.

units.la: Argum. 9. Referenda esset causa conversionis in complexiones individuales & in accidentia mera lautum convivium, in ebrietatem, adeoque in peccatum & recedentibus illis accidentibus prout non difficulter a subjecto removeri possunt, tam in proclivi esset hominem denuo ad statum peccati reverti, etiam hoc dato quod in eo esset semen Dei, & natura nova, quam non reverti ad peccatum.
units.tr: Argument 9. The cause of conversion would have to be referred to individual temperaments and mere accidents: a sumptuous banquet, drunkenness, and so sin. When those accidents recede, as they can easily be removed from the subject, it would be just as easy for a man to return again to a state of sin, even granting that there is in him a seed of God and a new nature, as it would be for him not to return to sin.

units.la: Argum. 10. Novus est fecundus partus & regeneratio à solo ministro suadente fierer. Atqui sic claudus ambulare, cæcus fuafione videre posset, & in peccatis mortuus refurgere.
units.tr: Argument 10. A new and fruitful birth and regeneration would be made by the persuading minister alone. But in this way a lame man could walk, and a blind man could see by persuasion, and the dead in sins could rise again.

units.la: Argum. 11. Necesse est motio congrua & non congrua habeant locum in actibus naturalibus liberis, & in omnibus actibus peccaminofis Diabolorum & hominum reproborum, quia Deus juxta præscientiam mediam operatur & movet in illis, & sic Dei motio non congrua vel erit causa peccati, quod absurdum, vel motio congrua non erit causa actus, vel moraliter, vel fupernaturaliter, boni. Respondet Suarez, habere in iis locum, sed Deum collocare homines in illa occasione, in qua præscit ipsos peccaturos, non ex intentione, ut peccent, sed ut bonum faciant; peccare vero eos fecundum voluntatem permittentem. R. At quid philosophari opus est hic de intentione Dei, qui est actus immanens in Deo, & nihil reale ponit in homine? Nam Deus est realis & externa caufa nempe non movens congrue, id faciens, ex quo infallibiliter sequitur peccatum, & fi de actu externo loquamur, nihil aliud agit ad productionem operis moraliter boni & supernaturalis. 2. Deum non congrue movere Diabolos jam in malo judicialiter obfirmatos, ea intentione ut bonum faciant Diaboli, quis audet afferere ? nam quæ lex jam est Diabolis proposita? 3. Supra dixit Iesuita, non conferre Deum dona specialissima gratiae omnibus. Quia (inquit) nec for-tasse expediebat, ut divina gratia simul & justitia magis ostenderetur. Ergo per hanc rationem fortasse Deus, si Iesuitae placeret, collocat homines in ea occasione ut peccent etiam ex intentione, ut haberet in quo divina gratia & justitia magis ostenderetur. Attende & animum adverte, Iesuita, ad haec.
units.tr: Argument 11. Congruous and incongruous motion must have a place in natural free acts and in all sinful acts of devils and reprobate men, because God works and moves in them according to middle knowledge. So God's incongruous motion will either be the cause of sin, which is absurd, or congruous motion will not be the cause of the act, whether morally or supernaturally good. Suarez replies that they have a place in these acts, but that God places men in that occasion in which he foreknows they will sin, not with the intention that they sin, but that they do good; they sin, however, according to his permissive will. Reply: But why is there any need to philosophize here about the intention of God, who is an immanent act in God and posits nothing real in man? For God is a real and external cause, namely one that does not move congruously, and by doing so infallibly brings about sin. And if we speak of external act, he does nothing else towards the production of a morally good and supernatural work. 2. Who dares to assert that God does not move the devils congruously, though they are already judicially hardened in evil, with the intention that the devils do good? For what law has already been proposed to the devils? 3. Above, the Jesuit said that God does not confer the most special gifts of grace on all. "Because (he says) perhaps it was not expedient that divine grace and justice be shown more together." So by this reasoning, perhaps God, if it pleases the Jesuit, places men in that occasion in order that they sin even with intention, "that in them divine grace and justice might be shown more." Attend and take note of these things, Jesuit.

units.la: Argum. 12. Neque potest esse par gratia in congrue vocato & non congrue vocato, siquidem converti major est gratia, quam non converti. Resp. Suarez. In genere motionis sive rei, aequalem esse utrobique vocationem, at vero in genere beneficii majorem esse gratiam converti, quam non converti, & congrue vocari quam incongrue. R. 1.
units.tr: Argument 12. Nor can there be equal grace in the congruously called and the incongruously called, since being converted is a greater grace than not being converted. Reply, Suarez: in the genus of motion or thing, the calling is equal on both sides, but in the genus of benefit, being converted is a greater grace than not being converted, and being called congruously is greater than being called incongruously. Reply 1.

units.la: Quid non obscurabunt Iesuitae distinctionibus suis evanidis? Quid, an non ista motio, qua Deus adhibet in conversione, est beneficium? Annon est beneficium quod Deus homines trahat? quod corda aperiat? quod det cor ad intelligendum? Nemo sanus id negabit. 2. Ex Iesuitis converti non est beneficium ita a Deo convertente, ut possit conversus Deo gratias agere, qui ipsum a non converso separaverit. Nihil enim in genere motionis & ut causa realiter influens Deus agit in converso, quod in non-converso. Ideoque est conversi beneficium naturale quod debet purae naturae arbitrii separationem facienti. 3. At major Dei dilectio erga congrue vocatum quam erga non congruè vocatum, est quia secundum duo diversa decreta, prædestinationis & providentiæ nimirum, ipsos vocat: unde disparitas dilectionis? à Dei absoluta libertate? Tum vicit Calvinus, imo potius Dei veritas triumphavit: an à meritis? & vincet Pelagius.
units.tr: What will the Jesuits not obscure with their flimsy distinctions? Is that motion, by which God applies himself in conversion, not a benefit? Is it not a benefit that God draws men, opens their hearts, and gives them a heart to understand? No sane person will deny it. 2. According to the Jesuits, conversion is not a benefit from God converting in such a way that the one converted can thank God for having separated him from the unconverted. For in the kind of motion, and as a really influencing cause, God does nothing in the converted that he does not do in the unconverted. Therefore conversion is a natural benefit of the convert, which must be credited to the separating of pure natural free will. 3. But God's greater love for the congruently called than for the incongruently called is because he calls them according to two different decrees, namely of predestination and of providence. Whence then comes the disparity of love? From God's absolute liberty? Then Calvin has won, or rather the truth of God has triumphed. From merits? Then Pelagius will win.

units.la: Argum. 13. Congrua vocatio stat hoc fundamento quod sit in Deo scientia media: at fundamentum hoc corruit, ut supra probatum.
units.tr: Argument 13. Congruent calling rests on this foundation, that there is middle knowledge in God; but this foundation falls, as was proved above.

units.la: Argum. 14. Stante Iesuitico hoc principio, [Deum obedienti dare efficacem concursum, non obedienti negare] tum ei qui semel obedit Deo vocanti, Deus ex justitia motionem congruam, qua infallibiliter obediturus est, dare tenetur; & hunc actum alia motione congrua, necessitate justitiæ, præmiabit, & sic qui semel obedivit, non potest unquam in posterum peccare, quod absurdum: & per eandem rationem, qui semel ponit obicem Deo vocanti, Deus ex justitia ei negabit motionem congruam, & per eam rationem semper deinceps, & sic nunquam obedibit: quod absurdum. Si vero ex absoluta libertate Deus dat, vel negat vocationem congruam, ad Calvinum redibunt Iesuitæ, & necesse est vale dicant, concursui Dei conditionali, qui pugnat cum libertate Dei absoluta.
units.tr: Argument 14. With this Jesuit principle standing, [that God gives efficacious concurrence to the one who obeys, and denies it to the one who does not obey], then God is bound by justice to give to one who has once obeyed God's calling a congruent motion by which he will infallibly obey. And by another congruent motion, from the necessity of justice, he will reward this act. So he who has once obeyed can never sin in the future, which is absurd. By the same reasoning, he who has once placed an obstacle to God's calling will be denied a congruent motion by God's justice, and by the same reasoning always thereafter, and so will never obey, which is absurd. But if God gives or denies congruent calling by absolute liberty, the Jesuits will come back to Calvin, and they must necessarily bid farewell to God's conditional concurrence, which fights with God's absolute liberty.

units.la: 6. Hanc vocationem Iesuitæ à scripturis non probant, sed ab Augustino solo. An id jure faciant, videamus, Sciendum itaque motionem dici congruam tribus modis. 1. Quando Deus movet per verbi suasoria argumenta voluntatem, ita ut in genere suasorio congruentiffimè moveat, siquidem intellectus, voluntas & affectus verbi genio & ingenio congruerent. Hoc modo congrue Deus vocat omnes in visibili ecclesia. At vero Iefuitæ nolunt affectus humanos verbo contemperari, sed verbum & Dei volitionem accommodari genio & dispositionibus individualibus affectuum humanorum, quam contemperatione ego nunquam potui intelligere.
units.tr: 6. The Jesuits do not prove this calling from Scripture, but from Augustine alone. Let us see whether they do so rightly. It must be known that a motion is called congruent in three ways. 1. When God moves the will by persuasive arguments of the word, so that in the persuasive kind it moves most congruently, since the intellect, will and affections agree with the nature and disposition of the word. In this way God calls all congruently in the visible Church. But the Jesuits do not want human affections to be tempered to the word; they want the word and God's volition to be fitted to the nature and individual dispositions of human affections. I have never been able to understand this tempering.

units.la: Nam contemperatio verbi, genio affectuum tantum potest intelligi tribus modis, 1. genio pure naturali. Atqui sic nulla effet causa, cur congrue vocatus pareret. Quæ enim influentia effet puræ naturæ, nisi qua elevatæ per gratiam? Pura enim natura non est tantarum virium, ut posset in actus supernaturales influere. 2. Si genio naturæ corruptæ nunquam sequeretur conversio. Nam animalis homo habet pro mera stultitia, ea quæ sunt Dei, nihilque magis ei sordet, qvam simplicitas euangelii. 3. Genio naturæ per gratiam prævenientem elevatæ. At sic, cū ex Iesuitis par gratia potest esse in converso, & non-converso, vocatio non effet sic congruentior converso, quam non-converso. At forte dant, quartum modum, nempe vocationis contemperationem cum complexione & individualibus difpositionibus superadditis puræ naturæ. At vero nec hoc, cum fanâ ratione, dici potest. Quæ enim convenientia est inter invisibilia, Dei æternam gloriam, fortem filiorum Dei nullis calamitatibus non oppressam?quippe necesse est fe cruci,fami,inediæ,algori,persecutionibus,dedecori,exilio,cupiditatū abnegatione per totam vitam exponant, & morti deniq; acerbissimæ & immaturæ(siquidem Deus ita volet) perpetiendæ sint parati: quæ inquam inter hæc & dispositiones individuales convenientia? Imo mihi videtur contrarietas non mediocris, & mirum est, scripturam nunquam meminiffe ullius dispositionis ejusmodi, aut occasionis, siquidem ex ea penderet conversio, vel non-conversio. Imo debebat Deus præcipue in scripturis regulas & præcepta tradidisse, quibus homines sese in tali loco, tempore, tristitia, vel lætitia convivali vel muficali aut hujusmodi collocarent, quo congruenter difponerentur ad Dei vocationem: ut taceam, quam nihil activitatis habeant hæ dispositiones ad voluntatem huc vel illuc flectendum, fatentibus jesuitis. 2. Congrue Deus movet, quatenus ita determinat voluntatem electorum quatenus novit genio libertatis naturalis convenire. Novit enim efficaciam gratiæ, & quomodo voluntate illæsa libertate impellat. Hoc etiam sensu vocationem efficacem congruam concedimus. 3. Ita ut actus præsciat, scientiâ mixta antecedenter ad motionem suam, & tum motionem suam contemperet ad genium voluntatis: hoc nos pernegamus.
units.tr: For the tempering of the word to the nature of the affections can be understood only in three ways. 1. By purely natural nature. But in that case there would be no reason why the congruently called should obey. For what influence could pure nature have, except that which is raised up by grace? Pure nature is not of such strength that it could flow into supernatural acts. 2. If conversion followed only from the nature of corrupted nature, it would never follow. For the natural man counts the things of God sheer foolishness, and nothing is more despised by him than the simplicity of the gospel. 3. By the nature raised up by prevenient grace. But in that case, since according to the Jesuits there can be equal grace in the converted and the unconverted, the calling would not be more congruent to the converted than to the unconverted. Perhaps they give a fourth way, namely the tempering of the calling with the complexion and individual dispositions added to pure nature. But neither can this be said with sound reason. For what agreement is there between invisible things, God's eternal glory, and the lot of the sons of God, who are never free from calamities? Indeed they must expose themselves for their whole life to the cross, hunger, famine, cold, persecutions, dishonour, exile and the denial of their desires, and be ready to suffer finally a most bitter and untimely death (if God so wills). What agreement, I say, is there between these things and individual dispositions? To me there seems to be no small contrariety. It is strange that Scripture never mentions any disposition of this kind, or any occasion on which conversion or non-conversion depended. Indeed God ought especially in the Scriptures to have handed down rules and precepts by which men might place themselves in such a place, at such a time, in sadness or in convivial or musical joy, or the like, so that they might be disposed congruently to God's calling. Not to mention how little power these dispositions have to bend the will this way or that, as the Jesuits themselves admit. 2. God moves congruently insofar as he so determines the will of the elect as he knows agrees with the nature of natural liberty. For he knows the efficacy of grace, and how to impel the will without harming its liberty. In this sense also we concede an efficacious congruent calling. 3. That God foresees the act, by middle knowledge antecedent to his motion, and then tempers his motion to the nature of the will: this we flatly deny.

units.la: 7. Citant ex Augustino illud : Ex quo apparet habere quosdam in ipso ingenio, divinum naturaliter munus intelligentiae, quo moveantur ad fidem, si congruat suis mentibus, vel audiant verba, vel videant signa: & tamen si Dei altiore judicio a perditionis massa non sint gratiae praedestinatione discreti, nec ipsa ei adhibentur vel dicta divina, vel facta per quae possunt credere, si audirent utique talia vel viderent. Locus hic videtur maxime favere Jesuitis : at non prodest iis. Nam 1. ait quosdam in ipso ingenio habere hoc munus intelligentiae, ut observat Tuissus. Atqui Jesuitae volunt omnes naturaliter posse moveri & permoveri, si adsit congrua vocatio. 2. Apparet (inquit pater) non ergo aliquid determinat, de modo vocationis. 3. Congruitas ista Augustiniana spectat ad substantiam vocationis, ut apparet ex verbis praecedentibus.
units.tr: 7. They cite from Augustine the words: From this it appears that some have in their very nature a divine natural gift of understanding, by which they are moved to faith if it agrees with their minds, or if they hear words or see signs. Yet if, by God's higher judgment, they are not set apart by the grace of predestination from the mass of perdition, neither are divine words or deeds applied to them by which they could believe, even if they heard such things or saw them. This passage seems to favour the Jesuits most, but it does not help them. For, first, he says that some have this gift of understanding in their very nature, as Tuissus observes. Yet the Jesuits want all people to be naturally able to be moved and persuaded, if congruent calling is present. 2. "It appears," says the Father; he therefore determines nothing about the mode of calling. 3. That Augustinian congruity concerns the substance of the calling, as appears from the preceding words.

units.la: Caeteri autem, ubi nisi in massa perditionis justo judicio divino, relinquuntur? Vbi Tyrij relicti sunt & Sidonij, qui etiam credere potuerunt, si mira illa Christi signa vidissent. Sed quoniam ut crederent non erat iis datum, etiam unde crederent est negatum. Non dicit, [sed quoniam ut crederent, non erit iis eo modo & tempore datum,] sed simpliciter negat iis esse datum. Tyrij ergo potuerant credere ex Augustino sic expositio, si Deus tali modo ipsos vocasset. Nempe igitur praescivit Deus Tyrios crediturōs antecedenter ad scientiam mediam. Ergo erant vere credituri in fide, ergo fallax erat scientia media & falsa, qua ipsos nunquam crediturus praescivit. Nam nunquam crediderunt. Nam tam contingens est non-credere Tyriorum, quam credere. Ergo scienti à medià Deus utrumque praescivit. At dices praescivisse Deum τὸ[?] credere, non absolute sed ex hypothesi vocationis congruae. At Resp. Vel animadversio Tyriorum ad vocationis sensum literalem erat libera, ideoque contingens, ac proinde tam non-credere, quam credere cohaeret contingenter cum vocatione illa, ex cujus positione Deus ipsos credituros praescivit. Nam quia libere se collocassent Tyrij in tali occasione, in qua erant convertendi hypotheticè, & Deus scientia media praescivit non futuritionem illius libertae collocationis in tali occasione, non poterat praescire fidem Tyriorum in hypothesi, quam nunquam ponendam praescivit eadem scientia media, nisi in infinitum rediret quaestio de positione illius libertae conditionis, & rursus de conditione illius conditionis, quod absurdum non admitteret Augustinus. 5. Tyrij credidissent, si congrua verba & signa audivisent, & vidissent, congrua nempe congruitate in secundo significato, quatenus moraliter movet & Physice voluntatem, illaesa libertate. 6. Non potest illic Augustinum loqui de modo applicationis vocationis, sed de ipsa substantia vocationis, quoniam causa altissima Augustino est divina absoluta praedestinatio, ut apparet ex verbis: atqui talis praedestinatio actuum liberorum Jesuitis est Chymerica fabula.
units.tr: Others, however, where are they left, but in the mass of perdition by the just judgment of God? Where were the Tyrians and Sidonians left, who also could have believed if they had seen those wonderful signs of Christ? But since it was not given to them to believe, it was also denied them whereby they might believe. He does not say [but since they were not to believe in that way and at that time, it was not given to them], but simply denies that it was given to them. The Tyrians therefore could have believed, according to Augustine's exposition, if God had called them in such a way. Surely then God foreknew by middle knowledge that the Tyrians would believe. Therefore they were truly going to believe, and therefore middle knowledge was fallacious and false, since by it he foreknew they would never believe. For they never believed. For the not-believing of the Tyrians was as contingent as their believing. Therefore by middle knowledge God foreknew both. But you will say that God foreknew "to believe" [τὸ πιστεύειν] not absolutely but from the hypothesis of congruent calling. But I reply: either the Tyrians' attention to the literal sense of the calling was free, and therefore contingent, and consequently both not-believing and believing cohere contingently with that calling, from whose supposition God foreknew they would believe. For since the Tyrians would have freely placed themselves in such an occasion, in which they were to be converted hypothetically, and God by middle knowledge foreknew not the futurity of that free placement in such an occasion, he could not foreknow the faith of the Tyrians in a hypothesis which, by the same middle knowledge, he foreknew would never be posited. Otherwise the question of the positing of that free condition would run back into infinity, and again the condition of that condition, an absurdity Augustine would not admit. 5. The Tyrians would have believed if they had heard congruent words and seen signs, congruent indeed in the second sense, insofar as it morally and physically moves the will with its liberty unharmed. 6. There Augustine cannot be speaking of the mode of applying the calling, but of the very substance of the calling, since for Augustine the highest cause is divine absolute predestination, as appears from the words. Yet such a predestination of free acts is a chimerical fable to the Jesuits.

units.la: 8. Citant Augustinum ad Simplicianum. Ve-rum est (inquit) multi vocati, pauci vero electi. Illi enim electi, qui congruenter vocati: illi autem qui non congruebant neque contemperabantur vocationi, non electi, quia non secuti, quamvis vocati. Ibid. Igitur non volentis &c. sed miserentis Dei, qui hoc modo vocavit, quo modo fit ei congruere ut vocantem non repuat. Resp. Non negarem Augustinum (quod res est) ita scripsisse ante exortam hæresin Pelagianam. Deinde Augustinus voce congruitatis ideo sæpissime utitur, quia præoccupare semper illud Pelagij & humanæ rationis voluit, quo ex omnipotentissima Dei flexione voluntatis liberæ sequi videtur compelli libertatem & fato cogi, quod & postea sæpius Pelagiani & Semipelagiani Augustino objecerunt. Ideo Augustinus omnipotentissimam illam flexionem exposuit per talem congruitatem moralem, qua Deus illæsa libertatis natura, ipsam, quo vult, flectebat, sicut & nos contra Jesuitas & Arminianos cogimur tradere prædeterminationem talem physicam, quæ tamen locum relinquat judicio, electioni vitali & indifferentiam libertatis naturalem, admirando modo, conservet, ideoque nostram congruitatem non Jesuiticam attruit, quippe inspirationes, attractiones omnipotentissimas aperte docuit Augustinus. Nec ob aliud dicitur veraciter omnipotens, nisi quia quicquid vult, potest, nec voluntate cujusquam creaturæ voluntatis omnipotentis impe- ditur effectus. Et idem. Deo volenti salvum facere nullum hominum resistit arbitrium. Sic enim velle & nolle in volentis & nolentis potestate est, ut divinam voluntatem non impediat, nec superet potestatem. Atqui in congrua vocatione est potestas resistendi Deo vocanti, & nolenti salvum facere, quia semper manet indifferentia Iesuitica ad volendum & nolendum in voluntate, positis etiam omnibus ad agendum requisitis. Neque hic ullum actum formalem omnipotentiæ divinæ, quem toties in Augustiniana congruitate vocationis inculcatum iterum atque iterum audiunt, quicunque in ejus scriptis vel paulo exercitatiores sunt. 2. Congruitate Augustiniana non fit nuda concio ab homine concionatore, sæpe oratore minime diserto: quod fieret, si sola excitante & suasoria actione Iesuitica perficeretur conversio. Nec dicere possunt Iesuitæ, Deum jam immediate è cœlis persuadere, imo eloquentia hominum ordinarie jam utitur, atqui Augustino, à quo audimus & discimus, est Pater cœlestis, cujus alia longe & excellentior est actio, quam prædicatoris suadentis in terris. Atqui si suasio hæc congrua staret, eadem est suasio Dei & prædicatoris, imo eadem numero. Unde est ergo congruitas? Certe non in, vel à suasione, aut ipsius accommodatione; sed à Deo movente & determinante voluntatem libertati congruenter. 3.Vocatio Augustini iplam cordis duritiem atque adeo contumacem potentiam resistendi aufert. Nam à nullo duro corde respuitur, ideo quippe tribuitur, ut cordis durities primitus auferatur. Atqui congruitas Iesuitica non aufert duritiem, quia manet indifferentia absoluta non parendi Deo vocanti. 4.
units.tr: 8. They cite Augustine to Simplicianus: "It is true," he says, "that many are called, but few are chosen. For those are chosen who are called congruently; but those who did not fit in with or accommodate themselves to the calling are not chosen, because they did not follow, although they were called." Also in the same place: "Therefore it is not of him who wills, etc., but of God who shows mercy, who called in such a way that it is congruous for the one called not to reject the caller." Reply: I would not deny that Augustine (as is the case) wrote this before the Pelagian heresy arose. Next, Augustine so often uses the word congruity because he always wanted to forestall that objection of Pelagius and of human reason, by which it seems to follow from God's almighty bending of the free will that liberty is compelled and forced by fate. The Pelagians and Semipelagians often objected this to Augustine afterwards. So Augustine explained that almighty bending through such moral congruity, by which God, with the nature of liberty left unharmed, bends the will wherever he wills. Likewise we too, against the Jesuits and Arminians, are compelled to teach a physical predetermination of such a kind that it nevertheless leaves room for judgment and vital choice, and wonderfully preserves the natural indifference of liberty. And so we do not ascribe to him a Jesuitical congruity, since Augustine clearly taught almighty inspirations and attractions. Nor is he rightly called truly almighty for any other reason than that whatever he wills, he can do, and his effect is not hindered by the will of any creature. And again: "To God, willing to save, no human will resists." For willing and not willing lie in the power of the one who wills and does not will, so that they neither impede the divine will nor overcome its power. But in a congruous calling there is a power of resisting God calling and unwilling to save, because the Jesuitical indifference to willing and not willing always remains in the will, even when all things required for acting are posited. Nor is there here any formal act of divine omnipotence, which those who are even a little practised in his writings hear inculcated again and again in Augustine's congruity of calling. 2. By Augustinian congruity conversion is not a bare sermon delivered by a human preacher, often a not very eloquent speaker. That is what would happen if conversion were accomplished by the sole exciting and persuasive action of the Jesuits. Nor can the Jesuits say that God now persuades immediately from heaven, but rather that he now ordinarily uses human eloquence. Yet for Augustine, from whom we hear and learn, the heavenly Father has an action far different and more excellent than that of a preacher persuading on earth. And if this persuasion were a congruous one, the persuasion of God and that of the preacher would be the same, indeed the same in number. Where then is the congruity? Certainly not in, or from, the persuasion or its very adaptation; but from God, who moves and determines the will congruently with liberty. 3. The calling of Augustine takes away the very hardness of heart and so the stubborn power of resisting. For it is rejected by no hard heart; it is given for this very reason, that the hardness of heart may first be taken away. But Jesuitical congruity does not take away hardness, because the absolute indifference to not obeying the calling God remains. 4.

units.la: Augustinus non ad liberum arbitrium refert efficaciam gratiae, quod faciunt Iesuitae. Nolunt enim congruitatem determinare voluntatem, sed ipsam posse absolute agere vel non. Atqui Augustinus hic admiratur. Iam si ad illam profunditatem scrutandam [inquit) quisquam nos coarctet, cur illi ita suadeatur, ut persuadeatur, illi autem non ita, duo sola occurrunt &c. O altitudo, & nunquid iniquitas apud Deum? Atqui quae altitudo, quod gratia fit efficax, quia ille non vult, hic vocatur, quando praescitur obediturus, hic quando praescitur non obediturus? 5. Congruitatis Iesuiticae fulcrum est scientia media, commentum Augustino, sanctis patribus, & scholasticis ignotum. Ausim dicere Augustinum nunquam intellexisse congruitatem Iesuiticam, & qui in scholasticis sunt versati, nuperum figmentum esse non possunt diffiteri. In hisce injuriis gratiae & providentiae divinae allatis, cum Iesuitis & Arminianis [illegible, ~8 letters] scholasticam non detrectabo. L A V S D E O.
units.tr: Augustine does not refer the efficacy of grace to free will, as the Jesuits do. For they are unwilling for congruity to determine the will, but hold that the will can act absolutely or not. Yet Augustine marvels here: "Now if anyone should press us to search that depth, why it is that to one it is so persuaded that he is persuaded, and to another it is not so, two things alone present themselves... O depth! Is there unrighteousness with God?" But what depth is there in this, that grace is made efficacious because this one is called when it is foreknown that he will obey, and that one when it is foreknown that he will not obey? 5. The prop of Jesuitical congruity is middle knowledge, an invention unknown to Augustine, the holy Fathers and the scholastics. I dare say Augustine never understood Jesuitical congruity, and those versed in the scholastics cannot deny that it is a recent fiction. In these wrongs done to grace and divine providence, against the Jesuits and Arminians [illegible, about eight letters], I will not shrink from the scholastic (argument). PRAISE BE TO GOD ALONE.
